loss to open-heart surgery and resuscitation of severely wounded battle casualties.

However, this practice has not met with general acceptance—even for low-or moderate-grade blood loss and trauma. Whole blood appears to remain the overwhelming modality of choice for fluid resuscitation, in spite of the known dangers associated with its use. Though the objections to use of crystalloid solutions by surgeons and internists are varied, a common belief is that only colloid solutions will achieve and sustain a satisfactory replenishment

of blood volume, and further, whole blood or red blood cells (RBC) are required to maintain the hemoglobin at desirable levels—generally thought to be 11, 12, or 13 gm/100 ml.

This communication presents a body of clinical experience with exclusive use of crystalloid solution as alternate therapy to blood transfusion in cases of high-trauma surgery with major blood loss. Though it describes, in many ways, extremes of clinical practice, it may contribute to a clearer understanding of results of nonhepatic fluid resuscitation, and help to define safe limits of its employment.

Thirteen consecutively studied cases of a group of surgical patients subjected to a wide range of traumatic procedures are presented (Table 1). All sustained major blood loss. None received blood or any blood fraction at any time. All were members of the Jehovah's Witness faith. Crystalloid solution in the form of Ringer's solution or lactated Ringer's solution was the sole or major resuscitative solution employed. Fluid administration was based on blood pressure or blood volume determination. No attempt was made to use blood loss as a basis for fluid administration.

### Methods

Blood volume was determined by an isotopic method with use of a gamma ray counter and iodinated serum albumin (RISA). Hematocrit levels were corrected for plasma trapping.¹⁸ Red blood cell mass and plasma volumes were corrected for whole-body hematocrit values.¹⁹ Administered fluid volumes and urine volumes were carefully recorded and totalled. A highly accurate weighing bed was employed for each patient's weight. Specific gravity of blood and other isosmotic fluids was assumed to be 1.0. Blood loss was estimated from the reduction in total RBC mass. The "expected blood volume" at any period was estimated to be the previously determined blood volume minus the blood loss sustained during the interval. Total retention of fluids was calculated as the difference between total administered volumes and total urine excretion, or alternately as the algebraic sum of the weight change plus the blood loss. Intravascular retention of administered fluid was calculated as the differ-

ence between the measured blood volume and the expected blood volume. Extravascular distribution of administered fluid was calculated as the difference between total fluid retention and intravascular retention. These methods have been extensively described elsewhere.⁸

### Findings in Present Study

Figure 1 shows the magnitude of operative blood loss of individual patients in relation to the extent of operative trauma. For the low-trauma group, blood loss was negligible. However, as noted later, these patients had sustained major blood loss prior to admission. For high-trauma surgery—mostly open-heart procedures—blood loss ranged from 21% to 66% with the mode clustering about 40% blood volume. Figure 2 relates the total volume of nonhemic fluids administered during surgery and four hours afterwards to the volume of blood loss sustained. In general, for major blood loss, fluid volumes of three to five times blood loss were administered. Patient 2 received 500 ml artificial colloid solution in the op-

erating room. No other patient received colloid solution during surgery or for four hours thereafter.

The general distribution of the retained fluid for the high-trauma group is indicated in Fig 3. Large-volume urination was an invariable result of this regimen. However, most of the fluid administered was retained. The intravascular space retained little, averaging 10% of fluid administered (range, 5% to 19%). Based on fluid volume retained, the intravascular retention averaged 16% (range, 8% to 28%). These figures do not include patient 2, since she received colloid during operation. Examination of Fig 3 reveals that as the volume of administered fluid increased, there was little if any intravascular gain. The liquid appeared to go to the extravascular spaces primarily, with most of the remainder eliminated as urine.

Though the intravascular retention of crystalloid fluid was a small percentage of administered fluid, the large volumes employed produced a physiologically significant volume increment. This is shown

# Comment

This communication describes key hematologic changes of 13 surgical patients whose clinical management perforce did not employ blood or any blood fraction at any time. The patients may be divided into two main groups, a low-trauma group consisting of two patients admitted with low RBC mass and hematocrit levels due to serious pre-surgical blood loss who were subsequently subjected to low-trauma surgery, and a high-trauma group consisting of nine patients with relatively normal blood indices who were subjected to acute, large-volume blood loss associated with heart surgery, mostly of the "open" type.

The low-trauma patients (6 and 7) were admitted with hematocrit values of 15% and 17% respectively, after continuous bleeding for a period of one to two weeks. Both were pale and weak. They were, however, alert, well-oriented, and cooperative. They did not evidence respiratory distress while lying in bed. Blood pressure was normal (120/80 and 140/80 mm Hg) and heart rates were increased (100 and 140 beats per minute). Immediate surgery was performed in both cases with operative blood loss less than 200 ml.

At five and ten days after the operation, respectively, these patients, both in the Intensive Care Unit concurrently, were sitting beside their beds, quite pale but alert and comfortable and reading the newspaper. Their respective hema-

The present data suggest that such distribution ratios are not meaningful, or at least not applicable under the conditions of this experience.

Although the crystalloid fluid was a poor "volume expander" in terms of efficiency, the large volumes resulted in a physiologically significant intravascular volume increment (20% to 64%) of blood loss. The degree of replenishment of intravascular volume was not related to the amount of blood loss, or to the volume of fluid administered. Hemodilution caused hematocrit values to fall to the range of the high 20's to

low 30's immediately after the operation and they continued to fall for the next three days to the range of the high teens to low 20's. This latter fall was the result of a stable RBC mass diluted by an increased plasma volume. Similar observations have been reported previously for patients treated with partial hemodilution. The replenishment of the RBC mass by RBC production was sluggish, regardless of the administration of various hematinic preparations employed in some patients. Immediately after the operation the RBC mass had decreased to 50%. Two weeks later it had increased to 65% of its initial amount.

Certain features of clinical management are worthy of note. It became obvious that fluids were best administered according to overt

physiological signs and symptoms.

The data strongly suggest that there is a limit to the safe employment of crystalloid solution alone as volume replacement for shed blood. Those patients sustaining a loss of up to 1,200 ml of blood apparently were able to tolerate volume replacement with crystalloid solution alone. For the six patients with blood losses greater than 1,200 ml, it was necessary to supplement the crystalloid infusion with colloid solution at some time in the first 24 hours after operation to maintain a satisfactory intravascular volume. When this was not done, ie, when the attempt was made to replace blood loss in excess of 1,200 ml with crystalloid solution alone, very large volumes were needed, and serious edema, especially pulmo-

nary edema, was manifested. In the postoperative period, patients whose hematocrit values were in the high or middle teens generally fared better with tracheostomy and respiratory assistance. Our impression is that in the lower ranges of RBC mass, weakness of the respiratory muscles can contribute to poor ventilation, insufficient gas exchange, and eventual vascular collapse. Meticulous hemostasis was of prime importance, since lost RBC mass could not be replaced for religious reasons.

We believe that this experience may be of value for surgery of more conventional patients, those who accept blood transfusion. It may be estimated that the number of transfused units of blood could be reduced by 50% if physicians would use crystalloid solutions for fluid resuscitation in place of the initial 1 or 2 units of blood employed for volume expansion. This single step alone would bring about a drastic reduction in hepatitis and effect a most desirable change in the quality of available stores of heterologous blood for transfusion. The fact that crystalloid solution alone, in the absence of artificial colloid solution, was able to be employed successfully in high-trauma surgery of adults with blood loss up to 1,200 ml is offered as support and encouragement for this practice.

# Answer to donor shortage?

THE EXPOSITOR, BRANTFORD, Tuesday, June 21, 1972 27

# 'Bloodless surgery' reduces hazards of transfusion

By C. G. McDaniel

AP Science Writer

CHICAGO (AP) — "We don't throw around a bottle of blood willy nilly anymore," says Dr. Stanley Dudrick.

Thus does one surgeon characterize a growing trend toward "bloodless surgery," when it is possible and applicable.

Two goals of bloodless surgery are to avoid potential hazards from transfusions, including transmitting the liver disease hepatitis, and to reduce the need for blood donors. At present, about seven million blood transfusions are given every year in the United States, and there's a shortage of donors.

Dudrick, of the University of Pennsylvania medical school and chief of surgery at the Veterans Administration Hospital in Philadelphia, has helped develop one alternative method of blood replacement.

This involves building up the blood before and after surgery with various nutrients, such as amino acids and iron, to make transfusions unnecessary.

Other techniques involve the heart-lung machine, lowering of blood pressure, and cryosurgery or freezing. There are still other procedures.

Not all patients can be treated with the blood build-up method, Dudrick said in an interview. They must be fairly healthy and the surgery must

not be urgent, to allow time to build up the blood.

Dudrick said: "It is amazing how fast patients come around" in response to the nutrient build-up.

It was "sort of a ritual" in the past to replace lost blood unit for unit, he said.

The blood-build-up technique has been used clinically at the University of Pennsylvania hospitals for about four years, he said, and has been used at major medical centres around the U.S. for the last two.

Surgeons do not uniformly accept the method, because it means extra work to build up patients before and after surgery, he said.

"The easiest thing to do is

to hang a bottle of blood," Dudrick said, noting that some still rely on the transfusion when it might not be necessary.

Dr. James E. Eckenhoff, dean of Northwestern University medical school, has been a leader in development of surgical techniques involving hypotension—the lowering of blood pressure—to reduce blood loss in certain problems.

This is particularly useful in surgery of the head and neck and the upper extremities, in neurosurgery and in plastic surgery, he said.

The hypotension technique, Eckenhoff said in an interview, "can markedly reduce

the loss of blood and the need for replacement."

This technique has had wider use in Britain, where Eckenhoff, an anesthesiologist, worked in perfecting it at Queen Victoria Hospital in East Grinstead.

A decade ago, surgeons replaced blood if the loss exceeded 400 or 500 cubic centimetres, about a pint, but now replace much of lost blood with nutrient solutions, he said.

The transfusion itself may cause death, he said, noting that one of every 4,000 to 5,000 bottles of blood has fatal effects.

In comparative studies, patients whose blood pressure

was lowered, required less than half the amount of replacement blood required by others undergoing the same procedures.

Eckenhoff said surgeons now think that patients who are not in severely deteriorated condition can sustain a loss of up to one quart of blood without replacement.

The Korean and Vietnamese wars also taught surgeons to work with less donated blood, Eckenhoff said, because there was not enough to meet the needs of men injured in battle.

A leading heart surgeon, Dr. Denton Cooley of the Texas Heart Institute, Houston, said he is not opposed to

blood transfusions but "the fact is evident now that most major surgery can be done without transfusion."

Cooley, noted for open heart surgery and as a pioneer in heart transplants, said some doctors use blood transfusions "as a crutch" or because the blood is available.

"We continue to do our surgery with a minimum of transfusions," Cooley said in an interview. "Our goal is to see how little we can use."

Four Harvard Medical School researchers—Dr. S. Mortimer J. Buckley, W. Gerald Austen, Allan Goldblatt and Myron B. Layer—have developed a technique for diluting the patient's blood, then

reinfusing his own after surgery.

The patient's temperature is lowered, slowing his metabolism. Eighty per cent of his blood is removed and stored. At the same time, the blood is replaced by three times as much nutrient solution as blood withdrawn. Circulation is maintained through the heart-lung machine.

With this technique, Buckley said, it is possible even to suspend circulation during the repair procedure on some patients, placing them in a state of suspended animation.

Other forms of bloodless surgery include cryosurgery, which involves freezing, to remove malignancies and treat certain other conditions.

ANESTHESIOLOGY, Vol. 33, No. 2, August, 1970

# The Anesthesiologist and the Cardiac Surgeon

Denton A. Cooley, M.D.\*

New and rapidly changing techniques in cardiac surgery have steadily increased the burden placed upon the anesthesiologist during the past two decades. Not long ago, the anesthesiologist had, and often exercised, the prerogative of recommending that operation be deferred because of an inordinate anesthetic risk. Now he is practically obliged by modern practice to accept the assignment and share the challenge, striving desperately with the surgeon to salvage the patient by his determined skill with intra- and postoperative anesthetic techniques, assisted by pharmacologic and respiratory support. Today, intensely cyanotic patients, many of them newborn infants, undergo thoracotomy for cardiac repair. Adult patients with advanced acquired heart disease are seldom refused operation unless irreversible myocardial damage or advanced pulmonary, hepatic, or renal disease is present. Recently, for example, moribund patients with terminal irreversible heart disease have undergone cardiac transplantation and recovered. The close alliance necessary between surgeon and anesthesiologist demands that the anesthesiologist continually familiarize himself with cardiac diseases and new surgical procedures designed to treat these diseases in order to anticipate the special problems during and after operation.

The era of open intracardiac surgery began about 15 years ago with the introduction of total-body hypothermia combined with caval inflow occlusion. The limitations of this method were many, and it was soon replaced by the technique of temporary cardiopulmonary bypass. Pumps and oxygenators have not yet been standardized in all centers, and wide varieties of both are used today with satisfactory results. For the past six years we have used exclusively the plastic disposable bubble diffusion oxygenator primed with 5 per cent

dextrose solution, and have kept the patient normothermic. In addition to its important advantages of convenience, economy, and absence of certain cardiopulmonary and hematologic complications, this method also allows surgeons to perform open-heart surgery on Jehovah's Witnesses without using blood—a special problem for the anesthesiologist who is concerned with blood replacement. We have done open-heart operations on 70 Jehovah's Witnesses without using blood before, during, or after operation. Disc oxygenators primed with fresh heparinized or even ACD bank blood still remain the choice in some hospitals. At one time a hyperbaric environment for cardiac surgery seemed an attractive prospect and was used in many newborn infants. Because of its cumbersome equipment, complicated physiologic problems (mainly respiratory), and hazard to personnel, most centers now use this method only for medical, and not for surgical, problems. The membrane-type oxygenators with ultra-thin silastic membranes have attracted interest recently; they promise prolonged cardiorespiratory support in the desperately ill patient. Other types of mechanical oxygenation are unsatisfactory for this purpose since they require prolonged direct exposure of blood to a gaseous interface. The membrane oxygenator will not, however, replace the simpler and more efficient bubble diffusion and filming oxygenators for open-heart surgery.

Almost daily advances are being made in surgery for congenital heart disease, as one anomaly after another becomes operable. One exciting example is the complete correction of transposition of the great arteries—an anomaly long considered to be incurable. Truncus arteriosus, another complicated defect, is correctable with a composite homograft of ascending aorta and aortic valve. This homograft has been used successfully in severe cases of tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonic valve atresia and in cases of transposition of the great vessels with large ventricular septal defect. Anesthesiology
August 1970

ent, the only remaining barrier to surgical repair of congenital cardiac anomalies is severe pulmonary vascular sclerosis and fixed pulmonary resistance.

Surgical treatment of acquired valvular disease now consists primarily of total valve replacement, although some indications for valvuloplasty remain. Thromboembolism is by far the most common and difficult complication of valve replacement with synthetic prostheses. Fortunately, these complications are rare in aortic valve replacement, in which prosthetic valves serve satisfactorily. For the mitral annulus many modifications of prostheses have been tried experimentally and clinically, yet none has proved entirely satisfactory; the search for an "ideal" mitral prosthesis continues. Recent reports of composite stinted grafts using homo- or heterograft semilunar valves or valves fashioned with autologous viable fascia lata are promising.

The cardiac surgeon still finds his major challenge in surgery for advanced primary myocardial disease. Coronary atherosclerosis is the most prevalent cause of this disease, although a variety of cardiomyopathies also are recognized clinically. Cardiac transplantation, first attempted clinically two years ago, has prolonged the lives of many patients. At least ten of about 150 such patients throughout the world have survived a year or more after cardiac transplantation. In one patient operated upon in our hospital a two-staged cardiac replacement was performed, using a total cardiac prosthesis for the first stage. The prosthesis supported circulation and life for 64 hours until it was removed and a cardiac allograft inserted. Although the patient died 32 hours after allografting, this case may represent a significant step forward in total cardiac substitution, since for the first time prolonged

circulatory support was successfully achieved. Hopefully, the experience will stimulate others to attempt similar bold techniques in dying patients, particularly when death in the operating room is the alternative.

Since the introduction of coronary arteriography using Sones' technique, revascularization of the ischemic heart has been attempted in a more deliberate, practical manner than previously, when less precise diagnostic methods were employed. During the past few years implantation of the internal mammary artery into the myocardium has been performed in several thousand patients, but within the past few months the technique has been replaced by a direct attack upon the occluded coronary artery. Using the autologous saphenous vein graft bypass so successfully employed for the occluded superficial femoral artery, cardiac surgeons are anastomosing coronary vessels one or two millimeters in diameter to aortic or coronary grafts. While results at this early stage are being highly acclaimed, one must maintain a healthy skepticism for the future of these operations; too often have new methods in the difficult area of cardiac surgery enjoyed initially spectacular but very brief histories. Meanwhile, the anesthesiologist must continue offering his cooperation, indulgence, and valued assistance to the cardiac surgeon in a mutual effort to improve and expand the surgical attack upon coronary disease.

"Death and sorrow will be the companions of our journey; hardship our garment, constancy and valor our only shield. We must be united, we must be undaunted, we must be inflexible." These impassioned words of Winston Churchill (1940) may serve to describe the task for these two comrades, surgeon and anesthesiologist, brought together in this struggle for progress in cardiac surgery.

## Open Heart Surgery

Without Blood Transfusion

Arthur C. Beall, Jr., MD; Ellard M. Yew, Jr.; Robert D. Bloodwell, MD; Grady L. Hallman, MD; and Denton A. Cooley, MD, Houston

DEVELOPMENT of the pump oxygenator for open heart surgery and clinical progress over the past decade now allow successful surgical correction of most congenital and acquired cardiac lesions. For many years, however, procurement of large quantities of blood necessary for priming most pump oxygenators used for these operations taxed blood banking facilities throughout the country and limited use of cardiopulmonary bypass in emergency situations. Demonstration of the adverse effects produced by such a pool of homologous blood further emphasized the advantages of eliminating this blood prime.¹

The feasibility of priming extracorporeal circuits with a variety of nonblood solutions soon was established,²⁻⁵ and in April 1962, we adopted a technique of open heart surgery using disposable plastic oxygenators primed only with 5% dextrose in distilled water.⁶ With this technique extracardiac blood loss usually was replaced with banked acid-citrate-dextrose blood as during any major operative procedure. However, our policy has been to limit transfusion to only that amount of blood absolutely necessary, in order to reduce the incidence of hepatitis and other complications of administering blood.

It now appears that many patients undergoing open heart surgery do not require blood transfusion either during the operation or at any time during the period of hospitalization. Furthermore, it is possible to offer benefits of such operations to individuals of the Jehovah's Witness religious faith, who will not accept transfusion of blood or any of its products.⁷ The purpose of this report is to review experience with open heart surgery using this technique with emphasis upon a group of 157 patients in whom no blood was necessary.

### Technique of Operation

This method of open heart surgery is illustrated diagrammatically in Fig 1. The superior and inferior venae cavae are drained by gravity into a disposable plastic oxygenator which is stretched on a metal frame. Raising or lowering the height of the frame adjusts flow rate by changing the distance between vena caval level and the base of the oxygenating column. Blood

is driven up the oxygenating column by the oxygen dispersion system as gas exchange occurs. Oxygenated blood then passes over stainless steel sponges coated with antifoam and through a filter into an angulated arterial reservoir. From the base of the reservoir a roller pump returns blood proximally through a common femoral artery into the aorta. Coronary sinus return and bronchial arterial blood is collected by a left ventricular sump and by an intracardiac aspirator and is passed through a cardiotomy reservoir into the base of the oxygenating column.

The oxygenator is primed with 5% dextrose in distilled water, 20 to 30 ml/hr of body weight, to which is added heparin sodium, 30 mg/liter of priming solution. In infants weighing less than 13.6 kg (30 lb) a single unit of fresh, heparinized blood is required due to the infant's small blood volume in relation to the priming volume of the oxygenator and tubing. Except in such infants all solution remaining in the oxygenator and tubing at the completion of the intracardiac procedure is returned slowly to the patient through the femoral artery. When necessary, banked, acid-citrate-dextrose blood is given intravenously to replace extracardiac blood loss, but such transfusion is used only for specific indications and is withheld unless blood loss exceeds that which is compatible with smooth recovery from operation.

# Clinical Material

During the four-year period from April 1962 until April 1966 this technique of open heart surgery was used in 1,818 patients admitted to St. Luke's Episcopal, Texas Children's, or Ben Taub General hospitals, Houston. Overall results were most gratifying as compared to those obtained using homologous blood priming. Among these patients were 157 in whom no blood was given at any time during the entire period of hospitalization.

Seventy-three of these 157 patients were male and 84 were female. They varied in age from 2½ to 67 years with an average age of 22.4 years. Although 11 of the patients belonged to the Jehovah's Witness religious faith and blood could not be used, transfusion was withheld electively in the other 146, since its use was not considered necessary.

The various operations performed are summarized in the Table. Although the majority of these open heart procedures without blood were for repair of congenital cardiac lesions, quite a number of more complicated operations such as aortic or mitral valve replacements were included. # Results

Among the 157 patients in whom open heart surgery without the use of blood was performed, there were only two deaths, a mortality of 1.3%. One death followed mitral valve replacement in a 56-year-old man who died suddenly of an uncontrollable arrhythmia on the day of his scheduled discharge from the hospital, at which time his hemoglobin level and hematocrit reading were within normal limits. The other death occurred in a 36-year-old woman after repair of a very complex congenital anomaly. In this patient of the Jehovah's Witness faith survival might have been possible with transfusion, but she steadfastly refused to accept blood and died on the fourth day after operation with a hemoglobin level of 6.8 gm/100 cc and an hematocrit reading of 21%.

Anemia did not prove to be a problem in this group of patients, as can be seen from Fig 2. Although hemoglobin and hematocrit levels fell to an average of 10.4 gm/100 cc and 31.9%, respectively, one week after operation, these mild blood loss anemias responded to oral administration of iron. # Comment

The described technique of open heart surgery using disposable plastic oxygenators primed with 5% dextrose in distilled water offers significant advantages over methods requiring pooled, homologous blood to prime the pump oxygenator. Various physiological functions appear far better maintained than when a blood prime is used,⁹ and this appears of particular importance in regard to renal function in patients with advanced acquired valvular disease.¹⁰ Preparations for operation are simplified considerably, especially blood banking requirements. And, elimination of the need to obtain large quantities of fresh, heparinized blood now allows immediate availability of cardiopulmonary bypass for emergency operations, such as pulmonary embolectomy.¹¹

In addition to the use of pooled homologous blood to prime various extracorporeal circuits, routine transfusion of banked blood to replace operative blood loss milliliter for milliliter has become far too commonplace with open heart surgery. The concept of keeping up with blood loss as it occurs is advantageous when blood loss is massive, but loss of large quantities of blood is not a necessary accompaniment of intracardiac surgery. Efforts toward minimizing blood loss during open heart surgery can reduce significantly amounts of transfused blood required and eliminate its need altogether in quite a number of patients, as illustrated by the present report.

Blood loss of 500 to 1,000 ml usually is well tolerated by an adult, and compensa-

tion for even larger losses is possible by use of plasma expanders. Even in those patients in whom some blood replacement is mandatory, the number of transfused units should be kept to the minimum necessary for smooth recovery of the patient. Until better screening techniques for blood donors are developed or until demand for blood is reduced, only by minimizing donor exposure associated with open heart surgery can the incidence of posttransfusion hepatitis associated with open heart surgery be lowered significantly from figures running as high as 21%.¹² Furthermore, reduction in the amount of blood given also reduces the possibility of transfusion reactions associated with human error or with minor blood group incompatibilities missed in routine crossmatching.

A significant result of this approach to open heart surgery has demonstrated that many patients requiring intracardiac repair actually do not need any blood during the entire period of hospitalization. This has allowed acceptance for operation of patients belonging to the Jehovah's Witness religious faith, rather than denying them benefits of needed surgery. Certainly one prefers to retain the option of using blood transfusion should it prove to be indicated, but such limitation often is outweighed by the risk inherent in the patient's cardiac lesion without correction should the surgeon refuse operation under terms imposed by the patient's religious convictions. Moral and ethical consideration of major surgery in Jehovah's Witnesses has been reviewed by Fitts and Orloff.¹³ Legal implications are perhaps even more complicated. However, unless the surgeon is able to treat a patient of this faith on terms imposed by this religion, regardless of medical circumstances, he must not accept the patient for treatment.

# Summary

With demonstration of the adverse effects of using large quantities of homologous blood to prime pump oxygenators for open heart surgery, we adopted a technique using disposable plastic oxygenators primed with 5% dextrose in distilled water. Extracardiac blood loss usually was replaced with

Among these patients were 157 with assorted congenital and acquired cardiac defects which were corrected by open heart surgery without the use of blood at any time throughout hospitalization. Eleven of these patients belonged to the Jehovah's Witness religious faith whose steadfast convictions would permit no blood or blood products of any type to be used. In the majority of those who received no blood, however,

transfusion was withheld electively because it was not considered necessary.

Anemia was not a problem in these patients, and there were only two deaths, one of which was totally unrelated to absence of blood transfusion. This experience reemphasizes that blood transfusion should be used only for specific indications, even in patients undergoing open heart surgery. Such an approach not only reduces possible transfusion reactions, but also other complications of blood therapy such as homologous serum hepatitis.

# Cardiac Valve Replacement for Congenital Mitral Valvular Disease in Children

By ROBERT D. BLOODWELL, GRADY L. HALLMAN, DAN G. MCNAMARA, AND DENTON A. COOLEY

PATIENTS WITH MALFORMATIONS OF THE MITRAL VALVE causing advanced hemodynamic changes and severe disability during childhood may be managed only by excision and replacement of the mitral valve. Structural alterations of valves in most patients with congenital mitral stenosis, mitral insufficiency, and complete atrioventricular canal defects prevent successful correction by valvuloplasty.

Improved design of prosthetic valves, including low-profile lenticular valves for patients with small ventricular cavities, permit valve replacement during childhood.¹⁻³ Cloth covered seating rings should decrease thromboembolic complications and permit incorporation by ingrowth of autologous tissue.³,⁴

This report is concerned with 21 children in whom mitral valve replacement was used for management of congenital valvular malformations.

# CLINICAL MATERIAL

Since November 1965, 21 children between 1⅛ and 15 years of age have undergone excision and prosthetic replacement of congenital defects of the mitral valve in our institutions. Only those with severe hemodynamic alterations or intractable cardiac failure and growth retardation were selected for operation.

Six patients had congenital mitral stenosis, 2 of whom had typical "parachute mitral valve" deformities (Fig. 1).⁵ Ten patients had congenital mitral insufficiency,⁶ one of whom had an associated septum secundum atrial septal defect and another recurrent mitral insufficiency after annuloplasty had been performed 3 years previously. Five patients had complete atrioventricularis communis, in one patient associated with pulmonary valvular stenosis. One of these patients was operated upon secondarily after a previous attempt at suture repair of the mitral valvular component of the defect.

Three patients ages 1⅛, 3¼, and 6 years had undergone resection of coarctation of the aorta, 2 weeks, 1 year, and 3 years previously. One of these patients with mitral insufficiency and a 15-year-old boy with mitral stenosis had a patent ductus arteriosus divided previously. Three patients underwent concomitant aortic valvulotomy.

Pulmonary hypertension was present in 14 patients including each of those with complete atrioventricular canal except the child with associated pulmonary stenosis.

### METHODS

Cardiopulmonary bypass was provided by a disposable plastic bubble oxygenator using the hemodilution technique under normothermic conditions. Elective ischemic cardioplegia was used in all patients except in 3 early cases. Double open-caged ball-valve prostheses were used in 4 patients and low-profile lenticular valves were used in all subsequent patients including each with atrio-ventricular canal and all except the first patient with congenital mitral stenosis. Cloth covered discoid valves were used in all patients during the past year. Anticoagulant drugs were omitted in several of the early patients since control of dosage is difficult in children, but this method of reduction of thromboembolic complications seems important enough to urge its use even in these young patients. Anticoagulants did not prevent recurrent thrombosis which lead to the death of one patient 9 months after mitral valve replacement.

### RESULTS

Follow-up of these children after valve replacement extends from 2 months to 2½ years (Fig. 2).

Two patients experienced thromboembolic complications. A 6-year-old girl has recovered without sequelae from a cerebral embolus which occurred 6 months after operation; no similar episodes have occurred in this patient during the past year. Recurrent thrombus formation in a 12-year-old girl led to her death 9 months after operation, despite secondary valve replacement and intense anticoagulant therapy.

Three early deaths occurred among the 21 patients, yielding a hospital

# COMMENT

While knowledge of the long-term fate of artificial valves is incomplete, certain children with severe disability due to advanced congenital deformities of the mitral valve can be managed only by valve excision and prosthetic substitution.9,11 Possibility of the need for secondary valve replacement to provide for increased cardiac output as the child grows12 is circumvented by the opportunity to employ a small-sized adult valve in most of these patients with a dilated mitral annulus.

Valvotomy is unsatisfactory for correction of congenital mitral stenosis due to the advanced nature of structural changes in such a valve. Mitral annuloplasty is preferred by some for correction of congenital mitral insufficiency.13 Although such procedures may result in symptomatic improvement and often decreased heart size, nearly all reported cases retain some degree of mitral insufficiency with persistent systolic murmurs.8,15 Our experience with annuloplasty in adults has been equally disappointing.

Experience with the radical repair of complete atrioventricular canal defects using a valve prosthesis in conjunction with patch closure of the confluent ventricular and atrial defects has provided an encouraging outlook for these patients for whom the previous outlook for operative correction was poor.

Cloth covered low-profile prosthetic valves provide a means of replacing the mitral valve in children with a decreased chance of postoperative thromboembolic complications and the potential of providing adequate valve function into adult life.

# SUMMARY

Certain congenital defects of the mitral valve causing severe disability during childhood can be managed only by valve excision and prosthetic substitution.

Mitral valve replacement was performed in 21 children for correction of congenital mitral stenosis in 6, isolated congenital mitral insufficiency in 10, and complete atrioventricular canal defects in 5. Three patients underwent concomitant aortic valvulotomy. Fourteen patients had pulmonary hypertension and 3 had undergone previous repair of coarctation. Nine patients were in congestive heart failure.

Three hospital deaths occurred in patients operated upon for intractable failure; one had associated endocardial fibroelastosis, another acute mitral

The low-profile discoid valve with minimal protrusion into the left ventricle is particularly suited for mitral replacement in children. Small adult-sized prostheses were used permitting growth and development of the children. Cloth covering of the seating ring permits incorporation by ingrowth of autologous tissue and decreased thromboembolic complications.

Although the long-term fate of prosthetic heart valves is uncertain, the management of severe congenital mitral deformities by valve replacement has provided remarkable clinical improvement in these children.

# TWO-STAGE SURGICAL TREATMENT OF COMPLEX CONGENITAL HEART DEFECTS

![img-23.jpeg](img-23.jpeg)

Grady L. Hallman, M.D.
R. D. Bloodwell, M. D.
D. A. Cooley, M. D.

MEDICAL COMMUNICATIONS
1966

Half of all infants born alive with congenital heart defects die before one year of age if surgical therapy is not undertaken. Principal physiologic derangements are:

(1) Cardiac failure due to left-to-right shunts as in patients with ventricular septal defect.
(2) Hypoxemia due to:

(a) Pulmonary stenosis and ventricular septal defect with decreased pulmonary blood flow and right-to-left shunt in tetralogy of Fallot.

(b) Inadequate mixing between semi-isolated pulmonary and systemic arterial circuits in complete transposition of the great vessels.

(3) Cardiac failure due to increased ventricular pressure in patients with aortic and pulmonary valvular stenosis (and intact ventricular septum) or coarctation of the thoracic aorta.

If medical therapy with oxygen, digitalis, etc., is not successful in controlling symptoms, surgical treatment becomes necessary to prevent a fatal outcome. Total correction of the anomaly is, of course, ideal therapy and is possible in some anomalies such as patent ductus arteriosus and coarctation of the aorta. "Open-heart" surgery is necessary in lesions such as total anomalous venous return, and pulmonary and aortic stenosis. The added risk of open surgery in infants should be avoided in certain anomalies that can be treated by a staged technique. A palliative operation is performed during early infancy and definitive, open operation is deferred until the patient has reached a more optimal age and size. This exhibit illustrates the two-stage approach to the treatment of infants with tetralogy of Fallot, complete transposition of the great vessels, and ventricular septal defect.

# COMMENT

Most infants who require shunt operations for tetralogy are less than 4 years of age, and many are in the first year of life. Although we occasionally use the standard anastomoses described by Blalock and by Potts, our current preference is for an intrapericardial anastomosis between the ascending aorta and the subjacent right pulmonary artery. This anastomosis involves minimal mediastinal dissection; it can be done readily even with a right arch; and it can be combined with other operations such as atrial septectomy should transposition of the great vessels be present. The principle advantage of this anastomosis lies in the ease with which it can be closed through the ascending aorta at the time of total repair.

# COMMENT

Atrial septectomy provides satisfactory palliation of hypoxemia in newborn infants with transposition of the great vessels. Often this operation must be performed as an emergency without antecedent cardiac catheterization or angiocardiography. At the age of 3 or 4 years definitive diagnostic studies are performed and the patient is evaluated to determine the feasibility of total repair. The presence of increased pulmonary vascular resistance, pulmonary stenosis, or ventricular septal defect greatly increases the risk of total correction. At present we avoid operating upon such patients except in unusual circumstances. The ideal candidate for complete correction is one with an intact ventricular septum and a pressure in the left ventricle less than 65 mm. Hg. systolic.

# COMMENT

Medical therapy can control cardiac failure in the majority of infants with ventricular septal defect. If heart failure is intractable or if repeated episodes of pneumonia occur, operation is necessary. In the early years of cardiopulmonary bypass in our institution (1956-1959) open-heart repair of ventricular septal defect during the first few months of life resulted in a mortality of 42%. These discouraging results led to the adoption of pulmonary artery banding as the procedure of choice when surgical therapy became necessary during the newborn period. Most of the patients who died after banding had multiple cardiac anomalies.

We believe that pulmonary artery banding is rarely indicated beyond 12 months of age. If a patient can be carried on medical therapy to this point, he can usually be followed for several years until open-heart repair can be done.

Total repair has been performed in our institution at an average age of 4 years. The defect is closed with a Dacron patch using temporary cardiopulmonary bypass and the pulmonary band divided. If the pulmonary artery cannot be dilated to normal caliber, the constricted area is opened with a longitudinal incision. This incision is then closed transversely or an elliptical patch of pericardium is sutured into it to widen this area.

ANNALS OF SURGERY, Vol. 173, No. 6, June 1971.

## Cardiovascular Surgery in Newborn Infants:

Results in 1,050 Patients Less than One Year Old

GRADY L. HALLMAN, M.D., DENTON A. COOLEY, M.D.

From the Texas Heart Institute of St. Luke's-Texas Children's Hospitals,
Houston, Texas 77025

THE highest mortality from congenital
heart disease occurs during the first year of
life. More than one fourth of infants born
alive with anomalies of the heart and great
vessels die before they reach one month of
age, and 60 per cent die before one year if
not operated upon.¹⁸,¹⁹ A variety of anomalies are capable of causing heart failure and
hypoxemia, the physiologic derangements
that constitute the main indications for operation. Medical therapy is employed initially but often provides inadequate relief.
In these cases survival depends on surgical
alteration of cardiac anatomy and function,
and operation must frequently be performed on an urgent or emergency basis.²⁻⁴

### Clinical Material

Between January, 1954, and October,
1970, 1,050 infants less than one year of
age underwent palliative or corrective surgical procedures for congenital cardiovascular anomalies. Sixty per cent were 3
months old or less, and 80 per cent were 6
months old or less (Table 1).

The main indications for operation were
refractory heart failure (as in patients with
left-to-right shunts or valvular obstructions), hypoxemia (as in patients with decreased pulmonary blood flow and right-to-left shunts), and tracheoesophageal compression (due to vascular ring anomalies).
When symptoms were not relieved by
medical therapy with oxygen, digitalis, and
diuretics, palliative or curative operation

was scheduled, frequently as an emergency.
In many cases the patient's critical condition precluded cardiac catheterization and
angiocardiography, so operation was performed on the basis of clinical diagnosis
alone.

### Results

Of the 1,050 patients in this series who
underwent palliative or curative operations
for congenital heart disease, 291 (28 per
cent) died (Table 2). Postoperative improvement in the 759 (72 per cent) survivors was gratifying, with significant relief of cardiac failure or hypoxemia. Since
total correction of certain complex anomalies during the newborn period is associated with formidable mortality, these infants were treated in two stages; a palliative operation was performed during the
first year of life and total correction deferred until later years when open-heart
technics could be applied with greater
safety.

### Anomalies Treated in One Stage

Total correction was accomplished in one
stage in 397 patients, most of whom had
anomalies correctable by closed technics,
although some required cardiopulmonary
bypass or caval inflow occlusion. Mortality
for this group was 21 per cent (Table 2).
One hundred and ninety patients had tricuspid atresia or miscellaneous anomalies
that could not be surgically corrected and
therefore were treated by one-stage palliative operations. Ninety-three of these patients died after operation.

Presented at the Annual Meeting of the Southern Surgical Association, December 7-9, 1970,
Boca Raton, Florida.

Patent Ductus Arteriosus. Most of these patients had large ductus and low pulmonary vascular resistance causing a high-volume left-to-right shunt that produced refractory cardiac failure. Through a left posterolateral fourth interspace incision the ductus was interrupted either by suture-ligature (usually sufficient in small infants) or division and suture (sometimes necessary in larger infants). Of the 168 patients with this lesion, 13 (5 per cent) died, usually as a result of associated, more complex cardiac anomalies.

Coarctation of the Aorta. Indication for operation in the 98 patients with coarctation of the aorta was cardiac failure. The coarctation was resected and end-to-end anastomosis performed through a left posterolateral incision in the fourth interspace. Interrupted sutures were used in many patients on the accessible ventral surface of the anastomosis to favor subsequent growth. An associated patent ductus, when present, was closed as the coarctation was resected. If an associated ventricular septal defect had been diagnosed by catheterization and the pulmonary artery remained tense after repair of the coarctation, a constricting band was placed around the pulmonary artery. Most of the 22 (22 per cent) patients who died had preductal coarctation or associated intracardiac lesions, or both.

Aortic Stenosis. Thirty-two patients, mostly in the first few weeks of life, had aortic stenosis producing severe heart failure that responded poorly to medical therapy. Cardiopulmonary bypass enabled aor-

tic valvotomy under direct vision. Ten (31 per cent) of these patients did not survive operation.

Pulmonary Stenosis. Pulmonary stenosis with intact ventricular septum produced severe heart failure requiring pulmonary valvotomy in 30 patients. Both closed transventricular valvotomy and open operation with caval inflow occlusion have been used in the past, but the preferred technic in recent years has been open valvotomy with cardiopulmonary bypass. Most of the nine (30 per cent) patients who died after operation had a small right ventricle.

Vascular Ring. Compression of the trachea and esophagus by anomalies of the aortic arch system (such as double aortic arch, right arch with left ligamentum arteriosum, and retroesophageal right subclavian artery) caused symptoms severe enough to warrant operation during the first year of life in 18 patients. A left posterolateral incision was used and the offending vessel was divided. Vessels were removed from the retroesophageal area when feasible, and the ductus or ligamentum was divided. The esophagus and trachea were dissected to release any constricting fascial bands. In most patients the anomaly causing compression was a double aortic arch. All 18 patients with vascular ring survived operation.

Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Drainage. Fifty-one patients with cardiac failure required operation for total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage. Supracardiac, cardiac, infracardiac and mixed types were encountered and all required cardiopulmonary bypass. The common pulmonary vein was anastomosed to the left atrium, the patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect was closed, and the connection between the pulmonary vein and systemic venous system was ligated. Twenty-nine patients (57 per cent) died after operation.

Tricuspid Atresia. Tricuspid atresia was surgically treated in 66 newborn patients.

Most had decreased pulmonary flow with severe hypoxemia and underwent systemic-pulmonary shunt for palliation.¹⁰ The few patients who had increased pulmonary flow due to associated ventricular septal defect or transposition underwent pulmonary artery banding. Occasional use of cavopulmonary shunts yielded discouraging results. Thirteen (20 per cent) of the 66 patients with this lesion died after operation.

Miscellaneous Anomalies. Complex, often incurable anomalies such as truncus arteriosus, atrioventricularis communis, single ventricle, and endocardial fibroelastosis were found in 124 patients referred for operation during the first year of life. Surgical efforts in these patients were generally palliative. In those with hypoxemia, systemic-pulmonary artery shunts were used to increase pulmonary blood flow. Atrial septal defects were created to promote intracardiac mixing in patients with transposition of the great vessels, and pulmonary artery banding was employed where in-

creased pulmonary blood flow was producing heart failure. In a few cases clinical or laboratory diagnosis was doubtful and exploratory thoracotomy was performed as a final, desperate effort. Even palliative procedures were not possible in many of these patients because of unfavorable anatomy. Mortality for this heterogeneous group of 124 patient was 65 per cent (80 deaths).

### Anomalies Treated in Two Stages

Four hundred and sixty-three patients had major anomalies that would require cardiopulmonary bypass for total correction (Table 2). To avoid the excessive risk associated with open heart procedures in the newborn period, we utilized a two-stage approach, with a closed palliative operation performed first, deferring total correction until later in life.

Tetralogy of Fallot. Severe hypoxemia was the indication for operation in 144 patients with tetralogy of Fallot. Since an effective and safe palliative procedure is

We used the Blalock³ and Potts³⁸ technics in earlier cases, but have recently preferred an intrapericardial anastomosis between the posterior aspect of the ascending aorta and the subjacent right pulmonary artery.⁸,³⁹ Mortality in this group of patients was 17 per cent (24 deaths).

Transposition of the Great Vessels. Patients with transposition of the great vessels, the most common cyanotic anomaly requiring operation during infancy, exhibited severe hypoxemia with or without congestive failure. Here again, a first-stage, palliative procedure was chosen to avoid the risk of open-heart repair during the neonatal period. We used a modified version of the Blalock-Hanlon¹ technique that improved intracardiac mixing by creation of an atrial septal defect.¹¹,¹²,¹³ However, since 1967 most infants requiring intervention for transposition have been treated by balloon atrial septostomy, as described by Rashkind,²¹ obviating the need for the Blalock-Hanlon operation. In patients with an associated ventricular septal defect causing increased pulmonary flow and pressure, the pulmonary artery was banded after the atrial septum was excised or balloon atrial septostomy performed. Some infants had pulmonary stenosis and also received a systemic-pulmonary artery anastomosis. Of the 171 patients who underwent operations for transposition, 43 (25 per cent) died.

Ventricular Septal Defect. Intractable heart failure caused by a ventricular septal defect warranted operation in 116 patients. Open-heart repair was used between 1956 and 1959 in 31 of these patients, and 13 (42 per cent) died. This high mortality prompted us to adopt a staged approach. Since 1959, 85 patients have undergone pulmonary artery banding with a mortality of 23 per cent. Mortality for the entire group

of 116 patients with ventricular septal defect was 28 per cent (33 deaths).

Pulmonary Valve Atresia. Hypoxemia was extreme in the 32 patients with pulmonary valve atresia. Systemic-pulmonary artery shunts were used in most of this group, since, except in rare instances, the usual small size of the right ventricle and pulmonary annulus made valvotomy impossible or impractical. Special care was taken to construct the anastomoses small enough to lessen the chance of cardiac failure. Fifteen patients (47 per cent) died after operation.

### Discussion

Rapid advances in surgical treatment of congenital heart disease during the last few decades have enabled correction or palliation of many cardiovascular malformations previously considered incurable. Accurate clinical diagnosis is more important today than ever before, since we now have an array of effective surgical procedures that, if performed promptly and appropriately in the newborn child, may save lives otherwise doomed at infancy. Moreover, improvement in technics of general anesthesia for small infants has lowered significantly the risk of thoracotomy in this age group.²²

The poor prognosis in general for infants with congenital heart disease not surgically treated holds true for individual lesions as well. Seventy-five per cent of infants showing symptoms of coarctation of the aorta die before they are one year old.²³ An average survival of only 5½ months has been reported for a group of unoperated newborn patients with transposition of the great vessels.³ Mortality during the first year of life for patients with tricuspid atresia is 66 per cent without operation; for tetralogy of Fallot it is 55 per cent.²⁴ All patients with pulmonary atresia and intact ventricular septum, and 80 per cent of those with total anomalous pulmonary ve-

nous drainage die during the first few months of life if not operated upon.¹⁵,¹⁶

If initial medical therapy is successful in patients with severe symptoms of congenital heart disease, operation may be deferred until an older, more favorable age is attained. But when medical treatment is ineffective in ameliorating these symptoms, as it so often is, operation should be performed without delay, and on a clinical basis alone if the patient is too ill to tolerate cardiac catheterization. Although hypoxemia and cardiac failure are the principal indications for neonatal surgery, experience has shown that other findings may signify the need for operation, for instance, syncope, increasing cardiomegaly, electrocardiographic evidence of left ventricular strain, or discovery on cardiac catheterization of significant gradients, shunts, or pulmonary hypertension.⁸

The best surgical procedure for an infant with congenital heart disease is that which will offer the most physiologic benefit with the least operative risk. Lesions such as patent ductus arteriosus or coarctation of the aorta can be safely corrected with closed technics. Total correction of anomalies such as tetralogy of Fallot or ventricular septal defect, on the other hand, requires extracorporeal circulation, an added risk in neonates. These anomalies are best treated in two stages using a palliative operation first (when medical therapy is not successful) and doing the corrective procedure later in life. Usually the palliative operation will salvage the patient until a more favorable age and size for open-heart surgery is reached. For some lesions such as total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage no consistently effective palliative procedure exists, and complete correction with cardiopulmonary bypass must be attempted. Other complex anomalies such as tricuspid atresia are not surgically correctable and palliative measures must suffice.

Most deaths in this series of 1,050 patients occurred within 12 to 24 hours after

operation; yet patients who survived usually did so with, and because of, dramatic improvement in hypoxemia and cardiac failure. This suggests that surgical intervention in these seriously ill infants must be definitive and provide major physiologic benefit if the patient is to survive more than a few hours.

This series included many patients who were extremely poor operative risks and many desperate cases of exploratory operations performed on the remote chance that a correctable or palliable lesion might be found. Had selection of patients been limited to those with lesions susceptible to correction or palliation, survival rate would have been greater. In view of the high mortality during the first year of life in unoperated infants with cardiovascular disease, we believe that the 72 per cent survival reported in this paper justifies aggressive surgical treatment in the newborn period when symptoms do not respond to medical therapy.

### Summary

Maximum mortality in patients with cardiovascular anomalies occurs during the first year of life when 60 per cent die unless operated upon. A variety of anomalies can cause hypoxemia and/or cardiac failure and when symptoms do not respond to medical therapy, operation must be performed to prevent fatal outcome.

Between 1954 and 1970, 1,050 infants underwent non-elective operations during the first year of life for major cardiovascular anomalies including patent ductus, coarctation, aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, vascular ring, total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, tricuspid atresia, tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great vessels, ventricular septal defect, pulmonary valve atresia, and miscellaneous anomalies. When feasible, corrective operations were performed. In patients with complex anomalies such as transposition of the great vessels a palliative operation was chosen, deferring

# Epsilon-Aminocaproic Acid for Bleeding After Cardiopulmonary Bypass

Allen I. Midell, M.D., Grady L. Hallman, M.D., Robert D. Bloodwell, M.D., Arthur C. Beall, Jr., M.D., James J. Yashar, M.D., and Denton A. Cooley, M.D.

ABSTRACT The effect of epsilon-aminocaproic acid (EACA) in reducing bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass was studied in 73 patients who underwent open-heart operations for the repair of intracardiac lesions and resection of ascending aortic aneurysms. Forty-eight patients received EACA prior to the onset of bypass and 25 did not receive EACA. Bleeding during and immediately after operation in patients with acquired lesions was substantially less in the treated group than in those who had not received EACA. The results of the study indicate that EACA may be effective in reducing bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass for acquired cardiac disease and that further use and study of this agent is justified.

Excessive bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass represents a serious problem which complicates the recovery of patients undergoing an open-heart operation. Profuse bleeding may occur in spite of reversal of heparin anticoagulation with protamine and in spite of adequate hemostasis during operation. Abundant experimental and clinical evidence has shown that various changes in the coagulation mechanism regularly occur after extracorporeal circulation \[1, 3, 6, 8, 9, 11-15, 17-19]. Changes occur in both the plasma and the cellular constituents of blood. One of the significant changes producing excessive postoperative bleeding is the release of a plasminogen activator which converts plasminogen to plasmin, resulting in fibrinolysis \[9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18].

Epsilon-aminocaproic acid (EACA), acting as a competitive inhibitor of plasminogen activator, has been effective in controlling hemorrhage in isolated patients experiencing excessive bleeding and has yielded similar results in the experimental laboratory \[3]. The purpose of our study was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness of EACA in controlling hemorrhage.

# MIDELL ET AL.

# CLINICAL MATERIAL

Seventy-three patients who were placed on cardiopulmonary bypass during repair of an intracardiac lesion or resection of an ascending aortic aneurysm are included in this study. Forty patients were male and 33 were female. The patients ranged in age from 1 to 81 years with an average of 46 years; the average age of the female patients was 41 years and of the male patients, 50 years. Five patients were below 12 years of age.

A variety of operations for congenital and acquired cardiac disease were included (Tables 1, 2). The two procedures performed most frequently were mitral valve and aortic valve replacement. These operations, together with resection of an ascending aortic aneurysm and mitral annuloplasty, comprise all the operations in this series done for acquired disease—52 patients, or two-thirds of the series. The remaining 21 operations were performed for correction of congenital heart defects, although the majority of the patients were adults when operated upon.

Cardiopulmonary bypass was conducted under normothermic conditions using a disposable plastic bubble oxygenator primed with 5% dextrose in water. Blood flow during bypass averaged 50 ml. per kilogram of body weight per minute.

Forty-eight patients received EACA\* intravenously immediately prior to the initiation of cardiopulmonary bypass, while 25 received no EACA. The patients were matched according to age and weight insofar as this was possible. The first 48 patients were studied by giving alternate patients EACA (125 mg. per kilogram of body weight) prior to bypass. From our experience with the first 48 patients, however, the advantages of EACA seemed so obvious that the remaining

### RESULTS

When the patients in each group were divided according to the operative procedure performed, it was seen that the bleeding that had occurred in certain categories of patients who had received EACA was significantly less than in the corresponding categories of patients who had not received EACA. This was particularly noticeable in patients with acquired cardiac disease requiring valve replacement. The average blood loss among those with acquired heart disease in the treated group was 575 ml. as compared with 1,360 ml. in the untreated group.

Among all patients with congenital heart disease, regardless of age at the time of repair, an average blood loss of 1,263 ml. occurred in the untreated group as compared with 952 ml. in the treated group. Patients with subaortic stenosis, ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, and anomalous pulmonary venous return all had less bleeding when treated with EACA, although there are relatively few patients in each category (Table 2) and the difference between the treated and untreated patients was not as marked as it was in those with acquired disease.

In the entire series, 2 patients required reoperation for bleeding in the immediate postoperative period. One of these had received EACA prior to bypass.

The first patient, a 1-year-old infant who was treated with EACA during correction of transposition of the great vessels, was bleeding from multiple diffuse points in the chest wall and mediastinum. The second patient, an adult who underwent repair of an atrial septal defect without receiving EACA, also was bleeding from multiple points in the chest wall.

If all the patients are classified according to the total amount of blood lost, it is evident that the great preponderance of patients treated with EACA lost less than 1,000 mL (Table 3). Twenty-one of the 24 patients who lost less than 500 mL had been treated with EACA; and of the 48 patients who received EACA, 44 (42 adults and 2 children) lost less than 1,000 mL in the postoperative period.

# COMMENT

Trauma to the cellular elements of the blood during cardiopulmonary bypass results in destruction of and damage to red cells and platelets. Clot-promoting and heparin-neutralizing factors released from these damaged cells result in a state of potential hypercoagulability. Intravascular clotting consequently occurs, resulting in an abnormal consumption of clotting factors. These developments in turn stimulate production of antithrombin activity and the release of plasminogen activator, which results in fibrinolysis \[11, 13, 18].

Activation of the fibrinolytic enzyme system has been described by several earlier investigators \[15, 18], but the degree and frequency of fibrinolysis and the factors affecting it remain obscure. Gans and Krivit \[11], in a study of 44 patients, found that plasminogen activator was released in 40 of the patients during extracorporeal circulation and that operations for acquired heart disease were associated with the release of significantly more activator than were operations for congenital defects. On the other hand, a recent study by Beall and his associates \[1] of 24 patients undergoing extracorporeal circulation with a plastic bubble oxygenator primed with 5% dextrose in water revealed the presence of plasminogen activators without actual fibrinolysis in most of the patients studied.

# EACA for Bleeding After Cardiopulmonary Bypass

In this study, we found no patient in whom the administration of EACA in the dosage described was deemed responsible for any untoward effect. Considerable mention has been made in the literature regarding undesirable effects of EACA. A fatal case of glomerular capillary thrombosis with renal failure has been reported recently, and the dangers of the effect of EACA on cardiac performance have been noted to be substantial \[4]. The cardiovascular effects appear to be mediated mainly through release of catecholamines and may result in arrhythmia and hypotension \[5, 16].

The results of this study indicate that EACA may be effective in significantly reducing bleeding after extracorporeal circulation, particularly in the case of acquired cardiac lesions that are treated with valve replacement. We realize this study is inherently limited by the relatively crude measurement of blood loss through chest tube drainage as well as the relatively small number of patients in the series. Nevertheless, it would appear from the results obtained that EACA may be effective when used during operation for acquired cardiac disease. The significantly high level of plasminogen activator previously shown to occur during operations for acquired heart disease may explain the favorable results noted with EACA in these patients \[9]. Despite the inability to demonstrate circulating fibrinolysins among 24 patients undergoing extracorporeal circulation in an earlier study from this institution \[1] and despite such factors as diminished circulating platelets, prolonged prothrombin time, altered fibrinogen levels, and inadequate techniques for control of bleeding, all of which may contribute to faulty hemostasis and are unaltered by EACA, we found that EACA helped to diminish postoperative bleeding in some of the patients studied.

# BABIES 'ICED'

# FOR HEART

# OPERATIONS

![img-59.jpeg](img-59.jpeg)

At the age of three months, Michele weighed only eight pounds. She had a congenital heart defect, and doctors at the University of Washington Hospital in Seattle gave her but a few weeks to live. Her condition was so grave that a surgical team headed by Dr. David H. Dillard decided to try open-heart surgery using a technique of surface-induced deep hypothermia they had developed in animal studies.

Michele was anesthetized with ether, placed on a plastic sheet, and lowered into a cooling tank where she floated on ice water. As thermometer readings dropped, bags of crushed ice were packed around her to lower her temperature still further. When her rectal temperature reached 78° F, she was removed from the tank and put on the operating table for the first incision. Her temperature continued to drift down and hit 61° F.

At this point, 4 cc of Young's solution was injected into the aortic root to induce cardiac arrest. The heart was stopped for 32 minutes while the surgeons corrected the routing of the tiny infant's pulmonary venous circulation that drained into the coronary

sinus. The surgical field was almost bloodless. Today, three years later, Michele is healthy, lively, and growing normally. Her IQ is 140.

Surface-induced deep hypothermia has since been used by the Seattle physicians on 25 other infants too young to tolerate the heart-lung machine. Without corrective surgery for congenital heart defects, says Dr. Dillard, none of these infants seemed likely to live. Eleven have survived the open-heart surgery.

The survivors include Michele and four others out of the ten infants who had total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, four of seven who had transposed great vessels, one of three who had pulmonary atresia, and one of three who had complex ventricular septal defects. The procedure has also been tried in cases of aortic atresia, aortic stenosis with hypoplastic left ventricle, and double outlet right ventricle, but these three infants died.

"Mortality can perhaps be associated with the anatomy and over-all condition of the infant," ventures Dr. Dillard, who acknowledges there are still too few cases for significant cor-

relation. "Our youngest patient was only a few days old," he notes, "but our youngest survivor was 42 days old." All who survived correction of great vessel transposition or total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage were younger than six months.

Dr. Dillard, who is associate professor of surgery, suggests that there is some "special problem, still undefined" in transposition of the great vessels. One boy with this defect went into a prolonged period of cardiac arrest two days after surgery and is now somewhat retarded, with an IQ in the 80 to 90 range. Two other infants had pulmonary insufficiency after initial recovery from surgery, and mild impairment of psychomotor development is suspected in one. None of the children who have survived, Dr. Dillard reports, evidence any neurologic damage from the hypothermia itself.

In the extensive research with dogs and puppies that preceded their clinical use of induced hypothermia, the Seattle investigators noted that some adult dogs had a high-stepping gait after circulation was stopped for an hour. In later tests, they found that

<sup>**Page 117**</sup>

[Open Page 117 of PDF](https://pdfs-noindex.themindscapeishere.workers.dev/1973%20Jehovahs%20Witnesses%20Alternatives%20To%20Blood%20Transfusions.pdf#page=117)

BCRC-36

# 'ICING' SABIES continued

perfusion of the brain with cold isotonic saline solution helped avoid this problem. They now use such perfusion with infants as well.

A nine-member team of surgeons, anesthesiologists, and pediatricians carries out the procedure. Dr. Hitoshi Mohri handles the actual cooling. A visiting scientist at the university, Dr. Mohri pioneered in the development of the technique while at Japan's University of Sendai and has assisted with the Washington modifications.

In the gradual cooling, temperatures fall to the desired level within one to three hours. Cardiac arrest is limited to about an hour, but the entire procedure may last as long as six hours. Rectal and esophageal temperatures are monitored continuously. As the temperature is reduced, low-molecular-weight dextran is given intravenously. Deep ether anesthesia, reports Dr. Dillard, seems to be critical in obtaining desired levels of cooling without ventricular fibrillation.

All body activity is markedly decreased as the temperature drops. Blood pressure falls to around 30 mm Hg. Liver and renal function are de-

pressed, insulin and growth hormone release are decreased, and all metabolic processes are slowed before circulation stops. The baby breathes room temperature air, and respiration is maintained by hand to keep ventilation at relatively normal levels. Because of the depressed metabolism, this results in respiratory alkalosis and helps compensate for the circulatory curtailment.

# 'The Pink Get Pinker'

After the operation, all deviations gradually disappear as the infant is warmed in a warm-water bath. The heart almost always resumes its heat spontaneously, but sometimes manual massage or electrical pacing is needed. Blood that has lain still begins to circulate again, moving through the new routes. The blood's oxygen tension reaches normal levels, and peripheral cyanosis disappears. Says Dr. Dillard: "Even the pink babies get pinker."

Postoperative advantages of hypothermia, the Seattle surgeon reports, are the absence of bleeding problems and minimal respiratory complications. The infants, he says, have gener-

ally required less intensive postoperative care than perfusion patients.

The prolonged period of suspended animation possible with this method, Dr. Dillard says, makes it possible to do complete corrections on some infants who would normally be put through staged procedures. But he notes that the time for surgery is limited and that there is a potential hazard of producing heart block.

"This is not a panacea for the problems of cardiac surgery in the small infant," Dr. Dillard warns. "Perhaps it may not even have a permanent place in such surgery. But, for now—while heart-lung perfusion techniques are undergoing refinements that can reduce mortality and morbidity in tiny infants and while surgical procedures themselves are being improved—we are salvaging babies. Some were moribund when we first saw them. They are growing up healthy."

# **PEDIATRICS**

# **COOLING THE INFANT HEART**

Deep hypothermia by surface cooling, plus limited bypass, provide "ideal conditions" for operations to correct congenital heart defects in neonates and infants, according to a team of New Zealanders. In describing a series of 37 such procedures, Drs. Brian Barratt-Boyes, M. Simpson, and John Neutze of Green Lane Hospital in Auckland told the American Heart Association meeting in Atlantic City that use of this technique holds the duration of total-body perfusion to a minimum, provides a completely bloodless relaxed heart, and obviates caval cannulation. All this, they add, leads to a "striking lessening of morbidity," including the pulmonary complications commonly attendant upon heart-lung bypass.

The infants in their series were cooled to a nasopharyngeal temperature of 26° C on a circulating water blanket under halothane anesthesia, and then to 22° C by a short period of total-body perfusion. Circulatory arrest at this temperature averaged 48 minutes, sufficient time to make the intracardiac repair. Postoperatively, 20 minutes of total-body perfusion brought the temperature back

up to 32° C, and rewarming by surface means raised it to 36° C.

Thirty-three of the 37 infants survived the procedure, including 25 aged eight days to a year. The conditions treated were transposition in 13, tetralogy of Fallot in nine, total anomalous pulmonary venous connection in six, ventricular septal defect in six, and atrioventricular canal

in three. Analysis of the four hospital deaths, say the doctors, "indicates that all were avoidable; it would appear, therefore, that if no errors are made either in surgical technique or postoperative management, every infant should survive no matter how young or how severely affected—provided the defects are completely correctable."

Experience Gained on Jehovah's Witnesses

## Heart Surgery Transfusions

Skipped by Cooley's Team

BY MIMI CROSSLEY
Chronicle Reporter

"It's like walking a tight-rope without having a net," says a Houston surgeon about performing heart surgery on Jehovah's Witnesses, who refuse blood transfusions.

Members of the religious sect usually cannot get doctors to operate on them. Except for Dr. Denton Cooley and a team of heart specialists from the Texas Heart Institute here.

The doctors say their experience with the religious sect has led them to believe that all heart surgery should be performed without transfusion if at all possible.

The Houston team's work is described in the current issue of the Journal of the American Medical Assn. The doctors are C. Wilton Simmons Jr., Bruno J. Messmer, Grady L. Hallman, and Cooley.

"Any patient receiving a transfusion runs the risk of hepatitis and reaction leading to shock," said Dr. Hallman. "But these complications are especially serious for heart patients. Most centers set aside eight to 10 bottles of blood for surgery on the arteries and as much as 20 bottles for open-heart surgery, just for one patient."

To get around the need for transfusions, said Hallman, great care must be taken during surgery so the patient will not bleed. If artificial grafts are needed to replace a worn-out artery, special preclotted materials are used to prevent leaking. A salt and sugar solution is fed into the patient's veins during the operation.

"But we always keep blood handy for patients who are not Jehovah's Witnesses," said Hallman, "just in case."

So far the Cooley team has found that the death rate following "bloodless" surgery is

no greater than when transfusions are used. Post-operative problems are fewer.

The medical journal article carries a report on 29 Jehovah's Witness patients, ranging in age from 17 months to 76 years. They were all operated on for disease of the arteries.

Hallman said the team is now preparing a report on 29 Jehovah's Witnesses who underwent open-heart surgery.

"We had previously tried heart surgery without transfusion on a few people. Then a Jehovah's Witness came to us for surgery. The word spread, and I guess we get most of them now," said Dr. Hallman.

The experience with the Jehovah's Witnesses confirmed the team's belief that transfusions should be avoided for heart surgery, and it is now their policy.
