# EXPERIENCE WITH THE SURGICAL USE OF A NEW ABSORBABLE HEMOSTATIC AGENT (SURGICEL ABSORBABLE HEMOSTAT)\*

CHARLES B. HANNA, M. D.

W. D. HASTINGS, M. D.

E. E. HAGUE, JR., M. D.

Spartanburg, S. C.

The use of the conventional gauze sponge to control capillary and venous bleeding during surgical procedures has certain obvious disadvantages, the most important of which is that it cannot be left in situ when the bleeding occurs within an organ or body cavity. Many materials have been offered as antihemorrhagic preparations only to fall short of the ideal. It is true that some were slowly absorbed but this slow absorption rate may retard wound healing. Absorbability, tissue reactivity and hemostatic effectiveness have also been reported to vary widely.

During the past year, we have had an opportunity to use Surgicel Absorbable Hemostat, a new truly absorbable hemostatic agent. It is an oxidized regenerated cellulose fiber in uniform diameter chemically consisting of polyanhydroglucuronic acid, a compound which is not only highly hemostatic but can be readily absorbed by living tissue. It has been suggested by Hurwitt et al that the acid

\*SURGICEL Absorbable Hemostat was supplied by Johnson & Johnson, New Brunswick, New Jersey.

nature of this compound may be responsible for its hemostatic action because of a styptic effect and its marked affinity for hemoglobin and other blood proteins. They have also suggested that the artificial clot formed when Surgicel is used, may act as a basis for the formation of the physiologic clot.

The material is pale yellow, light in weight, silky in texture and available in sterile form for clinical use. When exposed to blood, it turns dark brown as a result of the formation of hematin acid by the action of the polyanhydroglucuronic acid on hemoglobin. Since the gauze itself is acid with a pH range of 3.5 to 4.5, agents such as thrombin, if added to the gauze, would be destroyed and no advantage could be expected from their combination with oxidized regenerated cellulose.

# Materials and Methods

We have used oxidized regenerated cellulose (Surgicel) in 196 patients who underwent a variety of surgical procedures including skin grafts, thoracotomies, hemorrhoidec

# Case Reports

Case 1. Skull Fracture With Brain Injury

A 33-year-old woman was admitted to the Spartanburg General Hospital, December 26, 1961. It was reported that she had fallen down steps 48 hours before admission to the hospital and that she had been aphasic for 24 hours. She had an irregular depressed laceration measuring 2½ by 3 cm over the left parietal region of the scalp.

An x-ray film confirmed the presence of a compound enantiated depressed skull fracture. The only neurological finding was complete aphasia. A depressed skull fracture in Broca's area was the presumptive diagnosis. She was taken immediately to the operating room and, under local and Pentothal anesthesia, the wound was debrided and the depressed broken bone raised to its original position. There was loss of several fragments of severely comminuted bone. An irregular laceration of the dura and of the underlying brain was also evident. The brain bled freely and re-expanded but there was still an irregular laceration with several superficial small venules bleeding slowly. The edges of the bony depression were trimmed by the rongeur until they were smooth to the fingertip. Good hemostasis of bone was obtained with bone wax. A small piece of Surgicel was cut to correspond to the size of the depressed area of the brain (approximately 1½ by 2 cm) which was generally contused and was oozing fresh dark blood. The surrounding area was thoroughly irrigated with a #14 catheter and no evidence of any epidural or dural hematoma was found.

A fresh piece of Surgicel Absorbable Hemostat was then placed over the bleeding and cut area of the brain and no effort was made to suture the dura. A small Penrose drain was placed down to the dura and the wound was rinsed in layers.

On the fifth day after surgery, the patient began to talk. When seen about ten months later, she still had difficulty in phrasing some of her thoughts but had control of her tongue. In general, a good result was obtained and there was an almost normal return of the ability to speak. At one time she had slight tingling and numbness in her right arm but this was not localized and she showed no motor disability.

Surgicel was of benefit in controlling the venous

hemorrhage. There has been no evidence of any untoward reaction to it.

Case 2. Head Injury With Subdural Hematoma

A 10-year-old girl was seen immediately after an accident in which she was hit by a car. She was knocked unconscious but recovered consciousness in about 15 minutes. Skull x-ray films showed no evidence of any fracture or dislocation; however, there was subluxation of the third cervical vertebra over the fourth cervical vertebra. While the examination was being carried out, a generalized convulsion with dilatation of the left pupil and deviation of the eyes to the right occurred. Within 30 minutes this child was carried to the operating room. Bilateral trephination was done and revealed a subgaleal hematoma on the left and a subdural hematoma on the same side. These were evacuated. Because of the edema of the brain, the dura was not closed on the left but a Surgicel gauze pack was placed over the dural opening. A Penrose drain was placed down to the dura.

After surgery, she regained consciousness and moved all her extremities. There was a recurrence of fluid in the subgaleal region but this was gradually absorbed over a two-week period. The drain was removed on the third postoperative day and there was no evidence of any irritation or toxicity from the Surgicel pack. Five weeks after the injury, the findings of the neurological examination were normal. Case 3. Cholecystectomy.

A 35-year-old woman on examination was found to be in good health except for the presence of stones in her gall bladder.

Physical examination showed the patient to be well developed but very small. Her blood pressure was 106/70 mm Hg.

At surgery the gall bladder was found to be elongated and narrowed throughout its length and largely filled with stones. The cystic duct and cystic artery were isolated separately, doubly ligated with #0 chromic sutures near the common duct. The gall bladder was removed without difficulty. The gall bladder bed was sutured with #00 chromic. When there was a slight amount of bleeding, Surgicel gauze was placed over the gall-bladder bed and a Penrose drain was placed in the foramen of Winslow. After brief observation, all bleeding from the gall-bladder bed had stopped. No other abnormalities of the abdominal viscera were found. She was returned to her room in good condition.

This woman had a normal convalescence. The drain was shortened on the second day and removed on the fourth day after surgery with no evidence of any further drainage. The post-operative course was afebrile. The Surgicel was a good hemostatic agent and caused no untoward reaction.

Case 4. Removal of a Bone Cyst.

A 26-year-old male felt a sudden pain in his upper right arm when cranking a power lawn mower. On examination (in June, 1960), he was

The pathological studies made at the time of surgery (June 6, 1907), showed the lining of the cystic structure to be composed of dense connective tissue supported by abundant collagen. The actual lining cells showed interstitial hemorrhage and organizational reaction with an occasional multinucleated cell. This was thought to represent aneurysmal bone cyst. There was no evidence of malignancy.

The cyst was corrected and the lining removed. This left an opening 2½ by 3 cm in the lateral wall of the humerus. The cyst was 8 cm in length and the full diameter of the bone. The cyst wall was treated with phenol which was then neutralized with alcohol. After it was thoroughly washed out with alcohol, Surgicel sponge was placed over the opening in the bone. The arm was strapped to the side in a Velpeau splint. The skin healed per primum. The patient was followed by means of x-rays and clinical examinations. The bone chips served as a stimulus for new bone formation; however, a second cyst was found proximal to the first. This second cyst was about 7½ cm long. It was treated surgically in the same manner as the first cyst. At the time of the second operation (September 24, 1900), there was no evidence of any Surgicel remaining at the first operative site. New bone had replaced the defect in the wall of the humerus. The Surgicel had been completely absorbed during the time lapse between the two surgical procedures. Subsequently, the bone graft has completely solidified and the patient has a normal range of motion of the shoulder with no evidence of recurrence of cystic formation.

# Case 5. Hemorrhoidectomy

A 48-year-old woman presented a complaint of severe pain during bowel movements. Her general health was good. On examination she was found to have large combined thrombosed hemorrhoids. A combined hemorrhoidectomy was done with removal of the overlying skin and mucous as well as the hemorrhoids. Surgicel with cyelomethycaine lubricant was placed in the anal orifice to control slight capillary bleeding. Convenience was normal. The patient later came to our office for anal dilatation. The third day after surgery the fragments of Surgicel were passed without any discomfort with her first bowel movement. Healing was satisfactory. Surgicel acted as a satisfactory hemostatic agent for the minimal venous bleeding from the anal orifice. The patient had no untoward reactions.

# Case 6. Liver Biopsy

A 20-year-old nurse was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of abdominal swelling and soreness in the hepatic region. Two years previously she had been in the same hospital after a blood transfusion. At that time liver biopsy was done and confirmed the diagnosis of viral hepatitis. She responded well

to a high-carbohydrate, high-vitamin diet supplemented with choline chloride; however, she later developed a recurrence of the hepatitis and was critically ill, but again responded to high-carbohydrate, high-vitamin therapy. On admission in December 1962, she had abdominal distention and the liver was six cm below the right costal margin, very tender and smooth along its lower edge. In addition, she had an abdominal fluid wave. Her skin was pale but there was no definite jaundice. Liver studies were done and the haemodialysis test showed 14% retention at the end of two hours. Biopsy of the enlarged liver was done under local anesthesia. A wedge of the liver was excised. A plug of Surgicel was placed in the biopsy site and it was not necessary to suture the liver surface. The wound healed satisfactorily with no evidence of any toxicity or increased drainage as a result of the use of Surgicel. Pathological study confirmed recurrent hepatitis, virus type, with scarring.

# Comments

A number of reports have appeared in the literature which attest to the valuable hemostatic property and freedom from toxicity of Surgicel Absorbable Hemostat. Our experience has brought to light nothing contrary to these reports. It has only borne out and confirmed the findings of others. To cite only one report, Miller et al. point out that on the basis of their experience, Surgicel is particularly useful in controlling bleeding from the brain, liver and kidney. They also call attention to the fact that this preparation also helps to avoid additional trauma to the tissues from suturing or cautery which may be required if bleeding is to be controlled by other methods.

The Surgicel acted as a splint to the grafted areas of skin and controlled the capillary bleeding of the donor site. Around bronchial stumps, in the gall-bladder bed and over the disc spaces after laminectomy, a double layer of gauze seemed to work best. With diffuse bleeding of the pleura, a single sheet of gauze markedly reduced the generalized oozing. No post-operative increase in pleural effusion was noted. In muscle injuries, in tonsil fossae and after hemorrhoidectomies, the gauze was often used as a pad or plug. The carded fiber was also used as an anal packing after hemorrhoidectomies. The gauze and the carded fiber seemed to control oozing equally well. Both usually disappeared from the anal orifice

Our preference was for the gauze type of material since it could be cut without fraying and could easily be molded to the contour of the bleeding areas or organ. During more than a year's experience, we have observed no change in the physical properties of this material on storage and in no instance has any toxic or untoward reaction been observed. When used as an adjunct to good surgical technique, this absorbable hemostatic agent is an excellent aid.

# Summary

1. A new hemostatic agent, Surgicel Absorbable Hemostat, an oxidized regenerated cellulose compound of pure uniform fibers of polyanhydroglucuronic acid, has been used successfully in 136 patients who underwent surgery of various types including cholecystectomies, skin grafts, hemorrhoidectomies, bone surgery, tonsillectomies, thoracotomies, biopsies, brain surgery and other procedures.

IN EXTENSIVE SURGICAL OPERATIONS

S. GOLLUB, M.D., DAVID CHARLES SCHECHTER, M.D., TERUO HIROSE, M.D., F.A.C.S.,
and CHARLES P. BAILEY, M.D., F.A.C.S., New York, New York

CURRENTLY in the United States, the use of
nonhemic colloid solutions as plasma sub-
stitutes is practically confined to dex-
tran, either the 70,000 or the 40,000 molecu-
lar weight preparations. These solutions ful-
fill most of the criteria for an ideal plasma
expander. However, they do possess disad-
vantageous properties. These include physi-
cal instability resulting in the formation of
flakes of solid material; antigenicity mani-
festing itself by immediate or delayed hyper-
sensitivity reactions of varying severity; and
a clinical hemorrhagic diathesis associated
with defective blood clot formation, which
is apparently dose-dependent. Consequent-
ly, the search continues for more suitable
materials to serve as plasma expanders.

The glucopyranose polymer, hydroxy-
ethyl starch, made from waxy sorghum
cornstarch, has been thoroughly studied
pharmacologically by Murphy, Thompson
(6-9), and Walton and their associates and is
presently undergoing clinical appraisal. It is
physically stable during storage and appar-
ently nonantigenic. However, it has been
shown to be similar to dextran in eliciting a
bleeding diathesis in dogs. Clinical trial of
the material to date has been cautiously
limited to infusion in volunteers and in
hemorrhaging accident victims.

This study was designed to determine the
clinical response to hydroxyethyl starch
when given instead of dextran solution as a
plasma substitute to individuals subjected
to extensive surgical procedures.

From the Departments of Hematology and of Thoracic and
Cardiovascular Surgery, St. Petersburg Hospital, New York.
Supported by: Contracts No. DA-47-193-MD-2566 and No.
DA-47-193-MD-2566, U. S. Army Medical Research and De-
velopment Command.

# MATERIALS AND METHODS

The 26 patients in this series were adults,
of both sexes, who underwent extensive pul-
monary or cardiovascular surgical proce-
dures. They were divided at random into
three groups. Those in group A received
hydroxyethyl starch during an operation
not requiring extracorporeal circulation;
those in group B received hydroxyethyl
starch during cardiopulmonary bypass,
either by venoclysis or as a constituent of
the pump-oxygenator prime; and those in
group C received hydroxyethyl starch in the
recovery room, immediately after opera-
tion.

In each of these three groups, the patients
were given either 250 or 500 milliliters of hy-
droxyethyl starch infused over a period of
30 minutes. Blood samples were drawn im-
mediately before infusion. In the patients in
groups A and C, a subsequent specimen was
taken one hour after conclusion of the infu-
sion. The total volume of either Hartmann's
or glucose-water solution, but never colloid
or blood, administered during this interval
of one and one-half hours was less than 200
milliliters. Usually, it was about 100 milli-
liters. In group B, the second blood speci-
men was obtained near the completion of
the entire operation, after cessation of
heart-lung bypass, when the hypocoagula-
ble state from heparin had been corrected
by protamine sulfate, and this neutraliza-
tion had been confirmed by a protamine
titration method (2).

Parameters observed in all patients dur-
ing 48 hours after infusion of hydroxyethyl
starch included arterial and venous blood
pressure, electrocardiogram, inspection of

the skin for signs of hypersensitivity reactions or unusual bleeding, examination of incisions for evidence of oozing, and urinary output.

Hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelet count, Lee-White clotting time, recalcified plasma-clotting time, and thromboelastography were determined before and after hydroxyethyl starch infusion. Blood volume determinations were also made for the patients in groups A and C. The hydroxyethyl starch used throughout was 6 per cent hydroxyethyl starch in 0.9 per cent sodium chloride solution, with 0.93 degree of substitution.

# RESULTS

No alterations occurred in blood pressure, pulse rate, respiration, or urinary output. Anaphylactic reactions or unusual bleeding were not observed.

The results of laboratory determinations are presented in Tables I, II, and III. These include changes in blood volume, red blood cells, and platelet count as well as results of tests of the coagulation mechanism as reflected in the Lee-White whole blood-clotting time, plasma recalcified clotting time, and the thromboelastographic patterns of whole blood. It should be noted that the blood volume rose modestly in almost every patient as a result of the infusion. The net increase in blood volume generally exceeded the quantity of hydroxyethyl starch given. This finding suggests some shift of water from the extravascular to the intravascular compartment consequent to the colloid osmotic action of this solution. Similar results have been observed in our experimental investigations with this substance.

The changes in platelet count for the patients in groups A and C were negligible. In Group B—patients undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass—the drop in platelet concentration was marked. However, these decreases are entirely explicable on the basis of the effects of extracorporeal bypass on platelets and have previously been observed in the absence of administration of colloid

plasma expanders (10). These data indicate no deleterious influence on the number of platelets from hydroxyethyl starch administration. The results of the Lee-White clotting time test and the thromboelastogram also suggest that, in the amounts used, there was no adverse effect on platelet function. The findings were exceptional in Patient 12 and will subsequently be discussed.

The laboratory studies evaluating the gross coagulation mechanism indicate no appreciable changes in other parameters studied, with the exception of Patients 5 and 12. Otherwise, the studies are compatible with the interpretation that hydroxyethyl starch solution in the amounts employed did not disturb the hemostatic mechanism as gauged by the clinical or laboratory criteria.

Particular mention must be made of two patients. Patient 5 of group A exhibited grossly impaired coagulation tests in the postoperative period after receiving hydroxyethyl starch. However, at no time did she demonstrate any bleeding tendency. The laboratory values are consistent with the presence of an anticoagulant, such as heparin. We are inclined to attribute these results to traces of heparin in the sample. Patient 12 of Group B received 500 milliliters of hydroxyethyl starch by venoclysis during heart-lung bypass. During closure of the thoracotomy wound, a few hours after cessation of bypass, diffuse oozing occurred from the sternotomy, endothoracic walls, and cardiovascular incisions. Clots were present, but they were soft in consistency and unusually friable. Diffuse oozing persisted for approximately 20 minutes, and then subsided spontaneously without any special therapy having been employed. The subsequent course of the patient was uneventful. Examination of the coagulation parameters of this patient showed a low platelet count, a slight increase in the plasma recalcified clotting time, and abnormal k and ma values in the thromboelastogram. The platelet count, again, can be explained on the basis of the cardiopulmonary bypass

procedure. Such values, observed in the past, were not necessarily associated with bleeding manifestations. However, the combination of essentially unaltered whole blood and plasma-clotting times, together with impaired k and ma values of the thromboemogram presents findings qualitatively similar to those observed in dogs given sufficient hydroxyethyl starch to deliberately produce bleeding (3). We suspect that this patient exhibited a minor transient bleeding diathesis produced partly by the hydroxyethyl starch and partly by the lowered platelet count.

# DISCUSSION

This study was undertaken to determine the response to hydroxyethyl starch in cir-

cumstances of trauma combined with blood loss, such as the extensive types of surgical procedures cited herein. We intentionally employed smaller amounts of the agent than would ordinarily be needed, with balanced salt solution for supplementation. Patients were elderly for the most part, with multiple system derangements, and had been receiving complex medication regimens for long periods. Obviously, such patients are not comparable to healthy young volunteers or accident victims. The results indicate that the hydroxyethyl starch solution was well tolerated in all but one patient. This individual transiently exhibited a minor hemorrhagic diathesis qualitatively similar to that observed in experimental animals subsequent to infusion of much larger

728 Surgery, Gynecology & Obstetrics - April 1969

quantities of the same solution or dextran. Bleeding in this single patient was also complicated by the low platelet count.

Ballinger and his associates administered as much as 1,500 milliliters of hydroxyethyl starch in patients not operated upon without encountering any adverse effects. It should be pointed out, however, that their patients did not have the significant challenge to hemostatic function as did those of our series. Lee and his associates found "prolongation of the partial thromboplastin time in three patients and a minimal depression of fibrinogen in one patient. These changes were temporary. None were felt to be of clinical significance and were similar to studies made with 6 per cent dextran."

In general, this investigation confirms our experience with animal experimentation employing hydroxyethyl starch as a plasma expander in that the results are quite similar to those obtained with dextran. It would seem that the new plasma expander, hydroxyethyl starch, can be employed in the same clinical circumstances in which dextran would be indicated. The potential hazard of inducing a bleeding diathesis with hydroxyethyl starch appears likewise to be the same as that when using dextran. The treatment of this particular complication is entirely empiric to date.

# SUMMARY

The new plasma expander, hydroxyethyl starch, was administered to 26 patients un-

dergoing extensive pulmonary or cardiovascular surgery. In all but one patient, clinical and laboratory observations indicated the material to be well tolerated and without significant side-effects. Hemostasis was unimpaired. One patient, who had been subjected to extracorporeal circulation, exhibited a minor, temporary bleeding defect, possibly related to the starch infusion.

## Medical Briefs

### Blood Substitute for Surgery

A blood substitute that some day may aid surgeons performing delicate operations has been developed by Dr. Leland C. Clark, Jr., of the University of Cincinnati Medical Center.

The milky chemical suspension has been used to prime heart-lung machines and to replace 80 percent of an animal's blood supply during open-heart surgery. After operations, normal blood supply is restored.

The man-made blood substitute can carry up to 20 times as much oxygen as plasma dissolves. Use of the new fluid can eliminate the risk of hepatitis and other infections and does not require tissue-typing or cross-matching. Doctor Clark says. The blood substitute, developed under a National Institutes of Health grant, reportedly is inexpensive to produce and can be stored.

## 35 rats

BOSTON (AP) — After 35 rats survived an experiment in which all their blood was replaced by an artificial substance, Harvard University researchers have begun tests on monkeys and hope to extend the benefits to man.

If the work is successful, the substance could be used to preserve organs for transplants and to provide an alternative for patients who have built up a reaction to ordinary blood transfusions, Dr. Robert Geyer, the chief researcher, said yesterday.

The breakthrough, which came late last fall, had eluded the specialists for several years.

Dr. Geyer said that the closer complete transfer is approached, the more difficult the task becomes.

"TWO YEARS ago we were able to do 68 per cent," he said. "By juggling the ingredients — in amounts and molecular characteristics — we finally were able to achieve 100 per cent."

The blood replacement is made up of a class of compounds called fluorocarbons and is a liquid that can be milky white to dishwater grey to clear, Dr. Geyer said.

The important feature, he added, is that it carries oxygen to an organism's cells, a job previously done only by red blood cells.

"We were almost convinced as recently as last spring that our substance would have to have at least a few red blood cells," Dr. Geyer said, but the chemical used for the rats was totally artificial.

SINCE a body continues to produce new red blood cells all the time, it is important that they be able to mix with the artificial substance, which was the case with the rats.

Since the blood replacement, the rats have survived and gradually replaced the substance with their own blood.

The change to monkeys will provide more answers on the usefulness of the preparation to humans.

In the coming year the researchers plan to begin seeing if replacing blood in rats afflicted with leukemia helps to cure the disease.

Dr. Geyer said no human experiments are planned at this time, but it is hoped that "within several years" the preparation, or one like it, will be able to keep various human organs alive for days and weeks for transplants.

The Spectator, Thursday, January 4, 1973 47

# Replacement of Operative Blood Loss of More Than 1 Liter With Hartmann's Solution

Benjamin Rigor, MD; Peter Bosomworth, MD; and Benjamin F. Ruth, Jr., MD

A hundred patients each lost over 1,000 ml of blood while undergoing surgery and received two to three times that volume of Hartmann's solution. Postoperative mortality and morbidity were not affected by the lack of blood in the replacement regimen. Age group and physical condition of these patients were representative of the hospital population, and patients over 60 years old in American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) risk classifications 3 and 4 were included. Eighty-six percent of the group lost from 1 to 1.5 liters of blood; only 14% lost a larger amount. Serum electrolyte levels were unaffected. Hematocrit readings and total protein concentrations decreased but remained within physiologic limits. No unexpected complications were encountered in the postoperative period, and hospitalization was not prolonged. Only four patients required subsequent transfusions postoperatively.

\*Substantial blood losses can be effectively replaced with balanced saline solutions if these solutions are given in sufficient quantity. Evidence favoring this proposition is both experimental and clinical. During the past two years, we have used increasing quantities of balanced saline solution for blood replacement. Our clinical records indicate that in the past year, 100 patients who lost more than a liter of blood during surgery had their loss totally replaced with Hartmann's solution. This communication reviews the effect of this regimen on morbidity, mortality, and serum changes.

# Methods

All patients operated upon between March 1,

From the departments of anesthesiology and surgery, University of Kentucky College of Medicine, Lexington. Reprint requests to 800 Rose St, Lexington, Ky 40506.

1966, and Feb 28, 1967, having blood losses in excess of 1,000 ml and fluid substitution with Hartmann's solution alone were included in the study. One liter of this solution was given in the first hour of operation without regard to blood loss, and each milliliter of blood loss was replaced with 2 to 3 ml of this solution. Blood loss was determined by weighing sponges and adding this to the observed loss in the suction bottle. All patients came to surgery with a hematocrit reading of 30% or better. The patient's physical status was classified prior to operation by the anesthesiologist according to the American Society of Anesthesiologists' (ASA) standard classification. Values for serum electrolytes, plasma proteins levels, whole blood values, hematocrit, and hemoglobin were determined for most, but not all, patients before and after surgery.

# Results

All major types of operation were performed (Table 1), but only procedures in which large amounts of blood were lost were included in the study, as indicated by the classification of the general surgical procedures in Table 2. Total gastrectomy, hemipelvectomy, bilateral radical neck dissection, and abdominal perineal resections were accomplished without blood replacement with fluids other than Hartmann's solution. All age groups were represented except children less than 15 years old, in whom losses of more than a liter of blood represented a much larger proportion of the blood volume than in adults. Twenty-three percent of the patients were over 60 years of age, and 61% over 40, which reflects the average distribution of patients in surgery at our institution (Table 3).

The use of Hartmann's solution was not restricted to patients who were considered good risks (Table 4); 88% of those treated were fair to poor risks according to the ASA risk classification (classes 2, 3, and 4).

With four exceptions, the blood loss permitted without replacement ranged from 1,000 to 2,000 ml (Table 5), with the largest group (86%) having a loss ranging from 1,000 to 1,500 ml. Despite the unreplaced blood loss, the patients did well postoperatively. Sixty-two percent were capable of leaving the hospital by the end of the first week, and 92% by the end of the second week. Only four patients were given subsequent blood transfusions, three because of overt postoperative blood loss, and one because of hypotension (blood pressure was 68/0 mm Hg). Average urinary output was excellent: 2,100 ml (range, 835 to 3,670 ml) in the first 24 hours after operation, and 2,500 ml (range, 1,100 to 4,120 ml) in the

second 24 hours. No episodes of anuria or oliguria were encountered.

Twenty-two postoperative complications were encountered (Table 6), ranging from mild to severe. There was only one postoperative death; a patient with spongioblastoma died on the 14th postoperative day with a perforated Cushing's ulcer. Hospitalization did not appear prolonged for patients with operations of this magnitude (Table 7).

Laboratory observations indicated a slow fall of hemoglobin and hematocrit values (Fig 1) as late as 72 hours postoperatively, but the mean drop was within a restricted range, so that oxygen carrying capacity was still adequate. Total protein concentrations also fell postoperatively (Table 8), but began to recover toward normal values by the third postoperative day. Serum sodium, potassium, carbon dioxide, and chloride levels remained within physiologic limits (Fig 2).

Assuming that a risk of one death from transfusion complications per 1,000 transfusions and an incidence of 2% nonfatal transfusion complications would occur, we conclude that five patients were spared complications and a 26% possibility of at least one death occurring was avoided.

There are abundant experimental data indicating the effectiveness of balanced saline solutions in maintaining blood pressure following hemorrhage, when such solutions are given in sufficient amounts. In our laboratory, replacement of one third of the blood volume in dogs with Hartmann's solution sustains the animals very well indefinitely, and replacement of one half of the blood volume is tolerated for at least 24 hours. This solution was superior to dextran 70, (Macrodex) levarterenol (norepinephrine) bitartrate, phenoxybenzamine hydrochloride (Dibenzylne), and even whole blood in resuscitating animals in hemorrhagic shock. Some of these phenomena may be explained by Shires theories concerning the loss of extracellular fluid during operative stress and hemorrhagic shock.

Despite the persistent tradition that blood is the only effective replacement for blood loss, the practice of using saline solutions for part or all of blood substitution has gained ground in many centers. Clinical studies performed as early as 1960 indicated that patients supported with infusions of saline solutions alone tolerated subtotal gastrectomy well. Cooley et al and Gollub and Bailey reported the feasibility of using saline solutions alone during major cardiac operations when this was required by Jehovah's Witnesses. Trudnowski noted that liberal use of balanced saline solutions conserved a total of 750 ml of blood per patient in major operations, and Boba observed the usefulness of balanced saline solutions in supporting patients in a diverse group undergoing 28 major operations where blood transfusions would normally be used.

The major objections to the clinical use of buffered saline solution as a substitute for blood loss is the dilution of hemoglobin and protein that results. However, saline replacement of blood losses in the range suffered by these patients rarely reduced serum protein or hematocrit values below physiologic limits. Hematocrit readings between

# PLASMA-VOLUME REPLACEMENT WITH HYDROXYETHYL STARCH

BRITAIN is reasonably well served with blood-transfusion services, and for restoring blood and plasma volume the fluids commonly used are stored blood and plasma. Though dextran is often given, especially in an emergency, few will have experience with other plasma substitutes like hydroxyethyl starch or modified gelatin derivatives. Hydroxyethyl starch has a number of advantages. Supplied as a 6% solution in saline, it is comparatively cheap, and it is said to be reproducible in quality and stable on long storage. It has a molecular weight of about 400,000 and it is said to persist longer in the blood than other plasma substitutes—usually for about two weeks. This may or may not be desirable, according to clinical and other circumstances, but its persistence raises questions concerning long-term incorporation in cells and tissues. It is prepared from waxy sorghum starch, an amylopectin which is treated with ethylene oxide, thereby introducing hydroxyethyl groups.

In 1965 Bollinger et al.¹ reported that hydroxyethyl starch was as effective as dextran for treating haemorrhagic shock in dogs, and Solanke² found that it had no adverse effects when given intravenously to patients. Recently Solanke et al.³ compared the plasma-volume expansion produced in four groups of volunteer

patients given 500 ml. of hydroxyethyl starch, dextran-70, plasma, or a commercial gelatin derivative ("Haemaccel"). Plasma volume was measured by the dye-dilution method, using T-1824 (Evans blue) as a tracer as soon as possible before and after the infusion. The plasma-volume expansion with dextran, plasma, and haemaccel were about the same and similar in volume to the amount infused, but that obtained with hydroxyethyl starch was on the average more than twice the volume given. This extra effect must be due to the drawing of fluid into the bloodstream, and it is reminiscent of the immediate results after infusion of hyperosmolar dextran-40. The osmolarity of 6% hydroxyethyl starch is not stated, but presumably it too is hyperosmolar, though, unlike dextran-40, it is not excreted rapidly in the urine. Information on the duration of the plasma-volume expansion with hydroxyethyl starch in normovolemic and hypovolemic states is required. The Committee on Safety of Drugs might also state any potential hazards, since hydroxyethyl starch is not yet approved for clinical use in the United States.⁴

# Vascular Surgery in Jehovah's Witnesses

C. Wilton Simmons, Jr., MD; Bruno J. Messmer, MD; Grady L. Hallman, MD; and Denton A. Cooley, MD

Twenty Jehovah's Witnesses (age range: 17 months to 76 years) underwent central or peripheral vascular surgery for congenital or acquired disease. Two patients died: one (74 years old) from myocardial infarction, the other after a subsequent open heart operation. Hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit readings were not low enough in any patient to urge blood transfusion. Hospital convalescence averaged one week. Overall results compared favorably with results in other patients, indicating that a good outcome can be obtained in vascular surgery without blood transfusion.

PATIENTS WHO belong to the religious sect of Jehovah's Witnesses refuse to undergo any surgical procedure requiring blood transfusion, because it is forbidden by their literal interpretation of Bible passages such as Acts 14:20,29, which charge those believing in God "to abstain from . . . blood." The development of a hemodilution technique for cardiopulmonary bypass has allowed such patients to undergo open heart surgery without challenging their religious convictions; and since 1964, open heart operations in Je-

hovah's Witnesses have been extensively reported. Relatively little information exists, however, on other procedures carried out in members of this faith. Major noncardiac procedures such as pulmonary resections, gastric surgery, and rectosigmoid resections have been successfully performed in this center as well as various vascular operations. In this paper we detail our experience with Jehovah's Witnesses who underwent vascular procedures without blood transfusion.

# Clinical Material

A total of 20 Jehovah's Witnesses have undergone central vascular or peripheral vascular surgery in this institution since 1964. The patients

ranged in age from 17 months to 76 years. Seven patients had congenital vascular disease (Table 1). Three children, each 2½ years of age, and one 28-year-old woman underwent division and suture of patent ductus arteriosus. Coarctation of the aorta was resected in two other children. The youngest patient in the series, an infant of 17 months, had excision of an aneurysm of the left axillary artery that had resulted from giant cell arteries.

Among the 13 patients with acquired vascular disease (Table 1) five had resection of an aneurysm of the abdominal aorta. One of these five patients also received an aortobilateral popliteal bypass graft, and another underwent concomitant closure of a large arteriovenous fistula between the aneurysm and the left renal vein which had caused severe left ventricular failure. Aortofemoral bypass procedures were performed in three cases; aortorenal, in one. The oldest patient (76 years) received a bilateral femoral-popliteal bypass graft. One patient underwent bilateral thoracic sympathectomy with periaortic neurectomy for intractable angina pectoris, and another underwent bilateral transfemoral embolectomy. Thrombectomy of the superior vena cava was performed in a patient who had had occlusion following transvenous insertion of a pacemaker electrode.

During surgery 16 patients received 5% dextrose in lactated Rin-

### Results

Eighteen of the 20 patients in the series survived operation, and all but one of these 18 recovered without postoperative complications. Unilateral pleural effusion developed on the sixth postoperative day in a 72-year-old woman who had undergone thrombectomy for obstruction of the superior vena cava, but this cleared by the time of hospital discharge.

Two patients died. One was a 74-year-old man who had resection of an aneurysm of the abdominal aorta and an aortobilateral popliteal bypass procedure. Hypotension developed in this patient on the first postoperative day, and two days after operation, he sustained a cardiac arrest from which he could not be resuscitated. Autopsy showed an acute

myocardial infarction, hypertrophy of the left ventricle, severe coronary arteriosclerosis, and bilateral nephrosclerosis, in addition to generalized atherosclerosis of the great vessels and occlusion of the iliac and femoral arteries.

The other death occurred in a 52-year-old man who had undergone bilateral transfemoral embolectomy and then the next day had had a stenotic mitral valve replaced under cardiopulmonary bypass. Initial response was good, but severe anemia and jaundice developed later in the postoperative period. The patient's heart rate ranged between 88 and 120 beats per minute, and there were no premature ventricular contractions. A sudden cardiac arrest on the eighth postoperative day caused his death. No autopsy was performed.

Hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit values obtained in 19 of the 20 patients averaged 13.3 gm/100 ml and 39.7%, respectively, upon admission to the hospital, and 12.8 gm/100 ml and 38.4% in the immediate postoperative period (one to three hours after operation). Hemoglobin concentration was decreased after operation in 11 patients, remained the same in 2, and in 6 cases was increased immediately after operation but subsequently fell below the pre-

operative value. In ten patients determinations were made again 24 hours after operation and averaged 12.8 gm/100 ml for hemoglobin concentration and 38.6% for hematocrit reading. Sporadic determinations were made between the first and sixth postoperative days but did not show further significant decrease in blood values. Table 2 shows a typical course of hemoglobin and hematocrit value changes in a patient who underwent resection of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. The estimated blood loss during surgery was 400 ml. This patient received 1,900 ml of 5% dextrose in lactated Ringer's solution intravenously during the procedure, and 4,440 ml of 5% dextrose in 0.25N saline solution within the first 48 hours after surgery. There was a progressive decrease in hemoglobin and hematocrit values until the fourth postoperative day when both values stabilized. The patient was discharged six days after operation.

Hospital convalescence for this series of patients ranged from 4 to 12 days and averaged about one week.

### Comment

Vascular surgery is routinely performed in this hospital without blood transfusion unless specifically indicated. However, since blood loss in most vascular procedures—especially those involving the aorta and its larger branches—may be unexpectedly excessive and can occur

The Jehovah's Witness, whose beliefs bind the surgeon to withhold blood transfusion under any circumstances, undergoes vascular surgery with an added risk, particularly if the patient is a small child in whom even minimal blood loss represents a considerable portion of the total blood volume. If significant amounts of blood are lost at operation they cannot be restored; consequently, vascular operations in these patients demand utmost attention to technical detail.

Rapid and meticulous hemostasis is, of course, a fundamental requirement in all vascular procedures in Jehovah's Witnesses.

In patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm minimal dissection of the proximal aorta is advisable before the proximal clamp is placed. No attempt should be made to excise the aneurysm. The iliac arteries should be clamped without circumferential dissection, since this could injure the iliac veins. Ligature of the inferior mesenteric artery before opening the aneurysm is advantageous if it can be done without extensive dissection; otherwise, the orifice should be closed from the inside with a suture, immediately after opening the aneurysm. Blood loss from the lumbar arteries is usually slight after removal of the thrombotic and atherosclerotic material from within the lumen. Each bleeding orifice of a lumbar artery is oversewn with a single figure-of-eight suture starting at the proximal end. After the graft is anastomosed to the proximal aortic and distal iliac stumps, little

of the aneurysmal sac need be excised. It is simply sutured over the graft.

When a vascular prosthesis must be inserted below the diaphragm, it is our usual policy to employ knitted Dacron grafts which are preclotted to minimize immediate blood loss after removal of vascular clamps. In Jehovah's Witnesses, however, we favor woven grafts since their lower porosity eliminates initial blood loss through the graft.

Results in this series of Jehovah's Witnesses undergoing major vascular surgery compare favorably with results in other patients who receive similar operations. Whether in adults or children, hemoglobin and hematocrit values did not fall to levels that would indicate blood transfusion. Replacement of immediate blood loss with 5% dextrose in lactated Ringer's solution and administration of the same fluid during the early postoperative period was enough to keep the circulation stable. Lactated Ringer's solution is preferable to dextran 40, which may encourage diffuse capillary bleeding due to peripheral vasodilation, hemodilution, lowered blood viscosity, and prevention of erythrocyte aggregation.

All but two patients survived operation, enjoyed prompt recovery, and left the hospital an average of one week after surgery. No complications could be attributed to the nonrestored blood loss after the vascular procedure. One of the patients who died sustained a sudden cardiac arrest eight days after mitral valve replacement which was performed the day after bilateral femoral embolectomy. This death was related to the open heart procedure rather than to the vascular operation. Immediate

postoperative values for hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit reading were within reasonable levels (11.0% and 33.5% respectively) in the 74-year-old patient who died from acute myocardial infarction two days after resection of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Whether myocardial infarction occurred as a chance event or was precipitated by a combination of surgical stress, generalized cardiovascular disease, and advanced age is unknown.

Since it is our policy to avoid the use of blood transfusion whenever possible in all operations, the patient who is a Jehovah's Witness does not really represent a special case; and we can comply with his demands without undue concern. We have found that blood transfusion is not a necessary accompaniment to vascular surgery, but indeed has certain disadvantages such as the risk of hepatitis. Thus, blood is used cautiously during and after operations in our institution, and patients who refuse to accept blood can usually undergo major operations without prohibitive risk and enjoy favorable postoperative results.

Chapter 5

# COMPLICATIONS OF BLOOD TRANSFUSIONS

By BEN J. WILSON

BEN J. WILSON is a Hoosier, educated at Indiana University and trained in surgery at Southwestern Medical School. Upon the resignation of his former teacher, Dr. Carl Moyer, he assumed the duties of Professor of Surgery and Chairman of the Department at Southwestern. In spite of his heavy administrative load, he has found time to carry out a fruitful program of research in the fields of electrolyte balance and shock.

A surgical procedure carries the risk of doing harm while intending to benefit; similarly the therapeutic procedure of transfusing whole blood may do harm—often only annoying harm—may sometimes induce a serious illness, and occasionally is fatal. Before blood is given, the chance of injury must be weighed in the same manner that one assesses operative risk. The complications of transfusion that one should consider in his assessment of risk will vary according to the urgency of need for blood. When the clinical circumstances do not demand that blood be given, the specter of transfusion complications looms greater than when the patient's survival depends upon his receiving blood.

If a transfusion is mandatory, then, by definition, one cannot consider the risks of the therapy, but simply must be prepared to look for complications so that their presence can be detected and treat-

ment, if any, can be begun. But knowing what the complications of transfusion are, and their relative frequency of occurrence, one may change his definition of states in which transfusion is mandatory.

The specific complications that attend the infusion of homologous blood are briefly described below relative to incidence of occurrence, cause, manifestations and management. At the end of the discussion of complications an attempt is made to quantitate the cumulative mortality occurring annually in the United States as a result of 4.5 to 5 million blood transfusions given to more than 2 million recipients. In view of the frightening revelation of transfusion morbidity, a short section has been added in which some commonly used indications for blood transfusion in surgical patients are critically examined.

# IMMEDIATE COMPLICATIONS INCIDENT TO PROPERTIES OF BLOOD

# HEMOLYTIC REACTION

A hemolytic transfusion reaction may be defined as the occurrence of an increased

rate of destruction of red cells of the donor or recipient as a consequence of blood transfusion. The antibodies producing hemolytic reaction may be natural (ABO)

or acquired (Kell, Duffy, Rh, Lewis, and many others), and the titer of the culpable isoantibodies which react with the red cell antigens determines in part the rate of red cell destruction that follows transfusion.

When hemolysis is relatively slow, there may be few manifestations, perhaps only jaundice. Alarming symptoms and signs usually attend rapid hemolysis in a conscious person; these are chills, fever, back pain, anxiety, tachypnea, occasionally with cyanosis, hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria. A bleeding tendency develops in about 30 per cent of persons with a hemolytic transfusion reaction, and peripheral vascular collapse sometimes attends major reactions. All symptoms are masked in the anesthetized patient even though incompatible blood has been given. A reaction may not be detected during an operation unless it is recognized that generalized bleeding or shock may be a manifestation of a transfusion reaction. Hemoglobinemia can be found immediately after a major hemolytic reaction to blood transfusion, but hyperbilirubinemia does not appear for three to six hours. Anemia tends to develop within several hours or days, but this finding cannot be used for immediate confirmation of diagnosis. About 80 to 90 per cent of persons who have had a hemolytic reaction will suffer renal insufficiency.¹⁸

The diagnosis of a hemolytic transfusion reaction consists in the demonstration of increased destruction of red cells. The increased destruction may proceed at rates detectable only by measuring a shortened life span of red cells. However, the more dangerous hemolytic reactions are attended by rapid rates of red cell breakdown and may be detected by obtaining a sample of venous blood from the patient and performing the following tests recommended by Mollison:¹²

(a) Observe the plasma for brown or

pink discoloration which indicates the presence of liberated hemoglobin in excess of 25 mg. per 100 ml. Concentrations less than this require that a colorimetric determination be used to quantitate the amount of free hemoglobin. All precautions to prevent hemolysis must be observed when obtaining the blood sample: viz., use a clean dry syringe and a large-bore needle (no. 18 or 20), remove the needle before transferring blood into the citrate test tube, avoid drying or clotting of blood on the sides of the syringe or tube, avoid vigorous agitation of the blood sample, but gently mix the blood with anticoagulant before centrifugation.

If the sample is obtained more than twelve hours after the transfusion, hemoglobinemia may not be present even though a hemolytic reaction did occur, since the free hemoglobin may have been cleared. Methemalbumin may still be present, however, and can be detected spectroscopically by Schumm's test.³ A positive test indicates that a hemolytic reaction has taken place.

(b) Serum bilirubin concentrations may have risen three to six hours after a hemolytic reaction so that the plasma is grossly icteric. If not, the van den Bergh test may reveal an increase in the indirect bilirubin.

(c) Repeat the typing procedures on the recipient and perform a direct Coombs test. This will probably be positive if more than 100 ml. of incompatible blood was given to the patient, if the donor's plasma contained an antibody or if a group O donor's plasma contained an antibody that destroyed the recipient's cells.

If a sample of donor blood can be obtained, repeat the typing procedures and cross-match, using the indirect antiglobulin test.

(d) Differential agglutinations to determine donor cell survival may be the only means of establishing whether a hemolytic

A sample of urine obtained by catheterization may reveal red or brown discoloration due to hemoglobinuria, but since hemoglobinuria may be slight and of short duration, it is often not detected. Hemosiderinuria is regularly found, provided the plasma hemoglobin concentration exceeds 25 mg. per 100 ml.⁴ Blue particles indicate a positive test when the resuspended sediment of centrifuged urine is mixed with an equal volume of 5 per cent hydrochloric acid and 0.5 ml. of 10 per cent potassium ferrocyanide in water.

Recipients who are particularly likely to have a hemolytic reaction are those who have had previous blood transfusions, parous women with a history of hemolytic disease of the baby, and patients with hemolytic anemia.

The frequency of occurrence of hemolytic reaction is estimated by DeGowin to be 1 to 5 per 1000 transfusions. Dameshek stated that at least 1 in 500 transfusions is followed by a reaction of incompatibility. The incidence increases as human error increases. Technicians who are infrequently engaged in typing and cross-matching procedures are more likely to make mistakes which lead to the transfusion of incompatible blood. Reactions are occasionally unrecognized, and reports of reactions are often incomplete. A national average of 5 hemolytic reactions per 1000 transfusions probably reflects more nearly the actual incidence of this dangerous complication than does Dameshek's estimate of 2 per 1000 which obtains in blood banks that are well supervised, where many safeguards are practiced and where data are kept to permit an accurate accounting of reaction rates. Based on an incidence of 5 per 1000 and on 4.5 million transfusions given in one year, the number of hemolytic reactions would be 13,500 annually. By using a reported mortality for hemolytic transfusion reactions of 50 per

cent, the estimated yearly toll is the loss of about 6750 lives from this one complication of whole blood transfusion.

Since definitive treatment for hemolytic transfusion reactions is not known, recognition of a reaction is of vital importance so that the transfusion can be stopped immediately. The most common fatal complication, renal damage, is roughly a function of the volume of incompatible blood received. Except in the unconscious or anesthetized person, most hemolytic reactions will be manifest during infusion of the first 50 to 100 ml. of blood. It is therefore possible to reduce the number of fatal transfusion reactions by withholding the infusion of whole blood during anesthesia and by careful observation of conscious patients while the first 50 to 100 ml. of blood is injected.

Other factors influence the severity of renal injury that follows hemolytic reactions; e.g. the state of water lack or of extracellular fluid deficiency will exaggerate the injury and contribute to the development of acute renal insufficiency. Intense renal vasoconstriction, high hematocrit level and low blood pressure are other factors that have been shown to adversely affect renal function and recovery from hemolytic states. The therapeutic corollary is that an infusion of glucose in water should be started after a hemolytic transfusion as soon as the blood is discontinued, provided a water deficit is thought to exist. If no water deficit is present, a balanced salt solution should be injected intravenously, since it will tend to alleviate hypovolemia, lessen the intensity of vasoconstriction and reduce the hematocrit level.

In most instances of refractory renal insufficiency observed by the author that have followed hemolytic transfusion reactions, blood had been given during the emergency situation to the exclusion of electrolyte solutions to combat an existing hypotension or hypovolemia. In these in-

It is likely that the incidence of acute renal insufficiency following hemolytic reactions will be reduced if water and salt deficits are promptly made up and if buffered sodium solutions are used to correct hypovolemia immediately after a hemolytic reaction. If there is no urine flow in response to water or saline infusion, treatment of the subsequent anuric phase is as discussed in Chapter 8.

There is some evidence to suggest that a renal protective effect might be gained by the use of a ganglionic or adrenergic blocking agent to alleviate the renal vasoconstriction. But the safety to the patient and efficacy of the treatment are not sufficiently established to warrant its clinical use.

High fever attending hemolytic transfusion reactions should be lowered by antipyretics and physical cooling measures. Dyspnea, especially when attended by cyanosis, requires intermittent positive pressure breathing with oxygen.

# ALLERGIC REACTIONS

The incidence of allergic reactions varies from 1 to 5 per cent. Urticaria is the usual manifestation and may present as a few discrete wheals which do not itch or as giant erythematous wheals with intense itching. Occasionally severe asthma may follow transfusion (one to two persons per thousand), and in other instances facial and laryngeal edema may cause serious respiratory distress. Some reactions, especially in recipients with a history of allergy, are extremely dangerous and are attended by hypotension, cyanosis, tachycardia, facial edema and bronchial asthma. Intravenous epinephrine must be given for severe reactions, while oral or parenteral antihistamines are usually effective for the less ominous symptoms. Although allergic reactions to transfused blood are a common cause of morbidity, deaths do not often

occur. In an atopic person, or one with pulmonary insufficiency or myocardial disease, an allergic reaction can be fatal.

The illness induced by a transfer of antibodies may not be apparent immediately after transfusion, but is manifested later when the recipient comes in contact with an antigen which corresponds to the transfused antibody. Thus a patient who has received a transfusion from a person who has an allergy to strawberries may suffer asthma or urticaria when he next eats strawberries, months after his transfusion. Blood donors should be carefully selected to exclude those with distinct allergies.

The immediate allergic responses occurring as a result of passive transfer of antigens can be reduced in incidence by the administration of Pyribenzamine or other antihistamines to the patient before the transfusion. This preventive measure is indicated in those patients who have previously shown allergy following transfusion.

# PYROGENIC REACTIONS

A slight elevation of body temperature (99 to 100° F.) may often be found during or after blood transfusion, but ordinarily the fever subsides within two or three hours. In about 2 per cent of all recipients the febrile reaction is more severe and is generally attended by a feeling of coldness or by a shaking chill. The onset of fever is often delayed for one to three hours after the transfusion has begun, especially when the blood is given slowly. The fever usually subsides within eight hours. Most reactions of this kind are due to polysaccharides of high molecular weight derived from bacteria. These pyrogenic substances apparently do not produce fever until they are metabolized in some way in the recipient; thus a lag between infusion and the development of fever is characteristic. Pyrogens are particularly apt to contaminate the citrate solution which is used as an anticoagulant in the collection and

storage of blood. Pyrogen can be demonstrated with fair accuracy by a standard technique using intravenous infusion of the questionable substance into rabbits. When the pyrogen test is negative, other mechanisms may be at fault.

Evidence has been presented by Crosby and by Dameshek which establishes the presence of donor plasma pyrogenic factors, and this phenomenon may contribute to the frequency with which febrile reactions attend the infusion of blood. Warming the patient before transfusion and giving the blood at a slow rate tend to reduce the incidence and height of febrile reactions.

Febrile transfusion reactions have also been shown to occur as a result of isoantibodies against donor white blood cells and against platelets. These reactions are similar in many respects to those caused by bacterial pyrogens, except that they tend to occur more frequently in patients who have received previous transfusions. Febrile reactions due to these factors (leukoagglutinin, platelet agglutinins, plasma antibodies) can be prevented by using only washed red cells. Removal of the buff coat after centrifuging the donor blood will eliminate reactions due to the presence of white blood cells and platelets.

Since both red blood cell incompatibility and contaminated blood cause fever, a differential diagnosis of the various etiologies must be attempted whenever fever occurs as the result of a transfusion (see Hemolytic Reaction). One usually considers the consequences of pyrogenic reaction to be evanescent and trivial after having eliminated incompatibility or bacterial contamination as a cause. This attitude is unwarranted, however, for the author has observed several fatal pyrogenic reactions. In these instances the rectal temperatures reached 106 to 109° F., and the skin was pale, cool and dry. Absence of sweating during hyperpyrexia is evidence that the febrile reaction was in fact heat stroke.

An elevation of temperature regularly

follows the intravenous infusion of pyrogen to animals even though a prior injection of antihistamine has been given, so that one should not expect to alleviate or prevent febrile reactions to transfusions with antihistamines. In fact, one study has shown that any febrile response that follows the injection of Pyribenzamine and transfusion will be 2 to 4° F. higher than if no antihistamine is given.

Mild temperature elevations should be treated with aspirin. When the fever is high or rapidly rising, physical methods of cooling must be used as well as antipyretics. For temperatures of 104° F. or higher that do not respond to antipyretics or to topical sponging and fanning, the patient should be placed on a hypothermia blanket, or surrounded with ice, until the body temperature falls to 101° F. or less. During hyperpyrexia an intravenous infusion of glucose in water will abet the attempt to lower body temperature and will replace rapid insensible losses of water. If the expiratory phase of respiration becomes prolonged or labored during the high fever, or if cyanosis is seen, oxygen should be administered with a tightly fitted face mask, using 15 to 18 cm. of water pressure in the inspiratory phase.

# BACTERIAL CONTAMINATION

The contamination of blood with bacteria is more common than is generally appreciated. In one blood bank of a university hospital, cultures were made from random bottles of banked blood, and over 2 per cent of the bottles yielded bacterial growth. Not all the bacteria were pathogens, but this unrecognized incidence of contaminated blood is disquieting, especially when bacteria can be found even when no violation of collection technique can be discovered. Further, bacterial growth may proceed when no faults in refrigeration have occurred, for certain strains of gram-negative bacilli grow well at 4 to 10° C.

which is the ordinary refrigerator temperature span. These cryophilic bacteria are virulent, and their intravenous infusion during blood transfusion is nearly always rapidly fatal to the recipient.

If a bottle of blood that is contaminated with the more common warm growing bacteria is left at room temperature for several hours, the rate of bacterial multiplication is logarithmic, and lethally infected blood results.

The bacteria found by Pittman in contaminated blood were all capable of using citrate. In some instances this property of the contaminants causes clotting of the blood; in others hemolysis may be apparent. There are recorded instances of fatal transfusions of blood contaminated with millions of organisms per milliliter, yet there was no gross change in the blood. One must conclude, then, that continuous refrigeration of blood and a normal appearance are not assurance that the blood is not infected.

The symptoms mimic those of endotoxin shock with peripheral vasodilatation, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension and fever. When any of these symptoms occurs, the transfusion should be discontinued and a sample of the donor blood examined by smear and Gram's stain for the presence of organisms. If the contamination is heavy and is likely to be fatal, the organisms will be apparent by a smear. If the contamination is light, a culture may have to be made to determine the presence of bacteria. If samples of donor blood are not available, the patient's blood should be cultured. If the infection is due to the coli-aerogenes group of bacteria, the culture will usually yield growth.

Hypovolemia has been demonstrated in septic shock and is attended by a rising hematocrit level so that treatment of the shock requires replacement of volume with balanced salt solution. Antibiotics should be given in large doses intravenously, but sustained large doses are probably not

helpful, since the bacteremia is of short duration. Many of the disastrous immediate effects of contaminated transfusions are due to the toxins infused rather than the bacteria. The use of hydrocortisone administered intravenously is probably helpful in recovery from shock caused by bacterial toxins. These measures alone may be effective treatment. Recovery from shock should not be determined by blood pressure alone, for frequently the hypotension persists for a while after treatment has effected a functional recovery. Evidences of functional circulatory recovery are mental lucidity, warm extremities, increased urine flow rate and filling of peripheral veins. Unless a total assessment of the patient is used to determine whether recovery has occurred, the tendency to boost a moderately low blood pressure by means of vasoconstrictor agents may lead to overtreatment and unnecessary complications of therapy.

### BLEEDING TENDENCY

After whole blood transfusions, especially of large volumes, the development of a bleeding tendency is often observed even though no incompatibility is demonstrated. Howland¹⁰ found a hemorrhagic tendency in 35 per cent of patients who received 10 pints of blood, or more, during operation. The possible causes for this phenomenon are discussed in Chapter 6; hence only a list of factors that have been found responsible for hemorrhagic diathesis following compatible blood transfusions is given: decreased platelets, platelet defect, lack of factors V and VII, increased fibrinolysin, circulating heparin-like substances, hypoprothrombinemia and hypofibrinogenemia. Specific treatment will depend upon which one, or more, of these several mechanisms is found to be at fault in a given instance. Frequently multiple clotting defects are discovered, or occasionally no specific factor can be demonstrated, and

in these instances, when blood loss becomes cumulatively significant, one must give empiric treatment. The infusion of whole blood freshly collected in plastic containers frequently helps to supply some of the depleted plasma clotting factors, as well as platelets. As long as additional red cells are needed, fresh whole blood may retard the bleeding tendency while supplying red cells. When whole blood infusions are not imperative, fresh plasma can be used. Platelet-rich infusions should be used if there are contraindications to additional expansion of the intravascular volume and the platelet deficiency persists. Protamine sulfate in doses of 50 to 100 mg. intravenously and vitamin K3 oxide may be used to help stanch a bleeding tendency. If the situation is desperate, or if hypofibrinogenemia has been found, intravenous fibrinogen may be used, but because of its narrow therapeutic range of activity, expense, risk of causing hepatitis and its occasional fibrinolytic activity it should not be used indiscriminately. Bleeding tendencies that follow compatible blood transfusions often spontaneously cease within forty-eight hours.

Prevention of the development of a bleeding tendency can most effectively be done by restricting the use of whole blood after traumatic blood loss and during surgical operations to the minimum volume required to treat peripheral vascular collapse, without attempting complete replenishment of red cell losses. Injection of balanced isotonic sodium solutions during operations and after trauma can safely and effectively reduce the quantity of whole blood required. By avoiding massive transfusion, bleeding diatheses due to transfusions can be largely prevented.

# PULMONARY CONGESTION NOT ATTENDED BY CIRCULATING VOLUME OVERLOAD

Transfusions of small quantities of blood occasionally are followed by the development of hemorrhagic pulmonary edema (also called congestive atelectasis). If the causative transfusion was given to a conscious person, it will usually have been attended by a febrile reaction. But hemorrhagic edema has followed transfusions given to anesthetized patients who demonstrated no reaction to the blood and in whom no renal insufficiency ensued. Although no red cell incompatibility has been demonstrated, no gross overload of circulation has been obvious and no indication that left ventricular congestive failure has occurred, the lungs have become stiff and gaseous exchange insufficient after whole blood transfusions. The clinical signs are increased rate of respiration, expiratory effort early, inspiratory effort later marked by interspace retraction, cyanosis unrelieved by oxygen, absence of moist rales, and minimal auscultatory findings early, but sibilant rales may be heard and signs of patchy consolidation may later appear. As the respiratory insufficiency becomes more prominent there is arterial hypotension with rising venous pressure. The clinical course and postmortem findings are those of primary pulmonary vascular obstruction with intense pulmonary congestion and loss of compliance.

In my experience with this entity, treatment (positive pressure oxygen, digitalis, phlebotomy, bronchodilators) has relieved temporarily some of the signs, but has done little to stop the progression of respiratory insufficiency to death.

# IMMEDIATE COMPLICATIONS INCIDENT TO THE METHOD OF TRANSFUSION

# AIR EMBOLISM

The true incidence of this disastrous complication is not known because a report of air embolism is tantamount to admission of negligence. Most of the fatal air embolic episodes occur as a result of hydraulic pressure infusions in which air is pumped into the donor bottle to hasten the rate of flow. If the infusion is not terminated when the bottle is empty and while blood is still in the outflow tube, several hundred cubic centimeters of air may enter the vein in a few seconds. The air entrance may be so rapid as to produce an audible sucking sound. The possibility of this complication can be eliminated by the use of one of several devices in which air pressure is applied to the column of blood through a collapsible but impermeable partition. Air embolism has followed a loose connection between tubing and needle when the venous pressure at the point of venipuncture is subatmospheric.

If one sees air bubbles in the tubing or detects air embolism by a sucking sound, or if the patient has an untoward reaction, the intravenous infusion should be immediately discontinued. The signs of air embolism are essentially those of mechanical blockage of the right side of the heart or pulmonary arteries. Gasping respiration followed by apnea, distended peripheral veins, arterial hypotension, cyanosis and splashing crunching noises coincident with the heart beat are signs which are unmistakably due to air embolism. The patient must be turned on his left side and the head tilted down as soon as the source of air entry has been eliminated. If the volume of air is small or has slowly entered the vein, this position may allow blood to flow through the right ventricular outflow tract around the air block. But if the mass of air trapped in the heart is large, the excessive myocardial stretch renders the

muscle incapable of contraction. If a large needle (no. 15) is inserted into the heart, decompression may be effected and heart beat may resume. In the event of cardiac arrest, however, a thoracotomy with direct visualization of the heart is preferable, since arrest may be due to air having gained entrance to the coronary arteries through a patent foramen ovale, the left side of the heart and coronary ostia. Decompression of the dilated left and right chambers with a large-bore needle must then be done before manual systole will be effective in restoring the heart beat.

# CIRCULATORY OVERLOAD

Even when transfusions are considered mandatory, the risk of producing circulatory overload exists, especially if chronic blood losses are completely or rapidly replaced. Transfusions of excessive volumes will not ordinarily cause congestive heart failure in a recipient who has a sound heart, but rather will cause a plethoric syndrome characterized by livid cyanosis, tachypnea, flushing of the face and neck, increased venous pressure, patchy atelectasis, elevated systolic pressure, wide pulse pressure, loud heart sounds, slapping aortic second sound, laterally displaced apical impulse and elevated hemoglobin concentrations.

The treatment of this state is removal of blood by phlebotomy until the signs of plethora are relieved. If a concomitant extracellular fluid volume deficiency exists, recovery is hastened by simultaneous infusion of sodium salts and intermittent phlebotomy.

Although congestive heart failure is difficult to produce by overtransfusion in healthy adults with no previous heart disease, it is easily precipitated by blood transfusions of moderate volumes in the elderly, the anemic, the debilitated or persons

In fact, transfusions of whole blood have in my experience more readily produced heart failure than noncolloid salt solutions when the latter were being used for circulating volume replacement of operative losses. Heart failure may often be manifest as a pulmonary congestive state accompanied by a feeling of chest constriction and dry cough without frank pulmonary edema and frothy sputum. The absence of moist bubbling rales and frothy sputum does not negate the diagnosis of pulmonary congestion incident to myocardial overload and does not eliminate this state as being dangerous, for fulminant pulmonary edema may appear many hours later. In addition, the congested lung is vulnerable to the development of atelectasis, and the collapsed segment is highly susceptible to infection. The postoperative development of atelectasis and pneumonitis is likely augmented by transient unrecognized pulmonary congestion frequently induced by blood transfusions given during operation and anesthesia.

The treatment of circulatory overload producing congestive heart failure consists in phlebotomy, semierect sitting position, digitalis and positive pressure oxygen breathing with bronchodilators in a nebulized wetting agent. Diuretics usually are not required in the treatment of acute blood overloads.

Some of the thrombotic postoperative complications such as venous thrombosis of legs and pelvis, coronary thrombosis and cerebral thrombosis are possibly related to the polycythemic state and the attendant increase in blood viscosity that commonly follows transfusions, especially those given during abdominal operations. An increase in postoperative hemoglobin concentration over the preoperative level was seen in about half of 100 consecutive patients during major gastric operations even though no blood transfusions were given and electrolyte solutions were infused. The propensity to hemoconcentration is in-

creased by the injection of whole blood. That a thrombotic tendency is present in persons with polycythemia is well known.

Decreased renal function may be another manifestation of relative red cell overload. Oliguria has been observed to follow operations and trauma for which whole blood was given to the exclusion of electrolyte solutions with resultant high hemoglobin concentrations. Urine flow was restored in some of these instances by phlebotomy if hypervolemia existed, and by infusions of salt solutions.

Many clinicians, 8, 13 regard circulatory overload as the most common cause of death from transfusion, although it often is not coded as the cause of death. Even more frequently, overloads are probably a contributory cause of death. If these estimates of incidence of overload are accurate, a conservative estimate of the number of deaths following transfusions in the United States each year as a result of circulatory overload would be at least equal to the number of deaths computed to be due to hemolytic transfusion reactions, namely, 6750.

### CARDIAC ARREST

Cardiac asystole, ventricular fibrillation and various other less disastrous disturbances of rhythm and conduction (bradycardia, partial heart block, T wave elevation, prolongation of Q-T interval) may attend massive whole blood transfusions. In Howland's series of 130 patients who received 10 pints, or more, of blood in the operating room and in whom adequate replacement had been effected, 17 per cent died of cardiac arrest or fibrillation.

Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest are thought to have been caused by hypothermia (90° F.) incident to transfusion of cold blood, citrate toxicity, decreased ionized calcium secondary to citrate excess, hyperkalemia and acidosis from old banked blood. Perhaps a combination of these factors with or without myocardial overload
