as a result of an acute transfusional hypervolemia is sufficient to induce cardiac arrest during anesthesia.

Since the precise causes are not known, treatment must consist essentially in prevention, by avoiding massive transfusions by means of supplemental injection of sodium solutions (glucose in lactated Ringer's). Stirman¹⁸ produced in dogs fatal hemorrhagic shock that was irreversible when the shed blood was returned or when extra quantities of whole blood were infused; but when injections of isotonic sodium solutions were made before return of the shed blood, most of the animals survived. This unique property of sodium solutions to modify fatal hemorrhagic shock is not generally appreciated, but is singularly valuable in the successful management of operative (and traumatic) hemorrhage.

When it is anticipated that large volumes of blood will be required, the blood that is used should not have been stored for more than one week, and as many pints as possible should have been recently collected in plastic containers using heparin as an anticoagulant rather than citrate solution. This precaution would appear to be especially important when liver dysfunction is present, since citrate metabolism is dependent on blood flow to the liver and intact liver functions. The blood should be warmed to room temperature before injection. If only citrated blood is available, calcium gluconate (about 1 gm. for each 3 units of whole blood infused) can be given intravenously to prevent severe ionic calcium deficiencies from developing.

By electrocardiographic monitoring dur-

ing replacement of large quantities of whole blood, the conduction and rhythm abnormalities may be detected and specifically treated before arrest. In the event of cardiac arrest or ventricular fibrillation the course of action and details of treatment are as given in Chapter 12.

### THROMBOPHLEBITIS

Although thrombophlebitis is a common complication following intravenous injections of irritant fluids, it is not usual for a single blood transfusion to result in venous thrombosis at the site of vein puncture. The duration of the transfusion influences the incidence of local infection, so that if more than one transfusion is given through the same venipuncture, the possibility of infection and of thrombosis increases. This complication can be serious, since most hospital-acquired infections at the site of skin punctures and venous cannulations are due to resistant staphylococci. Fatal septicemias have been observed as the result of infection following indwelling venous plastic catheters.

Rotation of the site of infusion after six to eight hours will probably prevent infections and thrombosis more effectively than any other measure. If a given needle puncture site shows early signs of inflammation, or becomes painful, the infusion should be discontinued at that area. If distinct inflammatory signs are present over a thrombosed vein and the patient shows evidence of systemic infection, the vein should be ligated proximal to the thrombosed segment to prevent septic embolization.

### LATE COMPLICATIONS

#### TRANSMISSION OF DISEASE

One of the most serious current problems of transfusion therapy is the transmis-

sion of serum hepatitis to the recipient. The incidence apparently is increasing, and at present there is no certain way to preclude the possibility of transmission.

Methods for eliminating the infectivity of whole blood have not been found. Careful donor selection is helpful in reducing the incidence of giving infected blood, but since there are no practical and reliable screening methods for detection of the asymptomatic carriers of hepatitis virus, selection is an inadequate preventive measure. About 1 in 150 persons is estimated to harbor hepatitis virus, and in some professional donor populations the incidence is even greater; e.g. at the University of Chicago Hospitals there was one case of hepatitis for every 127 pints transfused. Five per cent of whole blood recipients in Osaka, Japan, acquire serum hepatitis. Some metropolitan hospitals in the United States have reported 3 and 6 per cent incidences of hepatitis in patients given blood transfusions. The reported incidence varies from the actual frequency as a result of the long incubation period of the disease of 60 to 160 days, when many patients are lost to follow-up.

The mortality rate of serum hepatitis varies from 2 to 25 per cent. In Allen's series one death occurred in every 500 recipients. This does not include the persons with serum hepatitis who develop chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis and subsequently die of these complications.

If one assumes a national fatality rate which is equal to that reported by Allen, serum hepatitis following blood transfusion would then cause death in 5000 persons each year. If Hoxworth's data, taken from transfusion experiences in Cincinnati, are projected on a national basis, the annual deaths from hepatitis due to blood transfusion are about 1700. The difference in hepatitis attack rate between these two series of blood recipients is probably due to the predominance of professional paid donors in one group, while family and friends of the patients contributed blood in the series with the lower attack rate. The number of deaths each year in the

nation due to hepatitis from blood transfusions is assumed to be 3309, which figure is an average based on these 2 reports of hepatitis among recipients.

At present there is no effective prevention or cure of serum hepatitis, although large doses of anti-inflammatory steroids may shorten the course of illness. The only way by which death from serum hepatitis can be eliminated is to avoid transfusion.

Diseases other than serum hepatitis may be transferred from donor to recipient. Transmission of brucellosis has been reported, and in Mexico the incidence of positive agglutination titers for brucellosis among donors is so high as to limit the availability of blood.

An illness resembling influenza was reported by Beutler and Dern to have been transmitted by blood transfusions.

Syphilis can be transmitted, and routine serologic testing of the donors does not infallibly prevent the use of infected blood because one third of persons with primary syphilis are serologically negative. Storage at 4° C. is helpful in reducing the transmission of syphilis, for after 4 days infected blood is probably no longer capable of causing syphilis in the recipient. Fresh blood, or that which is stored only a short time, can transmit the disease unless the recipient is given penicillin. The incubation period is one to four months, and the first manifestations are those of secondary syphilis. A positive serologic test for syphilis can also be transmitted to the recipient even though viable spirochetes are not; this positive test does not persist for more than about three weeks.

Malaria may be transmitted by transfusion and usually has a short incubation period of four to twenty days. The malaria plasmodia remain viable in refrigerated blood, so that storage does not reduce infectivity. Prophylaxis is made more difficult by the fact that quartan parasites may remain viable in the blood of a person for

Examination of blood smears for presence of the parasites is not a practical method of eliminating the transmission of malaria because the plasmodia are too few to find. In endemic areas prophylactic administration of quinine and other antimalarial agents to recipients is necessary to reduce the transmission of malaria.

### ISOSENSITIZATION

Anyone having had a previous transfusion is regarded as a dangerous recipient. His chances of having a complication with another transfusion are augmented by the isosensitization that probably occurred incident to the earlier transfusion. Hemolytic disease of the newborn and some other acquired hemolytic anemias are other examples of the late consequences of previous whole blood transfusions.

Actually, about 14,000 transfusions are

given daily in this country. The number becomes greater each year, so that a progressively larger segment of our population is falling into the dangerous recipient class. This would indicate that transfusions will become more hazardous and that the complication rate will increase unless more discrimination is used by the medical profession when prescribing whole blood infusions.

### TRANSFUSIONAL SIDEROSIS

Many transfusions are required to produce deposits of excessive iron in bone marrow and reticuloendothelial cells all over the body. If iron is given over a long period of time, as few as twenty blood transfusions may cause hemosiderosis. Ordinarily, the persons showing histologic evidence of transfusional siderosis have received 100 transfusions. There is no effective treatment. Intercurrent exotic infections cause death of many victims of siderosis.

### CUMULATIVE MORTALITY FROM COMPLICATIONS OF BLOOD TRANSFUSIONS

The annual mortality from only 5 complications of blood transfusion (hemolytic reactions, overload and serum hepatitis) is computed to be 16,500. Although some assumptions used in arriving at this figure may be challenged, one cannot dispute the fact that there is tremendous loss of life and induced illness from this procedure, which is intended to be therapeutic. In terms of disability and loss of life the sequelae of blood transfusions rival some of our major public health problems. The computed annual death rate from blood transfusions exceeds that reported for many common surgical illnesses such as rectal cancer, appendicitis, diverticulitis,

duodenal ulcer, cholecystitis or intestinal obstruction.²⁹

One must certainly consider when he prescribes whole blood that an illness may be inflicted on his patient which is far worse than the retarded recovery which is assumed, but not proved, to attend failure to replace all preoperative red cell deficits and all operative blood losses.

Since certain complications are unavoidable after transfusion, one's only means of prevention of transfusion morbidity is to avoid transfusion. In order to make this decision wisely, the validity of the commonly used indications must be critically examined.

### PREOPERATIVE TRANSFUSIONS

#### SPECIFIC DANGERS OF BLOOD TRANSFUSION GIVEN FOR ANEMIA

Causes of anemia, other than blood loss, may be masked by the infusion of blood. Pernicious anemia, folic acid deficiency or other specific anemia may seriously complicate the postoperative course when not recognized and treated preoperatively.

The inherent risks of transfusion are augmented in the person with chronic anemia who has received multiple transfusions in the past and in whom isosensitization likely has occurred, for additional transfusions may induce or precipitate an acquired hemolytic state.

Blood transfusions have a depressant effect on the bone marrow, and the resultant decrease in erythropoiesis may restrict the patient's ability to spontaneously restore red cell losses that occur during operation.

An increased circulating blood volume frequently attends chronic anemia as a result of plasma overexpansion. Whole blood transfusions are therefore likely to produce overload phenomena, since the total blood volume must necessarily be overcorrected in order that the hemoglobin mass be restored to normal. If the recipient cannot

regulate this overload by rapid extrusion of plasma from the vascular tree, some form of circulatory failure will ensue. The ability to extrude plasma is impaired in patients with chronic anemia.

Respiratory inefficiency, as measured by vital capacity, pulmonary compliance and oxygen consumption rates, attends rapid correction of chronic anemia by transfusion of whole blood or packed red cells.¹

#### LACK OF NEED FOR WHOLE BLOOD TRANSFUSION IN SOME PATIENTS WITH ANEMIA

Physiologic adjustments by plasma volume expansion, increased cardiac output and more efficient gaseous exchange frequently permit the patient with anemia to perform work without undue fatigue¹¹ and to undergo operation without untoward incident.¹²

Prior blood transfusions have been shown not to prevent shock or lessen mortality from subsequent hemorrhage if the animal was normovolemic, even though moderately anemic, before the transfusion.¹⁷

### TRANSFUSIONS DURING OPERATION

#### HEMORRHAGE WITHOUT SHOCK

This is not an urgent indication for blood replacement, provided there are no physiologic manifestations of hypovolemia and subsequent hemorrhage is not anticipated. When blood replacement is made for losses of less than 500 ml., one has taken the untenable position of recommending transfusion for blood losses of smaller volume than that lost by the donor, who was capable of walking out of the hospital after his contribution.

A direct relation exists between the volume of incompatible blood received and

mortality.¹⁴ The early subjective complaints that accompany hemolytic and other transfusion reactions cannot be sounded during general anesthesia in time to prevent administration of large, probably lethal, quantities of faulty blood. One should be particularly reluctant to give blood during the anesthetized state unless the need for it is urgent.

One other untoward reaction of blood transfusion during anesthesia is development of pulmonary stiffening and vascular engorgement if an episode of hypercapnia, hypoxia or asphyxia precedes the transfusion.²⁹ Since imperfect gaseous exchange

Electrolyte solutions have been regularly used on my surgical service during operations and general anesthesia and have been effective in obviating the risks of elective blood transfusions. The postoperative complications (pulmonary, wound, anastomotic) have actually been less as a result of this policy.21 The expected postoperative decrease in urine output which is supposed to be a manifestation of endocrine response to injury did not occur in those patients who received adequate electrolyte solutions during operation. Recently Randall has demonstrated that sodium retention need not attend major operations, provided operative losses of sodium salts are replaced.

### HYPOTENSION WITHOUT DECREASED BLOOD VOLUME

The elevation of blood pressure that follows blood transfusion in this hypotensive state is obtained at the dear price of overloading the intravascular volume and of masking the true cause of the hypotension

(e.g. bacteremia, mesenteric tug reflex, deep anesthesia, hyperthermia, and the like). Thus correction of hypotension by stuffing the patient with blood can deceptively indicate improvement instead of jeopardy during reflex, vasoparalytic, cardiogenic and other forms of normovolemic shock.

### SHOCK WITH REDUCED BLOOD VOLUME DUE TO PLASMA AND EXTRACELLULAR FLUID LOSSES

The empiric use of whole blood to elevate the blood pressure in shock states due to extracellular fluid volume depletion (intestinal obstruction, diarrhea, peritonitis, vomiting, and so on) is without rational basis and is not attended by functional recovery despite improvement in blood pressure.

Renal function did not recover even though whole blood transfusion successfully restored blood pressure in dogs suffering from shock due to extracellular fluid removal by peritoneal dialysis, but when this hypotensive shock state was treated with lactated Ringer's solution, glomerular filtration rate, urine flow and blood urea nitrogen all returned to normal.18

### POSTOPERATIVE TRANSFUSIONS

#### BLOOD LOSS ANEMIA

The effectiveness and safety of oral or parenteral iron therapy for blood loss anemia make blood transfusion a dangerous alternative that need not often be used in the postoperative period when the fear of additional blood loss is past.

#### WHOLE BLOOD TRANSFUSIONS FOR NUTRIMENT

Intravenous whole blood is an incomplete food and a grossly inefficient method

of feeding, since there is a slow and questionable entry of globin and plasma protein into the protein metabolic pool. Moreover, this method of feeding is expensive and dangerous. One may lose more calories by the febrile reaction attending transfusion than he gains by the calorie equivalent in the blood.

There is little critical evidence to support the use of whole blood as a source of antibodies to confer passive immunity or

# Transfusion Reactions

ORTHO DIAGNOSTIC REPORTER

Vol. 6, No. 1, 1971

"...because of the inherent dangers which can be reduced but not abolished, transfusion should be prescribed only when there is a justifiable indication..." The attending physician should recognize that he subjects his patient to a potential hazard each time he prescribes a blood transfusion.¹

Blood transfusion has become so commonplace in modern medical practice that the magnitude of its contribution to headline-making surgical advances and to the improved outcome of a great variety of medical diseases is often unappreciated. The hazards of blood transfusion are commonly underestimated—if considered at all. In order to practice rational hemotherapy, which necessitates weighing the possibility of injury against the anticipated benefit, the risks of blood transfusion must be clearly comprehended. In addition, awareness of the diversity of transfusion reactions contributes to the early recognition of their occurrence—one of the most important means of treating them successfully and of preventing their most serious consequences.

# "Toxicity" of Blood Transfusion

Approximately five to six million units of blood are transfused in the United States each year, and conservative estimates suggest that two or three percent of all transfusions are accompanied by some sort of adverse effect. Transfusion therapy is distinguished by the combination of frequent usage and a high reaction rate. However, the wide variation in reported reaction rates (from 10 percent to less than 0.2 percent) suggests that two uncertainties lurk behind the figures and their interpretation: First, what actually constitutes a transfusion reaction? And, secondly, how accurate is the detection and reporting of such reactions?¹,⁸,⁹,¹⁰

It is obvious that disinterest and conscious suppression of information invalidate the reported rate, but equally as important is the fact that physicians, nurses, and laboratory personnel are unfamiliar with the wide variety and diverse manifestations of transfusion reactions. Most of the symptoms of transfusion reactions are nonspecific, and in the critically ill patient, influenced by drugs, anesthesia, and complicating infections, it may be impossible to clearly delineate the role of transfusion in the causation of chills, fever, shock, or jaundice.⁷,⁸

# Transfusion Hazards Not Strictly "Reactions"

Broadly defined, a transfusion reaction is any unfavorable effect which occurs as a direct consequence of the transfusion of donor blood (whole or as components) into a recipient. However, a number of transfusion-induced ill effects are conventionally excluded in the narrower clinical usage of the term transfusion reaction, in part at least because their occurrence is relatively remote in time from the administration of the blood transfusion. Among these are the risks of:

(1) isosensitization of the recipient to antigens of erythrocytes (eventuating in transfusion incompatibility or hemolytic disease of the newborn), leukocytes, platelets, or plasma proteins (leading to febrile or allergic reactions with subsequent transfusions, or even to histo-incompatibility);

(2) transmission of disease, historically syphilis, but today preeminently viral hepatitis, and—resurgently—malaria;

(3) transfusion hemosiderosis, or the deposition of excess amounts of iron in the tissues which may ultimately develop in the chronically anemic patient receiving a great many transfusions over a period of months or years; and

(4) the special complications attendant upon massive transfusion (e.g., in excess of 5,000 ml to an adult recipient within 12 hours) which include citrate toxicity, acidosis, hypothermia, hyperkalemia, and a hemorrhagic diathesis.¹,³,⁸,¹¹

# Transfusion Reactions Proper

In its restricted application, the term transfusion reaction refers to an untoward or unanticipated response to the administration of blood. Reactions are manifold in causation and symptomatology. Transfusion reactions per se comprise five principal etiologic categories: (1) allergic reactions, (2) febrile reactions, (3) circulatory complications, (4) bacterial contamination reactions, and (5) hemolytic transfusion reactions. All transfusion reactions are expressed as any one or various combinations of a constellation of signs and symptoms which include headache; chills; changes in body temperature; apprehension; dyspnea; nausea; vomiting; tachycardia; alterations in blood pressure; cyanosis; itching; urticaria; abdominal, back, or chest pain; jaundice; discolored urine; hemorrhage; and others. It must be emphasized that early recognition of transfusion reactions is paramount in prevention of serious compli-

### Allergic Reactions

Though seldom serious, allergic reactions, in the form of skin rashes and itching are comparatively common, occurring in approximately one percent of all transfusions. Severe and life-threatening allergic reactions, such as laryngeal edema and anaphylaxis, are fortunately rare. Allergic transfusion reactions reflect an abnormality in the recipient rather than in the donor blood, and are prone to develop in individuals with histories of allergy and in those patients who have

previously experienced allergic transfusion reactions. The specific incitant is rarely identifiable, and it may be either a normal constituent of donor plasma or an incidentally present environmental allergen.2,6,13

### "Nonspecific" Febrile Reactions

A slight rise in body temperature is probably the most common form of transfusion reaction, particularly among multiply-transfused recipients. In a more severe reaction, the fever may reach 102° to 104° F, and may be accompanied by chills. Many of these reactions formerly resulted from the inadvertent administration of pyrogenic products of bacterial growth present in imperfectly cleaned, re-used transfusion equipment. With the introduction of disposable intravenous apparatus, this source has been largely eliminated although the "nonspecific" febrile response to transfusion continues to occur with some frequency.2,6,8,9,14

At least some febrile reactions are related to isosensitization of the recipient (via previous transfusion or pregnancy) to the leukocytes and platelets of the infused blood. A characteristic reaction complex has been noted in transfused individuals possessing strong leukoagglutinins, consisting of flushing and tachycardia, followed by a latent period, and then transient hypertension, severe rigor, and prostration. Development of these symptoms in susceptible patients can be avoided by removal of the offending cells of the "buffy coat" from the transfusion unit. Rare reactions based on isosensitization to donor plasma proteins have also been described, but a large proportion of the febrile reactions observed on any transfusion service presently defy explanation. Since fever accompanying transfusion may be a manifestation of more dangerous forms of transfusion reaction, it should be clear that the diagnosis of a "nonspecific" febrile reaction is a diagnosis by exclusion.2,3,8,9,15

### Circulatory Complications

Blood transfusions given too rapidly or in great quantity may precipitate heart failure and pulmonary edema, the so-called "circulatory overload" reaction. This complication usually occurs in the elderly, the very young, and in patients with pulmonary or cardiac diseases, but acute left-sided cardiac failure during transfusion also develops readily in profoundly anemic patients. Circulatory overloading is largely preventable by the substitution of packed red cells for whole blood in routine

Air embolism constitutes a real circulatory hazard when blood is rapidly administered under positive pressure from rigid containers. The replacement of glass bottles by compressible plastic blood bags has lessened the likelihood of this rare transfusion danger. However, it is still possible to introduce air into the recipient's circulation when starting a transfusion, and thereafter when the infusion tubing is changed, or as a result of a leaking adapter connection, or a needle hole in the line (while negative pressure exists in the cannulated vein).9,13

# Bacterial Contamination Reactions

Transfusion of banked blood contaminated by endotoxin-producing bacteria may give rise to a medical catastrophe. The unusual transfusion reaction due to grossly infected blood is characterized by immediate onset of profound shock accompanied by flushing and a warm dry skin—the remarkable "red shock" syndrome. This condition, actually an intense endotoxinemia, is associated with a mortality rate of over 50 percent even when recognized promptly and treated vigorously. The bacteria responsible for this extremely grave situation may gain access to the blood unit at the time of donation despite "adequate" antiseptic skin preparation, or may be contaminants of the equipment and container used for collection, or may be introduced by improper handling of the blood unit prior to or during transfusion. Entry into the blood container prior to transfusion probably represents the greatest risk, and this fact is responsible for the "24-hour limitation" imposed on

the preparation of blood components in a nonclosed system.1,2,9,13,14

# Hemolytic Transfusion Reactions

In its classic acute form, resulting from the transfusion of incompatible blood, the hemolytic transfusion reaction is the most feared complication of blood transfusion. Since actual hemolysis is prominent in some transfusion reactions, but transitory, inapparent, or absent in others, current views of the hemolytic reaction stress the concept of red cell survival. Thus, a hemolytic transfusion reaction is defined as the occurrence of signs of accelerated red cell destruction following transfusion.2,4,9,11

Ordinarily, the phrase "hemolytic transfusion reaction" connotes immunologically mediated red cell destruction, but other causes for hemoglobinemia in the course of blood transfusion are possible. One of these is gross contamination of donor blood by bacteria, as previously described. Other causes of nonimmunologic transfusion hemolysis include: (1) the transfusion of poorly preserved (overheated or previously frozen) blood, or of blood which is "outdated"; (2) the administration of blood under pressure through a fine gauge needle, or the use of certain types of pump-oxygenators in cardiac surgery, which lead to mechanical rupture of the red cells; (3) the transfusion of blood damaged by contact with glucose solutions; and (4) the introduction of medications which may directly lyse donor cells into the blood container.11,13

The true hemolytic transfusion reaction, caused by the in vivo combination of antibody with red cells possessing the corresponding antigen, logically can and does occur with several variations of donor-recipient pairing. Most frequently, the antibody is in the recipient's plasma and the susceptible red cells are those of the donor ("major" incompatibility). Conversely, antibody in donor plasma may adversely affect either the recipient's red cells ("minor" incompatibility), or other donor red cells concurrently transfused to the same patient ("interdonor" incompatibility). Severe hemolytic reactions are most likely when the antibody involved is that of the recipient, since transfused incompatible cells are exposed to a vast quantity of available antibody upon entering the circulation. In each of the other situations, the passively transferred antibody is diluted by the recipient's plasma volume. However, when the transfused antibody is high-titered or endowed with un

# Mechanisms of Hemolysis

The symptoms of the hemolytic transfusion reaction depend largely upon the manner in which the red cells are destroyed. Two mechanisms of in vivo red cell destruction by antibodies are recognized, namely intravascular and extravascular. Intravascular destruction involves the rupture of red cells within the bloodstream, resulting in the release of free hemoglobin into the plasma. It occurs rapidly and dramatically, and leads to more serious clinical consequences. Extravascular destruction is slower and occurs primarily in the liver and spleen through a process of trapping and subsequent breakdown of the antibody-coated red cells by sinusoidal reticuloendothelial cells. Extravascular destruction of red cells leads to elevation of plasma bilirubin concentration, but not to the liberation of hemoglobin. However, the two general mechanisms of red cell destruction are not sharply separated. Certain antibodies (such as anti-Rh), while primarily destroying red cells extravascularly, frequently cause sufficiently rapid cell destruction to produce hemoglobinemia—considered the hallmark of the intravascular mechanism.2,7,11,13

# Relationship of Serology to Pathophysiology

Some correlations have been established between the in vitro serologic properties of the red cell antibodies and their patterns of behavior in vivo. Complement-fixing antibodies which produce hemolysis in the test tube, such as anti-A and anti-B, cause rapid intravascular destruction of incompatible red cells. Incomplete (IgG) antibodies in general cause red cell destruction by the extravascular mechanism, and the coated red cells are cleared from the circulation predominantly in the spleen. If the antibodies are particularly potent and the rate of red cell destruction rapid, the liver plays a more prominent role in the sequestration process. Incomplete antibodies that bind complement bring about far more rapid clearance of incompatible cells than those that do not.2,3,7,11,13,17,18

Acute intravascular hemolytic reactions may begin with the first few milliliters of blood transfused, and are characterized by prompt appearance of hemoglobin in the plasma. Hemolysis of as little as 5 to 10 ml of incompatible blood will result in plasma hemoglobin

levels of 25 to 50 mg/100 ml and impart a pink color to the sample in hand. The hemoglobin released into the plasma is bound to a specific plasma protein, haptoglobin, and in the form of a haptoglobin-hemoglobin complex is removed from the circulation within a few hours by the reticuloendothelial system. If the binding capacity of plasma haptoglobin is exceeded (approximately 100 mg/100 ml hemoglobin), free hemoglobin begins to circulate in the plasma. Part of the circulating free hemoglobin is degraded to heme, which combines with albumin to form the brown pigment, methemalbumin. The latter can be detected in the plasma within 4 to 10 hours after in vivo hemolysis, and it persists for

The extent of the investigation and the sequence of procedures used will vary depending on the circumstances of the reaction and the facilities available. Cultural Varieties of Incompatible Red Cell Reactions

Transfusion of incompatible red cells can result in several patterns of transfusion reaction, each occurring at a characteristic time interval following transfusion. First among these, by virtue of its immediacy and gravity, is the frank acute hemolytic reaction wherein potent preformed antibodies cause intravascular destruction of red cells. The associated clinical picture consists of hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria, shock, oliguria progressing to anuria, occasionally a coagulation defect with generalized bleeding, and possibly death in renal failure. The second form of transfusion reaction, the anamnestic response, is delayed extravascular hemolysis developing three to ten days after transfusion as a result of secondary antigenic stimulation of antibodies which were initially latent. The clinical manifestations of jaundice and anemia reflect a mild form of hemolytic anemia. The third pattern of transfusion reaction is, in reality, an interpretative view of a puzzling observation, i.e., the occasional late (three to five weeks post-transfusion) abrupt onset of accelerated disappearance of donor cells in the absence of demonstrable antibody. It is thought that this type of red cell survival curve ("collapse curve") represents evidence of primary immunization to foreign red cell antigens.3,11,10,18,19

Laboratory Differential Diagnosis of Transfusion Reactions

Difficulties in the clinical diagnosis of the various forms of transfusion reactions stem from the fact that there is no sign or symptom, or group of signs or symptoms that is pathognomonic of a transfusion reaction, hemolytic or otherwise. As a result, all reported transfusion reactions must have laboratory studies, at least to rule out the possibility of blood group incompatibility, if not to conclusively establish the etiology of the reaction. For the purposes of the rapid recognition of the life-threatening form of acute hemolytic reaction, two tests deserve the highest priority: inspection of the post-reaction sample for hemoglobinemia, and performance of the direct antiglobulin test on the same sample. These two tests, if positive, provide direct evidence of red cell incompatibility.1,2,6,11,16

Conclusion

Blood transfusion continues to involve certain potential hazards. The point has been made that even if a donor in a planned autotransfusion receives back his own blood, he is still subject to many of the risks of transfusion. Only careful adherence to acceptable processing techniques and continual vigilance on the part of all personnel involved in blood transfusions can reduce the hazards to a minimum and ensure recipients the full benefits possible through transfusion therapy. In view of the risks cited, indications for transfusions must be critically evaluated. It is well to remember the rule that "lack of a clear-cut indication for a transfusion in itself constitutes a contraindication."3,20

# CHICAGO SURGICAL SOCIETY

Transfusion Reaction: A Reappraisal of Surgical Incidence and Significance.

Robert J. Baker, M.D., Sigfred L. Moinichen, M.D., and Lloyd M. Nyhus, M.D.

Although transfusion of blood and blood components in various clinical situations is a life-saving procedure, reactions to the infusion are common, reportedly in 3-6% of recipients. Recognition of these reactions is obviously important, as timely and appropriate treatment may prevent disastrous consequences or gross overtreatment.

A review of approximately 116,000 transfusions administered to 42,000 recipients during a six-year period (1961 to 1967) was undertaken, in order to delineate the significant signs and therapeutic principles in transfusion reaction, especially on

# CHICAGO SURGICAL SOCIETY

215

surgical services. The overall incidence of significant reactions within 24 hours of infusion was 2.21% of the units administered, manifested in 5.42% of recipients.

Analysis of the reactions in 2,281 recipients showed the following groups and distribution:

- (a) Allergic 45.6%
- (b) Febrile 43.5%
- (c) Hemolytic 9.9%
- (d) Miscellaneous 1.0%

The group of hemolytic reactions included six observed instances of unexpected diffuse bleeding encountered in anesthetized patients during the operation. Immunochemical investigation of donor and recipient bloods demonstrated verifiable incompatibility in only one patient. Overall, 64% of observed hemolytic reactions were not definable by currently available testing techniques, either before or after transfusion. The mechanisms apparently operative in these, and a scheme for modification or prevention of such reactions, were presented.

Immediate transfusion reactions were defined, their clinical characteristics detailed, and the rationale for specific treatment outlined. As the use of whole blood and blood products containing red cells increases, keeping pace with the increasing complexity of surgical procedures, a greater awareness on the part of all surgeons of the nature of these reactions and their management becomes correspondingly more important.

# On The Legislative Scene

A bill dropped into the House hopper by Representative Victor Veysey, Republican from California, would establish a national Blood Bank Program run by the Department of Health, Education and Welfare (HEW).

Charles Percy, Illinois Republican, and Vance Hartke, Indiana Democrat, have introduced a companion bill to Veysey's in the Senate.

# Blood: A Service or a Product?

The point of law in question is whether blood is a service or a product. Legally, a product is subject to warranty, in that its producer guarantees its quality. A service is not. So blood is declared a service for the purposes of those who manufacture this "service." Therefore, there has been a scramble by the legislatures of all states to pass laws in which transfusions are declared a service, from donor to patient, except for Illinois.

It does not seem fair that the doctor, the hospital and the blood bank should be protected against the risk of transfusion hepatitis and the patient not be. Ironically, the present laws are directed against the health of 100 percent of our population and against the financial interests of 98 percent of their constituents—those not engaged in the service of blood transfusion.

Whether a transfusion represents a product, a service or a combination of both is irrelevant to the patient if he contracts transfusion hepatitis. He may be mildly ill, moderately ill, severely ill, or he may die.

Once protective legislation (declaring blood to be a service) has been passed, there is no stimulus for the physician, the hospital or the blood bank to improve the quality of blood. They need only maintain the status quo. Although the patient has been subjected to 10 or more times the risk rate of contracting serum hepatitis from com-

mercial blood than if only volunteer blood is used, by law the blood bankers are saying that all blood carries equal risk. Medically, physicians know this is not true.

The patient has no choice as to whether he receives blood from a commercial high-risk donor population or a low-risk volunteer population. Even if the patient brings in volunteer donors in advance of his need, there is no guarantee that this responsible act will receive any consideration when he is transfused, even though his donors are of his own type. In no state do the laws require that blood banks are obligated to provide such patients with blood from volunteer sources in return for the patient's effort and foresight.

A California law does nothing to encourage blood banks, hospitals and physicians to improve the quality of blood they are now using. Backing similar legislation in Illinois are the American National Red Cross, the American Association of Blood Banks, the State Medical Society, the State Hospital Association, the Midwest Chapter of the National Hemophilia Foundation, and a variety of lesser medical or paramedical organizations. Why not in California, too?

Better they unite to form a vigorous national all-volunteer program, producing blood and its products that are uniform in excellence, and then labelling it as unpurchased.

### Informed Consent and Strict Tort Liability

Informed consent has no medical value in the case of transfusion hepatitis for several reasons. It is impossible for the lay patient to be informed adequately of the risk of hepatitis that transfusion may carry; and, it is unreasonable to expect him to understand the full range of complications of hepatitis. Furthermore, the patient may be under anesthesia before the decision is made to give him a transfusion, or he may be brought into the hospital unconscious and in urgent need of blood. With these acknowledged deficits, one nonetheless should carry out the charade of informed consent. But it would be much simpler for the patient's doctor to know the source of the blood before he gives it. He needs to balance risks against gains in making this decision. Without this knowledge, he cannot.

The strict tort liability theory assumes that there is a certain liability inherent in the cost of doing business. When there are so many at risk for transfusion hepatitis, why should not all share in the costs of the few who contract the disease? In our everyday life we have solved similar problems by suitable procedures, which also involve services that can be lifesaving. For example, we do not, as individuals, pay each time we use the Fire Department or the Police Department. Taxation insures that a person will not be charged for the service of putting out a fire in his home. In our community, the average cost of a fire call is \$2,900. These costs are shared by all and, as citizens, we are happiest when we have not had to use these ser-

vices. Why not also "tax" for unavoidable accidents in Medicine?

### Financing Tort Liability

About thirty thousand cases of post-transfusion hepatitis occur each year, according to the estimates of the National Research Council and the American National Red Cross. This is a reasonable guess. Further, they estimate that if an all-volunteer program were used, only about 3,000 cases would occur.

(Editor's Note—However, some authorities have reported that nobody really knows just how high the rate is. The Government's Center for Disease Control (CDC) in Atlanta says, "Because physicians often fail to report serum-hepatitis cases, the real hepatitis rate could be two to ten times Dr. Allen's estimate (or 35,000 deaths and 500,000 illnesses a year instead of 3500 deaths and 50,000 illnesses).")

However, Dr. Allen told "Inspection News," "This is no longer true.

"Last year, about 2,900,000 patients were transfused with a mean of 3.4 units of blood. 1.06% of these patients developed icteric serum hepatitis, an incidence rate of 304,000 (3.4 mean units of blood) or about 89,300 cases for each single transfusion. I have assumed that I might be wrong and have arbitrarily cut this figure to 1.3 or 30,000.

"Surely this is an unrealistically low figure. We assume that the 11,627 patients who received blood in our study received one unit of volunteer blood and we calculate from the least. Still, there were 0.3% of icteric cases here (if they were all volunteer blood), or 42,007 x .003, or 126,021 — 64 less than found. Do the same for 8,500,000 single units of blood given to 8,500,000 patients x .003 for a figure

### Borrowing Blood

Dr. Allen told Inspection News, "Patients who 'borrow' blood from hospital banks, replacing it with volunteer blood donated by friends, frequently receive 'high-risk' commercial blood with neither the patient nor his physician knowing it. Only when all blood becomes volunteer can the patient be guaranteed that the blood he receives is from a volunteer donor."

"Yes, I can show that 30,000 is unusually low."

This too is probably correct, assuming that doctors use blood more conservatively than at present. If each of the 3,000 patients who develop post-transfusion hepatitis were awarded an average of $20,000 each, the national total would be $60,000,000. This may be more than most blood banks make in profit.

But the strict tort liability theory could help enormously to improve our national blood program, if it were properly used. Costs of $60,000,000 per year could be readily met if you added $1.00 per year per person to each of the hospital insurance policies covering the 180,000,000 people currently insured.

This would create a large nest egg of \$186,000,000 per year, or about three times what is needed to get started. Later, these charges could be reduced according to experience.

A scheme such as this could cover other unavoidable medical accidents, and these considerations are not far away. Since the patient will already have paid his part, the cost of the doctor, hospital and blood bank should not be permitted to be passed on to the patient.

This plan seems a more reasonable approach than to introduce legislative methods that are designed to protect the selective interests of only 2 percent of our total population who one day may also need blood.

# Blood That Kills

By August Gribbin

AS HOWARD SCHMID prepared to undergo surgery, neither he nor his wife saw reason to worry about his necessary but uncomplicated blood transfusion. They didn't know that many U.S. hospitals routinely use "cheap," possibly contaminated blood from skid-row addicts and bums—blood that can make a simple transfusion riskier than the most delicate surgery.

Like most Americans, the LaGrange, Ill., couple also didn't know that most authorities agree that a national blood program could solve the problem, but that the organizations judged most qualified to act one up oppose this solution. So blood transfusions now kill at least 3,500 Americans and medically injure another 50,000 each year, says Stanford University's Dr. J. Garrett Allen, whom many researchers regard as the nation's leading expert on the blood problem.

Of every 150 patients over 40 years old who receive blood transfusions, one dies, Dr. Allen estimates. Howard Schmid, age 52, didn't know that either.

### The Hepatitis Menace

Schmid's heart operation in a Chicago hospital went "beautifully," says Mrs. Schmid. "My husband came home. He was feeling better than he had in years. Out walking and everything. Planning to go back to work."

Three months later Schmid awoke one morning with yellow skin and a 102-degree temperature. "We took him to the hospital. And—he died," says Mrs. Schmid. The cause of death: serum hepatitis from contaminated blood.

Serum hepatitis is one of two main forms of a group of liver infections generically called hepatitis. The other main type is infectious hepatitis. The diseases' symptoms are roughly the same; so are their treatments. But infectious hepatitis, nicknamed "dirt disease," comes primarily from contaminated food and water and shows up most often amid crowding, poor sanitation, and malnutrition.

Serum hepatitis, for more serious, comes principally from injecting or transfusing tainted blood. The blood of persons who have had infectious hepatitis, and their uninfected regular associates' blood, is especially suspect. The malady inflames the victim's liver, causing extreme pain, itching, weakness, diarrhea, nausea, fever, and yellowing of the skin.

Researchers haven't isolated the ultimate sources of serum hepatitis. They do know that its infectious agents flourish in the dirt and squalor of city slums and skid rows. And that's just where many commercial blood banks have set up blood-collection stations.

There commercial blood-bank operators are within easy reach of down-and-out donors and drug addicts who sell their blood for $3 to $5 per pint. Outside of skid-row sections, donors normally get $15 to $20 a pint for common types of blood. Rarer types bring $50, $60, or more.

### Danger Is Imported Too

The skid-row banks sell common types of blood to hospitals and to other banks for $40 to $50 a pint. One industry source says they net 100 per cent profit after processing and other costs.

The commercial banks also get such "cheap blood" from prisoners. Like addicts, prisoners frequently lie about past illnesses so they can earn a few dollars or special privileges for giving blood.

Some commercial banks also import blood from such willing sources as impoverished, medically backward Haiti. They extract and sell this blood's highly marketable plasma—which also can cause serum hepatitis.

### Everywhere the Dollar

Certainly not all commercial suppliers depend on convicts and derelicts as sources of blood. Many suppliers take extreme care in hiring "donors," who often are robust but cash-shy soldiers and college youths. And of course a tiny percentage of the blood from presumably healthy donors may contain hepatitis.

Richard Dice, president of the reputable, commercial Community Blood Services of Alabama, abhors the questionable practices of what he calls "relatively few blood bankers." Commercial banks vary in quality from place to assets, adding: "If you really dissect blood donating in this country, you'll find that the dollar is involved everywhere. The Red Cross levies fees for the blood it distributes to hospitals; nonprofit banks charge fees. Both have blood-replacement plans."

Under such plans, banks solicit blood from unpaid volunteers by promising them free blood should they ever need it. Some hospitals, which

frequently have their own blood banks, and some nonprofit banks "lend" blood, requiring the user to solicit replacement blood from acquaintances.

# Not All Blood Is Equal

Dice says the difference between the banks is not whether they are commercial or nonprofit, but how conscientiously they operate. Many of his colleagues agree wholeheartedly.

Doctors nonetheless make a huge distinction between "commercial blood," whose donors receive payment, and "volunteer blood," whose donors generally receive no cash. The difference can get fussy, because many noncommercial banks pay volunteers for their blood, calling the payment an "incentive." Blood obtained from "incentive"-paid donors sometimes is called volunteer blood.

Unpaid contributors' blood is generally considered much safer than that of paid donors. The promise of pay allegedly induces some donors to conceal disqualifying histories of hepatitis, past transfusions, allergies, or communicable diseases.

Statistics support the theory. Stanford's Dr. Allen reports that in one study blood traced to addicts in prisons and slums was found 70 times likelier to carry hepatitis than is blood from unpaid volunteers. Over-all, he says, commercial blood is 10 times likelier to harbor hepatitis than volunteer blood is.

Dr. Allen has been studying blood-transfusion problems since 1945. It was he who first discovered commercial blood's special health hazards. He has published widely. And many medical men regard him as the nation's leading authority on blood donating and hepatitis.

# Hepatitis Risk Understated

Commercial blood, which the Government says computes one-third of the U.S. supply, is currently indispensable. Without it, hospitals in some major cities would have to curtail transfusions. So it is almost universally available even to the altruistic volunteer whose blood donations to a nonprofit bank entitled him to free, safer volunteer blood.

No blood bank has centers in all states. The Red Cross, biggest of the banks, has 50 centers in 42 states. But the centers may not cover the entire state, and they can't always supply blood. So a volunteer donor requiring emergency transfusion in such areas simply gets what's available; the Red Cross or his own nonprofit bank only picks up the tab.

The common use of commercial blood is the biggest contributor to the serum-hepatitis rate among transfusion patients. Nobody knows just how high the rate is. The Government's Center for Disease Control (CDC) in Atlanta says, because physicians often fail to report serum-hepatitis cases. The CDC says the real hepatitis rate could be 2 to 10 times. Dr. Allen's estimate, or 35,000 deaths and 50,000 illnesses, a year instead of 2,500 deaths and 50,000 illnesses.

# Difficulties of Diagnosis

# Why the confusion?

First, some serum-hepatitis symptoms resemble those of other illnesses. Thus a doctor may diagnose hepatitis as something else—especially if he doesn't know that the patient has had a transfusion. Second, the disease takes two to six months to develop. After that time, both patient and doctor may fail to connect the hepatitis with a transfusion given while treating another malady from which the patient apparently has recovered.

Mrs. Schmid is suing Rush Presbyterian-St. Luke's Medical Center in Chicago for its alleged "failure to warn us that there might be a danger in using blood from paid donors." Had she known of the danger, Mrs. Schmid says, she could have obtained volunteer blood for her husband, whose membership in a fraternal organization made him eligible for free blood. Schmid's heart operation required 22 pints of blood costing about \$750 total. More than half of it was commercial blood.

Presbyterian-St. Luke's will not comment on Mrs. Schmid's suit beyond acknowledging it. The case has not been scheduled for trial.

There have been enough court cases, including Mrs. Schmid's, to help document and defuse the extent of the blood problem, but there haven't yet been enough court decisions to do much more.

Last October a jury in Billings, Mont., returned the first jury verdict favoring a victim in a post-transfusion hepatitis case. The jury awarded $32,941.41 damages to a Montana man who was disabled by serum hepatitis after receiving transfused blood taken from a woman who allegedly had hepatitis when she sold her blood to a commercial blood bank for a $5 "incentive." The blood bank is appealing the verdict. Lawyers on both sides agree that the case could become an important precedent.

Stanford's Dr. Allen testified as an expert witness at that trial, which brought to public view some of his mass of data on the blood problem.

Dr. Allen says an all-volunteer national blood program would cut the annual toll of hepatitis deaths and illnesses by 90 per cent. He estimates that hepatitis costs Americans \$67,000,000 a year, based on a study of 25,000 patients hospitalized by hepatitis.

# The System's Shortcomings

Moreover, Dr. Allen says he has evidence that:

- Inspection of blood banks under Federal jurisdiction "is minimal because inspectors who visit blood banks often are inexperienced, and even veteran inspectors fail to investigate thoroughly enough."

- Despite rules of the standards-setting American Association of Blood Banks, some commercial banks let donors give blood almost fortnightly, ignoring the eight-week recommended waiting period.

- Patients who "borrow" blood from hospital banks, replacing it with volunteer blood donated by friends, frequently receive "high risk" commercial blood with neither the patient nor his physician knowing it.

# One Investigation's Findings

Newsmen have corroborated many of Dr. Allen's allegations. NBC's Chronology program last October carried a critical report based on nine months of research. Various newspapers, including the New York Times and the Washington Post, have investigated the blood problem in their bailiwick. Among the best articles was a series by a three-reporter Chicago Tribune "task force."

The Tribune reporters spent two months digging, says Phil Caputo, head of the team. They sold blood. The next day different blood banks readily accepted them as donors, despite their arms' fresh needle marks.

In Chicago's grimly slums they found "winos who sold blood so often they had scar tissue on their arms," Caputo says. His team interviewed skid-row donors who survived solely on garbage, a diet rendering them easy prey for hepatitis.

The reporters learned from blood-bank donor lists that suspected hepatitis carriers were rejected by one bank and then accepted by others. They found that Scientific Blood Bank, Inc., a Chicago-based commercial supplier, paid skid-row "professional donors" with vouchers cashable only at a nearby liquor store that required what Caputo calls "a sizable purchase, not just a pack of cigarettes."

Scientific paid the same way in Washington, D.C., until it closed down its Capital operation two months ago. Scientific's blood-buying facility, located in a ghetto area, paid donors with \$5 vouchers stamped "Cash at Moe's Liquors only."

# No Purchase Necessary

The owner of Moe's, who doesn't want his name used "because all it'll do is make me catch more hell," says he charged Scientific 25 cents per voucher. "We didn't demand that those guys buy booze," he says. "Sometimes they bought it; sometimes they didn't."

Scientific shut down its Washington operations after local newspapers carried stories about its liquor-store vouchering. Asked by The National Observer to comment, Robert Gallagher, president of Scientific, said: "I don't want to be rude, but I honestly believe anything I say will come out wrong. In the past whenever I've talked to reporters it has always come out wrong."

Rep. Victor Veysey, Republican of California, has been thumping for months for reform of the nation's uncoordinated blood programs. He has introduced a Maine bill that would impose stiffer, broader Federal regulations on blood banks. Charles Percy, Illinois Republican, and Vance Hartke, Indiana Democrat, have introduced a companion bill in the Senate.

# THE NATIONAL OBSERVER

January 29, 1972

The Veysey bill would establish a national blood-bank program run by the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (HEW), which would be given regulatory authority over all blood banks. At such national regulation now exists, HEW's Division of Biological Standards (DBS) policies the 166 banks that deal in interstate commerce and supply most of the nation's blood. But most of the 5,000 American blood banks don't operate interstate, so they're subject only to state and local laws.

# Proposals and Accusations

Those laws are anemic at best. Only seven states assess blood banks. Only five provide for blood inspection. Seventeen states have no blood-bank laws at all, and in 21 other states the only laws relating to the industry are those exempting blood banks from legal claims or patents harmed by tainted blood.

Veysey's bill would require a national registry of blood donors. It would not know or suspected hepatitis carriers, enabling blood banks to exclude them as prospective donors. And it would require labeling commercial blood as "high risk" and volunteer blood as "low risk." At present, doctors often have no way of knowing the source or quality of blood they give their patients.

The Red Cross has been "lackadousical" for not expanding and trying to remedy the shortage of volunteer blood on its own, Veysey alleges. Dr. Jack J. Levin, the physician who is assistant director of the Red Cross blood program, says in response:

"We haven't expanded. We get no subsidy from Government and we must consider the others involved in blood collecting. Our program is a little more aggressive so far as efficiency and other things are concerned. This is our main thing. We want to improve what we have before we run off to expand."

# A Matter of Authority

Veysey also alleges that the DBS has been derelict in its duty by not requiring that commercial blood be so labeled. He says the DBS has clear authority to order labeling, to bring unregulated banks under its jurisdiction, and to prevent suppliers from accepting skid-row donors.

The DBS says it has no such authority. John N. Ashworth, chief of the DBS Blood and Blood Products Laboratory, says no one in DBS "understands exactly what the congressman and others are inferring in their criticism of us. We have no authority to interfere with private enterprise, but we do take action against blood banks that violate the law."

Forty-three DBS inspectors annually inspect the 200 installations of the 166 DBS-regulated blood banks. They examine equipment such as needles, autoclaves, and blood containers. They check records and monitor the bank's technicians for violations of proper medical techniques.

"In extreme cases of rule-breaking we have gone to court to get compliance," Ashworth says. "We've moved against three to five blood banks in the last decade, maybe it was six banks."

It was four. That's the total number of serious watchdog actions against blood banks since regulation began in 1902.

Veysey doesn't think DBS does enough. In fact, his bill stipulates that DBS shall not operate the proposed national blood program.

The transfusion-hepatitis risk would be minimal if doctors had an infallible laboratory test to detect serum hepatitis in blood. They don't, although many thought the Australia antigen was it. The antigen, first found in an Australian buxman, causes an observable reaction when introduced into blood containing serum hepatitis.

Last October the Association of American Blood Banks, which represents 1,000 commercial and nonprofit banks, ordered all its members to use tests based on the antigen. The DBS also required such tests. But researchers have found that the Australia-antigen test detects hepatitis only 25 per cent of the time, so the search for a more reliable detector goes on.

Because hepatitis detection is still unreliable, many authorities say the only solution to the nation's blood products is to use only low-risk volunteer blood nationals. And this, most agree, means creating a national blood program under a single agency.

The Red Cross, which ran the nation's blood program during World War II and afterward and is still the biggest blood banker, doesn't want the job. "I'm not so sure we could handle a national program," Dr. Levin says. "Even if we had a subsidy it would be difficult to recruit people to do the job."

# National Program Opposed

The Red Cross concedes the need for a national program. But besides declining the job itself, it isn't supporting Veysey's bill. In fact, officials of some autonomous state Red Cross chapters are lobbying against the bill. Some observers say these officials see a national system as a threat to their own blood collecting.

Commercial banks oppose the idea of a national system too. So does the blood-bank association. "We oppose a monolithic system. It would stifle research and creativity," says Mrs. Bernice Hemphill, a spokesman for the American Association of Blood Banks and head of the big, nonprofit Irwin Memorial Blood Bank in San Francisco.

Blood banks could supply enough volunteer blood by switching to other donor-recruitment systems, she says. Since last October, she adds, the Irwin bank has supplied only unpaid volunteers' blood to the 50 hospitals it serves.

Dr. Allen ascribes another motive to the association's opposition. The association vehemently denies his accusations, but he insists that:

"The 'nonprofit' blood banks make huge profits and want to protect them. I know: I had the embarrassment of running a bank that made such profits. The current fee structures make it practically

impossible not to clear money."

Dr. Allen says the blood banks camouflage their excess profits by paying \$50,000-a-year salaries to key executives. And he alleges that much of the banks' research grants goes to their own researchers. "There's no competition for the money as there would be if the grants were awarded impartially by the National Institutes of Health, for example," he says.

This sort of squabbling has provoked at least one clear, firm decision from a powerful sector: the 14,000,000-member AFL-CIO, which has co-operated closely with the Red Cross since World War II and which wants a national program begun.

Leo Perlis, head of the AFL-CIO's Department of Community Services and an activist in blood programs for more than 25 years, told The National Observer:

"The AFL-CIO is going to give the Red Cross one more year. If we don't see it improve its blood program, we're going to start lobbying hard to set up a national system without it."

"We're not only concerned with hepatitis, had as it is; we're concerned about the nation's values," Perlis adds. "It's about time we stopped thinking we can buy and sell every single thing. My God, when we start selling the blood from our bodies—and contaminated blood at that—we're going off . . . well, words fall me."

Words don't fall Richard Titmus, the British author of The Gift Relationship, a recent book on blood donating. He sees the American blood controversy as a moral issue constituting "one of the ultimate tests of where the 'social' begins and the 'economic' ends."

Titmus argues against considering blood a commodity to be bought and sold. To him, "Freedom from disability is inseparable from altruism." Many Americans are beginning to agree, if only because good blood is perhaps one thing the dollar just can't buy.

# Transplant

recipient
also got
cancer

Special to The Spectator

WASHINGTON — For the first time in the history of heart transplants, a recipient has died of a cancer apparently introduced in his body by the heart he received.

The case has been disclosed by the St. Louis University Medical Centre.

Vincent H. Dobelman, 45, was given a new heart at the St. Louis Centre last Feb. 8. It came from a man who died of a brain tumor but not, so far as the surgeons knew then, from a cancer.

The operation was the centre's first heart transplant.

DOBELMAN showed signs of rejection, the process by which the body sloughs off foreign cells. This was normal. It was treated, as usual, by so-called immuno-suppressive drugs.

It became known that Dobelman might face another problem. An autopsy of the heart donor had shown that he suffered not from a primary brain tumor (which is almost always an isolated condition, not affecting other parts of the body) but from a lung cancer which had spread to the brain.

On Nov. 11, Dobelman was readmitted to the hospital with "muscle aches" and "malaise." He developed more signs of rejection, and on Dec. 16 he died with a clinical picture of heart failure.

On autopsy, pathologists found extensive cancer in his heart, lungs and liver. It had obviously grown and spread fast, a common occurrence in kidney transplant patients who have also been inadvertently given new organs that bore cancerous cells.

"The extent of tumor growth," the St. Louis doctors' statement said, "is considered at this time to be a major contributing factor to the heart failure which caused his death."

THE DOCTORS also said it is not certain that the cancer found in the donor is the same one that struck Dobelman. "It is unlikely that a positive statement can ever be made in this regard," they added.

"It is highly probable that the tumor was in the heart when it was transplanted," said Dr. Vallee L. Wilman, chief of surgery and the man who directed the transplant effort.

Even a careful exterior examination of a heart before transplant or a biopsy of heart muscle could fail to show cancer cells, said one authority. Cancer does not actually take root in heart muscles, he added, but cancer cells may be present in the heart circulation, and thus get transplanted.

## Transmission of Disease by Blood Transfusion

Hepatitis,¹ syphilis, malaria, and brucellosis have all been transmitted to patients who were given whole blood or blood products. Hepatitis is by far the most serious disorder transmitted in this way, and the incidence of the disease in patients receiving an average of two bottles of blood is about 0.8%. When plasma from relatively large pools is used the incidence can reach the alarming figure of 11.9%, but if the plasma pool is prepared from less than 10 bottles the figure falls to 1.3%. After a massive blood transfusion—and between 10 and 20 bottles is commonplace in modern heart surgery—the risk is once again increased. This important hazard of blood transfusion is not as widely appreciated as it should be: one of the reasons for this may be the relatively long incubation period, which varies from 60 to 160 days before jaundice appears.

The signs and symptoms are better known. In addition to jaundice, about two thirds of patients have nausea, vomiting, and anorexia, joint pains are present in about a quarter and a skin rash may develop. The illness lasts about 30 days. Seven out of 134 cases reported by D. Lehane and his colleagues² died. The work of G. S. Mirick, R. Ward, and R. W. McCollum³ suggested that giving gamma-globulin may reduce the frequency of hepatitis after transfusion, and there is much to be said for adopting this form of prophylaxis with large transfusions.

Where malaria is endemic the transmission by transfusion remains a hazard. N. N. Duhanina and T. A. Zukova⁴ report 47 cases, including the transmission of quartan malaria to children who were given maternal blood as prophylaxis

against measles. Another 36 cases are recorded from Yugoslavia.⁵ Transmission of malaria by transfusion can be prevented by the administration of chloroquine diphosphate to the recipient before the transfusion. A dose of 600 mg. seems to be adequate.⁶

Transmission of syphilis is less likely because spirochaetes are unlikely to survive for more than 72 hours in stored citrated blood,⁷ and transmission of brucellosis, though reported,⁸ must be a rarity.

Most transfusion services do not accept as donors those who give a history of jaundice. Nevertheless, even after this step is taken the known incidence of homologous serum jaundice suggests that not less than 1 in 200 healthy donors are carriers of the virus. Whole blood from donors who have lived in areas where malaria is endemic should not be transfused, though there is no objection to the use of their plasma. It is also the practice to carry out serological tests for syphilis on donor blood samples and to exclude donors giving positive reactions.

# TRANSFUSION MALARIA SNEAKING UP

Until 1967, the U.S. had only about one case a year of transfusion-induced malaria. Since then, 27 cases have turned up, 12 of them since January 1970.

The Center for Disease Control, worried about the sharp upturn, wants the American Association of Blood Banks to tighten up and simplify its guidelines for accepting donations. It proposes that blood banks reject donations from any person who has lived in or traveled to a malarious area—not necessarily an entire country—within three years.

Current AABB guidelines permit donations within six months after leaving the malarious area if the donor is asymptomatic and has not taken antimalarial drugs. If drugs were taken, donations are not supposed to be accepted for two years after the chemotherapy ended. Permanently rejected are those with a

history of malaria or residents of a country where it is endemic.

CDC's complaint is not so much that the guidelines are too lax, but that they are not rigidly enforced, says Dr. Arthur S. Dover. He points out that if the guidelines had been strictly followed, only two of the 21 cases in which he has traced the infected donor would have occurred. He adds, however, that regardless of whose guidelines are in effect, the "serious problem" of donor misinformation remains. He says he knows of at least four cases in which the infected donor lied about his history.

AABB has balked at the CDC proposal, but is still mulling it over. It contends that the CDC guideline lacks flexibility and would cause the loss of many safe donors. "We've had quite a hassle," says Dr. Herbert A. Perkins, chairman of the AABB panel considering the proposal. "We differ on whether the restrictive pe

riod should be three years, two years, or only six months. What do you do, say, with the guy who passes through Saigon for 12 hours?" Dr. Perkins also contends that AABB's guidelines have not been in effect long enough—they were promulgated in January 1970—to have really been put to a test.

Dr. Dover says CDC chose the three-year limit for maximum safety, he reports one case in which the parasites had been in the donor for 32 months. "A two-year interval unnecessarily increases the risk," he says.

AABB's decision is expected to be worked out by the time of its annual meeting in Chicago this September. "We are giving the recommendation very careful consideration," says Dr. Perkins. "We want to get something that everyone will be happy with."

MEDICAL WORLD NEWS July 16, 1971 Vol. 12, No. 27, p12

# Transfusion Malaria

Sik: In November of 1970, we sent a communication to the journal Transfusion in which we reported that current standards for malaria prevention in blood banks were misleading and dangerous. These blood bank regulations were guidelines set by the American Association of Blood Banks Committee on Standards and the Center for Disease Control (CDC), Atlanta, Ga. At the time our paper was submitted, we hoped for early publication in order to bring the problem into the open and thereby facilitate the revision of standards.

We are particularly disturbed by some of the allegedly direct quotations and paraphrases from Dr. Herbert Perkins, chairman of the Standards Committee, AABB in your article:

(1) "... We differ on whether the restrictive period should be three years, two years, or only six months. . . ." Comment: We concur with the CDC that a restrictive period of only

# Letters to the Editor

six months or two years is insufficient. Furthermore, six months could be dangerous.

(2) "... What do you do, say, with the guy who passes through Saigon for twelve hours. . . ." Comment: He must be excluded as a blood donor for at least three years. Even though Saigon is relatively malaria-free compared with most of Vietnam, it takes only one infected mosquito a mere fraction of a second to bite and to transmit malaria. Accordingly, 12 hours is more than sufficient. This example is particularly dangerous, for drug-resistant falciparum malaria is prevalent in Vietnam.

(3) "... AABB's guidelines have not been in effect long enough—they were promulgated in January 1970—to have really been put to test. . . ." Comment: This statement presumes that the current guidelines are reasonable and safe. They are not.

Finally, when we sent our communication (which has not yet been published in Transfusion, or officially commented on by the AABB Committee on Standards) we mailed pre-publication copies to the AABB Committee on Standards, the CDC, and blood bank directors in the Chicago area, including Dr. Coye C. Mason, Executive Director, Chicago Blood Donor Service. Dr. Mason is also editor of Laboratory Medicine, and his staff inadvertently published our comments in Laboratory Medicine (Vol. 2, No. 1).

Interested readers may find there what we believe are safe, reasonable blood bank malaria standards.

# Graft-vs-Host Reaction

## Following a Single Blood Transfusion

William E. Hathaway, MD, Vincent A. Fulginiti, MD, Carl W. Pierre, MD, PhD, John H. Githens, MD, David S. Pearlman, MD,

Frederick Muschenheim, MD, and C. Henry Kempe, MD

The graft-vs-host (GVH) reaction occurred in an 11-month-old boy with thymic alymphoplasia and progressive vaccinia who had received a single whole blood transfusion. The principal manifestations of the GVH reaction were hepatosplenomegaly, dermatitis, diarrhea, aplastic anemia, and histiocytosis of the spleen and lymph nodes. The findings in this patient are quite similar to those of other previously reported cases of possible human runt disease. This case study emphasizes the dangers of smallpox vaccination or blood transfusion in infants with thymic alymphoplasia or one of the variants of this syndrome.

As recently as 1962, Nisbet and Heslop were able to write "runt disease is an entity entirely restricted to laboratory animals, and . . . has no known human counterpart in clinical medicine." Since then, several cases have been reported suggesting fatal graft-vs-host (GVH) reaction (runt disease) in humans. As in laboratory animals, this reaction appeared to occur when immunologically competent lymphocytes were transfused into immunologically deficient infants who had thymic alymphoplasia or "Swiss-type" agammaglobulinemia. The purpose of this paper is to describe another case of human runt disease which occurred in an infant with thymic alymphoplasia following a single transfusion of whole blood. The clinical and pathologic findings of this case will be compared with those of the previously reported cases.

### Report of a Case

An 11-month-old white boy was admitted to Colorado General Hospital, Denver, on Oct 27, 1968, for evaluation and treatment of progressive vaccinia. With the exception of oral thrush as an infant and occasional mouth ulcerations with slight fevers, he had been well until six weeks prior to admission when he was given a small-pox vaccina-

From the departments of pediatrics (Drs. Hathaway, Fulginiti, Githens, Pearlman, and Kempe) and pathology (Drs. Pierre and Muschenheim), University of Colorado Medical Center, Denver. Reprint requests to 4200 E Ninth Ave, Denver 80220 (Dr. Hathaway).

tion on the left upper arm. Two weeks later a single crusted lesion was noted. This lesion became surrounded by satellite vesicles which coalesced, enlarged, and appeared necrotic. During the two weeks prior to admission the patient had a febrile course and was treated with penicillin, sulfasoxazole, and tetracycline. On Oct 20, 1968, he was admitted to a hospital in Brooklyn, NY, where he was given a 10-ml intramuscular injection of vaccinia immune serum globulin was well as 10 ml of commercial γ-globulin. Daily body temperatures of 102-103 F (38.9-39.4 C) were recorded. A superficial surgical debridement of the lesion was done. The following day (Oct 21, 1968) a 125-ml whole blood transfusion (12-day-old Red Cross blood treated with anticoagulant acid citrate dextrose solution) was administered without reaction (male donor). The original vaccinial lesion became worse, two new lesions appeared, and the febrile course persisted in spite of additional antibiotic therapy (ampicillin and erythromycin). On Oct 27, 1968, he was transferred to Colorado General Hospital.

The history was unrevealing except for immunization with diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and pertussis vaccine and oral poliovirus vaccine without reaction. Pregnancy, birth, growth, and development were entirely normal. The father and mother, both 23 years old, were in good health. There were no siblings. Family history was noncontributory.

Physical examination revealed an acutely ill, well nourished, well developed, mildly dehydrated infant who weighed 8.8 kg (19.4 lb). The left upper arm was covered by a 15 x 15-cm, necrotic, crusted ulcer with an erythematous margin. Pustular vesicles were seen on the right eyelid and left ankle. The right knee was swollen, red, and tender. The liver edge was palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen was not felt.

Laboratory Studies.—Initial studies disclosed the following values: hemoglobin, 14.3 gm/100 cc; hematocrit 47%; white blood cell count, 15,000/cu mm, with S7 segmented neutrophiles, four bands, three large lymphocytes, two medium lymphocytes, one small lymphocyte, one monocyte, and two eosinophiles. Platelets were within the range of low average. Reticulocyte count was 1.6%. Coombs' test result was positive (1+). Urinalysis showed proteinuria (1+) and a few granular casts. Bacterial cultures of urine, blood, stool, nasopharynx, and vaccinia lesions revealed no pathogens. Blood electrolytes were normal except for a mild hyponatremia.
