The clinical impression was that the patient was undergoing a GVII reaction secondary to the blood transfusion he received prior to admission. In an effort to give passive vaccinia antibody therapy, a series of exchange transfusions with blood from recently vaccinated donors were instituted. Each exchange (Fig 2) consisted of three units of blood irradiated with 2,500 rads to render the lymphocytes nonviable. The patient tolerated the exchange transfusions very well, but failed to show clinical benefit. On the 13th day the infant had severe abdominal distension and melena and roentgenologic study showed pneumatosis intestinalis. Coagulation studies showed a prolonged prothrombin time and severe depression of prothrombin factor II, proconvertin factor VII, Stuart factor X, and proaccelerin factor V. Antihemophilic factor VIII was normal. Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma were given with cessation of bleeding. The remainder of his course was complicated by generalized edema, hypoalbuminemia, progression and necrosis of the vaccinial lesions, and deepening lethargy; he died on the 22nd hospital day. Figure 2 depicts the hematological data in relation to the patient's hospital course. In addition to the thrombocytopenia and granulocytopenia, a severe reticulocytopenia occurred just prior to his death.

Pathologic Findings.—At autopsy, the infant had a large, necrotic vaccinia enchar of the left shoulder and upper left anterior and posterior thorax and many satellite lesions on the face, arms, and legs. Raised, yellow-green, friable, vaccinial lesions were present on the tongue and in the esophagus and colon. Much nuclear and cellular debris as well as Guarnieri bodies were present at the margins of the lesions; there was minimal inflammatory response. The remainder of the skin was markedly edematous and a morbilliform eruption was visible. Histologically, the dermis was edematous. Mononuclear cells were scattered about adnexae and vessels. The epidermis showed hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, acanthosis, and epidermal proliferation of the basal layer; scattered dyskeratotic cells were seen (Fig 3). Lymphoid tissue was absent from the palatine tonsilar area, mediastinum, and small intestine and was markedly reduced in the appendix. The thymus weighed 1 gm and was present in the anterior mediastinum. It was composed of large fusiform epithelial cells, macrophages, and reticulum cells; no Hassall's corpuscles or small lymphocytes were seen. The lobular arrangement was well preserved (Fig 4). ### Comment

Runt disease is that form of GVH reaction which occurs in infants who are immunologically tolerant due to a disease state or immaturity, and who receive allogenic transfusions of immunologically competent lymphocytes. Secondary disease is the form of GVH reaction that occurs in individuals who have undergone immunosuppression by radiotherapy or chemotherapy, and who receive transfusions containing lymphocytes.

The clinical and pathologic findings of the GVH

6. Section of spleen. Periarterial lymphoid tissue is hypocellular. Small lymphocyte cuff is partly replaced by increased histiocytes. Similar cells surround small artery at left (×160).

![img-85.jpeg](img-85.jpeg)

reaction or runt disease in animals are well established, but the mechanism of the production of these manifestations is not well understood. The manifestations of human runt disease are similar to those seen in animals. Tables 1 and 2 summarize the clinical and pathologic findings which have been described in the reported cases of possible human runt disease. These findings include gastrointestinal symptoms such as severe diarrhea, dermatitis evidenced by an erythematous morbill-

iform rash, hepatosplenomegaly, hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, and usually, a rapidly fatal course. Pathologically, dyskeratosis of the skin, aplasia of the marrow, hepatic necrosis, lymphoid tissue depletion, and histiocytic and monocytic cell infiltration of the spleen, liver, lymph nodes, gut, and bone marrow are seen. Each of these clinical signs and pathologic lesions is not of itself specifically diagnostic of the GVH reaction; they can be seen in part in other diseases of the reticuloendothelial system such as severe infections or histiocytosis X. However, when these findings occur in an immunologically deficient infant with impaired delayed hypersensitivity, who has received infusions of whole blood, leukocytes, or bone marrow which contain immunologically competent lymphocytes, runt disease is a strong possibility. Proof of persistence of the graft in the form of appropriate sex chromosomal markers is additional evidence for the GVH reaction, although

there is evidence in animal experiments that the grafted cells need not persist after an initial period of time to mediate the pathologic reaction.⁷

The similarity of the cases of human runt disease (Tables 1 and 2) is striking, especially when one realizes that the severity of the GVH reaction may be dependent on several factors including (1) degree of immunosuppression of the host; (2) the genetic disparity of graft and host tissues, ie, the difference in histocompatibility genes; (3) cell dose of the graft (both numbers and types of cells); (4) complicating infection⁸; and (5) degree of lymphatic tissue depletion.⁹

The underlying immunologic deficiency disease in each of these patients and the present case was thymic alymphoplasia or Swiss-type agammaglobulinemia¹⁰⁻¹¹ or a variant of thymic alymphoplasia.¹²⁻¹⁶ In all of these cases except one (Kodawaki et al), intravenous injections of varying numbers of viable lymphocytes from genetically different individuals (allogenic cells) were given. It has been estimated that allogenic lymphocytes administered intravenously in a dose of 1 × 10⁷/kg of body weight are sufficient to produce fatal runt disease in mice, and that lymphocytes in a dose of 6 × 10⁷/kg can produce secondary disease in man.⁸⁻¹⁰ Acute GVH reaction was produced in an infant with maternal bone-marrow lymphoid cells in a total dose of 2.9 × 10⁷. In the present case lymphocytes were given in a dose of 2.8 × 10⁷/kg (assuming 2,000 lymphocytes/cu mm in the donor blood). It has been shown¹¹ that even 17-day-old bank blood contains viable lymphocytes capable of mitotic activity in tissue culture. Therefore, it is feasible that the single transfusion of 12-day-old blood given to our patient was adequate to invoke a GVH reaction.

The case of Kodawaki and associates⁷ and one of those of Hathaway et al¹ would appear to be chronic forms of runt disease in which gastrointestinal manifestations were the predominant symptoms. The other cases of Hathaway et al¹ and Miller¹ and the present patient all demonstrated an acute form of GVH reaction in which hepatosplenomegaly,

erythrodermia, and aplastic anemia were the prominent features. The case of Rosen and others¹⁸ may have been another example of the acute GVH reaction following a transfusion of maternal bone marrow.

Although there are no pathologic changes which are specific for runt disease in the human, several findings illustrated by the cases in Table 2 should be emphasized. Most of the infants showed a severe pancytopenia and depletion of hemic elements in the bone marrow. A myeloid hyperplasia preceded the aplasia in the present case and was prominent in the case of Kodawaki et al. A myeloid hyperplasia followed by hypoplasia of all hemic elements is characteristic of severe animal runt disease (J.H. Githens et al, unpublished data).

Dyskeratosis of the skin (Fig 3), which has been observed in all the cases in which a careful examination of the skin was made (including the present one), has been described as a very characteristic finding in human secondary disease.¹⁹ Although these same changes may be seen in "autoimmune disease" such as disseminated lupus erythematosus, when present, they are suggestive of a GVH reaction.²⁰

Monocytoid cellular infiltration in the portal triads and hepatic cell necrosis are quite specific pathologic changes in mouse runt disease²¹⁻²³ and secondary disease in primates.²⁴ In mice, the sites of necrosis are limited to the subcapular regions; this type of necrosis was not seen in the present case, although a few, small, focal necrotic areas were noted. These were difficult to interpret since vaccinia virus may have also been an etiologic agent. Mild monocytic cell infiltration of the portal triads was seen in this patient.

Monocytoid cell and histiocytic proliferation of the bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen was seen in the present case as well as in the other cases in Table 2. This finding is also characteristic of experimentally induced runt disease. However, cells staining positively with methyl green pyronin were seen infrequently in the cases of human runt disease although they are often described in experi-

mentally induced GVH reactions in animals, especially the dog. In the present case as well as in several of the others erythrophagocytosis and phagocytosis of nuclear debris were present, findings which have been seen in animal runt disease.

Thus, on the basis of clinical, hematologic, and pathologic findings, the present case can be considered as an example of human runt disease occurring in an infant with thymic alymphoplasia who received a single transfusion of whole blood. The propositus was also given exchange transfusions with blood obtained from recently vaccinated donors in an effort to administer large amounts of vaccinia antibody. This blood had been irradiated to decrease the risk of a GVH reaction; however, the amount of radiation given may not have been enough to render all lymphocytes nonviable. Nevertheless, the clinical manifestations of the

GVH reaction were already present before the first exchange transfusion. Our patient was extremely ill with generalized vaccinia, but appeared to become worse with the development of the manifestations of runt disease.

This case study emphasizes the serious danger of administration of even small amounts of lymphocytes (ie, a single whole blood transfusion) to a patient with thymic alymphoplasia or one of the variants of this syndrome.

## Partial Immunodeficiency and Graft-versus-Host Disease

If patients with defective cellular immunity are transfused with immunologically competent cells (ICC), graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) may result. It has occurred in several children with severe combined immunodeficiency (Hong, Gatti, and Good, 1968), but only once in a child with partial immunodeficiency—Wiskott-Aldrich disease (Douglas and Fudenberg, 1969).

We describe a child with partially defective cellular and humoral immunity, who developed a fatal illness, probably GVHD, after a blood transfusion.

### Case Report

The only daughter, birthweight 2940 g, of unrelated parents thrived until 5 months when an upper respiratory tract infection developed, progressing to bronchopneumonia. This partially responded to oral antibiotics, but anorexia, poor weight gain, and chronic diarrhoea persisted. When admitted to hospital aged 8 months, her weight was on the third centile; she passed 4 to 5 mucousy offensive stools daily, and had bilateral lower lobe pneumonia. The liver was 2-5 cm below the costal margin. The spleen was not felt; small axillary, cervical, and inguinal lymph nodes, and small tonsils were present. She had congenital right ptosis.

Her pneumonia improved on intramuscular antibiotics, but oral and cutaneous thrush developed, unresponsive to topical nystatin. Gastroenteritis (Esch. coli 0126) responded to oral neomycin and colomycin.

Low levels of immunoglobulins were detected, and parenteral immunoglobulin was started; two infusions of hydroxystibumidine cleared the candidiasis, and pentamidine was given intramuscularly for 14 days for suspected pneumocystis carinii. The pneumonia cleared but relapsed at 13 months. She responded again to intramuscular antibiotics and a course of pentamidine. At 15 months she was free of infection on lincomycin 50 mg b.d. orally, and immunoglobulin intramuscularly twice weekly. The diarrhoea persisted despite dietary exclusion of disaccharides, and her weight was static. Progressive anaemia at 15 months necessitated a 200 ml packed cell transfusion of 4-day-old acid citrate dextrose (ACD) blood, which was well tolerated. Aged 16 months she was transferred to Great Ormond Street for further investigation. Sequential haematological and immunological data are shown in Fig. 1. IgG was initially rather low, but rose above the level ascribable to the injections. IgM was normal, IgA low, and lymphocytes few, until the terminal illness. The haemoglobin fell progressively.

Other findings included normal platelet counts, and marrow; reticulocytes 1-4%; serum albumin 2-1-3-4 g/100 ml; blood urea 40-165 mg/100 ml (on high protein diet); normal urine; hypokalaemia; excess faecal disaccharides; cultures (including 3 blood cultures) grew no pathogens; patchy shadowing at bases on chest x-ray; dilatation of small bowel on barium meal.

Immunological function tests included anti-B isohaemagglutinin (group A Rh-) 1/4; ASO 40 U/ml (45 days after stopping immunoglobulin); antidiarrheic antitoxin 0-16 U/ml and anti-tetanus antitoxin 0-64 U/ml about 1 year after two doses of triple antigen, and 80 days after stopping injections of immunoglobulin. Skin tests to candida antigen and to DNCB were weekly and doubtfully positive (biopsy of the latter showed no

significant lymphocyte infiltration, and a burn cannot be excluded). Lymphocyte uptake of tritiated thymidine on phytohaemagglutinium (PHA) stimulation was significantly positive (counts/min unstimulated 486, 907, and 651; PHA stimulated 12,560, 4914, and 8684) though about tenfold less than parallel controls.

Over the ensuing 3 months the diarrhoea persisted despite numerous dietary manipulations, and she gained no weight. The immunoglobulin injections were discontinued, and she remained infection free on oral ampicillin, and her general condition improved. She was given KCl for gut loss of K. Discharge was planned, and she was transfused for anaemia.

At 18 months a 200 ml packed cell transfusion of 6-day old ACD blood from a female donor was given. Seven days later, pyrexia and a macular erythematous rash developed; this was attributed to ampicillin which was stopped. The fever persisted, the rash became confluent with generalized subcutaneous oedema, and striking generalized lymph node enlargement. There was a conspicuous fall in polymorphs and thrombocytes, marrow aplasia, and rise in immunoglobulins and lymphocytes (Fig. 1); the direct antiglobulin test was negative. She rapidly deteriorated and died in peripheral vascular collapse 15 days after transfusion. GVHD was diagnosed clinically.

At necropsy the lymph nodes were of normal size and distribution; the thymus was small (2-0 g). The lungs were clear; there was some small bowel dilatation, but no other macroscopical abnormalities. Histologically, the thymus showed typical thymic dysplasia (Fig. 2). The lymph nodes were hypocellular without follicular differentiation. There were very small amounts of organized tissue in the appendix and ileum; there was no lymphoid tissue in the tonsils. The spleen contained plasma cells but no lymphoid follicles.

The marrow was aplastic, but contained many plasma cells and large macrophages. There were phagocytic large macrophages deep in the dermis.

## Discussion

Deficiencies of individual immunological functions may occur in a wide range of combinations in any individual patient. Our child showed antibody response and cutaneous delayed hypersensitivity, and had measurable but reduced immunoglobulin levels, lymphocyte count, and lymphocyte transformation to PHA, in contrast to severe combined immunodeficiency cases, where all these parameters are usually grossly deficient.

The morbid anatomical findings were similar to those in severe combined immunodeficiency which is usually fatal in infancy (Berry, 1970); it is interesting that such findings may be compatible with measurable immunological function. Plasma cells in the marrow, and actively phagocytic macrophages in the marrow and skin, seen in our case, are not usual in severe combined immunodeficiency, and are suggestive of GVHD, though they could be related to her partial immunological function. Other features of GVHD (histiocytic infiltration of the reticuloendothelial system and erythrophagocytosis) were absent. Unfortunately, both

the donor and the recipient were female, so we were unable to demonstrate chimerism by chromosome studies.

The clinical course of her terminal illness was very similar to GVHD in animals, adults, and children with severe combined immunodeficiency.

In the latter it has followed transfusion of fresh blood, plasma, or marrow cells, given either for transfusion purposes, or as an attempt at radical treatment (Hathaway et al., 1965; Miller, 1967; Hong et al., 1968; Gatti et al., 1968; Kretschmer et al., 1969). In such patients, and in the case of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (Douglas and Fudenberg, 1969) GVHD has always been fatal, except when partly tissue-matched sib marrow has been infused.

Lymphocytes are capable of mitotic activity in vitro after 5 weeks storage in ACD blood (McCullough et al., 1969), and so are presumably capable of causing GVHD. The risk of blood, fresh or stored, to patients with severe combined immunodeficiency is well recognized. GVHD apparently following transfusion of stored blood in the presence of measurable humoral and cellular immunity in our patient suggests that blood transfusions should be avoided wherever possible in a wider range of patients with immunodeficiency. If unavoidable, old irradiated washed cells should be given.

## UNCONTROLLABLE POST-OPERATIVE HAEMORRHAGE AFTER INCOMPATIBLE BLOOD TRANSFUSION

BY

JAMES M. MOORE, F.R.C.S.Ed., F.R.F.P.S.

Senior Registrar, Hairmyres Hospital, East Kilbride

It has often been reported that a defect of coagulation may occur in obstetrical conditions and in pulmonary and prostatic surgery. For example, it has been noted in accidental haemorrhage, amniotic fluid embolism, intrauterine foetal death, and missed abortion (De Lee, 1901; Dieckmann, 1936; Moloney et al., 1949; Schneider, 1951; Reid et al., 1953; Barry et al., 1955), following pulmonary lobectomy (Soulier et al., 1952), and in metastatic carcinoma of the prostate (Tagnon et al., 1952; Swan et al., 1957). One of the features of these cases has been hypofibrinogenaemia.

That abnormal bleeding may occur as a transfusion reaction is not so well known, although it has been recorded by American authors on a number of occasions since it was mentioned by Drinker and Brittingham (1919). Muirhead (1951) found nine cases, while Friesen et al. (1952) investigated 11. Other examples are given by Wiener (1954) and Stefanini and Dameshek (1955). Krevann et al. (1957) studied two instances, and in a survey of the literature found 11 additional reports. No report of a case has been traced in British literature, although Mollison (1956) refers to the condition.

It is the object of this paper to give a clinical account of such a case which had a fatal termination.

### Case Report

The patient was a single woman aged 25 suffering from a chronic gastric ulcer. In the past she had undergone appendicectomy and tonsillectomy, and no excessive bleeding had been noted. Menstrual blood loss had been normal. There was no history suggestive of any allergic upset.

Operation.—A Billroth I partial gastrectomy was carried out, and it was uneventful. The anaesthetic consisted of

thiopentone sodium, tubocurarine chloride, gallamine tri-silindide, and nitrous oxide, and a pint (540 ml.) of carefully matched homologous group O rhesus-negative blood was given. The operation was completed at 12 noon.

A second bottle of blood was started at 12.30 p.m. When examined 15 minutes later the patient was rather pale, with a slight cyanotic tinge, and there was a little staining from a stab drainage wound. There was little change during the next two hours. At 2.45 p.m., when about two-thirds of the second bottle of blood (360 ml.) had been given, it was discovered that it was in fact group A rhesus-positive blood which had inadvertently been transfused. Immediately, carefully matched blood of the correct group was substituted and 1 pint (540 ml.) of 50% dextrose given in an attempt to minimize renal complications.

At 4 p.m. it was noted that venous blood sent for further cross-matching would not clot, and by then there was considerable fresh bleeding from the stab wound. Only a small amount of altered blood had been aspirated from the gastric tube during the afternoon, but at 6 p.m. there was 15 oz. (450 ml.) of fresh blood and the main wound had started to ooze. The patient became weaker despite continued transfusion, and another laparotomy was carried out at 7.45 p.m.

Second Operation.—About 4 pints (2 litres) of blood was found in the peritoneal cavity with a few clots. There was a general ooze from many areas involved in the previous operation. On opening the stomach more blood escaped, but again this arose from numerous areas, many not at the suture lines. Despite all attempts at haemostasis the ooze continued. The supply of matched blood for transfusion was temporarily exhausted during the operation, and 2 pints (1 litre) of 6% dextran in saline ("dextraven" and "intra-dex") was given. As nothing further of benefit could be done, the stomach opening was repaired and the abdomen closed with two drainage tubes.

It was now obvious that the patient had developed an abnormal haemorrhagic tendency.

Treatment.—4 ml. of "adrenoyl" (1.5 mg. of adrenochrome monosemicarbazone dihydrate) and 100 mg. of vitamin K analogue ("synkavit") were given intramuscularly. 10 ml. of 10% calcium gluconate was given intravenously and a rapid transfusion of matched group O rhesus-negative blood continued. After consultation with the director of the regional transfusion centre at 10 p.m. the patient was given 4 pints (2 litres) of fresh dried plasma alternating with blood, and 2 g. of concentrated fibrinogen fraction. At this stage there appeared to be a slight temporary decrease in the rate of blood loss. Fresh frozen plasma was requested for her, but her condition deteriorated and she died at 1.45 a.m. on the day following operation, before it could be given.

She had received a total of 17 pints (9 litres) of blood, 3 pints (1.5 litres) of processed plasma, and 2 pints (1 litre) of dextran, as well as the 4 pints (2 litres) of fresh dried plasma and fibrinogen mentioned above. In all, this represents the administration of approximately 20 g. of fibrinogen, of which half had been given after the haemorrhagic defect had been recognized. In spite of this, up to the time of death, bleeding continued from the drainage tubes in the abdomen and from the gastric tube.

### Relevant Post-mortem Findings

There was a large amount of blood and clot in the peritoneal cavity. The stomach was filled with a well-formed clot equivalent to about a pint (0.5 litre) of blood. No open vessels were identified, but there appeared to have been diffuse haemorrhage from the gastric mucosa, in which there were numerous slit-like defects several millimetres in length apparently communicating with submucosal haematoma. The liver and spleen were normal. Histological examination of kidney showed amorphous eosinophilic material, and desquamated epithelial cells in a few convoluted tubules. The lungs appeared oedematous, but there

were no histological changes, and selective staining showed
no significant intravascular deposits of fibrin.

Blood Examination.—A specimen of venous blood taken
at 3.30 p.m. on the day of operation failed to clot in 24
hours, even after the addition of thrombin in excess, indicat-
ing afibrinogenaemia. Marked haemoglobinemia was noted
soon after withdrawal, proving rapid destruction of the in-
compatible blood. A similar specimen taken two days before
operation eluted normally.

Investigations at the regional transfusion centre confirmed
that the patient was group O, rhesus negative, and that she
had received group A blood, which had been rapidly de-
stroyed. The pre-transfusion serum of the patient contained
an anti-A haemolysin, and it was considered that this was
responsible for the rapid haemolysis of the incompatible
cells.

### Discussion

The patient undoubtedly developed a haemorrhagic defect
associated with afibrinogenaemia. The development of
hypofibrinogenaemia has been described by Stefanini and
Daneshak (1955). Among the conditions mentioned as lead-
ing to the syndrome are haemorrhagic shock and haemolytic
transfusion reactions. The patient's condition was good
immediately after operation, which had not been associated
with significant loss of blood. Therefore, even if haemor-
rhagic shock can produce such a syndrome, it seems unlikely
that it was initially responsible for the onset of the fibrinogen
deficiency in this case. The trigger mechanism was almost
certainly the transfusion of blood of the wrong group.

Acquired hypofibrinogenaemia might theoretically result
from (a) defective formation of fibrinogen; (b) intravascular
clotting following the entrance of thromboplastic material
into the circulation, with consumption of fibrinogen; or
(c) depletion of fibrinogen by fibrinolytic or proteolytic
enzymes in the blood. In this case it is unlikely that there
was any defect in the formation of fibrinogen, as there was
no evidence of impaired liver function. It is possible that
intravascular clotting was the cause of the haemorrhagic
state, because Quick et al. (1954) have demonstrated the
thromboplastin-like activity of lysed red blood cells. How-
ever, there was no evidence histologically of abnormal fibrin
deposition in tissues; nevertheless a fibrin deposit could
have been destroyed by fibrinolytic enzymes, the presence of
which has been reported in some cases of this syndrome.

The response to treatment was disappointing although
there was post-mortem evidence of clotting. Stefanini and
Daneshak (1955) suggested that the average amount of
fibrinogen required in treatment was 2-4 g., but mentioned
that 8-20 g. might be necessary. Barry et al. (1955) recom-
mended 2-6 g. of the fibrinogen fraction in the treatment of
hypofibrinogenaemia of pregnancy, but if this was not avail-
able found triple- or quadruple-strength raw plasma equally
effective (1 pint (0.5 litre) of the latter strength yielding
4.4 g. of fibrinogen). In this case approximately 10 g. of
fibrinogen was given after the haemorrhagic defect had been
recognized, but it is possible that this amount might have
produced a greater effect if more of the fibrinogen had been
in a concentrated form and had been administered over a
shorter period. However, the failure of the patient to
respond suggests that there may well have been additional
factors involved.

Other coagulation elements may have been absent or
diminished—for example, prothrombin, Factor V, and
platelets (Greenwalt and Triantaphyllopoulos, 1954).
Krevens et al. (1957) studied two patients after 500 ml. of
incompatible blood and in both found hypofibrinogen-
aemia, hypoprothrombinaemia, and thrombocytopenia, with
reduction of Factor V activity in one. (Incidentally, they
could find no evidence of increased fibrinolytic activity, and
favoured intravascular coagulation as a probable cause of
these changes.) In treatment they advised fresh whole blood
supplemented by fibrinogen. It may be that the fresh
frozen plasma, containing some of these factors, would have
been of benefit.

Two pints (1 litre) of dextran 6% in saline was given
when matched blood and plasma were temporarily unavail-
able. In retrospect it is clear that this was inadvisable, as
a number of reports have incriminated dextran as a cause
of a haemorrhagic tendency (Carbone et al., 1954; Scott,
1955; McKenzie and Langlands, 1956). The mechanism of
the process is not clear, and suggestions made include inter-
action of dextran with fibrinogen, haemodilution, produc-
tion of thrombocytopenia, and prolongation of the bleeding-
time. The patient, of course, had developed abnormal
bleeding before the dextran was given, but it is possible that
the dextran aggravated the haemorrhagic tendency.

Friesen et al. (1952) described similar cases in which post-
operative bleeding occurred as a result of a haemolytic
transfusion reaction, when over 250 ml. of incompatible
blood had been given. They felt that fibrinolysis was an
important factor, but considered that a "heparinoid disturb-
ance" was present. Toluidine-blue dye, given intravenously
to two patients in a dosage of 15 mg. per kg. of body
weight, apparently corrected the bleeding tendency. Such
treatment might be worthy of a trial in any refractory case.

Treatment with corticotrophin (200 units intramuscularly)
or cortisone (400 mg. intravenously) has been recommended,
in addition to fibrinogen, by Stefanini and Daneshak (1955).

If the possibility of a bleeding state after incompatible
transfusion had been known, the second laparotomy would
probably not have been carried out, and appropriate treat-
ment might have been started earlier.

### Summary and Conclusions

A case is described in which there was fatal post-
operative bleeding, associated with afibrinogenaemia,
following a haemolytic transfusion reaction.

Treatment is discussed, and the following points may
be of value in controlling such a condition: (1) early
recognition of the fact that a haemorrhagic state has
developed; (2) administration of large amounts of the
fibrinogen fraction—for example, 2-6 g., repeated if
necessary—or the use of quadruple-strength recon-
stituted raw dried plasma if fibrinogen is not available;
(3) fresh frozen plasma, or fresh blood, if there is a
poor response to adequate fibrinogen; (4) avoidance of
dextran; (5) corticotrophin, cortisone, or toluidine-blue
dye intravenously, if not responding.

I am grateful to Dr. John Wallace, the director of the West of
Scotland Regional Transfusion Centre, and Dr. A. S. Douglas
for their assistance and advice. I should like to thank Mr. K. I.
Macrossan for permission to publish details of this case.

# Virus Hepatitis after Blood Transfusion

A. J. ZUCKERMAN, MD, M.SC, M.C.PATH, DIP.BACT.

Reader in Virology,

London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London

Infectious and serum hepatitis may be transmitted by any procedure that exposes a person to the blood or tissues of a carrier of the virus of hepatitis. Thus hepatitis may be transmitted not only by contaminated syringes and needles in medical and dental practice, by the transfusion of blood and blood products, by tissue and organ grafts but also by non-medical procedures including accidental scratches and cuts, tattooing, the barber's razor and Acupuncture. Mosley (1966) wrote that virus hepatitis is now the most important complication of the transfusion of blood and blood products, a fact that is perhaps not so widely appreciated.

In the early years of World War II it became apparent that high attack rates of hepatitis were associated with the transfusion of certain pools of human plasma. Presumptive evidence of the transmission of this infection by blood transfusion was noted as soon as the practice of transfusion became more widespread. The concept however of two distinct disease entities with widely varying incubation periods was accepted until 1962 when Allen & Sayman found that in almost 51 per cent of transfusion-associated hepatitis the incubation period was less than 60 days. Possibly the more important aspect of Allen & Sayman's work was that it stimulated the systematic observation, at least in some hospitals, of patients who received blood transfusion but there continues to be considerable controversy over just how common hepatitis may be.

In 1963 in the United States it was roughly calculated that about 1.8 million transfusions were given and it has been estimated that the incidence of clinical hepatitis associated with transfusion was 30,000 cases with nearly 3600 deaths. It should be particularly noted that no account was taken of the incidence of the anicteric form of hepatitis for which, in general, the accepted ratio is 1 overt case of jaundice for at least 10 actual infections, although in 1964 it was estimated that the true ratio of anicteric to icteric hepatitis after blood transfusion could be greater than 100 : 1 (Hampers et al. 1964). The figures for post-transfusion

hepatitis, both in the icteric and the anicteric form, published from a number of centres in Germany, Japan and the United States are remarkably high. Thus in a recent careful study in Germany Creutzfeldt et al. (1966) found the overall attack rate of post-transfusion hepatitis to be 14 per cent. A much higher incidence based on the elevation of serum transaminase activity, which is admittedly not specific, was noted by Shimizu & Kitamoto (1963) in Japan with an attack rate of 600 cases of hepatitis per 10,000 units of blood. Hampers' figures from Philadelphia (1964) gave an incidence of 870 cases per 10,000 units of blood. Recent figures in this country are not available but in 1949 Lehane et al. obtained an incidence of 0.8 per cent of jaundice after whole blood transfusion and the 1954 survey revealed an incidence of only 0.16 per cent in England and Wales and 0.36 per cent in Scotland. The frequency of anicteric hepatitis in the United Kingdom is not known, and at any rate it should be noted that in the early surveys the more accurate of the non-specific tests of liver damage such as the serum transaminases were not available. There is no reason to suppose that the incidence of transfusion hepatitis would be very much lower than those observed elsewhere even though commercially-supplied blood is not used in this country.

The overall mortality from post-transfusion hepatitis has been variously reported as 0.9 per cent (Allen & Sayman 1962); 2 per cent (Grossman et al. 1945); 12 per cent (Grady et al. 1964); and 27.5 per cent (Ratsoff et al. 1965). The morbidity and complications following serum hepatitis are probably similar to those which may follow infectious hepatitis, although no actual figures are as yet available for transfusion-hepatitis.

Reduction in the severity, but probably not incidence, of post-transfusion hepatitis has been reported by the prophylactic administration of gamma-globulin. However the routine use of gamma globulin with blood transfusion would rapidly exhaust the world supplies of this material. The risk of hepatitis in a recipient of blood in-

THE BRITISH JOURNAL OF CLINICAL PRACTICE

creases with the number of transfusions (Allen & Sayman 1962). In their excellent survey Creutzfeldt et al. (1966) go even further in stating that the number of units of blood transfused is the decisive factor influencing the risk of hepatitis. Sex, age, primary disorder of the patient and transaminase level of the blood donor had no significant effect on the incidence of transfusion hepatitis. Therefore reduction in the risk of hepatitis can be achieved by the judicious use of blood and the substitution of hepatitis-free blood derivatives. Note however that Mosley (1965) found that single-unit transfusions accounted for 16.9 per cent of all patients with transfusion-associated hepatitis. In the absence of specific laboratory tests for the virus of hepatitis the meticulous screening of potential blood donors and the avoidance of commercially obtained blood must continue.

Finally it should be noted that the risk of the parenteral transmission of virus hepatitis is not restricted to whole blood. Pooled human plasma carries an even higher risk than whole blood and the risk of hepatitis increases with the size of the pool. Similar observations apply to fibrinogen, and Mosley (1965) quotes the proportion of hepatitis associated with fibrinogen at 35 times greater than among patients transfused with whole blood at two large hospitals in the United States. It also appears that the attack rate of hepatitis is related to the size of the pool from which the fibrinogen is prepared. The risk with the use of antihaemophilic globulin is believed to be similar to that from fibrinogen. Thrombin also carries the risk of

transmitting hepatitis. Gamma-globulin, stable plasma protein solution, albumen, fibrin foam and plasminogen appropriately treated are free of infective hepatitis virus (W.H.O. 1964).

Any approach to the prevention and study of an infection requires initially information about the number and type of cases. Therefore, we require in this country basic epidemiological information on transfusion-hepatitis such as the incidence of the disease, the morbidity and mortality, and to be able to define the high risk patients. This can only be achieved by systematic observation and follow-up of all patients who receive transfusions of blood and blood products.

MEDICAL WORLD NEWS/November 24, 1972

# FOCUS ON THE NEWS

## FDA FINDS HOLES IN HEPATITIS SCREEN

The Russian roulette aspect of whole blood transfusion—with hepatitis as the lethal bullet—is a nightmare that physicians will have to live with for some time to come.

And for the cardiovascular surgery patient or the hemophiliac who gets large amounts of blood, there will continue to be added danger. Dr. Howard F. Taswell, director of the Mayo Clinic blood bank, has determined that out of 5,000 cardiovascular surgery patients, five, or one per 1,000, died from post-transfusion hepatitis.

To help tip the odds in favor of patients, the FDA is stepping up its

regulatory program of blood banks (www. Sept. 15). Dr. Harry M. Meyer Jr., director of the FDA's Bureau of Biologics, has just released the results of a tough test of the proficiency of banks under direct federal supervision in detecting hepatitis B antigen.

The 250 tested banks, about 5% of the total number of blood facilities in the U.S., each received a panel of 20 coded samples. Each panel contained duplicate samples of seven sera reactive for hepatitis B antigen—ranging from very strong to very weak—and six samples of nonreactive sera. With the exception of two

borderline samples, the bureau's labs were able to detect all positives by counterelectrophoresis using commercial reagents.

But granted that only 25% or 30% of hepatitis cases are Au-antigen-positive to begin with, the tested banks failed miserably in detecting the positive samples. Only 14 banks scored 100% correct in the test. An example of the inefficiency: 11 banks caught seven or fewer of the 14 positives, and two of these banks only caught four. Correct responses on individual samples ran from a low of 1.6% of the banks on weak samples, to 100% for the two strongly positive samples.

Erring on the safe side, a few banks labelled nonreactive samples as positive. Reproducibility was spotty when checked by duplicate positives—very few of the banks detected both of the very weak samples. On the other hand, 99.5% caught both very strong sera samples.

Dr. Meyer's results leave Au antigen screening programs in a tenuous position. But the bureau is taking some remedial steps. With another set of samples, FDA inspectors went to those labs that missed definitely positive sera—to observe the labs in action and detect procedural errors.

The test will be repeated periodically by the FDA to try to improve the blood screening picture.

Tuesday, June 27, 1972 65

### Blood donor clinics cut in prisons

TORONTO (CP) — A Red Cross official said yesterday blood donor clinics in most Ontario prisons have been discontinued at least temporarily because tests have revealed a high incidence of serum hepatitis in samples of prisoners' blood.

Dr. E. E. Tieman, assistant national director of blood transfusion services for the Red Cross, said it is likely that some of the clinics never will be reopened, although it is hoped most will.

He declined to give the exact number of prisons affected by the discontinuation.

Dr. Tieman said about 2,000 units of blood were collected last year from Ontario institutions, but the loss of such clinics likely would not seriously affect the overall collection of blood in the province.

The Red Cross began testing blood for serum hepatitis last year.

Dr. Tieman said such tests show the incidence of the disease to be much higher in prisons than among the general public. He said the disease — as opposed to infectious hepatitis — often is linked to the use of drugs and comes about through the use of a contaminated needle.

He indicated that the situation in Ontario appears worse than elsewhere in Canada.

TORONTO — About 22 of every 10,000 people who donate blood in Canada are capable of giving serum hepatitis to people who receive their blood, the first results of a new Red Cross screening program show.

In western Quebec, the rate rises to 47 per 10,000, and in pantotriaries, 67. The lowest rate, eight per 10,000, is found in rural areas.

SERUM HEPATITIS is a liver inflammation, often called jaundice, that is most frequently passed from person to person by either blood transfusion or the use of a hypodermic needle that hasn't been sterilized between uses by different people.

It is believed caused by a virus-like particle in the blood, called Australia antigen or hepatitis-associated antigen (HAA). HAA is in the blood of a person both before and after an attack of hepatitis, but it can also exist in carriers who never have any symptoms.

A year ago, the Red Cross started screening all its blood donations for HAA, the screening system has been extended to 16 regional centres. The Hamilton blood bank was included earlier this month.

# Pulmonary Edema Following Blood Transfusion Reaction

James P. Byrne, Jr., MD, Salt Lake City, and John A. Dixon, MD, Ogden, Utah

Severe pulmonary edema was observed in two patients following blood transfusion reactions. The amount of blood transfused was small and there was no evidence of fluid overload in either patient. The roentgenographic appearance is one of bilateral patchy infiltrates suggestive of interstitial edema. Hemolysis of erythrocytes with release of substances causing constriction of pulmonary arterioles or venules, or intravascular coagulation are possible pathophysiologic mechanisms. Therapy consists of the usual respiratory support measures. Dextran 40, heparin sodium, and isoproterenol may be of benefit.

We have recently observed the occurrence of severe and potentially fatal pulmonary edema in two patients following blood transfusion reaction. Pulmonary edema is a well-known complication following blood transfusion when it is due to overload of the intravascular compartment or embolization of particulate matter contained in the transfused blood during massive

The nail beds were cyanotic. The hematocrit value was 43%, and the white blood cell count was 17,300 cu mm. An x-ray film of the chest revealed bilateral patchy infiltrates in both lung fields with Kerley's B lines (Fig 1). Serum bilirubin level was 2.9 mg/100 ml. The urine did not contain free hemoglobin. Prothrombin time was 15 seconds for the patient and 12 seconds for the control. The platelet count was normal. Direct and indirect. Coombs' reactions were negative. The eosinophil count was normal and the serum fibrinogen level was 100 to 200 mg/100 ml (normal, > 200 mg/100 ml in our laboratory). Blood volume was 6.5 liters measured, 5.7 liters estimated normal. The patient was begun on a regimen of intravenously administered steroids and dextran 40.

He became increasingly tachypneic with respirations of 56 per minute and developed an almost continuous cough productive of copious amounts of white frothy sputum. The central venous pressure was 4 cm H₂O. The course of the blood gases is depicted in the Table. Respirations were assisted with a pressure cycled apparatus. Following blood and sputum cultures he was begun on a regimen of broad-spectrum antibiotics because of suspected pneumonia. The blood culture was negative and the sputum culture produced a scant growth of Staphylococcus aureus. The temperature returned to normal the afternoon of admission. During the next three days the x-ray films gradually cleared and the blood gases returned to normal levels (Fig 2 and 3). Gastrointestinal bleeding did not recur. The ABO and Rh typing were checked and found to be correct. It was not possible to obtain a sample of the blood given.

CASE 2.—A 16-year-old boy sustained a 32-caliber bullet wound to the left axilla. When seen in the emergency room his vital signs were normal. A rapidly expanding hematoma was apparent. There were diminished pulsations of the ulnar and radial arteries and motor and sensory loss in the median nerve distribution. The hematocrit value was 40%, and an x-ray film of the chest was normal.

The patient was taken to the operating room and the wound was explored.

The axillary artery was found to be completely transected and thrombosed. The damaged portion of artery was excised and a saphenous vein graft was placed. Two units of blood were given during operation. No problems were noted until on the fourth postoperative day when the hematocrit value was found to be 27%. Two units of blood were given. Shortly after completion of the second unit he had a severe shaking chill and developed a persistent cough productive of blood-tinged, frothy sputum. Respirations became rapid and he complained of chest pain. Auscultation of the chest revealed diffuse moist rales and wheezes. An x-ray film of the chest (Fig 4 and 5) revealed bilateral patchy infiltrates. Pulmonary emboli arising from the axillary vein were suspected but an axillary venogram was normal. Blood volume determination revealed a measured volume of 4.2 liters compared to 4.5 liters estimated normal. The patient was given heparin sodium. X-ray films of the chest 24 hours later revealed extensive clearing of the lungs and 48 hours after the reaction was almost completely clear. Five days after the reaction the x-ray film of the chest was normal and the patient was discharged.

# Comment

The criteria which suggest a type of pulmonary edema secondary to blood transfusion as an entity other than simple overload of the intravascular space are the clinical setting and the distribution of the edema on x-ray film. All of the cases reported have occurred in patients who were clearly not fluid overloaded but were hypovolemic as judged by calculation of fluid deficit, presence of orthostatic hypotension or a low central venous pressure. The x-ray film of the chest has revealed a picture of patchy infiltrates which are not perihilar as is usually seen in fluid overload or heart failure, but are present throughout the lungs. The edema is interstitial as evidenced by the presence of Kerley's B lines as in case 1.

Barnard¹ first reported the case of a leukemic patient who developed pulmonary edema following the transfusion of one unit of blood and died. He called this a hypersensitivity reaction but had no clinical or roentgenographic evidence to clearly establish the case as a new entity. Gould and Terranee² in a review of 100 cases of pulmonary edema diagnosed on x-ray film of the chest,

![img-94.jpeg](img-94.jpeg)

Fig 5.—Progressive clearing during ensuing 48 hours (case 2).

reported one case which occurred following a blood transfusion reaction. The edema was patchy throughout the lungs but they did not comment on the clinical setting. Hirsch and Caracta³ reported a patient with pernicious anemia who developed acute pulmonary edema while receiving a second unit of packed cells. The patient died and it was not possible to obtain roentgenograms or an autopsy. Philipps and Fleischner⁴ reported three cases in which the patients were clearly hypovolemic and developed pulmonary edema which was documented on x-ray film of the chest and was present throughout the lungs. Ward et al⁵ reported a similar case.

All of the cases of this syndrome so far recorded have described a similar situation; while receiving 1 or 2 units of blood the patient develops severe chills and a high fever. A cough productive of frothy sputum and tachypnea follows. There is either rapid progression to death or spontaneous resolution during three to five days.

The exact pathophysiology of this syndrome is unknown. An acute hypersensitivity response secondary to homologous blood is one of the most likely explanations. In the case reported by Ward et al,⁷ the patient developed urticaria and presumably a similar response could have occurred in the pulmonary capillaries.

CPE-51

They also found a high titer of antileukocyte antibodies in their patient's serum.

Diffuse intravascular coagulation is another etiology to be considered. Erythrocytes are known to contain large amounts of thromboplastin and hemolysis could release this factor and begin the coagulation process. As transfused blood is diluted very little before it reaches the lungs, this organ might be expected to react more actively than others. In case 1, the elevated bilirubin level suggests that hemolysis did take place and the prolonged prothrombin time and diminished serum fibrinogen level suggest that intravascular coagulation also occurred. However, a decrease in platelets was not noted. Hardaway⁴ found microthrombi and edema in the lungs of dogs dying of incompatible blood transfusions. Blaisdell et al⁹ have demonstrated the occurrence of intravascular coagulation in patients dying of post-traumatic pulmonary insufficiency secondary to interstitial edema and intra-alveolar hemorrhage. They postulate that tissue destruction causes release of tissue thromboplastin which initiates the coagulopathy.

This same mechanism may account for the "postperfusion lung" seen following use of the pump oxygenator. Grant et al¹⁰ have demonstrated increased thromboplastin in the blood of patients following cardiopulmonary bypass. Allardyce et al¹¹ have shown that microemboli occur during venovenous perfusion

in dogs and occlude the pulmonary capillaries. This did not occur with venoarterial perfusion. However, they also noted a marked decrease in the occurrence of such emboli if dextran was added to the pump prime.

Vasoconstriction is another mechanism whereby diffuse pulmonary edema may occur following transfusion reactions. In a series of experiments in sheep, Halmagyi et al¹² produced a marked increase in pulmonary arterial wedge pressure following injection of incompatible homologous and heterologous blood and various components of red blood cells. They postulate that destruction of red blood cells releases a substance which causes constriction of the arterioles and possibly also the venules. Veith et al¹³ have presented morphologic and functional evidence to show that pulmonary arteriolar constriction is the common mechanism underlying pulmonary damage secondary to shock, transfusion reaction, and pump-oxygenator procedures. Schramel et al¹⁴ and Keller et al¹⁵ noted the occurrence of hemorrhagic lung lesions following venovenous perfusion in dogs. They demonstrated increased pressure in the small pulmonary veins and suggested that venular constriction leads to engorgement and rupture of pulmonary capillaries.

Thus the basic abnormality underlying the pulmonary pathology noted in the two cases reported would appear to be obstruction to blood flow through pulmonary arte-

rioles or venules or both. Whether this is a result of microembolic phenomena or vasoactive substances is unclear. Both of these mechanisms may be operative. The lung is known to contain high concentrations of the substances necessary for fibrinolysis.¹⁶ Depending upon the efficiency of the fibrinolytic system, microemboli may not persist in some instances, thus unmasking the vasoconstrictive element.

Treatment at present is empiric and supportive with oxygen and a volume-controlled respirator. As noted, dextran may be of value as may steroids. Heparin is the accepted agent for the treatment of consumption coagulopathy and would seem to be of theoretical value. This was the only therapy given in case 2. However, there is no evidence that the intravascular coagulation which occurs in the lungs also takes place throughout the vascular space thus becoming a true consumption coagulopathy. Therefore, as Schramel et al¹⁴ point out, heparin may cause progression of the lesions. Isoproterenol may possibly be helpful and was found by Halmagyi et al¹⁵ to reverse the abnormalities of pulmonary hemodynamics associated with transfusion reaction.

# TRANSFUSIONS ARE DANGEROUS\*

BRUCE CHOWN, M.D., Winnipeg, Man.

AT LEAST HALF of all transfusions are unnecessary; personally I think the proportion is much higher than that. Every transfusion given to a girl or to a woman of child-bearing age carries a hidden threat, the threat of the death of her children. It does not matter how carefully the donor blood is selected, the threat remains.

Why do you transfuse? Why do you? Why do you? What is the proof that more than a small fraction of the blood that is daily poured into patients in the operating room alters the prognosis for the better? Blood has always had a mystical quality; its use in the operating room is more often mystical than scientific. And for women! Most transfusions given to women under the age of 45 are given in relation to pregnancy—for the bleeding associated with an abortion, with a vaginal delivery, with Caesarean section—even, God save the mark, for simple anaemia. I would hazard the guess that not 5%—no, not 1%—of transfusions so given have been life-saving. And I would hazard the guess too that at least as great a percentage has been death-dealing.

Death holds his cards close to his belly, and he plays them slowly; sometimes very slowly. So you forget. Or you don't know; you're no longer in the game when Death plays his trump. Let me tell you a story.

One day in 1951 Mrs. Schmaltz, let us call her, then three months gone in her third pregnancy, went to bed feeling well. In the night she woke to find her waters had broken, and early next morning she delivered herself of a fetus. For a day and a night she bled at home; then she went to the hospital. She was pale; her hæmoglobin was not measured. She was no longer bleeding. Next day towards noon she was taken to the operating room, curetted and, while still under the anaesthetic, given a transfusion. (Luck was with the operator; she didn't have a reaction.) Next day she felt fine and was given another transfusion, and a few days later she went home. Death played his trump card five years later when a baby was born to Mrs. Schmaltz with erythroblastosis, from which it died before it could be transfused. The erythroblastosis was not due to the Rh factor or to any of its kith or kin but to an entirely unrelated blood group system.

SPECIAL ARTICLE: TRANSFUSIONS 1057

The most careful selection of the donor blood under our present methods of selection would not have prevented the sensitization of the mother and the sequent death of the baby. And in this case there was no question of saving the mother's life; she was never in danger; the first transfusion was not given until 30 hours after admission to hospital and at least as long after bleeding had stopped; the second transfusion was given for no apparent reason. The giving of transfusions seems to be a conditioned reflex: abortion, transfusion; abortion, transfusion. So it goes. But why? Why? Let me tell you another story.

A 31-year-old woman was admitted to hospital in March 1954, suffering from an incomplete abortion. She was of a rare blood group, and, having had eight transfusions in connection with earlier abortions, had developed antibodies which reacted with the blood of almost all potential donors. While compatible blood was being sought, her blood pressure fell to 70/50 mm. Hg, her hæmoglobin from 8.5 to 5.8 g. per 100 ml. (from about 60 to about 35%). A compatible donor was found at last, but the patient had such a severe pyrogen reaction to the transfusion that it had to be stopped when 250 ml. had been given. No further transfusion was attempted: her hæmoglobin was 14 grams per 100 ml. within a month.

I tell you that story before you say to me about Mrs. Schmaltz, "It may not have been necessary to the saving of her life, but it shortened her convalescence." Did it? By how much? A week? Two weeks? Three weeks? Certainly with a bit of iron her hæmoglobin would have been up to normal within a month. And would she willingly have traded her baby's life for those few draggy weeks? Mrs. Schmaltz had changed doctors between 1951 and 1956, so the transfuser of 1951 never knew about the bad result of his "good" treatment.

I'll tell you some other stories another time.

# Special Article

# TRANSFUSION OF GIRLS AND WOMEN CAN KILL THEIR BABIES\*

A NOTE ADDRESSED MORE TO SURGEONS AND ANÆSTHETISTS, BUT APPLICABLE TO OTHERS

BRUCE CHOWN, M.D., Winnipeg, Man.

I ADDRESS THIS NOTE more to surgeons and anæsthetists than to others, although the facts are applicable to the practice of most doctors. A surgeon often knows a patient only for days, and an anæsthetist for hours or minutes; the bad effect of a transfusion that either one may give may not become apparent for years; it may never be known to the man who gave the transfusion. I illustrate by four cases, two surgical, one medical, one obstetrical or gynaecological.

In 1948 Mrs. B. had an operation for a herniated intervertebral disc, during the course of which she was given a transfusion. Neither she nor her family physician knew of this transfusion until the events of pregnancy indicated that it must almost certainly have taken place; it was then proven by the hospital record. Mrs. B.'s blood was first examined in May 1950 in the second month of her first pregnancy; it contained an anti-Rh antibody with a titre of 2. At four months the titre had risen to 256. At six months it was 1024 and the fetus died. Autopsy proved that the fetus had had erythroblastosis. In 1951 her next fetus also died.

On April 20, 1940, Adele S., aged 6, was playing round a bonfire; her clothes caught fire; she was admitted to the Children's Hospital, Winnipeg, with third-degree burns involving about two-thirds of the skin. There she remained for 125 months, during which time she received three transfusions, to the third of which, given some seven months after the first, she responded with a chill, sweating and fever. Fifteen and a half years later, on November 23, 1955, when she was in the second month of her first pregnancy an anti-Rh antibody with a titre of 1 was found in her blood. It continued at this level until three weeks before her expected date of delivery, when it rose to 256. Her attending obstetrician, Dr. J. R. Mitchell, induced labour at once. The amniotic fluid was yellow, containing 0.83 mg. of bilirubin per 100 ml. The baby, a boy weighing 5 lb. 45 oz., appeared very ill at birth. The cord blood hæmoglobin was 10.82 g., and the bilirubin 9.6 mg. per 100 ml. The baby was given four replacement transfusions in 48 hours by Dr. W. D. Bowman, and made a complete recovery; it was a close call.

When Mary N., then in her teens, had typhoid fever in 1936, she was given a transfusion of her mother's blood. She married six years later and the following year had a nice normal baby. The next year, however, she gave birth to twins, one hydropiac and the other

inaccurated. She was Rh-negative, her mother Rh-positive, her first child Rh-negative. It was eight years from the time of her transfusion to the death of her first Rh-positive babies. Seventeen years after that poisonous transfusion she lost her second Rh-positive baby, stillborn. Luckily her husband is heterozygous and can father some Rh-negative babies.

This is not written in criticism of the fact of transfusion in these cases, although the need in the first case is open to doubt. It is written to illustrate the fact that transfusion of girls or women may years later kill their babies; the time intervals between transfusion and disaster in these three cases was 2 years, 15 years and 8 years; we have been able to demonstrate Rh antibodies as long as 30 years after the last possible antigenic stimulus.

The inciting factor in each of the above cases was Rh-positive donor blood given to an Rh-negative patient. It may be objected that sensitization by this means no longer occurs. But this is not so. Mistaken typing of blood as Rh-positive or Rh-negative still occurs; a fatal transfusion reaction due to just such faulty typing was recently reported in this Journal. Beyond simple Rh-positive and Rh-negative incompatibility there are other incompatibilities. The Rh blood group system itself is complex. For example, about 20% of Rh-positive people are of such an Rh-positive subtype (CDe-CDe or R1R1) that about 80% of Rh-positive donors and practically 100% of Rh-negative ones are incompatible with them; the antibody that they are likely to develop is an anti-Rh antibody called anti-c. The following case is an illustration.

Mrs. McP., Rh-positive, suffered an accidental abortion in 1952, and, as part of her treatment, was given a transfusion of Rh-positive blood. In 1955 she gave birth to a baby who quickly became deeply jaundiced and required two replacement transfusions. The baby's erythroblastotic jaundice was due to the anti-c. Her next baby died in spite of transfusion.

I could cite you many other examples of transfusion sensitization from our files, but do I make my point? Transfusions of girls and women can kill their babies, often many years later.

# BLOOD

# TRANSFUSIONS

EVERY TIME you give a patient a blood transfusion, you're taking a chance that he'll suffer an adverse reaction. The odds are better—or worse—than one to 20. And the more blood you transfuse, the greater the chance of a reaction.

Two professors of surgery from the University of Illinois College of Medicine have arrived at these odds after reviewing the results of blood transfusion in nearly 48,000 patients. Drs. Robert J. Baker and Lloyd M. Nyhus conclude that the best way to avoid transfusion reactions is to avoid transfusion whenever possible.

But what if you find that you must give a transfusion?

Then, say the two physicians, you can at least avoid transfusing red cells unless they're needed to save the life of the patient. And never, they emphasize, use universal-donor or unmatched whole blood. "Colloid substitutes are equally effective in volume expansion and carry infinitely less risk."

And what if the patient reacts adversely to a transfusion despite these precautions?

For this not unlikely event, they recommend a three-step procedure: Stop the transfusion immediately; diagnose the precise nature of the reaction, assuming it to be hemolytic if there is any doubt; then give suitable treatment.

Dr. Baker and Dr. Nyhus have been primarily concerned with the immediate transfusion reaction, which they define as one that occurs during or within a few days after transfusion. These reactions, Dr. Baker told members of the American College of Surgeons at the annual meeting in San Francisco, are "frequently ignored by both medical and nursing staff, particularly if the reaction is transient or does not appear serious."

But according to the Illinois physicians, many of the immediate reactions are serious.

For diagnostic and treatment purposes, these reactions can be considered in three categories: those alterations in the blood that may accompany massive transfusion, sometimes called the "storage lesion"; idiosyncratic or sensitivity phenomena; and hemolytic reactions.

When you replace a major portion of a patient's blood volume over a relatively short period, there are likely to be considerable changes in the physiochemical properties of the circulating blood. Drs. Baker and Nyhus list the major changes as acidosis, hypothermia, citrate overload, hyperkalemia, hyperammonemia, coagulation defects, and a reduction in bacterial resistance.

The acidifying action of the acid

citrate dextrose solution in which blood is stored lowers the plasma pH to 6.8 in three days, and it continues to fall thereafter. If stored blood is given rapidly, the Illinois surgeons recommend that you give 44.5 mEq. of sodium bicarbonate intravenously with every five units of blood that is transfused.

Blood taken directly from the refrigerator and infused rapidly can produce a critical fall in myocardial temperature. Total body hypothermia can also increase tissue oxygen consumption, producing a further strain on the traumatized or hypovolemic patient. Warming the blood before transfusion is the obvious solution, but Dr. Baker warns against warming the blood as a unit. With this method, carbon dioxide may accumulate under pressure. Instead, he recommends in-line warming by running the blood through 15- to 20-foot lengths of plastic tubing immersed in a water bath.

Citrate overloading due to the transfusion of stored blood may affect both the myocardium and coagulation mechanisms by depleting ionized calcium. Ordinarily, you can probably transfuse one unit of whole blood every five minutes without giving additional calcium. However, infants, patients in hypothermia or shock, and those with preexisting liver damage do require calcium replacement therapy. There can be danger in giving either too much calcium or the chloride salt, especially to the hypothermic patient. But the administration of 1 gm. of calcium gluconate per liter of blood, say the Illinois doctors, "seems to be without significant hazard."

Stored blood is inevitably hyperkalemic, and the leaching of potassium from the red cells begins as early as the third day of storage. In small volumes, the amount of potassium ion infused is of little consequence. Not so for massive transfusion, especially in patients with renal insufficiency, or for multiple transfusions over a short period of time. In these cases you would be wise to request blood that is less than three days old. continued

DCRA-41

The allergic reaction is the commonest kind of transfusion reaction. In the Illinois study it occurred in one out of every 42 patients. Itching, erythema, and urticaria are the usual signs and symptoms. Sometimes there were chills and fever, not usually over 103° F., and rarely such respiratory difficulties as stridor, dyspnea, or wheezing. These effects seldom appear until more than half the unit has been transfused, sometimes not until after the transfusion has been completed.

The typical allergic skin reactions can usually be alleviated with intravenous antihistamines—Drs. Baker and Nyhus suggest 25 mg. of diphenhydramine—and epinephrine or steroids are rarely necessary. In this one instance, if this is all the reaction amounts to, it isn't necessary to stop the transfusion. But it is necessary, the Chicago clinicians note, if the patient has chills and fever and you have any doubt at all about the cause.

Less common than other reactions, but most serious of all, is the hemolytic transfusion reaction. The immediate severe reaction is usually the result of an error in crossmatching, labeling, or patient identification. Chills and fever may appear after infusion of as little as 15 to 20 ml. of blood and usually are evident by the time 100 ml. has been given. Other possible symptoms include tachycardia and pain in the chest, flank, or back.

With this reaction especially, Drs. Baker and Nyhus stress, you must stop the transfusion immediately. At the same time, take samples of the donor blood and of the patient's blood and urine and send them to the laboratory for tests to determine the causes of the reaction. Begin an intravenous infusion of 20 gm. of mannitol, 40 mg. of furosemide (Lavis, Hoechst), and usually 50 mEq. of sodium bicarbonate, preferably in 1000 ml. of dextrose or Ringer's lactate solution. And though the rationale—a theoretical modification of the antigen-antibody reaction—is unproven, the Illinois doctors recommend rapid IV injection of 500 mg. of hydrocortisone. You

can also give either isoproterenol or levarterenol (Levophed, Winthrop) to maintain tissue perfusion pressure.

Another type of hemolytic reaction is the depletion of essential coagulation elements, which can cause spontaneous bleeding. To treat this, you'll need to identify the specific defects, but the basis of treatment is administration of fibrinogen and fresh frozen plasma. If there is clot lysis, Dr. Baker recommends IV administration of 2 to 4 gm. of epsilon aminocaproic acid and adds: "Obviously, administration of fresh, compatible, rematched whole blood should be continued as needed."

Severe hypotension or shock may also be a hemolytic transfusion reaction. The mechanism is speculative, but Drs. Baker and Nyhus believe the changes can probably be reversed with IV isoproterenol, assisted ventilation, and the transfusion of compatible blood. Since pulmonary venular constriction appears to be a factor, you might try low molecular weight dextran to increase pulmonary perfusion. And, "as a last resort," give pressor agents such as levarterenol or metaraminol (Aramine, Merck Sharp & Dohme).

The Illinois study also indicates that "delayed hemolysis as a manifestation of hemolytic reaction is much more common than is realized." In these reactions, which occur after three to seven days, crossmatching may have been entirely accurate, but after infusion, the donor blood excites a rapid production of antibodies. Symptoms, if any, are usually slight, but the patient is often jaundiced and laboratory studies may reveal reticulocytosis, spherocytosis, or clumps of agglutinated red cells in the peripheral blood.

Transfusion can be lifesaving in patients who need it, and the possibility of early or late reactions is a chance you have to take. But for what Drs. Baker and Nyhus estimate to be "approximately 30% of patients" who receive transfusions that they don't need, either to save their lives or to speed their recovery, the chance simply isn't worth taking.

# LETTERS TO THE EDITOR

## BLOOD TRANSFUSION

To the Editor:

In the December 1 issue, I have just read an article by Dr. Bruce Chown of Winnipeg, regarding the danger of transfusions. This article I consider most timely, and coming from one as authoritative as Dr. Chown, it is doubly so.

I am one who had a large practice in the days before transfusions and did fairly well, I think. With the coming of transfusions a new era began, to be followed by the introduction of antibiotics. Both these are life-savers and, being new and expensive, met with immediate response by the medical profession (early in transfusion history the patient paid at least \$25.00 for a transfusion). The operation was also very dramatic and being new and expensive "must be good". So transfusion and antibiotics became everyday treatment with resultant danger from staphylococcus and antibodies.

I know of one surgeon who stated at one time that he would not do major surgery on a patient whose hemoglobin was below 70%. Just how many patients have developed hepatitis or other reactions, I do not know; perhaps he does not either.

One hospital I know of reported a greater number of transfusions for one month than had been given at the Toronto General Hospital the previous year. This was in the "key-day" of transfusions.

I hope there are fewer now. I will be looking forward to Dr. Chown's further articles.

120-121 Medical Arts Bldg., H. A. Gibson, M.D.,
Calgary, Alta., C.M., F.R.C.S.(Edin.),
December 11, 1937, F.R.C.S.(C.),

To the Editor:

I agree with Dr. B. Chown (Culvert, M. A. J., 77: 1037, 1937). Because I entered surgery before the flood of blood began, I am always amazed to see blood given for ordinary operations. It seems to be quite all right to take a pint of blood from a donor and let him walk home but wrong to lose a little blood during ordinary surgery! My belief is put into practice. In nearly 17,500 admissions to this general hospital we have not found it necessary to transduce more than a dozen times. Our mortality rates compare favourably with those of other institutions.

Dr. Chown will appreciate the article "Chance, Design, and Discovery in Medicine" by J. H. Dible, Professor of Pathology, Postgraduate School, London, England. It is found in The Postgraduate Journal, Vol. 29, at page 39. Because so many of your readers are far from libraries, perhaps you will let me quote:

"Medical progress is a study of trial and error, of false paths, of whole generations under the sway of wrong ideas leading to wrong treatment and God knows what in the way of casualties—and the old tale let goes on. A friend of mine said to me the other day. In the 18th century hundreds of people lost their lives through blood being taken out of them needlessly. Many people are being killed through blood being put into them needlessly, and I—who only that morning had seen the body of a young man, dead as the result of an incompatible blood transfusion, given after an operation of convenience—could only agree with him sadly." FRANK REGALL,

## Chapter I RELIGION, MEDICINE AND LAW

"The greatest dangers to liberty lurk in insidious encroachment by men of zeal, well-meaning, but without understanding."

BRANDERS

VERY FEW QUESTIONS, legal, religious, or medical have aroused as much concern in recent years as the cases involving the refusal of Jehovah's witnesses on religious grounds to accept blood transfusions for themselves or their children. Very often the issue becomes so surcharged with emotion that it is difficult to get a balanced view of the problem and to take into account all the relevant considerations that should be weighed. One statute has already been passed in connection with this matter and other statutory amendments have been demanded particularly in Ontario and in Saskatchewan.

The emotional view often taken of this subject would give a very quick reply: "Take the child away from the parents and let the doctors use their own judgment. They know best." In fact, the issue is not just that simple. At what point do we decide that the natural, God-given control of children by their own parents who love them and have their welfare at heart shall be overruled? Will the proposed medical discretion be confined to blood transfusion, or will professional men now be judges and masters to perform at will any operation — amputation, appendectomy, sterilization, etc.? Will their power of forced treatment be limited to therapeutic measures in which they can offer some assurance of effectiveness, or are they now getting carte blanche for unsure, dangerous and experimental treatment of unproved value? Who is going to accept liability when the "men of science" hand a corpse back to grieving parents and announce with scientific assurance that "the operation was a success, but the patient died"? What is to become of the law when the currently popular practice of blood transfusion goes the way of blood letting, sulfa drugs and

other medical practices which have enjoyed a brief fad of popularity and then disappeared? Are we prepared to accept the Nazi-Spartan theory that children belong to the state? If so, what supervision or state control is proposed to protect the people from medical abuses; or do doctors now become state officials without control and vested with unlimited discretion? Freedom of worship is guaranteed by the constitution and has been protected at great sacrifice. Does it now weigh so little in the scales of justice as to scarcely merit mention by those who in the name of "science" are prepared to trample constitutional liberties without a backward glance?

These problems are not simple. It is the function of the law to balance the claims which conflicting interests may have on its protection. This function has been well described by Mr. Justice Ivan C. Rand.

"In the structure of the law's myriad adjustments, built of the products of the reasoning mind, molding the life of the community, neutral in its nature and operation, should reside the security of the humblest citizen: security in life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, security against any attempts by the most powerful to invade his sanctities... the courts... are the special guardians of the freedoms of unpopular causes, of minority groups and interests, of the individual against the mass, of the weak against the powerful, of the unique, of the nonconformist — our liberties are largely the accomplishments of such men."

In order to deal with the "myriad adjustments" relevant to this issue and to strike a balance on them it is necessary to review this matter from the standpoint of religion and medicine, as well as law.
