# Chapter 2 THE OBJECTION OF JEHOVAH'S WITNESSES TO BLOOD TRANSFUSION IS ONE OF A NUMBER OF RELIGIOUS VIEWS THAT CONFLICT WITH CURRENT MEDICAL PRACTICE

A. Society commonly accepts the religious opinions of larger groups who decline to accept certain medical treatment, but the same tolerance is not shown toward minorities, such as Jehovah's witnesses.

Jehovah's witnesses are by no means the only religion whose opinions cause them to refuse to accept certain aspects of accepted medical practice. Other groups such as the Roman Catholics and Christian Scientists also have religious views which cause them to refuse at least some forms of medical treatment. Such refusal by these larger groups is a well-known phenomenon that both society in general and the medical profession are able to absorb with no apparent difficulty. At least one hears no great public outcry.

With respect to Jehovah's witnesses, however, though the number of cases has been very small, the highly dramatic treatment given them by the press seems to have convinced many that something new has been uncovered and we must be prepared to alter the law to cope with the situation.

Some understanding of these religious views and the resulting conflicts is essential to a proper grasp of this problem.

B. Jehovah's witnesses found their objection to the use of blood on the Bible.

Jehovah's witnesses make full use of surgery and other remedial treatment that is available. They are prepared to call in medical assistance, and to accept hospitalization or other essential treatment. Jehovah's witnesses only draw the line where the use of blood is concerned. Their point of view is entirely different from the groups who decline remedial treatment and depend on "faith healing".

It is a matter of interest in this connection that Christian objection to the use of blood is not original with the twentieth century. In the days of Roman persecution of Christians the Roman magistrates sought to ferret out believers in Christ by demanding that they consume blood. If they refused they were branded at Christians, subject for martyrdom, Tertullian, a famous Christian writer of the second century states, in addressing the Romans:

"Let your error blush before the Christians, for we do not include even animals' blood in our natural diet. We abstain on that account from things strangled or that die of themselves, that we may not in any way be polluted by blood, even if it is buried in the meat. Finally, when you are testing Christians, you offer them sausages full of blood; you are thoroughly well aware, of course, that among them it is forbidden; but you want to make them transgress."

In order to properly state the position of Jehovah's witnesses on this subject the writer has obtained an official statement from the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Pennsylvania, governing organ of Jehovah's witnesses. The view is stated as follows:

"Jehovah's witnesses are Christians. They follow the principles set out in God's Word the Bible. It is not Jewish principles but Christian principles that forbid the consumption of blood. The first council of the

Christian church held by the apostles themselves at Jerusalem issued the following ordinance as governing all the Christian congregation as recorded at the fifteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles the V. 28.29. For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things; that ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication; from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fate ye well." This powerful statement of necessary things condemns: idolatry, use of blood, use of things strangled without draining their blood, fornication. Note that in this short statement two of the four items prohibit blood. The Apostles determined these to be the necessary things for the congregations of the Christian church. These is certainly nothing temporary about the prohibition on fornication or idolatry. By the same token, the prohibition against blood is of equal permanence: "abstain from blood." It is a permanent and unchanging rule of the Christian church.

"The decision of Jehovah's witnesses to refuse blood transfusion has not been taken hastily. There is direct Biblical injunction against consumption of blood: the manner of taking it into the system is immaterial. Jehovah, the Creator, who made blood, has reserved it as sacred to himself. The blood is the life of the creature."

"From the beginning of the Scriptures, blood has been holy, reserved to God himself. This was first stated in the covenant or agreement Jehovah made with Noah immediately after the flood about 2300 B.C. — this was 855 years prior to the law given to Moses at Mount Sinai. The instruction to Noah was: 'Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you ... But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat ... Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed.' (Genesis 9:3-6) The flesh he gave to men for their consumption: the blood, the life, he reserved unto himself."

"The law given to Moses continued the principle of the sacredness of blood. It was not a dietary law, either to Noah or to the Jews. Leviticus 17:14 (AS) declares: 'For as to the life of all flesh, the blood thereof is all one with the life thereof; therefore I said unto the children of Israel, Ye shall eat the blood of no manner of flesh; for the life of all flesh is the blood thereof: whosoever eateth it shall be cut off.' Verse 13 states: 'And whatsoever man ... who taketh in hunting any beast or bird that may be eaten; he shall pour out the blood thereof, and cover it with dust.' Deuteronomy 12:23 (AS), 'Only be sure that thou eat not the blood; for the blood is the life; and thou shalt not eat the life with the flesh, Thou shalt not eat it; thou shalt pour it out upon the earth as water.'"

"The contention has been made that 'eating blood' is confined to consumption through the mouth. But if a patient is too weak to eat in the ordinary way, he is fed intravenously — nourishment is fed into his veins and he 'eats' or consumes it to sustain his body. Since intravenous feeding is eating, transfusion of blood into the veins is also eating for all practical purposes. Blood is fed into the veins for the purpose of nourishing or sustaining the body. The body consumes, 'eats' it; actually lives, maintains itself, on the blood of another. It is eating blood."

C. The beliefs of the Roman Catholic church, Christian Scientists and others cause their adherents to refuse at least some forms of medical treatment but such religious conflict with medical practice is considered quite acceptable though the result in lives lost may be much more serious than among Jehovah's witnesses.

There are a number of minority groups commonly described as "faith healers" who do not believe in any type of medical or remedial treatment. They rely on prayer and faith in the belief that this will effect the necessary remedy. Jehovah's witnesses do not accept faith healing, but are prepared to use medical treatment in general as long as blood is not involved.

By way of illustration, reference could be made to a controversy that arose in New York City in 1958. The Commissioner of Health created a religious storm when he directed medical doctors to stop disseminating birth control information and therapy in all city-owned hospitals. Since the city hospitals had patients of many different faiths there was understandably an objection to this ruling and it had to be rescinded. The Roman Catholic Archdiocese of New York condemned birth control therapy as one that "introduces an immoral practice into our hospitals which perverts the dignity and

nature of man". Doctors and nurses were reminded of "their grave obligation in conscience to in no way cooperate in such procedures." Similarly with the subject of therapeutic abortions: there are times when the continuation of pregnancy to full term will result in the death of the mother. There is also occasionally the situation where continuation to full term will result in death of mother and child both. Under such circumstances the normal medical procedure is induced abortion.

The Catholic view that the soul is more important than the body does not ordinarily accept the medical view that induced abortion may sometimes be an acceptable procedure. As stated by Lord Justice Denning, "It is simply a question of balancing the conflicting interests." In balancing these conflicting interests, it is important that fair weight shall be given to each.

(1) Family life and rights are sacred and are vital to the well-being of the nation

A very useful statement of proper legal approach to the various considerations of family, infant and community, is made by Mr. Justice Rand of the Supreme Court of Canada in Hepton v. Maat:

"It is, I think, of the utmost importance that questions involving the custody of infants be approached with a clear view of the governing considerations. That view cannot be less than this: prima facie the natural parents are entitled to custody unless by reason of same act, condition or circumstance affecting them it is evident that the welfare of the child requires that that fundamental natural relation be severed. As parens patriae the Sovereign is the constitutional guardian of children, but that power arises in a community in which the family is the social unit. No one would, for a moment, suggest that that power ever extended to the disruption of that unity by seizing any of its children at the whim or for any public or private purpose of the Sovereign or for any other purpose than that of the welfare of one unable, because of infancy, to care for himself. The controlling fact in the type of case we have here is that the welfare of the child can never be determined as an isolated fact, that is, as if the child were free from natural parental bonds entailing moral responsibility — as if, for example, he were a homeless orphan wandering at large.

"The view of the child's welfare conceives it to lie, first, within the warmth and security of the home provided by his parents; when through a failure, with or without parental fault, to furnish that protection, that welfare is threatened, the community, represented by the Sovereign, is, on the broadest social and national grounds, justified in displacing the parents and assuming their duties."

Welfare of the democratic nation itself requires respect for and maintenance of the family ties to the fullest extent. The point is well stated in Eversley on Domestic Relations:

"The relationship of parent and child is a strong and powerful tie. A proper regard for this tie is necessary for the cohesion of state as well as of family. It is a natural and necessary instinct which impels those who have brought children into the world to shield, nourish, and support them in their early years."

The very high regard in which the law holds the rights of the parents is well stated by Lord O'Hagan in Re Meads:

"The authority of a father to guide and govern the

education of his child is a very sacred thing, bestowed by the Almighty, and to be sustained to the utterness by human law. It is not to be abrogated or abridged, without the most coercive reason. For the parent and the child alike, its maintenance is essential, that their reciprocal relations may be fruitful of happiness and virtue; and no disturbing intervention should be allowed between them, whilst those relations are pure and wholesome and conducive to their mutual benefit."

The vital role of the family as recognized by our law is developed further in the case of Re Agar-Ellis, where Brett, Master of the Rolls, said:

"The father has the control over the person, education, and the conduct of his children until they are twenty-one years of age. That is the law. But the law of England has recognized the natural rights of a father not as guardian of his children but as the father, because he is the father. The law recognizes the rights of the father because it recognizes the natural duties of the father, which, if he breaks, he breaks from all that nature calls upon him to do; but if he breaks from these duties, the law may not be able to insist upon their full performance." The Master of the Rolls quoted with approval the words of Vice-Chancellor Bacon: "One of those principles (and it is the prominent one) is that this Court, whatever he its authority or jurisdiction, has no right to interfere with the sacred right of a father over his own children." It seems to me that in the word "sacred" the Vice-Chancellor has summed up all that I have endeavoured to express. The rights of a father are sacred rights because his duties are sacred duties."

Lord Justice Bowen in the same case discussed also the matter of parental discretion and the inadequacy of judicial machinery to replace it:

"Fancy the position of a child, with its father living, which the Court endeavours to bring up by judicial machinery, instead of leaving it to be brought up by parental care . . . Judicial machinery is quite inadequate to the task of educating children in this country. It can correct abuses and it can interfere to redress the parental caprice, and it does interfere when the natural guardian of the child ceases to be the natural guardian, and shows by his conduct that he has become an unnatural guardian, but to interfere further would be to ignore the one principle which is the most fundamental of all in the history of mankind, and owing to the full play of which man has become what he is.

"Now the Court must never forget, and will never forget, first of all, the rights of the family life, which are sacred . . . It is not the benefit to the infant as conceived by the Court, but it must be the benefit to the infant having regard to the natural law which points out that the father knows far better as a rule what is good for his children than a court of justice can . . . excepting cases of immorality, or where he is clearly not exercising a discretion at all, but a wicked or cruel caprice, or where he is endeavouring to withdraw from the protection of the court, which is entrusted with such protection by law, the custody of the infant. As a rule this court does not and cannot interfere, because it cannot do so successfully, or I should rather say because it cannot do so with the certainty that its doing so would not be attended with a far greater injury both to the infant itself and also to general social life . . . it is not more disagreement with the view taken by the

father of his rights and the interests of his infant that can justify the Court in interfering. If that were not so we might be interfering all day and with every family. I have no doubt that there are very few families in the country in which fathers do not at some time or other, make mistakes, and there are very few families in which a wiser person than the father might not do something better for that child than is being done by the father, who however has an authority which never ought to be slighted." (Italics added).

The foregoing statement shows clearly the recognition by the court of the important area of parental discretion in relation to the welfare of their children. Mere disagreement with the view of the father as to the interests of the child is no ground for state interference whether by the courts or Children's Aid Society. Since the law invests the parent with discretion, the parent is duty bound to exercise it according to his best judgment within the area of jurisdiction which is left to him. One might in these circumstances compare the lawful authority of the parent to the lawful authority given to any official acting within the scope of certain limited powers. Sometimes a parent will make grave mistakes, just as under the same circumstances and faced with the same human problem courts, doctors and Children's Aid officials would also make many mistakes. They may be able to interfere; but can they interfere with any certainty that their "doing so would not be attended with far greater injury to the infant and to general social life"?

Let us remember in the cases involving sick children—the parent did not make him sick. The parent was faced with an emergency decision in relation to the child's health. No one could guarantee what the result would be of the various possible forms of treatment offered. The parent did not abandon his discretion by refusing to take any treatment or refusing to call in such skilled help as he could find. However, having called in skilled help, he still had a duty as the person in authority to decide what form of treatment he would allow to be administered by his agent, i.e., the doctor.

The cases involving "faith healers" i.e., those who refuse remedial treatment of any kind for their children are really a complete abandonment of parental discretion. When parents abandon their function the state as parens patriae is entitled to enter. Jehovah's witnesses accept their parental responsibility and call in medical aid. They exercise their lawful discretion in determining what treatment they will accept.

A useful illustration of the problem of making a medical decision on behalf of an infant will be found in the case in In Re Hudson. In that case the child had a badly deformed arm which was developing much beyond the normal size of such member and was damaging the health of the child. The doctors wanted to amputate the arm, but the parents refused to agree to this suggestion.

The court considered the law in great detail and came to the conclusion that:

"The weight of authority is to the effect that in determining whether he will submit to an operation involving danger and uncertainty the injured person may exercise his judgment. In the case of a minor child the exercise of judgment in the matter of submission of the child to an operation involving danger and uncertainty is indubitably that of the natural guardian of the child if the natural guardian has not been displaced because of unfitness as a guardian."

Similarly blood transfusion is an operation of danger and uncertainty. Parents have a perfect right to refuse it if they think it is not in the interests of their child's welfare. The uncertainty of this matter has been admitted by Dr. Arthur Kelly, secretary of the Canadian Medical Association.

Dr. Kelly disagreed with those who seek to force this type of treatment:

"Patients and parents have a perfect right to accept or reject treatment offered. No doctor can be positive that a person will die if he doesn't get a transfusion or live if he does . . . The principle is an important one relating to the liberty of citizens. The same thing applies to any other medical treatment, and right or wrong, people have a right to decide."

Another American case in point is Re Tuttendario. There a society for care of children, without consent and over protest of parents, sought authority of the court for an operation considered necessary. The petition of the society was dismissed. The court said:

"We have not yet adopted as a public policy the Spartan rule that children belong, not to their parents, but to the state. As the law stands, the parents forfeit their natural right of guardianship in cases where they have shown their unfitness by reason of moral depravity. Even if the law had advanced so far as to consider defective judgment of parents in a critical case a good reason for depriving them of their guardianship, we would not be prepared to say that a clear case of defective judgment has been here made out. The science of medicine and surgery, notwithstanding its enormous advances, has not yet been able to insure an absolute correct diagnosis in all cases, and still less an absolute prognosis. There is always a residuum of the unknown, and it is this unknown residuum which scientists, by a necessary law for the development of science, disregard, but which parents, in their natural love for their children, regard with apprehension and terror. Cases are not unknown in which patients, apparently in defiance of logical reasoning, die within a few days after having been successfully operated on. Scientifically considered, such catastrophes merely establish the high average of successful operations and demonstrate the average safety of the patients who undergo them. The law of average, however, is of no benefit to the exceptional individual who succumbs. For him there is no longer a percentage of chances. His loss is total. It is this contingency which every adult person weighs whenever a serious operation is to be performed and no one has ever questioned his legal right to decide the question for himself. When, however, infants are concerned, the choice must be exercised by their guardians. In the case before us, the parents fear that the operation will result in their child's death. There is ever present in their minds the fact that of ten children born to them seven died at an early age. It may be neither absurd nor illegal to argue from this that there is an inherent constitutional weakness in the family which increases the peril of a serious operation and tends to put the patient in the class of those who succumb. At all events, such a conclusion is not so patently wrong that a court would or ought to interfere with it."

The science of medicine is unsure and the percentage of contingency that may satisfy a doctor or public official is not an adequate criterion for overruling the decision of a parent. To break down family control and responsibility by the substitution of official discretion that can assure nothing at all is to hold the family too lightly in the scale of justice. It is tearing at the fabric of democratic society to no good end.

(ii) Welfare of the child requires that it remain as part of the family

In the eye of the law, the welfare of the child is bound up with the maintenance of the family circle, unless the considerations are very, very serious. As stated above by Mr. Justice Rand, "The welfare of the child can never be determined as an isolated fact, that is, as if the child were free from natural parental bonds entailing moral

responsibility . . . The view of the child's welfare concedes it to lie, first, within the warmth and security of the home provided by his parents . . ." The family, with all its limitations, be they economic, cultural, educational or scientific, is still the God-given and legally recognized forum for the raising and training of our future citizens. The state and public officials may have more money, and may have more wisdom and scientific knowledge, but when it comes to the field of love, warmth and often down-to-earth common sense, public officials, especially in minor capacities, by no means distinguish themselves. The child is still better off with the warmth and security of the family circle. The adjustment and balance that can only come from family life can never be replaced by even the best-run institution. Our law has recognized these principles in declaring the rights of the family, and of the father, to be "sacred".

The proper place for the child is in the family, the backbone of all orderly government. The family is to democracy what life is to the human body. Drain away the warm family relationship and substitute the cold foster-parental care of the government, and democracy will perish as surely as does the body without breath. If the individual in a democracy is to retain his integrity, the family relationship must not be impaired by misapplied laws. The strength of the nation depends on the security of the family and family life.

A useful statement of the true principle of the family and the state was made by Mr. Justice Rivard in Hirsch v. Protestant School Commission:

"The child does not belong to the state; it belongs to the parents. Theirs is the inalienable right and the imperative duty of raising and educating the child. The state intervenes only for the purpose of creating media of education, organizing, subsidizing, assisting and protecting the school, controlling the use of funds which it assigns to such, inviting parents to fulfill their duty and filling in any lack in extreme cases of negligence and abandonment, but without ever encroaching on the rights of the father of the family and always subordinating its actions to such rights. The state assists the family, says Portalis, and does not supplant it."

This view of the law is certainly in conflict with the thinking of minor officials of the Children's Aid and the members of the medical profession who wish to be placed in a position that their decisions can override those of the parents. It has been publicly stated by certain of these officials that "children belong to the state".

The idea that children are the property of the state may be new to democratic thinking but it is not a new or original thought. Lycurgus, dictator of Sparta about the 5th century B.C., had the same idea. Sentiment was not going to rule him, but only scientific wisdom and the welfare of the state.

Plutarch's Lives tells us,

"Lycurgus considered children not so much the property of their parents as of the state, and therefore he would not have them begot by ordinary persons but by the best men in it. In the next place, he observed the vanity and absurdity of other nations where people study to have their horses and dogs of the finest breed they can procure, either by interest or money, and yet keep their wives shut up that they may have children by mine but themselves, though they may happen to be doting, decrepit, or infirm."

Lycurgus was not the only dictator who thought children belonged to the state. The Nazi dictator Adolph Hitler had exactly the same idea. He determined to raise children scientifically also as part of his "Master Race" theory. He was not interested in bumbling, time-wasting, unscientific family life as is practiced in the democratic states. This operation of science was discussed in the Canadian Doctor by the executive editor:

"In other countries the thin end of the wedge, with all good intent, has divided the individual from his right, by placing the state's right and scientific 'advancement' before the individual's inalienable right to live and worship according to his conscience before God.

"We witnessed, if we cast our eyes back to the Nazi era, the debasement of human right for 'Master Race' ideals, yet, if we take away the right of parents to choose the spiritual life for themselves and their children, whatever the cost, are we not approaching the thinking of those who, under the Nazi system, and under the guise of medical and scientific enlightenment took boys away from their parents, to train them for the 'Hitler Youth', or young girls to use them for breeding, out of wedlock, in a medically supervised environment, where all parents' training, love and faith were withheld from them, to their eventual destruction, morally and spiritually?"

Children have a God-given right to the protection of their own parents and to the loving care that can only come with the family. Official interference can easily result in meddling, harmful alike to the child, the family and the state.

(iii) Welfare of the community requires that family life be kept strong

The democratic state as parens patriae has through its courts always recognized its own limitations so far as custody and control of children is concerned. Democracy recognizes the worth, the intelligence and the responsibility of individual citizens and hence their right to control their own families.

The basic principle is well stated by Mr. Justice Rand in Boucher v. The King where he said:

"If we conceive of the governors of society as superior beings, exercising a Divine mandate, by whom laws, institutions and administrations are given to men to be obeyed, who are, in short, beyond criticism, reflection or censure upon them or what they do implies either an equality with them or an accountability for them, both equally offensive . . . the administrators of what we call democratic government have come to be looked upon as servants, bound to carry out their duties accountable to the public."

While our elected political leaders are, or should be, conscious of their true position in relation to the public, such consciousness does not always manifest itself in the case of minor officials. They may not realize that paternalism and interference in private affairs erodes away the personal responsibility of the people. This is destructive of democracy. It is damaging to the nation itself.

The comparative obscurity of the proceedings of minor officials in dealing with family affairs opens the door to oppression which the law would never knowingly countenance. Consider the warning of Mr. Justice Jackson of the United States Supreme Court in Barnette v. West Virginia State Board of Education:

"Such Boards are numerous and their territorial jurisdiction often small. But small and local authority may feel less sense of responsibility to the Constitution, and agencies of publicity may be less vigilant in calling it to account . . . There are village tyrants as well as village Hampden, but none who acts under color of law is beyond reach of the Constitution . . .

"The very purpose of a Bill of Rights was to withdraw certain subjects from the vicissitudes of political controversy, to place them beyond the reach of majorities and officials and to establish them as legal principles to be applied by the courts. One's right to life, liberty, and property, to free speech, a free press, freedom of worship and assembly, and other fundamental rights

These points are equally applicable to the problem under consideration. Officials demand that acceptance of blood transfusion shall be the orthodox, officially approved thinking. If one dares not to conform he becomes classified as a heretic. The "Big Brother" mentality cannot stand those who will not conform.

But it is a free people living under constitutional liberties that have made this country what it is. A citizen has been able to raise his family in security free from the pressures of required orthodoxy to any field of thought or opinion. The present pretext of breaking into the family circle under guise of doing good is specious. (iv) A child loved, controlled and cared for can never be a neglected child in any sense of the term

In this matter the statutory provisions speak of a "neglected child" as one where the state can take steps as parens patriae to protect the infant. When, however, a child is maintained in a home where the parents show it love, care, kindness as well as proper control and instruction, is there any substantial ground for holding it can be a neglected child?

"Neglect" is defined by Webster as "negligence, habitual want of regard". When parents seek, according to their best judgment to do what is for the welfare of their child, the dispute can only centre around official disagreement with the methods employed by the parents. There is no real neglect, no "habitual want of regard".

In the field of medical treatment, it may be recalled that at common law there was at one time no obligation on parents to obtain medical treatment of any kind. In certain cases children whose parents believed in faith healing had been allowed to die by their parents without any treatment at all but the parents were still acquitted of manslaughter.¹⁴

Following the acquittal in Reg. v Wagstaffe the British Parliament enacted the Poor Law Amendment Act,¹⁵ which placed a duty on the parents to provide proper medical service. The first case after the enactment of this statute was in 1875, Reg. v Downes.¹⁶ In that case the child had died without treatment and the parent was convicted of manslaughter because of the legal duty created by the statute. Subsequent cases have followed substantially the Downes case.¹⁷

Following the Poor Law Amendment Act above referred to (and our Canadian Child Welfare Legislation is substantially to the same effect) there is no doubt a duty on parents to obtain medical or other therapy that they regard as helpful or useful for their child. Parents no longer have a discretion to decide that they will have no medical treatment for their children. Complete refusal of treatment is an abandonment of parental discretion and duty. Such abandonment of duty makes it proper for the state as parens patriae to interfere. But such is not the case of Jehovah's witnesses. They do call in and use any treatment they regard as valuable to their children and spare no expense. At the same time, there still remains vested in them as parents an area of discretion. When different forms of therapy and healing are available parents must decide which one they will accept for their own children. As admitted by Dr. Kelly supra, "No doctor can be positive that a person will die if he doesn't get a

blood transfusion or live if he does". Because of this uncertainty the law wisely leaves the decision with the parents. If public officials or medical doctors, even with the best intentions, become entirely free and uncontrolled in their decisions relating to people's children, then the result in the long run can be much more damaging than the occasional mistakes that are made now. Parents may choose therapy that will result in the child's death or may refuse therapy that could perhaps give life. Doctors also can and do make erroneous decisions with equally fatal results. The law has placed the discretion as well as the responsibility in these matters with the parents, when it should be.

The state as parens patriae can interfere when it becomes necessary. The circumstances which ordinarily call for official action are set out in the child welfare legislation of the various provinces. The Child Welfare Act of Ontario¹⁸ is typical of such legislation. Provision is made for the Children's Aid Society to take custody of a "neglected child" defined as a child "who is an orphan and who is not being properly cared for;" "where the guardian is dead, ill, or in prison;" "living in an unfit or improper place;" "found begging or loitering in a public place after 9 p.m.;" "who is delinquent or incorrigible under circumstances tending to make him idle or dissolute;" "who is emotionally rejected . . . sufficient to endanger his emotional and mental development;" "a child whose life, health and morals may be endangered."

All these examples of abandonment, loitering, living in an improper place or with improper associates, begging, etc. — these are cases of neglect. It is to cover such circumstances of actual neglect that the statute is designed. Confined to such circumstances it can be very useful. So far as dealing with these situations, public agencies such as the Children's Aid fill a valuable function. It is when they leave the field of real neglect and get into the area of pretended neglect as a means of thought control that they leave their proper orbit and the door to abuses is opened. That is what is happening in the blood cases. It is a distortion of the law to pretend that loving parents such as Jehovah's witnesses who give their child and its welfare first place in their home are neglectful, showing "habitual want of regard". The neglect must be ejusdem generis with abandonment, begging and other instances of actual negligence to be within the statute.

The provision under which most of the Ontario cases have been taken is section 11 (1) (e) sub par. (x) of the Child Welfare Act which defines a "neglected child" as "a child when the person in whose charge he is neglects or refuses to provide or secure proper medical, surgical or other remedial care or treatment necessary for his health or well-being, or who refuses to permit such care or treatment to be supplied to the child when it is recommended by a duly qualified medical practitioner".

The point for determination in sub paragraph (x) is: What is proper medical treatment necessary for health or well-being? Some people have had the experience of going to several different doctors and of having been given completely different remedies by each. Under such circumstances, what is "proper medical treatment"? Each of these men giving different opinions and perhaps a different diagnosis of the cause of the trouble is a "duly qualified medical practitioner".¹⁹ How many different recommendations must a parent adopt before he has provided "proper medical treatment"? Or has the parent already made his child a "neglected" child by virtue of disagreeing with the first doctor and seeking the advice of others?

Suppose a situation where an enthusiastic young intern, being a "duly qualified medical practitioner" believes that a child should have a serious operation or have an in-

Some medical doctors quite properly object to the whole principle of trying to force their services on the people. Doctor patient relationship is too important to be upset by bureaucratic impatience with people.

A prominent British surgeon, T. T. Higgins, writes in The Times, London:⁴²

"However neatly surgery may be streamlined, most parents will still be averse to operations on their children. I share their aversion both as a parent and as a surgeon, but until better ways emerge operations upon children will be necessary, sometimes urgently so. It is for the surgeon to explain, persuade, and convince, his privilege to inspire trust and confidence. His task may on occasion be difficult, even exasperating; he may encounter ignorance, panic, religious scruples, half-baked so-called scientific knowledge — antipathetic bias of every kind. His patience may be sorely tried, yet he must persevere with simple explanations of the inescapable facts and with understanding sympathy. His highest reward is public faith in his judgment and integrity.

"To introduce into this delicate relationship the threat of official coercion as a final alternative to intimate personal persuasion may be legalistically convenient, but it is surely unwise. Is it really necessary?"

Note too the comment of Doctor Arthur Kelly, general secretary of the Canadian Medical Association, speaking in a personal capacity.

"It is perhaps better that the odd person die rather than the fundamental human right of refusing medical treatment because impaired. Doctors who take a reasonable view of their profession know they are not God. Accordingly disagreement with them is not an offence and a child is not a "neglected child" because the parent does so disagree.

A balanced warning on this subject is voiced by an editorial in The Times, London, showing the danger of exchanging parental discretion for official-medical discretion:

"The argument is compelling but not conclusive. Not all cases in which parents may differ with the hospital authorities are of the straightforward kind which is chosen as a model for the purposes of persuasion. There may be a difficult reckoning of risks and probabilities concerning which enthusiastic surgical opinion may argue one way and a parent's more general concern another. Again, the parent's objection may not always be one of principle: he may for good or bad reasons distrust that particular hospital; or his objection may be based on a deep, though unscientific, understanding of the child

and on his responsibility for its future, neither of which is shared by the doctors recommending an operation. Even if it is conceded that there are rare cases in which the court might properly intervene, the exercise of the discretion opens up dangerous possibilities of misapplication."⁴⁴

The possibility of an occasional useful decision is greatly outweighed by the many cases where official authority would be open to abuse. Let us not forget: "Doctors, like the rest of us, have to learn by experience; and experience often teaches in a hard way."⁴⁵ We are still a long way from medical infallibility.

Quite apart from misconstruction and misapplication of Child Welfare legislation, there is also the problem of procedure that leaves much to be desired. Under the Ontario legislation, for example, the determination of whether or not a child is neglected comes under Section 11 (1)(d) of the Child Welfare Act which allows the decision to be made by a county or district judge, a magistrate or a judge of a juvenile and family court. Since the latter officers are at times not trained lawyers and may not have the qualifications for serious judicial decision, the family courts sometimes become not much more than a rubber stamp for medical opinion. In effect a medical doctor makes the decision and the courts merely approve. In one case in which the writer acted there was disagreement among the doctors as to the necessity of a blood transfusion. The child's own doctor thought it was unnecessary. Two other doctors at the hospital thought it was. The family court judge was still prepared to award custody to the Children's Aid.

A section of the Child Welfare Act, Ontario, which appears to give protection to the parent in Section 16(4). The protection is illusory; unfortunately the section is honored more in the breach than in the observance. It provides: "The judge shall not proceed to hear or dispose of the matter until he is satisfied that any municipality that may be made liable to pay the rate in respect of the child has had reasonable notice of the hearing and that the parent or the person having the actual custody of the child has had reasonable notice of the hearing or that every reasonable effort has been made in the opinion of the judge to cause them to be notified." (Italics added)

It would seem normal as a matter of statutory construction that when the legislature provides for "reasonable notice" of the hearing in relation to a legal proceeding that there should be some opportunity for the parents to be prepared and to be represented. The words "reasonable notice of hearing" get very cavalier treatment in these proceedings. In some cases in Ontario provincial police cars rush the father to court and commence the proceedings forthwith without allowing him time to even communicate with his legal representative. This is what is known as "reasonable notice". In some cases there has been a categorical refusal to allow counsel time to attend even though this would not take more than two or three hours. The term "neglected child" gets very elastic treatment under these circumstances.

A proper legal statement of what the law and procedure should be is made by Mr. Justice Middleton in Re Chiemelowski:⁴⁶

"A parent's rights to the custody and upbringing of the child are sacred and not easily lost, and as a matter of general policy ought to be given effect save in unusual circumstances . . . the state steps in, and after due judicial inquiry, if the child is found to be in fact a neglected child, it is made a ward of the Children's Aid Society."

Magistrate O'Brien, of Wakefield, England, has written a warning against the "subtle tyranny" that can arise from the use and judicial extension of this type of legislation.⁷¹

"Your leading article on March 16 about the intention of the Sheffield Regional Hospital Board to use judicial procedures to circumvent a parent's refusal to consent to medical or surgical treatment for his child raises an issue of the first importance.

"The welfare state has brought into existence procedures by which the natural rights of parents over their children can be encroached upon out of the highest motives. Those of us who are magistrates are constantly under the temptation to assume that we know better than deviant parents and others how their children should be looked after; and social workers, too, are inclined to assume that their institutional homes are better than the apparently dreary and unattractive homes of difficult parents. The powers we possess are excellent in themselves, but their abuse can lead to a new and subtle form of tyranny over an awkward minority. This is most likely to happen where magistrates are keen and knowledgeable in their work and where social workers are efficient in interpreting the statutes and wishes of local authorities. Thus efficiency can be its own danger in this particular field.

"It is up to all of us—and especially, perhaps, magistrates—to resist any attempts whatsoever to extend our judicial powers at the expense of the proper rights of parents to decide their own affairs, subject to the community's need to protect itself and its citizens from the consequences of gross maltreatment and neglect."

It is perhaps not inappropriate to recall that there are still funerals being held every day despite the services of doctors, including blood transfusions. Patients still die. This is no answer to grieving parents. They are the real losers.

Some interesting questions of liability may arise, when, lacking adequate indications for it, a blood transfusion is administered with fatal results. Will the doctor be liable? Will the Children's Aid officials be liable? Will a lower court judge be liable if he has carelessly made an order on inadequate investigation? Other serious operations besides blood transfusion can have a similar tragic result and these difficulties can easily arise under such loosely drawn legislation.

In the light of these considerations it is submitted that community interests are certainly not being served by further impairing the rights of the parents. These "neglected child" provisions in the above statutes and others like them should be confined to neglected children in the ordinary sense of the word, i.e., those who are unfed and uncared for and abandoned. It is a distortion of the true intent and purpose of this statute to use it to force upon people a particular type of medical therapy to which they object, although they have called in and are prepared to provide any other form of medical attention for their children. "Proper medical treatment" is not necessarily confined to one single form of therapy. The parents provide hospitalization, medical treatment, surgery, etc. Such treatment is obviously "proper". To support the theory of the Children's Aid in these cases, it is necessary to rewrite the statutes and to place a duty on the parents to provide "every form of medical treatment" instead of "proper medical treatment". When medical opinion is uncertain about blood transfusion where is there any logic in the law making it certain? The law would become only gratuitous tyranny. Doubly damaging is the abandonment of due process of law in the streamlining of procedure and the abdication of the judicial function by judges who merely rubber-stamp medical opinion, this, in effect, making the doctor judge in his own case.

(v) Freedom of Worship and Its Preservation Is a Vital Right of the Individual, of the Family and of the State

This vital constitutional right cannot be weighed lightly in the scales of law and justice. As this is a religious issue that affects the individual, the family and the nation, proper weight and consideration must be given to the important feature of freedom of worship. It is one of the foundation principles of the life and the fibre of a free people.

No one's freedom is any safer than that of the most unpopular citizen. If the law reaches out to destroy and disrespect the religious liberty of Jehovah's witnesses, the freedom of others will quickly be jeopardized both by this proposed change in the law and by the precedent created. It is the function of the law to see issues of principle and to adhere to them rather than to abandon them in favour of expediency. The point has been stated by Mr. Justice Rand,

"It is not sufficient to define freedoms: they must be secured to every citizen without preference or discrimination. A rule of law is to be contradistinguished from the rule of man's despotism; . . . it is the rule of principle as against expediency. It admits of no concession or compromise . . ."

It is not when religious liberty is destroyed that forces which respect the constitutional principles must rally. It is at the beginning of these encroachments. Mr. Justice Sutherland sounded the warning in Associated Press v N.L.R.B.:

"Do the people of this land—in the providence of God, favored, as they sometimes boast, above all others in the plenitude of their liberties—desire to preserve those so carefully protected by the First Amendment: liberty of religious worship . . .? If so, let them withstand all beginnings of encroachment. For the saddest epitaph which can be carved in memory of a vanished liberty is that it was lost because its possessors failed to stretch forth a saving hand while yet there was time."

Religious liberty has been determined by the Supreme Court of Canada to be a principle of utmost importance

to the nation. In _Saumur v. Quebec_$^{24}$ it was stated by Mr. Justice Rand.

'The Christian religion, its practices and profession, exhibiting in Europe and America an organic continuity, stands in the first rank of social, political and juristic importance . . . From 1760, therefore, to the present moment religious freedom has, in our legal system, been recognized as a principle of fundamental character; and although we have nothing in the nature of an established church, that the untrammeled affirmations of religious belief and its propagation, personal or institutional, remain as of the greatest constitutional significance throughout the Dominion is unquestionable.'

The guarantees of religious liberty in Canada were written into the law in 1852 prior to Confederation, but pursuant to section 129 of the British North America Act this guarantee of freedom is still part of the law of Canada. The statute is entitled, 'An Act Respecting Rectories'$^{25}$ and provides as follows:

'WHEREAS the recognition of legal equality among all Religious Denominations is an admitted principle of Colonial Legislation; and whereas in the state and condition of this Province, to which such principle is peculiarly applicable, it is desirable that the same should receive the sanction of direct Legislative Authority, recognizing and declaring the same as a fundamental principle of our civil polity: Be it therefore declared and enacted by the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Legislative Council and of the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Canada, constituted and assembled by virtue of and under the authority of an Act passed in the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and intituled, An Act to re-suite the Provinces of Upper and Lower Canada, and for the Government of Canada, and it is hereby declared and enacted by the authority of the same. That the free exercise and enjoyment of Religious Profession and Worship, without discrimination or preference, so as the same be not made an excuse for acts of licentiousness, or a justification of practices inconsistent with the peace and safety of the Province, is by the constitution and laws of the Province allowed to all Her Majesty's subjects within the same.'

Mr. Justice Locke stated in the _Saumur_ case.$^{26}$

'The right in the free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship without discrimination or preference, subject to the limitations expressed in the concluding words of the first paragraph of the statute of 1852, existed at the time of the enactment of the British North America Act and was not a civil right of the nature referred to under Head 13 in Section 92 of the British North America Act.'

These judicial statements establish free exercise of worship as something that comes not by recent statutory provision but is actually an inherent liberty coming down from the common law of England.

In the case of _Chaput v. Romain_$^{27}$ there was before the Supreme Court of Canada a case where a number of policemen of the Quebec Provincial Police had interfered with a religious service of Jehovah's witnesses. The Supreme Court of Canada, in a unanimous time to nothing verdict, imposed damages on the police for this abuse of their authority. Mr. Justice Taschereau of the Supreme Court said:

'In our country there is no state religion. All religions are on an equal footing, and Catholics as well as Protestants, Jews and other adherents to various denominations, enjoy the most complete liberty of thought. The conscience of each is a personal matter and the concern of nobody else. It would be distressing to think that a majority might impose its religious views upon a minority, and it would also be a shocking error to be-

believe that one serves his country or his religion by denying in one province, to a minority, the same rights which one rightly claims for oneself in another province. In the circumstances of the present case, the preacher was only expounding religious doctrines in which he believed, which may have been opposed to the views of the majority of the citizens of the locality, but the opinion of a minority is entitled to the same respect as that of the majority.'

It will be noted that the statutory guarantee of religious liberty provides that it shall be 'without discrimination or preference' unless the practices are 'inconsistent with the peace and safety of the Province'. Religious liberty is placed on such an important basis that there must be no interference with it unless the free exercise of it would interfere with the peace and safety of the province itself. Anyone desiring to trench upon the vital freedom of religious liberty must show a very strong case. This is similar to the test suggested by Mr. Justice Holmes that there must be a 'clear and present danger'$^{28}$ to the welfare of the state before there is justification for destroying constitutionally guaranteed liberties. In the present instance there is nothing that in any way approaches a danger to the public weal. Under the circumstances, provincial legislation seeking to take away the liberty of a minority to make decisions founded upon its religious views would be unconstitutional. The province has no power to trench in this field but must leave it to Parliament, if indeed, even the federal authority has power to interfere with this right.

That religious liberty includes control and training of one's children is clear from _Chabot v. Lamourautière_,$^{29}$ where the Quebec Court of Appeal held that Roman religious training was unenforceable so far as Protestant children were concerned. Mr. Justice Pratt said, at page 802:

'On this subject it appears useful to recall that the right to give one's children the religious education of one's choice, like freedom of conscience, is anterior to positive law . . . In the one, _Re Agar-Ellis v. Lascelles_ (1878), 10 Ch. D. 49, at page 58, Sir Richard Malins, V.C., cited with approval the following words of another judge, Lord O'Hagan (_In Re Meades_ (1871), I. R. 5 E. Q. 98 at 103): 'The authority of a father to guide and to govern the education of his child is a very sacred thing bestowed by the Almighty, and to be sustained to the uttermost by human law. It is not to be abrogated or abridged, without the most coercive reason.''

Even those who support the idea of invading the family and the religious liberty of the family will often admit that this is an invasion of freedom. There has never been an invasion of religious liberty yet that its proponents could not justify on good humanitarian and patriotic ground.

'Courts may decide whether the public welfare is jeopardized by acts done or omitted because of religious belief; but they have nothing to do with determining the reasonableness of the belief. # B. A Review of Some of the Cases

It was recently stated by the Attorney General of Ontario that the procedure under the Child Welfare Act has worked "reasonably satisfactorily." He said also: "Any government should move slowly before putting in the hands of someone outside a family the complete right to exercise judgment about a child's health." How satisfactory is the law? Let us consider what is really happening in these cases.

The case that appears to have attracted the most attention in Canada is that of 14-year-old Donald Holland of Neepawa, Manitoba. It was as a result of this that new legislation was introduced in the province of Manitoba as already stated. Donald Holland was accidentally shot in the thigh by a .22 calibre rifle on his father's farm on November 4th, 1958. The femoral artery was severed but the surgeon in charge tied this off and for a time the boy seemed to make satisfactory progress, but he died ten days later. The day before his death the Children's Aid Society of Winnipeg sought to gain custody in order to give him a blood transfusion but the case was adjourned till the following day and during this period Donald Holland died.

The press impliedly accused the parents of this child of having caused his death. This was the view left with the public. Some doctors, however, were prepared to admit it was just not true.

Dr. H. Angus Boright of Montreal said in a letter to the Montreal Gazette:

"I would take exception to the article printed in The Gazette under the headline 'Denied blood by faith, boy dies of wounds.' This statement would seem to imply that had the boy received blood, his life would have

been saved. Perhaps such an implication is unfair to both the parents and the Jehovah's Witness sect in general . . . By implication the story suggests that the loss of blood was largely responsible for the boy's death, yet, although the accident occurred on Nov. 4, he did not die until Nov. 14. Such an interval is strong evidence against the likelihood that blood loss alone was responsible, for if such were the case death would have occurred shortly after the accident . . . blood transfusion per se would not necessarily have altered the ultimate course . . . The loss of a son is one thing not to be accused publicly (by inference) of partial responsibility for that death is the inhumane act of an irresponsible press."

Instead of the unquestioning assumption that the Holland child died for lack of blood transfusion, Doctor Boright shows that there is a very serious question about this. The assumption was unfair both to the parents and to Jehovah's witnesses. It was following this case that the provincial legislature passed the amendment analyzed under part IV of this study.

Strangely enough, at Edmonton, Alberta, there was a similar accident at the very same time, when another teenage child was shot in the leg. Her parents were not Jehovah's witnesses and much blood was transfused. She died anyhow. There were no headlines and no public outcry that blood transfusion be abolished.

A case in Toronto contemporaneous with that of Donald Holland was that of the child Lori Lynn Campbell, born at Newmarket, Ontario, on Monday, December 8, 1958. This baby was born with Rh blood incompatibility. A real wave of hysteria was whipped up by the press. One Toronto newspaper carried five large articles on blood transfusion in one day.

Saturday afternoon with law offices mostly closed, a sudden hearing was fixed. The father received one hour and fifteen minutes' notice to get from Newmarket, thirty-five miles, to the trial. The trial was held before a family court judge, known de jure as Judge Stewart, a former clergyman who had never been a lawyer. It is difficult to conceive a situation where injustice was more likely; an important religious-legal issue on trial before a clergyman whose whole background could only predispose him against the parents.

In another case involving baby Deborah Morris at Windsor, Ontario, there was a question of anaemia in a young child two months old, a premature baby. The doctors who sponsored the application of the Children's Aid Society were discharged from the case and a new doctor brought in. The latter was of opinion that the child had a good chance of survival without any blood transfusion. With the doctors disagreeing among themselves, the trial judge was still prepared to make the order. However, there was a delay and during this time the father, an American citizen, took the child out of the jurisdiction. Ultimately the child died anyhow in the United States but the autopsy revealed that there was an actual congenital deformity no amount of blood transfusion would have cured.

Following autopsy Dr. Oliver W. Hatterman of Columbus, Ohio, wrote the following statement for the parents:

"The untimely death of Deborah Morris was due to a congenital anomaly of the vascular supply of the kidneys as determined by autopsy. It is apparent from this finding that transfusion would not have been of any material benefit in influencing the ultimate outcome."

There have been a number of other cases of both children and adults, some of which are helpful in illustrating what really happens from a practical standpoint. At Reading, Pennsylvania, an interesting situation arose

Another case that caused considerable interest was that of seventeen-year-old Donna Jones of Hamilton. She had suffered from periodic internal bleeding from childhood and was in the Hamilton Hospital for treatment. Newspaper headlines proclaimed she was 'dying for her faith'; certain doctors announced they would see she got a blood transfusion, even against her will and that of her parents. After much publicity on the subject, Donna recovered without any blood transfusion. A week later she walked out of the hospital carrying her own suitcase. There were no front-page headlines that day.

A great deal of publicity also resulted from the case of Thryle G. Foster of Fredericton, N.B. Mr. Foster was travelling to New York in July, 1958, to attend the Divine Will International Assembly of Jehovah's Witnesses, which drew 253,000 people. Mr. Foster was involved in a serious accident in Connecticut which resulted in considerable loss of blood. He refused blood transfusion. It was stated he was 'committing suicide', 'undoubtedly going to die because of his foolish decision', 'could not survive', etc. The medical view seemed to be that there was no question he was going to die. Some weeks later, the 'amazed physicians' saw him leave the hospital well on the road to recovery and return to his home.

Interesting aspects of this subject are revealed by some of the decided cases.

In _Nevolayff v. General Hospital_$^{44}$ the hospital was sued after an intern entered the wrong room and gave blood to a patient who was not supposed to have it. She went insane as a result of the blood transfusion.

Another New York case was _Parker v. State_$^{45}$ where a patient died from jaundice contracted as a result of being transfused with infected plasma. The plasma had been released by the government. The plaintiff's action was dismissed on the ground that the use of such plasma, even though of dubious purity, was a matter of medical judgment and was not negligence.

A useful illustration of the complications that can arise is seen from the case of _Grambosi v. Putera_.$^{46}$ In this case the patient received a blood transfusion from which she contracted syphilis. The same doctor treated her for syphilis and she died from the treatment.

A recent case of _White v. Putera_$^{47}$ reveals a situation where a mother was killed by a blood transfusion. The jury assessed damages against the doctor of $150,000.00 reduced by the court to $135,000.00.

So far as young babies are concerned, there are, to the knowledge of the writer, at least six babies born with the Rh incompatibility in the Toronto area, who according to standard medical practice would probably have been transfused, but this has not been done. All are in good health today. _Merck's Manual of Diagnosis_, a standard medical work, states concerning babies with hemolytic disease: '... the outlook for infants varies with the severity of the anaemia present. Some will die regardless of treatment; others will survive only if properly treated, others will survive and be normal without treatment.' Some of those who do get transfusions die anyway, such as baby Wolfe at London, Ontario, who died April 5, 1960, after a transfusion.$^{48}$ If babies die without a transfusion, it is always said that they died for lack of one. If they die after a transfusion, it was because they didn't get it soon enough. No account seems to be taken of the fact that some children die anyway, with or without transfusion.

To sum up the Canadian cases it can safely be said that there has never yet been a trial of the issue in any serious judicial sense. Streamlined procedure in a lower court, after one hour's notice, and proceeding without counsel or chance to get witnesses is not really a trial, especially after several days of sensationally dramatized headlines, designed to sell newspapers, not to get at the truth. The present child welfare legislation is not working satisfactorily from the standpoint of giving people a fair hearing. When these cases are contested they should automatically shift out of the family court and come before a county or supreme court judge where there is a possibility of a more judicial hearing.

All these experiences and cases bring us back to the same sensible point made by Dr. Arthur Kelly: 'Patients and parents have a perfect right to accept or reject treatment offered. No doctor can be positive that a person will die if he doesn't get a transfusion or live if he does.'$^{49}$ 'It is perhaps better that the odd person die rather than the fundamental human right of refusing medical treatment become impaired.'$^{50}$

In the past five years in Canada there have not been, so far as can be ascertained, more than twenty cases of juveniles involving this issue. That comes to approximately four cases a year. Some of these patients have lived, others have died — some with blood and some without. Other children who might ordinarily have been transfused lived without such treatment. Nothing can really be proved beyond question either way.

In weighing up statistics it may be worthwhile to recall that in the cases that have been mentioned, the blood transfusion of only two mothers resulted in the death of five babies.$^{51}$ Those two transfusions alone have killed more babies than the average number of cases that arise in Canada in a whole year.

Can anyone say on these figures that there is an epidemic of some kind, a serious flaw in our law that all the forces of the state should be organized to overcome? Take away the drama and emotionalism and what really is left?

## Chapter 5 THE MEDICAL PROFESSION IS NOT ENTITLED TO UNCONTROLLED DISCRETIONARY POWER OVER OTHER PEOPLE'S FAMILIES

(a) Medical doctors already have too much power; the added authority now claimed would make a mockery of law

The claim is made by some that all medical doctors

should have uncontrolled authority to decide on medical treatment for other people's families even contrary to the wishes of the parents.

Is this thinking really sound? Should every doctor immediately become a public official with power to invade

the sanctity of the family and to remove children from the protection of their own flesh and blood? It is not accurate in these cases to say that the courts control; they have abdicated their function and merely approve medical decisions. This opens the door to many abuses. What valuable consideration can the doctors offer to justify the claimed extension of power?

Relevant to this matter is the inherent weakness of medicine as an inexact science; further weakness from the way it is practiced; and finally account must be taken of the fact that medical testimony in matters touching professional privilege is notoriously unreliable.

It is not the purpose of these comments to attack the practice of medicine as a profession. It can do much good; it can also do harm. It has competent men in it; also incompetent. The difficulty is that medicine has been placed on such a pedestal by some people that they hardly stop to look at the true situation. It is the purpose of this discussion to take it off the pedestal and look at the facts.

Medicine is an inexact science; it can't be anything else. This is not a reflection on the doctors: they didn't create the human organism with all its complexities and problems. Many of them do the best they can with the treatments they have to work with, but their best often leaves a great margin of uncertainty.

"Medical progress is a study of trial and error, of false paths, of whole generations under the sway of wrong ideas leading to wrong treatment and God knows what in the way of casualties — and the old tale yet goes on . . . in the 18th century hundreds of people lost their lives through blood being taken out of them needlessly; today people are being killed through blood being put into them needlessly."

states Dr. J. H. Dible, Professor of Pathology.

It is this area of uncertainty, of experimentation, of disputable values, where the law is now being asked to force on unwilling patients, a remedy of uncertain value. "The accepted treatment of today was risky yesterday; and will be obsolete to-morrow . . . proven to be wrong."

In this field of uncertainty the law should not meddle. That public respect for law shall be maintained, it must proceed on some reasonable certainty that the invasion of individual liberty is justified because of some compensating value. Otherwise the law comes in disrepute.

But here courts and police are supposed to rally in support of medical uncertainty. So when doctors abandon blood transfusion, along with blood letting, the parents will have been right after all and the tyranny and abuse will be laid at the door of courts and legislators. There is a certainty of invasion of the sacred family circle, and a certainty of destroying civil liberty: as a balancing consideration in favour of the destroying of liberty can only be offered the uncertainty that any good will result. Individual liberty cannot be held so lightly in the scale pan of justice.

There is one other motivating force that is not usually talked about much.

"Arrogance, the first and probably least excusable sin, is the greatest single cause of public resentment against the doctors. Condescension, aloofness, and evident conviction of superiority and infallibility do not win friends. Let's descend from our pedestal".

suggests Dr. Francis T. Hodgins. As admitted in this statement there is an unfortunate weakness in a very vocal segment of the medical fraternity of not being able to stand people disagreeing with them. This becomes evident in the strong medical pressure for more power.

Before determining to give uncontrolled discretion to every doctor regardless of ability or integrity, considera-

tion could well be given to the article "Does Canadian Medicine Need a Housecleaning?" written by a doctor (anonymously) for Liberty magazine:

"Instead of weeding out misfits, which give our profession a bad name, organized medicine concentrates on building itself up as a holier-than-thon priesthood. The Canadian Medical Association employs a Montreal publicity agent to 'interpret' the actions of its members to the public.

"What they conveniently mask is the gross carelessness of several doctors."

Instead of putting the people under the control of physicians the above writer recommends exactly the opposite:

". . . put the control of doctors under the thumbs of laymen. As J. C. McAree of the Globe & Mail pointed out: 'There is a theory that the governing bodies of doctors . . . are established for the protection of the public . . . The truth is that these bodies are formed for the protection of doctors.'"

"The public must grab the coat-tails of the medical profession and drag it back into the workaday world. The day of the priesthood is over."

Medical doctors are no worse than any similar group in any other profession: neither are they any better! No one would demand that every lawyer, engineer or geologist shall automatically become a public official with unreviewable power over people's lives and children. But still it is contended that every doctor, young or old, good or bad should automatically become a public official totally without control or supervision and able to seriously interfere with people's homes and families. Such a law is indefensible.

Already people can lose custody of children by court order if they fail to accept "proper treatment when recommended by a duly qualified medical practitioner". There is no duty on the practitioners to show any reasonable value to his recommendations or that there is a probability of some good. Neither is any account taken of the fact that a medical panel or a more experienced doctor might recommend something different. It is submitted that medical opinion is already treated with too much sanctity. More power would only lead to more abuse.

B. When any practice of the medical profession, or of a member is questioned, there is a conspiracy of silence to prevent the courts from getting full information. The full story of the dangers and doubtful value of blood transfusion has never been told in evidence

There is a legal fiction that the decisions in these cases are being made by the courts. In reality, the doctor states his opinion, there is no real chance as a rule for cross-examination, or the bringing of other testimony, and the lower court, under pressure, in effect rubberstamps the evidence of the doctor. He is the "duly qualified medical practitioner" who has recommended something. It is immaterial that other doctors might recommend the opposite. They are not called to give evidence.

This leads us to the further problem: how reliable is the evidence of the doctor?

Part of the difficulty in all this is the highly idealistic view taken by some, and judges are not entirely immune, of the quality and value of expert testimony. One would like to think that expert testimony is wholly impartial and indubitably a statement of the real factors in the case. Regrettably, this just is not the case. In truth and in fact, the situation is so serious that one well known doctor author has written a detailed study of medical testimony, part of which he entitles "The Myth of Impartiality."

The writer in question, Dr. Henry A. Davidson, makes the following commentary:
