such a patient can sometimes be kept beating for a week. I have never seen such a patient begin to breathe spontaneously and survive, and autopsy always shows advanced liquefaction necrosis of the brain, for it "died" several days before the heart did. When did the soul leave the body? Is turning off the respirator murder? Is there any moral or ethical difference in not starting the respirator, as compared to stopping it once it is started? An 85-year-old lady, suffering from arthritis, cataracts, and many pains, wanting to die for several years, has developed pneumonia, or heart failure, and is comatose. Must these medical illnesses be treated, forcing her, against her desire, to suffer longer? A cancer patient in a terminal state required narcotics for relief of pain, which produce semistupor to the point of inadequate fluid intake.

### Murder

The unlawful killing of a human being with afore-thought malice, expressed or implied, is known as murder. This, we agree, is illegal, immoral, and evil, and needs no further discussion. The physician who so acts with such malice, in his own or in someone else's interest, is a criminal, and should be prosecuted by law. Thou shalt not kill.

### Euthanasia

The act of painlessly putting to death a patient suffering with an incurable and distressing disease is called euthanasia. Though several attempts at passage of legislation to make such acts legal have been made, this has never become law in any state. The risks of error and abuse make this legally unacceptable. Theologically, this act is contrary to moral law because, if each human life is divine, man has no right to destroy it. This would be direct violation of the supreme dominion of God over His creation. Even if the patient requests death, the family approves of it, and the physician concurs, we must recognize that sometimes the patient's desire to die is a symptom of pathological depression, which is a mental illness that is often transient and curable. The family approval might be selfishly motivated to save expense or lessen their own hard-

And what physician can be certain that he can eliminate his own emotions and motives enough to be sure that he does not want the luckless patient to die, not only to end his suffering, but also to solve the whole burden of caring for him? And what authority should decide on all these quirks of human nature?

Yet, though civil law makes euthanasia a crime, there are certainly humanitarian arguments to be heard. Sometimes the issue is not life or death, but simply, should we not have some choice in what kind of death—agonized or peaceful? Should we not be able to do something for a loved one that we can do for a dog?

### Blessed Are the Merciful

Not only are physicians obligated to prolong life, but also to relieve suffering. This is legal; it is moral; it is ethical; it is good. Compassion and mercy are self-evident qualities that are inherent in the best of medical tradition. Though most of us agree that legalized euthanasia is not warranted, we do feel duty bound and morally justified in relieving suffering.

We have no argument that as long as there is any chance of cure, or of prolonging a reasonable life, it is our duty to treat the patient with every medical skill at our disposal. Yet, there are those circumstances, however, when we have every right to be certain that the patient is suffering the terminal events of advanced malignancy, for example. Here, each step we take can come under scrutiny—intravenous fluids, tube feedings, blood transfusions, tracheostomy, palliative ultraradical surgery. Our quandary is aptly expressed by the couplet, "Thou shalt not kill, but need not strive/Officiously to keep alive."

The Roman Catholic church has attempted to guide the physician in this area by stating that we have a moral obligation to utilize "ordinary" means to preserve life, but the use of "extraordinary" means is optional. However, the physician and the moralist do not use the terms ordinary and extraordinary in the same sense. The physician's definition of ordinary means of preserving life are standard, recognized, orthodox, or established medicines or procedures of that era, at that level of medical practice, and within the limits of availability, and his definition of extraordinary is a medicament or procedure that might be fanciful, bizarre, experimental, incompletely established, unorthodox, or not recognized. The moralist's viewpoint of ordinary ways of preserving life include not only normal food, drink, and rest, but all medicines, treatments, and operations which offer a reasonable hope of benefit for the patient, and which can be obtained and used without excessive expense, pain, or other inconvenience; extraordinary ways of preserving life are all medicines, treatments, and operations which cannot be obtained or used without excessive expense, pain, or other inconveniences for the patient or for others, or which, if used, would

not offer a reasonable hope of benefit to the patient.

Obviously, what may be ordinary to the specialist, may be extraordinary to the family physician; what is ordinary in a university hospital may be extraordinary in a small community hospital; what is extraordinary today may be ordinary tomorrow; and the same pain or inconvenience may be excessive for one patient, but not for another.

We realize that intensive efforts to maintain life can, in reality, become prolongation of dying, rather than prolongation of living. Many times these individual decisions are clear, yet at other times, indecision and doubt arise. In questionable cases, Laforet has stated that it is wiser to err on the side of active treatment rather than maintain "laissez faire" for the following reasons: (1) The physician is fallible, and the case may not be medically "hopeless." (2) The physician, by tradition, has been committed to active contention with disease. (3) The physician is not competent to determine fully the "quality" of a given life or whether longevity is "fruitless." (4) Even if without positive act, the physician who arrogates to himself the prerogative of determining whether life shall continue or terminate by default is in an uncomfortable moral position. (5) The discovery of new curative agents is an ever present possibility. (6) Spontaneous regression of malignancies in apparently hopeless patients has been documented. (7) Miraculous intervention is possible. (8) The physician may find that self-recrimination for errors of omission is harsher than for errors of commission. (9) Even a brief moment of mental lucidity in a moribund patient may be all-important for his spiritual welfare. (10) Extraordinary means of treatment may result in cure.

### The Solution

Life or death—who decides? Each physician could recite innumerable examples of different diseases, situations, and conditions, with many variables, that would make each decision as to measures of prolonging life a debatable one. Because of these countless variables, rigid rules are impossible. Our course of action becomes a matter of moral, ethical, and religious convictions.

Certainly, the physician's first thought must be the welfare of the patient. Since life is a gift of the Creator to the individual, the primary decision rightfully belongs to the patient, because the patient is the custodian of that gift. The physician's responsibility to the patient's family, to science, to the hospital, and to society are secondary.

It is proper for us to be merciful, but we must be human about it, and not pretend to be omniscient. It is always unwise for the doctor alone to make the decisions. Unilateral edicts are dangerous. Certainly, the patient and the family have some say in these matters as well as others meaningfully involved in the particular situation. Basically it often becomes a religious decision.

The patient's attitude toward death is profound-

ly influenced by his concept of life hereafter, and this varies according to the depth of his religious convictions, and varies with different religious faiths. Thus, this becomes a theological problem. Just as we should seek consultation medically with a specialist in certain diseases, so we should seek guidance in spiritual matters with clergymen, who are specialists in theology. Though the purely medical decisions should be made by the physician, consideration of the moral and spiritual aspects, as well as guidance of the family's thoughts and emotions, are proper functions of the clergy, either rabbi, priest, or minister. Thus the team approach of physician and clergy working together, with patient and family, is the ideal solution to this problem. At times, other professions may contribute constructively, such as lawyer, social worker, or nurse.

The physician should treat the patient within the dictates of the patient's religion, and not force his own religious convictions upon the patient. The physician may withdraw from the case if his own religious beliefs produce a conflict that he cannot conscientiously handle.

That we cannot give satisfactory answers to all questions that arise is not disturbing to me. What is important is our wrestling with these problems. One approach to this dilemma is already being made by the Department of Medicine and Religion of the American Medical Association, who has stimulated the formation, and guided the activities, of committees on medicine and religion in each state medical society. These, in turn, have assisted in the formation of district or county committees on medicine and religion, who are actively arranging meetings, seminars, and discussion groups between

physicians and clergymen in the interest of total care of the sick.

At a recent meeting of the Wyandotte County Medical Society in Kansas City, Kan, the program consisted of a panel composed of a rabbi, priest, minister, surgeon, internist, and psychiatrist, discussing this very subject of prolonging life. Each physician attending the meeting brought a clergyman as his guest. This type of interprofessional and interfaith communication and understanding is a proper approach to answering some of the ethical, moral, and spiritual problems that face the conscientious physician.

However, let us also realize that religion does not have sole claim on either morality or humanitarian compassion. There are physicians who do not perform within a religious frame of reference, whose reverence for life and devotion towards relief of suffering meet the criteria of highest level of integrity, morality, and love for fellowman.

The fact that this topic has appeared for discussion in this First National Congress on Medical Ethics and Professionalism is further reassuring evidence that the medical profession is deeply concerned that its science does not surpass its art; that we still treat the patient, not just the disease; that we be merciful humanitarians, not cold aloof scientists; and that we not delude ourselves and become "medically omniscient." For after all, there is only One who is Omniscient: we are His servants. I see no dichotomy, or even any dilemma. We can, without conflict, simultaneously serve God, our creator, medical science, our profession, and man, our patient, as we strive to improve ourselves in both the art and the science of the practice of medicine.

## Those doctors play God again

Who controls your body, you, or God, or the Canadian Medical Association?

At its convention in Winnipeg, the CMA has grandly accepted, after 103 years, the principle of male and female sterilization, for reasons other than medical but under conditions to be established by — who else? — the CMA.

One condition supported by some delegates but turned down by the majority would have provided that before performing the operation doctors consider the validity of the patient's reason for wanting sterilization.

"Please, sir, may I be sterilized? I have the money for it right here."

"Why do you want to be sterilized?"

"Well, my wife and I already have 10 kids and I'm out of work."

"Sorry, that's not a valid reason."

### What charter?

If the Government were to intervene in the private and personal life of the individual to this extent there would be an immediate public outcry. Under what charter have the doctors assumed this power? Sterilization is not illegal under the Criminal Code — why has the CMA forbidden it for so long?

Well, according to the association's past president, Dr. Jack Walters, who proposed the new sterilization policy at the Winnipeg meeting: "We're policy-makers for the country. If we say it is proper, ethical and legal then it has to be accepted."

That's quite a tall order — arbiters of what's proper, ethical and legal. Proper — by whose standards? Ethical — medically or socially? Legal — are come off it! The law is established by Parliament and administered by the judiciary; doctors, like everyone else, are subject to the law.

Playing God is an occupational disease of doctors. They are helped into it by legend, myth, superstition and the propaganda of the Canadian Medical Association. But what is a doctor, except a technician? We pay him to tinker with our bodies, just as we hire a mechanic to tinker with our ears, or a plumber with a leaky pipe. We would be outraged if the mechanic or plumber laid down conditions for repairing certain defective parts.

### Just his fee

That's because the car is ours, the plumbing fixtures are ours and we reserve the right to decide what's to be done with them.

All we grant to the tradesman is his fee. And so it should be with doctors.

The body is a temple, yes; but for its care or abuse we are responsible only to ourselves and God. A medical school degree doesn't confer on the doctor any spiritual powers or privileges not enjoyed by any other honest workman.

In his confrontation with the pro-abortion terminists in Vancouver the other day, Prime Minister Trudeau laboriously made the point that under the present law the doctors have been granted freedom to decide the issue. Wasn't that what the woman wanted?

In reply, the terminists, bless them, gave the PM a big horse laugh and a few were heard to boo and groan. I should think so.

# Phototherapy and the Jaundiced Infant

RICHARD P. WENNBERG, M.D., Seattle, Washington

In a test tube, bilirubin is converted to colorless compounds by light. A baby's jaundice skin can be bleached by the same agent. Light accelerates the decline of serum bilirubin and decreases the number of exchange transfusions required. Animal studies have indicated that light can cause metabolic changes, some of which are harmful to the young, but there is no evidence of harm to human infants. The risks, if any, are considerably less than risks of damage by excess bilirubin.

When crystalline bilirubin is dissolved in dilute sodium hydroxide and exposed to fluorescent light the solution gradually turns from yellow to amber to green, and finally to a slightly tinted, almost clear solution. As these events occur, the concentration of bilirubin falls rapidly. While the degradation products have not been determined with certainty, it is likely that bilirubin is photo-oxidized to biliverdin, then to a second yellow pigment and, finally, to other colorless compounds.

Although this instability of bilirubin has been known for years, a nurse is credited with recognizing the possible clinical importance of this phenomenon. In the mid 1950's the head nurse of a premature-unit in Essex, England observed that if a jaundiced infant were placed next to the window on a sunny day the jaundice in the exposed areas faded quickly. This led to a series of experiments reported by Cremer et al which demonstrated that serum bilirubin concentrations could be drastically reduced in jaundiced infants by exposure to sunlight or to artificial light.

Since this early work, phototherapy has been used in the management of physiologic jaundice in the premature, both in Europe and South America. Little attention was given to light therapy in the United States, however, until the study of Lucey and his colleagues was presented in 1968. Since then, several studies of the use of phototherapy in the prevention of hyperbilirubinemia in the premature have been presented.

Table 1 summarizes five controlled studies, representing a total experience with 521 infants. For most, the lighting was provided by a group of daylight fluorescent tubes delivering 300 to 500 foot-candles of light to the infant. The babies were naked except for protective eye shields and, in some cases, diapers. The results are remarkably uniform and indicate that light therapy will reduce the serum bilirubin concentration to 50 percent of the expected level in physiologic jaundice of the premature. The lesser values of only 17 to 19 percent reduction reported by Gupta and Rath are ascribed to the use of a less intense light source. They sim

ply improved the nursery lighting from the previous dim 10 foot-candle illumination to one of 90 foot-candles. As yet, effectiveness of light therapy in hemolytic disease of the newborn is uncertain, but available evidence suggests that light exposure accelerates the decline of serum bilirubin concentrations and decreases the number of exchange transfusions required.

In spite of these data, considerable doubt regarding the safety and efficacy of phototherapy has been expressed by several investigators. The reasons for this hesitancy are summarized in Table 2.

Primary concern is that products of photodecomposition might be as toxic as their parent compound, bilirubin. Bilirubin inhibits electron transport and uncouples oxidative phosphorylation. Photodecomposed bilirubin has no apparent effect on either of these systems in isolated mitochondria. Biliverdin, however, does inhibit nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) oxidase when the enzyme is isolated in vitro. On the other hand, biliverdin appears to be less fat soluble than bilirubin and thus probably does not cross lipoprotein membranes of cell walls readily. Furthermore, nobody has been able to demonstrate a significant amount of biliverdin circulating in light treated infants. The concentrations necessary to produce a toxic effect are probably never

attained in vivo. The remaining photo products have been shown to be water soluble, do not deposit in brain tissue readily, and are rapidly excreted without conjugation both through the liver and kidney minimizing the likelihood of any toxic effects."

A second question has been raised as to whether the photodecomposition products may displace bilirubin from albumin. I have recently looked at this problem in the laboratory at the University Hospital, using electrophoresis and spectrophotometric techniques, and have been unable to displace any bilirubin from albumin by the addition of photodecomposed bilirubin. On the other hand, Odell has shown that exposure of jaundiced serum to intense light can decrease bilirubin binding in vitro, possibly by photodecomposition of albumin itself. Porto et al have recently presented evidence of an increase in available bilirubin binding sites on albumin in those

babies treated with phototherapy."

A third concern—and possibly the area in which we are most ignorant—is the possibility that light therapy in itself may be hazardous. It has been suggested, without supporting evidence, that continuous light therapy could interrupt normal circadian rhythm. There have been animal studies to indicate that light exposure may alter endocrine metabolism, cause runting in rats, and cause retinal damage in monkeys. In the few children who have been carefully followed through the first year of life, however, there is no evidence that light treatment has any harmful influence on human growth. Since infants exposed to light have uniformly been blindfolded, the effects of prolonged phototherapy on the retina in premature infants are as yet unknown. While the risks of retinal injury are probably remote, it would seem wise to continue to blindfold all infants who receive intensive light therapy, at least until further evidence is available.

In evaluating the possible ill effects of light therapy it is well to consider that the intensity of artificial light used in phototherapy is only in the range of 400 to 500 foot-candles as compared with 5,000 to 10,000 foot-candles supplied by natural sun-

light. An infant placed next to a window may be exposed to much more intense illumination than one receiving artificial phototherapy.

In view of available data, the potential hazards of light therapy are probably very small compared to the known hazards of hyperbilirubinemia in the premature infant. Boggs and his colleagues have provided evidence that bilirubin concentrations in excess of 15 mg per 100 ml might produce mental and motor impairment. Kernicterus can occur in sick, premature infants with bilirubin concentrations of 12 mg per 100 ml or lower. The risks of repeated exchange transfusions are well known.

In spite of the usefulness of phototherapy in the management of jaundice, prophylactic treatment does present some potential clinical hazards as summarized in Table 3. Bilirubin is not only a poison—its presence also provides a warning of other diseases. If jaundice is prevented by prophylactic phototherapy,

These include hepatitis, syphilis, cytomegalic inclusion disease, toxoplasmosis, rubella syndrome, diabetic mother syndrome, hereditary forms of jaundice, and the many forms of hemolytic disease in the newborn. can result in severe, and occasionally fatal, anemia in early infancy.

Infection in the newborn is extremely difficult to recognize, and one of the signs of sepsis is unexplained jaundice. If all babies are treated prophylactically, this clue is lost. The stools of infants receiving light therapy are often brown or green and loose, which may add to the confusion since diarrhea is another presenting sign of sepsis. In addition, overheating of incubators has occurred from homemade phototherapy units and improperly ventilated commercial models; if this is not recognized, temperature instability in the infant may further mislead the physician.

Since the majority of bilirubin which is decomposed by phototherapy lies within or beneath the skin and not in the circulation, one might fail to recognize the severity of hyperbilirubinemia. Serum concentrations of 8 to 12 mg per 100 ml have been observed in infants who appear non-jaundiced except for the area under the blindfold. The extent to which dangerously high levels of bilirubin can be

masked by phototherapy is unknown.

An additional hazard of phototherapy has recently been observed with the introduction of high-energy blue fluorescent lamps. These lamps have been recommended because they possess approximately two times the radiant energy in the absorptive band of bilirubin than do daylight lamps. However, these lamps cast a blue hue over the infants, and instances of undetected, marked cyanosis have occurred. Thus, the advantage of increased energy output is more than outweighed by the risk of missing color changes (cyanosis, rashes) in the infants, and blue fluorescent lamps should not be used for phototherapy.

In summary, the available evidence indicates that phototherapy is effective and safe. However, patients receiving phototherapy must be followed carefully and theoretical problems which might arise from light therapy deserve continued study. Babies receiving phototherapy, especially when used prophylactically, require even more careful monitoring for early

signs of sepsis, undetected hemolytic disease, and marked hyperbilirubinemia.

Which infants, then, should be treated with light? While the selection of candidates is somewhat arbitrary, the following guidelines are suggested:

1. All infants who are jaundiced.
2. All infants with a known cause for hyperbilirubinemia. This includes hemolytic diseases, infections and infants with large hematomas or other internal bleeding, even before clinical jaundice becomes apparent.
3. All infants who are severely ill and thus at greater risk of kernicterus. Hyaline membrane disease, severe anoxia, or symptomatic hypoglycemia can be dangerous.
4. All premature infants under 1500 grams, because of the greater risk for physiologic jaundice and for kernicterus at low serum bilirubin concentrations.

# \*\* Blue Light and Jaundice

SIR,—Your leading article on blue light and jaundice (4 April, p. 5) was welcome in drawing attention to this method of treatment which, though first developed in Britain, has been almost totally neglected here ever since. However, you seem not to have been convinced firstly, that hyperbilirubinemia unassociated with haemolytic disease is potentially dangerous, and secondly, that phototherapy is both effective and harmless. There is, however, plenty of evidence from both in vitro experiments and clinical observation that hyperbilirubinemia is potentially dangerous. Kernicterus is such a serious condition that even if its incidence is low every effort must be made to prevent it from occurring.

Recent work by G. B. Odell and colleagues has shown that the major factor determining brain damage in jaundiced infants is the fraction of bilirubin which is dissociated from albumin and therefore free to diffuse into cells. In a careful study of infants who had been jaundiced during the neonatal period they found no correlation between the presence of brain damage at five years of age and the maximal serum bilirubin level, but that there was a significant correlation with the saturation of serum proteins with bilirubin in infancy. The saturation index provided a better assessment of the risk of hyperbilirubinemia than did the serum bilirubin concentration. Their series of cases included one infant with brain damage in whom the maximum serum bilirubin concentration was only 13.6 mg./100 ml., but the saturation index was abnormal. The risks are therefore greater in infants with hypopituinaemia. In practice it still remains difficult, however, to assess accurately when a jaundiced infant is in danger because, as your article points out, other factors like anoxia, respiratory acidosis, and the respiratory distress syndrome may be involved. But it is precisely when these conditions are present that exchange transfusion as a method of treatment becomes more difficult and dangerous. We submit, therefore, that in such circumstances the simple method of phototherapy is particularly valuable and, provided it is properly given, its effectiveness is unquestionable. It has one great advantage—that is that the infant can be effectively treated in the incubator without undue disturbance.

The dangers of phototherapy are at present hypothetical. No ill effects have been noted in any of the numerous reports which have so far been published on this method of treatment. It seems likely therefore that its dangers have been exaggerated. We would, however, agree that long-term follow up studies of treated cases are desirable and so in Chelmsford, where we have now treated over 500 cases, a follow-up study has been started.

R. E. Behrman and D. Y. Y. Hsia¹ summarized the conclusions of the Chicago symposium. Your assessment appears to have overlooked the positive recommendation they made that "phototherapy should be used for infants in whom the risks of hyperbilirubinemia are thought to outweigh the risks of this form of treatment." We disagree therefore with the opinion expressed at the end of your leading article that neonatal units are probably not justified in adding special lighting apparatus to the already long list of important equipment needed from limited funds. While we agree that the indiscriminate use of phototherapy should be discouraged, we maintain that more should be done to stimulate research into its correct application in suitable cases.—We are, etc.,

C. R. M. WARREN.

# Blue Light and Jaundice

SIR,—Inasmuch as I am an "enthusiastic" supporter of phototherapy, I feel that I should comment on the ultra-conservative editorial comment, "Blue Light and Jaundice" (4 April, p. 5).

Workers in this field² now recognize that bilirubin can produce learning difficulties in humans at lower serum concentrations than were previously realized. Previous studies have not detected these defects because of inadequate testing. It is for this reason that a safe and simple method to replace exchange transfusion is needed. The statement that phototherapy is "unduly to be adequate treatment" in preventing low bilirubin kernicterus is an opinion with which I certainly do not agree. Preliminary data suggest that this is the type of infant who will benefit. Phototherapy is also now widely being used to control mild haemolytic disease. There has been no convincing evidence published to support the original suggestion by Franklin³ that the photochemical products might be toxic. There is considerable evidence that these products are not toxic either in vivo, in vitro, and in human infants.⁴ I would ask that the author of this leading article and others read the Bilirubin Symposium⁵ quoted, and not just the summary as has apparently been done, for more data on this important point. I would also refer the reader to two recent articles,⁶ for more reassuring evidence in human infants. Published human clinical experience for several countries with phototherapy now numbers over 3,000 cases, and no serious toxic effects have been reported to date.⁷ More recent studies in two human infants with Crigler-Najjar syndrome employing ¹⁴C labelled bilirubin and phototherapy indicate that the breakdown products are rapidly and safely excreted.⁸

Early feeding may have limited the incidence of hyperbilirubinemia of prematurity in one nursery in England to less than 1%, but this has certainly not been the experience in the U.S.A. Where this problem has been studied carefully, one usually finds that from 10-25% of premature infants can be expected to develop serum bilirubin concentrations of over 15 mg./100 ml.⁷

The leader writer also cites a reference⁸ referring to a hypothesis that light might cause retrolental fibroplasia. This curious theory is certainly not widely held by many paediatricians.

I, and others, have not used "blue" light, but have employed broad spectrum light. One should not of course use "blue light," especially if you want to judge skin colour. Phototherapy units are now designed so that they not only allow better observation of the infant but also free access to the infant. The leader writer's quaint reluctance to allow even a minor change in the present lighting conditions in the nursery suggests that he knows that these conditions are indeed optimal for newborn infants. I challenge this idea. I am afraid that few doctors actually have any idea about the present lighting conditions in their nursery. Outdoor light on a bright day supplies 10,000 foot candles of broad spectrum light. I have found nurseries with 25 foot candles to 2,000 foot candles in the same nursery. Phototherapy units supply only about 300-500 foot candles of light. "Phototherapy" is, therefore, being carried out in many nurseries without physicians being aware of it. There are no data whatsoever to support the present "dim light" conditions present in many nurseries as being the best. Outdoor lighting is used to illuminate many nurseries and "long-term disadvantages" are not apparent.

I agree that we have much to learn about light and its effect on human infants. The present leading article implies, however, that we know the present highly artificial light conditions are good, so why change? I would suggest that we face our ignorance on this point, examine the currently available evidence without prejudice, and then make a judgement.—I am, etc.,

JEROLD LUCKY.

Department of Pediatrics,

University of Vermont,

Burlington, Vermont, U.S.A.

# PHOTODECOMPOSITION OF BILIRUBIN AND BILIVERDIN IN VITRO

J. DONALD OSTROW, M.D., AND ROGER V. BRANHAM

Department of Medicine, Case Western Reserve University, and University Hospitals, Cleveland, Ohio

Decomposition of bilirubin and biliverdin under intense fluorescent light was studied in vitro at pH levels ranging from 7.4 to 13.0. Photodecay of bilirubin was more rapid at a higher pH if albumin was absent, but more rapid at a lower pH if albumin was present, whereas biliverdin was more stable at a lower pH, with or without albumin. During illumination at lower pH levels, albumin stabilized biliverdin but accelerated decay of bilirubin; these effects were not altered by competitive uncoupling of bilirubin from albumin or by chelation of contaminant divalent cations with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid. Studies with a variety of fluorescent lamps demonstrated that wavelengths between 400 and 600 mμ were most effective in destroying bilirubin, ultraviolet light was less effective, and red light (>600 mμ) was ineffective. Photodecay of both bilirubin and biliverdin was oxidative, but exclusion of oxygen did not arrest photodecay of bilirubin if albumin was present also. Presumably, albumin itself or the vinyl side chain of bilirubin substituted for oxygen as a hydrogen acceptor. By radiochromatography and by reillumination of photoderivatives of ¹⁴C-bilirubin, it was shown that the process of photodecay proceeded from bilirubin to biliverdin to weakly diazo-reactive derivatives to highly polar, diazo-negative products.

Exposure of infants to fluorescent lights commonly is utilized to treat neonatal jaundice,² but the mechanisms involved and the products of bilirubin photodecay

Many investigators have approached this problem by examination of the photodecomposition of bilirubin in vitro,⁴⁻¹⁰ but the conditions employed often have been neither physiological nor standardized, and the factors affecting the kinetics of bilirubin photodecay have not been evaluated systematically. The present in vitro studies were performed to assess the effects of pH, albumin, oxygen, and the wavelengths of the incident light upon the photodecomposition of bilirubin and to determine whether biliverdin is an intermediate in the process.

The comparative studies of different fluorescent lights indicated that, taken as a whole, the blue-violet (400 to 500 mμ) and yellow-green (500 to 600 mμ) regions of the spectrum most effectively destroyed bilirubin, that red light (>600 mμ) was ineffective, and that ultraviolet light (300 to 400 mμ) had intermediate potency. The lesser effect of ultraviolet light may have been due in part to absorption by the glass walls of the vessel. The data comparing the pink and gold lamps suggested, however, that the spectral line at 440 mμ, close to the absorption maximum of bilirubin, may be most effective of all. Sisson's recent report²⁸ has confirmed these observations. Cremer and co-workers³ drew similar conclusions, but their data are limited by failure to adjust for radiant energy emitted in the different portions of the spectrum.

These findings have two practical implications. (a) In handling bilirubin in the laboratory, the pigment can be stabilized in serum or in physiological albumin solution by operating under red light and in albumin-free solutions by addition of EDTA or exclusion of oxygen. (b) The emission spectrum of lamps utilized for phototherapy of the newborn should be selected within the blue-violet and yellow-green portions of the spectrum to eliminate those wavelengths which most prominently generate unwanted side effects.³⁰

### Riboflavin Enhancement of Bilirubin

### Photocatabolism in vivo¹

Phototherapy has become a common therapeutic procedure in neonatal hyperbilirubinemia²⁻⁴. Despite the well-established efficacy of light therapy in reducing bilirubin levels, there have been reservations expressed with respect to exposing infants to light intensities of 300 to 500 foot candles, often continuously for periods of several days⁵. We have been examining the possibility

![img-101.jpeg](img-101.jpeg)

Fig. 1. Plot showing effect of FMN on rate of bilirubin photodecomposition by visible light in aqueous solution of 1% BSA, pH 7.4, under aerobic conditions.

of administering agents which would promote the photochemical decomposition of bilirubin in vivo, and might thus reduce either the exposure time or the light intensity necessary to reduce plasma bilirubin levels.

Experimental. Preliminary in vitro experiments indicated that monosodium salt of riboflavin 5'-phosphate (FMN) increases the rate of photochemical decomposition of bilirubin. Bilirubin solutions (3.36 × 10⁻⁶ M) were prepared in 0.05 M phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, containing 1% w/v bovine serum albumin (Armour fraction V), with and without 0.97 × 10⁻⁶ M FMN. These solutions were irradiated intermittently in 1 cm quartz spectrophotometer cells located 24 in. from a projector equipped with a 500 W tungsten lamp. Absorbance spectra were recorded, versus a buffer blank, on a Cary 15 spectrophotometer at appropriate time intervals. Studies were conducted at room temperature of 22-23°C, with solutions exposed to air. Initial bilirubin absorbance at 460 nm was approximately 40 times that of FMN, and the enhanced initial rate of decline in absorbance at 460 nm in presence of FMN, as illustrated in Figure 1, indicates acceleration of bilirubin photodecomposition by FMN.

Potassium iodide at a concentration of 10⁻⁴ M reduced the FMN enhancement of bilirubin photodecomposition, while showing no effect on rate of bilirubin photodecomposition in absence of FMN. This observation implicates the FMN triplet in the enhanced bilirubin photodecomposition. A further observation that the photolating of FMN is inhibited by the presence of bilirubin is compatible with

a mechanism whereby bilirubin quenches the FMN triplet. Detailed studies of this photochemical process will be considered in a separate report⁶.

Adult male jaundiced Gunn rats⁸ weighing 275-400 g were dosed with 75 mg/kg of FMN administered in 0.7 to 1.0 ml of normal saline solution via the penis vein every 9 h up to 36 h and then every 12 h for the duration of the experiment. Control animals were injected at the same time intervals with normal saline solution. The backs of both the control and the FMN treated rats were shaved and the animals were placed in individual cages under a light canopy containing four 60 W daylight fluorescent lamps (Sylvania). Constant light intensity was maintained throughout the experiment by daily monitoring of light intensity with a light meter and adjustment of the lamp-to-animal distance as required. Blood sampling was performed prior to and during the exposure period by a technique similar to that described by HURWITZ¹⁰. Plasma bilirubin concentration was determined by a modified Malloy-Evelyn colorimetric method¹¹. Riboflavin plasma levels encountered at the selected sampling times did not interfere with the assay for bilirubin.

Results and discussion. Both the albino and the hooded strains of Gunn rats responded to phototherapy. Preliminary studies conducted with light of 750-1100 foot candles intensity showed a rapid decline in plasma bilirubin levels, with no difference detectable for control and FMN treated rats. However, when rats were exposed to light of 300 foot candles, marked differences in rate of decline of plasma bilirubin levels were observed for the control and FMN treated animals, as illustrated in Figure 2. No change in plasma bilirubin was observed for FMN treated animals kept in the dark. In vitro studies have shown no competitive displacement of albumin-bound bilirubin by FMN at FMN concentrations up to 50 mg/100 ml.

![img-102.jpeg](img-102.jpeg)

Fig. 2. FMN enhancement of rate of plasma bilirubin decline in both albino and hooded Gunn rats exposed to daylight fluorescent lights at 300 foot candles intensity. FMN dosing of 75 mg/kg i.v., indicated by markings on the time axis.

<sup>**Page 298**</sup>

[Open Page 298 of PDF](https://pdfs-noindex.themindscapeishere.workers.dev/1973%20Jehovahs%20Witnesses%20Alternatives%20To%20Blood%20Transfusions.pdf#page=298)

FDDR-3/73

Riboflavin injected i.v. at a dose of 75 mg/kg can be observed to color the skin of either jaundiced or normal rats, suggesting that at this dosage level riboflavin, like bilirubin, is distributed to superficial tissues in appreciable concentration.

As shown in Figure 2, plasma bilirubin levels in jaundiced Gunn rats exposed to light of 300 foot candles intensity, in absence of FMN administration, decline at an apparent zero order rate to a new plateau level. Animals treated with FMN and exposed to the same light intensity exhibit virtually the same plateau plasma bilirubin as non-FMN-treated animals, but the plateau is achieved more rapidly in the FMN treated animals and at an apparent first order rate.

The results of these studies suggest that there is potential for improving the efficiency of bilirubin phototherapy through systemic administration of an appropriate agent. An improved efficiency of phototherapy which would either decrease the exposure time of infants to bilirubin lights or permit use of lower intensity light (perhaps even normal room lighting) would eliminate reservations with respect to some of the potential hazards cited for phototherapy¹. It is not suggested that FMN at the admittedly extraordinary dose level used in this study, nor at any other dose level, is suitable for this purpose on the basis of present knowledge. Currently an FMN dose-response study is being conducted in the Gunn rat model, and studies are in progress to determine whether FMN administration results in photo-products which differ from those produced by light exposure without FMN treatment.

THE LANCET, APRIL 18, 1970

### PHOTOTHERAPY FOR JAUNDICE

SIR,—Most pediatricians agree that exchange transfusion is not to be undertaken lightly. It has many hazards and, despite careful technique and special safeguards, a definite mortality, which must always be weighed against the risk of hemicterus. The suggestion that exposure to bright light could lower the bilirubin concentration of some infants sufficiently to avoid exchange transfusion was received with scepticism and indifference until very recently. The typical reaction mingled disbelief with the insistence that specimens were stored in the dark and examined promptly lest the bilirubin "went off".

The following case-history is of interest, since it concerns the use of light in an infant who would normally have been treated by exchange transfusion.

A girl was born on Nov. 18, 1960, at term after a normal pregnancy and labour. Weight 6 lb. 4 oz., condition satisfactory. The mother's blood-group is O Rh-positive and no antibodies were detected antenatally. The father's blood-group is A Rh-positive. The couple have one other child born in 1965; this child had severe early jaundice from presumed AO haemolytic disease and required three exchange transfusions.

Two hours after birth, she was jaundiced and pale. Her general condition was good and the liver and spleen were not enlarged. Venous blood haemoglobin was 11·6 g. per 100 ml.; Coombs weakly positive; group A Rh-positive. A blood-film showed many spherocytes. Serum-bilirubin 4·1 mg. per 100 ml.

Plant were made for an early exchange transfusion, which began eight hours after birth. Cannulation of the umbilical vein and then both arteries was unsuccessful. Assistance was summoned and the second operation, although able to insert venous

2. Behrman, R. E., Hsie, D. Y. Y. J. Pediat. 1969, 75, 718.

![img-103.jpeg](img-103.jpeg)

Fig. 1—Phototherapy technique.

The front of a fluorescent X-ray viewing-box is removed and placed over the cot, its 2 tubes approximately 25 cm. from the baby's skin. The baby is undressed, except for a bandage over the eyes, and is turned regularly. The temperature is monitored, here using an electric skin thermometer, to avoid cooling. Exposure is continued for as long as necessary, two or three days being usual.

![img-104.jpeg](img-104.jpeg)

Fig. 2—Changes in serum-bilirubin and haemoglobin levels.

and arterial catheters to 10 cm., was unable to withdraw blood from either site. It was considered inadvisable to attempt any further cannulation of the arteries and an X-ray was taken of the venous catheter in position. The umbilical vein had been perforated early in its course and the tip of the catheter was lying freely in the peritoneal cavity somewhere in the left hypochondrium.

By this time, the baby was too unwell to withstand further operation and it was decided to await return. At 16 hours, the serum-bilirubin had risen to 13·8 mg. per 100 ml. Extra glucose drinks were ordered. Norepinephrine 5 mg. 8-hourly was given by mouth, and continuous phototherapy was improvised (fig. 1). The skin blanched remarkably after only a few hours' treatment. Bilirubin and haemoglobin were estimated 12-hourly for the next three days until the bilirubin level began to fall (fig. 2). The initial sleep rise was not maintained and the maximum level was only 17·3 mg. (direct reacting 1·1 mg.) per 100 ml. on the third day. The baby made an uninterrupted recovery and a simple transfusion of 60 ml. of concentrated blood was given by scalp vein on the twelfth day. She has continued to make normal progress.

Special fitments for light treatment will undoubtedly become popular, but there is still too little information on the ideal quality and quantity of light needed for the maximum effect. It may well be that cumbersome cradles of 6 or 10 fluorescent tubes will prove unnecessary. Until more is known, there is much to commend the improvised use of an inverted fluorescent X-ray viewing box with the front removed, especially since this equipment is readily available.

London W.C.2.

# CONGENITAL NONOBSTRUCTIVE, NONHEMOLYTIC JAUNDICE\*

Effect of Phototherapy

RAFAEL GOMODISCHER, M.D.,
GERHARD LEVY, PHARM. D.,
JOSEPH KRASNER, PH.D.,
AND SUMNER J. YATFE, M.D.

SERUM bilirubin concentrations of newborn infants can be reduced by exposure to sunlight or artificial blue light.¹ These findings have been confirmed by many investigators in this country and (especially) abroad. More recently, phototherapy has been applied in a prophylactic manner to modify the degree of hyperbilirubinemia in premature infants.²

In the case reported below phototherapy was used successfully to reduce serum bilirubin concentration in an older infant with congenital, nonobstructive, nonhemolytic jaundice unresponsive to phenobarbital therapy.

# CASE REPORT

R.I.¹ (C.H. 477291), an obviously icteric infant with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (serum bilirubin as high as 95.4 mg per 100 ml, with a direct fraction of 0.3 mg per 100 ml), had required several exchange transfusions before admission at the age of 4 months. He had no evidence of hemolysis (half-time of ¹⁴Cr-tagged red cells was 25 days), and conventional liver-function tests gave normal results. Bilirubin in duodenal juice ranged between 1.2 and 5.2 mg, with direct fractions of 0.2 to 2.0 mg per 100 ml; however, the direct fraction was not identified further. A riboflavin test was also within normal limits, indicating no obstruction in the bile ducts. A 12-week course of oral phenobarbital (45 mg per day) administered before admission had not modified the jaundice in the serum bilirubin values. Defective intestinal absorption or rapid metabolism of the drug was not the cause of the lack of response since the concentration of phenobarbital in serum was very high (97 mg per liter). Phototherapy was started at 10 weeks of age (6-30-watt General Electric daylight bulbs 36 inches long). The infant was exposed male, and his eyes protected with neutral-density glasses. A precipitous fall in the serum bilirubin value occurred within 3 days (to 19.6 mg per 100 ml), with a further fall to 9.0 mg per 100 ml in the subsequent three days (Fig. 1). The deep-gold-yellow discoloration of the skin changed to green, followed by a return to normal color; the urine became dark green for 3 or 4 days shortly after initiation of phototherapy. The light was changed to 8-40-watt General Electric blue light bulbs 48 inches long (intensity of 350 footrandles measured at 45 cm from the light source) for 12 hours per day, and serum bilirubin concentrations were maintained between 6.3 and 8.3 mg per 100 ml for 60 days. The only abnormal sign on physical examination was the persistent mild scleral icterus. Discontinuation of phototherapy (Fig. 2) for 57 hours resulted in a sudden increase in the serum bilirubin from 7.9 to 11.7 mg per 100 ml preceded by reappearance of skin jaundice. When light treatment was reinitiated jaundice disappeared,

Studies of glucuronide-conjugating capacity of the infant and family members are summarized in Table 1. The patient excreted less than 5 per cent of an oral dose of 20 mg per kilogram of salicylamide as the glucuronide. Normally, about 50 per cent is glucuronidated and excreted into the urine. On the other hand, N-acetyl p-aminophenol (15 mg per kilogram by mouth) was eliminated normally, with a biologic half-life of 2.7 hours, and 47 per cent of the dose was excreted as the glucuronide. The normal response to N-acetyl p-aminophenol could have various interpretations: multiplicity of glucuronyl transferases; particular structure of this substrate (absence of a carboxyl group), making it more accessible to the active site of an abnormal glucuronyl transferase; and the fact that the rate-limiting factor in the metabolism of N-acetyl p-aminophenol is a step other than the glucuronide-conjugating process.

This finding suggested that the patient possessed (at least in skin) the genetic potential to glucuronidate bilirubin. We therefore turned to pharmacologic agents other than phenobarbital, to which the patient had not responded. Nifedipine (diethylsuccinamide) has been shown to enhance bilirubin conjugation and excretion in animals and to decrease serum bilirubin concentration in newborn infants. The patient received nifedipine orally in a dose of 37.5 mg per kilogram per day for 13 days and 75 mg per kilogram per day for 9 days (Fig. 1) without noteworthy modification of the serum bilirubin concentrations (6.3 to 8.3 mg per 100 ml).

Developmental-neurologic examinations were carried out at the ages of 19 weeks and 3 days, 19 weeks and 4 days and 21 weeks and 6 days and at 28 weeks. On examination on the first 2 occasions, abnormal neurologic findings, which although minor were considered important, included a consistent degree of head lag, inappropriate for age, on pull to sitting from the supine position. The Gross Motor Quotient at that time was 84, whereas the General Developmental Quotient, on the basis of adaptive and language behavior, was 97. After he had received phototherapy for 10 days, a 3d evaluation (performed at the age of 21 weeks and 6 days) showed no head lag on pull to sitting, on repeated trials, and the Gross Motor Quotient was 96. When the pa

tient was examined for the last time at the age of 28 weeks just before discharge from the hospital, he attained a Gross Motor Quotient of 114 and a General Developmental Quotient of 107. Development was considered to be normal in all respects, and there were no abnormal neurologic patterns.

## DISCUSSION

Congenital nonobstructive, nonhemolytic jaundice appears to present itself clinically in two different forms. Most patients respond to administration of phenobarbital with a marked lowering of serum bilirubin concentration, presumably by an enhancement of bilirubin glucuronide formation. The remaining patients tend to have higher serum bilirubin values and are more prone to kernicterus. These studies demonstrate that phototherapy can be a valuable therapeutic measure in patients with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia who do not respond to phenobarbital. A previous report from France based on several clinical failures indicated that such an approach was ineffective in this disease. No explanation for these discrepant results is now available other than a difference in experimental conditions (less light). The mechanism of action of light on bilirubin metabolism in man is unknown. Ostrow has demonstrated in icteric Gunn rats that phototherapy converts tissue bilirubin to water-soluble diazopositive derivatives that are apparently similar to the bilirubin catabolites found normally in Gunn-rat bile. In vitro it is possible to reduce the concentration of unconjugated bilirubin in solution with human albumin after exposure to light of certain wavelengths. As the bilirubin decreases, first biliverdin and then a series of compounds (some diaza reactive) appear in the solution. These products have not been fully identified, but the best available evidence suggests that they are, in part, pyrrolic segments of bilirubin. Most importantly, the derivatives appear to be less toxic (and more polar) than bilirubin itself. The photo-oxidative effect is proportional to the radiant energy emitted over a wide spectrum (300 to 600 mμ), with the blue-violet and yellow-green portions most effective.

The in vivo effects of light may be quite different from the preceding in vitro observations. The effects are more fleeting in the newborn infant, and identification of the oxidative products (including biliverdin) in the plasma has not been possible. Patients such as the present one with chronic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia afford a unique opportunity to supply some of the answers to the questions previously raised. Other biologic effects of light that should be mentioned include effect on biologic rhythms of body temperature, physical activity, adrenocortical secretion and food consumption. In animals, light has a profound influence on gonadal weight and ovulation. Many of these effects are probably mediated via photoreceptors in the retina, and it is therefore possible that covering the eyes, which has been employed in the newborn infant in

# EFFECTIVE PHOTOTHERAPY IN CONGENITAL NONOBSTRUCTIVE, NONHEMOLYTIC JAUNDICE\*

MYRON KARON, M.D., DANIEL IMACH, M.D., AND ALLEN SCHWARTZ, M.D.

CONGENITAL nonobstructive, nonhemolytic jaundice (the Crigler-Najjar syndrome) is characterized by the presence of indirect hyperbilirubinemia caused by a deficiency in the activity of the transferase forming bilirubin glucuronide. In 80 per cent of those affected "kernicterus" develops, usually early in childhood or in some cases after a long asymptomatic course. Attempts have been made to lower the concentration of serum bilirubin by the use of resins or by exchange transfusion or hemodialysis (or both). These measures have had only limited success. More recently, phenobarbital has been demonstrated to decrease serum bilirubin in some but not all cases of the Crigler-Najjar syndrome.

![img-107.jpeg](img-107.jpeg)

In the past two years considerable attention has been focused on the ability of light to decrease the serum bilirubin of normal and premature infants. This interest in phototherapy followed the early observations that daylight could cause the in vitro degradation of bilirubin. In view of these observations and because of sporadic reports that the blood level of bilirubin in the Crigler-Najjar syndrome could be reduced by phototherapy, light treatment was instituted in a newborn infant in whom this abnormality had recently been diagnosed.

# MATERIALS AND METHODS

# Patient

S.C. was the product of a full-term pregnancy. His mother was a 26-year-old primigravida. The pregnancy was complicated by edema during the last 2 months, treated with quinethazone, a nonmercurial diuretic, during the last week of gestation. Delivery was spontaneous, with vertex presentation after an uncomplicated 6-hour labor. The Apgar rating was 8. Physical examination at birth was innumerable. The patient weighed 4140 gm (9 lb, 2 oz). Jaundice was noted at 36 hours of life. Exchange transfusions were performed at 3 and 4 days of age to control hyperbilirubinemia (Fig. 1).

The patient was transferred to the Childrens Hospital of

The arrows at the top of the bilirubin curve indicate exchange transfusions. Direct-reacting bilirubin was always less than 10 per cent of the total and is not shown.

The total serum bilirubin was 34 mg, with an indirect fraction of 33 mg per 100 ml. The BUN was 2.5 ng per 100 ml. Galactose, urobilinogen and bilirubin could not be detected in his normal urine. The protein-bound iodine was 7.4 μg per 100 ml. The stool color varied from yellow to green to brown.

X-ray films of the skull were normal. An extensive family history failed to reveal a single case of jaundice on either side of the family. There was no consanguinity.

A presumptive diagnosis of Crigler-Najjar syndrome was made when a defect in ability to conjugate orally administered sodium salicylate was demonstrated (Table 1).

### Phototherapy

Phototherapy was given in the hospital with the use of a Bill-line, consisting of a bank of 11, 20-watt daylight fluorescent bulbs, shielded by ½ inch of plexi-glass placed approximately 25 to 25 inches from the child and at home using 4, 40-watt bulbs or a distance of 23 inches. The child's eyes were bandaged, and he was left male or occasionally covered by a diaper. The fluorescent bulbs were replaced after 400 hours' use.

### Bilirubin Determinations

Bilirubin determinations were performed on capillary blood by the method of Malloy and Evelyn. Total and direct fractions were assessed after 30 minutes of incubation.

\*Olympic Surgical Co., Seattle, Wash.

### Salicylate Studies

Sodium salicylate (USP) was administered orally on 3 separate occasions (Table 1) in a single dose of 500 mg, and a 24-hour urine collection obtained. We each took a single dose of 1 gm of sodium salicylate. The control children, 2 male infants 3 and 4 months of age, were given sodium salicylate, 40 mg per kilogram of body weight, orally before collection of 24-hour urine specimen.

Free salicylate was determined by the method of Brodie et al. with the use of 5-ml aliquots. Salicyluric acid was determined by extraction with dichloroethane, 1-ml aliquots being used. Total glucuronides were determined by incubation of 5-ml aliquots of urine with 2400 units of beta-glucuronidase in 0.1M potassium acetate buffer, pH 8.1.

### RESULTS

### Light Therapy

The course of the first two months of this infant's life is summarized with respect to bilirubin and hemoglobin concentration in Figure 1. Two exchange transfusions using Type A positive blood were performed on the third and fourth days of life as indicated by the arrows at the top of the bilirubin curve. The indirect bilirubin rose steadily after these exchange transfusions to a level of 33 mg per 100 ml. The child underwent two additional exchange transfusions of 450 ml of Type A blood each over a five-hour period, reducing the bilirubin to a level of approximately 10 mg per 100 ml. Both phototherapy and phenobarbital orally in a dose of 5 mg every eight hours were instituted. The phenobarbital treatment was discontinued after four days. The light treatment was given for three days out of five and was discontinued at the age of 16 days when the bilirubin level had reached a plateau of 8 to 10 mg per 100 ml. With the light off, the serum bilirubin rose at a rate of 1 mg per 100 ml per day, determined by the slope of the best fit line, to a level of 15 mg per 100 ml (Table 2). At

# Salicylate Determinations

The percentage of salicylate excreted as glucuronide by the patient in three separate collections of urine was at least one third to one fourth of normal (Table 1). The proportion of sodium salicylate excreted as the free acid ranged between 2 and 10 per cent. The major metabolite of the urine was salicyluric acid. The patient's mother excreted less salicyl glucuronide than the adult controls.

# Growth and Development

Measurements of height and weight during the first five months of life remained entirely normal. Developmental and neurologic examinations at three and five months of age also gave normal re-

\*For a follow-up report on this patient, see Correspondence, page 197.

sults, the patient pulling himself to standing position at five and a half months. His sleep patterns were not affected by the light treatment; he had slept through the night since the age of six weeks. An electroencephalogram taken at the age of three months was normal. An ophthalmologic examination after five months of phototherapy was within normal limits.

# DISCUSSION

# Phototherapy

These results indicate that phototherapy, which has been shown to cause the nonenzymatic degradation of bilirubin into water-soluble products in vitro, can control the level of indirect serum bilirubin in an infant with the Crigler-Najjar syndrome. Furthermore, the use of this modality of treatment for more than five months, the longest duration of phototherapy reported to date, has resulted in no demonstrable toxic effects or disturbances of growth. These findings are in agreement with studies in animals indicating that the degradation products of phototherapy are not toxic to nervous tissue.

The gradual rise in serum bilirubin from a level of 7.5 to 8 mg per 100 ml at three months to 10 to 11 mg per 100 ml at five months (Fig. 2) most probably represents pigment production from an increased red-cell mass. An alternative explanation would be a decrease in the efficiency of phototherapy. This possibility was investigated by withdrawal of therapy at the age of five months (Fig. 2 and Table 2). By that time, the bilirubin production rate had risen almost twice to between 1.8 and 2.0 mg per 100 ml per day (Table 2). In spite of this, light was able to decrease bilirubin at the rate of 0.6 mg per 100 ml per day, indicating that the amount of bilirubin degraded was still in the range of 2.4 to 2.6 (1.8 + 0.6, 2.0 + 0.6) mg per 100 ml per day. This is essentially the same as that observed at the age of one and a half months, suggesting that the increased bilirubin production rather decreased degradation is the most likely explanation for the higher pigment level in the serum in the face of continued phototherapy.

The exact nature of the water-soluble breakdown products induced by phototherapy is not known. Studies in a child and in the Gunn rat, both with a deficiency in glucuronyl transferase, have indicated a remarkably constant rate of bilirubin turnover involving alternate pathways of bilirubin degradation. These pathways yield colorless, polar, diazo-negative breakdown products that are excreted in urine and bile. Goldstein has recently demonstrated that the heme contained in Heinz bodies is primarily converted to diazo-negative water-soluble metabolites. The relation of the water-soluble degradation products produced through these alternative pathways to those induced by phototherapy is a matter for speculation and investigation.

# PHOTOTHERAPY FOR JAUNDICE

To the Editor: We have followed the patient (S.C.) described by Drs. Karon, Imach and Schwarz in "Effective Phototherapy in Congenital Nonobstructive, Nonhemolytic Jaundice" (page 377, this issue of the Journal) since he was born months of age. He has continued to receive phototherapy for approximately 12 hours each night.

At six and a half months of age, bilirubin levels ranged between 11.4 and 12.8 mg per 100 ml over a two-week period. A four-week course of phenobarbital was started while nightly phototherapy was continued. The dosage of phenobarbital was 135 mg per day (15 mg per kilogram) in three divided doses. During this period, indirect bilirubin, measured twice weekly, varied between 11 and 15 mg per 100 ml. (Simultaneous direct bilirubin determinations were always less than 1 mg per 100 ml.) The only effect of the phenobarbital was increased drowsiness.

In the last four months, the bilirubin levels have ranged between 10.6 and 16.4 mg per 100 ml while phototherapy has been continued for an average of 12 hours a night. On the basis of an estimated blood volume of 70 ml per kilogram, a 1 per cent hemolysis rate and the conversion of 1 gm of hemoglobin to 35 mg of bilirubin, the estimated bilirubin production rate had risen to 34.5 mg per day by the age of 11 months.

The patient is now 12 months of age. Developmental milestones are within normal limits for his age, his having walked and started monosyllabic words at the age of nine months. He is an alert and active child whose only abnormality on physical examination is skin and scleral icterus. The hemoglobin has ranged between 11 and 12.8 mg per 100 ml in the last four months. Height and weight are just above the fiftieth percentile for age. Because of the lack of response to phenobarbital, he probably represents the Type I glucuronyl transferase deficiency of Arias et al. (Amer J Med 47:397, September, 1969). The phototherapy (during which the eyes are covered) has had no apparent ill-effect.

Because the likelihood of the development of kernicterus at higher levels of bilirubin maintained over long periods is unknown, the present phototherapy regimen will be continued.

# PHOTOTHERAPY OF SEVERE UNCONJUGATED

# HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA: FORMATION AND REMOVAL OF LABELED BILIRUBIN DERIVATIVES

Edward W. Callahan, Jr., M.D., M. Michael Thaler, M.D., Myron Karon, M.D.,
Karinne Bauer, and Rudi Schmid, M.D.

From the Departments of Medicine and Pediatrics, University of California, San Francisco;
Department of Pediatrics, University of Southern California, and
Children's Hospital of Los Angeles

ABSTRACT. Formation and disposition of the photodegradation products of bilirubin was studied in two infants with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Crigler-Naijor syndrome) who responded to phototherapy with a marked and sustained fall of serum bilirubin. During exposure to light, tracer amounts of ¹⁴C-bilirubin were infused at constant rates for periods of 10 and 24 hours. Radioactivity in bilirubin and in its photoderivatives was determined in serially collected samples

of plasma, urine, and bile. Direct evidence was obtained that light converts bilirubin in vitro to more polar, predominantly diazonegative, and presumably less toxic derivatives which are rapidly excreted in bile and urine without detectable retention in the plasma. These findings provide experimental support for the use of phototherapy in the management of hyperbilirubinemia in infants. Pediatrics, 46:841, 1970, PHOTOTHERAPY, HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA, PHOTODEGRADATION PRODUCTS.

NATURAL or artificial light has been found to be effective in lowering the serum bilirubin level of infants with neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.¹⁻³ This reduction is thought to result from photodecomposition of bilirubin because in vitro the pigment is rapidly degraded by exposure to light.⁴,⁵ Studies of the degradation products prepared by exposing solutions of analytically pure bilirubin to light showed that, in contrast to the parent pigment, the photoderivatives are water-soluble and diazonegative.⁶ Furthermore, when infused into experimental animals, they appeared to be less toxic than bilirubin and to be readily excreted in bile and urine.⁶,⁷

Comparable studies in human subjects have not been reported, and little is known about the kinetics of bilirubin metabolism in icteric patients undergoing phototherapy. Of further concern is the recent sug-

gestion that the photodegradation products formed in vivo and in vitro may differ qualitatively.⁸ Since phototherapy is being utilized for the routine treatment of infants with neonatal hyperbilirubinemia,⁹ it would be desirable to clarify the effect of light on bilirubin metabolism and disposition by direct studies of icteric infants under illumination. As an essential part of such an investigation, assurance should be obtained that the photoderivatives of bilirubin formed in vivo are either non-toxic or are rapidly eliminated from the organism. Unfortunately, the transient nature of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and the problems inherent in studies of newborn infants have prevented such investigations.

A unique opportunity to carry out analogous studies arose when two infants of 5 and 7 months of age with severe, congenital, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia

# PHOTOTHERAPY OF HYPERBILIRUBINEMIC INFANTS

![img-109.jpeg](img-109.jpeg)

FIG. 1. Patient 1. Specific radioactivity of serum bilirubin (dpm/μg) during and after infusion of ¹⁴C-bilirubin. Horizontal arrow indicates the period of exposure to light; horizontal bar indicates the duration of labeled bilirubin infusion.

(Crigler-Najjar syndrome) were found to respond to phototherapy with dramatic and sustained reductions in serum bilirubin levels.¹⁰,¹¹ During phototherapy, both patients were infused for prolonged periods with tracer amounts of ¹⁴C-bilirubin. Plasma, urine, and bile were collected, and the disposition of the infused labeled pigment was determined.

# PATIENTS AND METHODS

# Clinical Data

The historical, clinical, and laboratory findings in each patient and their responses to phototherapy were described in detail elsewhere.¹⁰,¹¹ At the time of study, Patient 1 was 5 months old and weighed 7.5 kg. Shortly after birth, his serum bilirubin rose to levels in excess of 30 mg/100 ml, necessitating repeated exchange transfusions. Phototherapy was begun after the last exchange transfusion had reduced the serum bilirubin from 33 mg/100 ml to 10 mg/100 ml. With daily illumination of 12 to 15 hours' duration, it was possible to maintain the serum bilirubin concentration around 11 mg/100 ml (range, 10 mg/100 ml to 13 mg/100 ml).

Patient 2\* was 7 months old when studied and weighed 8 kg. Severe hyperbilirubinemia developed in the immediate neonatal period and was only transiently amelio-

rated by several exchange transfusions. After phototherapy had been instituted, the serum bilirubin concentration fell from 35 to 9 mg/100 ml, where it stabilized on daily illumination of approximately 12 hours' duration. At the time of study, the bilirubin concentration ranged from 8 to 11 mg/100 ml.

Phenobarbital had been administered to each patient for more than 1 month without noticeable effect on the hyperbilirubinemia.¹⁰,¹¹

# Phototherapy

During the 5 days of investigation, Patient 1 was exposed continuously to 350 foot-candles of illumination provided by six, 30-watt General Electric "daylight" bulbs contained in a light candle at a distance of 23 in. In Patient 2, an initial period of 48 hours of continuous illumination (350 foot-candle intensity provided by 11, 20-watt "daylight" fluorescent bulbs at a distance of 20 in.) was followed by a 36-hour period without light treatment; subsequently, the infant was treated with light for 8 hours daily.

# Isotopic Studies

¹⁴C-bilirubin was prepared and its specific activity was determined by methods reported previously.¹ Immediately before administration, the pigment was recrystallized and then dissolved under sterile conditions in pyrogen-free 0.1 N NaOH and 5% human albumin. This solution was infused into an arm vein at a constant rate of 2 ml per hour delivered by a Harvard infusion pump.† During infusion, the solution was protected from light and kept at 4°C with ice packs. Patient 1 was infused for 10 hours at a rate of 32 μg of ¹⁴C-bilirubin per hour \[specific activity, 6,500 disintegrations per minute (dpm) per microgram], and Patient 2 was infused for 24 hours at a rate of 15 μg of ¹⁴C-bilirubin per hour (specific activity, 14,000 dpm per microgram).

Multiple blood samples were drawn from

the opposite antecubital vein during and after the infusion and the serum was separated by centrifugation. Bile was aspirated by duodenal intubation. Urine was collected continuously by external drainage through light-shielded tubing. All serum, bile, urine, and stool samples were frozen immediately and kept in the dark until analyzed.

# Analytical Procedures

The serum bilirubin concentration was measured by the conventional diazo method¹² and by the Weber-Schalm solvent partition method.¹³ Bilirubin was crystallized from the serum, and its specific radioactivity was determined by liquid scintillation counting.¹⁴ Radioactivity was also assayed in whole serum and in the lower, non-polar phase of the Weber-Schalm system. By comparing the measured specific radioactivity of the bilirubin crystallized from the serum with the specific activity

calculated from the total ¹⁴C-activity and the analytically determined bilirubin concentration of the serum, it was possible to detect the presence, if any, of labeled pigment derivatives.

The bile specimens obtained by duodenal aspiration were only slightly colored and exhibited concentrations of diazo-reacting pigment in the range of 0.5 to 1.5 mg per 100 ml, so that direct crystallization of the bilirubin was not possible. An indirect approach was therefore chosen: the apparent specific radioactivity of bilirubin in the bile was estimated by dividing the total of ¹⁴C-activity of each bile specimen by the content of diazo-reacting pigment in the sample. All assays were carried out in quadruplicate, with all four determinations yielding virtually identical values. Since at any given time the specific radioactivity of bilirubin in the bile cannot exceed that of the pigment in the serum,¹⁵ any excess radioactivity in the bile not accounted for by ¹⁴C-bilirubin indicates the presence of labeled diazonegative bilirubin derivatives. Total radioactivity in urine and feces was quantitated by methods described previously.¹⁶

# RESULTS

The specific radioactivity of the serum bilirubin during and following the constant

infusion of tracer pigment is shown in Figures 1 and 2. During the infusion, the specific activity in both patients increased at a similar rate, but in neither instance had it reached a constant value by the time the infusion was completed. Thus, despite the extended infusion periods, complete and homogeneous mixing of the infused tracer with the endogenous miscible bilirubin pool could not be achieved. In Patient 2, in whom the infusion lasted 24 hours, the pattern of the specific activity of the serum bilirubin (Fig. 2) suggests that mixing of the tracer pigment with the miscible bilirubin pool may have been more nearly complete than in Patient 1, who received a much briefer infusion. After completion of the infusions, the specific radioactivity of the serum bilirubin initially fell rapidly followed by a slower exponential decline (Fig. 1 and 2). The first rapid component presumably indicated additional mixing of the tracer with the endogenous bilirubin, while the second, slower decline probably reflected the rate of turnover of the total pigment pool. However, it should be noted that, because of the incomplete mixing at the end of the infusion periods, analysis of these disappearance curves in terms of first-order kinetics may not be strictly applicable.

Bilirubin was crystallized from 16 individual serum samples and its specific radioactivity was determined. The specific activity was also calculated by dividing the total radioactivity in each serum sample by its bilirubin content. The ratio of the two specific activities so determined in all samples averaged 0.97; in no individual serum sample did the two values differ by more than 10%. These findings indicate that virtually all radioactivity in the serum was accounted for by isotope in intact ¹⁴C-bilirubin while the concentration of radioactive bilirubin derivatives in the serum was insignificant.

Bile specimens were obtained from both patients; in Patient 1 all bile samples were collected during phototherapy; in Patient 2, specimens were aspirated during phototherapy and 22 hours after cessation of illu-

mination. In five individual bile specimens obtained from both patients during phototherapy, the apparent specific radioactivity of diazo-positive pigment exceeded the simultaneously determined specific activity of the ¹⁴C-bilirubin in the serum by factors ranging from 2.3 to 6.3. This indicates that most of the radioactivity in the bile during phototherapy was present in diazonegative pigment derivatives rather than in intact bilirubin. After cessation of phototherapy in Patient 2, the relative amount of these labeled derivatives in the bile decreased sharply, as indicated by a reduction of this factor to 1.6, i.e., less radioactivity was present in the bile in diazonegative derivatives in comparison with bile collected during phototherapy.

The radioactivity excreted during the first 5 days of the study accounted for 35% (Patient 1) and 29% (Patient 2) of the infused dose. Most of this label was present in the stool; stools collected during the study periods contained 83% and 72% of the recovered ¹⁴C-activity, while the urine contained 18 and 28%, respectively (Fig. 3 and 4). None of the radioactivity in the urine was present in the form of intact bilirubin.

On the basis of the level and specific activity of the serum bilirubin and the plasma volume (estimated from the hematocrit and body weight), the fraction of the infused isotopic pigment that is bound to albumin in the vascular compartment may be calculated. On the fifth day of the study, this compartment contained 22% (Patient 1) and 24% (Patient 2) of the administered pigment. Since the extravascular space for albumin is approximately 1.5 times the plasma volume,¹⁷ the extravascular pool of bilirubin¹⁸ may be assumed to have been about 34% (Patient 1) and 37% (Patient 2) of the infused label. Thus, at the conclusion of each study, at least 90% of the infused labeled pigment was accounted for in the organism and the excreta.

# DISCUSSION

These studies represent an initial attempt to investigate with tracer technics the fate of bilirubin in patients with hyperbilirubinemia undergoing phototherapy. Our investigative approach differed from that used in two previous studies of untreated patients with severe hyperbilirubinemia (Crigler-Najjar syndrome).¹⁵,¹⁶ In these earlier studies, pulse labeling was used to
