introduce the isotopic tracer pigment into the miscible bilirubin pool. After an initial mixing period which lasted 12 to 24 hours, the pool exhibited a single exponential rate of isotope disappearance which permitted calculation of the rate of bilirubin production and turnover, and estimation of the pool size.¹⁵,¹⁶ A third patient studied with a similar pulse tracer technic had a significantly lower serum bilirubin level,¹⁷ presumably reflecting a partial deficiency of the conjugating apparatus.¹⁸ In this patient, the ability to conjugate and excrete bilirubin, although at greatly reduced rates, may have prevented adequate mixing of the injected tracer pulse with the total endogenous pigment pool (apparent mixing with the plasma pigment pool required 1 hour) which could explain the implausible turnover rate of plasma bilirubin calculated by the pulse tracer technic. As a result, the kinetic data obtained in this patient are difficult to analyze and interpret.

Difficulties of a similar nature were anticipated in the present studies because phototherapy presumably reduces the serum bilirubin level by enhancing the degradation of pigment in those portions of the bilirubin pool directly exposed to light. This would be expected to disturb the homogeneity of the miscible pigment pool and to complicate its characterization by means of first-order kinetics. Therefore, we attempted to achieve uniform labeling of the miscible bilirubin pool with prolonged infusions of tracer pigment at a constant rate. A similar method was found to yield satisfactory results in patients with Gilbert's syndrome and with normal subjects in whom a constant specific activity of plasma bilirubin usually is reached within the first 10 hours of infusion.²¹ In Patient 1, 10 hours of constant infusion of ¹⁴C-bilirubin were inadequate for uniform labeling, as the specific activity of the serum bilirubin failed to reach a plateau (Fig. 1). The tracer infusion was, therefore, extended to 24 hours in Patient 2 (Fig. 2); but, despite this, homogeneous distribution of the infused ¹⁴C-bilirubin in the miscible pigment pool was not

achieved. However, the characteristics of the specific activity disappearance curve of serum bilirubin in Patient 2 suggest that, by prolonging the infusion, more nearly complete mixing was obtained as compared to Patient 1. The absence of uniform labeling, which may have been a direct result of phototherapy, prevented accurate calculation of the dimensions and kinetics of the total bilirubin pool and made a quantitative appraisal of the bilirubin degradation rate during phototherapy impossible. In planning future isotopic studies of this type, these methodological aspects should be given prime consideration.

Despite these problems, the present studies provide conclusive evidence that phototherapy converts a portion of the body's bilirubin to pigment derivatives that are rapidly eliminated from the blood. This is evident from the observation that radioactive bilirubin derivatives were not detectable in the serum, while they were plentiful in the bile, particularly during periods of phototherapy. Thirty-five and 29% of the infused isotope was recovered in stool and urine collected during the first 5 days in Patients 1 and 2, respectively. Approximately three fourths of the eliminated isotope was recovered in the feces, with the remaining fraction appearing in the urine. The isotope fraction excreted in the urine was considerably larger than that in previously studied untreated patients with the Crigler-Najjar syndrome¹¹,¹⁸,¹⁹ and in jaundiced Gunn rats.¹⁹ While enhanced isotope excretion in the urine may be attributable to phototherapy, this cannot be established with certainty because all earlier human and murine studies employed pulse labeling rather than continuous tracer infusion.

At the conclusion of the study, 57% (Patient 1) and 53% (Patient 2) of the infused label was accounted for by isotope in the plasma and in the excreta. Since at least another 34 and 37%, respectively, of the labeled pigment was distributed in the extravascular albumin space,¹⁸,¹⁹ less than 10% of the infused isotopic pigment was unaccounted for. Therefore, it is improbable

that phototherapy reduces serum bilirubin levels by means of displacement of pigment from its albumin carrier or through significant redistribution of pigment between plasma and tissues.

The exact location of the photoconversion of bilirubin to its derivatives remains to be determined, but the skin and/or the percutaneous vascular compartment appear to be the most important sites because they are directly exposed to the highest intensity of illumination. This interpretation is supported by the observation that, during phototherapy, exposed areas of the skin lose their icteric color despite continuing hyperbilirubinemia, while areas shielded from light (e.g., under eye patches) retain their yellow color.

In the Crigler-Najjar syndrome, as in Gunn rats, the inability to conjugate and, hence, to excrete intact bilirubin results in the deposition of this pigment by alternate metabolic pathways. In these circumstances, the major mechanism for pigment elimination is the breakdown of bilirubin to more polar, diazonegative, and water soluble derivatives of undetermined chemical structure which are readily excreted in the bile and urine; other, relatively minor pathways include direct transfer of pigment across the intestinal mucosa into the gut lumen and excretion of small amounts of unconjugated bilirubin in the bile. When the capacity of these alternate excretory pathways equals the rate of pigment production, a steady state is reached characterized by elevated and relatively constant levels of serum bilirubin. The bilirubin derivatives in the bile and urine of our patients on phototherapy qualitatively resembled those found in human and murine hyperbilirubinemia without treatment. This may suggest that exposure to light simply accelerates the breakdown of bilirubin by mechanisms similar to those normally operative in patients with the Crigler-Najjar syndrome and in Gunn rats. Definitive proof for this concept will require chemical identification and structural analysis of these pigment derivatives.

These observations in patients with congenital hyperbilirubinemia document for the first time that light converts a portion of the bilirubin pool in man to more water-soluble derivatives that are efficiently excreted in the bile and urine. The findings are directly applicable to neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and lend strong support to the recent recommendation that environmental illumination should be a standard feature of newborn nurseries.

MEDICAL TRIBUNE

# Hyperbilirubinemia Prevented With Phototherapy

## 88 Prematures Studied In First U.S. Trials

Medical Tribune—World Wide Report

ATLANTIC CITY, N.J.—Nearly all premature infants develop hyperbilirubinemia to some degree, and in an estimated 10 to 20 per cent it reaches dangerous levels predisposing to possible brain damage.

An apparently successful method for preventing its development was reported on here by Dr. Jerold F. Lucey, of the University of Vermont College of Medicine, at a joint session of the American Pediatric Society and Society for Pediatric Research annual meetings.

The procedure—entailing use of phototherapy to reduce serum bilirubin levels—originated close to a decade ago with Dr. Robert Cremer in England and has since been widely applied in Europe. However, the Vermont studies are reportedly the first of their kind here in the United States.

Dr. Lucey said that in controlled clinical trials over the past year in 88 premature infants, total serum bilirubin levels in all treated infants were held below the 20-mg./100 ml. level considered indicative of the need for exchange transfusion.

### Serum Bilirubin Levels Given

None had a level higher than 11 mg./100 ml. In contrast, during the treatment period, about 20 per cent of control infants had levels ranging between 15 and 20 mg./100 ml., Dr. Lucey reported.

Treatment was given to every other infant below 2,500 Gm. in birth weight in the premature nurseries at Mary Fletcher and DeGoesbriand Memorial Hospitals in Burlington. (The two have recently been merged to form the Vermont Medical Center.) Treated and control groups were comparable with respect to birth weight and initial weight loss, gestational age, and fluid intake, it was noted.

Phototherapy with artificial blue light was provided by a "homemade" light chamber placed outside the baby's incubator. Infants remained under the lights from 12 through 144 hours after birth, and serial bilirubin determinations were performed.

These and earlier experimental studies showed the effect to be limited to serum

![img-113.jpeg](img-113.jpeg)

Incubator in which premature receive phototherapy to prevent hyperbilirubinemia.

bilirubin, Dr. Lucey emphasized. There was no change in levels of serum albumin, protein binding, free fatty acids, or uric acid.

He pointed out that the phototherapy procedure has not become popular in this country because of concern over the possible toxicity of photochemical decomposition products of bilirubin.

"The method has been extensively used in England, France, and Brazil, and there has been a unanimity of opinion there that there is no damage. We have been slower to appreciate this," Dr. Lucey said.

### 100 Treated Cases Needed

"Although statistically significant differences were shown between our treated and control groups," he added, "we feel we will need to have at least 100 treated cases to have a convincing case for phototherapy." Dr. Mario Ferreiro of Chile, who has been working in Vermont with Dr. Lucey on this project, has returned to South America and is also conducting trials there.

"They have a higher incidence there of very small babies, under 3 pounds in birth weight," Dr. Lucey pointed out. "It is important to prove the value of the treatment in that group because serum bilirubin is most likely to reach dangerous levels in the very small premature."

Experimental studies have indicated that the significance of a given serum bilirubin level depends in part on the presence of other abnormalities, he observed.

"For example, the presence of hypoglycemia, acidosis, anoxia, low serum protein, and such appears to set up some babies for kernicterus and possible brain damage at lower levels of serum bilirubin than would otherwise put them at risk."

"If we can control this one variable—the serum bilirubin concentration—we may be able to improve the outlook for these babies."

The report was in collaboration with Dr. Ferreiro and with Jean Hewitt, of the Department of Pediatrics.

# ARTICLES

# EFFECT OF ENVIRONMENTAL ILLUMINATION IN PREVENTION OF HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA OF PREMATURITY

Frank Giunta, M.D., and Jageswar Rath, M.D.

From the Providence Lying-In Hospital, Providence, Rhode Island

ABSTRACT. A controlled study involving 90 babies weighing under 2,500 gm was done by placing 47 completely exposed infants, except for diapers, under environmental lights averaging 90 footcandles and 49 fully clothed infants under lights averaging 10 footcandles. A significantly lower serum bilirubin occurred in the light group from the second to the sixth day. Only three babies developed in

direct bilirubin levels over 15 mg/100 ml in the light group against 14 in the control group. Exposure to this intensity of environmental lighting seems to be of much value in the routine treatment of premature infants for the prevention of hyperbilirubinemia. Pediatrics, 44:162, 1969, PHOTOTHERAPY, HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA, PREMATURITY, PREMATURE INFANTS.

PHOTOTHERAPY as a method of reducing hyperbilirubinemia was first reported in 1958 by Cremer, Perryman, and Richards¹ in England. Later, studies done in France,² Italy,³ Uruguay⁴ and, more recently, in the United States by Lucey⁵⁻⁶ demonstrated that exposure to light could influence serum bilirubin levels. Various devices are now commercially available for intensive light therapy.

It was noted, however, that all previous studies¹⁻⁴ and available equipment utilized high intensity illumination ranging between 200 and 500 footcandles. Because of this, a study was done to determine the effects of brighter illumination of the premature nursery on bilirubin levels. It was hoped that the benefits of phototherapy could thus be obtained without using phototherapy units.

# MATERIAL AND METHODS

An alternate case series of 96 consecutive babies weighing less than 2,500 gm at birth at Providence Lying-In Hospital from February 1968 to July 1968 were placed either in a brightly lighted nursery exposed except for diapers or under the usual dim nursery light and fully clothed.

Serum bilirubin, blood hemoglobin, Coomb's test, blood group, Rh factor, and blood glucose were determined for each

baby soon after birth. Thereafter, a bilirubin and hemoglobin were obtained every 12 hours for 6 days.

Capillary blood was collected by heel prick. Babies with positive Coomb's test were excluded from the study, as were seven who died soon after birth and five who were transferred to regular nurseries by their physician.

Early feedings were encouraged. The initial glucose solution feeding was given at 12 hours of age, except for those with respiratory distress syndrome or other problems requiring intra-arterial or intravenous therapy. Milk formulas were started as soon as these were tolerated.

No differentiation of race or sex was made in the selection of babies. Bilirubin determinations were done by the Evelyn-Mallin method. The colorimetric determinations for direct and total serum bilirubin were obtained by recording the optical density at 540 mμ using a Coleman Junior Spectrophotometer. The direct reacting bilirubin was read exactly 60 seconds after the addition of diazo reagent. Six milliliters of methyl alcohol was then added, and 10 minutes later it was read as the total serum bilirubin. The indirect serum bilirubin was determined by subtracting the direct from the

total bilirubin. The indirect bilirubin was used in our study because this, more than the total bilirubin, has influenced our treatment of infants with hyperbilirubinemia. The Somogyi-Nelson method was used for blood glucose determinations, and the Cyanmethemoglobin method was used for hemoglobin determination.

The lights used were two fixtures with four 8 ft, 75 watt fluorescent cool white light tubes in each fixture. They were suspended 2 ft from a 9 ft ceiling in a room 17 by 11 ft. The minimum distance of the infant from the nearest light source was 4 ft (Fig. 1 and 2). The spectral energy distribution curve of a cool white fluorescent tube shows a continuous spectrum, including all the visible wavelengths, from 3,800 Angström units to 7,500 Angström units and a maximum energy at 5,800 Angströms. The light tubes are low brightness light sources, even though the total light output is high and they produce less total heat for a given amount of light

than a filament lamp.

A Westinghouse light meter, calibrated to read the intensity of the incident light directly in footcandles, was used to make the illumination measurements. The light at the level of the baby's skin averaged 90 footcandles. Babies were placed in the room soon after birth and were continuously exposed to this illumination for six days. Eye shades were not used. No special attention was given to changing the position of the infant, other than with routine handling. The control group was kept clothed and under illumination averaging 10 footcandles. Both groups were kept in Isolettes or Gordon Armstrong incubators. Clear plastic or glass, such as that used in these units, transmits about 90% of light. Our readings were taken inside the units.

In addition, the mean of the 6-day total and the mean of the highest indirect bilirubin in the 6-day period are all noted. These averages are all found to be lower in the light group.

The Analysis of Variance was used to analyze the bilirubin data. There was no significant difference between the groups on the first day (p > .05). However, there were highly significant differences on the last day (p < .01) and for the average of the 6 days (p < .01).

Table III shows the highest indirect bilirubin value found in the 6-day period for babies in the two groups. In the light-treated group, only three babies developed indirect bilirubin levels over 15 mg/100 ml against 14 in the control group. One of the three in the light group went over 18 mg/100 ml.

She was the smallest baby in the series, with a birth weight of 1,219 gm, and had severe hyaline membrane disease. She developed an indirect bilirubin level of 22.3 mg on the fifth day, but after clinical evaluation the pediatrician decided not to do an exchange transfusion.

Seven of the babies in the control group had indirect bilirubins over 18 mg/100 ml. One of these infants had an exchange transfusion because of a rapidly rising indirect bilirubin at 47 hours and a reading of 18.2 at that time. Another baby in this group was given 2 gm of salt-free albumin intravenously at 93 hours of age because of an indirect bilirubin of 20 mg/100 ml in the hope of increasing the albumin-binding capacity for bilirubin.

# DISCUSSION

All past studies¹⁻⁴ have employed high intensity illumination with ranges of 200 to 500 footcandles of light. This study shows that environmental lighting of the intensity used by us is effective in reducing bilirubin levels in premature infants, but not with as good results. Lucey⁶ was able to maintain bilirubin levels under 12 mg/100 ml. Our lighting resulted in a definite shift to lower levels of bilirubin. Only three babies in the light group concerned us because of elevated bilirubins while there were 14 in the control group.

In addition to the reduction of bilirubin, another benefit of good lighting is the com-

fort and ease of performing most close visual procedures by physicians, nurses and technicians without supplemental lighting. The lights provided fairly uniform general illumination over the entire room. There was no problem with glare on variation in brightness, which are the usual causes of eye fatigue and headache. Our intensive care nurses enjoy working in the well lighted room and cannot conceive of working in a dimly lighted room again. They speak of more illumination rather than less. Babies are more easily monitored. Jaundice, cyanosis, respiratory changes, and monitoring equipment show up much better.

Just as there has been much skepticism about the effects of light in lowering bilirubin levels, so also there has been much hesitation in using them because of fear of untoward¹⁰ effects. Studies by Broughton, Rossiter, Warren, and Goulis,¹¹ Ostrow,¹² and Blondheim and Kaufmann¹³ have shown no evidence of toxicity from the by-products of photochemical reaction on bilirubin. More recently, Diamond, Lucey, and Schmid¹⁴ injected newborn guinea pigs with photodecomposed bilirubin and found that the end products were readily excreted by the kidneys with no detectable toxic effects. The bi-products are water soluble and do not pass the blood brain barrier. With our present knowledge, the photochemical breakdown products must be considered safer than the unconjugated bilirubin, which is known to be toxic.

In our study no detectable toxic effects were noted during the hospitalization of the 47 babies treated under lights, and there were no evident neurologic or visual problems in 26 follow-up reports from pediatricians 4 to 9 months after discharge. Therefore, for routine care of premature infants and for any infant who develops much jaundice regardless of the cause, exposure to high intensity illumination would be advisable. If this is not available in a particular hospital, the best lighting that can be mustered should be used and the baby should be completely exposed for maximum effect of phototherapy.

The smaller the hospital the greater is the need for high intensity illumination, since such hospitals have the least experience with exchange transfusions. Environmental lighting of much higher intensity than that used by us can be designed by lighting engineers to give the level desired with comfortable brightness ratios and a minimum of glare. These should be considered for existing nurseries and in planning the illumination for new nurseries. Every large hospital treating a greater number of premature infants could have a room with high intensity environmental illumination so that a number of babies may be treated in the room at the same time. For this reason, we are converting a small room in our nursery into a light room. This can be accomplished by using a panel of fluorescent lights in the ceiling to give diffuse, no glare illumination on the baby at levels of 500 footcandles or more, which is greater than the intensity of light from a phototherapy unit.

# SPECULATION

Compared with the levels of illumination ordinarily encountered in nature, we have literally been working in the dark when it comes to lighting in our nurseries. Daylight in the shade measures 100 to 1,000 footcandles and direct sunlight measures from 5,000 to 10,000 footcandles. Comfortable general lighting of much higher intensity than that available with present day phototherapy units is practical and not difficult.

Blondheim and Kaufmann¹⁴ showed that with comparatively weak light of up to 40 footcandles, there was no destruction of bilirubin as measured by the indirect diazo reaction. No significant difference in the bilirubin levels on the first day of our study and in the higher intensity study of Lucey, Ferreiro, and Hewitt¹⁵ was noted. It would be of value to determine if levels of 500 to 1,000 footcandles can produce a much more rapid breakdown of bilirubin, thereby helping to lower some of the more rapidly rising bilirubins which develop from hemolysis on the first day.

# ARTICLES

167

The relative efficiency of various colors of light was investigated by Blondheim and Kaufmann,¹³ who found that the wavelength used in illuminating the bilirubin was not critical. Most previous work specified use of blue light. In our study cool white lights were used and found to be effective. It is likely that the intensity of light rather than the wavelength will ultimately prove to be the activating factor and that one day our nurseries may be illuminated to give the same effect as daylight. If this happens, it will take us back to the day when a nurse in England¹ noted that babies exposed to sunlight did not become as jaundiced as infants away from the light.

# SUMMARY

Under a controlled study at the Providence Lying-In Hospital, 47 babies, unclothed except for diapers, were treated under lights averaging 90 footcandles, and 49 controls were kept routinely clothed in rooms averaging 10 footcandles of light.

Environmental illumination of the intensity used by us was found to be significantly effective in reducing the hyperbilirubinemia of prematurity but not to the degree obtained by the much higher intensity illumination used by others.

With light treatment

Hamilton Spectator, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 1968 29

# New hope for premies

Special To The Spectator

LOS ANGELES — One cause of brain damage in premature infants is being controlled at Los Angeles County-University of Southern California Medical Center by a novel treatment which is attracting national attention in the U.S.

PREMATURE infants are highly susceptible to jaundice, a condition due to a buildup in the blood of a substance called bilirubin. If the bilirubin level gets high enough, it causes permanent brain damage.

In infants with bilirubin levels above a certain point, the usual treatment is to drain all the infant's blood and transfuse a new supply. Doctors consider this a drastic procedure in a tiny premature baby and they are reluctant to do it except as a last resort.

As an alternative to transfusion, doctors at County-USC's newborn center recently began exposing jaundiced babies to white light from fluorescent lighting fixtures attached above their basins.

AS ODD as it seems, the method works, according to Dr. John Hodgman, associate professor of pediatrics at USC and director of the newborn service at the medical center.

The penetration of the light through the infant's thin skin causes a chemical reaction in the bilirubin flowing through tiny capillaries and veins just beneath the skin.

The effect, Dr. Hodgman said in an interview, is to break down the bilirubin into byproducts which are thought to be eliminated. The bilirubin level falls and, it is believed, the danger of brain damage from this cause is reversed.

THE IDEA of using light to decompose bilirubin did not originate with Dr. Hodgman's group. Laboratory technicians have known for years that test tube samples of blood being studied for bilirubin must be kept in the dark or else the bilirubin breaks down.

But it was not until about 10 years ago that an Englishman, Dr. R. J. Cremer, first used light to treat jaundice in the newborn. Since that time

it has been used in England, Italy, South America and South Africa.

DR. HODGMAN'S contribution has been to apply the scientific method to learn whether the treatment really works. She did this by comparing its results with those obtained by treatments conventionally used in the United States. Dr. Jerold Lucey, of the University of Vermont, chairman of the fetus and newborn committee of the American Academy of Pediatrics, has also been conducting controlled studies of the light treatment method.

Bilirubin is produced when red blood cells die. It cannot get out of the bloodstream until it is transformed into by-products which can be eliminated.

IN NORMAL individuals an enzyme breaks down the bilirubin. This enzyme does not become active until after birth. In premature infants it takes longer for the enzyme to become active.

Thus, if the enzyme does not make its appearance for several days after birth, the bilirubin accumulates and may reach a level high enough to cause damage to the brain and central nervous system.

The pediatrician believes that newborn jaundice is one of the principal reasons why premature infants have a much higher incidence of brain and nervous system malfunctioning than babies who are born at full term.

IN VERY small babies — those weighing three pounds

or less — the incidence of brain damage is about 60 per cent. It is much lower in heavier prematures, but nevertheless a significant risk.

Dr. Hodgman says the light treatment is much safer and simpler than the exchange transfusion method.

Because it is safer, it can be used to treat babies with bilirubin levels far lower than those for whom doctors would be willing to do an exchange transfusion.

She believes a degree of brain damage may have been occurring in babies who have a bilirubin level that is above normal but not high enough to risk a transfusion.

THE NEW treatment is expected to prevent damage in babies in that category.

Because the light method has not been in use long enough under controlled conditions, it is not possible to state definitely the long-term results.

For example, while it is known that the light changes the bilirubin in such a way as to eliminate the jaundice, nobody knows for sure what effect if any, the byproducts have on the body. The byproducts produced by this method are not the same as those occurring when bilirubin breaks down naturally in the body.

HOWEVER, animal studies and other kinds of experiments indicate that the by-products are harmless to the brain and the liver.

"I think the problem is large enough and the risk of bilirubin great enough to justify taking a chance on the long term results," Dr. Hodgman said.

"It's no longer enough that we are able to make these babies survive. They must also be as productive as possible. Anything that decreases the chances of brain damage is worthwhile."

# Phototherapy and Hyperbilirubinemia of the Premature

Joan E. Hodgman, MD, and Alberto Schwartz, MD, Los Angeles

Phototherapy to prevent hyperbilirubinemia in the premature infant was tested with 47 light-treated and 51 control infants with birth weights of 1,250 to 1,500 gm (2 lb 10 oz to 3 lb 4 oz). All infants had a negative Coombs' test. Treated infants were continuously nursed under a light chamber for 24 hours to 6 days of age. Bilirubin equaled or exceeded 15 mg/100 cc in 25.5% of the controls and none of the light-treated infants. Treatment was as effective in Negro and Mexican-American infants as in white infants. The only difference noted in clinical behavior was the appearance of green stools in light-treated infants. Evaluation of growth and development of these infants will be necessary to establish the benefits and safety of phototherapy.

The first clinical application of the decomposition of bilirubin by visible light was reported by Cremer et al¹ in 1958. They exposed jaundiced infants to sunlight and then to artificial light and observed a decrease in indirect bilirubin levels with both light sources. Since Cremer's study, phototherapy has been

used effectively to treat infants with hyperbilirubinemia in Brazil,²⁻⁴ Italy,⁵ and France.⁶ The first controlled study in the United States using phototherapy to prevent the development of hyperbilirubinemia in premature infants was reported by Lucey et al⁷ in 1968. In an effort to test their results in a different population, a controlled study of phototherapy was carried out in the Premature Center of the Los Angeles County-University of Southern California Medical Center from January to July 1968.

### Methods

Ninety-eight premature infants with birth weights of 1,250 to 2,000 gm (2 lb 10 oz to 4 lb 6 oz) were selected for study at 24 hours of age. Coombs' test performed on cord blood was negative in all infants. Infants with birth asphyxia, respiratory distress, hypoglycemia, suspect infection, and other problems were purposely included in the study. The infants were randomly assigned to treatment and control groups. Forty-seven infants were exposed to a light cradle over the incubator starting at 18 to 20 hours and continuing until 6 days of age, for five days of continuous treatment. They were nursed naked, but the eyes were covered by gauze eye pads held in place with adhesive tape. Fifty-one control infants were also nursed in incubators but without light cradles or eye pads. Total bilirubin determinations were performed on all infants at least

daily, from the start of treatment through the eighth day, by a modification of the method of Evelyn and Malloy.⁸ The reaction was observed at one minute when quantities of direct bilirubin greater than 1 mg/100 cc could be detected. If a direct reaction was present, a quantitative test for direct bilirubin was performed. Feeding schedules and other routine care was the same in the two groups. All infants were given 1 mg vitamin K₁ oxide an admission.

The light cradles were constructed to fit over the incubators leaving the ports exposed to provide ready access to the infants (Fig 1). Each cradle held ten 20-watt cool white, trigger start, fluorescent bulbs giving 450 foot candles of light intensity at the level of the infant in the incubator. All infants were kept at a skin temperature of 97.6 F (36.4 C), and no problems in heat control were encountered in the incubators used with the light cradles.

### Results

Clinical data demonstrating the similarity of the control and study infants are presented in Table 1. The mean birth weights and gestational ages were almost identical, and the two groups did not differ significantly in any of the areas. Five deaths occurred within 72 hours of birth due to hyaline membrane disease or intracranial hemorrhage; two in treated and three in control infants. Kernicterus was not found at autopsy in these early deaths.

Daily mean total bilirubin levels and range are shown graphically in Fig 2. Total bilirubin levels are reported because a reaction indicating more than 1 mg/100 cc of direct bilirubin was not observed in these infants. The initial bilirubin was not significantly different in the two groups. Levels in the study group remained essentially unchanged during the period of phototherapy, and showed no rebound after therapy was discontinued. The relatively narrow range of values in the study group as contrasted to the much wider range in the control group is clearly demonstrated. The levels in the control group were significantly different from the study group from the second through the seventh days, with P values <0.01 to 0.001.

Fig 2.—Mean and range of daily total bilirubin levels.

form a distinct subpopulation. Comparison of peak levels for light-treated and control infants by race revealed no difference in the response of the three racial groups. Phototherapy was as effective for Negro infants as for white.

Infants were admitted to the study only if the Coombs' test on the cord blood was negative. In our laboratory, the Coombs' test reliably identifies infants with hemolytic disease due to the Rh factor, but may not identify as many as one half of those due to ABO incompatibility. The incidence of ABO incompatible blood types between mother and infant was the same in the two groups. Three type O mothers in the light-treated group, and four in the control group, had infants with blood types of A or B. The highest peak bilirubin level in these infants was 12 mg/100 cc.

The number of infants who achieved or exceeded bilirubin levels of 12, 15, and 20 mg/100 cc are presented in Table 3. Two infants in

the light-treated group had peak bilirubins of 12 and 13 mg per 100 cc, respectively, and none exceeded this value. Of the control infants, 25% developed bilirubins of 15 mg/100 cc or more. Three of these reached 20 mg/100 cc at which time exchange transfusion was performed.

The clinical behavior of the infants while in the nursery was closely observed. The only difference in the two groups was the development of loose, green stools in many of the light-treated infants. These stools were distinctive in appearance and were not accompanied by changes in feeding behavior or by weight loss.

# Comment

The importance of preventing hyperbilirubinemia in the premature infant depends on the effect of bilirubin levels in excess of 12 to 15 mg per 100 cc. In our center, as in many others, exchange transfusion is regularly performed in an effort to prevent the bilirubin levels rising above 20 mg/100 cc. The major area of

The recent report of Stern and Doray⁹ of 23 premature infants with kernicterus at autopsy is of particular interest, as kernicterus occurred in 18 of the patients at levels below 20 mg/100 cc. Phototherapy effectively prevents hyperbilirubinemia in the premature. In our 47 light-treated prematures, one infant had a peak level of 12 mg/100 cc and one a level of 13 mg/100 cc. The remainder were all below 12 mg/100 cc. Obes-Polleri,¹¹ Lucey et al,⁷ and Porto and Hsia¹² have reported series of infants managed with phototherapy with comparable results. The effectiveness of phototherapy is related to the intensity of the light and the rate at which the bilirubin levels are rising. It cannot be expected to reliably control rapidly rising bilirubin levels. Hyperbilirubinemia not due to hemolytic disease, which is characterized by slowly rising levels during the first days of life, can be controlled or prevented. In addition, phototherapy can be administered as readily to sick infants as to healthy ones, as no handling of the infant is necessary.

None of the infants in either the control or treated groups developed significant amounts of direct acting bilirubin. During phototherapy, indirect bilirubin may be changed to water-soluble dipyrroles which are excreted in the bile. As glucuronide conjugation of indirect bilirubin is not increased during phototherapy, no increase in direct-acting bilirubin would be expected.

The most appropriate light intensity and intervals of treatment for prevention of hyperbilirubinemia have not been established. Effective light intensity may be considerably less than that used in our study and the others referred to above, where

infants were nursed under light chambers. Guinta and Roth ¹³ studied the effect of increasing the room light in nurseries to 200 foot candles at the level of the infants. When premature infants were nursed unclothed except for diapers in these nurseries, significantly lower bilirubin levels were reported from the second to the sixth day compared to control infants in dimly lighted nurseries. Apparently yet another variable which must be considered when evaluating premature infant care is intensity of environmental light. Intermittent light exposure has been used successfully to both treat and prevent hyperbilirubinemia.¹²,¹⁴ Intermittent exposure would have theoretical advantage over continuous exposure if it more closely approximated normal diurnal changes. Further study is required to establish the most effective pattern.

Before it can be recommended, phototherapy must be demonstrated to be safe as well as effective. The photo-decomposition products of bilirubin must be less toxic than the parent compound, and no untoward effects of light, either short-term or long-term, be demonstrable in the infant.

Studies on toxicity of photo-decomposition products of bilirubin have been complicated by the fact that the products have not been completely chemically identified. Several authors have studied the breakdown products resulting from light exposure of bilirubin in vitro. These products have been shown to be water-soluble and nontoxic when added to tissue slices of brain and liver or injected into laboratory animals.¹⁵⁻¹⁷ However, the breakdown products formed from exposing bilirubin to light in vitro may not be the same as those formed in vivo.

Studies of photo-decomposition in vivo have been limited to the Gunn

rat. Ostrow¹⁸ exposed adult Gunn rats to visible light following injection of bilirubin labeled with radioactive carbon. He recovered water-soluble diazo-positive derivatives which were rapidly excreted in the bile, and more slowly in the urine, demonstrating that glucuronide conjugation was not necessary for excretion of these products. They were similar to bilirubin catabolites normally found in Gunn rats, but appeared to be different from in vitro photo-decomposition products.

The evidence that breakdown products of bilirubin are not toxic to infants rests on clinical observation in the nursery and on follow-up study. The only clinical difference in infants' behavior during phototherapy observed in our own infants and reported in other studies has been the appearance of loose green stools. These presumably represent the excretion of breakdown products in the bile. No abnormal neurologic findings or changes in behavior have been noted in the nursery in controlled studies.⁷,¹¹⁻¹⁹ Although phototherapy has been used clinically for over ten years, and infants have been considered normal on follow-up study, no detailed studies on follow-up study of concurrent treated and control groups have been published. Unpublished data from three studies (J. F. Lucey, oral communication), Obes-Pollori,¹⁹ and Hodgman and Teberg²⁰ show no increase in neurologic or behavioral abnormalities in treated as compared to control infants.

No direct information is available of the effect of continuous light on the eyes of the premature infant. Permanent retinal damage has been reported in albino rats,²¹ normal rats,²² and piglets.²³ Monkeys, on the other hand, showed no retinal damage after one month's exposure (T. Kuwabara, written communication,

Oct 23, 1968). The authors of all the studies carried out in infants recommend covering the eyes while the infant is under the lights. No visual damage has been reported in light-treated infants. Odell et al²⁴ have reported changes in albumin, as well as bilirubin, following light exposure in vitro. There is indirect evidence that albumin-binding is not adversely altered in vivo as the 2-(4-hydroxy-benzine azo) benzoic acid (HABA) binding capacities reported by Lucey et al⁷ were not different in control and treated infants.

The long-term effects of phototherapy are only currently being investigated in a consistent manner. Preliminary data from Ballowicz¹⁹ suggest that continuously light-exposed nursing Gunn rats are significantly smaller than the controls. Two other workers have not found retardation of growth using the same animal model (J. F. Lucey, oral communication, Oct 16, 1969).²⁰ Preliminary studies on infants have also given conflicting results. Of the infants reported in our study, more light-treated babies were below the 10th percentile on growth curves during the first year than were controls.²⁰ Retardation of growth has not been encountered in follow-up studies of Lucey (oral communication, Oct 16, 1969) and Obes-Pollori.¹⁹

Endocrine function in both animals and man is influenced by light exposure.²¹,²⁶ The possible effect of phototherapy in the nursery on later endocrine function is entirely speculative. Some of the effects are mediated via the autonomic nervous system from receptors in the retina rather than from surface exposure and would constitute a theoretical indication for covering the eyes. Subtle or unexpected long-term changes in growth and behavior induced by light exposure of the infant

# Conclusions

Phototherapy used as described was effective in preventing hyperbilirubinemia in the premature infant. The incidence of total bilirubin of 15 mg/100 cc or greater in control infants was 25.5%, while the highest total bilirubin in the treated group was 13 mg/100 cc. Infants were

nursed naked in the incubators, and their eyes were bandaged while under the lights. Phototherapy was effective for sick premature infants and did not interfere with their care. Negro and Mexican-American infants responded as well as white infants to treatment.

There is no evidence that photodecomposition products of bilirubin are acutely toxic. The only difference noted in clinical behavior in the nursery both in our infants and in the published studies was the ap-

pearance of loose green stools in some of the light-treated infants.

Evidence of the safety of phototherapy from long-term studies is fragmentary and conflicting. The long-term effects need further evaluation by continued follow-up studies of light treated and control infants.

This investigation was supported by a grant from the John A. Hartford Foundation.

MEDICAL WORLD NEWS/June 13, 1969

# BLUE LIGHT FOR BABIES

## IN BILIRUBIN PERIL

Since it was introduced in America 2½ years ago to prevent jaundice in premature infants, phototherapy has both excited and dismayed pediatricians. While the technique seems effective and is simpler, safer, and cheaper than exchange transfusions, many wonder where the yellow went. But now the technique is being put to an even more controversial use—to treat neonates with hemolytic disorders due to Rh and ABO incompatibilities.

Chief among proponents of this new use is Dr. Thomas Sisson, associate professor of pediatrics and director of neonatal research at Philadelphia's Temple University. Dr. Sisson contends that phototherapy is indeed effective once serum bilirubin levels are high and rising rapidly.

To prove that treatment can be as effective as prevention, Dr. Sisson undertook a controlled study using continuous light with 50 infants whose jaundice was due to ABO incompatibility. Using a fluorescent blue light and plexiglas shield against ultraviolet emissions, Dr. Sisson started irradiating randomly selected infants only when serum bilirubin levels reached 10 mg%. And he kept bathing the infants in the light until concentrations fell below 7.5 mg%. On the average, this took three days.

Not one infant of the group exposed to the light required an exchange transfusion, Dr. Sisson reported to the Atlantic City meeting of the Society for Pediatric Research. But three of the controls did. "We have not studied infants with Rh hemolytic disease in a similarly controlled fashion," he notes, "but rather, have used phototherapy on all. Exchange transfusion was necessary only in the most severely affected. And in those few instances where irradiation was adjunctive therapy, the number of expected repeat transfusions was reduced."

For phototherapy to be effective in

these cases, Dr. Sisson says, the light must be in the blue visible range, where the most active photodecomposition of bilirubin occurs. Most nurseries use "Daylight" bulbs with only 60% of the energy as the blue type at the effective wavelength. The blue light is equally effective in white and Negro infants, says Dr. Sisson, although it does hasten darkening of the skin of Negroes.

Dr. Gerald Ente, associate director of the nursery for the newborn at Long Island's Meadowbrook Hospital, takes issue with Dr. Sisson on the last point. Though he finds light therapy effective in hemolytic diseases, he does not consider it as effective in Negroes as in whites, even for prophylactic purposes. "It is significant," says the New York pediatrician, "that in 2½ years, the only baby who received phototherapy and needed a transfusion was Negro. Probably the melanin pigment blocks penetration of the effective radiation." In 50 black infants exposed to light on a preventive basis in his nursery, the average serum peak bilirubin level was 9.6 mg%. In 30 white babies, the peak level was 8.9 mg%.

Dr. Ente, who was one of the first to use the light units, has studied "a few" Rh and ABO babies. "We tried to predict whether they would have needed exchange transfusions had they not undergone the light therapy," he says. "Only three out of 20 actually needed exchange." He adds: "If my colleagues had known what I was doing, they'd have killed me. But I watched those kids like a hawk." Nevertheless, because of the pressures, Dr. Ente dropped the preliminary study.

Objections to the technique are both real and imagined, he suggests. Some physicians argue that the light may damage the eyes, cause growth retardation, overheat the baby, or adversely affect circadian rhythms. And since there is no real knowledge of what happens to bilirubin once it is

![img-119.jpeg](img-119.jpeg)

Shielding infants' eyes ensures safety of controversial phototherapy, says Temple nursery chief, Dr. Norman Kendall.

photoexposed, there are those who contend that it may not be detoxified.

But a good part of the reluctance seems to stem from the unfortunate—and for some pediatricians, traumatic—experience with oxygen therapy. "We had no idea that the oxygen was actually causing retrolental fibroplasia in infants with hyaline membrane disease," recalls Dr. Sisson. "Once bit, twice shy."

While phototherapy has its theoretical disadvantages, concedes Dr. Ente, "the main objection to it seems to be that it goes against the medical mind. Doctors say, 'It's not scientific, this physiotherapy-type device.' Actually, it's too simple."

"People are worried about a machine," says pioneer phototherapist Jerold Lucey of the University of Vermont, who started it all in the U.S. "I wish we had put the babies outside in the sun, where they'd get 20 times more light. Who'd worry about doing that? Man has been walking around

FERH-36

in sunshine since shortly after the earth's crust cooled, and not too many bad effects have been noted."

Dr. Lucey has observed 77 light-treated infants for over two years and has found no evidence of neurotoxicity or growth retardation. Thousands of babies have also been treated safely in Uruguay and France, he notes. Dr. Lucey is continuing to keep tabs on the treatment in Europe and South America. Since the eyes of infants are routinely shielded, there is believed to be no danger that the light damages them. But Dr. Sisson stresses that the eyes must be well covered. In studies he has conducted, unshielded piglets showed destruction of cells in the outer retinal layers after fewer than 12 hours of exposure.

The biggest unknown in phototherapy is the chemical effect of the light. "Photodecomposition of bilirubin is, as far as we know, an oxidative process," says Dr. Sisson. "We should be concerned, then, that the light may affect or stimulate other oxidative processes in the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and blood." According to Gerard Odell, associate professor of pediatrics at John Hopkins, it does. Test-tube studies he has conducted

indicate that light affects plasma albumin as well as bilirubin. If it is damaged, then it is no longer capable of transporting bilirubin out of the body. "The fact that light lowers serum bilirubin levels doesn't mean the bilirubin has necessarily left the body," Dr. Odell warns. "It may be displaced into the tissues." Until evidence is produced that the amount of bilirubin recovered outside the body is equal to the amount altered, he says, he will continue to object to using light.

According to in vitro studies by Dr. Nasrollah Hakami of Seattle's King County Hospital, biliverdin, one of the early breakdown products of bilirubin, inhibits the mitochondrial enzyme nucleic acid dehydrogenase. Thus, by inhibiting the activity of necessary enzymes, bilirubin could be toxic to brain cells. "But," says Dr. Sisson, "we don't know whether biliverdin is actually produced in vivo." Until some highly sensitive ways of measuring bilirubin products in vivo are found, the battle lines will probably remain right where they are.

# SUMMARY

From the Department of Clinical Puericulture (Head: Prof. G. P. Salvioli), University of Bologna.

G. P. Salvioli and P. Dallacasa: Personal experience with light in the management of paraphysiological and Rh- and ABO-isolimmunisation-induced neonatal bilirubinaemia. — Results with light treatment in 79 cases of paraphysiological and Rh and ABO isolimmunisation-induced neonatal bilirubinaemia hospitalised in the Bologna University's Puericulture Clinic from January to August 1970 are reported. Collateral therapy included i.v. cortisone and 5% glucose perfusions. The treatment proved satisfactory in the immunological cases and its early use is recommended. Follow-up tests performed for a number of months in 64% of the series (haemochromocytometry, EEG, ecc.) revealed anaemia of average gravity in only 2 ABO and 1 Rh erythroblastosis foetalis cases.

Blood bilirubin values must be carefully and constantly controlled during the treatment. A watch must also be kept on parenteral liquid administrations, particularly with respect to glucose solutions, to prevent hypoglycaemia and dehydration as possible complications of light therapy. The early commencement of feeding is also recommended as a means of avoiding marked increases in blood bilirubin levels. Overall evaluation showed that statistically significant falls in blood bilirubin levels were obtained in paraphysiological and ABO isolimmunisation subjects; in Rh cases, the upward trend of the blood bilirubin curve was halted and exsanguinotransfusion was rendered unnecessary.

### PHOTOTHERAPY IN RHESUS HÆMOLYTIC DISEASE

MARK McC. REID\*
E. MARKS

GARTH McCLURE
J. H. ELWOOD

Special Care Unit, Royal Maternity Hospital, Belfast,
and Department of Social and Preventive Medicine,
Queen's University, Belfast

Summary A controlled trial of the use of phototherapy in the management of infants with rhesus hæmolytic disease is reported. Phototherapy was administered for 4 days, starting after the transfer of infants from the labour ward to the neonatal special-care unit. Forty-five phototherapy-treated infants required 50 exchange transfusions while seventy-eight control infants required 132 exchange transfusions. This difference is significant at the 1% level. 19 late exchanges were required in

- Present address: Lurgan and Portadown Hospital, Lurgan, County Armagh, Northern Ireland.

the treated group, compared with 92 in the control group. This is again significant at the 1% level. In the treated group no ill-effects were noted during or after phototherapy. It is suggested that phototherapy can reduce the requirements for exchange transfusions in rhesus hæmolytic disease.

### Introduction

THE management of the neonate with rhesus hæmolytic disease and consequent hyperbilirubinaemia has been by exchange transfusion.¹ McMullin et al.⁴ demonstrated that phenobarbitone administration could significantly reduce the number of exchange transfusions required. Phototherapy has been used in the treatment of neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia, but we could find no published reports of its successful use in rhesus hæmolytic disease. We have investigated the use of phototherapy in rhesus hæmolytic disease in a controlled trial.

### Patients and Methods

The trial was carried out over a period of 11 months in the special-care unit, Royal Maternity Hospital, Belfast. All babies with rhesus hæmolytic disease were admitted to the trial. The treated group received phototherapy for 4 days as soon as the results of the cord-blood analysis and Coomb's test were received; this was always within 2 hours of birth. There were no other dissimilarities in the management of the control and treatment groups. None of the infants received phenobarbitone during this period nor did any of the mothers receive phenobarbitone in the last 2 weeks of pregnancy. The criteria for exchange transfusion were: (1) cord-blood serum-bilirubin 4 mg. per 100 ml. or more, (2) cord-blood hæmoglobin less than 12 g. per 100 ml., and (3) serum-bilirubin above 19 mg. per 100 ml. An early exchange transfusion was defined as being one done because criteria (1) and (2) were fulfilled; a late exchange was done if criterion (3) was fulfilled.

Serum-bilirubin estimations were done approximately every 8 hours (or more frequently when the infant's clinical state indicated) in the hospital laboratory by technicians who did not know to which treatment group the infants belonged.

Exchange transfusions were performed via the umbilical vein using acid-citrate-dextrose blood prepared not more than 4 days previously. All infants who required an exchange transfusion received a 48-hour course of ampicillin and cloxacillin. Feeding was started within 6 hours of delivery. Phototherapy was administered using a 160 W phototherapy unit (Air Shields (U.K.) Ltd., Southend-on-Sea). The infant's eyes were bandaged and covered with dark glasses to avoid possible retinal damage.⁵

There were more patients in the control group than in the treatment group because we had only one phototherapy apparatus. This does not affect the statistical significance of the trial.

### Results

The treated and control groups were similar with respect to mean birth-weight, cord bilirubin level, and Apgar score (table 1); the difference between the average gestational ages arose by chance, and almost certainly did not affect the results of the trial. 50 exchange transfusions were required for the forty-five infants in the phototherapy group, an average of 1.1 per infant, with twelve (27%) out of the forty-five receiving no transfusions, compared with 132 trans-

fusions on the seventy-eight infants in the control group, an average of 1·7 transfusions per infant, with twenty-four (32%) receiving no transfusions. The total number of exchange transfusions required in the phototherapy group was significantly less in the control group (P<0·01) (table II).

The difference in the number of exchange transfusions was due to significantly fewer late transfusions (table III): twenty-six (33%) of the controls required two or more late exchanges while only four (9%) of the treated infants required repeat transfusions.

Three infants died—one in the phototherapy group and two in the control group. The infant in the phototherapy group who died was born at 27 weeks' gestation, weighing 1045 g., Apgar score 8; this child died at 74 hours of age from respiratory failure due to the respiratory-distress syndrome, confirmed at necropsy. This infant received two exchange transfusions, one early and one late. The two infants who died in the control group were also very immature. The first was born at 31 weeks' gestation, weighing 1480 g., Apgar score 3; this child received an early exchange transfusion and died at the age of 7 days from intestinal obstruction, and was found at necropsy to have obstruction of the large bowel due to congenital peritoneal bands. The second infant was born at 29 weeks' gestation, weighing 1160 g., Apgar score 5; this child died at 38 hours of age after having had four exchange transfusions, one early and three late. This child, who died from respiratory failure due to the respiratory-distress syndrome, was found to

have cerebral haemorrhage at necropsy. None of the infants given phototherapy seemed to have any ill-effects, in that we noticed no change in their motor activity, no diarrhea, and no increased incidence of eye infection, although two had a transient erythematous rash which was of no great significance.

### Discussion

Phototherapy has been used in the treatment of neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia for more than 15 years. Despite the theoretical risk of ill-effects caused by photochemical breakdown products of bilirubin, no short-term or long-term ill-effects have been recorded after the clinical use of phototherapy. This is probably not surprising, because Lucey noted that many infants have been exposed to twenty times the intensity of light supplied by phototherapy apparatus simply by being placed next to a window on a bright day.

There are few references to the use of phototherapy in rhesus haemolytic disease, and those that there are refer to a few cases rather than a series of patients. Behrman et al. thought that repeat exchange transfusions might be avoided by the use of phototherapy, but produced no convincing evidence for this claim. Others thought that phototherapy would not be an effective method of avoiding repeat exchange transfusions where the rate of bilirubin production was very much higher than in "physiological hyperbilirubinaemia". However, we have found a significant reduction in the number of exchange transfusions required when phototherapy was used in the treatment of rhesus haemolytic disease. As one might expect, the effect is to reduce the number of late rather than the early exchange transfusions. Sisson et al. have shown that the frequency of severe hyperbilirubinaemia and exchange-transfusion rates can be reduced by the use of phototherapy in ABO incompatibility.

The technique of phototherapy in the treatment of neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia can be usefully extended to the treatment of rhesus haemolytic disease. Any method which reduces the level of bilirubin, and also the need for exchange transfusions, must be welcomed because prolonged exposure to high levels of bilirubin may adversely affect the psychomotor development of infants in later life. Furthermore, an exchange transfusion, even in skilled hands, carries a definite morbidity and mortality, with the risk of infection, air embolus, vessel trauma, and hepatic damage. Although we had no deaths immediately after exchange transfusions, there were several instances of significant bradycardia and respiratory depression during the exchange transfusions which might not have occurred had the exchange not been required. Another benefit is the reduced requirements for blood. The phototherapy apparatus is easy to use and its cost should be rapidly recouped by the reduction in the demands for blood and the purchase of transfusion equipment.

We thank Prof. I. J. Carrè and Dr. W. A. B. Campbell for their permission to study their patients, and also for their advice and encouragement.

# Hazards of Exchange Transfusions

Infants who start life with erythroblastosis severe enough to require exchange transfusion never quite catch up with their unaffected peers, according to the results of a University of Pittsburgh study involving almost 4,000 children.

The study confirms what many physicians have long suspected: Erythroblastosis fetalis may result in permanent neurologic deficits, even in apparently healthy survivors.

"Among children who are healthy enough to attend school, it seems that blood group incompatibility and exchange transfusion pose hazards for IQ, vision, and hearing," says Dr. Edward R. Schlesinger, chairman of the department of maternal and child health. "The differences from normal are small, but they are consistent and tend to be where we would expect them to be—among the more severely affected."

Dr. Schlesinger's conclusion developed from a review of the health and school records of 1,865 children who had jaundice at or immediately after birth. The children were born at Magee-Women's Hospital or treated for jaundice at Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh. In all the cases included in the study, jaundice was attributed to

erythroblastosis fetalis, ABO incompatibility, or hyperbilirubinemia.

For each case, Dr. Schlesinger and his research team, which included Dr. Sati Mazumdar, associate research professor of maternal and child health and biostatistics, selected a control, matched for sex, race, and birth weight.

"We then made every effort to get the children's subsequent health records. We sent the parents a questionnaire covering the health history and present status of each child, and followed up by letter or phone call until we had an 80% response on the index cases and a 70% response on the controls."

From the follow-up, the team obtained 475 matched pairs of children for whom they had results of vision and hearing tests. The greatest number of poor scores on both tests was concentrated in the group of children who had erythroblastosis fetalis treated by exchange transfusion, Dr. Schlesinger reported at the American Public Health Association meeting in Philadelphia.

Among the controls, only 5% had poor vision—defined as 20/40 in the best eye. But 9% of children with a record of neonatal jaundice had poor

vision by the same criteria. And almost the same percentage of children in each group had a hearing loss of 35 decibels or more, usually in the right ear, with a smaller deficit in the left.

A similar pattern appeared in the IQ test results obtained from school records of 306 matched pairs of children. Average IQ of the index cases was 110, and of controls, 112. But for children who had the most severe Rh disease—those who underwent exchange transfusion at Children's Hospital—average IQ was 109 vs 113 for their controls. Children with erythroblastosis requiring only small transfusions, on the order of three ounces, achieved IQ scores that differed from their controls by less than a point.

Children born of mothers with ABO incompatibility showed about the same deficits as those with Rh disease. Children who had hyperbilirubinemia in the neonatal period, on the other hand, had no deficits when compared with their equally low-birth-weight controls.

Dr. Schlesinger speculates that hearing loss in children who have had exchange transfusions could be caused by streptomycin, given along with the transfusion to prevent infection.

"But the entire problem of Rh incompatibility would be eliminated if the new Rh antibody were used universally," says the Pittsburgh researcher. Current estimates indicate that 8% of white women of child-bearing age in the U.S. should have the Rh antibody, but only one in four is getting it.

The Massachusetts State Health Department is currently testing an Rh antibody preparation manufactured by its State Laboratory Institute. According to Dr. Morton Madoff, director of biological laboratories at the institute, the state can produce the preparation at a cost of \$6 per dose.

Clinical tests with the Rh antibody preparation are being conducted in six Boston hospitals under an investigational new drug application. If it is licensed, says Dr. Madoff, "we could immunize every Rh-negative woman of child-bearing age in the state."

## NEWER PEDIATRIC PROCEDURES

- Exchange transfusions seem to be on their way out as far as pediatricians are concerned. According to Dr. Julian B. Schorr, director of Clinical Services of the Greater New York Blood Program and a practicing pediatric hematologist, the total number of such transfusions in his own practice has decreased by about 70%. Exceedingly few of those still done are for ABO incompatibilities and the jaundice of premature infants, with Rh incompatibility accounting for the rest.

- Phototherapy has done a great deal to cut down on the need to transfuse neonates (MWN, June 13, '69). It has also reduced the incidence of repeat exchanges by slowing the bilirubin "rebound" phenomenon.

- In addition, Dr. Schorr says that several groups of physicians have been testing the use of phenobarbital in prospective mothers a couple of weeks before birth, or in their newborn babies (MWN, June 3, '66). This drug enhances the bilirubin-clearing mechanism when given in doses that do not induce drowsiness. And, for the Rh-incompatibility problems, there is Rh-immune globulin, which hopefully will become a mainstay in the obstetrician's practice.

26H

MEDICAL WORLD NEWS January 16, 1970

## Controlled trial comparing agar, intermittent phototherapy, and continuous phototherapy for reducing neonatal hyperbilirubinemia

Low-birth-weight infants, less than 24 hours of age, were randomly assigned to one of four therapy groups: (1) Agar, 125 mg, by month every 3 hours for 4 days beginning at 18 hours; (2) exposure to blue light, 200 to 300 footcandles 12 hours daily for 4 days (intermittent light); (3) exposure to blue light continuously for 4 days (continuous light); and (4) no therapy. Infants with a positive Coombs test or sepsis were excluded. From the second day on, infants who received light continuously had significantly lower mean bilirubin concentrations than any of the other three groups. Infants who received intermittent light or agar had daily mean values which were not significantly different from those of the control subjects except on Day 4.

Harold M. Maurer, M.D.,\* Clare N. Shumway, M.D., David A. Draper, M.D., and Ali A. Hossaini, M.D., Richmond, Va.

PHOTOTHERAPY, regardless of skin pigmentation, is effective in both prevention and treatment of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Despite its frequent and widespread usage, little information is available as to how to best apply it. There is no information available to evaluate the optimal duration of light exposure or whether exposure should be continuous or intermittent. The

intensity, duration, and pattern of light exposure have varied considerably among the groups of infants who have been subjected to phototherapy by different investigators. Therapy has been continued for varying periods of time, continuously or intermittently, through the sixth day. One purpose of our study was to determine whether intermittent phototherapy is as effective as continuous phototherapy in reducing neonatal hyperbilirubinemia in low-birth-weight infants.

The second purpose of our study relates to the recent report by Poland and Odell. They evaluated the role of the enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin in the production of physiologic hyperbilirubinemia in nine full-term infants delivered by cesarean section. Poland and Odell gave a formula supplemented with agar, U.S.P., for the first five days of life starting at the twentieth hour. Ten infants were given the same formula without agar. Agar is thought to stabilize bilirubin in aqueous solution and prevent its bacterial conversion and reabsorption from the intestinal tract. No rise in serum bilirubin concentration occurred after the thirteenth hour of life in the agar-fed infants. More bilirubin was excreted in the feces within the first five days in infants fed formula with agar than in the control subjects. These results suggest that the reabsorption of bilirubin from the intestine can be a major cause of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and that agar may be of therapeutic value in controlling the projected rise in neonatal serum bilirubin concentration. Our second purpose was to determine whether agar-supplemented feedings modified the course of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia in low-birth-weight infants, and to compare its effect on serum bilirubin concentration to that of intermittent and continuous phototherapy.

#### METHODS

Low-birth-weight infants (less than 2,500 Gm.) less than 24 hours of age were randomly assigned to one of four groups: Group 1 (17 infants) received agar powder (U.S.P., Difco Laboratories, Detroit, Mich., Lot No. 554882), 125 mg. in the first 5 ml. of each

formula (Similac with iron), beginning at 18 hours and continued at 3 hour intervals for 4 days (32 doses); Group 2 (18 infants) was exposed to blue fluorescent light (eight 20 watt lamps, F20T12/B, Westinghouse Corp., Bloomfield, N. J.), 200 to 300 foot-candles, 12 hours daily for 4 days (intermittent phototherapy); Group 3 (19 infants) was exposed to blue fluorescent light continuously for 4 days (continuous phototherapy); and Group 4 (15 infants) received no therapy. Infants with positive Coombs tests, potential ABO incompatibility, or sepsis were excluded. Infants receiving phototherapy were placed nude in the Isolettes. The distance of the lamps to the superior surface of the infant was 40 cm.

The intensity of the lamps was monitored daily. All infants received 1 mg. of synthetic vitamin K$_{1}$ intramuscularly. Serum bilirubin concentrations were determined daily with a direct-reading spectrophotometer. Statistical analyses were performed using analysis of variance and Duncan's multiple range test.

#### RESULTS

Infants in each group were similar with respect to mean birth weight, mean gestational age, sex distribution, and race (90 per cent or more were Negro (Table I)).

From the second day on, infants who received continuous phototherapy had significantly (p < 0.05 on Day 2; p < 0.01 on Days 3 to 6) lower mean serum bilirubin concentrations than any of the other three groups (Fig. 1). In contrast, infants who received intermittent phototherapy or agar-supplemented feedings had mean values which tended to be lower than those of the control subjects on Days 4 through 6, but

Side effects of therapy were minimal in both light-treated groups and consisted of occasional mild diarrhea. Agar supplementation was well tolerated and no significant (p > 0.05) weight loss occurred as a result of its potential laxative effect during therapy.

# DISCUSSION

It is strikingly apparent from our data that continuous phototherapy during the first four days of life is significantly superior to either intermittent phototherapy or agar-supplemented feedings in lowering the concentration of serum bilirubin in low-birth-weight infants. Its effect is obvious by the second day of life and is still apparent by the sixth. In contrast to continuous phototherapy, the use of intermittent phototherapy (12 hours daily for 4 days) or agar-supplemented feedings results in little, if any, significant serum bilirubin reduction, when compared to no therapy. Our findings indicate that continuous phototherapy results in the lowest bilirubin concentrations in low-birth-weight infants. In a study by Porto and

associates,² in which blue light (40 watt fluorescent lamps) was turned on 75 per cent of the time during a 4 day period and resulted in lowered bilirubin levels in low-birth-weight infants, no comparison was made with continuous therapy.

With respect to agar, our results in low-birth-weight neonates failed to confirm the earlier findings of Poland and Odell.³ They reported no further rise in neonatal serum bilirubin concentrations in full-term infants when agar-supplemented feedings were instituted. The dosage of agar employed in our study (approximately 0.5 Gm. per kilogram of body weight per day) is similar to the dosage used in their trial. Agar, U.S.P., is a dried hydrophilic colloidal substance obtained from various species of algae.⁴ It is rich in hemicellulose. It has been extensively used in the preservation of meat, confections, bakery products, ice cream, and cheese.⁵ It has also been employed medicinally as a colloid laxative and is used in commercially prepared infant formulas in the form of carrageenan. Poland and Odell postulate, on the basis of in vitro studies, that agar protects bilirubin from the action

# Chemical Variables and New Lamps in Phototherapy

GERALD ENTE\[1], EDWARD W. LANNING, PETER CUKOR, AND RICHARD M. KLEIN

Department of Pediatrics, Nassau County Medical Center, East Meadow, New York, and The Bayside Research Center, GTE Laboratories, Incorporated, Bayside, New York, USA

### Extract

In vitro studies were undertaken to measure the effects of varying concentrations of albumin and flux on the photodecomposition of bilirubin.

By using an experimental model, the effect of albumin on photodegradation of bilirubin was determined. Synthetic crystalline bilirubin solutions (20 mg/100 ml, pH 7.4) were exposed to the same flux levels for periods of 4.5 hr. The only variable in this series was the concentration of albumin, ranging from 0.5 to 5 g/100 ml. As the concentration of albumin increased, the reaction rate decreased (Fig. 5).

The efficiency of phototherapy was studied by varying flux levels while maintaining other variables constant. Figure 6 shows a nonlinear relation between reaction rate and flux, in which higher flux levels resulted in less decomposition per amount of flux (i.e., efficiency). More than twice the flux level was required to attain a twofold increase in decomposition rate. The effect of light flux was such that continuous use of the lowest practical level is to be recommended.

Data are given on the comparison of the relative effectiveness of cool white, high intensity blue, and two experimental lamps. The four lamps were tested at conditions of constant distance and constant flux. The high intensity blue lamp was twice as effective as the cool white. The two experimental lamps showed a 17% increase over the blue lamp (Figs. 2 and 3).

The effect of time on the spectral output of the fluorescent lamps in an experimental model was determined by using a spectral radiometer. The energy dropoff within the 420- to 480-nm region at 200 hr was approximately 20% for blue lamps and averaged 7.5% for the experimental lamps.

### Speculation

As with any new drug used on the neonate, the effects of phototherapy must be categorized, and the procedure must be standardized. Further investigations are needed to determine exact in vivo decomposition products, optimal timing of exposure, differences in skin attenuation, toxicity reactions, site of action, and photobiologic and photochemical alterations and interreactions.

### Introduction

Successful treatment and prophylaxis of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia with phototherapy—the use of magnetic waves of visible light—have been reported by

many investigators in this country and abroad over the past 13 years \[1-5, 9-14, 18, 19, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30]. Many questions regarding the physical hazards of phototherapy have been posed by investigators who have observed harmful effects produced in animals after ex-

The in vitro studies reported herein were designed to measure the effects of variations in concentrations of albumin and flux (see Table 1) upon the photodecomposition of bilirubin. Also, experimental lamps were tested.

# Materials and Methods

# Apparatus

A light exposure box was built which allowed simultaneous exposure of three solutions by three different lamps. A Reeder thermopile \[31] was used to measure the total flux (watts per square centimeter) of each lamp. The response of the thermopile is linear within 2% over the entire visible portion of the spectrum. One-millimeter precision cells \[32] were used to expose solutions to lamps as well as to measure absorption spectra. Absorption spectra were obtained with a Cary model no. 14 recording spectrophotometer \[33].

The lamps utilized in the tests consisted of two commonly used lamps, the cool white (GE F20T12CW) and high intensity blue (GE F20T12B), and two experimental lamps, A and B (Fig. 1). Lamp A was phosphor no. L7352 \[16] and Lamp B was no. FPB 533C \[23].

# Reagents

Standard phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) was prepared according to the method of White et al. \[29]. Crystal-

line unconjugated bilirubin \[34] and crystallized human albumin \[34] were used. Bilirubin was routinely recrystallized from methanol-chloroform solution. The first batch was subjected to ascending thin layer chromatographic analysis on silica gel plates, and no separated impurity spots were observed. The infrared spectrum of bilirubin prepared in this manner was obtained in a potassium bromide pellet. The spectrum showed only those bands assigned to bilirubin. After the pellet was exposed to daylight for several days, its spectrum showed no significant change. In this manner, it was established that bilirubin in a solid dry state was relatively insensitive to light. Test solutions were prepared by dissolving the appropriate amount of bilirubin in a minimum amount of 0.1 x sodium hydroxide solution. Albumin was added and the volume was adjusted with phosphate buffer. Bilirubin concentration ranged from 7.5 to 30 mg/100 ml and albumin concentration from 0.05 to 5.0 g/100 ml.
