# Test Procedure

In the light exposure tests, portions of the test solutions were transferred to the 1-mm cells, and their absorption spectra were recorded. The cells were then placed in the light exposure box for irradiation by the appropriate lamps. Each sample was placed at a distance from the lamp which provided the desired flux as measured with the thermopile at the front surface of the cell, except for those runs in which constant distance was employed. The lamp to sample distance varied from approximately 3 to 18 inches. Concurrently, a reference sample was prepared for monitoring any dark reaction. Periodically, the absorption spectra were obtained for both the test and reference samples in order to measure the bilirubin absorption as well as to observe any change in spectral shape. No temperature changes were observed.

In order to measure the relative effectiveness of the different lamps, samples of synthetic icteric serum were exposed to radiation from each. The concentration of bilirubin at any given time was inferred from the absorbance at 455 nm, and the rate of decomposition was measured by the decrease in absorbance at this wavelength. The lamps were tested under conditions of constant distance and constant flux.

![img-122.jpeg](img-122.jpeg)

Fig. 2. Reaction rates for different lamps at constant flux. The experimental lamps are 17% more effective than the high intensity blue lamps used in clinical phototherapy. Cool white fluorescent lamps are only half as efficient as the high intensity blue.

To ascertain the effect of albumin on photodegradation of bilirubin, 20 mg/100 ml solutions of bilirubin were exposed at pH 7.4 for periods of 4.5 hr to the same flux levels. The only variable in this series was the amount of albumin.

Finally, a series of tests was made to determine the effect of varying flux levels while maintaining all other factors constant.

To measure the effect of time on the spectral output of the fluorescent lamps, the maintenance of the four lamps was tested with a spectral radiometer. Light from a 4-inch section of the middle of the lamp was allowed to pass through a monochrometer to a photomultiplier. The output of the photomultiplier was digitized and fed to a computer that corrected the results for instrument spectral sensitivity. The computer then printed out the energy emitted by the lamp for each 2-nm interval. Blue, cool white, and two experimental lamps were measured with this equipment.

# Results

Figure 2 compares results of bilirubin sample exposures to the four test lamps. Samples were so placed that the total light flux was constant. This shows that, after 5.5 hr of irradiation, the high intensity blue lamp was twice as effective as the cool white. Moreover, the experimental lamps exhibited a 17% increase over the GE blue lamp.

In actual clinical use, lamps are placed at a fixed distance from the infant. A test run was therefore made under the conditions of constant lamp to sample distance. The results (Fig. 3) are quantitative differences which can be attributed to different lamp fluxes. For example, the blue lamp was 1.6 times as effective as the cool white, as contrasted to the factor of 2.0 found in the previous measurements. This is partially explained by the fact that at a fixed distance the flux level of the cool white was 10% greater than in the constant flux level experiments.

Figure 4 shows lamp maintenance data for a typical cool white lamp \[35]. The percentages of initial output obtained after 100 hr of operation for the two experimental lamps were 91% for A and 94% for B. For the cool white lamp, the value was 96% and for the blue lamp the value was 85.7%. The percentage of initial output for the blue lamp in the 420- to 480-nm region at 200 hr was 80.9, indicating a 20% dropoff at 200 hr. Moreover, the energy output after 200 hr was constant for every 2-nm reading within this interval.

Increasing albumin concentrations retarded the photodecomposition process. Figure 5 shows the effect of

## Discussion

The ideal lamp for phototherapy is one that exhibits all of its emission between 450 and 460 nm. However, practical fluorescent lamps emit bands of greater than 10-nm width. The broad spectrum cool white lamp exhibits most of its phosphor emission between 500 and 700 nm. The blue lamp emits maximal energy at 450 nm and is more suitable. Confusion occurs here because we are not concerned with footcandles or lumens (see Table I), but are interested in the actual specific energy, which is measured in microwatts per square centimeter, or flux, for the specific nanometers or wavelengths involved in the process of photodecomposition of bilirubin. So, although a cool white bulb gives a higher footcandle reading on a light meter, it lacks flux comparable to the blue lamp. Again, the blue bulb gives a lower footcandle reading and emits a high relative energy concentration in the 420- to 480-nm zone.

Seeking effective narrow band phosphors, we selected two phosphor systems (Fig. 1). Most of their energy output was found to be in the desired wavelength region and their peak emissions were 4-5 times as great as that of the blue lamp.

The spectral output of all fluorescent lamps decreases as a function of time. The qualitative form of this deterioration is similar for all fluorescent lamps; i.e., phosphor decay is characterized by a relatively rapid dropoff in the first 100 hr, followed by a more gradual steady decline. The severity of the deterioration can therefore be judged by the amount of deterioration at 100 hr. For example, Figure 4 shows a lamp maintenance curve for a cool white lamp \[35]. The shape of this curve is similar for all fluorescent lamps; that is, the brightness approaches an asymptote. The percentage of initial output obtained after 100 hr of operation for the two experimental lamps (91% for A and 94% for B) indicates that the lamps will have a very long life (thousands of hours) under normal operating conditions.

Because of the long predicted lifetime of the experimental lamps as compared with that found by Sisson et al. \[28] for the presently used blue lamps, the maintenance of these lamps was tested. Our data showed only a 10% dropoff in spectral output at 200 hr, as opposed to 44% reported by Sisson et al. \[28].

Varying concentrations of albumin were investigated. One mole albumin is capable of binding two moles of bilirubin under our experimental conditions \[21]. Since the molecular weights are in the ratio of ≃

100/1, 100 ml of 1% solution of albumin is sufficient for binding 20 mg bilirubin. Figure 5 shows the effect of increasing albumin on the reaction rate of bilirubin. Apparently, the albumin-bound bilirubin complex is more stable than free bilirubin, so that, as the concentration of albumin is increased, the reaction rate decreases. This result shows that although more albumin is desirable because of increased binding of bilirubin, which prevents deposition in tissue, it is disadvantageous in that it retards the rate of photodecomposition.

We studied the efficiency of phototherapy by varying flux levels while maintaining all other factors constant. Efficiency is defined as (percentage bilirubin decomposed per unit of time) (total light flux). The lamps having the greatest efficiency will therefore theoretically accomplish the destruction of bilirubin with the least exposure of total radiation to the infant. The nonlinear relation between increasing flux and bilirubin decomposition as shown in Figure 6 means that higher flux levels result in less decomposition per unit flux. One implication of Figure 6 is that the most efficient use of phototherapy is the use of the lowest possible flux level necessary to maintain the desired bilirubin concentration. It is further suggested that continuous exposure is preferable to an intermittent mode. With intermittent use, light might be on for 2 hr and off for 2 hr. The "on" period must produce the same amount of decomposition as 4 hr of continuous exposure. In order to achieve this, twice the decomposition rate must be attained. Figure 6 shows that much more than twice the flux level is required to attain a twofold increase in decomposition rate. Thus, the intermittent mode of therapy would require exposure to much more light. The effect of light flux is such that the lowest practical level is recommended. Moreover, continuous exposure is recommended to provide more efficient decomposition per unit of flux. Clinically, this was confirmed by Jurado-Garcia \[13].

## Conclusions

The experimental lamps, chosen on the basis of their emission spectra, are found to be 15-20% more effective than the high intensity blue lamps used in clinical phototherapy. Cool white fluorescent lamps are found to be only half as efficient as the blue lamps. These results are similar regardless of albumin, flux, or bilirubin level. Increasing albumin concentration retards the photodecomposition process. The effect of light flux is such that continuous exposure at the lowest practical level is recommended.

# Factors Influencing the Effectiveness of Phototherapy in Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia

THOMAS R. C. SISSON, M.D.; NORMAN KENDALL, M.D.; RONALD E. DAVIES, Ph.D. AND DANIEL BERGER, M.S.E.E.

The rate of photodecomposition of bilirubin in vivo and in vitro depends upon the intensity of the light used for irradiation and also upon the spectral distribution of the emitted light. The action spectrum of bilirubin, the wavelength of visible light to which it is photoreactive, is equally important in producing a photochemical reaction. These studies indicate that bilirubin is most effectively decomposed by light emission in the blue range, 420 to 460 nanometers, and that the greater the energy output of the light source in this wavelength interval the more rapid the degradation of bilirubin. A significant loss of energy was found in the fluorescent lamps employed in phototherapy after 200 hours of use. This energy loss was found sufficient to retard the rate of bilirubin decay in vivo.

The effects of light on bilirubin metabolism in the jaundiced newborn infant appear to be related to:

1. The action spectrum of bilirubin.
2. Spectral radiant intensity.\*
3. The character of the plasma in which bilirubin circulates.
4. Hemolytic processes and the rate of red cell destruction.
5. The maturity of the irradiated infant.
6. The purpose of the irradiation—preventive or therapeutic.

Our studies have shown that the rate of bilirubin photodecomposition both in vivo and in vitro depends upon the intensity of the light used and upon its spectral distribution. The greater the energy output of the light source the more rapid has been the degradation of the bilirubin irradiated.

Plasma with a low content of protein, in particular

albumin, is characteristically found in premature infants. Free or unbound bilirubin may, therefore, circulate in high concentration with consequently greater risk of kernicterus. If free fatty acids are present in great amount they will compete with bilirubin for binding sites on albumin.

The rate of red cell destruction that may occur to a pathologic degree in the infant is of particular importance, whether due to fetomaternal blood group incompatibility, sepsis or other causes. Upon this process depends not only the increment of plasma bilirubin per unit of time but the ability of the infant to handle the quantity of bilirubin produced.

Newborn infants who are immature have difficulty in adequately conjugating bilirubin to permit its excretion, even without hemolytic disease. This is believed to account in large measure for the higher incidence of hyperbilirubinemia among prematures. Other factors of hypoxia, acidosis, etc. also play an accompanying role in this circumstance.

All these elements bear upon the purpose of phototherapy. If a prophylactic effect is sought as in the premature infant, the intensity of light and time of exposure are quite different than for the treatment of hyperbilirubinemia as an already existing condition. In the latter situation the length of time of treatment cannot be as leisurely as for prophylaxis. If the plasma concentration of bilirubin is rapidly increasing, as it must also in the tissues, the rise may

The action spectrum of bilirubin is of primary importance in the consideration of phototherapy, not only in the evaluation of its clinical effect, but also in the study of bilirubin metabolism itself. Knowledge of the rate of photodecay of this pigment irradiated under various types of visible light is incomplete, as is identification of its breakdown products. Evidence is accumulating that the photodecomposition of bilirubin is a very complex process involving products with different rates of appearance, and perhaps of differing molecular composition under varied experimental conditions, and not all identical with those in the human infant. It should be stated, if only parenthetically, that the action spectra of the breakdown products should be investigated, for were they to vary widely from those of bilirubin itself the composition of the light sources for phototherapy might be quite different from those in use at this time.

It seems a logical extension of these relationships to employ those areas in the visible spectrum to which bilirubin is most reactive. Since ultraviolet

radiation should be avoided in the clinical use of phototherapy, our attention has not been focused on the effects of UV light except to a minor degree.

Not only has the action spectrum of bilirubin been of interest, but also the determination of the spectral radiant intensity of a variety of light sources under conditions of use and in comparison one with another.

# Materials and Methods

The following fluorescent lamps of 20 watt input were used as light sources: red (F20T12/R), pink (F20T12/P), yellow (F20T12/GO), green (F20T12/G), blue (F20T12/B), daylight (F20T12/DA), Vitalite®, special narrow-band blue (Westinghouse).

Solutions of bilirubin (20 mg/100 ml) in human serum albumin (3.3 gm/100 ml) buffered by Sorenson's phosphate buffer to pH 7.4 were divided into 2.0 ml aliquots and placed in small plastic Petri dishes. These were exposed to the various fluorescent lamps for 30, 60, 120, and 240 minutes at a distance of 9.6 cm.

Spectral analyses were performed on each sample in a Cary Model 14 scanning-recording spectrophotometer.

The energy output of each light source when new, and in some instances after varying periods of use, was measured by a spectroradiometer attachment to the Cary Model 14. Energy is expressed in microwatts per square centimeter per nanometer.

# Results

# Light Source Characteristics

We had noticed that the response of hyperbilirubinemic infants to phototherapy was less marked when the lamps had been in use for over 200 hours. Figure 1 is a graphic representation of the energy output of blue fluorescent lamps when new and after 89, 108, and 200 hours of use.

A marked drop-off of energy, especially in the wavelengths of peak output (420-460 nm), was observed. The decrement varied from 44 to 49, after 200 hours in the range of 400 to 480 nm, which encompasses almost all the effective emission of these lamps in the blue portion of the spectrum. The data are presented in Table I.

It was apparent from these observations that the loss of energy in this rather narrow spectral range was substantial, and it was obvious from repeated clinical studies that the decrease of energy did affect the rate of decline of serum bilirubin in vivo. The clear implication is that the photodecomposition of bilirubin is dependent upon the spectral radiant intensity of the light source.

It was also observed that the decrease of serum bilirubin concentration was slower when fluorescent lamps of broad spectral distribution, ie "daylight"

In summary, lamps of higher energy output were more effective clinically, and this was confirmed by in vitro studies which demonstrated a faster rate of decomposition of bilirubin in that static system (Fig. 4). This was so whether the lower energy output was due to energy loss from lamp use over a period of time or as a characteristic of the particular lamp. These findings support the concept that the spectral radiant intensity of the light source influences the photodecomposition of bilirubin.

### Action Spectrum

In order to determine if there is indeed a fairly specific action spectrum for the photochemical degradation of bilirubin, this compound was irradiated in vitro in two solvent systems. One employed pooled exchange transfusion serum of an infant with severe hemolytic disease of the newborn; bilirubin concentration was 7.5 mg/100 ml. The second employed bilirubin in buffered human albumin. Two ml aliquots were irradiated as described before. These bilirubin solutions were exposed to light from fluorescent lamps with differing emission spectra, which are listed in Table II.

The change in optical density of bilirubin in buffered human serum albumin after 30, 60, and 120 minutes of irradiation under the various light sources is illustrated in Figure 3. These changes represent a loss of optical density as bilirubin was decomposed.

# Breakdown Products

There is disagreement among investigators as to the identity of the products of bilirubin photodecomposition. Because of the difficulty of studying the metabolism of this pigment in the newborn infant, recourse has been made to the Gunn rat, and to artificial serum-bilirubin solutions. The results of these studies are hard to transpose to the infant despite the sophistication of technics since different conditions obtain in the human.

Some investigators have reported the appearance of biliverdin following irradiation. We have encountered a greenish-brown pigment upon exposure of bilirubin solutions in vitro. However, we have observed absorption peaks at 375 and 650 nm, characteristic of biliverdin, only in artificial solvent systems, not in adult or infant plasma and serum from hyperbilirubinemic patients. By extraction methods and thin layer chromatography several pigments have been demonstrated, some of them evanescent in nature, but none having the solubility or spectral features of biliverdin.

The development of absorption peaks at 360, 410-415 (in the absence of heme pigments), 490, and 560 nanometers has been intriguing but beyond our capacity to further identify. These various peaks do not all appear in a single solvent system, but the appearance of the bilirubin solutions, depends upon the make up, and upon pH. Some appear to be of a transient character. At this time we have some doubt that biliverdin is formed in the infant from the photodecomposition of bilirubin, but believe rather that a series of breakdown products is formed with differing rates of formation and decay: their synthesis and

degradation under continued irradiation of the infant may overlap, to further obscure this already highly complex process.

# Conclusion

We have concluded that the photodecomposition of bilirubin is dependent, among others, on two major factors; its action spectrum and the spectral radiant intensity of the light source used. It is known that the shorter the wavelength of emitted light the greater the kinetic energy of the photons reaching the irradiated object. Ultraviolet light will effectively decompose bilirubin in vitro. Its use in phototherapy is not recommended, however, because of the danger of injury to tissues, especially at wavelengths 330 nm and below.

Our studies have led us to conclude that blue light, with a maximum output between 420 and 460 nanometers, is the most efficient practical fluorescent light source for phototherapy, and that if rapidity of response is an important consideration in the treatment of jaundice of the newborn an adequate energy output from the light source of at least 90 $\mu\mathrm{w}/\mathrm{cm}^2$ in that spectral interval should be used. These recommendations do not necessarily hold for the prophylactic irradiation of the newborn who has not developed hyperbilirubinemia before the institution of phototherapy.

One cannot yet say what is the minimal amount of light energy effective in the treatment of neonatal jaundice, nor indeed is the optimal amount known precisely. However, if light is to be used as a form of therapy it may logically be managed as would be a drug or chemical compound for a specific therapeutic purpose, which it should achieve in the safest yet most expeditious manner. The prevention of kernicterus will not permit of half measures, especially in the immature neonate wherein brain damage may occur at relatively low serum bilirubin concentrations. Therefore, the proper type of light which will decompose bilirubin in the shortest period of time with safety, would be the optimum.

The term "footcandle" as a unit of measure of light intensity in phototherapy should be discarded. Footcandles and lumens are units of measure of illumination from any light source, in reference to the photoreceptivity of the retina. A more precise unit of measurement is microwatts per square centimeter per nanometer ($\mu\mathrm{w}/\mathrm{cm}^2/\mathrm{nm}$), which is an expression of the light energy reaching the object of irradiation at each wavelength emitted by the particular source of light. This measurement does not assume an action spectrum which the other visible units of measurement do, making them inapplicable for even qualitative determinations of such radically different action spectra as the photodecomposition of bilirubin.

Though the method to determine the action spectrum of bilirubin reported here is crude, it offers

# Discussion

GERALD ODELL asked about the susceptibility of the protein-bound bilirubin to photodecay and why salicylate is far more effective than Gastrisin in isolating bilirubin away from human albumin. The question can be raised as to whether part of the Gastrisin molecule is transmitting the photomergy to the bilirubin. OSTROW replied that by adding the bilirubin onto the albumin, there is apparently an acceleration of decay and suggests that albumin itself is involved in the oxidative process. It may be one of the things that is taking the hydrogens out, or at least, the oxidizing agent. GERALD ODELL then said that when he stored jaundiced serum for six months in the refrigerator, the van den Bergh reaction would be the same, but the spectral curve with the sharp peak at 460 mμ becomes flat or dull. He assumed that it was denatured albumin that made the difference. OSTROW replied that in the dark, albumin always stabilizes bilirubin, while this is not always true in the light, suggesting that albumin is photoactivated. The lack of change in the diazo reaction suggests that these are clearly bilirubin derivatives and not chloroform related.

PETER BROUGHTON asked whether he had followed the decay in the serum of a jaundiced patient. OSTROW said that Blendheim had published such curves. He felt the differences in

the green color may be due to rates and not qualitative. For instance, the pattern would change if you altered the proportion of methanol to chloroform.

AUDREY BROWN asked if there is any data that would suggest that the human infant is putting out such alternate products normally in bile. Both OSTROW and ROGER LESTER had never performed chromatography on normal bile.

IVAN DIAMOND asked if photodecay of bilirubin includes the biliverdin step. OSTROW replied that in albumin, the green color remains for a long time, while in alkali it is very transient. KRASNER said that he could not identify biliverdin in a nondynamic system. OSTROW said that he had isolated biliverdin in the jaundiced serum of an infant after exposure to light.

COLEMAN WHITLOCK asked if these colorless products formed by photoactivity were urobilin or urobilinogen. RUDI SCHMID said that all of these compounds are bacterial reduction products and are not related to phototherapy.

ROGER LESTER explained how botanists used the evolution of oxygen by plants as an indication of the forms of light used. He felt it was important to think of bilirubin and its spectrum in terms of its sitting in an aqueous solution and when bound to protein. Bilirubin usually has two peaks of maximal absorption—one at 450 to 460 mμ and the other at 315 mμ. LEONORE BALLOWITZ emphasized that if you use continuous light on a plant, it will destroy the photoreceptors and the plant will fail to grow. However, if you use intermittent therapy, such as night and day, it will grow satisfactorily.

DONALD SILBERBERG asked what was known about retinal damage from light. SISSON replied that he had recently done an experiment wherein the two eyes of one piglet were accidentally exposed to light for slightly less than 12 hours and the retinas were badly damaged. The piglet became blind. Electron microscopic examination revealed that the discs of the photoreceptor rods were edematous and distorted; disintegration and vacuolization had occurred, demonstrating irreversible damage to the outer retinal layers (visual cells—rods in particular) of newborn piglets six weeks after 12, 24, 48 and 72 hours of exposure to the same phototherapy lamps used in his study of jaundiced infants. MICHAEL THALER quoted Wurtman as saying that the light receptors have a fantastic sensitivity, something in the order of 10⁻⁴. Using the best patching available, we can only reduce that to 10⁻⁴. Thus, current patching technics do not approach the sensitivity of the receptors. Furthermore, in the premature, the macula is a developing organ, which makes it more sensitive to damage. SISSON measured the light transmission through the eyelid of a stillborn infant and found that 2 to 3% of light from a monochromator reached through the eyelid to the photocell. The usual type of patch also lets through about 3% of incidental light. DONALD SILBERBERG commented that the corneal sensitivity of young infants is very low and one must be careful not to keep an eye open as it is patched.

# Relationship of phototherapy and skin color -- Reply

# Reply

To the Editor:

In a recent symposium, Sisson and co-workers reported that the decrease of serum bilirubin concentration was slower when fluorescent lamps of broad spectrum distribution such as "daylight" and "Vitalite" are used in place of blue lamps in which the spectral distribution was more monochromatic. At 440 nm, the daylight type of lamp had but 55 per cent, and the vitalite had but 35 per cent of the energy of the blue light. At 460 nm, the daylight lamp had approximately 65 per cent, and the vitalite had about 45 per cent of the energy of the blue light.

In comparing our data with those of Dr. Eute, it becomes apparent that while there is no difference in the peak serum bilirubin levels between Negro and Caucasian premature infants when both are exposed to blue light turned on

75 per cent of the time, a difference begins to emerge when one reduces both the duration of exposure to 25 per cent of the time and the intensity of the light at 440 to 460 nm, to about 50 per cent through the use of daylight or vitalite lamps instead of blue lamps.

This emphasizes the importance of using adequate phototherapy, particularly in infants with dark skin pigment, and might help explain why this form of treatment has met with success and failure among some Negro infants.

### Effect of Light on Serum-bilirubin

During serial estimations of the serum-bilirubin in jaundiced infants we noticed that their serum-bilirubin is highly photosensitive in vitro (Cremer, Perryman, Richards, and Holbrook 1957). We have studied this sensitivity and tried to apply it therapeutically.

![img-134.jpeg](img-134.jpeg)

Fig. 3—Effect of sunlight on serum-bilirubin.

When icteric serum of infants is illuminated by white light, and the temperature is kept constant at 20°C, the characteristic 420 mμ absorption peak decreases and the absorption at the red end of the spectrum, around 550-650 mμ, increases a little (fig. 1). At the same time the measured serum-bilirubin level is reduced and electromotive force (E.M.F.) measurements show a positive

increase in the oxidation/reduction (rodox) potential of the system (fig. 2). This indicates that, under the action of light, bilirubin undergoes photo-oxidation or dehydrogenation to biliverdin or some intermediate products. These substances are more polar, and therefore probably more easily excretable, than is bilirubin.

Bilirubin (van den Bergh indirect pigment), the type of pigment greatly predominating in icteric infants, is some two or three times as photosensitive as is conjugated bilirubin (van den Bergh direct pigment) (fig. 3).

These findings emphasise the need for special precaution in laboratories doing routine bilirubin estimations on jaundiced infants. We now make a practice of enclosing all our blood-specimen tubes in light-tight containers if immediate analysis is not feasible. We have found that specimens left in bright daylight may lose as much as 30% of their serum-bilirubin in an hour.

Fig. 4 shows the distribution of the photosensitivity effect over the visible spectrum.

### Clinical Applications

The subjects chosen for this study were all infants in the premature babies unit of the hospital. The sister in charge of the unit had earlier reported the apparent fading away of the yellow pigmentation in the skin of jaundiced babies when they had been a short time in sunlight. It was decided, therefore, to expose jaundiced infants to sunlight and assess the results quantitatively by serial determinations of serum-bilirubin.

Before the exposure the general trend of the serum-bilirubin level was established by the micro-method devised for this

![img-135.jpeg](img-135.jpeg)

Fig. 4—Spectral distribution of the photodestruction of serum-bilirubin.

purpose (Perryman, Richards, and Holbrook 1957). To avoid overheating or excessive ultraviolet radiation, the babies were placed naked in direct sunlight for fifteen to twenty minutes (according to the sun's intensity) and then withdrawn for similar periods before again being exposed to the sunlight. During the exposure the infants' eyes were protected by a simple plastic shield.

Jaundice quickly disappeared from the exposed areas of skin but persisted in areas which remained in the shade.

After this intermittent sunlight treatment, bilirubin levels were again measured.

Fig. 5 shows a typical result of this treatment. Table I records the initial level and drop in serum-bilirubin in 13 premature infants with twenty test exposures. These had the so-called "physiological jaundice" of prematurity, and in all (except case 13, where there was a rise) there was a definite drop in serum-bilirubin during the exposure. In general, we found that the higher the initial serum-bilirubin level and the longer the exposure-time, the greater the fall in serum-bilirubin.

In view of these results, we sought a source of artificial light instead of sunshine. Guided by our work on the spectral distribution of the photosensitivity (fig. 4), we examined various light sources. Finally the apparatus illustrated in fig. 6 was devised.

This consists of a hemicylindrical stainless-steel reflector suspended on a movable gantry and adjustable for height. Eight 24 in. light blue fluorescent 40-watt discharge tubes

This equipment gives light of very high intensity in the region of 420-480 mµ without any dangerous ultraviolet or X-ray components. The height

- Intermittent illumination: 6 hours on, followed by 2 hours off.

### Discussion

Our results so far are insufficient for a complete statistical appraisal, but they encourage further work. From our biochemical studies, it has become clear that a complex series of chemical changes is involved.

Under the action of light, bilirubin seems to be dehydrogenated, and the role of hydrogen acceptors and photocatalysts is being investigated. Several compounds accelerate the photodestruction of serum-bilirubin in vitro—α-methylene-blue at a concentration of 10 µg. per ml. of serum, similarly toluidine-blue and cresyl-blue, though they are less effective, and riboflavine. We suggest that the difference in degree of response to light treatment between one jaundiced infant and another and also the complete failure of some to respond may be related to lack of essential hydrogen acceptors

or other factors in the circulating plasma. We have found that in the first few days of life ceruloplasmin is absent from the blood-serum, which may have a bearing on this problem.

No prospect can be entertained that this light treatment will prove a substitute for exchange transfusion in the erythroblastotic infant with active haemolysis, but the method may be turned to clinical advantage in controlling the level of serum-bilirubin in cases of jaundice of prematurity.

# Summary

In some cases of neonatal jaundice the serum-bilirubin level is reduced by sunlight or by suitable artificial-light treatment.

# Experience and Reason

## Briefly Recorded

"In Medicine one must pay attention not to plausible theorizing but to experience and reason together. . . . I agree that theorizing is to be approved, provided that it is based on facts, and systematically makes its deductions from what is observed. . . . But conclusions drawn from unaided reason can hardly be serviceable; only those drawn from observed fact." Hippocrates: Precepts.

(Short communications of factual material are published here. Comments and criticisms appear as Letters to the Editor.)

### Natural Variations in Environmental Illumination in a Newborn Nursery

Phototherapy as a means of reducing hyperbilirubinemia was first reported in 1958 by Cremer, et al. Numerous studies since then have demonstrated the effectiveness of its use.

Tentative guidelines on the use of phototherapy have been formulated from data presented at a symposium on bilirubin metabolism in the newborn. These suggest that 200 to 400 foot-candles of the spectrum of wavelengths between 300 and 600 nm will be effective in reducing the serum bilirubin and recommend the use of equipment designed to deliver this intensity of illumination.

The possibility that environmental lighting conditions might effect neonatal bilirubin levels has been raised by Gupta and Rath who demonstrated that a modest increase in environmental lighting intensity (to 90 footcandles) had a statistically significant effect in reducing the hyperbilirubinemia of prematurity. Thus the intensity and duration of illumination present in any nursery might play a significant role in explaining both the considerable variation in the incidence of hyperbilirubinemia from one nursery to another as well as the reported seasonal variation in neonatal bilirubin levels.

During the course of a study to evaluate the use of phototherapy in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit of The Montreal Children's Hospital, we collected data on the natural variation in environmental lighting intensity depending on the amount of available sunlight, time of day, and the location of the infant within the nursery. These data are presented as an index of the variations in natural illumination which probably occur in any nursery irrespective of whatever artificial lighting is employed.

# RESULTS

The measurements of available environmental light under different outside conditions are shown in Figures 2 to 6. From these it can be seen that the amount of illumination received by any infant varied from 15 to 2,500 footcandles depending upon his or her location in the nursery, the time of day, and the amount of sunlight present.

# DISCUSSION

Lucey and others have suggested that increases of illumination in nurseries to 100-200 footcandles, coupled with a liberal policy of exposure of unclothed infants to this light, is a safe and effective method of preventing the hyperbilirubinemia of prematurity. The data of Giunta and Rath demonstrated that infants exposed to environmental lighting averaging only 90 footcandles had significantly lower serum bilirubin levels than control infants exposed to environmental lighting averaging 10 footcandles. The data presented here suggests that ex

posure to natural sunlight yields far greater illumination levels than either of the two groups have judged as effective in controlling hyperbilirubinemia. Moreover, within our nursery the position of the baby in relationship to the source of external light appears to play a major role in determining the amount of such illumination received. Such differences as the total area and orientation of the windows coupled with variations in the local practice of nursing the infant minimally clothed allow for wide fluctuations in effective light exposure.

# SUMMARY

Measurements of the natural variation in environmental lighting depending on the amount of sunlight, visibility, the time of day, and the location of the infant within the nursery have shown a wide variation in intensity of illumination received by any infant ranging from 15 to 2,500 footcandles depending on the interplay of these factors. Both the physical structure of the nursery and the amount of sunlight available are major variables in determining the ultimate amount of light to which an infant is exposed. Both of these factors need to be taken into consideration in the architectural design of nurseries and the assignation of optimal illumination standards.

The Journal of Pediatrics
December 1969

# Studies on the effect of

phototherapy on neonatal
hyperbilirubinemia among
low-birth-weight infants
II. Protein binding
capacity

Sergio O. Porto, M.D.,\*

Rosita S. Pildes, M.D., and

Harold Goodman, M.D.

CHICAGO, ILL.

ONE of the unresolved questions of
phototherapy in the clinical management of
neonatal hyperbilirubinemia is the binding
of the photooxidative derivatives of albumin.
Theoretically, if these derivatives were to
bind with albumin, they could compete with
bilirubin for binding sites in much the same
way as do salicylates and sulfonamides and
increase the likelihood of kernicterus devel-
oping.¹

Previously, using 2-(4-hydroxybenzeneazo)
benzoic acid (HABA) as a means of mea-
suring dye binding capacity, Lucey and co-
workers² reported that the sera of light-
treated babies who had low serum concen-
trations of bilirubin had the same binding
capacity as the sera of control babies who
had high serum concentrations of bilirubin.
On the other hand, using the same HABA
binding method, Sisson and co-workers³ have
shown that phototherapy causes an increase

From the Department of Pediatrics, Loyola
University-Stritch School of Medicine and
the Loyola University Hospital; the Department
of Pediatrics, University of Illinois School of
Medicine and the Cook County Hospital;
and Grant Hospital.

This investigation was partially supported by grants
from the Illinois Mental Health Fund and the National
Institute of Health.

\*Fellow, Ely Lilly Company, Indianapolis, Ind.

in albumin binding capacity when there is a
decrease in the serum concentrations of bi-
lirubin.

Recently Odell and co-workers⁴ have
developed an albumin saturation index based
upon the amount of bilirubin displaced from
albumin after the addition of sodium sali-
cylate. The present paper describes a con-
trolled study employing this technique on
the sera of low-birth-weight infants who re-
ceived phototherapy with blue fluorescent
light.

# MATERIALS AND METHODS

Studies were carried out on the 29 Negro
infants described in the preceding paper.⁵
Blood samples were collected by heel punc-
tures daily while the lights were turned off.
The saturation of albumin with bilirubin was
determined according to the micromethod
of Odell and co-workers.⁶ For these studies,
20 µl of separated serum was pipetted into
2 cuvettes containing exactly 1.0 ml. of
0.1M phosphate, pH 7.37. The maximum
absorption of each sample of serum was lo-
cated between 460 and 465 mµ, and the
spectrophotometer was set at this wave-
length. To the control cuvette, 50 µl of 25
mM. sodium salicylate was added. The cu-
vette samples were mixed by inversion and
replaced in the spectrophotometer and read.
The differences in optical density between
the cuvettes was again measured.

The saturation index (S.I.) is calculated
by the following formula:

$\frac{\Delta\text{O.D. } 460 \text{ m}\mu}{\text{bO.D. } 460 \text{ m}\mu} \times 100 = \text{S.I. (\% O.D. } 460 \text{ m}\mu)$

where ΔO.D. 460 mμ represents the absolute
difference between the measurement of the
control cuvette and that of the cuvette to
which salicylate was added, and bO.D. 460
mμ is the optical density of the control cu-
vette after excluding the optical density at
460 mμ caused by nonbilirubin chromogen.

larity in the patterns of the saturation index
and the serum bilirubin concentrations of

the two groups. In the control group, there was an increase of the saturation index corresponding to the increased concentration of serum bilirubin, and a fall of the saturation index corresponding to the decreased concentration of serum bilirubin. In the study group, there was no significant change in the saturation index and no change in the serum concentration of bilirubin until Day 6, when there was a rebound in both the saturation index and the serum bilirubin value. As with the serum bilirubin concentrations, the saturation index was significantly lower in the study group, as compared with the values in the control infants on Day 3 (p < 0.05), Day 4 (p < 0.01), and Day 5 (p < 0.001).

Furthermore, the correlation coefficient between the saturation index and the ratio of the concentrations of the serum bilirubin expressed in milligrams per 100 ml. and the

total protein in grams per 100 ml. was r = +0.604 (p < 0.01).

# SUMMARY

These data indicate that the photooxidative derivatives of bilirubin are not bound to albumin, or at least, show less affinity to albumin than either bilirubin or salicylate. These observations add to the growing body of data that these products of phototherapy are probably nontoxic and harmless.

The Journal of PEDIATRICS 613

## Effects of photodegradation products of bilirubin on myelinating cerebellum cultures

Cultures of myelinating cerebellum were exposed to media containing bilirubin and human serum albumin and to identical media in which the bilirubin had been partially degraded by light. Starting concentrations of bilirubin were 30 mg. per cent. Cultures exposed to irradiated media in which the remaining diazotisable bilirubin was below 14 mg. per cent (representing a bilirubin to human albumin ratio of approximately 0.8:1) did not damage the cultures. Unirradiated media produced characteristic and severe damage.

Donald H. Silberberg, M.D., Lois Johnson, M.D., Henry Schutta, M.D., and Linda Ritter, B.A.

PHILADELPHIA, PA.

SINCE the introduction of phototherapy for the treatment of neonatal jaundice in 1958, a question has persisted regarding the potential neurotoxicity of the photodegradation products of bilirubin.

Evidence exists that bilirubin is converted transiently into biliverdin and then into a variety of smaller molecules which are principally dipyrroles. There is conflicting evidence regarding the toxicity of the breakdown products in various experimental

From the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine.

Supported in part by United States Public Health Service Grants Nos. NB-08197-01, NB-08075-02 (Dr. Silberberg), SR01 NBO-6919 (Dr. Johnson), and RO1 NB-HD-06899 (Dr. Schutta).

Part of this work has been presented at 21st Annual Meeting American Academy of Neurology, April 25, 1969, Washington, D. C., and at a Symposium on Bilirubin Metabolism in the Newborn, June 6, 1969, Chicago, Ill.

systems. Broughton and associates found that a solution of bilirubin which had been exposed to light for 32 hours had no effect on the oxidative phosphorylation of suspensions of brain or liver mitochondria. However, Hakami and associates described inhibition of mitochondrial NADH-oxidase by the early photodecomposition products, which they presumed were largely biliverdin. Biliverdin has proved to be nontoxic to myelinating cerebellum cultures in our previous studies. In this study we have exposed myelinating cerebellum cultures to media containing light-irradiated bilirubin and its photodecomposition products in order to study the possible neurotoxicity of the breakdown products.

In previous experiments we have seen that bilirubin produces characteristic morphologic changes in the large neurons of these tissue cultures. At the ultrastructural level we have

seen complex, electron-dense, intracytoplasmic whorls and enlargement of mitochondria. Neuronal and glial swelling, accompanied by myelin degeneration, start within about 4 hours of exposure to toxic concentrations of bilirubin. Swelling of the cell proceeds to vacuolization and eventual complete disruption within 24 hours in severely damaged cultures, and all visible myelin disappears.⁷

# MATERIALS AND METHODS

Culture technique. Fragments of newborn rat cerebellum were explanted onto collagen-coated cover slips and maintained in the Maximow double-cover slip assembly as previously described.⁷ Cultures were fed twice a week with a medium consisting of 25 per cent fetal calf serum, 75 per cent Earle's balanced salt solution with glucose added to a concentration of 600 mg. per cent, and zinc-free insulin added to a concentration of 0.2 units per milliliter. Under these conditions, 95 per cent of cultures myelinate starting about the tenth day in vitro.

Experimental media. We have incorporated bilirubin into medium in which adult human serum has been substituted for fetal calf serum so that the final albumin concentration in the medium is 2.0 Gm. per 100 ml. Phosphate-buffered saline was used to facilitate pH control.⁸ A bilirubin level of 30 mg. per 100 ml. was used. The medium was then exposed to two 15 watt blue fluorescent bulbs, used less than 200 hours, at a distance of four inches. Bilirubin was measured by a standard diazo method.⁹ Media containing identical amounts of bilirubin were kept in the dark at the same temperature as the experimental media for the same periods of time. In addition, media not containing bilirubin were exposed to the blue light for the same periods of time. Well-myelinated cultures 14 to 17 days in vitro which had been obtained from littermate newborn rats were exposed to these media and observed for 24 hours. Fifty-one cultures were exposed to unirradiated bilirubin media; 103 cultures were exposed to identical medium which was

first irradiated with blue light for 3, 4, 6, or 24 hours; 61 cultures were exposed to medium not containing bilirubin which was irradiated for the same period of time (Table I). The pH of the media was controlled so that the pH remained low enough to assure toxicity in the presence of bilirubin in the unirradiated media.¹⁰, ¹¹

# OBSERVATIONS

All cultures were observed by bright field microscopy before, during, and after specific experiments. Representative cultures were fixed in glutaraldehyde, embedded in Araldite, cut into one micron sections, and observed with Nomarski interference contrast optics (Zeiss). Using this technique to supplement routine bright field optics, we were able to detect by light microscopy the appearance of the characteristic intracytoplasmic whorls which occur in large neurons in response to bilirubin damage. This technique was used to examine 17 cultures which had been exposed to irradiated bilirubin media for 24 hours. These cultures appeared undamaged when examined by bright field microscopy in the living state. Only cells which were definitely identifiable as neurons were counted, for a total of 511 neurons; 443 neurons in 17 cultures which had been exposed to irradiated but nonbilirubin-containing media were also examined (Table II).

Under our experimental conditions we found a relatively constant rate of decrease in the level of bilirubin in response to expo-

It also shows that the whorls are not uniquely caused by bilirubin damage, but are a relatively nonspecific indicator of damage. Most cultures contain an area of necrosis within the center of the explant (central necrosis). This area has probably suffered from poor diffusion of oxygen or nutrients, and most of the abnormalities in control neurons occur within this area. The abnormalities noted as "other abnormalities"

are chiefly the occurrence of intracellular lipid droplets, a frequent nonspecific finding.

As noted in Table II, one irradiated bilirubin culture was omitted from the results because it contained 47 neurons with whorls out of a total of 52 neurons. Since only recognizable neurons were counted, we could not include the many smaller neurons which cannot be distinguished from large glial cells in these unstained cultures. However, we did count any cell containing an intracytoplasmic whorl, even if not an obvious neuron, and thus probably increased the apparent proportions of damaged cells. Conversely, if any neurons were sufficiently damaged to have lost their normal architecture but did not contain whorls, they would not have been counted. This was not probable, since the over-all condition of both experimental (irradiated) and control cultures was excellent as observed in the living state by bright field microscopy.

Since the experimental cultures were exposed to the photodegradation products of bilirubin as well as to the remaining intact bilirubin, it is appropriate to state that we could see no evidence of cytotoxicity of the photodegradation products in this experimental system. Both the experimental and control media contained 2.0 Gm. per 100 ml. (0.3 mM.) adult human albumin in whole serum, providing binding sites for both bilirubin and photodegradation products. While the culture model differs in many respects from the in vivo occurrence of kernicterus, we feel this can be used as additional evidence for the safety of phototherapy for the prevention of kernicterus.

# SUMMARY

Cultures of myelinating cerebellum were exposed to media containing bilirubin and human serum albumin and to identical media in which the bilirubin had been partially degraded by light. Starting concentrations of bilirubin were 30 mg. per cent. Cultures exposed to irradiated media in which

the remaining diazotizable bilirubin was below 14 mg. per cent (representing a bilirubin to human albumin ratio of approximately 0.8:1) did not damage the cultures. Unirradiated media produced characteristic and severe damage.

We appreciate the technical assistance of Mr. Dennis Martell, Mr. Tony Mignano, Miss Sandra Valenta, and Mr. Arthur Siegel, who developed and printed the photomicrographs.

## Briefly Recorded

PSD-62

"In Medicine one must pay attention not to plausible theorizing but to experience and reason together. . . . I agree that theorizing is to be approved, provided that it is based on facts, and systematically makes its deductions from what is observed. . . . But conclusions drawn from unaided reason can hardly be serviceable; only those drawn from observed fact." Hippocrates: Precepts.

(Short communications of factual material are published here. Comments and criticisms appear as Letters to the Editor.)

### The Question of Diarrhea and Phototherapy

The effectiveness of phototherapy in reducing the serum bilirubin in neonatal jaundice has been well documented. A report of diarrhea appearing shortly after the institution of phototherapy has been published, and other authors have noted green loose stools in infants receiving light therapy. The lack of published data on this association prompted the present study.

#### MATERIAL AND METHODS

The charts of the 600 infants with a birth weight below 5 pounds (2,268 gm) born at Charity Hospital between February 1, 1970 and January 31, 1971 and admitted to the Newborn Intensive Care Unit were reviewed. Two groups were defined. The phototherapy group consisted of infants who received a minimum of 24 hours of light therapy during the first 7 days of life. Figure 1 shows the distribution of the duration of phototherapy during the first week of life of the infants studied. With eyes shielded, infants in this group were placed under the lights continuously for 7 of every 8 hours. Those who received therapy on other schedules (i.e. longer intervals between treatments) were excluded, as were those who died before 7 days of age. The light treatment was provided with commercially available phototherapy units having eight 20 watt daylight fluorescent bulbs adjusted to the height of the incubator top (14 in.). The intensity of light at the level of the infant was approximately 800 footcaudles. Jaundiced infants were given light therapy upon a physician's order; however, no rigid criteria controlled the initiation of phototherapy or the length of exposure.

The control group consisted of all infants who received no phototherapy at any time. Table 1 shows the characteristics of the phototherapy and control groups in regard to race and

birth weight. Routinely, infants not requiring intravenous fluids were placed on the same formula according to a standardized schedule based on birth weight. For the purposes of this study, diarrhea was defined as the occurrence during the first 7 days of life of one or more stools described in the nurses notes as "loose," "liquid," "semi-liquid," "watery," or "trothy." Stools described solely as "green" were not included, nor was the etiology of the diarrhea considered. In the phototherapy group, diarrhea was recorded regardless of its temporal relationship to the therapy.

### RESULTS

Table II shows the incidence of diarrhea in the phototherapy and control groups. Thirteen of the 76 infants receiving light therapy (17.1%) had at least one episode of diarrhea, as did 55 of the 371 in the control group (14.8%). The difference in the incidence of diarrhea in these two groups was not significant (X² = 0.09).

### COMMENT

Other authors have reported loose green stools in infants receiving phototherapy.⁴,⁵ The present study was concerned, not with the color, but only the consistency of stools. Green stools, unaccompanied by diarrhea, were not considered because of the possible confusion with meconium stools. The minimum of 24 hours of phototherapy for infants in the treatment group was chosen arbitrarily, since a lesser amount of exposure was felt to be insufficient for evaluation.

This study was made on a retro-prospective basis with the patients divided by treatment

TABLE II
INCIDENCE OF DIARRHEA IN PHOTOTHERAPY
AND CONTROL GROUPS

|  Group | Number of Cases | Infants with Diarrhea | Percentage  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  Phototherapy | 76 | 13 | 17.1%  |
|  Control | 371 | 55 | 14.8%  |

and then the charts followed to determine the occurrence of the disease condition. The observations were made by experienced personnel—the nursing staff for many years have described in their notes infants' stools according to definite criteria. In addition, both groups were cared for in a single unit by the same personnel; therefore, the quality of care was similar. The data presented here do not support the hypothesis that there is a significant increase in the incidence of diarrhea among low birth weight infants receiving phototherapy. A carefully controlled prospective study would be useful for further evaluation of this question.

### SUMMARY

In a series of 600 infants with a birth weight below 5 pounds, the incidence of diarrhea among those receiving more than 24 hours of phototherapy was 17.1% (13/76), whereas the incidence in controls was 14.8% (55/371). This study fails to confirm a significantly increased incidence of diarrhea in low birth weight infants receiving phototherapy.

THE LANCET, DECEMBER 5, 1970

# EYE-SHIELD FOR USE IN PHOTOTHERAPY

SIR,—Phototherapy is increasingly being used for treatment of hyperbilirubinemia of the newborn, and there has been concern over the possibility of damage to the infant's retina and macula. No commercial eye-shield is available.

Initially we used gauze pads folded in half and taped over the eyes. This method is time-consuming. Our practice is to uncover the eyes for a minimum of two hours in twenty-four, but, using the gauze pads, the less conscientious helpers tended to neglect this routine. Several infants had conjunctival discharge and inflammation; and others had skin irritation from constant changing of the tape. To overcome these problems we designed a simple eye-mask made of drawing paper (see accompanying figure). Two sizes were made—one for premature and the other for full-term infants. The tapes consist of strips of rubber band stapled to the paper. These make it easy to attach the mask with the correct tension.

The masks are lifted above the eyebrows while the infant

1195

![img-151.jpeg](img-151.jpeg)

Dimensions of mask.

is being fed, and there is no longer the temptation to leave them continuously in place. They have proved time-saving, and to date there have been no cases of conjunctivitis or eye infection. Ideally, an eye-shield for phototherapy should be contoured, and fitted with soft material on the inner surface; probably it should also allow some light to filter through. It is to be hoped that a manufacturer will produce such a mask.

## DRUGS AND LIGHT FOR THE PREVENTION AND TREATMENT OF NEO-NATAL JAUNDICE

The enzyme system for conjugating bilirubin is often deficient in neonates, especially the immature. Unconjugated bilirubin is not excreted well, and if the concentration in plasma exceeds about 20 mg/100 ml,¹ unbound unconjugated bilirubin may pass the blood-brain barrier² and cause permanent damage - kernicterus. The treatment of jaundiced infants is aimed at preventing this damage.

Exchange transfusion was originally developed for treating rhesus incompatibility and has been the main method for lowering plasma bilirubin in the jaundiced neonate. But exchange transfusion has a mortality of at least 1%,³ and may need to be repeated frequently in the first week of life. Recently, two new approaches to the prevention of kernicterus have been introduced. One came from the finding that various drugs, particularly phenobarbitone, induce the synthesis of the liver enzyme which conjugates bilirubin. The other followed the discovery that illumination of icteric serum in vitro reduced the concentration of bilirubin in it, and this provided a rationale for exposing jaundiced infants to light.

DRUGS - Phenobarbitone, like alcohol, dicophane (DDT) and many other drugs, induces the synthesis of various drug-metabolising enzymes in liver microsomes, among them glucuronyl transferase,⁴ the enzyme which conjugates bilirubin. Neonates have little glucuronyl transferase. Moreover the inducing effect is greater in immature animals.⁵ As phenobarbitone crosses the placenta, its administration to the mother should induce glucuronyl transferase synthesis of the foetal liver, thus equipping the child to conjugate bilirubin at birth. This would enable the child to produce bilirubin glucuronide which is easily excreted, and which does not enter the brain. However in rats bilirubin itself induces glucuronyl transferase⁶ and it is therefore possible that in babies endogenous induction is already occurring once jaundice has developed. The high incidence of jaundice in premature babies may be partly due to protein deficiency which is known to impair enzyme induction. Early feeding of such babies reduces the incidence of excessive bilirubinaemia.⁷

Phenobarbitone may also reduce jaundice by increasing bile flow⁵ ⁸ and recently it has been shown to induce a protein which may take up bilirubin within liver cells.⁹ This mechanism may be important, as the relative scarcity of binding sites in the neonate might be limiting bilirubin conjugation and so excretion.

Treatment of mothers with phenobarbitone (50 - 150 mg daily for 3 to 50 days before delivery) has consistently reduced plasma bilirubin concentrations in their infants, whether those with Rhesus or ABO-group incompatibility were excluded¹⁰ or included.¹¹ Similar results have been obtained with intravenous infusions of ethanol for 3 to 96 hours before delivery.¹² All these trials were adequately controlled, but it is not clear from any of them how much an infant at special risk is likely to benefit. A special study is still needed in mothers for whom early induction of labour is planned.

Treatment of Infants - Prophylactic treatment from birth has given unimpressive results both in normal and in underweight infants,¹⁰ ¹¹ and certainly seems less effective than treating the mothers.

In infants with jaundice, phenobarbitone treatment has given inconsistent results. In a well controlled trial in Hong Kong Chinese infants with bilirubin levels between 10 and 20 mg/100 ml, the drug reduced the need for exchange transfusion for hyperbilirubinaemia from 45% to 4%.¹³ However in jaundiced Caucasian children with a bilirubin of less than 12 mg/100 ml, and without haemolytic disease, phenobarbitone did not seem to reduce bilirubin levels.¹⁴ ¹⁵ The latter two trials must have included many babies in whom the jaundice was so mild as to require no treatment. The discrepancy might be due to differences in the types of jaundice treated, or to a racial difference.¹⁶

Unwanted effects attributable to phenobarbitone used to prevent or treat jaundice have not been reported in either mothers or children. Defective blood clotting, resembling that of vitamin K deficiency, has however been found in babies of mothers who were given anticonvulsants in pregnancy. Both phenobarbitone and phenytoin were involved.¹⁷ ¹⁸ Some theoretical risks which would not manifest themselves until later life have also been predicted.¹⁹ For example, brain damage might be caused by reduced steroid hormone levels in the body if steroid metabolism were increased. As the trials have reported effects only in the neonatal period, the development of the treated children should now be closely observed.

LIGHT - The exposure of jaundiced premature infants to daylight or artificial light (wavelength 420 - 480 nm) significantly reduced serum bilirubin concentration, particularly the unconjugated fraction, and also caused the yellow to fade in all but the shaded areas.²⁰ This effect is trivial or does not occur in children born at full term, or with haemolytic jaundice or sepsis;²¹ the mechanism remains unknown. Artificial light has been used either continually or intermittently up to the sixth day of life and its intensity has varied between 300 and 500 foot-candles. Other infants have been exposed to intermittent direct sunlight for up to two hours daily.²⁰ The eyes were shaded and the body temperature monitored; with these precautions no unwanted effects have yet been noted.

CONCLUSION - Administration of phenobarbitone to mothers in the last weeks of pregnancy will reduce the plasma bilirubin of their newborn infants. The effects on bilirubin levels of giving the drug to babies is less clear and needs further study. Plasma bilirubin can also be reduced in premature children by exposing the child to sunlight or special artificial light. The two approaches are therefore to an extent complementary. The routine use of phenobarbitone for this purpose in late pregnancy is not justified at present, but it seems worth considering for mothers in whom it is planned to induce labour before term.

# PHYSIOLOGIC JAUNDICE: THE ENTEROHEPATIC CIRCULATION OF BILIRUBIN\*

RONALD L. POLAND, M.D., AND GERARD B. ODELL, M.D.

Abstract To evaluate the role of the enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin in "physiologic" hyperbilirubinemia, nine full-term infants delivered by cesarean section were given a formula supplemented with agar for the first five days of life starting at the 20th hour. Agar stabilizes bilirubin in aqueous solution and prevents its bacterial conversion. Ten infants were given the same formula without agar.

No rise in the serum bilirubin concentration oc-

IMMATURITY of hepatic function has been cited as the major cause of "physiologic jaundice" in the newborn and increased bilirubin production a secondary contributor to hyperbilirubinemia. This hypothesis gained its greatest support from studies that reported reduced glucuronyl transferase activity in livers of neonatal guinea pigs. Brown and Zuelzer¹ found virtually no conjugation of bilirubin in liver tissue from four-day-old animals, although neonatal hyperbilirubinemia does not occur in this species. Gartner and Arias² subsequently reported that newborn guinea pigs have a partial decrease in conjugating ability for bilirubin, but not of sufficient degree to result in nonconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Dutton et al.³ indicated that the activity of glucuronyl transferase is proportional to the concentration of uridine diphosphoglucose (UDP) glucuronic acid in the assay system used, and Strebel and Odell⁴ have since found the specific activity of bilirubin glucuronyl transferase of liver in four-day-old rats is comparable to that in adult animals. Other investigations have also demonstrated the presence of bilirubin glucuronyl transferase activity in fetal and newborn human infants.⁵⁻⁶ In view of this more recent evidence on the probable adequacy of hepatic glucuronyl transferase to conjugate the bilirubin that is normally formed, other mechanisms for physiologic jaundice appear to warrant consideration.⁷

curred after the 13th hour of life in the agar-fed infants. More bilirubin was excreted in the feces within the first five days in infants fed formula with agar, and these infants also lost less weight than the controls. By the sixth day, total fecal bilirubin excretion from birth was similar in both groups. These results suggest that the reabsorption of bilirubin from the intestine can be a major cause of neonatal physiologic jaundice.

Circumstantial evidence suggests that the enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin contributes to physiologic hyperbilirubinemia, but this mechanism has not been quantitated. Condie,⁸ as early as 1859, commented that jaundice in the newborn was related to "the want of a free evacuation of the meconium." In 1937 Ross et al.⁹ demonstrated that anicteric infants had greater stool excretions of bilirubin during the first few days of life than comparable icteric infants. More recent clinical observations have shown that marked neonatal hyperbilirubinemia can be anticipated in clinical circumstances associated with abnormal bowel function such as obstruction of the upper intestinal tract,¹⁰ delayed passage of meconium¹¹ or fasting.¹²

The feces of newborn infants, unlike those of adults, contain bilirubin and β-glucuronidase activity and negligible amounts of umbilinogen and urobilin.¹³ Intestinal β-glucuronidase activity has also been described in the human fetus.¹⁴ The absence of an intestinal bacterial flora for the reduction of bilirubin to umbilinogen and the presence of β-glucuronidase in the intestine during fetal and neonatal life presents a unique circumstance whereby bilirubin diglucuronide secreted into the intestinal tract could be hydrolyzed and the resulting bilirubin reabsorbed. Duodenal infusion of bilirubin in laboratory animals has demonstrated a more rapid absorption of nonconjugated bilirubin than its diglucuronide,¹⁵ and similar results have been reported in humans with biliary fistulas.¹⁶,¹⁷

Previous attempts to demonstrate that enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin contributes to neonatal hyperbilirubinemia have involved orally administered medicinal charcoal and the synthetic resin.

cholestyramine, to adsorb intestinal bilirubin.¹⁰,¹⁸ The feeding of charcoal was associated with a reduction in the maximum concentration of the serum bilirubin only if initiated before 12 hours of age in full-term infants. No effect on the serum bilirubin levels during neonatal life was found when cholestyramine was given to premature infants. Measurements of bilirubin excretion in the stools were not made in either study.

In vitro studies of the action of intestinal bacteria on bilirubin in this laboratory demonstrated that agar in thioglycollate broth protected bilirubin from either oxidation or reduction during bacterial growth. Agar is an aqueous extract of seaweed that has been separated into agarose and agaropectin.¹⁰ Agar has been extensively used in the preservation of meat, fish, confections, bakery products, ice creams and cheese.²¹ It has also been employed medicinally as a colloid laxative.²²

Studies of acute and prolonged agar feeding in jaundiced Gunn rats have been conducted in our laboratory. The results, as yet unpublished, indicated that the chronic feeding of agar in laxative doses²³ was associated with increased fecal bilirubin excretion, improved growth rates, lower mortality and partial protection from bilirubin nephropathy. Because of the encouraging results found in vitro and in the animal studies, permission for further study in human infants was granted by the Institutions Committee for Clinical Investigation, and authorization from the appropriate representative of The Surgeon General's Office of the Army was granted.

### MATERIAL AND METHODS

The capacity of agar to protect bilirubin from bacterial alteration was tested in vitro. Bacterial colonies were isolated from stool culture plates, inoculated into nutrient broth and incubated at 37°C. After 24 hours of incubation, 1.0 ml of the bacterial culture was pipetted into each of two sets of thioglycollate medium (8 ml per tube), of which one had been prepared to contain 0.07 per cent agar. Crystalline bilirubin (12.0 mg) was freshly dissolved in 10 ml of 0.01 N sodium hydroxide, and 1.0 ml was pipetted into each tube (final vol 10 ml, pH 7.4, bilirubin 11.5 mg per 100 ml). One set of thioglycollate tubes was not inoculated with bacteria and served as controls. All tubes were incubated at 37°C, periodically examined for bacterial growth and analyzed for bilirubin concentration at 48 hours by the method of Hargreaves.²⁴ Typical results are summarized in Table 1.

The control tube with agar maintained its original bilirubin concentration whereas a small loss was observed in the control tube without agar. Tube sets 1 to 5 showed good bacterial growth, but the original bilirubin concentrations were maintained only in the tubes that contained agar. Each of these tubes had either gram-negative rods or cocci. Tube

set 6 had been inoculated with staphylococci, and bacterial growth occurred only in the tube with agar. As indicated, the bilirubin concentration remained stable in both these tubes even in the absence of agar. A number of agar preparations have been tested in vitro for their capacity to stabilize bilirubin solutions and considerable variation has been noted. The U.S.P. agar used in the present feeding studies was one of the most effective lots, but the essential components responsible for this capacity have not been identified.

Healthy full-term infants delivered by cesarean section were selected for study because they would be in the hospital nursery for at least six days. Infants of mothers who were diabetic or had had preeclampsia were not included. The indications for cesarean section were maternal pelvic dystocia or a history of a previous section delivery. After delivery and evaluation of the infants, their parents were informed of the nature of the study, and permission was granted in each case.

Nothing was given by mouth for the first 12 hours after delivery; glucose feedings were given at 12 and 16 hours of life and formula feedings (Modilac, Gerber, 20 calories per ounce) were begun at the 20th hour. The agar-fed infants received 250 mg of agar powder (U.S.P.) in the first 5 ml of each formula beginning at 20 hours of age and continued at four-hour intervals for 24 doses.

Umbilical-cord blood from all infants was analyzed for ABO blood type and Rh factor, and a Commis test was performed. Capillary-blood samples were collected daily between 7:30 and 8:00 a.m. for measurement of serum bilirubin. On alternate mornings a blood hematocrit, examination of the peripheral blood smear and reticulocyte count were performed. The serum bilirubin measurements were done by one of us (B.L.P.), who employed a 1:10 dilution according to the method of Malloy and Evelyn.²¹ The other blood analyses were done by the routine methods of the hospital's laboratory. Daily weights were recorded for each infant.

All the infants' stools were collected for six days in Saran Wrap, which was used as inner liners for the diapers. Each 24-hour sample was analyzed daily. The stools were scraped from the plastic liner into a Waring blender, suspended to a final volume of 100 ml

Aliquots of 1 and 2 ml were analyzed for bilirubin by oxidation to biliverdin by addition of 1 per cent hydrogen peroxide in hydrochloric acid as described by Evelyn and Malloy.²⁵ The method was modified by inclusion of 1 per cent l-ascorbic acid to the reagent blank to prevent autooxidation of bilirubin in the blank tube.

The daily determinations of stool bilirubin were expressed as cumulative values by division of the sum of the bilirubin excretions to date by the weight (in kilograms) and the age (in days) of the infant. Thus, the six-day values represent the average fecal bilirubin excretions for the first six days of life in milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day. This means of analyzing the data was selected to minimize the differences due to the day-to-day variations of stooling.

The results of the control and agar-fed infants were statistically compared by the use of the Student's t-test. Since the fecal bilirubin values in Case 1 of the agar-fed and Case 2 of the control infants far exceeded any of the others, these results were excluded in the t-test computations using an r-ratio for outliers. All the stool-excretion data were included when the results were evaluated by the rank-sum test.²⁶

# RESULTS

There were nine agar-fed infants (four males) and

10 controls (six males). The birth weights, gestational ages, and frequency of blood-group incompatibility were similar (Table 2). None of the infants had positive Coombs tests or abnormal blood smears. The initial and subsequent hematocrits were comparable, as were the mean reticulocyte counts (Table 2). The agar-fed group, however, lost less weight (p less than 0.01) than the controls.

The serum bilirubin concentrations in the control infants (Fig. 1) rose from a value at the 13th hour of 4.1 ± 0.5 (mean ± S.E.) mg per 100 ml to a maximum of 7.5 ± 1.4 mg per 100 ml on the fourth day of life. The agar-fed infants had a similar initial mean serum bilirubin concentration of 4.1 ± 0.9 mg per 100 ml (Table 3). In contrast to the controls, there was an increase in the serum bilirubin on subsequent days. Only one of the agar-fed infants demonstrated a rise greater than 1 mg per 100 ml from the initial serum bilirubin value, whereas five control infants showed an increase of more than 5 mg per 100 ml during the same period.

Although there were marked differences between the study groups in their rates of bilirubin excretion during the first three days of life, the cumulative excretions were not significantly different by the sixth day of life (Fig. 2 and Table 4). The agar-fed infants had excreted much more of the total (six day) bilirubin eliminated in the first three days of life, whereas the control infants demonstrated a progressive increase in the stool excretion of bilirubin.

# DISCUSSION

No complications were observed with the administration of agar to the infants. The dosage of agar employed (0.5 g per kilogram of body weight per day) is within the laxative range recommended for adults, but no diarrhea or bulky stools were noted in the agar-fed infants. Unfortunately, stool weights were not measured before dilution, so that greater stool volumes could have been excreted by the treated infants.

The smaller weight loss found in the agar-fed infants is of interest but cannot be adequately explained by the present study. It is possible that the agar was responsible for greater water retention in the intestinal tract, but no evidence of distention was noted. It is also conceivable that the avoidance of bilirubin retention in the agar-fed infants prevented the development of a mild bilirubin nephropathy comparable to that described in the chronical

reduce neonatal hyperbilirubinemia have employed agents that can increase hepatic glucuronyl transferase activity such as phenobarbital, diethylnicotinamide and ethanol or exogenous administration of uridine diphosphoglucose as additional substrate for the conjugation of bilirubin. All these procedures have reduced the degree of hyperbilirubinemia quantitatively, but all infants so treated have shown the same qualitative pattern of neonatal jaundice, with a progressive rise of the serum bilirubin beyond the first day. By contrast, the serum bilirubin levels in the agar-fed infants qualitatively differed by the absence of any further increase after the initiation of agar feedings. The simultaneous elimination of further hyperbilirubinemia and the greater rates of excretion of bilirubin in the meconium stools strongly suggest that the agar feeding was responsible for the reduction in hyperbilirubinemia by blocking the enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin.

The daily cumulative excretion rates of bilirubin in our control infants were similar to the values reported by Ross et al., whereas the rates in the agar-fed infants were two to four times greater during the first four days of life. The initially low excretions of bilirubin in the control infants might be interpreted as either a primary failure in hepatic excretion or a consequence of an exaggerated reabsorption of bilirubin from the intestinal tract. The greater stool excretion of bilirubin in the agar-fed infants supports the latter interpretation. The sequestration of bilirubin within the intestine by agar associated with a possible cathartic-like action would result in a more rapid passage of intestinal contents and less intestinal reabsorption. The results of previously reported early feeding studies are compatible with the influence of early stimulation of intestinal motility on neonatal jaundice. In the present study early feedings were not used, and the findings are therefore more consistent with the interpretation that agar prevented intestinal reabsorption of bilirubin by reducing the available concentration.

By the sixth day of life, the total amounts of bilirubin recovered from both groups of infants did not statistically differ and averaged 4.0 mg per kilogram per day. This value represents between 50 and 70 per cent of the derived daily production of bilirubin, which has been estimated to range between 6 and 8 mg per kilogram per day in normal full-term infants from the rate of carbon monoxide production and red-cell life-span plus shunt bilirubin formation. Since the content of umbilinogen and umbilin in meconium stools is negligible, the discrepancy between the present recovery data for bilirubin and its theoretical rate of formation reflects either alteration of bilirubin in the intestine and during the collection procedure or some other mechanism for bilirubin metabolism in the infant. The error in recovery is probably much greater, for at birth the infant has to
