eliminate bilirubin already existent within the meconium formed during fetal life in addition to that formed daily from porphyrin synthesis and heme catabolism.

The present results suggest a sequence of events that can account for much of physiologic jaundice. In utero the fetus conjugates some bilirubin and excretes it into the intestinal tract where β-glucuronidase activity hydrolyzes the bilirubin glucuronide. By reabsorption from the intestine, the bilirubin of fetal origin can still be cleared by the placenta. The newborn, deprived of placental clearance, must excrete bile pigment derived from two sources: that reabsorbed from meconium and that produced from daily porphyrin metabolism. When the enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin is interrupted, newly born infants can excrete their fetal bilirubin load without its return to the circulation. The current report supports the proposal that the reabsorption of the bilirubin that is within the intestinal tract at the time of birth may be primarily responsible for physiologic jaundice. Further studies are needed, however, before the clinical use of agar for the management of certain types of hyperbilirubinemia can be recommended.

# Prophylaxis of Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia With Phenobarbital

THOMAS F. HALPIN, MD, ALBERT R. JONES, MD, FACOG, H. LEE BISHOP, MD and SAUL LERNER, MD, FACOG

In an effort to lower the incidence and severity of neonatal jaundice, 96 mothers were each given 20 mg of phenobarbital each night, beginning at the thirty-second week of gestation. Previous reports have suggested that such treatment stimulates the glucuronyl transferase system in the fetal liver and lowers the incidence of hyperbilirubinemia in the newborn. Serum bilirubin levels during the first four days of life were compared with those of 114 control mothers and infants. Treatment lowered the mean neonatal bilirubin at 72 hours after birth from 8.5 to 6.4 mg %. While 24.6% of control infants had serum bilirubin levels greater than 10 mg % at 96 hours, only 7.3% of the treated infants had levels greater than 10 mg % at this time. This study concludes that treating mothers with phenobarbital is an effective adjunct in lowering the incidence of neonatal jaundice.

SIGNIFICANT PROGRESS has been made in prevention of Rh sensitization and the treatment of hyperbilirubinemia secondary to Rh disease and ABO incompatibility. Physiologic jaundice, however, continues to be a source of concern and has recently been the subject of several investigations.

Physiologic jaundice is thought to reflect a relative inability of the newborn's liver to conjugate and excrete bilirubin due to immaturity of the glucuronyl transferase system. Odell¹ in an excellent review article, pointed out, that the problem of physiologic

hyperbilirubinemia in the neonatal period is undoubtedly more complex than simply immaturity of the glucuronyl transferase system. Hyperbilirubinemia (total serum bilirubin greater than 12 mg %) may be the result of either increased bilirubin production or decreased bilirubin excretion after birth which may also be caused by: a) decreased erythrocyte life span in neonates, b) inhibition of the glucuronyl transferase system by steroids of fetal or placental origin, c) decreased bilirubin transfer from plasma into liver cells, d) lack of bilirubin degradation into urobilinogen in the intestine due to absence of bacterial flora at birth and e) persistent patency of the ductus venosus.

Nevertheless, induction of glucuronyl transferase by administering phenobarbital to the mother seems to be a workable approach to preventing neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Brown and Zuelzer² demonstrated this possibility first in guinea pigs and their work was later confirmed by Gartner and Arias.³

In 1962, Catz and Yoffee,⁴ using Swiss-Webster mice, were able to induce conjugation of bilirubin in the offspring by pretreating pregnant mice with phenobarbital.

Six years later, Trolle⁵⁻⁶ was able to reduce the incidence of jaundice in newborns from 22.6 to 5.0% by pretreating the mothers with phenobarbital. He demonstrated that phenobarbital is more effective when administered to the pregnant woman near term than when administered to the newborn. In 1970, Doxidias⁷ reported his ex-

HALPIN ET AL

perience with neonatal hyperbilirubinemia in Greece and in several islands off its coast. He concluded that "phenobarbital appears to be a sound and logical approach to preventing severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia." However, Cunningham,¹ Ramboer,² and Walker³ were unable to demonstrate the benefits of prenatal phenobarbital or its direct administration to the neonate after icterus developed.

Other objections to the use of phenobarbital are known. Maurer¹¹ suggested that phenobarbital administered for 2 weeks or longer before delivery "altered the usual course of physiologic hyperbilirubinemia in the neonatal period." He cautioned that the drug is known to stimulate the activity of liver microsomal enzymes that metabolize steroid hormones and long-term effects on the fetus and newborn are not known. Behrman and Fisher¹² warned that treatment with a drug causing central nervous system depression must be carefully considered.

Mountain¹³ reported 2 infants out of 16 whose mothers were treated with phenobarbital prenatally, had clinical evidence of hemorrhagic disease and in 8 of the children, there was a decrease in Factors II, VII, IX and X which was severe in 7 of the 8. These were in mothers who had been taking barbiturates to control epilepsy during pregnancy. All of the infants responded to vitamin K₁.

The effectiveness of phenobarbital treatment is further obscured by factors such as race and sex. Yeung and Field¹⁴ reported a higher incidence of neonatal idiopathic jaundice in Chinese than in Caucasian infants. They attributed this to immature liver function. Kokosky et al¹⁵ report that newborn males have higher serum bilirubin levels than do newborn females. They also report that Caucasians have higher bilirubin levels than do Negroes, but that control Negroes still had higher mean bilirubin levels than phenobarbital-treated Caucasians. They reported no immediate side-effects in

newborn infants treated with phenobarbital.

Doxidias¹ reported a large series of control and treated patients, starting treatment between the thirty-second and thirty-eighth weeks of pregnancy. The infants of mothers who had ingested less than 1 g of phenobarbital, had bilirubin levels on the fourth day of life which were no lower than those of the controls. However, bilirubin levels on the fourth day of life were 4 mg % or less in 60% of the infants whose mothers had ingested 1 g or more of phenobarbital and in only 23% of the controls.

We have observed for some time what was felt to be an increasing occurrence of neonatal jaundice—perhaps due to greater alertness and early diagnosis. The anxiety of the mother whose infant is jaundiced has also been observed, particularly when these infants require extended hospitalization with its attendant expense. The risks to the neonate from hyperbilirubinemia and the subsequent neurologic deficits are well known. More recently, subtle degrees of hyperbilirubinemia have been implicated in subtle intellectual and psychomotor retardation in later years. Boggs et al.¹⁶ indicate a positive relationship between increasing levels of neonatal serum bilirubin and the incidence of low motor and/or mental scores attained at eight months of age. These relationships do not begin abruptly at the 20 mg/100 ml level of serum bilirubin, but may be seen to rise progressively and to become substantial at a concentration of 16 to 19 mg/100 ml. This data, if valid, would suggest that efforts toward preventing or ameliorating neonatal hyperbilirubinemia are desirable.

The present study was undertaken with an effort toward preventing and/or reducing neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.

# MATERIALS AND METHODS

Two hundred thirty-five consecutive pregnant Caucasian patients from the authors' private practice constitute the group of patients studied. Randomization was achieved

Further analysis reveals that the incidence of infants with serum bilirubin greater than 10 mg % at 72 hours is 30.7% in the control group and only 14.6% in the treated group. At 96 hours, 24.6% of the control group still have serum bilirubins in excess of 10 mg%, while only 7.3% of the treated group still have this degree of bilirubinemia (Figure 2).

The total group of 210 infants were then divided into four groups: a) formula-fed controls, b) breast-fed controls, c) formula-fed treated and d) breast-fed treated.

A difference appears when the total group of 210 infants are separated according to sex. Phenobarbital-treated females had lower serum bilirubin curves than phenobarbital-treated males and similarly, control females had lower serum bilirubin curves than control males. In fact, the curve for phenobarbital-treated males is nearly the same as that for control females (Figure 3).

# DISCUSSION

The present study suggests that treatment of the pregnant female during the last 8 to 10 weeks of gestation with a minimum total dose of 1 g of phenobarbital, produces significant reductions in serum bilirubin levels of the newborn during the first 96 hours of life. Since the effects of minor degrees of hyperbilirubinemia—ie, 10 to 15 mg%, upon subsequent neurologic development are unknown, but have recently become suspect,¹⁶ pretreatment with phenobarbital is considered advisable. From a more immediate and pragmatic point of view, because the fall in serum bilirubin occurs earlier in the treated infants, pretreatment will shorten the hospital stay of many infants being observed for neonatal icterus.

It should be noted that pretreatment with phenobarbital does not exclude later use of phototherapy by the pediatrician or the use of agar, if Poland and Odell's¹⁷ recommendations become clinical practice, but is merely an additional method of preventing or ameliorating neonatal icterus.

It is of some interest that breast-feeding the infants in this series produced no statistically significant elevation of serum bilirubin despite reports that progesterone metabolites, specifically pregnanediol 3α, 20β,

in breast milk interfere with bilirubin conjugation by the newborn's liver.¹⁴,¹⁵

No instance of hemorrhagic disease was seen in the 96 infants whose mothers were treated with phenobarbital, despite Mountain's¹³ warnings. This is probably due to the fact that all of the infants were routinely given vitamin K₁ immediately after birth.

# NEONATOLOGY

# CHARCOAL THERAPY OF NEONATAL JAUNDICE

A Preliminary Report on a Promising Method for Reducing the Need for Exchange Transfusions

JOHN P. CANBY, Maj., MC.

Chief, Pediatric Service, Martin Army Hospital, Fort Benning, Georgia

IN neonatal jaundice, a frequent problem in newborn nurseries, exchange transfusion has been the only effective method to date of controlling the bilirubin levels.

Recently, several authors have discussed the "enterohepatic bilirubin shunt" in man—so named because any unconjugated bilirubin which may reach the intestinal lumen is rapidly reabsorbed (shunted) into the blood stream. The following study was performed to take advantage of this phenomenon, using charcoal to adsorb bilirubin and block this circulation. The preliminary results, which seem to show a marked reduction in the need for exchange transfusions, form the basis of this report.

# METHODS

All newborns exhibiting an unusual degree of jaundice from whatever cause were admitted to the study. Although Rh and ABO incompatible patients were included, the severe jaundice in most of the infants had no demonstrable cause and was looked upon as "idiopathic."

For this study, an unusual degree of jaundice was defined as a total serum bilirubin level higher than 10 milligrams per 100 milliliters at 24 hours of age, or 15 milligrams per 100 milliliters at 48 hours of age.

Activated charcoal (Darco 60),\* suspended in water as a 10 per cent solution, was fed at the first sign of an unusual degree of jaundice. It was given by gavage in 5-cc. increments, each containing approximately 0.5 Gm. of charcoal, every two hours. This program was continued until age 120 hours with normal full term infants and up to age 168 hours with the smallest premature infants, or until the abnormal serum bilirubin levels had fallen to more acceptable levels.

In the nursery at Fort Benning, a community with a resident population of approximately 115,000 which is predominantly white, the newborn infants are fed 5 per cent aqueous glucose solution starting at age 12 hours. Breast nursing or cow's milk formula is begun at 24 hours of age. Mothers are generally discharged on the second day post-partum.

During the period of the study, all infants observed to be unusually jaundiced were fed only cow's milk formulas. Penicillin, streptomycin, kanamycin, and occasionally chloromycetin were the only antibiotics administered in the nursery. Vitamin K was administered as a 1 milligram dose once only, on discharge from the delivery room. The technics of feeding, bilirubin determination, and drawing of

blood, and the criteria for doing an exchange transfusion, did not change during the study.

The data for the control group were obtained by retrospective study of all records of infants receiving an exchange transfusion from January 1, 1963 to November 30, 1963.

The experimental study group, which was compared statistically with the control group, consisted of (a) those infants with serum bilirubin levels corresponding to those in the "obligatory" or "indeterminate exchange" zones (whether or not hemolysis was evident) of Allen and Diamond,³ and (b) all infants who received an exchange transfusion during the study period December 1, 1963 to May 16, 1964.

A comparison of the data from the control period and the period of this preliminary experimental study showed that the relative proportions of stillbirths, previable births, premature births in various weight groups, birth weights of term infants, Rh sensitized and ABO sensitized infants were nearly equal in each group.

Although occasionally a venipuncture was performed, most of the serial bilirubin readings were done on heel puncture blood collected at four to eight hour intervals, using the technic of Meites and Hogg.⁴ Macro bilirubin tests were performed by the technic of Mallory and Evelyn.⁵

Exchange transfusion was carried out whenever it appeared as if the indirect bilirubin reading would exceed 20 milligrams per cent by the fifth day of life. The exchange transfusions employed 400 to 500 cc. of whole blood per exchange—an amount equivalent to two infant blood volumes.

## RESULTS

During the period January 1, 1963 to November 30, 1963 (the control period) there were 3,009 live births; 53 exchange transfusions were performed on 27 infants; and one death occurred during an exchange transfusion.

During the experimental study period (December 1, 1963 to May 16, 1964) there were 1,562 live births, yet only 12 exchange trans-

fusions performed on nine infants seemed necessary. There were six other infants in this group who developed serum bilirubin levels in the "indeterminate" zone, and two other infants who developed serum bilirubin levels in the "obligatory" exchange zone. These were given charcoal orally and are included in the statistical tabulations.

When the experimental and control groups compared statistically by the chi square technic, the observed difference of the exchange transfusion rates between the two groups could be expected to occur, by chance alone, less than one time in 1,000. Of course the significance of this finding is affected to some extent by the fact that eight of the infants in the experimental group required no transfusion. Although there is no assurance that the total serum bilirubin levels of the latter infants would have exceeded 20 milligrams per 100 milliliters, all but two eventually did attain levels of 18 to 20 milligrams per 100 milliliters. In no infant was the direct serum bilirubin reading greater than 1 milligram per 100 milliliters. It is reasonable to assume that all eight infants would have required one or more transfusions, had charcoal not been administered.

## DISCUSSION

During the first few days of life, bilirubin metabolism differs from that in the normal child. Due to "immaturity" of the infant's liver, with relative lack of glucuronyl transferase, excretion of conjugated bilirubin is impaired with resulting accumulation of serum bilirubin, mostly as indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin.⁶ The feces of newborn infants contain large amounts of unconjugated bilirubin,⁷⁻⁹ and this content is increased in hemolytic disease of the newborn. Presumably, the bilirubin is transported across the intestinal mucosa cells into the intestinal lumen from the blood stream. Furthermore, there is absence of bacterial reduction of excreted bilirubin and large amounts of beta-glucuronidase, of probable visceral origin, are to be found in the intestinal lumen, possibly contributing to the presence of free bilirubin

in the intestine. As a result, an abnormal amount of unconjugated bilirubin thus becomes available for reabsorption into the body from the gastro-intestinal tract.

Lester and Schmid, using C¹⁴, have demonstrated that unconjugated lipid-soluble bilirubin is absorbed readily from the intestinal tract whereas conjugated water-soluble bilirubin is not absorbed, thus preventing reabsorption of a potentially toxic material. Previously, it had been demonstrated that humans afflicted with Crigler-Najjar syndrome, as well as the animal counterpart, the Gunn rat, have an enterohepatic bilirubin "shunt." Since most of the bilirubin in the newborn is present as unconjugated bilirubin, there should also exist the potentiality for an enterohepatic bilirubin shunt in the infant.

Ulstrom has recently confirmed that such a "shunt" does exist in the normal full term infant.¹⁶ By feeding normal newborn infants activated charcoal at four hours of age, he was able to cause a significant reduction in the maximum serum bilirubin concentrations attained, as compared with control infants. Furthermore, by the use of C¹⁴ labeled bilirubin, he was able to show that bilirubin solutions could be rapidly decolorized by addition of activated charcoal by adsorption onto the charcoal. Such activity was not impaired in vitro in the presence of added muconium or newborn stool.

It would seem, accordingly, that prevention of reabsorption of unconjugated bilirubin from the gastro-intestinal tract might effectively prevent high blood levels of unconju-

gated bilirubin from occurring in some individuals. That such is possible was shown by Lester in Crigler-Najjar rats, and by Lottsfeldt in a human with biliary atresia with the aid of the resin cholestyramine.¹⁷⁻¹⁹ Since charcoal seems to be more effective than cholestyramine in adsorbing bilirubin in vitro,²⁰ it should be more effective than cholestyramine in vivo.

MEDICAL WORLD NEWS

February 17, 1967

# Charcoal Each Day Keeps Jaundice Away

A New Jersey pediatrician is feeding charcoal to icteric infants to reduce their serum bilirubin, clear the jaundice, and eliminate the need for full exchange transfusions.

After preliminary testing in more than 100 babies, the new regimen is now routine procedure at Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital in Camden, N.J. Several years ago, Dr. Anthony J. Repici, chief of the hospital's pediatric service, heard the treatment discussed at a medical meeting, though where, and by whom, he does not recall. Since then, having used charcoal extensively, he estimates that the need for exchange transfusion at the hospital has been cut by more than 90%. "We've had no toxicity and no trouble from the charcoal."

All jaundiced newborn babies with serum bilirubin levels over 10 mg% are given 0.5 gm of charcoal in their formula every three hours, Dr. Repici says. Since the practice at the Camden hospital has been to wait until the serum bilirubin reaches 20 mg% before undertaking full exchange blood transfusion, the charcoal regimen affords treatment at an earlier stage. Therapy is continued until the serum bilirubin stabilizes at less than 10 mg%. Although all types of hyperbilirubinemia are treated with charcoal, Dr. Repici has obtained the best results in infants whose jaundice is not caused by Rh incompatibility.

Charcoal's Action Undetermined

Charcoal is distasteful to the babies, and it is hard to get them to take it and keep it down. The nurses assigned to Dr. Repici's busy neonatal service, which cares for 3,000 infants each year, dislike giving the charcoal feedings. But, says the Camden pediatrician, they find it far preferable to the three-hour preparation required for a full exchange transfusion.

Neither Dr. Repici nor Dr. Robert L. Breckenridge, the pathologist with whom he monitors the babies' bilirubin levels, is certain of the charcoal formula's mode of action. "We believe that charcoal absorbs bilirubin from the intestinal tract," the pediatrician suggests. "The more you draw off, the more will go into the intestine, so that the large excess of bilirubin in the body will be drawn out."

At Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital, he says, the mortality rate from full exchange transfusions is less than 1%. But at other hospitals, where the risk of the transfusion may be as high as 5%, Dr. Repici points out that the

nonsurgical treatment could have a decided advantage.

The New Jersey pediatrician has been using charcoal for several years. But "I can't say this is the last word in treating neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. We intend to get more data on what is taking place. But we are doing something for these babies."

# The Lancet · Saturday 13 December 1969

# ETHANOL IN PREVENTION OF HYPERBILIRUBINÆMIA IN THE NEWBORN

A Controlled Trial

RICHARD WALTMAN

GABRIEL NIGRIN

FRANK BOSUBA

C. PIPAT

Departments of Obstetrics and Gynecology and Pediatrics of the Brooklyn-Cumberland Medical Center, Brooklyn, New York 11201

Summary Ethanol was administered intravenously to 26 near-term and term pregnant patients before labour and during early labour in various doses to determine the effect on bilirubin levels in the newborn. 18 patients at term, free from obstetric complications, were randomly selected as controls. A statistically significant reduction of serum-bilirubin levels in infants in the third, fourth, and fifth days of life was observed in the group whose mothers were treated with more than 100 g. of ethanol prior to delivery. The findings suggest a simple, safe, and expedient agent which may be used to prevent raised levels of bilirubin in the newborn—levels which may affect mental and motor development in the first year of the infant's life.

# Introduction

SEVERAL clinical reports have advocated the oral administration of barbiturates during the last two to eight weeks of pregnancy,¹⁻³ as prophylaxis against high serum-bilirubin levels during the first week of the infant's life. It has been shown in rabbits, guinea-pigs, and mice that the enzyme glucuronyl-transferase, which is deficient in the first few days of life and is obligatory for the conjugation of free bilirubin, is enhanced by phenobarbitone injected into the pregnant animal several days before birth of the offspring.⁴,⁵ At the molecular level, many lipid-soluble drugs when administered to animals or to man induce an increase in the endoplasmic reticulum of the hepatocyte. These microsomal membranes are associated with drug-detoxifying enzymes. The functional counterpart of the morphological alteration results in an increase in hepatic enzymatic activity.⁶ Ethanol has been shown in rats as well as humans to be oxidised not only by hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase (A.D.H.) but by an adaptive microsomal enzyme system different from alcohol dehydrogenase.⁷,⁸ Microsomal enzyme induction initially stimulates oxidative enzymes but its activation eventually spreads to enzymes involved in hydroxylation, reduction, and glucuronidation.⁹ The possibility of induction of bilirubin glucuronidation by ethanol prompted us to

administer this agent to near-term and term pregnant patients and to observe the effects on bilirubin levels in the newborn during the first five days of life.

We have studied three groups:

Group A received 100-115 g. of ethanol from three hours up to ninety-six hours (median time twenty hours) prior to delivery (15 cases).

Group B received 100 g. or less of ethanol from less than three hours to more than ninety-six hours prior to delivery (11 cases).

Group C (control) received no ethanol (18 cases).

We excluded patients who received phenobarbitone or phenylhydantoin and patients with severe pre-eclamptic toxæmia because of reported low neonatal serum-bilirubin levels¹⁰ in the infants of such patients. Diabetics, Rh-isoimmunised, or bleeding patients, and patients whose personal history revealed mild-to-moderate consumption of alcohol during the last month of pregnancy were excluded.

# Method

150 ml. of 95% ethanol prepared as a sterile solution in the hospital pharmacy was added to 850 ml. of physiological saline thus making a 14.25% solution of ethanol. The solution was administered intravenously, generally at 2 ml. per minute and occasionally at up to 4 ml. per minute (found not to be well tolerated). The patients' blood-pressure and pulse-rate and the fetal heart-rate were carefully noted during the period of administration. Blood specimens were drawn at prescribed regular intervals for determination of maternal serum electrolyte and ethanol levels. Giggling and euphoria were observed, but nausea and/or vomiting was noted only at rates of 4 ml. of ethanol per minute. The sedation in labour consisted of small doses of pethidine (meperidine) and promethazine hydrochloride ("Phenergan")—drugs whose administration during labour does not effect serum bilirubin levels in the neonate.¹¹ The Apgar score at one and five minutes after birth was recorded. Cord-blood was drawn at the time of delivery for Rh typing and bilirubin determination, and bilirubin levels were determined daily for the first five days of life by the method of Malloy and Evelyn¹² (micro-modification) from the infant's heel-prick blood. All infants were carefully followed in the nursery by the paediatric staff, and no significant differences were noted in the infants of the control versus the ethanol-treated group relative to feeding, behaviour, or weight-loss.

# Results

Mean serum-bilirubin levels were significantly lower in the ethanol-treated patients (group A) at the third, fourth, and fifth day of life than in the controls (group C) (P<0.001) (see accompanying table). 11 patients who received less than 100 g. of ethanol either less than three hours or more than ninety-six hours before delivery are not charted (group B). Their infants showed mean serum-

Discussion
The administration of moderate amounts of ethanol to pregnant women from three to ninety-six hours before delivery resulted in significantly lower levels of s.d. in term or near-term infants. The mechanism remains to be elucidated. It was

Plasma-total-bilirubin levels in ethanol-treated and control groups.

The difference between the highest mean level in the treated group (4·75 ± 0·345 mg. per 100 ml.) and the control group (7·51 ± 0·634 mg. per 100 ml.) is highly significant (p<0·001).

noted by Remmer,¹⁸ and confirmed by Conney and Burns,¹⁹ that administration of phenobarbitone to rats enhanced liver microsomal drug-hydroxylating activities (N.A.D.P.H.-dependent drug-metabolising and steroid-hydroxylating enzymes). This enzymatic activity was accompanied by a proliferation of the endoplasmic reticulum of the liver parenchymal cells which was evident on electron-microscopic sections. The phenomenon was regarded not as a damaging or toxic effect on the hepatocyte but as an adaptive reaction to foreign substances.¹⁸ The process was non-specific since many substances (including over 200 lipid-soluble carcinogens, insecticides, and foreign and non-physiological agents) stimulate enzyme synthesis.¹⁹ Depending on the duration of treatment and the dosage of xenobiotic agents, the oxidative enzymes are first stimulated, and the inductive effect spreads to enzymes involved in hydrolytic, reductive, and glucuronic-acid-transferase activity. Though membrane proliferation and enzyme induction are intimately related, the response to the administration of puromycin and actinomycin D (inhibitors of D.N.A.-dependent R.N.A. synthesis) suggests that two different genes and messengers are involved.¹⁷ Many drugs and foreign agents, including bilirubin, are excreted in the urine as glucuronides—some by direct esterification, others after prior hydroxylation. The final steps in glucuronidation involve U.D.P.G. dehydrogenase, a supernatant enzyme, and a microsomal enzyme, glucuronyl transferase, both deficient in the newborn and increased in rats by the administration of phenobarbitone. In rats the increase in drug-hydroxylating enzymes as well as the U.D.P.G. dehydrogenase after treatment with drugs is rapid, but the glucuronyltransferase enzyme increase is characterised by a two-day lag period.¹⁸ Bilirubin metabolism in the newborn has been reviewed by Odell¹⁹; ethanol metabolism by Isselbacher and Greenberger²⁰ and Lieber²¹; and the effect of phenobarbitone and jaundice by The Lancet.²² Phenobarbitone was found to effect bilirubin metabolism through an enhanced hepatic uptake, conjugation, biliary excretion, and bile-flow. Recently, Lieber and DeCarli³ have reported that the chronic administration of alcohol to humans acts like phenobarbitone by increasing hepatic microsomal drug-detoxifying enzymes as well as proliferation of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. In addition both these substances increase the microsomal cytochrome P450 (focal point where molecular oxygen, substrate, and reducing-power meet) and enhance cholesterol biosynthesis. Yet after only two days of ethanol consumption by volunteers, alterations in hepatic architecture were observed.²³

Ethanol passes easily through biological membranes and placenta and reaches the fetus readily. Yet when mothers receive ethanol and are quite inebriated their infants generally show no respiratory depression at the time of delivery.²⁴ The fetal liver possesses only a fraction of the A.D.H. of the adult; the activity increases linearly and becomes comparable to that in the adult's liver at five years.²⁵ Even with low fetal ethanol levels, and a deficiency of A.D.H. activity, enhanced adaptive microsomal stimulation may result. 90–98% of the ethanol absorbed is completely oxidised and the remaining 2–10% is eliminated primarily

through the lungs and the kidneys.²⁹ By contrast, the transplacental fetal localisation of phenobarbitone, especially in the region of the 4th ventricle (site of the respiratory centre) and the fetal liver, results in the retention of this xenobiotic drug for a considerable time.³⁰

It has been reported from a survey of 23,000 cases³¹ that s.m. levels in the newborn above 7.5 mg. per 100 ml. may be associated with low mental and/or motor scores at eight months of age. We suggest that ethanol be administered in high-risk deliveries, where a raised serum-bilirubin level might be anticipated or is suspected.³² Perhaps premature infants and term Chinese and Indian infants, who apparently have an immature liver functional capacity for bilirubin conjugation,³³ should be carefully selected for further investigation. Premature infants especially should be studied. In these infants kernicterus may ensue at serum-bilirubin levels of 12 mg. per 100 ml. or less when these are associated with acidosis, asphyxia, hypoglycaemia, or respiratory distress syndrome—not unusual accompaniments of premature births.³⁴

This treatment involves the pleasant oral consumption of small amounts of alcoholic beverage during the last week or two of pregnancy. Several patients with a history of alcohol consumption during the last few weeks of pregnancy bore infants who showed relatively low levels of s.m. during the first five days of life. Inductive effects on other enzyme systems must also be evaluated.

We thank Dr. Alan Reid, director of laboratories, for the chemical determinations, and the entire resident staff of the departments of obstetrics and gynecology and pediatrics for cooperation. We are especially indebted to Dr. Sheldon Blatcher for the computerised statistics and review of the manuscript.

# The Lancet · Saturday 26 December 1964

# IMMEDIATE FEEDING OF PREMATURE INFANTS WITH UNDILUTED BREAST-MILK

VICTORIA SMALLPRICE
M.A., M.D. Land., F.R.C.P., D.C.H.
CLINICAL DIRECTOR

PAMELA A. DAVIES
M.B. Glog., M.R.C.P., D.C.H.
EDITORS

PEDIATRIC DEPARTMENT, UNITED OXFORD HOSPITALS

THE timing of the premature baby's first feed, and no less its content, have for some years been controversial matters. During the late 1940s the hazards of aspiration and the presence of oedema were advanced as reasons for starving the infant during the first 48 hours of life or longer (Clifford 1947, Smith et al. 1949). That this regimen led to improved survival was not unanimously accepted (Yippö 1954, Gleiss 1955), but the advocates of starvation probably outnumbered its opponents, at least in this country and the United States, during the 1950s. Although in the past few years starvation has been less rigorously practised, premature infants are seldom fed intensively in the first few days. The placenta nourishes these infants, if not always effectively, then at least continuously, until they leave the uterus. It seems irrational to interrupt the process just when the infant is exposed to greater risks than he will meet during the next four decades. Suspecting that some of the complications of this period might be caused or prolonged by delayed and inadequate nutrition, we carried out a trial of immediate feeding, which we have briefly reported elsewhere (Smallprice and Davies 1964).

# Patients and Methods

The trial was started on Nov. 1, 1962, and continued until March 31, 1964. Infants with birthweights of 1-2 kg. (2 lb. 3 oz.-4 lb. 6 oz.) were chosen. The mortality among those weighing less than 1 kg. is so high that we excluded them from the trial. Those between 1 and 2 kg. should all be viable, and this is the real challenge. 119 infants weighing between 1 and 2 kg. were either born in or admitted to the Radcliffe Infirmary, Oxford, during this 17-month period. 8 had to be excluded from the trial—2 because of esophageal atresia, 5 during the early part of the trial who died within 4 hours of delivery without being fed, and 1 whose admission from outside was delayed until the 4th day—leaving a total of 111 infants. All the very immature babies, and many of the larger ones, were fed from birth by indwelling tubes. Shortly after delivery, a polyvinyl feeding tube was passed through the nostril to the stomach taking care that it was well down; the tube could occasionally be seen through the thin abdominal wall as it entered the

| --- | --- | --- |
|  No. of infants | 111 | 45  |
|  Birthweight (g.) |  |   |
|  1000-1500 | 40 (38%) | 12 (27%)  |
|  1501-2000 | 71 (64%) | 33 (73%)  |

7374

stomach. It was then securely fixed, right across the cheek, with waterproof adhesive. Tubes were changed weekly. Early bottle or breast feeding was encouraged, so that the tube could be dispensed with as soon as possible.

We followed a fixed schedule of feeding during the first 4 days of life. The 24-hour periods were calculated from the time of birth, and not from the time of the first feed. Undiluted human breast-milk was given throughout in the following amounts:

|  Day | oz. per lb. body-weight | ml. per kg. body-weight (approx.)  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  1 | 1 | 60  |
|  2 | 1½ | 90  |
|  3 | 2 | 120  |
|  4 | 2½ | 150  |

As the trial progressed, most babies were getting their first tube-feed within 2 hours of birth. For very small or distressed infants the 24-hour total was divided into hourly portions to lessen the bulk of feed entering the stomach at any one time. The interval between feeds was lengthened to 2 and then 3 hours as soon as possible, but, when necessary, hourly feeding was continued for the whole 4 days. A third of the babies had small regurgitations, which were not allowed to interfere with the schedule. 3 infants, all below expected birthweight, had an initial period of bilestained vomiting, abdominal distension, and delay in the passage of meconium. After examination, feeds were continued and increased as usual, and the symptoms persisted only for a short time. There was no diarrhea. We adopted the standard birthweights for gestational age for singletons (kindly supplied by the National Birthday Trust from their perinatal-mortality survey of 1958); any infant whose birthweight was lower by more than twice the standard deviation than the standard weight we regarded as under expected birthweight.

This was not a controlled trial, but we have included for comparison observations made during the same 17-month period on 45 babies of comparable birthweight at the Churchill Hospital, Oxford. These babies were not fed until 4-32 hours after delivery. The majority had some feed during the first 24 hours, but the amount, and the rate of increase over the 4 days, were considerably less than in our trial. We describe the babies in the trial proper as "early-fed", and those at the Churchill Hospital as "late-fed". We made certain comparisons with a third group: infants weighing 1-2 kg. born before this trial, who were starved for at least 24 hours; these we call "late-fed".

Blood-sugar was estimated only in early-fed infants. In 50 of them an 'Autoanalyser' glucose-oxidase micro-method for true glucose was used, and in 27 others the method of Folin and Wu for total reducing substance. Two or more estimations were made on consecutive days during the first 4 days of life, and the lowest value for each infant was recorded.

Serum-bilirubin was estimated in both early-fed and later-fed infants if they were even slightly jaundiced. This was done in the laboratory of whichever hospital the infant was in, both laboratories using the same modification of the Tannhauser method. Proven cases of blood-group incompatibility were excluded.

# Results

Table 1 shows the birthweights of the infants, and the incidence of multiple pregnancy, respiratory distress, and deaths.

# Blood-sugar

In 27 early-fed infants the mean lowest value for total reducing substance was 60.1 mg. per 100 ml.

# Serum-bilirubin

The maximum bilirubin levels of 75 early-fed infants and 30 later-fed infants are shown in fig. 2. Of the early-fed, 13 (16%) had levels of 15 mg. per 100 ml. and above, 1 of these, with a reading of 19·5 mg. per 100 ml. on the third day, had an exchange transfusion. He had not been admitted until 8 hours after birth, and did not have the full schedule of feeds in the first day. 21 (70%) of the later-fed infants had levels of 15 mg. per 100 ml. or over. Exchange transfusion was necessary in 8.

The mean maximum bilirubin level for the 75 early-fed infants was 10·1 mg. per 100 ml., and for the 30 later-fed infants it was 16·6 mg. per 100 ml. The difference between these two is statistically significant at the 5% level. In the past, when infants were starved for 24 hours or longer, bilirubin levels at the Radcliffe Infirmary followed the same pattern as in the "later-fed" group at the Churchill Hospital.

# Times of Regaining Birthweight and First Passage of Meconium

Table II shows figures for 3 groups of infants; early-fed, later-fed, and late-fed. The differences between the early and late groups in times of regaining birthweight, and of first passage of meconium, are significant at the 5% level.

# Discussion

# Choice of Feed and Technique

Various kinds of feed have been advocated for premature infants (Corner 1960, Silverman 1961), including human breast-milk (Heas and Lundeen 1949, Crosse et al. 1954). Breast-milk is today scarce, and we have reserved it particularly for the all-important first few days of life. Wilkinson (1963) says that the newborn kidney is often judged immature by standard tests, but in fact it functions adequately when the infant is fed human breast-milk, and there is only a very small residue of water, sodium, and potassium to be excreted. Cow's milk, on the other hand, has a higher sodium, potassium, and chloride content. There is no real evidence that the premature infant's digestion is impaired, though fat absorption may vary

TABLE II—TIMES OF FIRST PASSING MECONIUM AND OF REGAINING BIRTHWEIGHT

|   | Early-fed | Later-fed | Late-fed  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  First meconium passed:  |   |   |   |
|  No. of infants | 90 | 34 | 28  |
|  Mean time (hr.) | 16·8 | 23·0 | 47·4  |
|  Birthweight regained:  |   |   |   |
|  No. of infants | 84 | 35 | 137  |

(Gordon and McNamara 1941). Diluting the milk merely reduces the number of calories, dilutes the gastric juice, and presents the kidney with an extra load of water, so we give undiluted breast-milk from the start. We see no merit in prolonged feeding with glucose; for, in the period of weight loss after birth, energy is provided by catabolism of protein, fat, and carbohydrate (Widdowson 1961), and it seems logical to provide them as soon as possible. McCance (1959) has emphasised the stabilising effect of growth in the newborn, and the importance of maternal milk in effecting this growth.

The alleged dangers and difficulties of early feeding of small premature babies have been overstressed. Apart from the 3 infants with temporary functional intestinal obstruction, we did not see significant vomiting, abdominal distension, or diarrhea, described as hazards in many standard pediatric textbooks. We do not wish to under-rate the risk of aspiration, but, with modern feeding techniques, which can be quickly taught by an experienced nurse, it should seldom occur. Even with the prevailing shortage of staff we feel that delayed feeding entails a greater risk. True aspiration pneumonia in infants is nearly always associated with some other gross lesion. The one infant who was found to have an aspiration pneumonia at necropsy also had a sizeable ventricular haemorrhage. In a few infants who came to necropsy, milk was found in the nasopharynx and sometimes in the trachea; but Gardner

1351

(1958) has shown that this can occur after death, and we have confirmed his findings. Food may, of course, well up the œsophagus in a moribund infant, because of decreased tone.

The indwelling polyvinyl nasogastric tube scarcely disturbs the infant. The tube should be well down into the stomach, and may pass on to the duodenum. The baby breathes almost entirely through the nose, but seldom seems worried by the tube in one nostril. When nasal infection occurs, which is not often, there tends to be more discharge from the intubated nostril. Gastrostomy with a blow-off vent (Berg et al. 1946) is said to avoid the supposed hazards of nasal obstruction, and, by allowing food to escape through the vent, to lessen the danger of reflux and aspiration. But tube-feeding is a very much simpler procedure, and our nursing staff has been eminently successful with it.

We do not favour intravenous feeding, because we think the infant's greatest need is milk.

### Hypoglycæmia

The levels of blood glucose and total reducing substance in early-fed infants show the wide range of values characteristic of the first few days of life; 8 infants had levels of 20 mg. per 100 ml. or less, but none had convulsions. Among the last 4000 babies born at the Radcliffe Infirmary there has been only 1 case of symptomatic hypoglycæmia—in a larger baby than those in this series, who should have had more feed in the first 24 hours. Recent studies of symptomatic neonatal hypoglycæmia (Cornblath et al. 1959, 1964, Brown and Wallis 1963, Neligan et al. 1963) have shown the susceptibility of infants below expected birthweight (particularly males and the smaller of twins), the risk of permanent cerebral damage, the quick response to intravenous glucose, and the inefficacy of oral glucose. Factors other than low blood-sugar levels are almost certainly implicated when symptoms arise. Cornblath et al. (1964) suggested that the low glycogen stores at birth, together with an abnormally sensitive insulin-release mechanism, are responsible. Melichar et al. (1962) have shown that in newborn babies, fat, either in breast-milk or as free fatty acids, produces a rise in blood glucose. We believe that symptomatic neonatal hypoglycæmia is largely due to delayed or inadequate feeding. This could explain the different incidence in various centres (Farquhar 1963, Wybregt et al. 1964).

### Hyperbilirubinæmia

We repeat that this was not a controlled trial. Two laboratories were involved, but they worked closely together, and several of the higher levels in the later-fed group were checked in the second laboratory. In addition, factors known to be associated with jaundice (Barton et al. 1962, Wood et al. 1962) were more frequent in the early-fed group. We therefore regard the difference in bilirubin levels as genuinely significant. The direct correlation between increased weight-loss and hyperbilirubinæmia, reported by Taylor et al. (1963), is relevant.

Hubbell et al. (1961) found that bilirubin levels 72 hours after birth were significantly lower in early-fed than late-fed infants. Laurance and Smith (1962) suggested that early feeding would lower bilirubin levels, and Lardinois (1963) thought that the volume offered was even more important than the content. On the other hand Haworth and Ford (1963) found no difference in bilirubin levels, nor, incidentally, in blood-sugar levels, between babies starved for 36 hours, and others fed from the age of 4 to 6 hours on 5% glucose. Too gradual an increase in calories

could account for their results. Brown (1962) cited Johnson and Day (1957), who described the depression of leucocyte motility by bilirubin, and Bernstein and Landing (1962), who tentatively ascribed necrosis of testicular epithelium and islets of Langerhans to bilirubin intoxication. It is surely right to keep the bilirubin levels as low as possible, and reasonable to suppose that nourishment provides a healthier cellular milieu than starvation for the maturation of the enzymes necessary for bilirubin conjugation. We feel that the rate of increase is as important as the content and time of starting feeds.

### Respiratory Distress

Wilkinson et al. (1962) have shown that early feeding with undiluted breast-milk will rapidly correct the chemical chaos in the extracellular fluid of newborn infants who have undergone surgery; this supports McCance's (1959) concept of growth as all-important in maintaining normal homœostasis.

Respiratory distress presents a more complicated problem. According to Nicolopulous and Smith (1961), excessive tissue destruction, shift of water from cells to extracellular space, hyperkalæmia, and excessive excretion of sodium occur in the first 48 hours in all premature infants, but especially those with respiratory distress. Beard et al. (1963) demonstrated prolonged acidosis and increased catabolism when infants with respiratory distress and low Apgar scores were deprived of fluid and calories in the first 48 hours.

The reported results of intravenous treatment with glucose and alkalis are inconsistent (Usher 1963, Hutchison et al. 1964). Such regimens supply calories, but they need constant attention and adequate laboratory facilities. We suggest that, until larger controlled trials prove the need for an intravenous regimen, these infants should be fed from the beginning. It is not true that infants with severe respiratory distress cannot be fed. 38 of them, fulfilling the diagnostic criteria of Usher (1961) and Miller (1962), were fed according to our schedule. 19 died, all but 4 weighing less than 1·5 kg. (3 lb. 4 oz.). Several had associated conditions such as intraventricular hæmorrhage.

### Nutrition and Growth

Recent evidence suggests that, when the birthweight is small, delay in regaining it is associated with later neurological abnormalities and intellectual impairment (Freedman 1961, Churchill 1963, Drillien 1964). Drillien (1964) found that children subjected to early starvation often developed handicaps, and suggested that delay in feeding might have serious after-effects. Spastic diplegia is the commonest neurological abnormality of infants of very low birthweight (McDonald 1963). Churchill (1963) found the premature infants with spastic diplegia had taken considerably longer to regain their birthweight than normal infants of similar birthweight. Dehydration caused by prolonged withholding of food may well alter the cerebral blood-flow. Infants below expected birthweight often have a high hæmatocrit at birth, so dehydration is especially dangerous for them. We cannot yet, of course, report on the neurological sequelae of our trial.

Stoch and Smythe (1963) emphasised the importance to brain growth of nutrition in infancy. Hammond (1961) thought that, in the growth of malnourished animals, brain took priority over other tissues. Låt et al. (1961) showed that restricting the food of suckling rats in the first 3 weeks of life not only impaired growth, but also reduced activity, inquisitiveness, and capacity to learn, regardless of how much they were fed after this early period.

# Conclusion

The Lancet (1963) said: "We need to know whether the simple matter of the time of feeding the premature baby is important or not. It could affect his whole future." We believe it may, because early and adequate feeding not only lowers his serum-bilirubin level, but almost eradicates symptomatic hypoglycaemia. Even more important may be the correlation in very small infants between spastic diplegia and delay in regaining the birthweight. We have shown that this delay can be reduced.

We are very conscious that many well-meant "advances" in the care of the premature baby over the last 20 years have been disastrous. Perinatal mortality for infants weighing 1-2 kg. at birth was lower in the single full year of the trial (1963) than in any year since 1952 when records were first available. This does not suggest the upsurge of a dangerous new regimen, though the improvement must be maintained. Minor difficulties were encountered at the beginning, but the scheme is now a matter of routine and has been extended to larger sick infants. It has been carried out despite an almost continuous staff shortage, and much credit is due to those members of the nursing staff who have pioneered it, and obtained supplies of breast-milk despite early discharge of the mothers.

The arguments for early and adequate feeding of these babies seem to us forceful. It is fully justified if hyperbilirubinæmia can be reduced and symptomatic hypoglycæmia largely eradicated; still more if shortening the period taken to regain birthweight reduces neurological sequelae. We think that it made the early neonatal course of these infants less complicated, and their resistance to infection greater. Although only a large controlled trial could settle these matters finally, it was necessary to show that this type of feeding is possible.

We are grateful to Dr. Hugh Ellis who generously allowed all babies in this weight group to be under the care of one of us (V. S.) during the period under review; Dr. R. H. Wilkinson who undertook the biochemical investigations; to our colleagues in the neonatal department; and to Sister Barbara Tubbs and Sister Moira Campbell who have been responsible with their staff for the care of the babies. Mr. D. Golding, of the Oxford Regional Hospital Board, kindly undertook the statistical analysis.

# THE USE OF THE BIOFLAVONOID COMPOUNDS IN THE PREVENTION OR REDUCTION IN SEVERITY OF ERYTHROBLASTOSIS FETALIS

WARREN M. JACOBS, M.D., F.A.C.S., Houston, Texas

ERYTHROBLASTOSIS FETALIS is major cause of fetal loss, as well as of certain cases of cerebral palsy. Since the incrimination of the Rh-Hr system about 15 years ago as the prime factor concerned with the production of erythroblastosis fetalis, countless articles dealing with this subject have appeared. The ideal solution to this problem would be to find some substance that would either prevent this antigen antibody reaction from taking place, or prevent placental transmission of the fetal cells which initiate the reaction, or even prevent placental transmission of the antibodies themselves. To date, although many substances have been tried, nothing has been found that would accomplish any of these ends. At present the management of erythroblastosis fetalis is based upon treatment of the affected baby after delivery has taken place (1, 2). The value of exchange transfusion is well known and will not be discussed here.

# THE RATIONALE FOR USE OF THE BIOFLAVONOID COMPOUNDS

The mechanism of Rh iso-immunization is based upon the concept that Rh positive fetal cells enter the maternal circulation through some break in the placental capillary system. Once these cells are in the maternal circulation antigen antibody response is set up with production of Rh antibodies. These then freely cross the placental barrier back into the fetus and attack and destroy the fetal red cells. Since the maternal and fetal bloods do not mix, it is logical to think that the fetal cells cross the placental barrier

From the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Baylor University College of Medicine, Houston.

because of some break in the capillary system. Javert states that in normal pregnancy varying degrees of decidual bleeding take place. He further states that the normal conditions which cause decidual bleeding are dilatation, engorgement, and stretching of the veins to the breaking point, and trophoblastic erosion, invasion, and perforation of the decidual veins. Mengert and his associates, in working with cells tagged with radioactive iron and also using cells with sickle cell trait, have shown that in a normal pregnancy a certain small number of fetal cells gain entrance to the maternal circulation, probably through some break in the capillary system. Increased fragility in the capillary bed is a venular defect. In 5 human subjects observed with spontaneous petechia formation in the bulbar conjunctiva, Lee, Goebel, and Fulton stated that the petechia were associated with venular changes. These latter consisted of annular and saccular widening, with reduced venular blood flow velocity in the widened portion, a turbulence of blood flow, and an observed escape of red cells from this distorted segment. In most instances, it was possible to see that the walls of the venule usually had a tricornered tear through which the blood cells escaped. It is conceivable that this may be the mechanism for the escape of fetal cells into the maternal circulation. Since the bioflavonoids oppose this action it is possible that when given during the course of a pregnancy this crossover of fetal cells may be reduced or even prevented. Since the bioflavonoids have an antihistamine action, this may also be of benefit, since Rh-Hr sensitization is an antigen antibody reaction.

GVTP-18

234 Surgery, Gynecology & Obstetrics - August 1956 Vol. 103

However, it must be stated that the anti-histamine drugs have been tried in the past without much success. Finally, increased capillary fragility in the baby is a prominent feature of erythroblastosis. These three factors then—prevention or reduction in capillary fragility of the placenta, antihistamine reaction, reduction or prevention of capillary fragility in the baby—are the basis for the use of bioflavonoid compounds in the treatment of Rh iso-immunized women.

# MATERIAL AND METHODS

Since most Rh negative women never develop antibodies, it would be a long and almost impossible task to evaluate the results of this therapy in all such patients. In this report only mothers with previous definite evidence of immunization are used. It is generally agreed that once immunization has occurred, each additional Rh positive child will be affected, and probably somewhat more so than his predecessor. Obviously, antibodies which are already present cannot be reduced or destroyed, but it is hoped that further crossover of fetal cells and additional iso-immunization may be prevented or kept at a minimum. This report deals with 6 cases of previously Rh immunized mothers treated with cvp, the trade name of a bioflavonoid compound, during the course of their present pregnancy. Twelve such mothers received therapy with cvp, but 6 were discarded from the series, 5 because the babies proved to be Rh negative (all of these husbands were heterozygous positive), and 1 because the previous history of immunization was doubtful. The dosage of cvp used in these patients was 6 capsules daily, which consists of 600 milligrams of the bioflavonoid compound. This therapy was started before the fourteenth week of pregnancy, since it is believed that crossover does not occur prior to this time.

# CASE REPORTS

CASE 1. Mrs. P. M., a 25 year old white para 1-0-0-1, was Rh negative. Her husband was heterozygous Rh positive, genotype CDE/c(d)e.

The patient had received intramuscular Rh positive blood when she was an infant. Results of titer studies made prior to her first pregnancy were as follows: blocking titer, positive undiluted strength only; agglutinating titer, negative; indirect Coomb's test, negative. Her first delivery was in January 1954. The results of titers prior to delivery in this pregnancy were as follows: blocking titer, 1 to 32; agglutinating titer, negative; indirect Coomb's test, strongly positive.

The baby was a male, weighing 6 pounds 9 ounces. Moderately severe erythroblastosis was present. He was treated by exchange transfusion. The neonatal period was essentially uneventful but secondary anemia developed about 7 days after delivery. He was treated by 2 additional simple transfusions and left the hospital about 3 weeks after birth.

The patient's last menstrual period had been on September 3, 1954 and the expected date of delivery was June 10, 1955. cvp in a dosage of 6 capsules daily was begun on October 15, 1954. Initial titer studies showed the following results: agglutinating titer, negative; blocking titer, 1 to 16; indirect Coomb's, strongly positive. Her prenatal course was essentially uneventful. At 38 weeks' gestation, results of titers were as follows: agglutinating, negative; blocking, 1 to 32; indirect Coomb's, strongly positive. Labor was induced by amniotomy on May 30, 1955, in approximately the thirty-ninth week of gestation. Delivery was performed by outlet forceps and left mediolateral episiotomy after a 6 hour uncomplicated labor.

The baby was a 6 pound 9 ounce male, in good condition. Results of laboratory studies on the cord blood were as follows: hemoglobin, 18 grams; red blood cell count, 5 million; Rh positive; direct Coomb's, positive; serum bilirubin, 3.5 milligrams per cent. The baby at this time still showed no evidence of jaundice and appeared to be a healthy infant. Exchange transfusion was done because of the patient's past history and because the baby did have a strongly positive direct Coomb's. The attending pediatrician and the obstetrician, who had also taken care of this patient and her baby during her first pregnancy, both believed that this baby was healthier than the first one and probably could have survived without an exchange transfusion. The baby had an uneventful neonatal period and left the hospital with the mother on the fifth postpartum day.

CASE 2. Mrs. H. G., a 34 year old white para 3-0-1-2, was Rh negative. Her husband was heterozygous Rh positive, genotype CDE/c(d)e.

Her first child was Rh positive with no evidence of erythroblastosis; the second child, Rh negative. Her third pregnancy terminated in a 7 month stillborn due to hydrops fetalis.

Her last menstrual period had been on September 25, 1954 with the expected date of confinement July 2, 1955. cvp in a dosage of 6 capsules daily was begun on January 1, 1955. Results of initial titer studies were: blocking titer, negative; agglutinating titer.

Her last menstrual period was on October 9, 1954. The expected date of confinement was July 16, 1955. cvp therapy in the dosage of 6 capsules a day was begun early in January 1955. Initial titer studies showed: agglutinating titer, negative; blocking titer, 1 to 8; indirect Coomb's, strongly positive. Her prenatal course was essentially uneventful. At the thirty-sixth week, results of the titer studies were as follows: blocking titer, 1 to 16; agglutinating titer, 1 to 2; indirect Coomb's, strongly positive. Labor was induced with pitocin on June 20, 1955, and spontaneous delivery with midline episiotomy was accomplished after an uncomplicated 6 hour labor.

The baby was a 4 pound 12 ounce female in good condition, with no gross evidence of erythroblastosis at birth. Laboratory studies on the cord blood were reported as follows: hemoglobin, 19 grams; red blood cell count, 5.8 million; Rh positive; direct Coomb's, strongly positive; serum bilirubin, 6.3 milligrams per cent. Because of the past history of this patient and because of the strongly positive direct Coomb's test, exchange transfusion was done. The baby had an essentially uneventful neonatal period and left the hospital with the mother on the fourth postpartum day. It was the opinion of both the attending pediatrician and the obstetrician, who had also taken care of this patient in her last pregnancy, that this baby was less affected than the last one, and could probably have survived without an exchange transfusion.

CASE 6. MRS. A. S., a 29 year old white para 4-0-0-4, was Rh negative. Her husband was heterozygous Rh positive, genotype CD2r/c(d)e.

The blocking titer just prior to delivery in this pregnancy was 1 to 512, and a strongly positive reaction to an indirect Coomb's test was obtained on the mother at this time.

Her last menstrual period was on December 24, 1954. The expected date of confinement was October 1, 1955. Therapy with GVP in a dosage of 6 capsules a day was begun on February 1, 1955. Initial titer studies showed: blocking titer, 1 to 256; agglutinating titer, negative; indirect Coomb's, strongly positive. Her prenatal course was essentially uneventful. At the thirty-seventh week titer studies were reported as follows: blocking, 1 to 512; agglutinating, negative; indirect Coomb's, strongly positive. Spontaneous labor was uncomplicated and delivery occurred on September 22, 1955.

The baby was a 7 pound 8 ounce female, in good condition, with no jaundice noticed at birth. Laboratory studies on cord blood were reported as follows: Rh positive; direct Coomb's, weakly positive; hemoglobin, 20 grams; red blood cell count, 5.4 million; serum bilirubin, 5.0 milligrams per cent. Because of the past history, and because the baby had a positive Coomb's, an exchange transfusion was done. The baby had an uneventful neonatal period and left the hospital with the mother on the fourth postpartum day. It was the opinion of both the pediatrician and the obstetrician, who had taken care of this patient in her last pregnancy, that this baby was a healthier baby and less affected than her predecessor.

# DISCUSSION

The seemingly most dramatic results were obtained in Cases 2, 3, and 4. These patients, although having delivered erythroblastotic infants before, showed no titer rise throughout their pregnancies, and the present infants were completely unaffected, as evidenced clinically and by laboratory studies. In Cases 1, 5, and 6, base-line titers were present early in gestation, which apparently represented holdover antibody titers from previous immunization. In all of

these the titer rise was only slight. One would expect that under ordinary circumstances these infants would be at least as severely affected as their predecessors, and probably more so. However, it was the opinion of the attending physicians in all of these cases that these infants were healthier and less affected than the previous ones. These infants received exchange transfusion because it would not be fair to compromise the current principles of therapy of erythroblastosis fetalis on the basis of an unproved drug, but it was believed by all concerned that because these infants were only mildly affected exchange transfusion probably was not necessary. It would be rather presumptuous to forecast a cure-all for erythroblastosis fetalis on such a short series of cases. However, based on these cases, there is evidence that the bioflavonoid compounds do have some value in the prevention or reduction in severity of erythroblastosis fetalis. Only similar studies with larger series of cases such as these will give the ultimate answer, and such studies are now being undertaken. For the present time, however, it must be emphasized that the best available treatment of erythroblastosis fetalis is the proper timing of delivery and exchange transfusion in the newborn infant. These principles should not be put aside in favor of an, as yet, unproved drug.

Surgery, Gynecology & Obstetrics January 1960

## FURTHER EXPERIENCE WITH BIOFLAVONOID COMPOUNDS IN RH IMMUNIZED WOMEN

WARREN M. JACOBS, M.D., F.A.C.S., Houston, Texas

In 1956, a preliminary report dealing with the use of bioflavonoid compounds in Rh immunized mothers was published (1). Much has been written on the effect of bioflavonoid compounds on prevention of capillary fragility, and it is fairly well accepted that the mechanism of Rh iso-immunization is based on the concept that Rh positive fetal cells enter the maternal circulation through a "break" in the placental capillary system. Many investigators have shown with various techniques that, in normal pregnancy, varying degrees of capillary placental "breaks" occur with decidual bleeding and escape of fetal cells into the maternal circulation. If these capillary "breaks" could be eliminated or reduced, thus eliminating or reducing the transfer of Rh positive cells into the circulation of an Rh negative mother, the degree of iso-immunization might possibly be minimized. In Rh negative mothers previously immunized by Rh positive blood transfusions or pregnancy, further iso-immunization might be prevented. Rh antibodies are small and freely cross the placenta, hence antibodies already present would not be affected, but if further transfer of fetal cells could be prevented, further degree of iso-immunization might be forestalled. Six cases were presented in an attempt to illustrate this point, but 6 isolated cases prove very little.

It is believed that if a comparison of Rh negative mothers given bioflavonoids throughout their pregnancy could be made with a similar group not given bioflavonoids but otherwise handled identically, i.e., pre-

term delivery if feasible and early exchange transfusion to the newborn infant, more evidence as to the value of this drug could be ascertained.

### MATERIALS AND METHODS

Seventy-one Rh negative mothers immunized by either pregnancy or blood transfusion with Rh positive blood, i.e., having delivered one or more erythroblastotic infants or having received a transfusion with Rh positive blood and having demonstrated Rh antibodies in the non-pregnant state, were studied during a given pregnancy which resulted in an Rh positive baby. The final outcome in this group was compared with that in a group of 32 Rh negative mothers similarly immunized, but having received bioflavonoids in the form of CVP capsules of from 400 to 600 milligrams daily, beginning early in pregnancy and continuing until delivery. The two groups were otherwise managed identically—preterm delivery if feasible and prompt exchange transfusion to the newborn.

### RESULTS

Group 1 consisted of mothers who had delivered 1 or more infants with mild to moderate erythroblastosis but survived, or mothers who had been immunized with Rh positive blood but had had no previous pregnancy.

Thirty-two such patients in the nonbioflavonoid group were observed. One infant was a hydropic stillborn; 9 were severely jaundiced and anemic and died in the immediate neonatal period in spite of attempts at exchange transfusion. Twenty-two were moderately affected, were given one or more exchange transfusions, and survived.

From the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Baylor University College of Medicine, Texas Medical Center, Houston.

The survival rate was 22 of 32, or 68.8 per cent.

Sixteen such patients in the bioflavonoid group were observed. One infant was severely affected (hydrops) and died shortly after birth. Fifteen were moderately affected and all survived after exchange transfusion. The survival rate was 15 of 16, or 93.7 per cent.

Group 2 consisted of mothers who had delivered 1 or more live-born infants who died in the neonatal period in spite of all attempts at therapy.

Twenty-four such patients in the non-bioflavonoid group were observed. Seven infants were hydropic stillborn and 17 died in the immediate neonatal period. None survived in this group.

Six such patients in the bioflavonoid group were observed. One infant was a hydropic stillborn; 2 died in the immediate neonatal period; 3 survived after 1 or more exchange transfusions. The survival rate was 3 of 6, or 50 per cent.

Group 3 consisted of mothers who had delivered 1 or more previous stillborn infants.

Fifteen such patients in the nonbioflavonoid group were observed. All 15 delivered hydropic stillborn infants.

Ten such patients in the bioflavonoid group were observed. Two infants were hydropic stillborn. Two died almost immediately after birth. Six infants survived after 1 or more exchange transfusions. The survival rate was 6 of 10, or 60 per cent.

SUMMARY

A total of 71 patients in the nonbioflavonoid group produced a total of 22 surviving infants, or 30.9 per cent, whereas a total of 32 patients in the bioflavonoid group produced a total of 24 surviving infants, or 75 per cent.

Offhand, these results would seem striking but it must be admitted that the bioflavonoid group is small by comparison and that larger numbers of patients must be treated before more definite conclusions can be reached. # Some aborted babies revive on their own: MD

WINNIPEG (CP) — Abortion is a form of "legalized killing" and cannot be justified by the "illogical" and "indacrous" arguments put forward to justify it. Dr. C. C. Merry, a pathologist at the Winnipeg General Hospital, said yesterday.

He told about 1,500 delegates to the Canadian Hospital Association meeting that examination of the developing babies that have been killed by a abortion shows that these are humans.

Some aborted babies have revived on their own, he said. One baby boy was

"found whimpering in a garbage bag by the hospital incinerator, waiting to be burned." He said those who take part in abortions become "blase" to such occurrences.

He said he had brought photographs of aborted fetuses to the meeting, but that these "had been censored." Officials at the meeting said the slides could not be shown.

Merry described the slides he would have shown, saying these would have illustrated that abortion "is the destruction of human life."

"Some doctors and churches try to justify abor-

tion by calling it necessary for the social and mental health of the mother or by saying that the unborn child is "something less than human," he said. He called this argument ludicrous.

"If we are to solve our social and economic problems by killing, it is totally illogical to destroy that unborn child."

Why not then destroy grossly abnormal children such as hydrocephalus—those suffering from water on the brain—who cost society about \$6,150 a year to keep? he asked. A similar logic should call for the killing of large numbers of senile persons who are kept in

chronic hospitals for about \$12,000 each a year.

Merry said aborted infants have been used for medical experimentation, that doctors and nurses who take part in abortions eventually become brutalized and hardened and that abortions have helped promote sexual irresponsibility.

"Canada is the only country in the world to have legalized abortion for non-medical reasons before contraception was made legal—by a matter of some two weeks," he said.

The Spectator, October 20 1973

# Doctor's statement attacked

This week, Dr. W. W. Watters of McMaster University made the statement that abortion should be regard-

ed as part of family planning and that the government should support this policy.

There are many people who would find this statement repugnant. Abortion is no more a part of family planning than is infanticide and the government has no more moral right to permit the former than it does the latter. Population control in some form is now considered necessary, but it cannot involve the taking of human life.

In addition to Dr. Watters' enthusiastic advocacy, it is also saddening to see the indifference of most of the medical profession to what is a life and death issue. However, some of us remain convinced that abortion constitutes the destruction of life and is an immoral and unethical solution to the wide range of problems which can confront the pregnant woman.

Anthony T. Kerigan, MD,
Hamilton.

The Spectator, Friday, June 6, 1969

# Legalized abortion called case of 'selective slaughter'

OTTAWA (CP) — Legalized abortion is "selective slaughter." Senator Ethel Belisle (PC-Ontario) told the Senate yesterday during debate on second reading of proposed Criminal Code amendments.

"Abortion is a crime against humanity, a ruthless, cold-blooded elimination of a human life already in existence," he said.

He was supported by Senator J. M. Macdonald (PC-Nova Scotia) who called abortion "a crime which calls to the very heavens for vengeance" because it is perpetrated on defenceless beings.

THE CODE amendments, already approved by the Commons, would empower three-member committees to allow therapeutic abortions in approved hospitals where it was certified a mother's life or health was endangered by continued pregnancy.

The bill would also permit homosexual acts between consenting adults in private.

Senator Belisle said legal

homosexuality in Canada would be a menace, not only to youth, parents and the family, but to society itself.

"To vote for these amendments is to vote for more crime and violence," he said. "We need stronger laws against sin and crime, not the licensing of homosexuality."

BOTH SENATORS expressed fears that more liberal abortion laws would lower the value of human life and might lead to removal of other groups from the law's protection.

"If we accept this in principle, we need only the passage of time to reach the position of placing a lower value on other stages of human life whether it be the aged, the infirm, the deformed person or those who don't agree with us," Senator Belisle said.

"The theory that abortion will not be forced on anyone does not stand up when one considers that it is forced on the unborn child."

Senator Macdonald warned that once the sanctity of human life is attacked at the weakest point, "then step by step it can be brought into question all along the line."

ABORTION WAS a serious violation of moral law. To pass the amendment would be an act contrary as well to the "noble tradition of the legal system" which was meant to protect life, not destroy it.

Senator Belisle said it has been established by outstanding medical experts that the fetus after five days is a human being. To kill an innocent human being was wrong.

"Society must protect the human fetus as it does the baby fresh from the maternity ward," he said.

Large numbers of persons totally rejected any suggestion that abortion was the cure-all for squalor, misery and hunger.

"EVEN THOUGH we know that many babies leaving the hospital will live in the slums

of Toronto, Montreal or in impoverished Indian settlements, no one seriously advocates a compulsory abortion law such that the child is not to be brought into these miserable surroundings.

"We know that there are better answers than this."

Senator Belisle said abortion would seem to answer many problems of the welfare state which promised security from the cradle to the grave and then allowed abortion to remove the possibility of any access to the cradle.

England had a great housing shortage. This would appear to be one of the reasons for passing a law allowing abortions for social reasons.

"We here in Canada are now faced with a housing shortage, while in the city of Toronto people who are unable to find homes are turning their children over to the Children's Aid Society. Do we contemplate the same solution there?" he asked.

Debate on the amendments was adjourned.

4 The Spectator, Tuesday, December 12, 1972

# Abortions rise by almost one-third

OTTAWA (CP) — Abortions in the first six months of 1972 increased by nearly 33 per cent over the same period in 1971. Statistics Canada reported yesterday.

Hospitals reported 18,891 abortions on Canadian residents in the first half of 1972, up from 14,168 for the same period in 1971. There were 16 abortions performed on women with foreign residence.

In terms of the number of live births, the abortion rate is one for every 10 live births or 10.1 per cent.

THE FIGURES were reported in the daily bulletin is-

sued by the health and welfare division of Statistics Canada.

All provinces showed increases compared with rates for the first half of 1971. The largest increase in actual numbers was in Ontario, where there were 9,844 abortions in six months of 1972 compared with 7,387 in the same period in 1971 — an increase of 35 per cent.

The largest percentage increases were in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. They showed an increase of 300 per cent based on half-

year figures of 34 in 1972 and 6 in 1971.

NEWFOUNDLAND, which reported 77 abortions in the first half of 1972 compared with 30 in the same period in 1971, had a percentage increase of 136 per cent.

British Columbia again had the highest rate of all provinces, the report said, with 22.4 abortions for every 100 live births. However, it showed the smallest increase — 16 per cent — compared with the 1971 period.

Newfoundland had the lowest abortion rate with 1.2 abortions for 100 live births.
