When to clamp the umbilical cord—whether immediately after delivery or a few minutes later—has been a controversial question for years. Now a South African obstetrician goes beyond even those who advocate late clamping. He says flatly that the cord should not be clamped at all on the mother's side.

The time needed to complete the third stage of labor and the blood loss in this period can be greatly reduced if the cord is left unclamped and allowed to bleed, claims Dr. Michael C. Botha, senior resident in the department of obstetrics and gynecology at the University of Cape Town. Dr. Botha, who is spending the year as a fellow in gynecologic surgery at the University of Louisville, maintains that clamping obstructs the normal mechanism of third-stage labor and can actually create the complications of retained placenta, postpartum hemorrhage, and Rh isoimmunization.

At the root of Dr. Botha's ideas

# UNCLAMPED

# CORD SEEN

# AS MOTHER'S

# HELPER

are his observations that primitive Bantu women traditionally do not touch the cord until after the expulsion of the placenta and that they seem to find the third stage of labor far less troublesome than Western sophisticates. He reports in the South African Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology (Vol. 6, No. 2) that he saw the unusual obstetrics cases occurring in a population of 26,000 Bantu over a ten-year period. "I found many other complications, but a retained placenta was seldom seen. If called to a case, I usually found that only the terminal part of the membranes was still in the vagina and had merely to be lifted out.

Blood transfusion for a postpartum hemorrhage was never necessary."

When bearing-down pains begin, parturient women of the most primitive Bantu tribes squat on their haunches, as if defecating. Once the infant is born, the woman remains in the squatting position, watching her new baby. The placenta then delivers itself without any maternal effort. After the placenta has been delivered—by gravity—the membranes usually remain in the vagina. The woman then raises herself on her haunches, and the membranes fall out. Only then does she attend to the cord.

Besides avoiding certain postpartum complications, this method of delivery also seems to result in a blood-gain for the infant. Dr. Botha cites a 1965 study indicating that about 89 cc of blood flows down the cord from the placenta after delivery of the child—blood that would be wasted if the cord were clamped and cut early.

With these findings in mind, Dr. Botha has managed 800 parturient white women over the past ten years, using oxytocic drugs, letting the cord bleed, and applying the Brandt-Andrews maneuver to help in the expulsion of the placenta. In none of these cases was the placenta retained, nor did any of the women suffer a postpartum hemorrhage that made a blood transfusion necessary.

To assess more precisely the effects of leaving the cord unclamped, Dr. Botha did a comparative study of 60 consecutive deliveries among white women. He clamped the cord in 30 and left it unclamped in the other 30. The cases were selected irrespective of age or parity, and the deliveries were all normal.

In these patients, the uterus was not handled until after the expulsion of the placenta, and the placenta was not handled until the mother felt the urge to bear down after the birth of her baby. The blood from the cord and from the uterus was collected separately and measured.

The third stage of labor was much quicker when the cord was left unclamped than when it was clamped, says Dr. Botha. The mean duration was 3.5 minutes when the cord was

# UNCLAMPED CORD continued

eight or more minutes after delivery of the infant showed the placenta in situ.

The function of the uterus in the third stage of labor, notes Dr. Botha, is to separate the placenta, to expel it, and to control hemorrhage. All this is effected by contraction and retraction. At delivery of the infant, micro-separation has already occurred due to the uterine retraction that takes place in the second stage. The placenta separates because it cannot reduce its own surface area, although the surface to which it adheres does shrink. The same applies to the membranes. "This separation can be illustrated by sticking a postage stamp to a piece of stretched elastic," says Dr. Botha. "When the elastic is allowed to shrink, the stamp will peel off."

The placenta is forced in the direction of least resistance, toward the lower segment of the uterus and the vagina. "If the cord is bled, this process is so rapid that retraction has not yet taken place in the cervix, and the placenta, reduced in size, is expelled without resistance into the vagina. If the patient is sitting on her haunches, the placenta will fall out by gravity."

Hemostasis depends on the criss-cross arrangement of the uterine muscle, and the tortuous course of the maternal blood vessels supplying the placental site runs through the interstices of these muscles. "These gaps are closed by retraction, thus obliterating the supply of blood to the placental site. Greater retraction, therefore, favors less bleeding."

So, says Dr. Botha, anything that promotes retraction will quicken separation and expulsion and will reduce the blood loss. Allowing the placental end of the cord to bleed freely or keeping the cord intact until the placenta is completely expelled, he says, has this effect.

"In both methods, the placental volume is reduced and, therefore, uterine contents are reduced by approximately 90 cc of blood," the South African obstetrician says. "Retraction takes place, squeezing more blood out of the placenta and reducing in size still further."

If, on the other hand, the cord is clamped, then the "counterresistance

from the placenta may be so great that retraction may come to an end. The placenta will then be separated by retroplacental blood, which, in my opinion, is not normal but abnormal. This takes place slowly, and by the time the placenta is separated, the cervix has also retracted. The placenta is bulky, due to the blood it contains, and expulsion is difficult. If expulsion is not possible, the inevitable result is that in a certain percentage of cases the placenta will be retained, with associated postpartum hemorrhage."

Finally, as other investigators have shown, Rh-negative women bearing Rh-positive babies rarely develop antibodies when the placenta is allowed to separate and to be delivered spontaneously with the cord unclamped. This finding, says Dr. Botha, fits in with other evidence that the major risk of isoimmunization occurs during the third stage of labor.

# Two Reasons in 300 Years

The reasons given for clamping the cord are few and somewhat tenuous, says Dr. Botha. In a 1909 textbook on obstetrics, Dr. J. G. Williams reckoned that tying the maternal end of the cord served only to avoid bloodying the bedclothes. And the great Glasgow obstetrician J. M. Munro Kerr later referred to the maternal ligature as a means of knowing if the cord had been lengthened so as to see if the placenta had separated. According to Dr. Botha, these two statements are the only reasons given in the literature dating back to 1682 for clamping the maternal end of the cord.

"It would appear," he concludes, "that we have interfered with normal labor since the 17th century, that we have, in fact, obstructed the normal mechanism by clamping the cord, thereby creating a number of complications." Therefore he advises giving oxytocics to help the uterine muscle retract, severing the cord after the birth of the child and allowing the placental end to bleed, and, when the bleeding has stopped, removing the placenta during the next contraction. This procedure, Dr. Botha notes, is now routine at the University of Cape Town.

# Preliminary Communications

# TRANSPLACENTAL FETAL HÆMORRHAGE AFTER PLACENTAL INJURY DURING DELIVERY OR AMNIOCENTESIS

TRANSPLACENTAL hæmorrhage may result from operative procedures that damage the placental site. Such bleeding into the maternal circulation may occur during cæsarean section or manual removal of the placenta.¹ We here report further evidence of significant bleeding into the mother's circulation during these procedures, and also during amniocentesis. As amniocentesis is now a common elective diagnostic procedure, we think that this complication and its possible significance should be known.

# OUR STUDY

Fœtal cells were detected in the maternal circulation by the acid-elution technique of Kleihauer and Betke.² The technique and its sensitivity are described elsewhere.³ We estimated the quantity of fœtal cells in the maternal circulation from the number of fœtal cells seen during a 10-minute scan of a slide preparation.⁴

TABLE I—PLACENTAL TRAUMA AND BLEEDING

|  Diagnosis | No. of women studied | No. of women with more than 1 ml. fœtal blood in their circulation  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  Normal delivery | 121 | 1  |
|  Cæsarean section | 87 | 10  |
|  Manual removal of placenta | 15 | 3  |

Table I shows that trauma to the placenta may cause such bleeding. Cæsarean sections were performed because of difficulties in labour, previous sections, placenta pravis, pre-eclampsia, and cephalopelvic disproportion. The frequency of fœtal hæmorrhage seemed to be independent of the indication for the cæsarean section. In most cases specimens were taken only after delivery, and one could not be certain whether the transplacental hæmorrhage had occurred before or after the procedure. In one patient in the cæsarean section group, a sample taken before surgery was negative, whereas after delivery it was estimated that about 8 ml. of fœtal blood had entered the maternal circulation. At times the quantities entering the maternal circulation were large. Only one subject in the normal group was estimated to have received as much as 4 ml. of fœtal blood, whereas seven of the cæsarean group and all three in the manual-removal group had more than 6 ml. of fœtal blood in their circulation. The largest amount was 20 ml.

Thirteen women were studied immediately after amniocentesis had been performed for the antenatal assessment of Rh haemolytic disease.¹ In four the procedure was unsuccessful and the surgeon thought he had entered the placenta with the needle. In two of these four patients the aspirated blood was examined and found to be of vital origin. In all four women, massive transplacental passage of fœtal cells had occurred (table II). The estimated volume of fœtal blood lost into the maternal circulation varied from 10 to 50 ml. These women all had anti-D antibodies before they were tapped. In the three women carrying Rh-positive fœtuses, an antibody rise of two dilutions or more was found 2 weeks after the procedure.

# DISCUSSION

The importance of manual interference with the placental site was brought to our attention recently by observations in three severe cases of anæmia of the newborn, which were proved to be the result of transplacental fœtal hæmorrhage. In two of these three patients, the baby had been born by cæsarean section, and delivery had been through the incised placenta. Although this has not been a common cause of this form of neonatal anæmia,⁵ Apley et al.⁶ have described a case of fœtal exsanguination owing to transplacental bleeding after injury to the placenta by a Drew-Smythe catheter. Two cases, probably similar, have been reported by Russell et al.¹⁰

Our findings suggest that operative procedures which damage the placenta can cause massive transplacental hæmorrhage, possibly resulting in fœtal exsanguination or isoimmunisation of the mother.¹¹⁻¹³ These results confirm those recently reported by others of the dangers of cæsarean section and manual removal of the placenta.¹⁴ They further indicate that amniocentesis may cause fœtal hæmorrhage into the maternal circulation, presumably by damage to the placenta. In our cases the bleeding was of a magnitude which was capable of compromising the life of the fœtus and causing a rise in the antibody titre in the mother.

ORIGINAL ARTICLES

THE LANCET

# TRANSPLACENTAL HÆMORRHAGE AFTER EXTERNAL CEPHALIC VERSION

ANDREW POLLOCK

M.B. Glanz, M.C.Path.

TERROR STERNSTROM, PHYSICIAN OF HÆMATOLOGY, SOUTHERN GENERAL HOSPITAL, GLASGOW S.W.1

Summary A pregnant woman had an attack of hæmoglobinuria after external cephalic version under anæsthesia. This was shown to be due to leakage of incompatible blood from her fetus into her own circulation. The case may have important implications regarding Rh sensitisation.

# Case-report

THE patient, a 22-year-old primagravida, had been well throughout pregnancy and had no relevant past medical history. At 35 weeks an attempt at external cephalic version was unsuccessful and this was repeated, still unsuccessfully, after the patient had been sedated. 1 week later she was admitted to hospital, where external cephalic version was performed under general anæsthesia by an experienced operator who stated that no unusual degree of force was used.

The patient's subsequent progress gave no cause for anxiety until 4 hours later when she passed dark-red urine. No red blood-cells were seen on microscopic examination, but on spectroscopy, the urine showed the characteristic bands of oxyhæmoglobin, and this (measured as oxyfomethæmoglobin) was present in a concentration of 0·2 g. per 100 ml. Further investigation of the pigment showed that it was resistant to alkali denaturation (Berke 1959) in the manner of fetal Hb, while on starch-gel electrophoresis (Hutchison et al. 1961) performed the next day, it moved well ahead of normal adult Hb but just behind a fresh sample of fetal Hb.

The patient's Hb level and red-blood-cell indices were normal. There was a leucocytosis (18,700 per cmm.) but, apart from a neutrophilia, the stained film showed no abnormality. The reticulocyte-count was 2%, and the direct Coombs test was negative. On a film stained after elution in citric-acid buffer (Kleihauer et al. 1957) however, occasional fetal red blood-cells were seen. The plasma contained free oxyhæmoglobin, and Schuman's test for methæmalbumin was strongly positive.

The patient's blood-group was O Rh positive, and her serum contained anti-A and anti-B at a titre of 1/64. No irregular antibodies were detected by Coombs or enzyme techniques.

She was symptom-free throughout, and her temperature and pulse-rate remained normal. The fetal heart-rate at the onset of the hæmoglobinuria was 160 per minute, but this fell to 140 per minute over the next 2 hours and remained steady. She passed a further specimen of reddish urine containing a trace of Hb 5 hours after the first, but no Hb could be detected in the next specimen the following morning. Very occasional fetal cells could still be detected in blood-films up to 1 week later.

It was clear that a transplacental hæmorrhage had occurred, and although the volume of urine voided was not known accurately, the fetal blood-loss was estimated to be at least 25 ml. It was predicted that the child's blood-group would be A or B, and 4 weeks later this prediction was confirmed when the patient gave birth to a live girl, blood-group A, a low forceps operation being required because of delay in the second stage of labour. The child was rather limp at birth but was rapidly revived and has remained well. 2 days after birth the child's Hb level was 16·3 g. per 100 ml., and the direct Coombs test was negative. At this time the anti-A titre of the mother's serum was 1/64 and a weak α-hæmolysin was present. The placenta showed evidence of a small area of separation.

# Discussion

Levine et al. (1941) were the first to postulate that fetal-maternal hæmorrhage was the cause of Rh sensitisation and hæmolytic disease of the newborn. Cases showing presumptive evidence of fetal-maternal bleeding were subsequently recorded (Wiener 1948, Wickster 1952), but

it was only in 1954 that Chown (1954) described a case of massive transplacental hæmorrhage with clear serological proof of fetal red blood-cells in the mother's bloodstream. Hæmorrhages of this magnitude are probably rare: only one case leading to severe anaemia in the infant has been seen in the past 4 years at this hospital (1800 deliveries a year). Evidence of an incompatibility reaction is rarer still, and although Chown (1954) reported a probable transfusion reaction of this type, I have been unable to trace a record of another case showing hæmoglobinuria.

In contrast, the importance of small leaks from the fetal to the maternal circulation has become increasingly apparent, since a simple method for the detection of fetal red blood-cells in blood-smears has been available (Kleihauer et al. 1957). Several groups of workers have investigated the occurrence of these leaks (Taylor and Kullman 1961, Fraser and Raper 1962, Zippursky et al. 1963a, b, Woodrow et al. 1965), and their relationship to Rh sensitisation is clearly established. Many workers consider that most of the sensitising leaks happen at or about the time of delivery (Woodrow et al. 1965), and the prophylactic use of high titre γ-globulin to prevent sensitisation is based on this assumption. Krieger (1966), however, concluded from a serological study that two-thirds of Rh-sensitised mothers are affected before delivery. The incidence of transplacental hæmorrhage is increased by manoeuvres such as casarean section, manual removal of the placenta, amniocentesis (Zippursky et al. 1963a, b), and forceps delivery (Taylor and Kullman 1961), as well as after accidental hæmorrhage (Fraser and Raper 1962).

Despite these observations little attention seems to have been paid to the possible effects of manipulations performed before delivery, even though the dangers of external cephalic version (particularly under anæsthesia) are well known, and include separation of the placenta (Greenhill 1960). Further work is in progress to determine the incidence of transplacental hæmorrhage after cephalic version. Blood-samples from fourteen patients undergoing external cephalic version without anæsthesia have so far been examined as part of a larger series (Pollock and Chen 1968). In twelve, where blood-samples taken before and after cephalic version were available, no fetal cells were seen in either specimen. In a further two cases only samples taken after cephalic version were available and in one of these specimens, from a patient who had a small accidental hæmorrhage after version, a significant number of fetal cells was seen. Meanwhile, I suggest that the risk should be considered before attempting this manipulation on a Rh-negative patient, particularly since sensitisation at this stage cannot be prevented by injection of γ-globulin, since this might cross the placental barrier and cause hæmolysis of the fetal red blood-cells.

I thank Dr. J. W. Whitelaw and Dr. T. E. Torbet for helpful comment.

# Drug-Induced Hemolysis: Biochemical Considerations\*

NASROLLAH T. SHAHIDI, M.D.

It has been known for many years that certain drugs often referred to as "hemolytic" will cause red cell destruction in some susceptible individuals. Among various biochemical defects which predispose to drug-induced hemolysis, erythrocyte glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G-6-PD) deficiency is by far the most common. It has been estimated that there are at least 100 million individuals with G-6-PD deficiency. While occasionally the drug itself may act as an "oxidant," in most instances, however, the biotransformation products of the "hemolytic" drugs are responsible agents. Major biologic reactions involved in formation of "oxidant" metabolites in vivo are deacetylation of aromatic acetamido compounds, N- or ring-hydroxylation of aryl amines, ring-hydroxylation, and O-dealkylation of phenolic compounds. It is believed that "oxidants" either by autooxidation or through coupled oxidation with oxyhemoglobin generate hydrogen peroxide or free radicals which, if not destroyed by cellular defense mechanisms, will oxidize reduced glutathione, hemoglobin and SH dependent enzymes. These oxidative processes will eventually damage the red cell membrane leading to the leakage of potassium and hemoglobin.

# Introduction

The fact that certain drugs possess hemolytic effects has been known since the end of the last century. The hemolytic activity of phenylhydrazine and acetylphenylhydrazine was first described by Dreschfeld in 1888.¹ Smillie was probably the first to draw attention to the individual susceptibility to the hemolytic effects of drugs.² He reported severe hemolytic anemia in a small percentage of his patients treated with betanaphthol for hookworm. Similar observations have been made following the use of 8-aminophenolone derivatives as antimalarials.³,⁴ These latter observations led to the discovery of an intrinsic abnormality of red cells⁵ and low concentration of reduced glutathione (GSH)⁶ which was later shown to be due to a deficiency of erythrocyte glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G-6-PD).

Among various biochemical defects which predispose to drug-induced hemolysis, erythrocyte G-6-PD deficiency is by far the most common. Other erythrocytic defects such as hemoglobinopathies

DRUG-INDUCED HEMOLYSIS: BIOCHEMICAL CONSIDERATIONS

predisposing to hemolysis by drugs, defective synthesis of GSH, or GSH reductase deficiency are scarce. Abnormal drug biotransformation resulting in excessive formation of oxidant metabolites in vivo, as recently described, is probably also uncommon.

According to a recent WHO report there are more than 100 million persons with G-6-PD deficiency. Since these individuals are potentially susceptible to a variety of commonly used drugs, one is always faced with the possibility of iatrogenic hemolysis. Since the discovery of G-6-PD deficiency a voluminous body of literature has appeared. Most investigations, however, have focused on the quantitative and qualitative aspect of G-6-PD. The nature of hemolytic agents, the biochemical mechanism leading to hemolysis and particularly the interaction of hemolytic drugs, or their biotransformation products, with various G-6-PD mutants, have not been fully explored. The aim of this discussion is to focus attention on these less emphasized or still debated aspects of drug-induced hemolysis.

For a better understanding of the hemolytic action of some of the well-known drugs the first part of this paper will be concerned with the discussion of their biotransformation and the nature of their active ("oxidant") metabolites. The second part will be devoted to the discussion of the effects of these "oxidants" on the red cell, and the mechanism whereby they cause hemolysis.

# I. The Nature of "Oxidants" Derived from Some of the Well-Known Drugs

Most drugs when ingested undergo significant biochemical transformation. The products of biotransformation are not only different chemically, but also pharmacologically from the administered drugs. Among various biochemical reactions involved in the biotransformation of common "hemolytic" drugs deacetylation of aromatic acetamido compounds, N-hydroxylation of aryl amines, ring-hydroxylation of aryl amine and phenolic compounds and O-dealkylation are of particular interest. Table I summarizes some of the well-known drugs and the products of their biotransformation suspected to cause red cell damage. While in most instances these metabolites have been isolated from the urine or blood in man, occasionally conclusions have been drawn from animal studies. Although many of the reactions which drugs undergo in laboratory animals are found to occur in man, the rate of these reactions, however, is often different. Furthermore, not only does man differ from laboratory animals in the rate of biochemical reaction involving drugs, but various groups of people differ from one another in this respect. Consequently, in addition to the nature of toxic metabolites, their concentration in the blood and the rate of their inactivation have to be considered.

11

etanilid and acetophenetidin, the well-known analgesics, have been reported to cause hemolysis in G-6-PD deficient individuals following therapeutic doses. These compounds can also induce hemolysis, although to a lesser degree, in normal subjects when taken in large "toxic doses." Upon ingestion a small part of these drugs is deacetylated in man and in most laboratory animals. Acetanilid which undergoes more extensive deacetylation is far more hemolytic than acetophenetidin. N-acetyl p-aminophenol which is the major metabolite of these compounds undergoes no significant deacetylation and this drug has been found to be innocuous to patients with G-6-PD deficiency. The concentration of deacetylated products depends not only on the rate of deacetylation, but also on the rate of reacetylation. According to Bray and associates, the deacetylase from rabbit liver has significantly higher activity for the ortho-substituted aromatic acetamido compounds than for the para-substituted drugs. While deacetylation remains an important step for the production of "toxic" metabolites, N- or ring-hydroxylation are essential steps. These latter biologic reactions, as most other reactions involving the metabolism of lipid-soluble drugs, are catalyzed by NADPH dependent enzymes in liver microsomes. Thus, aniline and p-phenetidin which are respectively deacetylated products of acetanilid and acetophenetidin, are assumed to undergo both ring- and N-hydroxylation. Phenylhydroxylamine, which is the product of N-hydroxylation of aniline, oxidizes hemoglobin in the presence of oxygen. Nitrosobenzene is the reaction product of phenylhydroxylamine. It has been shown in cats that one mole of phenylhydroxylamine produces up to 50 equivalents of methemoglobin. The mechanism whereby phenylhydroxylamine produces several equivalents of methemoglobin was elucidated by Kiese et al. These investigators showed that in the red cell nitrosobenzene is reduced back to phenylhydroxylamine by electron transfer from NADPH. The reaction is catalyzed by NADPH dependent diaphorase. It should be recalled that the same diaphorase is responsible for the reduction of methylene blue and similar dyes. Indeed, as shown by Lohr and Waller, the rate of methemoglobin formation with nitrobenzene is significantly slower in G-6-PD deficient red cells as compared to normal erythrocytes. The fact that acetanilid, which is partially transformed to phenylhydroxylamine, does cause hemolysis in G-6-PD deficient individuals, suggests that either other biotransformation products of acetanilid are involved or the nitrosobenzene is reduced outside of the red cell. These questions remain unanswered. The role of o-aminophenol in the production of methemoglobinemia has also to be considered. In this respect, it is of interest to note that animals who excrete more o-aminophenol as compared to p-aminophenol are more susceptible to the toxic effect of aniline. From studies by Kiese, however, it seems

that N-hydroxylation plays a more important role in the aniline-induced methemoglobinemia than ring-hydroxylation. Acetophenetidin (phenacetin) differs from acetanilid in that it has an ethoxy group in para position to the aromatic nitrogen. This analgesic is less extensively deacetylated than acetanilid and, as a result, its hemolytic activity is not as great as that of acetanilid.

The possibility of N-hydroxylation of p-phenetidin resulting in the formation of p-ethoxyphenylhydroxylamine and its product of oxidation, nitrosophenetol was investigated by Baader et al who found no relationship between the concentration of blood nitrosophenetol and that of methemoglobin. From their studies they concluded that other metabolites were probably involved in p-phenetidin-induced methemoglobinemia. Recent studies have indicated that ring-hydroxylation of p-phenetidin resulting in the formation of 2-hydroxyphenetidin may play a role in acetophenetidin-induced methemoglobinemia.

Sulfanilamide and its derivatives, which are also known to cause severe hemolysis in G-6-PD deficient individuals, belong to the aniline family and consequently are subject to similar type biotransformation. Except in the dog the main biochemical reaction of sulfanilamide is acetylation. A small portion of this compound undergoes ring-hydroxylation with the formation of 3-hydroxysulfanilamide both in man and in laboratory animals. This compound which is an o-aminophenol could oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin. More recent studies have shown that both rat and human liver microsomes catalyze N-hydroxylation of sulfanilamide in the presence of NADPH and molecular oxygen. It has been further demonstrated that p-hydroxyaminobenzolsulfonamide and its product of oxidation p-nitrososulfanilamide are more potent methemoglobin formers than 3-hydroxysulfanilamide.

Acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), which is one of the most widely used drugs, is known as a mild hemolytic agent in individuals with G-6-PD deficiency even in high doses. However, severe red cell destruction following ingestion of ASA has been reported on several occasions to occur following therapeutic doses of aspirin.

It is known that upon ingestion ASA is rapidly deacetylated and thus converted to salicylic acid. It is obvious as judged by structural formulas that neither ASA nor salicylate are redox compounds. The hemolytic effect of salicylate which will be discussed later is probably partially due to ring-hydroxylation of this compound. Roseman and Dorfman have reported that 3% of a 1.8 gm dose in man is converted to gentisic acid. Higher values, 4 to 8%, have been reported by Kapp and Coburn. The occurrence of traces of other congeners such as 2:3-dihydroxy benzoic and 2:3:5-trihydroxy benzoic acid have also been reported. It has been shown that gentisate can markedly stimulate pentose phosphate pathway.

DRUG-INDUCED HEMOLYSIS: BIOCHEMICAL CONSIDERATIONS

This action has been ascribed to the loss of electrons resulting in the formation of 2-carboxy-1,4-benzoquinone. Our studies have revealed that the incubation of gentisate and hemoglobin as intact red cell, results in the accumulation of methemoglobin accompanied by a drop in GSH (Table II).

Finally, 8-aminoquinoline drugs deserve particular emphasis for not only are they useful as antimalarials, but also because of their historic place in the discovery of biochemical abnormalities of sensitive erythrocytes. Although several reports have indicated that primaquine in vitro can cause red cell damage, there are reasons to believe that the hemolytic effect of primaquine is due to the product of its biotransformation. First of all, in vitro, primaquine is not more deleterious to G-6-PD deficient erythrocytes as compared to normal cells; secondly, it has been found that following ingestion of primaquine, the clinical onset of hemolysis appears two to four days after the ingestion of the initial dose. In addition, during administration of primaquine an anticatalase factor has been demonstrated in the plasma of both normal and G-6-PD deficient individuals. This anticatalase activity, which could not be demonstrated in the plasma until four to six hours after drug administration, reached a maximum in eight hours and was maintained for at least another 16 hours. From the study of Zubrod and associates it seems that the highest plasma concentration of undergraded drug is reached in six hours and thereafter it falls rapidly and is barely detectable after 24 hours. The first step in the biotransformation of primaquine is the O-dealkylation of 6-methoxy group followed by hydroxylation at 5 position on the quinoline ring. Josephson and associates have identified 5, 6 quinoline-quinone derivative which is thought to be the active metabolite. Quinoline-quinone derivatives are redox compounds and capable of

## II. The Mechanism of Action of "Hemolytic" Drugs or Their Biotransformation on Red Cells

There is now ample evidence to suggest that redox compounds either by autooxidation or coupled oxidation with oxyhemoglobin result in the formation of hydrogen peroxide or free radicals. The involvement of radicals or hydrogen peroxide in the formation of methemoglobin by redox compounds in the presence of oxygen has been considered since 1878 by Hoppe-Seyler. The formation of H₂O₂ by phenylhydroxylamine in the presence of oxyhemoglobin was demonstrated by Rostorfer and Cormier. That free radicals may also appear in the reaction of phenylhydroxylamine was suggested by paramagnetic resonance absorption studies by Wahler and associates. Using irreversible inhibition of catalase by 3-amino-1, 2, 4-triazole as an indicator of hydrogen peroxide, Cohen and Hochstein have shown that hydrogen peroxide is produced by a variety of "oxidants." However, some hemolytic compounds such as acetylphenylhydrazine seem to possess both properties, namely, to generate hydrogen peroxide and to catalyze directly the interaction between NADPH and oxygen.

The free radical or hydrogen peroxide do not attack hemoglobin or other red cell constituents in the same fashion. For instance, while coupled oxidation of oxyhemoglobin and ascorbic acid or phenylhydrazine produces methemoglobin, but also a significant amount of sulfhemoglobin (denatured hemoglobin), the coupled oxidation of aminophenols or phenylhydroxylamine with oxyhemoglobin produces methemoglobin and no noticeable amounts of sulfhemoglobin. No ready explanation for these findings is presently available.

It has been shown that reduced glutathione is oxidized more rapidly than hemoglobin when red cells are exposed to a variety of oxidant compounds. Methemoglobin and sulfhemoglobin appear only after depletion of GSH.

The mechanism whereby "oxidant" agents cause hemolysis in vitro or in vivo remains unknown. It is obvious that there is no direct relationship between methemoglobinemia and hemolysis. Methemoglobinemia may be present in drug-induced red cell damage in high concentration in normal individuals in whom little or no hemolysis occurs. On the other hand, if the methemoglobin-containing cell is rapidly destroyed, such as in G-6-PD deficient individuals, methemoglobinemia is absent or only moderate. The

From various investigations it is apparent that hemolysis of red cells is more related to erythrocyte GSH.⁴¹ It is now well established that this compound which is present in high concentration in red cells is maintained in the reduced form through the action of glutathione reductase which is a NADPH dependent enzyme.

It has been proposed⁴² that H₂O₂ generated at low concentration within the red cells is detoxified mainly by glutathione peroxidase. This enzyme which was described by Mills⁴³ is GSH dependent. Inadequate regeneration of GSH as in G-6-PD deficiency would curtail the activity of this enzyme and would result in the accumulation of hydrogen peroxide. However, the role of catalase in the detoxification of hydrogen peroxide has also been emphasized.⁴⁴ A recent report by Paniker and Iyer⁴⁵ suggests that both catalase and glutathione peroxidase are involved in the detoxification of hydrogen peroxide produced by diffusion technic. Recent studies have shown that disappearance of intracellular GSH, as caused by N-ethylmaleimide, does not result in appreciable hemolysis in vitro.⁴⁶,⁴⁷ In addition, G-6-PD deficient red cells may rapidly become GSH depleted when incubated with acetylphenylhydrazine or related compounds,⁴⁸ and yet they are not more sensitive to hemolysis than normal cells similarly treated.⁴⁹,⁵⁰ Using various sulfhydryl inhibitors Jacob and Jandl⁵¹ have shown that blockade of the membrane SH group of red cells results in their rapid trapping in the spleen. Weed and associates⁵² have shown that low concentration of oxidant compounds causes membrane injury as evidenced by leakage of potassium and entry of sodium. Another important factor in drug-induced hemolysis is enzyme inhibition or inactivation by hemolytic drugs or products of their biotransformation. The oxidant drugs can exert their damaging effect on enzymes through various mechanisms. The oxidation of Fe++ in iron-containing enzyme such as catalase is to be expected. Indeed, it has been observed⁵³ that the activity of catalase decreases markedly in G-6-PD deficient individuals as early as 24 hours after the initial dose of primaquine. It has been shown that some redox compounds in low concentration inhibit catalase.⁵⁴ Inactivation of SH dependent enzymes by SH oxidation is another possible mechanism. It has been suggested⁵⁵ that oxidative destruction of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GA-3-PD), an SH dependent enzyme, may play a role in the mechanism of drug-induced hemolysis. Powell et al.⁵⁶ however, could not demonstrate a drop in GA-3-PD during primaquine-induced hemolysis in sensitive subjects. Studies by Kosower and associates⁵⁷ indicate that a decline in the concentration of GSH

following incubation of red cells with acetylphenylhydrazine is not associated with a decrease in the activity of GA-3-PD. However, a decrease in the activity of GA-3-PD as induced by N-ethylmaleimide may occur in the terminal stage where the cellular GSH has completely disappeared. There has been more agreement on the inhibition of hexokinase by "hemolytic" agents such as phenylhydrazine.⁵⁸,⁵⁹ Mohler and Williams⁶⁰ have shown that the ATP content of G-6-PD deficient red cells incubated in vitro with phenylhydrazine decreases more markedly than in normal red cells incubated under the same conditions.

Finally, another mechanism affecting the enzyme system of red cells is the direct inhibition of certain red cell enzymes by hemolytic drugs. It has been known for many years that atabrine and quinine,⁶¹ as well as sulfanilamide,⁶² inhibit G-6-PD. Nitrofurantoin has been shown to inhibit glutathione reductase.⁶³ The inhibitory effect of several drugs known to induce hemolysis in G-6-PD deficient subjects has been investigated by Desforges and associates⁶⁴ on yeast G-6-PD and 6-phosphogluconic dehydrogenase. These investigators found that these two NADPH dependent dehydrogenases were inhibited by most common hemolytic agents. Data on the inhibitory effects of drugs on various mutants of G-6-PD are not available. Such studies may explain individual variation in response to the same drug. Our own interest in this aspect of drug hemolysis began with the study of a nine-year-old boy with G-6-PD deficiency associated with congenital nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia. The patient, as previously reported by Westring and Pisciotta,⁶⁵ developed severe intravascular hemolysis following therapeutic doses of aspirin on several occasions. Although it has been repeatedly emphasized that salicylates are mild hemolytic agents in patients with G-6-PD deficiency even in high dosage, the review of the literature revealed that acute red cell destruction following ASA ingestion has been reported.⁶⁶⁻⁶⁸

Since salicylate itself is not a redox compound and has no oxidative properties on hemoglobin it was thought that a metabolite of salicylate, probably gentisic acid, was the hemolytic agent. On this basis the red cells from this nine-year-old patient were tagged with ⁵¹Cr and transfused into a normal compatible individual who then received 75 mg/day of gentisic acid. This resulted in no noticeable change in the ⁵¹Cr ½ T. However, when 150 mg of gentisic acid were given, which is approximately equivalent to 3 gm of salicylate, the chromium ½ T was reduced by 50%. Further increase in the dosage of gentisic acid resulted in further decrease in red cell survival. The survival of the red cells of two other patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (A type) known to have taken salicylates without side effects was not effected even with doses of gentisic acid as high as 450 mg. ## Discussion

TIMOS VALAES asked why small children are much more sensitive to drug-induced hemolysis than older adults with the same kind of defect. SHAHIDI replied that the drug may be present in higher concentrations in children because of differences in the metabolism or handling of the drug.

SUMNER YAFEE raised the question whether gentisic acid itself would cause hemolysis and pointed out that in normal subjects, the rate of formation of gentisic acid constitutes less than 1% of all metabolites formed by salicylates. SHAHIDI replied that gentisic acid did not cause hemolysis in normal subjects indicating that only in this patient is the red cell metabolism different. According to various investigations it seems that 3 to 8% of therapeutic doses of salicylate are converted to gentisic acid.

RUDI SCHMID commented on the fact that there is increasing evidence that hemoglobin is destroyed by the oxidative processes such as hydrogen peroxide or other oxidizing agents, and this hemoglobin is no longer related to bilirubin. He pointed out that when Heinz bodies or heme exposed to phenylhydrazine is given to the animal, it is not converted to bilirubin but is excreted in the form of other labeled metabolites which are different from bilirubin.

TIMOS VALAES mentioned that all newborn infants with Heinz body formation also showed extreme jaundice. SCHMID agreed with this and explained that in every case of Heinz body hemolytic anemia, there is a vast overproduction of bile pigment, but emphasized that it has not been possible to show a quantitative relationship between the anemia and the jaundice.

AUDREY BROWN asked whether the Heinz bodies are unstable in drug-induced anemia. SCHMID did not know, but said that if you take Heinz bodies produced in vitro and inject them into animals as in experimental protoporphyrin, the heme is to a large extent not recovered as bilirubin or CO₂, but comes out in bile in the form of other labeled breakdown products. SYDNEY GELLIS asked how you make Heinz bodies. SCHMID described the method published by Jandl where you take a hemoglobin solution and expose it to phenylhydrazine in the presence of air, and get a precipitating material from which you can spin off Heinz bodies. BROWN pointed out that red cells of newborn infants uniformly act like G-6-PD deficiency red cells in forming Heinz bodies. SCHMID said that red cells in the newborn and particularly in the premature are sensitive to many of these drugs and cited a report where a baby was rubbed with camphor in the chest for respiratory distress and came down with a massive nasopharyngic hemolytic anemia. ROGER LESTER asked why the Heinz bodies do not get converted to bilirubin. SCHMID replied that when heme is attacked by hydrogen peroxide and other oxidative reductive compounds, there is no longer a substrate for heme oxygenase and this leads to a different pathway for metabolism.

## Aspirin and the Newborn

Obstetricians might do well to warn their patients that they should not take aspirin products for early labor pains, a study at the University of Alabama Medical Center suggests. Salicylate was found in the cord serum from 9.5% of 272 neonates tested, but most of the mothers were not aware that products they had taken contained aspirin. In normal infants, transitory salicylate toxicity probably has very little effect, says Dr. Paul Palmisano. But he adds that it could be harmful to those threatened by hyperbilirubinemia. One infant had a serum salicylate level of 10.9 mg%. Dr. Palmisano notes that this level ties up 0.35 mg% of the infant's serum albumin, which appears to play a role in averting jaundice in the newborn.

# Curb hexachlorophene in the nursery?

In an action disputed by many clinicians, FDA early this month advised the nation's doctors (via its Drug Bulletin) to discontinue using 3%-or-more hexachlorophene (HCP) products for total-body bathing of infants, and to have those in the nursery wash their hands "scrupulously" before and after handling each infant. The Bulletin noted that with the concurrence of the American Academy of Pediatrics "we recommend dry skin care or washing with plain soap and water or tap water alone for infant care."

FDA also proposed that the makers (Winthrop produces the most widely used cleanser, pHisoHex) be required to warn users on the label: "Do not use for total body bathing," and "rinse thoroughly after use." The safety action was based on a Winthrop study in which rhesus monkeys scrubbed with pHisoHex daily for three months were shown to have lesions in the cerebellum and brain-stem and accompanying HCP plasma levels of 2.3 µg/ml, not much higher than levels found in neonates discharged from hospital.

The agency challenged HCP efficacy, too, declaring that (based on NAS review findings) "whereas there is no doubt that HCP bathing decreases skin coloniza-

tion of gram-positive organisms, there is a lack of substantial evidence that HCP washings by themselves will prevent staphylococcal disease. . . ."

Winthrop had 30 days to protest the FDA labeling proposal. A spokesman pointed out that "our researchers scrubbed five to ten times as much pHisoHex into the monkeys' skin for 90 days instead of the three to six days a baby would receive it; and there wasn't the slightest sign of neurotoxicity in the monkeys at sacrifice. These findings must be balanced against 22 years of pHisoHex use on millions of babies without a single recorded case of neurotoxicity when used as directed."

Dr. Louis Gluck, professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Diego, whose studies at Yale in the early 1960s helped establish the safety and effectiveness of pHisoHex, called the FDA action "abominable." He added: "The agency doesn't have the hard data to justify its precipitate action, which risks an epidemic of Staphylococcus in nurseries. The simian lesion has never been observed in babies. At this point, the average practitioner doesn't know what to do."

# Hexachlorophene and "Skin Protection" in the Newborn

By now most pediatricians have heard that not only the safety but even the need for hexachlorophene for routine bathing of infants is being questioned by the FDA and other regulatory agencies. From their review of published studies, a Committee of the American Academy of Pediatrics has placed a number of general principles on record:

1. The levels of hexachlorophene which may be attained in the blood of newborn infants receiving daily baths with a three per cent solution are close to levels which are neurotoxic for adult rats. Similar brain lesions have been produced in monkeys by applying hexachlorophene to the skin in high doses.
2. "At this time there is little microbiologic justification for routine, daily hexachlorophene baths for newborn infants. . . . There is no documented experience where this technic has arrested a serious nursery epidemic. . . . The use of hexachlorophene increases colonization with gram-negative organisms and the incidence of gram-negative disease."
3. "For reasons that have not been defined, the problem of serious staphylococcal disease in nurseries has not been of major importance during the last five years, as

it was ten to 15 years ago." This epidemiologic subsidence has been unrelated to whether hexachlorophene was used for the skin care of the newborn infants.

4. Because of these considerations, "The safety of daily bathing of infants with hexachlorophene-containing solutions has not been established. . . . The use of hexachlorophene for total body bathing of newborn infants in hospital nurseries or at home is contraindicated."
5. At present the Committee on Fetus and Newborn recommends dry skin care for the newborn infant. Washing when needed should be with tap water, either alone or with plain nonmedicated soap.
6. "The two most important factors in the transmission of infection from infant to infant are hand contact and breaks in technic. These factors can be minimized by scrupulous hand washing before entering the nursery as well as just before and just after handling each infant. Either iodophor preparations or a three per cent hexachlorophene emulsion are recommended for hand washing."—Condensed from a "Statement" of the Committee on Fetus and Newborn, American Academy of Pediatrics, 1972.

WILLIAM M. MARINE, M.D., M.P.H.\*

Berkeley, California, and Atlanta, Georgia

Newborn health indices were measured before, during, and after a demonstration
nurse-midwife program introduced to relieve a health manpower shortage at a
county hospital in rural California. During the program, prenatal care increased,
and prematurity and neonatal mortality rate decreased as the county hospital.
After the 3 year program, prenatal care decreased while prematurity rose from
6.6 to 9.8 per cent (p < 0.02) and neonatal mortality rate rose from 10.3 to 32.1
per 1,000 live births (p < 0.005). No significant changes occurred in the same
indices for births elsewhere in the county throughout the period of study. It is
concluded that the discontinuation of the nurse-midwives' services was the major
factor in these changes, and it is suggested that nurse-midwives be used more
extensively.

MORE INFANTS die in the United
States than older people with diabetes, breast
cancer, and tuberculosis combined.¹ In 1968,
when our infant mortality rate was 21.7 per
1,000 live births, over 75,000 American-born
infants died during their first year of life.²
Our rank among 7 "advanced" countries
in infant deaths has declined from fourth to
seventh since 1950.³

About two thirds of infant deaths in the
United States occur during the first month
of life.⁴ Since most of those first-month, or
neonatal, deaths are associated with pre-
maturity, significant reduction in neonatal
mortality rate depends on reduced pre-
maturity.⁵

It has been demonstrated that prematurity
(and in turn neonatal deaths) can be re-
duced by providing prenatal care to more
pregnant women. Although 12 visits are
generally recommended,⁶,⁷ studies have
shown that infants whose mothers have had
any prenatal care have a lower risk of being
premature⁸,⁹ and, hence, a lower risk of
dying during the first month of life. In addi-
tion to more prenatal care, another way of
reducing neonatal deaths may be with im-
proved care during labor and delivery, and
during the infant's first few days of life.

Reducing neonatal deaths with nurse-midwives 51

These objectives of improved and more extensive care might be easily achieved were it not for the shortage and maldistribution of physicians in maternal and infant care in the United States. With the available physician manpower and the predicted increase in American births, Hellman recently estimated that by 1980 about half of all deliveries in this country would be on the ward services of hospitals without assignable physicians.¹⁰ This shortage in manpower for deliveries reflects similar shortages for prenatal and postnatal care.

One proposed solution to these shortages is the more extensive use of nurse-midwives, or nurse obstetric assistants (NOA's) as they are sometimes called. A nurse-midwife is a registered nurse who has had additional formal training (from 6 to 24 months) in maternal and infant care so that she can manage normal pregnancies. Nurse-midwives are never independent practitioners; they always function within the framework of a physician-directed health service. With NOA's managing normal pregnancies, physicians can concentrate on the few abnormal pregnancies.

The effectiveness of nurse-midwives in reducing infant mortality has been demonstrated abroad, and in the U. S. by the Frontier Nursing Service in Kentucky since 1935.¹¹ With few states allowing nurse-midwives to practice, however, few opportunities were available to test further the feasibility and the potential benefits of nurse-midwives. Such an opportunity became available from 1960 to 1963 with the nurse obstetric assistant (NOA) program at Madera County Hospital in California.

The Madera County NOA Program. This program was established in response to critical problems at the county hospital in the late 1950's. Serving mainly the medically indigent in a poor agricultural county of about 40,000, the 148 bed hospital was plagued with serious physician and nurse shortages. The full-time staff had been ranging from two to five general practitioners. There were no Board-certified specialists in any field in the entire county. More than

half of the pregnant women received late prenatal care or none at all, and it was estimated (but not documented) that about one fifth of the 400 annual deliveries there were not attended by physicians. The prematurity and neonatal mortality rates were much higher than at the two other hospitals in the county.¹²

Attempting to solve these problems, the Health Department established a 3 year, \$68,400, demonstration nurse-midwife (NOA) program with special legal permission from the State for the nurse-midwives to perform normal deliveries. From July, 1960, through June, 1963, two nurse-midwives managed most normal pregnancies, from prenatal care to labor and delivery, and the care of mothers and infants after delivery. But beyond "routine" care, they overcame many cultural and educational barriers to motivate many more women to seek prenatal care. When a woman first came to the prenatal clinic, she was examined by a physician. If no abnormality were found, she was then assigned to a nurse-midwife for the remainder of her pregnancy. By the middle of the program, the two nurse-midwives were managing the vast majority of the pregnancies and performing 78 per cent of the hospital deliveries. They were assisted by hospital staff physicians, who managed complications as they developed, and by obstetricians and pediatricians from a neighboring county who consulted for a total of a half-day, on the average, each week. At the end of the 3 years, the program was initially evaluated. Significant improvements during the program included: (1) more prenatal care given more frequently to a larger proportion of expectant mothers; (2) a greater proportion of mothers returned for routine 6 week postpartum examinations; (3) a decrease in the prematurity rate (based on a birth weight of 5½ pounds or less); and most importantly, (4) a decrease in neonatal mortality.¹³

Despite these improvements, the program was not continued beyond its initial 3 year demonstration period. The Council of the California Medical Association refused to

support a permanent change in the State law which would have permitted nurse-midwives to practice as they had during the program. Soon after the program, there were indications that the situation had deteriorated with the neonatal mortality rate for all births in the county increasing from 17.6 (per 1,000 live births) in 1963 to 30.0 in 1964, the first full year after the program.¹³

This retrospective study (performed in 1968) was done to determine whether the situation had, in fact, grown worse after the discontinuation of the program. It is a second evaluation of the NOA program, comparing parameters of medical care and infant health and deaths, during and after the program. The discontinuation of a medical care program that was thought to be beneficial is a rare occurrence in American medicine, and thus offers an unusual opportunity for critical examination of possible cause-and-effect relationships.

# Materials and methods

Two studies were done comparing parameters during and after the program: (1) a County Records Study, comparing data abstracted mainly from birth and death certificates for January, 1961, through June, 1962 (during) and 1965 (after), and (2) a Vital Statistics Records Study comparing data abstracted mainly from state birth and death records for January, 1961, through June, 1963 (during) and January, 1964, through June, 1966 (after). There was a high correlation between data of the two studies and between data from different sources, such as birth certificates and hospital charts.

County records study. Data gathered in the initial earlier evaluation (before vs. during) of the program for January, 1961-June, 1962 (during) was used along with data we gathered, using the same methods of data collection, for the 1965 (after) period. From all county certificates of live birth and fetal death, data were abstracted on mothers' obstetric histories and demographic characteristics and infants' birth weights (with prematurity defined on the basis of a birth weight of 5½ pounds or less).

We did not use the increasingly accepted definition of prematurity based on weeks of gestation because this information was missing from many birth certificates.

All infant deaths of infants born in Madera County in the "during" and "after" periods were recorded. Infant deaths were traced by Bureau of Vital Statistics records and the California Death Index. Each infant death was matched with its birth certificate to confirm it as a Madera County birth. Because of the relative stability of the county population and our efforts to determine if infants born in the county to noncounty residents died anywhere in the state, we felt that few, if any, infant deaths were missed.

For all Madera County Hospital live births and fetal deaths, data on prenatal and postpartum care were abstracted from mothers' hospital charts. The 60 per cent of county births not occurring at the county hospital were grouped together under the category "other." (Only 2.5 per cent of these did not occur in hospitals.)

Public health nurse records were used to determine how many of the mothers had postpartum home visits.

Vital statistics records study. From state Bureau of Vital Statistics records, data were accumulated for live births and fetal deaths for January, 1961-June, 1963 (during) and January, 1964-June, 1966 (after). Infant deaths were determined as in the county records study. This study provided data for longer time periods, but in slightly less detail, than did the county records study.

Other data. County welfare department personnel were interviewed regarding eligibility requirements for county hospital clinics. Information was obtained, from public health nurse files, on the number of mothers attending the county hospital prenatal clinic. The number of county hospital outpatient clinic visits, inpatient days, and average daily census, and number and turnover of hospital physicians were obtained from the hospital administrator.

show that the prematurity and neonatal mortality rates of county hospital births increased significantly after the program. The prematurity rate increased by almost 50 per cent, and the neonatal mortality rate more than tripled.

There were no significant changes in the fetal mortality rate (based on stillbirths after the twentieth week of gestation), in the total infant mortality rate, nor in the postneonatal mortality rate (based on deaths from the end of the first month to the end of the first year of life).

While the prematurity and neonatal mortality rates increased among county hospital births after the program, there was no significant change in any of the mortality or prematurity rates among infants born elsewhere in the county, as shown in Table I (B).

Analysis of county records study data (1965) showed that premature infants had more than a tenfold greater chance of dying during the first year of life than mature infants; of the premature infants, 16.4 per cent died during the first year of life; of the mature ones, only 1.4 per cent died.

Prenatal care.

Over-all use of county hospital clinic. When the program became fully operational

in late 1960, there was a large increase in the number of expectant mothers attending the prenatal clinic (Fig. 1). In 1961, total visits reached an annual peak of 1,905, compared with 1,231 in 1959. The ratio of prenatal clinic visits to total births rose significantly, from 3.57 in 1959 to 4.62 in 1961. Visits reached a quarter peak of 560 in July-September, 1961. In January, 1961-June, 1963 (during), the average number of visits for women receiving prenatal care was 4.5; in January, 1964-June, 1966 (after), it fell significantly to 3.6.

After the program, the number of visits dropped sharply, even below preprogram levels. At the same time that there was an abrupt decrease in the number of prenatal clinic visits at the county hospital in mid-1963, there was a 27 per cent decline in total outpatient clinic visits. In February and May, 1963, eligibility criteria for the use of county hospital outpatient clinics (including the prenatal clinic) were made stricter. No detailed written information is available to document these changes, but a welfare department employee, who was involved in determining eligibility before and after these changes, observed in an interview that these changes had a great effect on reducing clinic utilization. She also stated that there were

Postpartum care. The increased amount of postpartum care brought about by improved coordination through public health nurse home visits during the program was maintained afterward. No objective data could be obtained to indicate amount of postnatal care to infants.

Changes in Madera County population and health care resources. The total population of the county and its composition were relatively stable. The county hospital maternity population was also stable, with a higher percentage of Mexican-American and Negro mothers, mothers under the age of 20, and fathers employed in farm labor, as compared with the population delivering elsewhere in the county. There were no significant changes in the characteristics of the county hospital maternal population after the program. However, while the overall county births decreased by 15 per cent after the program, the number of births decreased by 23 per cent at the county hospital and only by 10 per cent elsewhere in the county.

The physician population in the county was also quite stable, increasing only from 20 to 25 from 1958 to 1965, and then decreasing to 23 in 1967, with the vast majority still being general practitioners. In 1958, only one physician did specialty work in obstetrics and gynecology; in 1961 and 1963, there were no physicians practicing this specialty; and in 1965 and 1967, one physician did specialty work in both surgery and obstetrics.

At the county hospital, the average number of full-time staff physicians per year went from a low of 2.9 in 1959 to a high of 5.1 in 1962. The hospital had no interns or residents. The number of staff physicians was approximately the same during and after the program. The inpatient to physician ratio during the program was 23.2, and decreased to 16.9 after.

# Comment

Significant increases in neonatal mortality rate and prematurity among county hospital births occurred after the discontinuation of

the NOA program (Table I, A). There were no significant changes among the other indices for county hospital births, although there was a trend of an increased postneonatal mortality rate during the program and a decreased postneonatal mortality rate after it.

Since this was a retrospective study with many uncontrolled variables, we investigated several possible explanations for the increased neonatal mortality and prematurity rates after the program.

First, we found no unusual events, such as nursery epidemics or an increased multiple-birth rate, to account for these increased rates. In addition, there was no countywide trend of increased prematurity and neonatal deaths since these rates did not change among infants born elsewhere in the county (Table I, B).

Second, there was no significant change in the number or types of doctors on the county hospital staff nor in the entire county after the program to account for these increased rates.

Third, we noted that the total births at the county hospital declined by 23 per cent after the program while the total births elsewhere in the county only declined by 10 per cent. This raises the possibility that some low-risk mothers who were delivered normally at the county hospital went elsewhere to be delivered after the program, possibly as a result of the stricter eligibility criteria then. Such a shift would have left a higher percentage of high-risk mothers at the county hospital, possibly accounting for these increased rates. No evidence among data gathered on the maternal population during and after the program, however, indicated such a shift. But even if one were to assume that such a shift occurred, it alone cannot reasonably account for the increased rates: there are still significant increases when one extrapolates a uniform decrease in birth rates after the program for both the county hospital and elsewhere in the county.

While prematurity and neonatal mortality rates increased among county hospital births after the program, prenatal care for mothers being delivered there decreased. Twice

as many women received no known prenatal care after the program and far fewer women made six or more visits (Tables II and III). Part of this decrease in prenatal care may have been due to the stricter eligibility criteria.

The prenatal care of one identifiable group of mothers at high risk, those having previous fetal deaths, reflected the over-all decrease in prenatal care. This suggests that the decrease in prenatal care, which affected the county hospital maternity population in general, also affected those with high-risk pregnancies.

Pooled data on all county births for 5 years (Table IV) indicate the lower risk of fetal deaths and prematurity among women receiving any prenatal care, and further corroborate studies by others.¹,⁸,³⁴ The value of prenatal care per se, then, is clearly established. However, the relation of the content and quality of prenatal care and of care during and after delivery to prematurity and death is another matter.

Indirectly we measured this content and quality of care during pregnancy and after delivery by calculating the neonatal mortality rates for infants whose mothers had about the same amount of care during and after the program. As seen in Table V, the neonatal mortality rates of infants whose mothers began prenatal care in the first two trimesters (who received about the same amount of care) was almost four times greater after the program than during it. This suggests that the quality of care, both prenatal care and care during and after delivery, was lower after the program. Table V also indicates that the neonatal mortality rate of infants whose mothers had no prenatal care at all (only care during and after delivery) almost doubled after the program. Since the amount of care for all these infants was about the same, this increased trend suggests that the quality of care during

and after delivery was lower after the program.

We found then that there were significantly higher prematurity and neonatal mortality rates, significantly less prenatal care, and probably a lower quality of maternal and infant care for births occurring at the county hospital after the discontinuation of the nurse-midwife program. We believe that the discontinuation of the nurse-midwife program created new manpower shortages in the prenatal clinic, on the maternity ward, and in the newborn nursery. These manpower shortages, it appears, brought about both lower quantity and probably lower quality of care for mothers and infants. And, finding no other reasonable explanations, we conclude that this lower quantity and probably lower quality of care were the main causes of the increased prematurity and neonatal mortality after the program.

As Hellman recently predicted, the physician shortage in maternal and infant care is likely to grow much worse in the next decade unless appropriate steps are taken. Currently, only six states and New York City in this country permit nurse-midwives to practice. On the basis of our study, we recommend that similar nurse-midwife (or NOA) programs be set up elsewhere, at least on a trial basis, especially where there are critical physician shortages and high prematurity and neonatal mortality rates.

AMSTERDAM...Although 70% of babies born in the Netherlands are delivered at home by GPs and midwives, the Dutch can boast one of the lowest

---

infant mortality rates in the world. A report by the U.S. National Center for Health Statistics shows that Holland has reduced infant mortality by one half in each of three periods--1900 to 1922, 1923 to 1939, and 1948 to 1964. In 1930 infant mortality was 50 per 1,000 live births and by 1964 it had been reduced to 15.

The country's low infant death rates, as compared with those in the U.S., England, and Wales, reflect Holland's long tradition of basic infant care in the family, aided by district nurses and supported by social security measures and a rising standard of living, the report observes.

Another study, which deals specifically with midwifery in the Netherlands, notes that a maternity aide assists in most home deliveries. The aide stays in the home for ten days after the infant is born, acting as a nurse and also doing the cooking and laundry.

# U.S. professor says

TORONTO DAILY STAR

76 Wed., Oct. 15, 1967

# Nurses could do all deliveries

Special to The Star

CHICAGO—A Harvard professor of medicine says nurse-midwives could take over most of the child deliveries in the United States and free scarce physicians for other duties.

The system operates in Sweden, where the infant mortality rate is far lower than in this country, said Dr. David D. Rutstein.

In Sweden, the trained midwife follows the patient through pregnancy, reports untoward events to the physician and enables him to follow the patient more closely than the unaided doctor in the United States, he said.

"At term, if the pregnancy has been normal, the nurse-midwife, working under the supervision of the physician, is in attendance on the patient from the moment she arrives in labor until she is delivered," Rutstein pointed out.

"In contrast, when one walks into the labor room of an American hospital, one finds the inexperienced husband

rather than the trained midwife holding the hand of the patient."

Because of the midwife's ability to perform normal delivery, it is unnecessary to schedule these in Sweden "as busy American physicians are forced to do," said Rutstein, adding:

"As a result, in normal deliveries in Sweden, membranes are rarely ruptured, drugs to induce labor are infrequently prescribed, instruments are less commonly used and there are fewer surgical interventions.

"It is not surprising for Sweden to have a lower infant mortality rate than the United States."

In a book, "The Coming Revolution In Medicine," published yesterday by the Mit Press, Rutstein said that in view of our unsatisfactory infant mortality rate," it is necessary to study Sweden's system and those in all other western countries where the nurse-midwifery system operates.

# Air pollution 'unseen killer' of infants

By BETTY LOU LEE
Spectator Staff

TORONTO — Sudden unexplained deaths of infants — so-called crib deaths — and some forms of mental retardation in children may be linked to various air pollutants, a Chicago chest specialist said yesterday.

Dr. Bertram W. Carnow, director of the Environmental Health Resource Centre and professor of occupational and environmental medicine at the University of Illinois, has spent more than five years directing research into the effects of air pollutants on human health.

In a retrospective study of 1,600 infants who died suddenly in their beds during the past four years in Chicago, Dr. Carnow found that there was a "very significant correlation" between the time that they died and the amount of sulphur dioxide in the air in their neighborhood.

"WE THINK they die of severe respiratory infection, probably viral, that pollution aggravates. Infants are at high risk. They have a limited ability to resist a hostile environment, and the pollution may be the added insult that killed them."

Checks of the post-mortem findings on the babies on whom autopsies were done showed that most of them had problems in

their windpipes and bronchial tubes, and some had pneumonia.

"One of the biggest problems is that air pollution affects children more than other people, and they have nothing to say about it," Dr. Carnow said at a press conference.

He was able to correlate the deaths with air pollution because of a sophisticated pollution information system that has recorded the differing levels of sulphur dioxide and particulate matter in each square mile of the city for every 15 minutes of a day.

HE ALSO believes that many children in Chicago are mentally retarded because

of a combination of malnutrition and lead pollution of the air.

He became particularly concerned when he found that his own four-year-old daughter had an almost toxic level of lead in her blood, that decreased when she stopped playing outdoors.

Dr. Carnow said a lot of publicity has been given to lead poisoning in children from eating lead-based paint, or food stored in some types of pottery. But lead in the air, particularly from automobile exhaust, may be more hazardous. When lead is eaten, he said, the body absorbs only about five per cent of it. It gets into the

(Continued on Page 3)

# Pollution — straw that broke infant health

Continued from Page 1)

circulation only after going through the liver, where much of it can be detoxified.

But inhaling it from the air, 60 per cent is absorbed. It gets directly into the blood stream from the lungs, when the blood exchanges carbon dioxide for oxygen.

BECAUSE LEAD particles inhaled are small, they also tend to stay deep in the lungs.

Dr. Carnow said traffic policemen and gas station attendants have been found to have high blood levels of lead, and he has applied for a research grant to study any correlations between retardation and blood lead levels in children. He thinks children whose homes are along expressways and other major traffic arteries may be particularly susceptible.

Another study done at his centre has linked lung cancer to air pollution. It has been known for some time that there is a higher rate of lung cancer in cities than the country, but his centre analysed all the air pollution and lung cancer statistics from studies in 48 states and 20 countries. They found that a similar conclusion could be drawn from them all.

FOR EVERY microgram of benzopyrene in 1,000 cubic meters of air, there is a five per cent increase in the incidence of lung cancer. Benzopyrene is an aromatic hydrocarbon, a byproduct of combustion of fossil fuels, including gasoline. It is known to produce cancer in experimental animals.

"If we could reduce air pollution by 30 per cent we could reduce lung cancer by 20 per cent," said Mr. Carnow. "This doesn't

negate the importance of smoking — probably accounts for the other 60 per cent.

"But these things act synergistically (each one enhances the action of the other). The smoker who lives in a city and works in an asbestos factory — the poor devil doesn't have a chance. His chance of getting lung cancer is 90 times that of someone who has none of these factors."

THE CHICAGO group also has a study of hospital admissions related to air pollution under way, but some preliminary figures show that heart and lung problems aren't the only things aggravated by a high pollution index.

At Cook County Hospital, primarily a charity hospital where people have to sit for hours in the emergency department to be seen, there has been an unusual incin-

ence of intense headaches during high pollution episodes. These pains are so severe the patients are willing to wait to be seen by a doctor.

Another hospital reports an increase in patients with epileptic attacks during high pollution.

And Dr. Carnow says the emphasis on air pollution research has uncovered some possibly dangerous industrial standards.

"There has been a realization that industrial workers are subjected to tremendous levels of pollution."

Dr. Carnow was brought to Toronto by the York-Toronto TB and Respiratory Disease Association and the University of Toronto. He gave both a medical seminar and a public address yesterday.

THE SPECTATOR, Hamilton, Canada, February 5, 1972 pp 143

28 The Spectator Monday, October 26, 1970

# MD invents delivery chair

BUENOS AIRES (AP) — Childbirth should not be taken lying down, an Argentine doctor says. He advocates a natural vertical position which he says people used before doctors introduced the "modern torture" of the delivery table.

Dr. Tucho Perrini, honored by the Argentine Medical Association for his studies, has invented a special chair for delivering babies.

"Look at the ease with which mothers give birth in taxis and trains, without assistance of any kind," he says.

"The seated or squatting position obviously plays a decisive role in the ease and speed of birth."

A biologist who later obtained a medical degree, the 52-year-old general practitioner says women in so-called primitive societies still deliver in a vertical position.

When physicians interfered in this heretofore private act about 200 years ago, Perussi claims, they placed the mother on a table as a matter of convenience and their own pride.

"Of course, it was easier for the doctor to work. And physicians could not be seen in such a humble position, on their knees, in front of the patient."

Perussi's device, resembling a dentist's chair permits the obstetrician to stand

while delivering the baby.

A study of 3,520 babies, half of them delivered in Perussi's chairs and half on the conventional table, indicated that chair-delivered infants had a better record of blood pres-

sure, temperature, pulse and other physiological signs.

The chair assists the mother in pushing out the child and she does not need the physician's help in expelling the placenta, Perussi says.
