# BRITISH MEDICAL JOURNAL

LONDON SATURDAY 9 NOVEMBER 1968

## Smoking during Pregnancy

During the last trimester of pregnancy the rate of growth of the foetus depends on a number of factors of which the more important are its sex, the number of previous pregnancies, the size of the mother, and the number of foetuses in the uterus. Some of these variables may have a considerable effect on birth weight. Females at term are on average 5 oz. (140 g.) lighter than males, first-born are 4 oz. (113 g.) lighter than second-born, and babies of short mothers are often a pound (454 g.) or more lighter than those of tall mothers.¹ The average weight of a twin of 38 weeks' gestation is about 1½ lb. (680 g.) less than that of a singleton of the same gestation, and a triplet weighs ¾ lb. (340 g.) less than a twin.² Other influences which retard foetal growth are maternal disorders such as hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Serious defects of the foetus such as anencephalus and mongolism may also be associated with impaired growth.

While most of these variables are not susceptible to control, there is one important cause of retardation of foetal growth—tobacco smoking—which we ought to be able to influence. The first evidence of the effect of tobacco smoke on birth weight came from animal experiments,³ but there have since been a number of human studies all of which have shown that women who smoke during pregnancy have, on average, smaller babies than women who do not smoke. The smallness of these infants cannot be explained by differences of parity or duration of gestation,⁴ or of maternal size, or social class.⁵ These results have recently been confirmed by C. S. Russell, R. Taylor, and C. E. Law,⁶ who also showed that differences of age, education, and work done during pregnancy between smokers and non-smokers could not account for the differences in birth weight. It seems to be established beyond all doubt that smoking during pregnancy has a restricting effect on foetal growth.

The extent to which growth is impaired depends on the amount smoked.⁷ On average, smoking causes a depression of birth weight of about 6 oz. (170 g.), but growth is unaffected by smoking before the start of pregnancy,⁸ and if the mother stops smoking early in pregnancy normal foetal growth can be expected.⁹

The mechanism by which smoking retards foetal growth is not fully understood. It has been suggested that non-smokers eat more than smokers and indulge particularly in foods of high sugar content.¹⁰ But it seems that there is no difference between smokers and non-smokers in their weight halfway through pregnancy, and both groups gain equally in weight over the next 10 weeks.¹¹ Furthermore there is some evidence that maternal dietary intake has to be seriously curtailed before foetal growth is impaired.¹²

A more likely explanation, suggested by C. R. Lowe,¹³ is that smoking restricts the blood flow to the placenta and so reduces the quantity of nutrients to the foetus. This view is consistent with what is known about the action of nicotine on the cardiovascular system and with the haemo-

dynamic hypothesis which has been advanced to explain variations in foetal growth rates in experimental animals.¹⁸ ¹⁹

It may be asked whether the infants of smoking mothers, because of their smaller size, are less likely to survive and develop normally than the infants of non-smokers. It is well known that small babies in general are at greater risk of disability and death than babies of normal size, but there is some evidence that infants whose low birth weight has been caused by smoking are more likely to survive than infants of the same weight whose mothers did not smoke.¹⁶ Since there is some risk that this statement may be misinterpreted, it should be pointed out that it means only that if a patient has a small baby one would prefer the smallness to be due to smoking rather than to some other condition.

It is possible that when contracted pelvis was a greater obstetrical problem than it is today some benefits could have been claimed for cigarette smoking during pregnancy, because, by causing the foetus to be smaller than normal, it reduced the possibility of disproportion. The earlier studies in fact showed that smoking women required surgical induction and forceps delivery less frequently than non-smokers,¹⁷ and there was little difference in the perinatal mortality of the two groups. But the 1958 British Perinatal Mortality Survey showed that the rate was 40% higher when mothers smoked during pregnancy, and this was not due to parity or social-class differences between smokers and non-smokers.¹⁸

T. M. Frazier and colleagues¹⁹ also recorded higher stillbirth and neonatal mortality rates for the offspring of smokers;

and Russell, Taylor, and Law²⁰ found that smoking women had a much higher foetal and infant wastage than non-smokers; the combined death rates from abortion, stillbirth, and neonatal death were respectively 79 and 41 per 1,000 pregnancies.

There are many more women smoking now than there were some years ago, and this is reflected in their rising mortality from lung cancer. It seems that the time has come when women should be told frankly that if they smoke they not only put their own lives in jeopardy but, if they continue to do so during pregnancy, also expose their unborn infants to an unnecessary risk.

# Survey finds link between infant mortality, cigarettes

WASHINGTON (AP) — New evidence linking cigarette smoking to stillbirths and newborn infant deaths was cited yesterday in the seventh annual U.S. government report on smoking and health.

The document suggests "the strong association between cigarette smoking and higher rate fetal and infant mortality among smokers' infants."

The report said several recent studies have demonstrated a "statistically significant relationship between cigarette smoking and an elevated mortality risk among the infants of smokers" and that the risk increases proportionately with the number of cigarettes smoked.

And, the report adds, "new evidence suggests that, if a woman gives up smoking by the fourth month of pregnancy she will have the same risk of incurring a fetal or neonatal loss as a non-smoker."

STUDIES HAVE shown that "the fetus of a smoking mother may be directly exposed to agents such as carbon monoxide within tobacco smoke" at levels which produce stillbirth in animals, the report said.

A mother's smoking habit will not influence the child's sex, according to the studies, and "no firm conclusion" can be made about any relationship between maternal smoking and congenital malformation.

Experiments with animals do suggest, however, that the mother's milk may contain nicotine and nitrosamines, the

latter powerful carcinogens which pass through to suckling young.

The offspring of smoking mothers are nearly twice as likely to have a low birth weight at delivery, the report says, but they grow faster the first six months because "a toxic influence" has been removed.

THE REPORT says clinical studies involving healthy, young men have shown that cigarette smoking impairs exercise performance "especially for many types of athletic events and activities involving maximal work capacity."

Pipe and cigar smokers experience death rates "slightly higher" than those of non-smokers but "substantially lower" than those of cigarette smokers, the report said.

The reason, it says, are that pipe and cigar smokers either do not inhale or do so infrequently or slightly.

"As a result, the harmful effects of cigar and pipe smoking appear to be largely limited to increased death rates from cancer at those sites which are exposed to the smoke of these products," the report says.

Although cancers of the mouth, larynx, pharynx and esophagus are serious, it says "they account for only about five per cent of the cancer mortality among men."

IN THE first official study of the health hazards of smoking the relatively new little cigars, criticized by some as cigarettes in disguise, the report said "it is reasonable to conclude that

smoking little cigars may result in health defects similar to those associated with smoking cigarettes if both are smoked in the same way.

"Smoking those brands of little cigars which can be inhaled by a significant portion of the population in a manner similar to the present use of cigarettes would probably result," the report says, "in an increased risk of developing those pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases which have been associated with cigarette smoke."

Dr. Merlin K. DuVal, who

recently resigned as assistant health secretary of the department of health, education and welfare, told Congress the report "reiterates, strengthens and extends the findings in earlier reports that cigarette smoking is a major health problem in the United States."

He said new research confirms that cigarette smoking is a major cause of lung cancer and chronic bronchitis and contributes to chronic bronchopulmonary disease, cardiovascular disease and other ailments.

Babies Could Be Saved

A medical correspondent of the London Times writes: "Hundreds of infant lives could be saved each year if expectant mothers could be persuaded to give up smoking by the end of the fourth month of pregnancy." The research showed that the risk of a baby dying just before or shortly after birth is increased by 28 percent if the mother continues to smoke during pregnancy.

# Smoking stunts (fetal) growth

New findings that extend previous evidence of smoking's baleful influence during pregnancy are presented in the latest report prepared by the National Clearinghouse for Smoking and Health. In a statement accompanying the report, Dr. Merlin K. DuVal, lame-duck HEW Assistant Secretary for Health, notes that the latest evidence not only "strongly indicates a causal relationship between cigarette smoking during pregnancy and low infant birth weight," but points to "a strong, probably causal association" between smoking and a higher rate of fetal and infant mortality.

"When a variety of known or suspected factors that also exert an influence on birth weight have been controlled, cigarette smoking has consistently been shown to be independently related to low birth weight," says pediatrician H. Stephen Williams, assistant medical director of the reporting panel. There is new evidence, he goes on, suggesting that if a woman gives up smoking by the fourth month of pregnancy, her risk of delivering an infant of low birth weight is similar to that of a nonsmoker. The effect of smoking on fetal growth, he says, reflects the number of cigarettes smoked daily during a pregnancy, not the cumulative effect of smoking before pregnancy.

The NCSH report cites recent studies indicating that smoking is most strongly associated with a higher rate of stillbirths among poorer women. Blacks have a higher stillbirth rate than whites in this country, it notes.

Twelve retrospective and prospective studies have revealed a statistically significant relationship between a mother's smoking habit and her chance of delivering a dead child, according to the report. It adds that in three of these studies—each of them of sufficient size to allow adjustment for other risk factors—a highly significant independent association between smoking and infant mortality was established. And it is this adjustment, says Dr. Williams, that partly explains the discrepancy be-

![img-163.jpeg](img-163.jpeg)

Dr. Williams links cigarettes to a higher infant death risk, too.

tween these studies and others in which no link was demonstrated.

There is a seeming paradox here, however. The NCSH paper notes that within groups of infants of similar birth weight, the offspring of nonsmokers appear to have a higher mortality rate than do those of smokers. According to the report, though, the reason is "that the infants of nonsmokers within such similar-birth-weight groups are, on the average, gestationally less mature than the infants of cigarette smokers. Available evidence indicates that within groups of similar gestational age, infants of lower birth weight experience a higher mortality risk."

Available evidence also strongly supports the idea that cigarette smoking is one cause of fetal growth retardation, says the report. The causes of the excess deaths among smokers' babies are those associated with small-for-date infants.

Two epidemiological investigations cited suggest that smoking may possibly affect lactation, too. Studies in rats have demonstrated that nicotine can interfere with the usual suckling-induced rise in prolactin, the pituitary hormone that stimulates milk secretion in mammals. The report ad-

![img-164.jpeg](img-164.jpeg)

mits that "with only limited numbers of women and without control of other potentially significant variables, no firm conclusions can be drawn." Nevertheless, there is evidence indicating that nicotine passes into breast milk, and the report notes that results from experiments with mice suggest that nitrosamines—known carcinogens—pass through the milk to the suckling young.

Emphatically ruled out on the basis of available evidence is the suggestion that maternal cigarette smoking can influence the sex of newborn infants. And given the considerable variation in the design of the 42 studies reviewed by the NCSH, no firm conclusion can be made at this time about the relationship between maternal smoking and congenital malformation.

One intriguing finding was that smoking mothers seem to run a significantly lower risk of developing pre-eclampsia than do nonsmokers. But this possible benefit from smoking does not impress Dr. Williams. "If a woman who smokes during pregnancy develops pre-eclampsia," he remarks, "her infant has a higher mortality risk than that of a nonsmoker with pre-eclampsia."

## RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION\*

WILLIAM J. JABLONSKI, M.D.†

BOSTON AND DORCHESTER, MASSACHUSETTS

ALTHOUGH most medical centers perform exchange transfusions on newborn infants if the bilirubin reaches levels of 18 to 20 mg. per 100 ml. in the first few days of life¹⁻⁴ there are many who doubt its necessity as a routine procedure at these levels.⁵⁻⁸ Since the decision to perform an exchange transfusion is based essentially on the risks inherent in the procedure itself versus those associated with the concentration of serum bilirubin, more precise knowledge of these hazards would enable the operator to make his decision on a more rational basis. Moreover, there is still wide variation in the literature about the dangers associated with these factors.⁹⁻¹²

The present study was undertaken in this institution, therefore, to determine the risks of exchange transfusion and of different levels of bilirubinemia in newborn infants.

### MATERIALS AND METHODS

St. Margaret's Hospital is a maternity hospital with approximately 5000 deliveries per year. In recent years about 100 exchange transfusions have been performed annually, as a rule by the responsible pediatrician and the pediatric resident.

Throughout this paper the term "bilirubin" will refer to the total serum bilirubin concentration, expressed in milligrams per 100 ml. (van den Bergh micromethod) since most of the exchanges were performed on the basis of this value. The indirect bilirubin usually remained only about 1 or 2 mg. per 100 ml. below the total bilirubin.

To correlate these determinations with those of other hospitals a sample of serum obtained from an infant during exchange transfusion was sent to five other hospitals in the Boston area. The total bilirubins ranged from 12.4 to 16.5 mg. per 100 ml. The average determination was 14.5 mg., and that obtained at St. Margaret's Hospital was 16.0 mg. per 100 ml.

This study was then divided into three parts: the mortality figures associated with exchange transfu-

sions over a seven-year period were studied; the records of 100 infants who underwent exchange transfusion were analyzed for various pre-existing factors; and a follow-up study on 204 infants with hyperbilirubinemia was attempted.

### RESULTS

#### Mortality

The statistics on all exchange transfusions performed between 1954 and 1960, inclusive, were reviewed. Accurate records of the number of exchange transfusions performed and the indications for these were obtained from the blood bank. Reasonably accurate information on all the deaths was available. During this period there were 558 replacement transfusions, with 26 neonatal deaths. The distribution by years, indication and mortality is shown in Table 1. In 1960 the average number of exchange transfusions per infant requiring the procedure was 1.7 for hemolytic disease and 1.2 for physiologic jaundice. The condition of infants before transfusion who died during or shortly after the procedure was studied; the results are shown in Table 2. The great majority of those who died were in poor condition before exchange transfusion.

In an attempt to determine the mortality due to the procedure itself, only infants with unexplained hyperbilirubinemia were analyzed. It was believed that patients with erythroblastosis fetalis had so many complicating factors that an accurate representation of the true state of affairs in this group would not be possible. There were 6 deaths in the 263 transfusions performed for nonhemolytic jaundice. In only 4 cases was there any possibility that exchange transfusion contributed to death. These included 2 small premature infants weighing 1049 gm. (2 pounds, 5 ounces) and 1757 gm. (3 pounds, 14 ounces), a premature infant weighing 2381 gm. (5 pounds, 4 ounces), who tolerated the procedure poorly and died afterward, and an infant with hyaline-membrane disease and kernicterus who went into heart failure during the procedure and died several hours later. In the other 2 cases it was thought that the procedure could not reasonably be

# DISCUSSION

Kernicterus has long been the dreaded complication of jaundice in the newborn period. In 1950 Allen, Diamond and Vaughn demonstrated that kernicterus could be prevented in erythroblastotic infants by the use of exchange transfusions, and in 1952 Hsia and his associates showed an increasing incidence of kernicterus with higher levels of bilirubin

FIGURE 3. Neurologic Defects on Twelve-Month Follow-up Study (Actual Number of Cases Noted in the Bars).

in these infants. Allen and Diamond then recommended exchange transfusion on infants with hemolytic disease whose bilirubin levels exceeded 20 mg. per 100 ml. whereas several British workers considered 18 mg. an indication for exchange transfusion in newborn premature infants. In general these recommendations have been widely followed. However, the same levels of bilirubin that were recommended as an indication for exchange transfusion in erythroblastotic infants have been applied to cases of unexplained neonatal jaundice, even though these are widely different problems. The present series included no cases of kernicterus in infants with jaundice of unknown etiology and with peak bilirubin levels ranging from 15 to 20 mg. per 100 ml. Gerrard has described the clinical course of a large number of infants with kernicterus and noted that 50 out of 52 cases were manifest clinically by the fifth day of life. Since the average stay of infants born at St. Margaret's Hospital is five days, it appears unlikely that any significant number of cases of kernicterus were undiagnosed before discharge.

Although neonatal jaundice without hemolytic disease is commonly associated with prematurity, the majority of the infants in the present experience were full term.

They questioned the validity of applying the same criteria and treatment that are used for hyperbilirubinemia caused by erythroblastosis fetalis to uncomplicated hyperbilirubinemia of prematurity.

The present results are compatible with these suggestions, with no evidence that in so-called uncomplicated hyperbilirubinemia the risk is greater in infants with peak bilirubin levels of 25 mg. than in those whose levels do not exceed 15 to 20 mg. per 100 ml. However, it has been shown that hypoxia and certain drugs such as sulfisoxazole increase the incidence of kernicterus with given levels of bilirubin. Infants with these complicating factors should not be considered in the class of those described as having uncomplicated or physiologic jaundice. However, since both the present experience and that reported in the literature show the mortality due to exchange transfusion to be in the range of 1 or 2 per cent, owing to the lack of very large numbers of infants followed with bilirubin levels above 20 mg. per 100 ml., it cannot be stated definitely that the risk of kernicterus does not exceed that of exchange transfusion in infants with levels of 20 to 25 mg. per 100 ml. It is of note, however, that this report and those by Newns and Norton and Killander, Muller-Eberhard and Sydin discuss a total of 133 full-term infants with bilirubin levels in excess of 20 mg. per 100 ml. without a single case of kernicterus, and papers by Hugh-Jones and his associates. ### SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS

A study was undertaken to determine the relative risks of exchange transfusion and of kernicterus for given levels of serum bilirubin in newborn infants. The mortality due to exchange transfusion was approximately 1.5 per cent. In 204 infants with neonatal jaundice of undetermined origin and bilirubin levels greater than 15 mg. per 100 ml. there were 45 with levels over 20 mg. and 9 with levels over 25 mg. per 100 ml. There were no proved cases of kernicterus in the group. At follow-up study there was no greater incidence of neurologic deficit in the 19 infants whose bilirubin levels rose to 20 to 25 mg. per 100 ml. than in the 58 whose levels never exceeded 15 to 20 mg. per 100 ml. It is believed that in uncomplicated hyperbilirubinemia in full-term and larger premature infants there is no indication for exchange transfusion unless the bilirubin reaches at least 25 mg. per 100 ml.

# Minimizing Risk

in Exchange Transfusion

CARL POCHEDLY, M.D., Meadowbrook Hospital, East Meadow, New York

![img-168.jpeg](img-168.jpeg)

Certain precautions are essential to minimize risk while performing exchange transfusion. The baby should receive no formula for eight hours before the exchange. The stomach should be suctioned to remove gastric contents. Facilities should be available for tracheal intubation. An electronic cardiac monitor should be used. Donor blood should be warmed. If the baby is premature or severely ill, an attempt should be made to control the pH of the donor blood.

Despite various technical advances, such as a new disposable exchange transfusion kit, exchange transfusion is still not an innocuous procedure. Sudden death continues to occur. The overall mortality rate is between 0.5 and 4.0 percent, depending on how many premature or severely ill infants are included in the statistics. If the risk is to be minimized, the danger points of exchange transfusion need to be clearly defined (Figure 1).

# Stresses of Exchange Transfusion

Exchange transfusion imposes a tremendous physiologic stress on a newborn infant. There are three main sources of acute stress: cooling of the baby, rapid blood volume changes and acidosis.

# HYPOTHERMIA

Cooling of the baby may be caused by room air, by inefficiency of the infant warmer or by cold donor blood. The use of

ice-cold donor blood for exchange transfusion is the most dangerous of these factors since it causes selective chilling of the heart. During massive transfusion in adults, Boyan found a much higher incidence of cardiac arrest when cold blood was used than when warm blood was given.

If the umbilical catheter is inserted to a depth of more than 6 to 8 cm., the tip comes to lie in the right atrium and cold donor blood is then injected directly into the heart. The injection of cold donor blood may cause a serious arrhythmia by chilling the sinoatrial node or by vagal stimulation. Since the foramen ovale is patent for some time after birth, it is even possible for cold unmixed blood to reach the left side of the heart and the coronary arteries. When using cold acid-citrate-dextrose (ACD) blood for exchange, these arteries are perfused with blood that is not only cold but also acidotic, with a low PO₂, low ionized calcium and high serum potassium. Hoy suggested that this combination of factors could precipitate cardiac arrest.

To avoid hypothermic stress, the donor blood is passed through a coil of plastic tubing immersed in a water bath kept at 39° C. and inserted halfway along the donor set. The blood is warmed to within 5° C. of the water bath temperature as it moves through the 25 feet of tubing in the immersed coil (Figure 2).

# HEMODYNAMIC STRESS

The degree of hemodynamic stress becomes apparent when one compares the magnitude of blood volume changes in a baby during exchange transfusion with the proportionate changes in a double-volume exchange transfusion on an adult.

The total blood exchanged (double blood volume) for a 3-kg. baby is 500 ml.; for a man weighing 70 kg., it would be 12,000 ml. The aliquot of blood exchanged per unit

Acidosis is due to the ACD solution used to prevent coagulation of donor blood. The pH of ACD blood usually ranges between 6.5 and 6.9. During a double-volume exchange transfusion, about 85 percent of the infant's blood is replaced with citrated donor blood. Povey showed that this often causes

# The Author

CARL E. POCHEDLY, M.D.

is director of pediatric hematology at Meadowbrook Hospital, East Meadow, Long Island, N.Y. A graduate of Western Reserve University School of Medicine, he served his internship at Akron General Hospital and his pediatric residency at Children's Hospital of the District of Columbia. He obtained a Master of Medical Sciences degree at Ohio State University. He completed a fellowship in pediatric hematology at New York Medical College and currently serves as consultant in pediatric hematology to several Navian County (N.Y.) hospitals.

the baby's pH to fall from the physiologic level of 7.4 to 7.0 or lower. The healthy infant adapts to this tremendous acidotic stress remarkably well. However, the premature or sick infant, who is already acidotic or who has had a previous exchange transfusion, may collapse under the heavy load of citrated donor blood. The acidotic stress from using ACD blood is much greater in infants who cannot ventilate adequately and who consequently have a high PCO₂ and low pH at rest. Barrie proved that acidosis depresses cardiac function and impairs the binding of bilirubin by albumin.

Postexchange acidosis can be lessened by a slow rate of transfusion. To reduce the citrate load with ACD blood, 150 mL of plasma may be removed from the unit of donor blood before use. The addition of sodium bicarbonate or tris (hydroxymethyl) aminomethane (THAM) to alkalinize or buffer the blood has also been advocated but overdose may result in alkalosis. The use of donor blood anticoagulated with heparin is another effective way to avoid postexchange acidosis. However, no single protocol for handling the problem of acidosis in the high-risk infant requiring exchange transfusion has been generally accepted.

The question of citrated versus heparinized blood is controversial. Each type has its advantages and disadvantages. Blood preserved with ACD solution can be used as long as three days after collection but, according to Varga, it has a very low pH and causes acidotic stress. Furthermore, citrate produces a fall in the blood calcium level, which necessitates the infusion of calcium gluconate. If given improperly, this infusion of calcium may cause severe bradycardia or intravascular clotting.

Heparinized blood has a physiologic pH but must be used within 24 hours of collection. Heparin also causes a rise in the plasma concentration of nonesterified fatty

Johnson stated that this condition is potentially hazardous because the serum bilirubin then does not indicate the risk of kernicterus. The use of heparinized blood to avoid accentuation of acidosis may be advisable in premature or severely ill infants.

In view of the severe physiologic stress from cooling, rapid blood volume changes and acidosis, the morbidity and mortality of exchange transfusion are quite low.

# Hazards in Technique

Lucid descriptions of exchange transfusion technique are available in the literature.

![img-172.jpeg](img-172.jpeg)

FIGURE 3. Items needed for resuscitation of infants during exchange transfusion: caffeine sodium benzoate and epinephrine 1:1000; sterile syringe; laryngoscope; endotracheal tube; infant face mask and hand resuscitator.

Some of the hazards associated with this procedure are: airway obstruction, cardiac arrest, congestive heart failure, air embolism, perforation of the umbilical vein and infection.

# AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION

Aspiration of the stomach does not ensure removal of all the gastric contents. The only way to be certain that the stomach does not contain a potentially lethal collection of coagulated milk is to restrict the infant to glucose-and-water feedings during the eight to 12 hours before exchange transfusion. When there is the slightest chance that an exchange transfusion may be necessary, no milk should be given. Direct laryngoscopy, tracheal intubation and direct suctioning may be lifesaving for a baby with sudden respiratory obstruction during exchange transfusion. Facilities should be immediately available for direct laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation (Figure 3). Someone who knows how to use them should be present.

# CARDIAC ARREST

Unexplained cardiac arrest is a well-known complication of exchange transfusion. Arrhythmias and cardiac arrest are partially attributable to hypothermia, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia and acidosis. When ACD blood is used for exchange transfusion, it should be less than three days old and calcium gluconate should be given during the procedure. Infants who die during or soon after exchange transfusion may show sudden cardiac arrest, bradycardia followed by cardiac arrest or tachycardia followed by congestive heart failure. Atrial, nodal and ventricular arrhythmias have been recorded during exchange transfusion. However, the infant may show obvious distress only with the onset of ventricular fibrillation.

Monitoring the heart intermittently with a stethoscope taped to the chest does not

provide adequate appraisal of the infant's cardiac status. Although this method is simple, it is unreliable. Rapid changes in heart rate, soft beats, dislodgement of the chest piece, poor sound conduction or unfamiliarity with the stethoscope may lead to serious inaccuracies. Even experienced observers have difficulty in rapidly estimating cardiac rate and evaluating quality of the heart sounds. The heart rate may remain unchanged despite evidence of imminent heart failure. ECG monitoring should be used to

help provide early and accurate warning of impending danger (Figure 4).

Exchange transfusion should be stopped if the heart rate varies outside the range of 100 to 160 per minute or if abnormal ECG changes appear. Robinson stated that the most serious changes indicating ventricular embarrassment are bradycardia; widening, notching or low voltage of the QRS complex; S-T deviation and spiking of the T waves.

# CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE

Heart failure due to overloading the baby's circulation with donor blood may be the result of carelessness. Inaccurate measurement of blood volumes may occur during injection and withdrawal by careless overshooting or undershooting the 20 ml. or 10 ml. mark on the syringe. This may cause serious overloading of the baby's circulation or postexchange anemia. Albumin loading before or during exchange transfusion is of doubtful value and may lead to hypervolemia and cardiac overload.

# AIR EMBOLISM

Shock from air embolism may result from aspiration of air through the umbilical catheter. This may occur while the venous pressure is being measured or it may be due to air entering the stopcock system at loose fittings. When the infant is making strenuous inspiratory efforts against some obstruction, such as laryngeal spasm, air may readily be aspirated through an open umbilical catheter. The inserted catheter should be closed or kept under constant observation whenever it is disconnected.

# PERFORATION

Sandal reported that forceful insertion of the umbilical catheter may cause perforation of the umbilical vein. Perforation is most likely to occur when using a catheter of

hard plastic or a plastic catheter with a sharpened point. If a soft plastic catheter with a rounded end is used, the risk is greatly reduced. Undue trauma to the umbilical vein may also lead to ascending phlebitis and thrombosis.

# INFECTION

Sepsis may result from the use of infected blood or from nonsterile technique. Serum hepatitis may follow.

Portal hypertension may follow septic thrombophlebitis of the umbilical vein. Because of this danger, fluids should not be administered parenterally through an indwelling umbilical vein catheter and catheters should not be left in the umbilical vein between exchange transfusions. If the umbilical area seems infected, or if undue difficulty is encountered in catheterizing the umbilical vein, another site for transfusion should be used.

Other hazards include rupture of the spleen and postexchange bleeding from the umbilical stump. Transfusion reaction is also a possibility. This results from using blood not compatible with the serum of the mother, since a newborn infant has no significant blood group antibody production of his own. Viega warned that blood from a donor with sickle cell trait should not be used.

# A WARNING ON CATHETERIZING NEONATE'S UMBILICAL VEIN

Catheterization of the umbilical artery or vein of newborns, which has become standard practice for diagnostic and therapeutic measures in many hospitals, is not without significant risk, warns a Florida team. In a 3½-year study of 259 infants in respiratory distress or in danger of developing this condition, the researchers found that nearly 10% had complications that could be linked to catheterization. In two cases, these complications—thrombosis and infarction—were considered severe enough to have been the possible cause of death.

Drs. Edmund A. Egan II and Donald V. Eltzman of the University of Florida College of Medicine in Gainesville report in the American Journal of Diseases of Children (Vol.

121, No. 3) that 16 neonates had clinical complications with this technique, and autopsy complications were documented in 12 cases. In three cases, there were both clinical and autopsy complications.

Among the 16 patients with clinical complications, five had a loss of pulse. Two of these subsequently developed gangrene. Infection occurred in five patients, accidental hemorrhage in three, and cardiac arrhythmia in three. In addition, extravascular placement of the catheter occurred in two cases.

While the other clinical complications have all been reported previously by other investigators, Drs. Egan and Eltzman indicate that cardiac arrhythmias have not. Normal sinus rhythms were restored in all

three infants upon removal of the catheter.

Catheterization complications were revealed in 12 out of the 68 autopsies in the series. Evidence of thrombosis was found in six cases, and in four, this complication was associated with infarcts. Hemorrhage without apparent thrombosis was seen in three cases, and inflammation unrelated to the primary disease, in three.

The team notes that catheterization facilitates therapy that includes supplemental oxygen, buffers, and fluids to treat neonatal respiratory distress. But they conclude that "an awareness of the possible complications is essential for any physician using this procedure to care for severely ill patients."

# Catheter linked to arterial thrombosis

AN UNEXPECTEDLY high incidence of arterial thrombosis is associated with umbilical artery catheterization.

Of 100 consecutive admissions to a neonatal intensive care unit, 79 neonates had umbilical catheters inserted, 86% of which were arterial.

Significant arterial thrombus formation was demonstrated in 18 of 21 infants submitted to aortography when the catheter was withdrawn.

Fifteen other umbilically catheterized infants died and of the 12 autopsied, seven had minimal to extensive arterial thrombus formation.

Umbilical arterial catheterization should be reserved for carefully selected patients. Speculatively, the authors are now placing the tip of the umbilical artery catheter much lower in the aorta, at the bifurcation, hoping to lessen the hazard of the procedure. — "Umbilical artery catheterization: Demonstration of arterial thrombosis by aortography." W. A. Neal et al, Pediatrics, July 1972.

APRIL 5, 1969 THE LANCET

### COPPER CONTAMINATION IN EXCHANGE TRANSFUSIONS

SIR,—The free non-carruloplasmin copper level in the cord sera of 11 normal babies, measured by the atomic absorption method of Blomfield and MacMahon,⁴ has been found to have a range of 7–19 (mean 11) μg. per 100 ml., which is similar to the adult normal range of 5–15 (mean 9) μg. per 100 ml. In a series of 10 infants in our hospital with haemolytic disease of the newborn, the first blood-samples removed before exchange transfusion had a plasma-free-copper range of 13–176 (mean 62) μg. per 100 ml. In 6 infants, undergoing exchange transfusions in a nearby maternity hospital, the plasma-free-copper range was 9–37 (mean 15) μg. per 100 ml. In our hospital metal 4-way stopcocks were often used, whereas the maternity hospital was routinely using disposable plastic transfusion sets. The disposable plastic sets were found to be copper-free, but squirting 5 ml. of copper-free deionised water through 7 sterilised metal stopcocks resulted in copper contamination of 3–384 (mean 96) μg. per 100 ml. The copper released did, however, tend to diminish with subsequent water rinsings. Since changing from metal stopcocks to plastic disposable 3-way stopcocks, the plasma-free-copper levels in 10 infants before exchange transfusion have been 6–37 (mean 14) μg. per 100 ml.

In patients with acute or chronic copper poisoning, one of the effects is intravascular haemolysis,⁵ and copper also enhances agglutination of red cells,⁶ so that an excess of copper could conceivably contribute to the haemolytic process. In addition, copper may compete with bilirubin for binding sites on albumin, thereby increasing the toxicity of the bilirubin, or, in its free state, may act as an enzyme poison, perhaps causing brain and liver damage as in Wilson's disease. The normal

732 APRIL 5, 1969

newborn infant indeed resembles patients with Wilson's disease in having a high level of copper in the liver and a diminished ability to synthesise caruloplasmin. With the metal stopcocks further potential hazards were residual dried blood, and a white turbidity which was thought to be due to silicone grease.

In view of these results, replacement of metal stopcocks for exchange transfusions by disposable plastic stopcocks or exchange-transfusion sets is advocated.

BRITISH MEDICAL JOURNAL 3 APRIL 1971

# Osteomyelitis after Exchange Transfusion

M. E. QURESHI, S. P. PURI

British Medical Journal, 1971, 2, 28-29

Gangrene of the big toe after exchange transfusion has been described but not to our knowledge osteomyelitis. We report osteomyelitis and gangrene in the big toe occurring in two out of 406 babies given exchange transfusions.

# Case 1

A male infant, born by induced labour at 36 weeks' gestation because of rhesus insemination, was clinically normal at birth with an Apgar score of 9/10 at three minutes. His weight was 2,480 g. Cord blood results were: direct Coombs test positive; haemoglobin 108%; bilirubin 3.4 mg/100 ml; blood group A Rh-positive. Because of increasing jaundice, 86 hours after birth exchange transfusion was carried out with the two-catheter continuous technique (Saling, 1959; Ara and Holman, 1966) employing intravenous infant-feeding tubes (Warne Surgical Products)—a 4.5 F.G. size catheter for the umbilical artery and a 6 F.G. size for the umbilical vein. After 530 ml of 1-day-old acid citrate dextrose whole blood, group AB Rh-negative, had been exchanged uneventfully within two hours and 45 minutes, the catheters were left in situ for 60 hours filled with dilute heparinized saline solution and stoppered with three-way taps. Prophylactic antibiotics were not given.

About 24 hours after removal of the catheters the baby became lethargic and slow to feed, resented handling, looked ill, and had a rectal temperature of 38° C. The whole of the right lower limb was swollen, with pregangrene discoloration on the middle of the sole, dorsum of foot, and lower third of shin. The right femoral artery was weakly palpable as compared with the left, but the microcirculation in the leg was satisfactory. The leg was held immobile in a position of slight flexion and abduction at the hip and slight flexion at the knee. Thromboembolism of the arterial tree of right lower limb was diagnosed, but as bone infection could not be ruled out blood culture was done and antibiotic cover with Ampiclox (sodium salts of ampicillin and cloxacillin) was started. Radiological examination of the leg was normal at

this stage. To improve the microcirculation the baby was transfused with 45 ml of Rhomacrodex on three occasions (Gruber et al., 1965), and since the haemoglobin was only 50% a packed cell transfusion was given.

After 48 hours the general condition improved. The discoloured patches disappeared except on the tip of the big toe. Staphylococcus aureus grown from the blood culture was resistant to penicillin but sensitive to cloxacillin. After a week the swelling of the limb disappeared, except at the lower end of the femur. Repeat x-ray examination showed decalcification of the lower end of the femur and erosion of the metaphysis area indicative of osteomyelitis. The tip of the right big toe developed dry gangrene, which gradually separated in about 10 days. The antibiotics were continued for six weeks. Repeat x-ray examination of the lower limb four weeks later showed improvement in bone texture and periosteal reaction in the metaphysis area. The baby was discharged home, aged 10 weeks, with normal movement of the hip and knee joints.

# Case 2

A female baby was born on 3 March 1970 to an Rh-negative mother who had received intrauterine transfusions for rhesus incompatibility, the last one four days before spontaneous delivery at the 32nd week. The baby weighed 1,906 g, had an Apgar score of 9/10 at five minutes, appeared to be hydropic, and had a palpable liver (four fingerbreadths) and a palatable spleen (three fingerbreadths). Cord blood results were: haemoglobin 37%; bilirubin 5.0 mg/100 ml; direct Coombs test positive; blood group O rhesus-positive. The first exchange transfusion was begun five hours after birth with rhesus-negative acid citrate dextrose partially packed blood by the two-catheter continuous technique. Altogether 360 ml of blood was transfused, while 326 ml was taken out. During the exchange 1 ml of 10% calcium gluconate was given after every 100 ml of blood; 84% sodium bicarbonate was given according to the Astrup results. A course of cephaloridine was started.

Another exchange transfusion was carried out on 5 March and a third on the next day because of a rising serum bilirubin. On 7 March 80 ml of packed cells was transfused because the haemoglobin had fallen to 53%. Next day the baby showed signs of paralytic ileus, and for five days was treated with intravenous fluids (including 10% dextrose) through the umbilical vein catheter and nasogastric suction. Two days later she developed sclerema n. onatum and was given a five-day course of corticosteroids. During the last 48 hours the fluid therapy was given through the arterial umbilical catheter because the venous catheter became dislodged. The arterial catheter was removed after 10 days. On the same day petechial haemorrhages were seen over the body and the baby passed blood-stained stools. The right leg was swollen, the tip of the right leg toe was blue, and there was a pinch of bruising on the little toe and right knee, with the skin bruising easily. X-ray examination of the right leg showed nothing abnormal. After a transfusion of 80 ml of fresh whole blood no fresh bleeding occurred and the petechial haemorrhages faded away.

Six days later the tip of the big toe became gangrenous. Signs of an infection in the right knee joint developed, and one week later pus was aspirated from which Escherichia coli was grown. This was found resistant to cephaloridine and sensitive to gen-

tamicin and kanamycin. Blood culture also grew E. coli and Staph. aureus. Treatment with gentamicin and cloxacillin was started and within a few days the swelling of the knee abated and the baby started to move the leg. The tip of the big toe demarcated into dry gangrene, which separated on 9 May.

The antibiotics were stopped after four weeks when the leg appeared normal and x-ray examination showed that the infection had settled. The baby was discharged home on 18 May when 11 weeks old and weighing 3,410 g.

# Comment

Prolonged umbilical vein catheterization may cause local thrombosis, umbilical vein phlebitis and pyaemia, liver necrosis, and pulmonary embolism. (Scott, 1965). Portal hypertension (Thompson and Sherlock, 1964), bowel perforation (Corkery et al., 1968; Orme and Eades, 1968), and myocardial infarction have also been documented (Van Der Hauwaert et al., 1967). Umbilical artery catheterization has also been associated with a few complications. Gupta et al. (1968) reported complications in 10% of 335 babies, which included bleeding, clinical signs of arterial obstruction, and arterial thrombosis detected at necropsy. Only one baby lost the tip of the big toe. Cochran et al. (1968) reported complications in 8% of 387 babies. Gluteal muscle necrosis has been described (Ulan and Swyer, 1968).

The clinical picture in our two cases can be explained only by thrombosis induced by the catheter in the arterial tree with superimposed infection. When the catheters were removed multiple embolization must have occurred, affecting

the skin, the big toe, and lower end of the femur. In the second case the infection was not controlled so suppuration became widespread. These are the only two cases with permanent sequelae in the 406 babies we have exchange transfused in the past four years.

We are grateful to Dr. B. Gans and Dr. C. A. Holman for permission to record these cases and for helpful advice and criticism. Our thanks are due to our resident pathologists for their help and to the nursing staff of the premature baby unit for their devoted nursing.

### UNEXPLAINED DEATH FROM EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION

WILLIAM C. TAYLOR, M.B., CH.B., LLOYD C. GRISBALE, M.D., AND

ALLAN G. STEWART, PH.D.

EDMONTON, ALBERTA

DURING the 11 years that have elapsed since the introduction of exchange transfusion for the treatment of hemolytic disease of the newborn, attention has been periodically focused on the fact that this procedure is not without its dangers and may occasionally be associated with unexpected fatality. Allen and Diamond¹ have recently pointed out that, with few exceptions, it has been impossible to explain the deaths that arise during or shortly after exchange transfusion. Walker and Mollison² have listed the causes of death occurring in association with hemolytic disease of the newborn in England and Wales during the years 1953 and 1955. In 88 (16 per cent) of 550 deaths, the fatality arose during or within 4 hours of exchange transfusion. The immediate cause of death was not apparent in these cases but, from the clinical information available, it seemed that death should not otherwise have taken place at that time.

The following case reports are presented in the belief that they represent a sequence of events which must occur in a certain but at present unknown proportion of sudden deaths arising during exchange transfusion.

From the Department of Pediatrics, University of Alberta and University of Alberta Hospital, Edmonton, Alberta.

### CASE REPORTS

CASE 1.—Cardiac Arrest During Exchange Transfusion.—

This female infant was delivered by cesarean section on the tenth of September, 1957. Cesarean section was performed at 35 weeks' gestation because of a rise in maternal D antibody titer to ¹/₃₂, and because of the death of the 3 preceding siblings from hemolytic disease. The infant weighed 2,220 Gm. She cried spontaneously and on examination appeared normal except for yellow staining of the vernix and the umbilical cord. The spleen was not palpable. The cord blood serum bilirubin was 6.4 mg. per cent, hemoglobin 9.5 Gm. per cent, hematocrit 26 per cent, and reticulocyte count 14.4 per cent. The direct Coombs' test was positive.

The first exchange transfusion was carried out within one hour of delivery. Using a 10 c.c. syringe, 415 c.c. of blood were withdrawn and 384 c.c. of packed cells injected. Throughout the 1-hour procedure the infant's condition remained satisfactory. Following the exchange, the serum bilirubin was 2.5 mg. per cent, the hemoglobin 13.4 Gm. per cent, and the hematocrit 35 per cent.

At the age of 7 hours, the serum bilirubin had risen to 9.0 mg. per cent and a second exchange transfusion was given. Using the same technique as before, 310 c.c. of blood were withdrawn and 290 c.c. injected in less than 1 hour. The infant's condition remained satisfactory throughout and periodic electrocardiographic (ECG) tracings taken with a direct writing

# CASE 2—Cardiac Arrhythmia During Exchange Transfusion.

Experience with electrocardiography in 50 exchange transfusions performed on 36 infants has revealed one other example of gross cardiac arrhythmia. This infant weighed 2,160 Gm, and was of 35 weeks' gestation. The cord blood hemoglobin was 7.0 Gm. per cent and the bilirubin 6.82 mg. per cent. He received an exchange transfusion at the age of 1 hour, using 5-day-old partially packed blood. After injection of 185 c.c. of blood in 15 c.c. aliquots, the heart rate was suddenly slowed although the infant's general condition remained satisfactory. The ECG showed marked sinus bradycardia and occasional ectopic beats (Figs. 5 and 6). The arrhythmia was uninfluenced by injection of 1.5 c.c. calcium gluconate (10 per cent solution) and persisted until the end of a cautiously executed exchange of 150 c.c. of blood. The bradycardia consisted with periods of normal ECG configuration. ECG tracings taken on the first, second, third, and seventh days after the exchange transfusion were not remarkable and the infant's subsequent progress was uneventful.

# DISCUSSION

Two examples of 2:1 auriculoventricular heart block detected by electrocardiographic examination during exchange transfusion have been reported by Joos, Yu, and Miller (Table I). One infant, transfused with donor blood containing a plasma potassium of 8.0 mEq./L., developed parasystoles and 2:1 block intermittently during the fourth and fifth 100 c.c. of the exchange. The arrhythmia was uninfluenced by calcium administration and the infant's serum potassium did not rise above 5.40 mEq./L. The second infant, a premature weighing 1,190 Gm., was transfused with donor blood containing a plasma potassium of 18.6 mEq./L. Arrhythmia consisting of 2:1 heart block developed during administration of the second 50 c.c. of exchange, persisted for 4 minutes, and then reverted to normal rhythm following the intravenous injection of 0.1 Gm. of calcium gluconate. The serum potassium just before the onset of the 2:1 block was 9.12 mEq./L. This baby died within 24 hours of the exchange transfusion. Autopsy revealed the findings of prematurity, severe hemolytic disease of

Case I which showed a sudden progression from a state of slow nodal rhythm, without associated clinical features, to complete cardiac arrest in a period of 4 minutes suggested that there was a possible interrelationship in this group of cases. acting over a short period of time, severely embarrassed the heart action. Hyperpotassemia was not considered to be a likely cause. Serum potassium levels up to 7.8 mEq./L. have not been considered unusual (McCance and Young⁸) during the normal newborn period. Sudden cardiac arrest occurred with a potassium level as low as 4.5 mEq./L. in the infant reported by Pew.⁹ In addition, Bolande⁸ has reported 1 infant with a serum potassium of 17 mEq./L. who did not develop cardiac arrest during exchange and who survived the exchange transfusion for a period of 17 hours. A comparison of the potassium in the donor blood and the potassium in the infant's circulation in Table I suggested that most infants could handle comparatively large loads of infused potassium. This confirmed the observations of Campbell⁷ and of Bolande.⁸

The possibility of cardiac arrest from hyperpotassemia also appeared unlikely from the experimental work of Baker and his co-workers.⁹ They have reported the use of potassium citrate in the arrest of the perfused isolated hearts obtained from 4 still-born fetuses of 16 to 20 weeks' gestation. A concentration of potassium citrate equivalent to 14.8 mEq./L. (calculated as tripotassium citrate) had to be directed as a continuous infusion into the coronary circulation to produce cardiac arrest. The volume of the potassium citrate solution required to produce this effect was not specified. Effer and his co-workers¹⁰ have reported the use of potassium citrate solutions equivalent in strength to 230.0 mEq./L. (calculated as tripotassium citrate) and 6-20 c.c. volume to produce cardiac arrest in children undergoing cardiac surgery.

In both reports the potassium solutions were directed into the coronary arteries and there was no opportunity for dilution to occur from mixture with venous blood. They have not, however, reported on the efficacy of weaker solutions of potassium. In exchange transfusion, the donor blood has ample opportunity to become diluted with the infant's venous blood before being directed to the coronary circulation.

Hypocalcemia was also considered as a cause of cardiac arrest. In 9 out of the 10 cases, calcium was given as a prophylactic measure during the exchange transfusion. In 2 cases of heart block and one of cardiac arrest, there was no response to immediate administration of calcium. It appeared unlikely, therefore, that calcium deficiency per se was the cause of the cardiac phenomena.

Pew¹ drew attention to the fact that his case of cardiac arrest followed shortly after the introduction of a bottle of cool blood into the exchange transfusion and that the heart felt cold when it was massaged. In Case I no attempt was made to warm the blood other than allowing it to stand at room temperature for about 10 to 15 minutes. Information with regard to warming of the blood is not available on the other cases. Hoff and Stansfield¹¹ and Deterling and his co-workers¹² have provided experimental evidence in the dog that ventricular fibrillation could develop when the body temperature was reduced below 73° F. or the local ventricular temperature below 50° F.

One factor which has not been given much consideration in previous reports is the effect that the acid-citrate dextrose anticoagulant mixture

has on reducing the pH and CO₂ combining power of donor blood. On samples of donor blood tested at this hospital, the average pH was 6.2 and this level varied little with the duration of storage. In Case 1, severe and irreversible acidosis was an outstanding feature following the third replacement transfusion. Deterling demonstrated that the ventricular fibrillation induced in dogs by hypothermia did not develop when the blood was maintained in a state of alkalosis by hyperventilation.

At the present time it is not possible to state that any one specific factor or combinations of factors is responsible for the occurrence of cardiac arrest in infants undergoing exchange transfusion. According to circumstances several or all of the following factors may be present: hyperpotassemia, hypocalcemia, cooling of the heart, acidosis, prematurity, and the disease process of hemolytic disease. There may be other factors at present unsuspected. The combined use of electrocardiography and adequate biochemical study is one way of further elucidating the problems involved and, at the same time, ensuring maximum safety for the infant.

# SUMMARY

Attention is drawn to the fact that sudden and unexpected death may occur during or shortly after exchange transfusion for hemolytic disease of the newborn.

One case is reported of bradycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and cardiac arrest after 70 c.c. of blood had been exchanged. A second case is reported of bradycardia and arrhythmia developing after an exchange of 185 c.c. of blood.

These cases are compared with 8 other case reports in which there is a similarity of clinical or electrocardiographic findings. It is not possible from the data available to determine a common etiological factor for the sudden alteration in cardiac function.

It is suggested that possible factors which might be operating singly, or in combination, are hyperpotassemia, hypocalcemia, hypothermia, acidosis, prematurity, and the disease processes of hemolytic disease.

Twenty-five minutes after beginning the exchange (after removal of 90 ml. and replacement of 70 ml.), the infant suddenly became dusky and cardiac rhythm was irregular. The procedure was discontinued. The trachea was suctioned, with little return, and oxygen was given without improvement. Respirations became irregular. An electrocardiogram 15 minutes after the end of the transfusion showed gross irregularity in ventricular rhythm, coupled beats, variable R-S, QS, and RSR waves, depressed S-T, and inverted T waves. Thirty minutes later, after intubation, external cardiac massage, and intermittent positive pressure, electrocardiogram showed a sine wave pattern with rare ventricular complexes. Adrenalin was given without prolonged benefit. The face and neck appeared swollen. Heart beat ceased at 2:25 A.M., 7 hours after admission, and 1½ hours after the exchange.

Dr. WILLIAM PFEFFER\* We are presented an infant with erythroblastosis, in itself not remarkable. However, the outcome was not only remarkable but unexpected. It is unfortunate that the issue here is not an isolated example, but has been seen before in this institution and has been reported in the literature fairly frequently. Very briefly, let us note some of the salient points in the protocol. This 6-hour-old boy presented at the hospital with a very high degree of bilirubinemia, a degree which all would agree necessitates immediate exchange transfusion if the very likely possibility of further rise of bilirubin and ultimate kernicterus is to be avoided. The infant seemed to be in good condition; he was vigorous, the skin was red, the hemoglobin was not only adequate but quite high, 22 Gm. per cent. The culture from the umbilicus perhaps sounds frightening, but I don't believe that the infant survived long enough for the Staphylococcus to cause any trouble.

One thing I would like to emphasize is that although the details of delivery are unknown,

\*Dr. Pfeffer is Associate in Medicine, The Children's Hospital Medical Center, and Instructor in Pediatrics, Harvard Medical School.

we are told that the mother received no medication during the pregnancy. Drugs given to the mother during delivery may be extremely important whether babies become jaundiced or not. However, we cannot follow this up, and let us assume that there is no problem in this area.

As is quite proper, exchange transfusion was carried out shortly after admission here. This procedure was begun at 12:45 in the morning. Perhaps this is significant because it is my opinion that the skill, awareness, and alertness of the operator has something to do with the outcome of any exchange transfusion. Possibly at quarter to one in the morning, judgment was not as good as might be. I am in no position to be too critical of the outcome in this baby because the same thing has happened to me on more than one occasion.

Neutralized heparinized Group O, Rh negative blood was used. At the onset of the exchange, the infant was in good condition; the venous pressure was 50 mm., a measurement we would consider normal. Between 30 and 80 mm. pressure by direct measurement of the height of the column of blood above the umbilicus is usually considered normal. This is, of course, a relatively inaccurate method of measurement, but it seems to be clinically useful. Exchange transfusion was begun by removal of 30 c.c. of blood. Now, I am not sure that this harmed the baby, but I think it was more blood than was actually necessary to remove. It is my custom to remove blood in quantities as large as this only if the baby has evidence of hydrops or of high venous pressure. If there is no elevation of venous pressure, it is my custom to form a deficit, but to form a deficit slowly, removing 10 c.c., replacing 5, the next time removing 15 and replacing 10, so as to carry along with a deficit of about 10 to 15 c.c. of blood during the exchange. If, as is possible, after 30 c.c. of blood were removed, a further 20 c.c. were removed, we would then have a deficit of 50 c.c. In a baby with a large blood volume and high venous pressure, this would be beneficial, otherwise not. In this baby, 20 c.c. may have been reinjected, and then 20 c.c. removed. I assume that the exchange went along fairly slowly because 25 minutes elapsed before 50 c.c. were removed and 70 c.c. replaced. This is good. It is my personal feeling that while rapid exchange can be done with impunity in some babies, it is not always possible. Some babies do much better with a slower exchange, and some babies do better with smaller increments and withdrawals of blood.

Suddenly, after 25 minutes, the infant became dusky, cardiac rhythm became irregular, and from this point on, the course of the disease was downhill.

Unfortunately, we do see some babies who have sudden changes in condition, but in most babies who are having adverse effects there is some small warning, which I shall describe later, which will enable the operator to slow his rate of exchange or even to discontinue it. If one has exchanged over 200 c.c. of blood, termination of the procedure is the safest plan; repeat exchange transfusion after 6 hours can be carried out if necessary. Apparently, the heart bore the brunt of the baby's difficulty. The electrocardiogram would appear to me to show irritation of the ventricle, premature ventricular beats, and as suggested by Dr. Nadas when I consulted him 2 days ago, the other findings could possibly be interpreted as evidence of myocardial ischemia. In any case, the myocardium was not very healthy and the infant died shortly thereafter, one and one-quarter hours after the exchange transfusion with the comment that the face and neck appeared swollen. At the end of 500 c.c. exchange, with no increase in venous pressure, I have seen one baby develop marked congestive failure with accumulation of large amounts of pericardial and pleural fluid, very loud moist rales in the chest, and a picture of drowned lung at autopsy. Whether or not this process was present in this baby, or whether this explains the swelling, I do not know. In any case, I assume that this represents an unexpected effect related to exchange transfusion, rather than effect of erythroblastosis, which did not seem too severe in this baby. When the baby is in as good condition initially as this one was and dies at the age of 7½ hours, some special explanation is required.

There is no question in my mind that exchange transfusion should have been carried out. What happened to the baby? Why did it happen? How could this be prevented in the future?

My experience with this procedure is centered in the years 1950 through 1960, during which time I performed between 800 and 1,000 exchange transfusions and observed between 1,000 to 1,200 babies with erythroblastosis as well as other infants with jaundice. I will say, to reassure any operator who loses a baby, that I have lost at least 12 to 15 babies during my years of experience in exactly the same way. I wish I knew more about what went wrong. In the past, pathologic examination of babies

who have died under these circumstances has usually been unrevealing.

Let us, for a moment, go over some of the known untoward effects of exchange transfusion and some of the untoward effects that do not occur, but that we worry about. It has become obvious that any baby with hydrops or severe anemia, or severe erythroblastosis, is immediately a worse risk for exchange transfusion than one in good condition, and, therefore, any mortality figures are going to show a more serious effect of exchange on the babies who are more sick. Since any sick baby is a candidate for adverse reaction to exchange, exchange should be done more slowly and, in my opinion, should be done to only half the quantity that one would ordinarily use. An exchange of 200 to 300 c.c. in a baby with severe anemia, enlargement of liver and spleen, and elevated venous pressure usually is sufficient to result in immediate clinical improvement. Further exchange should then be deferred to see if bilirubin rises. Frequently, in this type of baby, marked elevation of bilirubin does not occur and further exchange may not be necessary. In general, if an exchange transfusion of 500 c.c. occurs in a sick baby, this type of untoward reaction becomes almost common before the end of the exchange.

The possibility of embolization has always bothered us. When you put the catheter into the umbilical vein, particularly when the baby is over 24 hours old, and suck out a 2 cm. clot, which is 3 mm. in thickness, you wonder what would happen if instead of sucking it out, you inadvertently pushed it forward. So far as I know, this has never occurred. Some years ago Dr. Landing made a careful study of the lungs of babies who died shortly after exchange and was unable to demonstrate any embolic phenomenon there or anywhere else. There have been several cases reported, and I have seen at least one, of a septic thrombus forming. (In my case, in the radial artery 2 days after exchange.) I think this is an unusual complication. Air embolism should not occur, with any care.

Septicemia is sometimes difficult to distinguish from asymptomatic bacteremia found in babies after exchange transfusion. The incidence of positive blood cultures following an exchange transfusion is fairly high, but I have seen only one or two babies who have had clinical evidence of septicemia with fever and illness. Probably septicemia is not a problem here. The umbilical vein may be ruptured, usually close enough to the surface that the rupture is ob-

It is quite possible to form a false passage in the cord dividing Wharton's jelly as one goes along for a surprisingly large distance, even to 3 or 4 cm. Fortunately, one is able to check this. The rule is: Do not inject blood until you can withdraw blood freely and in large amounts. There has been at least one instance of blood being poured out into the retroperitoneal space when blood was given, not in the vein but into the cord substance. Hepatic necrosis has been reported twice, and I have seen one case. These babies die after 2 or 3 days of lethargy and apparent hepatic coma. The timing excludes this possibility in the present child. Hemolytic transfusion reactions, in the usual sense, do not occur, perhaps because of the age of the baby and relative inadequacy of his antibody system. Adrenal hemorrhage has occasionally been seen, I think, more or less as an incidental finding.

Dr. Van Praagh, in 1961, recorded several cases of ruptured spleen, none of which were diagnosed before death and all of which, in retrospect, had in common enlargement of the abdomen with difficulty in feeling the liver and spleen, profound anemia and pallor, and death with diagnosis made only at autopsy. This is something to be considered in a baby who is not doing well because it is a curable disease, once the diagnosis is made.

Any baby from whom you remove more blood than his vascular system is capable of losing will have an adverse reaction. I have seen this at least once: a 3 pound baby who inadvertently had about 40 c.c. of blood removed before any was injected. He promptly went into shock and died very soon thereafter. I think, perhaps, that the adverse effect of decrease in circulating blood volume, or the swings in pressure involved, may enter into this case, perhaps only as an auxiliary factor. Perhaps in this baby, sudden congestive failure caused swelling of the face and neck, and perhaps cardiac tamponade from pericardial fluid.

Dr. Van Praagh's study in 1961 is interesting in regard to this case because he analyzed 882 patients from this hospital with erythroblastosis; 650 received a total of 902 exchange transfusions. Of these babies, 82 died and 32 per cent of them died during or within 6 hours of exchange transfusion. This comes to 3 per cent of deaths in association with exchange transfusions. Of this number, 1 per cent (that is, one third of the babies who died) showed no adequate cause of

death at autopsy. In 13 babies there was evidence that cardiac irregularity and arrhythmia played some role in the death of the baby. These figures agree with other figures quoted in the literature. Boggs reports, from Philadelphia, an incidence of only 0.2 per cent death during exchange transfusion in babies who are vigorous and healthy at the time exchange is done. However, he does have 73 babies who were classified as being weak or having early kernicterus, and in this group 13 per cent died during or shortly after exchange transfusion. It is not surprising that 46 per cent of hydropic or moribund babies died during or shortly after exchange transfusion. My own experience would closely parallel that recorded by Van Praagh.

Babies showing this reaction, fortunately, are recognizable clinically. I have no figures on how often a reaction of this kind occurs during exchange and how often a bad outcome is averted by proper steps. I would think that such a figure would be very high, perhaps as high as 25 per cent, and perhaps more if your worry quotient is low.

What can be done? You can learn more by watching the baby's face, respiration, and color than you can by electrocardiographic monitor or even with a nurse listening with a stethoscope. The babies who get into trouble usually begin to show some clinical evidence of difficulty in the form of a weak cry and pallor, of a distressed expression on the face, if you will. I think everybody knows what I mean. The pulse rises. The patient becomes lethargic, and pinching the ear does not result in crying. When such symptoms appear, exchange should be discontinued immediately. You can often proceed again in a few minutes with the exchange, going more slowly and more cautiously than before. If this happens twice during an exchange, discontinue the procedure and try again some 6 hours later. Some babies act a little differently. Some babies have immediate, unforeseen cardiac arrest. Some seem to have apnea with a closed glottis. It is not always possible to blame lack of calcium for this because I have had this occur 10 minutes after having given calcium. Since this baby received heparinized blood, we cannot blame citrate binding of calcium because heparin causes no difficulty of this sort. Heparinized blood has several other advantages; you are required to use fresh blood, excluding increased levels of potassium. There may be some benefit when the blood is still warm from the donor.

the only untoward effect of exchange transfusion by using heparinized blood at this hospital in approximately 200 exchanges, an incidence of 0.5 per cent. I would like to have another visit on a Clinical Pathological Conference after 1,000 have been done, because my own feeling is that, although the citrate may be contributory, it is not the entire cause of these deaths. The temperature of the blood ordinarily does not seem to be a deciding factor. We have used cold blood many times with no adverse effects. The electrolyte balance probably is not a problem, although it is quite obvious that potassium and calcium levels are important if blood over 5 days old is used. I feel that the speed of giving the exchange transfusion, the volume of blood removed, and the volume of blood reintroduced each time is very important. I wish I knew more about the possible reflex changes that might occur, but from a common sense viewpoint, 20 c.c. of blood in a baby of this size is a large amount, comparable to 500 c.c. of blood in an adult. If you take from an adult one pint of blood by phlebotomy 20 times over a period of one hour, the incidence of syncope

in these donors is going to be considerably raised above what happens with a single bleeding. It has always been my opinion, that these babies die because of reflex changes initiated by rapid changes in pressure and volume within the heart or within the great vessels around the heart. Whatever the cause of these deaths, the most important preventive factors are good clinical judgment in the use of exchange transfusion and acute observation of the baby during the procedure.

DR. VANTAGE. First, I would like to remind you that not long ago we discussed here a child who, after the fourth exchange transfusion, had a massive fatal pulmonary embolism. Second, some of the comments made this morning recall a story of a child at another hospital who went into profound collapse with virtual cessation of cardiac activity following the intravenous injection of 20 c.c. of radioisotope dye. This was a very small infant and this must have represented a relatively large volume quickly given; if nothing else, it resulted in major distention of the cardiac chambers or a momentary period in which no oxygen was getting to the tissues. That child ultimately was left with what appeared to be anoxic cerebral damage.

To return to the questions at hand—one properly should not take a case that has so many complications for a Clinical Pathological Conference, but it was of interest for several reasons.

The mottled puffiness of the head and neck was associated with massive subcutaneous emphysema, the external evidence of mediastinal emphysema, pneumothorax, and the blebs of interstitial emphysema in the lungs. Air had dissected along pulmonary veins to rupture into the pericardial space, and, since bubbles were found in coronary arteries, it must have ruptured into a pulmonary vein at some point. Some confirmation that this occurred while circulation was still present is the presence of interstitial hemorrhage in the lung. The hemorrhagic response and involvement of the coronary arteries indicate that this air embolism is at least a terminal phenomenon associated with attempts at resuscitation, perhaps. When air embolism has complicated exchange transfusion, no pulmonary, mediastinal, or subcutaneous emphysema has been reported.

When emphysema of this sort and degree exists, one thinks, of course, of high pressures in the airway, but just as often one finds that some, at least partial, obstructive factor is present in the airway. Indeed, this infant has a moderate degree of aspiration, including squamous, meconium bodies, and thick material containing peculiarly acid-fast substances (Fig. 1). This acid-fast material, which is also present in bronchial epithelium (Fig. 2), is unusual and one suspects that a good deal is unknown about the pregnancy and delivery of this child. For one, a decreased volume of concentrated amniotic fluid is suggested. Moreover, postmaturity or dysmaturity is suggested. Other findings which might suggest intrauterine disturbances are: (1) some excess of fetal glomerulosclerosis in the kidney; (2) an unusual amount of splenic lymphoid tissue for a severe erythroblastotic infant (we often think that there is an inverse relationship between severity of erythroblastosis and amount of lymphoid tissue in spleen; (3) a liver which actually is less than half the expected weight, unlike the overweight liver expected in the usual erythroblastosis; and (4) a small thymus.

I have seen small livers of this sort under at least two circumstances: in infants thought to have ABO erythroblastosis and in infants considered to be dysmature. It is not easy to say why this liver is small; there is no evidence of necrosis, although anoxic vacuoles are present. Certainly, neither congestion nor erythropoiesis, while present, are very marked. Curiously, hyaline masses are occasionally found in walls of small portal veins. Could this represent ancient thrombosis or embolism? The element of endotheliation of these masses suggests origin prior to transfusion (Fig. 3).

Careful gross and microscopic study of the heart revealed no abnormality, such as hemorrhage or necrosis. Perhaps one anatomic fact is of interest, however. The artery supplying the area of atrioventricular node is a terminal end artery, branching from the right coronary artery. This circulatory area might then be as a premium where delivery of blood to the coronary circuit fails or decreases for any reason.

To emphasize once more, the evidence of erythroblastosis (such as extramedullary erythropoiesis), while present is definitely not severe.

In summary, there are several peculiarities in the disease presented by this infant, most of which point to the possibility of a grossly abnormal pregnancy, despite the lack of supportive
