Dr. PEFFER. Where did this air come from, and why?

Dr. VAVTER. I assume air introduced via the airway and partially trapped by aspiration dissected into the interstitium of the lung and silence to other sites. I also assume that this may be related to resuscitation after the exchange transfusion was interrupted.

Dr. NADIS. Are you saying that this might be associated with external cardiac massage or even that these troubles with air might have developed after cardiac massage?

Dr. VAVTER. It is possible that the evidence for intravital dissection of air may depend on the fact that external massage was used to support the circulation long enough to produce hemorrhages and for air to enter the coronary arteries.

Dr. PEFFER. Then, since you feel that the air embolism may not have developed during the exchange, but after it, we are left with no anatomic explanation for the poor tolerance to the exchange, or, in other words, why the baby died.

Dr. VAVTER. That is what I was trying to imply.

Dr. PEFFER. Now, in relation to your statement about volume changes, I think it is interesting to point out that, quite frequently, while doing the exchange, the baby shows evidence of distress after you have finished injecting the 20 cc. and is likely not to show distress while removing it. I think the injection of blood is something that has to be carried out more slowly than the removal of blood.

It is also important to point out that this is not something that happens to that isolated 1 per cent, but that probably this mechanism is operative in almost all of these babies. If the baby is going enough, or if we are fortunate enough to catch it in time, we get away with it in all but this 1 per cent.

In closing I would make a plea for a bit of common sense in this situation. There is a vast amount of discussion about the figure of 20 mg. per 100 ml. of bilirubin being the magical figure

below which you do not find kernicterus, above which you do, to the point where the nervous obstetrician can look at a baby's report, see that it is 19.5 mg. per 100 ml. and go to bed happily; if he sees 20.5, he calls the pediatrician and says that a quick exchange is needed, or "we will be used if anything happens."

I have had two or three babies die of kernicterus whom I have followed closely. All of them died after one or two exchanges, in which we followed the criteria of trying to keep the level of bilirubin below 20. In other words, they died in spite of exchange transfusion, using the criteria as outlined in the literature. During the same time I have lost at least 12 babies who died as a result of the exchange. I do not wish to imply that 20 mg. per cent is not a useful figure on which to base the need for exchange transfusion. However, I would like to point out a few things. Kernicterus does occur with bilirubin below 20; it occurs very commonly with bilirubin above 30, and third, no one is quite sure that a bilirubin level of 22 or 23 mg. per 100 ml. for a period of 6 hours, or 12 hours, or 22 hours, or 36 hours, is going to produce kernicterus. We do know, however, that exchange transfusion is not a procedure which is to be taken lightly, as is shown by today's case and other cases. I shudder every time people say that exchange transfusion is conservative treatment for erythroblastosis. At times exchange transfusion is the only treatment, but I hate to think that anyone thinks of exchange transfusion as being conservative in borderline cases. The level of 20, therefore, is one which is to be taken as a useful guide and not as an absolute indication. All too frequently pediatricians are pushed by a sense of legal responsibility to do an exchange transfusion when a wait of perhaps 6 to 12 hours might be better for the patient.

This baby obviously needed an exchange, but there are many other babies in whom the indications are less definite. There is one eminent clinician, whom we all respect deeply, who has made the bold statement that he would exchange no full-term baby at any level of bilirubin who did not have blood grouping incompatibility disease. Now, perhaps that is extreme, but it is a very valid viewpoint and indicates a healthy respect for the dangers of this procedure. As Dr. Nadas said, the mechanism of death in these babies is a subject about which we know very little. This subject is a very important one. I think that usually we are lucky in not having such complications more often.

# Myocardial infarction during exchange transfusion in a newborn infant

Myocardial infarction was demonstrated in a newborn infant who developed cardiac failure during an exchange transfusion and died shortly afterward. Possibilities for the pathogenesis of the thrombus are discussed.

Luc G. Van der Hauwaert, M.D., Marcel C. Loos, M.D., and

Luc K. Verhaeghe, M.D.

LOUVAIN, BELGIUM

ALTHOUGH EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION is safe and can be a lifesaving procedure for the treatment of hemolytic disease of the newborn, complications and deaths are occasionally encountered. In a recently reported series of 902 exchange transfusions,¹ the risk of death associated with the procedure was 4 per cent per patient and 3 per cent per transfusion. About one half of the deaths were related to a cardiac arrhythmia which developed during transfusion.

Because myocardial infarction has not been previously described as a complication of exchange transfusion, the following case is being reported. The diagnosis would not have been suspected without electrocardiographic monitoring during the procedure. This observation and a similar complication recently reported,² in which severe electro-

cardiographic changes were attributed to coronary air embolism, may shed some light on the causes of rhythm disturbances and cardiac deaths during exchange transfusion.

# CASE REPORT

This female infant was the fourth-born child of young parents. The first and second child had been normal, but the third pregnancy had resulted in a full-term stillborn infant affected by hemolytic disease. Delivery was induced at 35 weeks because of a rise in maternal Rh antibody titer to 1:64. The infant weighed 3,050 grams at birth. She was edematous, limp, and icteric. The heart rate was slow (90 per minute), and the respirations were irregular and shallow. The liver was felt 4 cm. below the costal margin. The Moro reflex was abnormal. The cord blood bilirubin was 7.5 mg. per cent (0.25 mg. direct bilirubin), hemoglobin 70 per cent, red blood cell count 2.15 million per cubic millimeter. Numerous normoblasts were found in the peripheral blood. The results of the Coombs test were strongly positive.

A few hours after birth the infant became more icteric, but the general condition seemed to

Exchange transfusion with heparinized blood, via the umbilical vein, was carried out when the infant was 3 hours old. Technical difficulties were encountered, and the catheter had to be replaced and manipulated before a satisfactory blood flow could be obtained. As a routine procedure during the transfusion of critically ill infants, the electrocardiogram was monitored throughout the procedure. The pretransfusion tracing (Fig. 1, A) was normal, showing regular sinus rhythm at 160 per minute, a P-Q interval of 0.12 second and a QRS axis of plus 120°.

After 110 c.c. of blood had been exchanged, the infant suddenly became cyanotic and very limp. The respiration became slow and gasping. The ECG revealed 2:1 atrioventricular block with a ventricular rate of 80 per minute and a short episode of complete atrioventricular block (Fig. 1, B). After a few minutes the condition improved, while the ECG (Fig. 1, C) revealed regular sinus rhythm at 170 per minute with a prolonged P-Q interval (0.24 second). The QRS complex was profoundly altered and showed a deep Q wave in II, III, aVr, and an elevation of the ST segment varying from 0.2 to 0.3 mv. in the same leads. These changes were interpreted as a severe disturbance of depolarization, but the possibility of a posterior myocardial infarction was not yet seriously entertained. After an interruption of 30 minutes, the condition had improved and the transfusion was resumed. However, after a total volume of 250 c.c. had been transfused, the procedure had to be abandoned because the heart rate again became irregular and dropped to approximately 30 per minute. The ECG showed recurrence of complete atrioventricular block. The general condition remained precarious and did not respond to the administration of oxygen and intramuscular nikethamide. Later, sinus rhythm with a P-Q distance of 0.14 second was restored, but the deep Q wave and the current of injury in II, III, and aVr remained. Twelve hours after the exchange transfusion the infant suddenly became apneic and died.

Autopsy was restricted to the heart, which weighed 20 grams and had a normal gross appearance. Before any incision was made, the orifices of the coronary arteries were cannulated and a barium sulfate suspension, consisting of 45 parts of Alubar Wander and 55 parts of 10

per cent formaldehyde, was injected by hand under minimal pressure. The size of the particles was 2 x. Roentgenograms were taken on fine grain films (Structuria D2 Gevaert) and magnified to three times the natural size. Subsequently the heart was fixed in formaldehyde. On the angiograms the left coronary artery system was normally distributed and even its smallest ramifications, up to the precapillary level, were seen to fill. The major branch of the right coronary artery was equally normal. Upon close inspection, and after comparing roentgenograms taken in various exposures, it was noted that the terminal arteries of the posterior descending branch of the right coronary artery (according to Spaltebohl's classification the ramus ventriculi sinistri posterior) were not filled with radiopaque material. This branch was the major vessel supplying the posterior part of the left ventricle.

The heart valves appeared normal. A post-mortem thrombus was found in the right atrium. The foramen ovale was widely patent, measuring 4 by 7 mm. The myocardium seemed to be healthy.

The histological examination of the heart was based on multiple transverse sections from the atria to the apex, made by means of a microtome set at a thickness of 7 x. Every twentieth section of the ventricular mass was studied after staining with hematoxylin, eosin, and safranin. The major histological finding was a large zone of fresh infarction involving the subendocardial layers of the posterior and diaphragmatic parts of the left ventricle (Figs. 2A and 2B). The myocardial fibers in this region took a deep eosinophilic stain, and their demarcation from the healthy myocardium was rather sharp. In some places, striation of the muscle fibers was weak; in other infarcted zones it had completely disappeared. The myocardial nuclei were hyperchromic, pyknotic, or karyolytic. Parts of the infarcted area were infiltrated with mononuclear elements and interstitial fluid.

The histological structure of the wall of the coronary arteries was normal throughout. Approximately four fifths of the peripheral arteries and arterioles in the infarcted area contained fresh thrombi which had blocked the passage of the barium sulfate suspension (Fig. 3). All occluded vessels belonged to the same posterior descending branch of the right coronary artery. In the healthy myocardium no blood clots were found, and, as consistently seen with the tech-

nique employed, the barium sulfate suspension entered the smallest arterioles.

# DISCUSSION

The sequence of events suggests that myocardial infarction in this newborn baby, severely affected by hemolytic disease, occurred during, and as a complication of, exchange transfusion. Although the baby was in cardiorespiratory distress, as are most newborn infants with hydrops fetalis, the pretransfusion electrocardiogram was normal. The sudden deterioration while transfusing coincided with the development of electrocardiographic disturbances.

The etiology of this infarction remains unproved. Possibly it was due to a paradoxical coronary embolus. This exceptional form of embolism has been reported in adults. In this patient thrombotic material may have derived from the umbilical vein and reached the heart via the ductus venosus. It is conceivable that a blood clot was dislodged during manipulation of the catheter. Unfortunately the umbilical vein could not be examined, as the autopsy had to be restricted to the heart. The anatomical and hemodynamic requirements for paradoxical embolism were certainly fulfilled. The foramen ovale was widely patent and the physiological pulmonary hypertension of the newborn baby is expected to be associated with relatively high pressure in the right atrium. A further temporary increase of right atrial pressure during transfusion may have produced a right-to-left shunt and passage of an embolus through the foramen ovale.

The alternative explanation is that a thrombus developed in situ, possibly as a result of congestive heart failure and circulatory stasis; the infant presented with hydrops fetalis and was in poor cardiac condition before the transfusion was started.

Electrocardiographic changes during exchange transfusion, similar to the ones described, have recently been reported. The evidence of injury disappeared after 28 minutes and was tentatively attributed to

transient coronary ischemia caused by air embolism. The infant made an uneventful recovery. Unexplained disturbances of rhythm have been observed by many authors. Out of 25 infants who died during or soon after an exchange transfusion, no less than 13 were considered to have died as a result of cardiac arrhythmia,² but unfortunately the electrocardiogram was not monitored in this series and no details concerning the pathology of the myocardium and the coronary vessels were presented. Bradycardia,¹,²,⁸,⁹ prolongation of the P-R interval,² 2:1 atrioventricular block,⁸ cardiac arrest,¹,¹⁰,¹¹ severe tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation⁸ have been encountered during exchange transfusion.

Hogg¹² studied the hearts of 40 infants who died of hemolytic disease, and he found small infarctions in 6 of them. No clinical or electrocardiographic findings were mentioned. However, the infarcts measured only 1 to 2 mm., and it appears unlikely that they played any role in the clinical course and fatal outcome.

Myocardial infarction is extremely rare in the newborn infant. Congenital malformations of the coronary arteries include the aberrant origin of one or both of the coronary arteries from the pulmonary artery. Idiopathic arterial calcification¹³,¹⁴ involving the coronary system is probably the next-to-most frequent cause. Coronary thrombosis in a newborn infant has been attributed to thickening and irregularity of the coronary intima.¹⁵ None of these anatomical changes were found in this patient.

# SUMMARY

A case of fatal myocardial infarction which occurred in a newborn infant during exchange transfusion is reported. Its thrombotic origin was demonstrated by postmortem coronary angiography and histological studies. The etiology remains obscure. Although it is possible that the thrombus developed in situ, the entertained hypothesis is that it resulted from a paradoxical coronary embolus, which had originated from the cannulated umbilical vein.

## Neonatal Peritonitis and Exchange Transfusion

Peritonitis is a fairly uncommon condition in the newborn baby. A. G. Birtch and colleagues¹ saw 99 cases during 25 years at the Children's Medical Center in Boston and P. P. Rickham² saw 17 in three and a half years in Liverpool. About four cases per year were seen, therefore, in two busy neonatal surgical units. Most of these babies had meconium peritonitis, and the usual cause of it is antenatal perforation of the gut above a congenital intestinal obstruction. The clinical picture is that of the obstruction, and the operative treatment and prognosis are not much affected by the presence of meconium in the peritoneum.

Bacterial peritonitis, due generally to a postnatal perforation, is much less common. About half of these cases are due to perforation of a peptic ulcer, as was shown in the excellent review of H. E. Thelander³ in 1939. The majority of other cases are due to intestinal perforations. Very occasionally perforated appendicitis or Meckel's diverticulitis will be seen in the newborn, but most babies with intestinal perforation have an apparently spontaneous lesion of the large, or less often the small, intestine. Perinatal sepsis, trauma, vascular insufficiency, and pressure from faecal masses have all been suggested as possible causes.

It is therefore remarkable that in this issue of the B.M.T. two articles should record 10 examples of this rare and obscure condition following soon after exchange transfusion.

This has only previously been recorded in sporadic cases. Mr. J. J. Corkery and his colleagues, of Sheffield, report four cases at page 345, and Drs. R. L'E. Orme and Sheila M. Eades six cases at page 349. The clinical picture was remarkably consistent. A newborn baby was given one or more exchange transfusions, apparently without technical difficulty. Some hours or days later the baby refused to feed or vomited. Five of the 10 babies passed blood per rectum, and all were found to have abdominal distension. Of the eight children who had an abdominal x-ray three were found to have a pneumoperitoneum and five showed signs of intestinal obstruction.

To the paediatric surgeon these are the essential signs of neonatal peritonitis, of which abdominal distension is the sign which is unfailingly present. The importance of investigating this sign whenever it is seen cannot be overemphasized. The delay which sometimes occurred before transfer to a surgical unit may have been due to a belief that the signs were those of septic umbilical phlebitis, a rare complication of exchange transfusion, but this is unlikely to produce progressive distension and certainly not pneumoperitoneum.

Nine of the 10 children had a laparotomy, which showed a perforation of the colon, and in the tenth child multiple perforations of the bowel were found post mortem. Some complex surgery was needed, and one of the eight survivors required separate resections of jejunum, ileum, and colon. To have achieved these results in a condition with a high mortality is most creditable. There is certainly nothing to be gained by delaying surgery when this condition is suspected.

What remains unsolved is the reason for this association of colonic perforation and exchange transfusion. It seems reasonably certain that the agent must be the catheter in the umbilical vein, and this might produce septic, haemo-

9 November 1968

Leading Articles

BRITISH MEDICAL JOURNAL

341

dynamic, or embolic complications. The cases reported this week are similar to those described by J. E. S. Scott,⁴ and he thought his were due to perinatal sepsis. There seems insufficient evidence on this point, and the suggestion of a Schwartzman type of anaphylactic reaction⁵ is also unproved.

What is certain is that exchange transfusion can seriously affect the circulation of the newborn.⁶ The site of the catheter tip during transfusion is crucial, and J. W. Farquhar and H. Smith firmly recommend that the catheter should never be inserted more than 7-8 cm.⁶ Even so, considerable variations in portal venous pressure still occur with varying rates of injection, and little is known about patency of the ductus venosus or about portal and systemic vascular pressures during transfusion. Systemic hypotension and portal hyper-

tension or embolism could at times occur, and Drs. Orme and Eades reasonably adduce evidence from adult patients that necrotizing enterocolitis may be associated with systemic hypotension. The occurrence of rectal bleeding in five of the ten babies lends support to the concept of a vascular lesion.

It is now necessary to recognize a new complication of exchange transfusion. Why it is rare in comparison with the large number of transfusions given is not yet clear. However, provisional acceptance of the vascular theory of origin certainly emphasizes the importance of scrupulous technique. The ready availability of the umbilical vein in the newborn only makes it the more necessary to remember the call of W. Walker and P. L. Mollison⁷ that exchange transfusion should be recognized as a skilled manoeuvre, to be undertaken only in centres where the necessary experience and skill are always available.

# Colonic Perforation after Exchange Transfusion

J. J. CORKERY,\* M.CH., F.R.C.S., F.R.C.S.I.; V. DUBOWITZ,† M.D., PH.D., B.SC., M.R.C.P., D.C.H.

JAMES LISTER,‡ M.B., F.R.C.S.ED.; A. MOOSA,§ M.B., CH.B.

Brit. med. J., 1968, 4, 345-349

Summary: Four patients are reported in whom perforation of the colon followed exchange transfusion for haemolytic disease of the newborn. This association seems to be more than coincidental, and possibly the perforation is due to a vascular accident occurring as a mechanical result of the exchange transfusion. The insidious onset of colonic perforation may be recognized early by the passage of blood per rectum. There is no place for conservative treatment, and once the diagnosis has been made treatment must include broad-spectrum antibiotics and laparotomy.

# Introduction

Spontaneous perforation of the colon in the neonate is a well-recognized but rare surgical emergency. We wish to report four cases treated at the Children's Hospital, Sheffield, in which the perforation followed exchange transfusion for haemolytic disease of the newborn, to suggest a way in which the transfusion may have led to the perforation, and to indicate some of the difficulties in early diagnosis.

![img-187.jpeg](img-187.jpeg)

# Case 1

This patient was the eighth child of a rhesus-negative mother and a homozygous rhesus-positive father. Four of his siblings had had exchange transfusions because of erythroblastosis foetalis; he was delivered by caesarean section because of delay in the first stage (mother's history) and weighed 5 lb. 5 oz. (2,410 g.) at birth.

When he was 5 hours old an exchange transfusion was performed for haemolytic disease. The abdomen was noted to have been moderately distended at that time and the rectum was empty. At 48 hours a second exchange transfusion was carried out because of a rising serum bilirubin. He tolerated this procedure well but six hours later passed blood per rectum. On the sixth day, because of abdominal distension, abdominal paracentesis was performed and gas and fluid were obtained. He was started on intravenous fluids and antibiotics. The following day he passed changing stools. On the eighth day he was transferred to the paediatric surgical unit of this hospital.

On examination he was moderately jaundiced though well hydrated. The abdomen was distended and there was oedema of the abdominal wall. No masses could be felt in the abdomen, and bowel sounds were absent. Rectal examination revealed a little blood-stained faeces. An x-ray film showed dilated loops of small bowel, but no free gas.

At laparotomy a large collection of faeces was found in the left side of the peritoneal cavity. The small bowel was inspected, and no perforation was found. The proximal transverse colon contained gas. A narrowed segment of bowel was noted in the region of the splenic flexure, but owing to adhesions and sailing could not be examined thoroughly. The actual site of perforation was not located. Peritoneal lavage was performed, a proximal colostomy made, and the abdomen closed with drainage. A swab taken from the peritoneal cavity grew Pseudomonas pyocyanea and Escherichia coli. Postoperatively he was treated with antibiotics, and made a good recovery.

Two months later a barium enema showed "an extremely narrow" segment, about 2 cm. long, proximal to the splenic flexure (Fig. 1). At 10 weeks of age a second laparotomy was performed. Frozen section revealed normal innervation in the rectosigmoid region. The narrow segment of bowel at the splenic flexure was excised and an end-to-end anastomosis was performed. Macroscopic examination failed to reveal a lumen in this narrow segment. A month later his colostomy was closed, and he has made uneventful progress ever since. He was last seen at the age of 2½ years, when he was free of complaints and was developing normally.

FIG. 1.—Case 1. Barium enema through distal limb of transverse colostomy showing a structure at the splenic flexure.

# Case 2

A female child, the second baby of a rhesus-negative mother and a homozygous rhesus-positive father, was born at the Jessop Hospital for Women, Sheffield, following induction of labour at 37 weeks' gestation. Her birth weight was 6 lb. 4 oz. (2,835 g.). The cord bilirubin was 4.6 mg./100 ml., and an exchange transfusion

Apart from a number of mucous vomits she remained well, but at 48 hours her general condition deteriorated rapidly. There was progressive abdominal distension, and she developed peripheral cyanosis and tachycardia. An x-ray film of the abdomen (Fig. 2) showed free gas in the peritoneal cavity, and she was transferred to the paediatric surgical unit.

![img-188.jpeg](img-188.jpeg)

FIG. 2.—Case 2. X-ray film of abdomen showing pneumoperitoneum.

At that stage she was still slightly jaundiced, but was active and not acutely distressed. The abdomen was tensely distended and tympanitic. No masses could be felt. Rectal examination revealed normal meconium. At laparotomy a few hours after admission free gas, pus, and fibrinous exudate were found in the peritoneal cavity. There was no free meconium. A small pinhole perforation was found in the caecum on its antimuscarinic border. Peritoneal lavage was performed and the faecal perforation exteriorized. The affected portion of caecum was excised for biopsy, but unfortunately was lost. A swab taken from the peritoneal cavity grew E. coli. Postoperatively antibiotics were continued, the caecostomy was closed after nine days, and, apart from a pseudomonal infection of her wound, she made a straightforward recovery. When last seen at 10 weeks of age she was gaining weight, and appeared normal in every way.

### Case 3

A male infant, the third child of a rhesus-negative mother, was born at home at full term weighing 7 lb. 13 oz. (3,543 g.). Cord blood bilirubin was 5.0 mg./100 ml., and the Coombs test was positive. Ten hours after birth he was noticed to be jaundiced, and was admitted to hospital. Shortly after this he passed normal meconium. At 24 hours an exchange transfusion was performed because of a rising serum bilirubin and a falling haemoglobin. He tolerated this procedure well, but four hours afterwards passed a small amount of blood and mucus per rectum. Over the next 24 hours his general condition began to deteriorate, and he began to vomit. At 48 hours he was admitted to the paediatric surgical unit.

On admission he was jaundiced (total bilirubin 12 mg./100 ml.) and lethargic. There was moderate distension of the abdomen, and a mass could be felt in the left hypochondrium. This was thought to be an enlarged spleen. An x-ray film of the abdomen (Fig. 3) showed some distended loops of gut with a suggestion of free peritoneal fluid but no free gas. These appearances were thought to represent a paralytic ileus in a septicemic baby. The next day he developed twitchings due to hypocalcaemia, which was

corrected with intravenous calcium gluconate. Because of persistent abdominal distension and aspiration of bile-stained fluid from the stomach, laparotomy was performed when he was 4 days old.

![img-189.jpeg](img-189.jpeg)

FIG. 3.—Case 3. Erect x-ray film of abdomen showing distension of small bowel, with a few fluid levels and a suggestion of free peritoneal fluid. Note the absence of free intraperitoneal gas.

A lot of clear yellow fluid was found in the peritoneal cavity. A large yellow mass in the region of the splenic flexure, corresponding to the mass felt preoperatively, proved to be faeces in the colon, covered only by an extremely thin layer of serosa. There was no trace of the muscular or mucosal layers in the region of the splenic flexure, over an area about 2.5 cm. in diameter. The serosal layer was so thin that immediately an attempt was made to mobilize the affected bowel it burst, and there was gross faecal soiling. There were numerous purplish red patches on the antimuscarinic border of the descending colon distal to the splenic flexure and down to the mid-sigmoid colon. The affected segment of colon was resected. A terminal right transverse colostomy was performed. The distal end of the sigmoid colon was oversewn and dropped back into the peritoneal cavity. A swab from the peritoneal cavity grew E. coli. Culture of a segment of the umbilical vein grew E. coli (same sensitivities as the peritoneal one), Proteus vulgaris, and Streptococcus faecalis. Postoperatively he made a slow but steady recovery. At 6 weeks bowel continuity was restored, and he has remained perfectly well ever since.

### Case 4

A male child was born to a multiparous rhesus-negative woman. Birth weight was 5 lb 2½ oz. (2,340 g.). Cord blood bilirubin was 4.5 mg./100 ml., and exchange transfusion was carried out when he was 4 hours old. He had one apnoeic episode towards the end of this procedure, but recovered spontaneously. At 24 hours another exchange transfusion was done because of a bilirubin level of 24 mg./100 ml. There was no difficulty during this procedure. At 48 hours he passed some blood per rectum, together with normal meconium. At 65 hours a third exchange was done because the bilirubin was again rising. After a further 22 hours he was noted to have abdominal distension, and began to vomit. There were no further bowel movements. Oral fluids were withheld, and the abdominal distension was thought to decrease a little. The next day oral fluids were restarted and retained. There was, however, a slight increase in the degree of abdominal distension. The bilirubin was 24 mg./100 ml. at this stage, but exchange transfusion was not repeated because of his poor general condition. When he was 5 days old his serum bilirubin rose to 28 mg./100 ml., and a fourth exchange transfusion was performed. He seemed a little better after this, and tolerated feeds. On the sixth day the abdominal distension increased rapidly. The bilirubin then was 13.6 mg./100 ml. On the seventh day an x-ray film of his abdomen showed an extensive pneumoperitoneum, and he was transferred to the paediatric surgical unit. Since birth he had had a four-day course of oxytetracycline followed by a combination of penicillin and streptomycin up to the time of admission.

Laparotomy was performed on the seventh day of life. At operation a large amount of gas and faeces was found free in the peritoneal cavity. The whole of the anterior wall of the descending colon was necrotic (Fig. 4). In the sigmoid colon there were a few necrotic spots on the antimesenteric border. The caecum and transverse colon were intact. The affected segment of bowel was excised, and proximal and distal colostomies were performed. A swab from the peritoneal cavity grew Str. faecalis and Pristus vulgaris. Postoperatively he had a very stormy course, and developed extensive sclerena. However, he eventually recovered, and his progress has been satisfactory. At 5 months of age the colostomy was closed and bowel continuity restored.

![img-190.jpeg](img-190.jpeg)

# Histology

The histological appearance of the damaged bowel was similar in the three cases in which material was available for examination. The lesion showed progression from necrosis confined to the epithelium through necrosis involving epithelium and muscle and extending to full-thickness loss. In places there was a mild inflammatory reaction at the edges of the affected areas, together with scattered extravasation of red cells.

# Discussion

# Diagnosis

Spontaneous perforation of the colon in the newborn is rare, and its association with exchange transfusion in four cases seems more than coincidental. It is suggested that the perforations in these cases occurred after second, first, first, and third exchange transfusions, and in retrospect a distinct, diagnostic sequence of events can be recognized. All patients were well at birth apart from their haemolytic disease and a weight of just over 5 lb. (2,270 g.) in two of them; in three the first abnormal sign was the passage of blood per rectum 4 to 15 hours after exchange, and this was followed within 24 hours (in Case 2 within 40 hours of the sole transfusion) by general non-specific deterioration, with lethargy, poor peripheral circulation, abdominal distension, and usually vomiting. The pattern was so recognizable that in our fourth case the diagnosis was made over the telephone to the referring paediatrician 90 miles (130 km.) away. The diagnosis may be confirmed by x-ray films showing free intraperitoneal gas (Fig. 2) or less dramatically showing fluid levels in bowel and a suggestion of free intraperitoneal fluid (Fig. 3). Abdominal paracentesis does not seem to have a place in the diagnosis, though therapeutic aspiration of free intra-abdominal gas may greatly increase the respiratory reserve preoperatively.

# Aetiology

Though rare, spontaneous neonatal colonic perforation has been reported in the literature with many suggested causes. In

small-bowel and large-bowel perforations localized bowel wall defects (von Sury, 1912; Moretti, 1949), primary vascular insufficiency (Paltauf, 1888; Helbing, 1908), and hypertrophy of the crypts of Lieberkühn coupled with thinness of the bowel wall and lymphoid hyperplasia (Boikan, 1930; Lattes, 1943; Maguire and Moore, 1950) have been suggested. In the colon specifically bacterial and fungal infection (Levin and Isaacson, 1960; Waldhausen et al., 1963), meconium and faecal plugs (Zachary, 1957), and haemangiomatous malformations of the bowel wall (Haas, 1958) have been put forward as causes.

Linkner and Benson (1959) reported a neonatal gastric perforation in a child with erythroblastosis without exchange transfusion, and Nienhuis (1963) an intrauterine colonic perforation in a child with haemolytic disease who later required exchange transfusion. However, the association between exchange transfusion and colonic perforation has been noted by Waldhausen et al. (1963), Forshall (1964), and in particular in a well-documented case by Hermann (1965), who suggested that the Shwartzman phenomenon was an aetiological factor. Thomas and Brockman (1966) could find no firm evidence for this theory, and agreed with Waldhausen et al. in placing bacterial infection as the most important causal factor.

That colonic perforation following exchange transfusion should not be grouped with all "spontaneous" perforations in the neonate is suggested by its apparently good prognosis. All our cases survived; so did Hermann's (1965) one case and two of the three cases reported by Wagget (1968). The general mortality of neonatal colonic perforation is very different; of the seven cases of Waldhausen et al. (1963) the only survivor was the one who had had an exchange transfusion, and both patients of Levin and Isaacson (1960) died. Thomas and Brockman (1966) found 26 cases of uncertain aetiology, 17 were operated on, and only eight survived, all after operation; there is no record of whether or not exchange transfusion was associated in these cases.

Studying some of the hazards of exchange transfusion, using a catheter inserted into the umbilical vein, Mintz and Vallbona (1960) demonstrated that in the presence of upper respiratory tract obstruction markedly negative pressures are obtained in the catheterized vein during inspiration. It is common experience during the procedure of exchange transfusion that if the patient strains or cries and the fluid level in the umbilical catheter can be observed the pressure within the umbilical vein can be seen to be raised by forcible expiration. Farquhar and Smith (1958) noted disturbances in 7 out of 19 patients during exchange transfusion. In two patients in whom the catheter was inserted 11 cm. into the umbilical vein, cyanosis of the lower half of the body associated with pallor of the upper half was noted; increased venous filling and retrograde flow in the superficial veins were observed. These indicated that at that time there was a functional obstruction of the inferior vena cava. On withdrawing the catheter these signs subsided spontaneously and apparently without having produced any ill-effects. "Shock"—that is, the infants suddenly became quiet, their body temperature dropped, and they developed some abdominal distension which was not due to hepatomegaly—was noted in three of these cases, and no blood chemistry changes explained this.

The umbilical vein runs, in the free border of the falciform ligament, to join the left branch of the portal vein in the porta hepatis. From the point on the left portal vein opposite this junction the ductus venosus runs on the posterior surface of the liver to join the left hepatic vein just before it enters the inferior vena cava (Johnston and Whillin, 1949). Van Loghem et al. (1949), by catheterizing the umbilical veins of neonatal cadavers under x-ray control, have shown that usually it is easy to pass a catheter through the umbilical vein into the inferior vena cava via the ductus venosus. When the catheter had been inserted to a length of about 12 to 14 cm. it had reached the inferior

Most people who perform exchange transfusion assume that the exchange is of inferior vena cava blood. This may be so, but with the tip of the catheter proximal to the ductus venosus there can be little doubt that some at least of this exchange takes place in the portal circulation. Perhaps in a quiet child in whom there is a low central venous pressure this fraction may be very small, but if the central venous pressure is raised, say, in a restless child, much of the injected blood may enter the portal circulation. Some of this will flow centrally, but some will also flow peripherally and thus raise the portal pressure relatively suddenly. Similarly, a narrow ductus venosus will

However, experimental injection of an opaque medium into the umbilical vein of cadavers has indicated the ease with which the portal venous system may be outlined, as shown in Figs. 5 and 6. That a vascular lesion was primarily responsible for the perforations in the four cases reported here is suggested by the fact that in three of these the passage of blood per rectum was the earliest sign that something was amiss, as it was in two of Wagger's (1968) three cases. This would suggest that a haemorrhagic infarct had occurred at the time of the exchange transfusion. It is suggested that, for one of the reasons already referred to, a vascular catastrophe of some sort (such as severe arteriospasm, venospasm, or sudden occlusion of the venous drainage due to a small retrograde embolus) occurred, resulting in infarction of the bowel wall with perforation, and in Case 1 an ischaemic stricture was produced in the region of the splenic flexure in addition. Further support is lent to this suggestion

in that in the resected specimen in Case 3 there were numerous red patches on the antimesenteric border of the descending colon. These were acutely congested patches that had not actually infarcted, and in Case 4 similar patches in the sigmoid colon actually showed full-thickness necrosis which had not perforated, presumably because of the proximal perforation.

Why these lesions should be more common in the colon than in the small bowel is difficult to explain if the condition is due to vascular changes resulting from back pressure. Cases 1, 3, and 4 perforated in inferior mesenteric vein territory, but Case 2 involved superior mesenteric vein territory, and Schaffer (1960) described a case in which there was an "unexpectedly excellent result" in a "miracle baby" who had two ileal perforations closed at laparotomy, and these occurred after an exchange transfusion. More small-bowel perforations may be reported once the association between bowel perforation and exchange transfusion becomes more appreciated; but it may be that the more complex venous system of the small bowel damps down any sudden rises in portal pressure more effectively than the large-bowel venous system. Continuous monitoring of the injection pressure during exchange transfusion could avoid large and dangerous pressure variations.

## Perforation of the Bowel in the Newborn as a Complication of Exchange Transfusion

R. L'E. ORME,\* M.A., M.R.C.P., D.C.H.; SHEILA M. EADES,† M.R.C.P.ED, D.C.H.

Brit. med. J., 1968, 4, 349-351

Summary: Spontaneous perforation of the bowel without evidence of intestinal obstruction is reported in six infants who had exchange transfusions for rhesus incompatibility, and in a seventh who had prolonged intravenous fluids via the umbilical vein. The pathological findings resemble those found in acute necrotizing enterocolitis in adults, which is known to be associated with arterial hypotension. The cause in these infants may also be due to a period of hypotension during the transfusion, and hypoxia and superimposed infection may also play an important part.

### Introduction

"Spontaneous" perforation of the bowel in the newborn, where perforation occurs in the absence of intestinal obstruction, was first described by Siebold (1826). Thelander (1939) reviewed the world literature up to 1939. Of her 85 cases 65 occurred in the neonatal period. Thomas and Brockman (1966) found 26 further cases in the colon between 1946 and 1965, and Fonkalarud et al. (1966) reported 19 cases of "spontaneous" perforation in a study of neonatal peritonitis. Some of the earlier cases may have been associated with meconium ileus due to cystic fibrosis or Hirschsprung's disease.

We describe six cases of "spontaneous" perforation in newborn infants who had had exchange transfusions shortly beforehand.

### Case 1

A male infant weighing 3.2 kg. was delivered normally following induction at 36 weeks. The mother's blood group was O negative

- Senior Registrar in Paediatrics, Devon and Easter Clinical Area.
  † Consultant Paediatrician, Devon and Easter Clinical Area.

with rhesus antibodies present 1 in 40. There was no asphyxia at birth. Cord blood results were: group O positive; Coombs test positive; Hb 70%; bilirubin 9.7 mg./100 ml. Three exchange transfusions were carried out without difficulty in the first 48 hours, calcium supplements being given. No antibiotics were used.

At the age of 34 hours he became reluctant to feed and passed small quantities of bright blood rectally. Abdominal distension developed. Bowel sounds were normal. At 72 hours periumbilical oedema and erythema developed. Portal vein thrombosis was suspected. An abdominal x-ray picture was suggestive of ileus. There was no gas under the diaphragm.

Laparotomy at 150 hours showed faecal peritonitis with two perforations of the large bowel, in the caecum and descending colon. The affected bowel was resected and an ileostomy fashioned. Postoperative recovery was good. Microscopy (Fig. 1) showed an acute colitis with extensive necrosis of the mucosa and submucosa. Associated vessels were thrombosed, but it was not possible to say whether this was primary or secondary.

### Case 2

A male infant weighing 3 kg. was delivered by lower segment caesarean section for foetal distress after induction at 38 weeks. The liquor was meconium-stained. The infant had white asphyxia and required endotracheal oxygen for resuscitation. Maternal blood group: A negative, with antibodies 1 in 20. Cord blood: group O positive; Coombs test positive; Hb 85%. Exchange transfusion was carried out at three hours with calcium supplements. Strontomycin was given.

At the age of 4 days the infant developed bilious vomiting and passed blood and mucus rectally. Abdominal distension, grunting respiration, and periumbilical oedema and erythema followed. Bowel sounds were absent and peritonitis was suspected. An x-ray film of the abdomen showed gas under the diaphragm. At operation three large perforations were found in the sigmoid colon. The affected bowel was resected with an end-to-end anastomosis.

### Case 3

This female infant weighing 3 kg. had a normal delivery at 38 weeks. There was no birth asphyxia. The mother's blood group was rhesus negative with antibodies. Cord blood results: Coombs test strongly positive; Hb 82%; bilirubin 3.2 mg./100 ml. An exchange transfusion was carried out at two hours. Oxygen was required during the procedure. On the fourth day abdominal distension and bilious vomiting developed. She continued to pass meconium but no blood. X-ray examination of the abdomen showed fluid levels. At operation multiple gangrenous areas of bowel necessitated resection of 6 in. (15 cm.) of jejunum, 7 in. (17.5 cm.) of ileum, and 7 in. (17.5 cm.) of transverse colon. Postoperative recovery was excellent, and when last seen, aged 3 years, she was well. Microscopy showed extensive necrosis of the mucosa, which extended into the submucosa and in places through the entire wall. Haemorrhage into the coats of the gut and a mononuclear exudate into the serosa were found. There was no evidence of mesenteric thrombosis. The appearances were compatible with a diagnosis of acute necrotizing enterocolitis.

### Case 4

This infant, a female weighing 2.6 kg., was severely asphyxiated at birth and required two exchange transfusions for rhesus incompatibility. At the age of 4 days she developed vomiting and abdominal distension but still passed meconium. A straight x-ray film of the abdomen did not show obstruction. The symptoms subsided and she was discharged home at two weeks. However, vomiting and frequent loose motions recurred later, and x-ray films now showed fluid levels. A barium enema demonstrated an ileocolic fistula. At operation two loops of ileum and jejunum were adherent to the splenic flexure. Each of these communicated separately with the lumen of the colon. The affected length of colon was excised and the holes in the small bowel were closed. Microscopy showed that the perforations were lined by necrotic tissue infiltrated with acute inflammatory cells. The intramural

nerve plexuses were normal. Subsequent rectal biopsy confirmed this.

### Case 5

A female infant weighing 2.1 kg. was delivered normally following induction at 34 weeks. Maternal group A negative with antibodies 1 in 256. Cord blood results: group A positive; Coombs test positive; Hb 92%; bilirubin 4.5 mg./100 ml. Exchange transfusions were carried out on the third and fourth days, the first with some difficulty. Signs of intestinal obstruction now developed, with vomiting and abdominal distension, which was treated conservatively with gastric aspiration and intravenous fluids. After an initial improvement she collapsed and died. Necropsy showed multiple perforations of the bowel.

### Case 6

This male infant weighing 2.4 kg. was delivered normally. The maternal blood group was rhesus negative with antibodies. Cord blood: Coombs test positive; Hb 84%; bilirubin 3.5 mg./100 ml. Two exchange transfusions were performed, at 41 and 65 hours. At the age of 6 days bilious vomiting and abdominal distension developed. Bowel sounds were absent. At laparotomy a large perforation of the transverse colon was found and closed. Postoperative recovery was complicated by a faecal fistula. At the age of 3 months a second episode of obstruction was found to be due to adhesions and a Richter's hernia of the proximal duodenum. Since the second operation he has thrived. Pathological findings are not available.

We also record a seventh case in which prolonged intravenous fluids via the umbilical vein were given, but no exchange transfusion.

### Case 7

This infant, a male weighing 1.5 kg., was born into a bucket in a caravan. On his admission the rectal temperature was 82° F. (27.8° C.), pulse 80. The temperature rose to 92° F. (33.3° C.) over eight hours. Antibiotics were given.

At 12 hours he became apnoeic and was treated with intermittent positive-pressure respiration and dextrose via umbilical vein catheter. A chest x-ray film showed hyaline membrane appearances. On the third day jaundice developed, the bilirubin reaching 12 mg./100 ml. No blood group incompatibility was demonstrated. Attempts to wean the infant off the respirator failed and he died aged 7 days. Necropsy revealed a perforation of the ileum, and microscopy showed non-specific inflammation and necrosis, reported by the pathologist as similar to those in Case 1.

We have found four other cases associated with exchange transfusion in the literature (Nienhuis, 1963; Waldhausen et al., 1963; Hermann, 1965; Schaffer, 1963). In Nienhuis's case the perforation was thought to have occurred in utero and thus would have preceded the transfusion.

### Clinical Manifestations

Though spontaneous perforation of the bowel in the newborn is well documented we believe insufficient emphasis has been laid on the early manifestations, which may lead to a mistaken diagnosis. We think it helpful to divide these into two groups, early and late, as follows:

- (a) Early.—(1) Refusal to feed. (2) Passage of blood and mucus rectally. (3) Abdominal distension. (4) Bilious vomiting. (5) Absent bowel sounds. X-ray examination of the abdomen may be normal at this stage or show distended loops of bowel (Case 1 and the case described by Hermann, 1965).
- (b) Later, after perforation has occurred.—(1) Erythema and oedema of the anterior umbilical wall. This may suggest a diagnosis of umbilical sepsis and cellulitis, or portal pyaemia and thrombosis in a baby who has had umbilical catheterization. (2) Grunting. (3) Pallor. (4) Hypothermia. (5) Peripheral circulatory failure. X-ray examination of the abdomen now shows gas under the diaphragm.

## Discussion

The aetiology of this condition has never been satisfactorily elucidated. A variety of possible causes have been suggested, including congenital weakness of the bowel wall (Rudnew, 1915; Fischer, 1928; Bolkan, 1930) and trauma (Fonkalsrud et al., 1966). Infection, either generalized septicaemia or primary peritonitis, has been incriminated (Waldhausen et al., 1963; Hermann, 1965; Thomas and Brockman, 1966). Hypoxia due to asphyxia or the respiratory distress syndrome is a factor (Lloyd et al., 1964; Thelander, 1939).

We think that in our cases the association between exchange transfusion and subsequent perforation is more than coincidental and that the cause is likely to be vascular, related to local vasomotor disturbances, or systemic hypotension exacerbated by hypoxia.

The term "necrotizing enterocolitis" has been used to describe the pathological findings in these infants (Waldhausen et al., 1963; Hermann, 1965; Fonkalsrud et al., 1966). The lesions in this condition are diffuse non-specific areas of necrosis with acute inflammation, which has not followed obstruction to a major blood vessel supplying the bowel. Hermann (1965) believed that this was due to an anaphylactic reaction of the Shwartzman type. This requires a sensitizing dose of antigen locally, followed after an interval by a second dose intravenously, causing necrosis at the site of the sensitizing dose. In this case sensitization of the bowel wall by bacteria could occur during colonization of the bowel. Umbilical catheterization later could introduce further bacteria into the circulation.

However, necrotizing enterocolitis has been widely described in elderly adults, and in them its association with hypotension is well recognized. McGovern and Goulston (1965) described 33 cases of "ischaemic enterocolitis," in 19 of which hypotension was recognized before the onset of symptoms, and in another seven in which they considered there was microscopical evidence of hypotension in the form of zonal necrosis of the liver or epithelial necrosis in the proximal zonal tubules. Kay et al. (1958) described another 16 cases, all of which were associated with an acute hypotensive episode, though these authors suspected that the colitis preceded rather than followed the hypotension. Marston (1962) has postulated that, as arterioles obey Laplace's law, the smaller the blood vessel the narrower is the margin between rupture on the one hand and collapse on the other. Small falls in pressure in the mesenteric vessels can therefore exceed the critical closing pressure of minute vessels in the bowel wall and cause widespread shutdown. Because these vessels vary in length and position, and are affected by the tone and diameter of the bowel wall, the resulting changes may be patchy.

We can find no recorded evidence of systemic blood-pressure readings during exchange transfusion. We are endeavouring in this unit to monitor the blood pressure in the aorta during the procedure in some cases and hope to present our findings in a future paper.

Another possibility (Kay et al., 1958) is that the anatomy of the vessels in the bowel wall is such that shunting may take place, bypassing the mucosa. Such shunts are well recognized in the lung, and in the respiratory distress syndrome hypoxia increases the flow through the shunt. It is interesting to speculate that hypoxia might have a similar effect on shunts in the bowel wall. Once ischaemia has occurred bacteria in the bowel could proliferate and invade the bowel wall and the effect of their endotoxins might be superimposed. Coliform endotoxins are sympathomimetic, and, possibly by potentiating adrenaline, can bring about further vasoconstriction and ischaemia of the bowel wall (Lillehei, 1957).

## Exchange Transfusion and Perforation

SIR,—We were interested to read the reports of Mr. J. J. Corkery and others (9 November, p. 345) and Drs. R. L'E. Orme and Sheila M. Eades (p. 349) on perforation of the bowel in the newborn period as a complication of exchange transfusion. Perforation, however, is only the most dramatic result of mesenteric vascular occlusion, and is not inevitable.

At a meeting of the South West Paediatric Club on 26 May this year, and again at a meeting of the Neonatal Society in London on 17 October, we presented six personally studied cases of neonatal gut infarction. Two of our cases had been preceded by at least one prolonged and technically

difficult exchange transfusion. In the first of these two cases there was a positive blood culture for E. coli associated with bowel necrosis extending from the caecum to the descending colon. Our second case had diarrhoea for seven days, which preceded the onset of abdominal distension and peripheral circulatory collapse owing to necrosis and perforation of the terminal ileum only. Unfortunately both these infants died without laparotomy being undertaken, and at necropsy we were able to demonstrate antemortem thrombi in the ductus venosus and portal vein in the first and in the portal and splenic

veins in the second. We note that in the series quoted there is no comment on the state of the portal vein in those infants who died. A fuller report is being prepared for publication.—We are, etc.,

E. S. MUCKLOW.

# Spontaneous Perforation of the Bowel in the Newborn Following Exchange Transfusion

W. R. CASTOR, M.D.,\* Port Arthur, Ont.

RECAUSE of the increasing number of reported cases, perforation of the gastrointestinal tract in the newborn must be considered more common than was once acknowledged. Without early recognition and immediate operation there is little chance of the infant's survival.

The term "spontaneous" is restricted to those cases occurring within the neonatal period, not associated with a more distal obstruction or known incident of trauma, such as perforation of the rectum by a thermometer or of the colon by a cleansing or barium enema. Various theories of etiology for spontaneous bowel rupture have been suggested, such as mural defects, peptic ulceration, laceration from birth trauma, meconium stasis and infection. A smaller group, composed chiefly of those cases in which the distal ileum and colon are involved, has not been explained.

This presentation reports two cases of colon perforation following exchange transfusion in erythroblastotic newborn infants. Reported instances of spontaneous perforation of the gut in the first 14 days of life are surveyed in order to demonstrate the similar clinical features and radiographic findings, despite the apparent variations in cause.

Case 1.—The mother was 52 years old, para III, gravida, IV, Group A, Rh-negative, with mild dia-

\*Radiologist, Department of Radiology, The General Hospital of Port Arthur, Port Arthur, Ontario.
Reprint requests to: Dr. W. R. Castor.

betes. At the 30th week of gestation and again at the 34th week Rh antibodies were present with a titre of 1:8. Amniocentesis at the 34th week recovered fluid of optical density that placed it in Liley's mid-zone. Because of the diabetes and the presence of antibodies it was considered advisable to induce labour when the 37th week was reached. Spontaneous delivery of a male child weighing 9 lbs. 8 oz. followed the administration of an intravenous oxytocin drip. The infant was Rh-positive and the direct Coombs' test was negative. The cord blood showed a bilirubin of 7.8 mg. per 100 ml. and the hemoglobin was 20.2 g. Jaundice was evident in the child at birth; the following day the bilirubin rose to 16 mg. and the indirect Coombs' test was positive. No abnormal abdominal findings were apparent. By the third day the bilirubin was 22 mg. per 100 ml. An exchange transfusion was given, using 500 c.c. of Group O blood. The umbilical venous pressure was recorded as 8 cm. of water at the commencement and 30 cm. of water during the exchange transfusion. On the fourth day the infant's stool was streaked with blood; later in the evening the child was irritable and refused its feeding, and its rectal temperature was 101° F.

Early in the morning of the next day abdominal distension, bile-stained vomiting and respiratory distress became evident. Radiographs demonstrated marked pneumoperitoneum (Fig. 1). Operation was performed without delay. A perforation of the transverse colon was repaired and a colostomy performed. From the margin of the perforation gangrenous tissue was obtained and a swab from the abdominal cavity resulted in moderate growth of E. coli. The infant tolerated the procedure well; the colostomy was subsequently closed and the patient discharged from hospital.

CASE 2.—A 36-year-old woman, para V, gravida VI, Rh-negative, presented with symptoms suggestive of acute pelvic inflammatory disease. A pregnancy test gave a positive result. A Papanicolaou smear from the cervix was positive and at the twelfth week of gestation conization of the cervix was performed. The pathologist reported carcinoma in situ with no evidence of invasion. The pregnancy continued uneventfully to term and the patient was delivered spontaneously of a female infant weighing 6 lbs. 7 oz. Some jaundice was noticed; the cord blood gave a positive Coombs' test, the bilirubin was 8.2 mg. per 100 ml. and the hemoglobin was 10.7 g. There was some suspicion of a congenital cardiac anomaly. Eight hours after birth an exchange transfusion of 440 ml. was given, and 460 ml. was removed, the deficit being allowed because of increased right-sided pressure. Following this the bilirubin was 7.0 mg. and the hemoglobin 13.4 g. On the third day, because the bilirubin had risen to 15.5 mg. with a fall in hemoglobin to 10.7 g., a repeat exchange transfusion was necessary, during which slight cardiac embarrassment occurred. Thirty-six hours later the baby refused its feeding, the abdomen became distended and free air within the abdomen became apparent by radiography (Fig. 2). An operation was performed within 12 hours and disclosed gangrene of the left transverse colon extending down to the sigmoid region, with multiple perforations. Resection of the diseased bowel and colostomy were necessary. Microscopic examination of the surgical specimen showed marked congestion of all vessels and early infarction in one area. The

serosa and attached mesentery were edematous with acute inflammatory infiltration. Inflammatory cells were present throughout the bowel wall and the mucosa was superficially ulcerated. Culture of the swab from the infant's abdominal cavity yielded a scanty growth of staphylococci and diphtheroid bacilli. The colostomy was closed within four weeks and the baby was later discharged from hospital.

The following illustrative cases have been collected from the literature:

CASE 3.¹⁸—A full-term male infant received an exchange transfusion at 4 hours and a second at 48 hours. On the fourth day abdominal distension and pneumoperitoneum were evident. An operation within 24 hours revealed perforation of the terminal ileum. Two days later re-operation was necessary after recurrence of the clinical picture of perforation and two more ileal perforations were repaired. The infant survived.

CASE 4.²⁴—On the second day following an exchange transfusion for Rh incompatibility, marked abdominal distension became apparent and there was radiographic evidence of fluid within the abdomen. No mention of pneumoperitoneum is made in the description of the case. At operation, perforations of the transverse colon were present. Because of the extent of the disease, resection of the terminal ileum, ascending colon and transverse colon was necessary. The patient survived.

# CLINICAL FINDINGS

Generally, there is no indication at birth that
anything is amiss, as the infant is usually
vigorous and healthy in appearance. One to five
days later the neonate possibly refuses feeding
and abdominal distension develops, frequently
followed by severe respiratory distress. Some
cases show blood in the stool before the appearance of the distension. The diagnosis is confirmed by radiographic evidence of pneumoperitoneum.

# RADIOLOGICAL FINDINGS

In the supine view of Case 1 massive intraperitoneal free air is apparent as it outlines the
peritoneal cavity and is divided centrally by the
faint linear shadow of the falciform ligament
(Fig. 1). On the erect film the gas is seen to have
accumulated above the liver and spleen with
elevation of the diaphragm. In Case 2 a chest
study before perforation included an anteroposterior recumbent and lateral projection using
a horizontal beam, and failed to demonstrate
pneumoperitoneum. From the emergency plain
film of the abdomen (Fig. 2a) radiographic
indications of pneumoperitoneum are more
subtle. The air-dome sign is present, as is the
falciform ligament sign, while the evidence from
the erect view (Fig. 2b) is pathognomonic of
free air.

The literature calls attention to the radiographic signs of free air on the anteroposterior
supine view; several of these are mentioned,
such as the air-dome sign, 19 the falciform liga-

It is partly under-exposed, obscuring the already subtle and frequently unfamiliar signs of free air beneath the dome of the abdomen, and a second view would be most desirable as a safety factor. Minute amounts of free air are best detected by an erect film, but when there is perforation of the bowel a large volume of air is present, which is a strong argument for the routine use of recumbent projections with the x-ray tube in a horizontal plane, so that no manipulation of the baby is required.

Gas may be present within the abdomen secondary to pneumomediastinum, having been compressed from the mediastinum into the perivascular spaces and into the retroperitoneal region,⁴ but this is usually not a diagnostic problem. Purposely to demonstrate gas within the scrotum, to which it makes its way through the open processus vaginalis,⁴ is unnecessary and increases gonadal irradiation. Gas may be present in the portal vein in cases of severe necrosis of the colon but also, as demonstrated by Schmidt,²⁰ following administration of fluid via the umbilical vein.

# DISCUSSION

All the cases of spontaneous perforation of the bowel that have been reviewed present in a way that is strikingly similar and show similar radiographic findings, although no common pathogenesis has been described. In cases other than those involving the stomach, enterocolitis and necrosis are repeatedly demonstrated at operation or autopsy; it is curious why rupture is seen most commonly in the colon and so infrequently in the small bowel, except for the terminal ileum. To account for the distribution of the lesion in the gastrointestinal tract, the portal vein appears to be a common denominator. Its hemodynamics are altered during an exchange transfusion and, in essence, reversal of the physiologic process occurs. But other local factors must exist in the bowel wall; otherwise the incidence of spontaneous rupture of the bowel would be much greater in association with exchange transfusions. Swenson²³ has pointed out that infants with Hirschsprung's disease are prone to enterocolitis which may lead to perforation, and in cases of meconium plug syndrome, necrosis may develop in the adjacent bowel wall. In our cases, no abnormality of the alimentary tract was suspected at birth and the baby survived surgical correction of the perforation with no such abnormality becoming apparent later.

Table II indicates the relationship of the age of the majority of patients at perforation to the postnatal period of transition within the portal circulation. Meyer and Lind⁸ found that functional closure of the ductus venosus occurs during the first minute of life owing to the decrease in pressure with the cessation of placental blood flow, while organic closure may not be completed until the twentieth day. With the beginning of intestinal function, blood flow through the portal vein increases considerably, while there is a distinct alteration from the oxygenated placental blood. The same authors claim that acute pathological lesions can be observed as a consequence of the postnatal change in liver circulation.⁹ According to Potter,¹⁰ acute necrosis of the liver unaccompanied by evidence of infection is not uncommon in young infants, especially newborns, and the amount of involvement varies. Potter describes similar changes suggestive of infarction following exchange transfusions, where partial thrombosis of the ductus venosus was found. The colon that was removed in Case 2 had an appearance very similar to that described in other reported cases. An area of early infarction was present; the veins were congested while the arteries were relatively unremarkable (Fig. 3). In some cases reported as necrotizing enterocolitis,¹,²⁴ the pathological description resembles that of our case. According to Robbins,¹⁷ occlusion of venous return will lead to infarction in about 18 hours. The macroscopic changes progress from intense congestion with a dusky red to purple hue, and a fibrinosuppurative, somewhat granular exudate appears later, followed by ulceration of the mucosa which is inevitably complicated by secondary bacterial contamination. Perforation of the wall may occur within the next two or three days. Any stage of the process may be seen, depending on the duration.

demonstrated that in only 3 out of 30 cases of blind placement (without radiological guidance) did the tip of the catheter enter the inferior vena cava. Rudolph et al.,¹⁸ when cumulating the right atrium using the umbilical vein, found that there is a tendency for the catheter to enter the portal vein. In both of our cases of exchange transfusion a high right-sided pressure was noticed.

It is reasonable to assume that transient portal hypertension, or even stasis in one or more tributaries of the portal vein, can be present, causing venous thrombosis and/or hemorrhagic infarction in a small or large portion of the bowel. Why the terminal ileum and colon are most often affected in cases associated with erythroblastosis is not apparent, and whether erythroblastosis is a primary cause cannot be determined from the series reported.⁷,¹¹,¹⁹ Potter¹² notes intestinal tract lesions in erythroblastosis which she attributes to replacement of Peyer's patches by erythropoietic cells. I would rather conclude that a complication of portal fetal circulation and/or the exchange transfusion is responsible. Neonatal portal vein thrombosis can occur as a complication of exchange transfusion¹³ or independently of it.² Furthermore, increased frequency of bowel perforation is not reported in erythroblastotic babies who have not received exchange transfusion, while on the other hand seven cases following exchange transfusions are on record. It is more difficult to assign this pathogenesis to Case 7, as the process appeared to have occurred before delivery, but the interference with the cord circulation may be of significance.

Surgical correction of the condition is mandatory and should be performed as soon as possible; bowel resection and temporary colostomy are frequently necessary. A grave prognosis is suggested by the perusal of the literature, but the majority of the reported cases which were associated with erythroblastosis survived. Case 5 was an exception, but operation was not performed. Of six cases of perforation with necrotizing colitis reported by Waldhausen, Herendeen and King,²⁴ the lone survivor was an erythroblastotic baby.

CASTOR: EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION 939

Summary Two cases of spontaneous perforation of the colon following exchange transfusions for erythroblastosis are described. Five additional cases have been reported in the literature and these are briefly described. The importance of the radiological signs of pneumoperitoneum in the newborn and the need for prompt surgery to repair or resect the necrotic bowel are emphasized. It is postulated that the condition may be a complication of the transition in the fetal portal circulation following delivery and/or a complication of the exchange transfusions.

Résumée L'auteur présente deux cas de perforation spontanée consécutive à une exsanguine-transfusion pour érythroblastose. Il passe brièvement en revue les cinq cas supplémentaires qui ont été cités dans la littérature. Il souligne l'importance des signes de pneumopéritoire chez le nouveau-né et la nécessité d'une correction chirurgicale rapide ou de la résection de la portion d'intestin nécrusé. Il émet l'hypothèse que cette pathologie peut être une complication de la transition dans la circulation porte du fétus après l'accouchement ou une complication des transfusions sanguines d'échange, ou, peut-être des deux procédés.

# Bowel perforation after exchange transfusion in

# the neonate: Review of the literature and report of a case

J. M. CARALPS-RIERA, M.D.

B. D. COHN, M.D., F.A.A.P.

BROOKLYN, N. Y.

From the Departments of Surgery, Maimonides

Medical Center and State University of New York

Downstate Medical Center

Bowel perforation following exchange transfusion in the neonate has often been designated as idiopathic. However, review of the reported cases and a recent experience in our institution suggest that exchange transfusion itself may be an etiologic factor.

# ETIOLOGY

Several possible pathogenetic mechanisms in bowel gangrene and perforation in the newborn infant following exchange transfusion have been discussed previously.

Sudden pressure increase in the portal system. If the baby cries or strains, the pressure in the inferior vena cava may suddenly rise, and if the catheter tip is proximal to the ductus venosus, retrograde flow into the portal system may result.²

Hypoxia or hypotension. Either condition may precipitate widespread small-vessel collapse or arteriovenous shunting to protect the cerebral and coronary blood supply.¹¹ Resultant bacterial growth may compromise the integrity of the bowel wall; coliform endotoxins, in particular, are known to have sympathomimetic effects.¹

Schwartzman reaction localized to the bowel. This possibility was pointed out by Hermann.³

Embolism from the umbilical vein. This appears to be the least likely of the proposed mechanisms.⁶

In the cases reviewed, clear-cut hypoxic episodes during or preceding exchange trans-

Received for publication April 24, 1970.

Vol. 68, No. 5, pp. 895-898

fusion were present in only 11 patients. However, the blood pressure was not continuously monitored; therefore, it is not possible to determine the significance of hypoxia as an etiologic factor in the reported cases. In most of the patients, there was no record of the pressure at which the blood was transfused, and donor or umbilical vein blood specimens obtained before or after transfusion were not cultured.

Although the evidence in favor of hypoxia as the most likely etiologic factor is not conclusive, this appears to be the most reasonable possibility, either as the primary cause or as the result of increased portal pressure or hypotension.

# CLINICAL MATERIAL

To date, 20 cases of bowel perforation after exchange transfusion have been reported; this literature includes the present case.²⁻⁵, ¹⁰, ¹¹, ¹²⁻¹⁶ In three instances, the sex of the patient was not reported; of the remaining 17, 11 were male and 6 were female. Eleven patients had multiple transfusions, with five being the maximum. Nine presented with multiple perforations. No relationship between the number of transfusions and the number of perforations could be recognized. The interval between transfusion and perforation varied from a few hours to four days.

The colon was affected in 14 instances,²⁻⁵, ¹⁰, ¹¹, ¹⁴ the small and large bowel in four,¹¹, ¹⁴, ¹⁵ and the terminal ileum alone in one.¹³

Pediatric surgery

Surgical exploration was undergone by 18 patients. The infants' ages at this time ranged from a few hours to 28 days. All but two of these patients survived. One died of pulmonary complications on the eighth postoperative day; the other, who had been treated conservatively for 28 days before laparotomy, died during the immediate postoperative period.

Two patients were treated conservatively. One died, and the autopsy findings disclosed multiple perforations involving the small and large bowel.¹¹ The other baby was reported to have recovered.¹¹ However, since proof of the diagnosis and follow-up data were not presented, it is difficult to accept this as a case in which conservative treatment of bowel perforation was successful.

# DIAGNOSIS

Bowel gangrene should be suspected in any newborn infant in whom abdominal distention develops after exchange transfusion. The bowel sounds may be absent or hypoactive and the abdomen tender. The patient may vomit bilious or mucous material, and blood may be present in the stool.

Pneumoperitoneum seen in an abdominal plain film confirms the diagnosis. Several patterns of intraperitoneal air distribution have been described: the air dome sign,⁸ the falciform ligament sign,⁹ the football sign,¹⁰ and air in the scrotum.⁸,⁹ The presence of gas in the portal vein branches cannot be considered as diagnostic of bowel gangrene secondary to vascular abnormality because it has also been seen following the administration of fluids via the umbilical vein.

# TREATMENT

Emergency treatment consists of intubation for nasogastric suction, rehydration, and intravenous antibiotics. Until culture reports become available, penicillin and kanamycin offer broad coverage. If pneumoperitoneum is present, needle paracentesis may facilitate respiratory exchange.

If perforation is suspected, laparotomy is mandatory. The surgical procedure depends

upon the findings. Primary resection and anastomosis, with or without diverting colostomy, diverting colostomy alone, ileostomy, Hartmann procedure, and suture of the perforation, with or without proximal colostomy, have been done. Irrigation of the peritoneal cavity with antibiotic solution may help to prevent postoperative complications.

# PATHOLOGY

Microscopic examination of the resected bowel has disclosed essentially similar findings, varying from areas of mucosal ulceration and inflammatory changes in all layers of the wall to necrosis and perforation. Areas of congestion in the antimesenteric border, with or without infarction, have also been present in most specimens.

# PROPHYLAXIS

The possibility of bowel damage from exchange transfusion must be kept in mind. The use of a radiopaque catheter¹⁰ or injection of contrast material will allow placement of the catheter in the inferior vena cava. The administration of a sedative prevents sudden increase in inferior vena cava pressure. Also helpful in reducing the hazards of the procedure are meticulous aseptic technique and culture reports on umbilical vein blood specimens taken before and after transfusion.

# CASE REPORT

A male infant was delivered after 40 weeks' gestation by low forceps extraction. The mother was 21 years old and para 2-1-0-3. The baby's Apgar score was 9 at one minute and 10 at five minutes. The mother's blood type was Rh negative. The antibody titer had increased from 1:16 on March 26, 1969, to 1:256 by August 21.

Physical examination indicated that the infant was full term and in no distress. When the baby was nine hours of age, jaundice was observed. The baby's blood type was A, Rh positive. The Coombs test gave a value of 3+. The serum bilirubin level was 2.8 mg. per 100 ml.; twelve hours later, it was 7.2 mg. per 100 ml. (direct, 0.4) and at 2 P.M., 9.7 mg. per 100 ml. Exchange transfusion was performed when the infant was 21 hours of age and the serum bilirubin level was 10.4 mg. per 100 ml. The procedure was well tolerated.
