On the next day, the patient was still jaundiced and less active; the sucking reflex was poor but the baby cried lustily. A nasogastric tube was passed and the baby was given glucose in water.

On the following day, three days after birth, the patient was lethargic, manifested a poor sucking reflex, and did not tolerate feedings. At 10 P.M., the baby's abdomen was very distended and the bowel sounds were absent. The temperature at this time was 100.4° F., the heart rate, 180 beats per minute, and the respiratory rate, 52 per minute. The passage of a rectal tube did not relieve the distention. Gastric suction yielded a small quantity of greenish mucoid material. The stool gave a 2+ positive reaction to the guaiac test. There was tenderness and rebound tenderness in the lower abdominal quadrants.

An x-ray examination of the abdomen disclosed free air under both hemidiaphragms. To improve the baby's respirations, an abdominal tap was done and 100 c.c. of air removed. Intravenous administration of fluids was started and penicillin and kanamycin were given. Blood cultures taken before and after exchange transfusion were negative.

Laparotomy was performed eight hours later, when the infant was 3 days and 9 hours old, and about 200 c.c. of fecaloid material were removed from the peritoneal cavity. The colon from the splenic flexure to the distal sigmoid was gangrenous with a large antimesenteric perforation of the sigmoid colon. After a left hemicolectomy was performed, an end-transverse colostomy with a sigmoid mucous fistula was fashioned. The peritoneal cavity was irrigated with a four percent kanamycin solution.

Pathological examination disclosed recent hemorrhagic infarction in the specimen, with marked peritonitis; the presence of ganglion cells was noted.

The colostomy started functioning 20 hours after the operation; by the fourth day, full-strength formula was being given. The baby remained afebrile and the reflexes were normal. On the seventh day, a subcutaneous wound infection was noted and the skin opened; the wound was irrigated with saline solution and packed. Escherichia coli grew in cultures taken from the wound. On the twenty-ninth postoperative day the patient was discharged. Continuity of the bowel is to be re-established eventually.

### SUMMARY

Review of reported cases of bowel perforation following exchange transfusion in the neonate suggests that the blood replacement procedure per se may be a factor in the etiology of this complication.

Of the proposed pathogenetic mechanisms, hypoxia of the bowel, either as the primary event or secondary to hypotension, appears to be the most likely factor in most instances. The diagnosis should be suspected whenever abdominal distention develops following exchange transfusion. Pneumoperitoneum in an abdominal plain film is diagnostic of the condition.

Laparotomy is mandatory if perforation is suspected. The pathologic findings in specimens of resected bowel are essentially similar, ranging from mucosal ulceration and inflammatory changes affecting all layers of the bowel wall to necrosis and perforation.

To the 19 previously reported cases is added that of a male infant in whom signs of abdominal distress developed approximately two days after exchange transfusion. The infant responded well to colectomy and end-transverse colostomy.

# Neonatal Colonic Perforation After Exchange Transfusion: A Case Report

A. A. Kerr MB MRACP, Paediatric Registrar

Paediatric Department, Wellington Hospital, Wellington

# SUMMARY

The case of a severely affected rhesus sensitised infant is described in which four exchange transfusions were followed by perforation of the large bowel on the fifth day of life, which was successfully treated by primary closure. The relationship of colonic perforation to exchange transfusion and its pathogenesis is discussed. From a survey of reported cases it is apparent that colonic perforation is directly related to exchange transfusion but the exact pathogenesis is not understood.

# INTRODUCTION

Spontaneous perforation of the large bowel in the neonatal period is a rare event, but its occurrence following exchange transfusion has recently been emphasised by Corkery, Dubowitz, Lister and Moosa (1968), and Orme and Eades (1968) in Britain, and Castor (1968) in Canada. A further case is presented here.

# CASE REPORT

Female baby G.O., Wellington Hospital Number 227601, was born on 13.9.69, to a Group AB, rhesus negative mother who had had two previously unaffected infants but during this pregnancy amniocentesis had shown a severe degree of Rh incompatibility in spite of low serum antibody levels earlier in the pregnancy.

At 36 weeks' gestation, labour was induced by artificial rupture of the membranes and the child was born vaginally after a normal labour. Birth weight was 2.73kg. At birth she was clinically anaemic, had gross hepatosplenomegaly with a distended abdomen, her heart rate was 150 with normal heart sounds and she had slight indrawing and grunting respiration with bilateral crepitations. The cord blood findings were Hb 4.4g/100ml, bilirubin 6.1mg/100ml with a strongly positive Coombs' test, and the blood group was AB Rh positive.

Her first exchange transfusion at two hours was of 500ml in 10ml cycles and because of a high venous pressure of 15cm a deficit of 20ml was left. The polythene catheter was inserted only 4ml into the umbilical vein. Her second exchange transfusion at 184 hours was of 440ml during which the baby had a short

Her fourth exchange transfusion at 67 hours was uneventful.

Citrated blood, warmed by passage through a coil, was used for all the exchange transfusions which were performed over 60 to 80 minutes in 10ml cycles. Prophylactic kanamycin 15mg intramuscularly 12 hourly was administered after the first exchange. She was digitalised after the second exchange.

On her fifth day, 40 hours after the fourth exchange, she was noted to have marked abdominal distension with oedema of the lower abdomen and legs, absent bowel sounds, but no vomiting and normal bowel motions. At that stage abdominal x-ray showed a pneumoperitoneum (Figure 1). At laparotomy, performed at the age of 110 hours, there was a loosely walled-off abscess in the left paracolic gutter with some minor soiling of the immediate area. The peritoneal cavity also contained free fluid and a large volume of air. The transverse colon showed a 7 x 3mm hole proximal to the splenic flexure. This appeared to be in an area of infarction and a biopsy from the edge showed non-specific acute inflammation. This defect was closed in two layers. The area was drained through the left hypochondrium. Cultures from the peritoneal fluid and later from the drainage site grew Escherichia coli sensitive to kanamycin.

For the post-operative period she was maintained on intravenous fluids and her antibiotic was changed to cephaloridine. Five days post-operatively she showed signs of digitalis toxicity and her drugs were stopped temporarily. At this stage there was some twitching of her limbs and her serum calcium was 1.8mEq/L and blood sugar was 12mg/100ml. Extra glucose was added to her infusion and supplementary calcium gluconate was given. Over the next few days her condition improved and she was changed on to normal oral feeding. Apart from a top-up transfusion of 100ml the rest of her admission was uneventful.

When seen at the age of five months her development was normal.

## DISCUSSION

Although exchange transfusion is a major procedure in the newborn, involving as it does replacement of 95 percent of the infant's total blood volume, in experienced hands it seems to carry little risk in terms of mortality. Weldon and Odell (1968), in a series of 351 exchanges in 232 infants gave a mortality rate of 3.1 percent.

There seems little doubt that such a rare event as colonic perforation following exchange transfusion is more than a coincidence and is a complication of the procedure. One feature of this complication however, is its relatively benign course as compared with other types of spontaneous perforation. There were only two deaths in the 12 cases reported by Corkery and others (1968), Orme and Eades (1968) and Castor (1968). Hermann's (1965) case (which survived) and the only survivor of the six cases of Waldhausen, Herendeen and King (1963) both fall into this group of post-exchange perforations. The mortality for other types of spontaneous perforation seems to be at least 75 percent (Brennan, 1967; Corkery and others, 1968).

region of the portal vein and ductus venosus (Figure 2). That this is so is further evidenced by a case described by Orme and Eades (1968) in which perforation of the ileum occurred following infusion of dextrose via an umbilical catheter in a premature infant with hyaline membrane disease. The mechanism of this remains speculative. That profound alteration in blood flow during infusion can occur is demonstrated by two cases described by Farquhar and Smith (1958) in which manipulation of the umbilical catheter and re-insertion to 11cm resulted in cyanosis of the lower half of the body associated with increased venous filling over the trunk and the abdominal veins draining superiorly. They felt that the catheter was in the portal system and attributed the apparent inferior vena caval obstruction to spasm of the ductus venosus spreading to the vena cava. Corkery and others (1968) in studies on two cadavers demonstrated rapid back flow of the infused radio-opaque dye up the portal and mesenteric veins. They suggested that spasm of the small vessels in the mucosal wall due to the variation in portal pressure resulted in necrosis with consequent perforation. Micro-embolism from the catheter site could produce a similar picture. The removal and replacement of blood during the exchange may also lead to episodes of systemic hypotension which, in association with increased sympathetic nervous discharge as expected during a traumatic procedure, may lead to bowel necrosis as is postulated in the mechanism of shock.

A local effect of the polyvinyl-chloride (PVC) catheters which have recently gained widespread popularity has been suggested by Rogers and Dunn (1969). They point out that human umbilical arteries perfused with Ringer-Lacke solution show clear-cut responses to normal physiological stimuli for up to 12 hours after birth. However, when PVC apparatus is used for the perfusion the responses are abolished. The implication is that toxic substances are leached out from the PVC and during exchange transfusion may cause either direct chemical necrosis or alteration in the normal portal vasculature.

![img-201.jpeg](img-201.jpeg)

Although the size of the biopsy was very small, no bowel resection having been done, the histological appearances in this case were of non-specific inflammation. These findings are the same as most others have found and because of this an infective aetiology has been suggested. Scott (1963), described six cases of colonic perforation unrelated to exchange transfusion which he attributed to perinatal sepsis leading to intestinal gangrene. He based his assumption on the histological picture with support from peritoneal swabs which grew coliform bacilli in four cases and Candida albicans in one, Waldhausen and others (1963), in their six cases demonstrated Pseudomonas aeruginosa in four of them and ascribed the condition to this organism. However, these cases were not associated with exchange transfusion and the high mortality in both these series suggests a different syndrome to that of post-transfusion perforation.

Hermann (1965) has taken the infective theory a stage further and suggested a Shwartzman-type

reaction to explain the vasculitis present in the histology. His case was similar to the present one with moderately severe rhesus incompatibility requiring four exchange transfusions and followed within 24 hours with abdominal distension and poor feeding due to perforation of the colon. He postulated that the colonic mucosa was sensitised by the bowel flora and was later challenged by organisms introduced via the umbilical vein at the time of exchange transfusion.

The possibility that the general metabolic upset during the exchange is a causative factor has been suggested and the use of citrated blood has been questioned on these grounds. Farquhar and Smith (1958) demonstrated an early rise in plasma citrate followed by a flattening off at a much higher level during exchange transfusion. These changes were associated with a reciprocal drop in the serum ionised calcium while the total calcium tended to rise gradually throughout the exchange. The potassium usually remained constant although a few cases showed episodes of hyperkalaemia. None of these changes, however, could be related to any clinical abnormalities observed. Also the severe and prolonged acidosis of the respiratory distress syndrome and cyanotic heart disease has not been associated with bowel perforation.

None of these explanations accounts adequately for the occurrence of the perforation in the colon in preference to other parts of the gut.

FIGURE 3.—Diagram to show the sites of perforation following exchange transfusion as described in 18 cases from the literature and the present case.

Figure 3 shows the sites of 25 perforations in the 13 cases referred to above (Corkery and others, 1968; Orme and Eades, 1968; and Castor, 1968) as well as the present case and five others Castor described from the literature. It will be noted that these are distributed equally between the drainage areas of the superior and inferior mesenteric veins but that there is a predominance of large bowel perforations. No explanation can be suggested for this other than a local susceptibility of the colon wall.

# ENTERO-COLITIS FOLLOWING EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION

J. M. Beck, F.R.C.S., Principal Paediatric Surgeon, Baragwanath Hospital,
M. Dinner, F.R.C.S.(Ed.), Chief Surgeon, Transvaal Memorial Hospital for Children
and

J. Chappel, F.C.S. S.A., Senior Surgeon, Transvaal Memorial Hospital for Children

Since the articles by Corkery et al. (1968), Orme and Eades (1968)
and Castor (1968) exchange transfusion has been recognised as one of
the causes of neonatal gastro-intestinal perforation. In several previous
reports (Waldhausen et al., 1963, Forshall, 1964, Hermann, 1965 and
Nienhuis, 1963) of perforations of the bowel in babies the association of
jaundice and exchange transfusion has been mentioned. The present
paper reports five babies who developed entero-colitis after exchange
transfusion, and the suggestion arising from our experience is that these
cases should have conservative management unless there is evidence of
gastro-intestinal perforation. The similarity of this condition to ischemic
colitis in adults as described by Marston et al. (1966), Watt (1968) and
McGovern and Goulston (1965) is discussed.

# Material

From 1967 to 1969, approximately four and a half thousand
exchange transfusions were performed by the South African Blood
Transfusion Service in Johannesburg (Shapiro, 1970). In this period five
babies were admitted to the paediatric surgical unit with evidence of
entero-colitis following exchange transfusion. The apparent incidence of
this complication is 1:900 exchange transfusions.

# CASE REPORTS

Case 1. A 10-day old African male weighing 5 lb. 10 oz. was admitted one week after an
exchange transfusion. Twelve hours after the transfusion he had passed blood per
rectum, followed by several more blood-stained stools. He had vomited feeds inter-
mittently and for two days prior to admission he had been vomiting bile and had had no
bowel action.

On admission the baby was shocked and hypothermic with gross abdominal distension,
oedema and discolouration of the abdominal wall. Following rapid resuscitation a
laparotomy was performed. There was gross faecal peritonitis with discolouration and
necrosis of the transverse colon and splenic flexure which had a large, ragged perforation
on its anti-mesenteric border. Resection with proximal colostomy was performed. The
baby died twelve hours later.

Case 2. A seven-day old African male weighing 4 lb. 12 oz. was admitted five days after
exchange transfusion. He had passed blood-stained stools the day after the exchange
transfusion, and had refused feeds before the appearance of the bloody stool. Abdominal
distension and bile-stained vomiting developed, and bowel actions ceased.

On admission there were signs of gastro-intestinal perforation. Vigorous resuscitation
was necessary. An x-ray showed pneumoperitoneum.

At laparotomy the descending colon and proximal sigmoid colon were necrotic and

avascular with multiple small perforations. The bowel proximal to this had a greyish discolouration but was thought to be viable. Left hemicolectomy and transverse colostomy were performed. The mucosa of the colostomy showed small, superficial ulcerations.

The colostomy failed to work but remained apparently viable. The baby died two days post-operatively.

Case 3. An Asiatic male infant, whose birth weight was 5 lb. 11 oz., was admitted to hospital on the 3rd day of life with haemolytic jaundice due to ABO incompatibility. Exchange transfusions were performed on the 3rd and 4th days. The baby became shocked during the second transfusion but recovered quickly.

He developed severe diarrhoea with blood-stained stools during the next few days. He also had abdominal distension and bile-stained vomitus. Septicaemia was diagnosed and he was treated with broad spectrum antibiotics, intravenous fluids, and naso-gastric suction. He eventually recovered four weeks later but had a disaccharide intolerance.

He made slow progress after discharge from hospital. At the age of 18 weeks he was admitted with low intestinal obstruction and an upper abdominal mass. There was a one-week history of absolute constipation.

Barium enema showed a stricture at the splenic flexure with proximal faecal impaction.

Laparotomy showed a tight fibrous stricture at the splenic flexure and a fistula between the terminal ileum and the ascending colon. Massive mesenteric lymphadenopathy was present. Subtotal colectomy with ileo sigmoid anastomosis was performed. The resected colon showed mucosal ulceration at the stricture with fibrosis of all layers of the bowel wall. The lymph nodes showed reactive hyperplasia only.

This baby is now well and can take a full normal infant's diet.

Case 4. A male infant, weighing 6 lbs. and suffering from RH incompatibility, developed moderate abdominal distension and passed stools mixed with fresh blood six hours after his third exchange transfusion. Investigation showed a platelet count of 30,000 per cu. mm., normal bleeding and clotting time and a PI of 82%.

X-rays showed intra-mural gas in the descending colon and distension proximal to the splenic flexure.

The baby was treated with broad spectrum antibiotics, naso-gastric suction and intravenous fluids, and made a good recovery after three days.

One month later when the baby had irregular loose stools a barium enema was performed. This showed a constant area of narrowing in the descending colon. Apart from dietary management no therapy was given and four weeks later the baby was perfectly well. A repeat barium enema was normal at this time.

Case 5. This infant developed severe abdominal distension and bile-stained vomiting 2 days after its second exchange transfusion. He had passed a blood-stained stool a few hours after his last transfusion. On admission he had marked oedema and discolouration of the abdominal wall and x-ray showed pneumoperitoneum. After rapid resuscitation a laparotomy was performed. The terminal ileum and colon were necrotic, and there were multiple small perforations. Total colectomy and ileostomy were performed. There was a stormy post-operative course but the baby eventually recovered and ileo-rectal anastomosis was possible. Since then the baby has been well.

# DISCUSSION

The 5 cases have certain features in common. All the babies were jaundiced and needed one or more exchange transfusions. Within one day, usually a few hours, of exchange transfusion all the babies passed blood or blood-stained stools. There was a varying degree of abdominal distension and the babies showed signs of shock. In those cases where early

41

symptoms and signs were overlooked, perforation and peritonitis developed, but the babies treated early did not develop free perforations. The presenting features in these cases are similar to those discussed by Corkery et al. (1968) and Orme and Eades (1968) who describe early manifestations of impending perforation and late manifestations after the advent of perforation. The symptoms are similar to those of entero-colitis in premature babies and secondary to other lesions (Touloukian et al., 1967).

# Management

The disease usually affects the colon and terminal ileum but cases of more widespread involvement of the gastro-intestinal tract have been recorded, Orme and Eades (1968). Not all affected babies develop free perforation and, as illustrated by case 4, complete recovery is possible. Once an early diagnosis has been made, the process can be arrested in a proportion of babies by vigorous conservative therapy consisting of naso-gastric suction, intravenous fluid and broad spectrum antibiotics. During this stage the baby must be kept under continuous observation and, if there is any deterioration in his condition, laparotomy must be performed. Serial x-rays of the abdomen may be of assistance in assessing progress, particularly if there is intra-mural gas. (Touloukian 1967). Barium enema and other contrast studies should be avoided for fear of causing perforation.

There is no doubt that laparotomy must be performed if there is a perforation, and in these cases rapid resuscitation is necessary so that operation may be performed as soon as possible. Resuscitation must be directed to restoration of blood volume, correction of acid-base and other metabolic disturbances, correction of coagulation defects, and maintenance of adequate respiration. At operation appropriate resection is better than attempts at repair of perforations, and proximal colostomy or ileostomy is better than primary anastamosis.

This management differs from that recommended by Corkery et al. (1968) who suggest early operation in all cases. We think that it is possible to prevent perforation by early vigorous conservative therapy. This policy is in agreement with that suggested by Touloukian et al. (1967) and by Stevenson et al. (1970).

# Pathology

Ischemic colitis in adults has been described by Marston et al. (1966). Transient, stenosing and gangrenous forms were described. The patients were elderly people with underlying vascular disease and colitis was precipitated by a hypotensive episode. The majority of patients gave a history of passage of blood and mucus per rectum, accompanied by disturbance of bowel function and abdominal pain. Apart from the age difference the presentation, radiological features and progress of these patients were very similar to those in the babies presented in our series. The findings in McGovern and Goulston (1965) series of fatal cases in adults were similar.

J. M. Beck, M. Dinner and J. Chappel

In the babies under discussion histological examination was carried out only in one acute case. In this patient (Case 5) there were patchy changes throughout the resected specimen with mucosal ulceration and features of haemorrhagic infarction. The histology of the specimen in Case 3 who had a stricture showed mucosal ulceration with surrounding inflammation and fibrosis at the site of the stricture.

It is unlikely that any of the babies had any pre-existing vascular disease, but three of the babies had had two or more exchange transfusions before developing the ischemic colitis.

Some portal venous damage may have been caused by one of the earlier transfusions rendering the bowel more susceptible to effects of hypotension. It may be argued that sensitisation for the development of the Schwartzman reaction is equally likely (Hermann, 1965). Alternatively with the relatively unstable and sensitive cardiovascular system of the newborn, hypotension alone may be sufficiently severe to precipitate ischemic bowel damage, particularly at the junction of superior and inferior mesenteric territories.

Intestinal mucosa is the most sensitive part of the bowel to the effects of ischemia, and ulceration results Marston (1966). Intestinal motility would be affected next and either spasm or distension might occur, both of which have demonstrably adverse effects on local circulation. Mucosal ulceration allows invasive infection by normal intestinal flora and further necrosis develops (McGovern and Goulston, 1965 and Marston et al., 1966). Possibly the infection is responsible for the intramural and intravenous gas bubbles which can be demonstrated radiologically and at operation in some, but not all, cases. The larger bacterial content of the terminal ileum and colon is as likely to be the cause of the more frequent involvement of this area of the gastro intestinal tract as any peculiarities of local arterial supply or venous drainage.

# SUMMARY

Five cases of entero-colitis occurring after exchange transfusion in jaundiced babies are presented. The features are similar to the transient, stenosing and gangrenous types of ischemic colitis in adults described by Marston. Non-operative management is recommended unless there is evidence of perforation or the patient's condition shows deterioration while on adequate conservative therapy.

# Intestinal perforation in the newborn infant

## as a complication in umbilical vein infusion or exchange transfusion

H. C. SOMMERSCHILD, M.D.\*

UPRALA, SWEDEN

From the Pediatric Surgical Clinic, Akademiska

sjukhuset, Upsala University Hospital

Intestinal perforation in the newborn is usually due to mechanical obstruction (atresia), traumatic damage (enema) or volvulus with gangrene (malrotation), but spontaneous perforation is not uncommon (necrotizing enteritis).

It seems, however, that spontaneous perforation as a complicating factor in an uneventful exchange transfusion through the umbilical vein in a healthy newborn infant is a new experience.

### CASE REPORT

A male infant was born Nov. 22, 1966, to a healthy, primagravida mother. It was a normal delivery five weeks before term. The birth weight was 2,070 grams. There were no complications during the infant's first three days of life. On the fourth day, an exchange transfusion through the umbilical vein was done with no irregularities. During the following 24 hours, the infant developed vomiting and abdominal distention. An x-ray examination of the abdomen revealed pneumoperitoneum. A laparotomy was immediately performed, and generalized peritonitis was found. From the cecum to the splenic flexure, the colon was dilated and gangrenous, as in necrotizing colitis, with three perforations in the transverse colon. From the splenic flexure to the rectosigmoid, the colon appeared normal. The affected part of the colon was resected and an ileostomy was constructed. The macroscopically normal part of the colon was biopsied, and the oral end was left as a colostomy. However, the patient died on the sixth postoperative day and an autopsy was performed.

Histologic examination. The entire wall of the colon showed stasis, hemorrhage, and infarction. Leukocyte infiltration was marked at the sites of

Accepted for publication Feb. 22, 1971.

\*Present address: Pediatric Surgical Dept., Rikshospitalet,

Oslo University Hospital, Oslo, Norway.

perforation; it was marked most on the mucosal side of the wall. Microthrombi could not be identified, not even by Leudrum staining for deposits of fibrin. In the normal part of the colon, there was no evidence of aganglionosis.

Bacteriology. Bacterial cultures from tissue specimens from the heart, lung, spleen, and liver revealed the presence of Klebsiella and pyocyanes; the interpretation was septicemia.

### MATERIAL

We have found 20 more reports of similar cases in the literature.1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 13-18 From this total of 21 cases, there are detailed reports regarding 18 (Table I).

Prematurity. At least six patients (30 percent) weighed less than 2,500 grams at birth.

Umbilical vein catheterizations. One patient had an umbilical vein infusion for seven days to treat respiratory distress syndrome. Seven patients had one exchange transfusion, while in ten cases this procedure was repeated one to three times.

Symptoms. In nine patients (50 percent), the abdominal symptoms began within 24 hours following the exchange transfusion. In the other cases, perforation was suspected two to four days after the procedure.

Localization of the perforations. Twelve patients (65 percent) had perforation of the colon. In two other cases, both the colon and the ileum were perforated. Two patients had perforation of the ileum only, and in two cases, the localization was not specified. Nine of the patients (50 percent) showed a single perforation, while the others had a more extensive affection of the intestine.

Operations. Two patients did not undergo

# RESULTS

Histologic examination. Reports are available in 13 cases and they are all similar. They show cell infiltration, capillary stasis, and hemorrhages throughout the intestinal wall with necrosis and ulceration. In a number of patients, the changes fulfilled the conditions of necrotizing enteritis, while in others they were localized to the areas of perforation. Microscopic thrombi were found in four patients.²⁻³⁰, ¹⁵ In two other cases⁴ (this author's case), they were investigated despite lack of indication. In the remaining case reports, this phenomenon was not discussed.

Bacteriology. Swabs for bacterial culture were taken from the peritoneal cavity in eight patients. Examination revealed the presence of Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Proteus, and pyocyanco, but without any common pattern.

Mortality rate. The over-all mortality rate was 25 percent. As evident from Table II, there was an overrepresentation among the deaths of low birth weight, multiple perforations, and complicating conditions. There was, on the other hand, no correlation between death and operative procedure, day of life of the exchange transfusion, the number of such procedures, or time elapsed from the exchange transfusion to the initial signs of perforation. The operations were, in all cases, performed immediately following the perforation.

# DISCUSSION

Today we consider the procedure of exchange transfusion through the umbilical vein as an established method of treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, although

![img-202.jpeg](img-202.jpeg)

The material presented here does not indicate that the difference in prognosis is caused by diagnostic or therapeutic conditions. The perforations complicating exchange transfusions in the newborn infant consequently are suggested as having a common, specific etiology, the pathogenesis being primary, microvascular catastrophes. 1, 4, 5, 10

So far, the etiologic mechanisms remains unknown although several theories have been proposed. Hermann discussed the possibility of an allergic Shwarzman reaction as a response to bacterial toxins. The experimental basis for this is supported by the report of Rapaport and co-workers. Our patient fulfilled the criteria for necrotizing colitis and hence the condition could have been based upon a Shwarzman reaction. However, the Lendrum staining of the histopathologic specimens did not in fact reveal the intravascular deposits of fibrin so characteristic for that reaction. Moreover, the fact that seven of the newborn infants had only one exchange transfusion does not support this hypothesis as a predominant factor.

The proposal of Lloyd that the diving reflex, if abnormally and locally enforced, may be responsible for spontaneous intestinal perforation in newborn infants does not seem to fit into this particular clinical picture, as all the babies thrived until signs of perforation appeared. Moreover, all the exchange procedures were reported to be unremarkable.

The patients considered here seem to have only one important common denominator, i.e., the exchange transfusion through the umbilical vein. This procedure, however, may be performed in different ways at the different hospitals. It is therefore tempting to suggest that the causal factors may correlate to the type of exchange procedure.

Meyer and Lind have shown that the ductus venosus closes within a few days after

Fig. 1. The relevant anatomic interrelation showing the umbilical vein entering the left main branch of portal vein. (From Corkery, J. J., Dubowitz, V., Lister, J., and Mossa, A.: Colonic perforation after exchange transfusion, Brit. Med. J. 4: 345, 1968.

birth. As a result of this, the catheter through the umbilical vein finds its way to the desired position in the inferior vena cava in only 20 percent of the procedures. In the other 80 percent the tip of the catheter is found either in the effluent or the affluent branches of the portal vein. The diameter of the portal vein in the newborn infant is 2 to 3 mm, and the catheters usually are of 5 to 8 Ch, i.e., 2 to 2½ mm. With such a catheter in a portal vein branch position in the mesenteric direction, there exists a real risk of inducing great pressure variations during the procedure, even when done by expert hands. Pressure readings are widely used but are carried out in the static phase of the procedure. In fact, we know very little about the hemodynamic conditions during the exchange transfusion.

The primary damage is probably the change in the microcirculation, such as hemorrhage and thrombosis, because the capillaries in the intestinal wall have an extremely small pressure difference between rupture and collapse.

The predominance of colonic perforation may indicate, as observed in other diseases,

### SUMMARY

The complication of intestinal perforation
in exchange transfusion in newborn infants
has been brought to our attention during the
last two to three years.

Twenty case reports are traced and one
more presented.

The survival rate is 75 percent in contrast
to the 15 percent rate which occurred in
spontaneous perforations of mixed etiology.

Analysis of the 21 cases gives no evidence
that the difference in the prognosis is caused
by diagnostic or therapeutic conditions. These
patients, therefore, are suggested to have a
common etiology.

Mechanical circumstances in the exchange
procedure may create the risk of great pres-
sure variations in the microcirculation in the
intestinal wall. The capillaries, particularly
those in the colonic mucosa, are very sensi-
tive to such variations. Hemorrhage and/or
thrombosis may therefore be the result of
these variations, leading to the development
of necrosis and perforation.

### ADDENDUM

After submitting the manuscript, I have seen,
in the Pediatric Department, Rikshospitalet, Oslo
University Hospital, another particular patient
with case history and symptoms relevant to the
problem discussed.

The fourth child of healthy parents was de-
livered four weeks before term with no perinatal
problems other than hyperbilirubinemia. The
mother was typed Rh negative and the father was
Rh positive.

The first exchange transfusion was given im-
mediately after birth; the second was given at 40
hours post partum; and the third was adminis-
tered during the third day of life. The exchange
transfusions were performed at different hospi-
tals, but were all reported to be uneventful. Fol-
lowing the second exchange transfusion, the baby
vomited once, the abdomen became distended,
and some fresh, coagulated blood was discharged
per annum. The general condition deteriorated. In-
testinal perforation was suspected, and the pa-
tient was referred to the pediatric clinic, Riks-
hospitalet, Oslo, where the third exchange trans-
fusion was performed. There was some fresh
blood from the anus the first two days. X-ray
investigation revealed slight evidence of paralytic
ileus, but no free air in the peritoneum. Symp-
toms of peritonitis never developed. The baby
made a rapid recovery and was referred to the
parents 16 days post partum; the patient was
symptomless and thriving.

Indeed, this may have been an actual perfora-
tion, immediately and spontaneously sealed, not
giving cause to peritonitis. The main symptoms,
however, were the melena and the distended ab-
domen following the administration of an ex-
change transfusion. It is assumed that this par-
ticular case represents the situation in which the
damage to the intestinal wall is restricted to the
mucosa, leaving the muscular and serosal layers
intact. The patient therefore illustrates the first
step in a pathogenetic sequence which eventually
leads to frank perforation. The demonstration of
this first step seems extremely rare and has never
before been reported. It strongly supports the
pathogenetic theory proposed.

# Erythroderma and Erythroblastosis Fetalis

To the Editor.—The appearance of a rash during the course of therapy for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia has been recognized.¹⁻³ The first report associated a macular erythematous rash in the use of phototherapy for the reduction of serum bilirubin. The second report noted the occurrence of a macular erythematous rash as a possible complication following intensive transfusion therapy for severe hemolytic disease of the newborn. No other references relating hyperbilirubinemia and a macular erythroderma could be found in the available literature. This communication further documents our clinical observations of this peculiar skin reaction in four severely affected erythroblastotic infants, none of which were exposed to bilirubin reduction lamps.

Report of Cases.—CASE 1.—A 1.0-kg (4 lb 2 oz) male infant was delivered spontaneously at 33 weeks gestation. He had received three intrauterine transfusions beginning at 28 weeks gestation. The total cord bilirubin value was 4.6 mg/100 ml, and the cord Coombs test was 2+ reactive. The total bilirubin value peaked at 14.0 mg/100 ml at 48 hours, and the direct reacting bilirubin peaked at 2.6 mg/100 ml on the tenth day. One exchange transfusion was required on the first day. A generalized macular erythematous rash appeared on the third day and was gone by the fifth day.

CASE 2.—A 2.3-kg (5 lb 2 oz) moderately hydropic male infant was delivered by cesarean section at 36 weeks gestation. He had received four intrauterine transfusions beginning at 28 weeks of gestation. The total cord bilirubin value was 4.8 mg/100 ml, and the cord Coombs test was 2+ reactive. The total bilirubin and direct reacting bilirubin values peaked at 22.1 mg/100 ml and 14.5 mg/100 ml, respectively, at 84 hours. Two exchange transfusions were required, the first at 3 hours and the second at 70 hours of life. A generalized macular rash appeared on the third day and cleared by the fifth day. Maternal and infant titers for cytomegalovirus, rubella, and toxoplasmosis were negative.

CASE 3.—A 2.3-kg (5 lb 1 oz) hydropic female infant was delivered following induction of labor at 38 weeks gestation. No fetal transfusions had been performed. The total cord bilirubin value was 5.2 mg/100 ml, and the cord Coombs test was 4+ reactive. The total and direct reacting bilirubin values peaked at 20.2 mg/100 ml and 12.4 mg/100 ml, respectively, at 96 hours of life. An exchange transfusion was per-

formed on the first and fourth day of life. A generalized macular erythematous rash appeared on the third day and cleared by the fourth day.

CASE 4.—A 2.0-kg (4 lb 8 oz) moderately hydropic female infant was delivered following induction of labor at 35 weeks of gestation. No fetal transfusions had been performed. The total cord bilirubin value was 10.0 mg/100 ml, and the cord Coombs test was 3+ reactive. The total bilirubin value peaked at 36.5 mg/100 ml on the fifth day. The direct reacting bilirubin fraction rose to a peak of 13.9 mg/100 ml on the seventh day. A total of nine exchange transfusions was required throughout the first four days of life to control the persistently rising levels of unconjugated bilirubin. On the third day a generalized macular rash appeared and lasted until the fifth day.

Comment.—Four severely affected Rh-isoimmunized infants have been described wherein a generalized macular erythroderma developed following intensive transfusion therapy. The rash occurred on the third day and cleared by the fifth day in all four patients. It was faint, evanescent, and varied in intensity from time to time during its 24 to 48 hours of existence. The maculae were 2 to 4 mm in diameter, blanched easily with pressure, and at times appeared circinate. In the first report¹ a very similar rash occurred in moderately-to-severely jaundiced infants undergoing phototherapy for bilirubin reduction, but the etiology of the hyperbilirubinemia was not indicated. None of our patients received phototherapy at any time. The rash was noted to coincide with a plateau in the rise of bilirubin levels seen in both our patients and those previously reported. Giunta¹ proposed that the rash resulted from the rapid pooling of pigment or breakdown products of the photochemical reaction of light and bilirubin in the skin. This would imply a toxic feature of the photooxidized products, but to date phototherapy has not been related to any specific toxic tissue effects of either the light itself or the breakdown products.²⁻⁴

CDS J. E. SCHAEFER, MC, USN
LCDR M. D. CUNNINGHAM, MC, USN
LCDR J. W. MACE, MC, USN
San Diego, Calif

# OUR CARE OF NEWBORN INFANTS

IS OFTEN NOT GOOD ENOUGH

We should not be smug about the medical care given to newborns; infant mortality in the U.S. is higher than it is in many advanced nations. Infant mortality in Sweden, for instance, is only 60% of that in the U.S.; in the Netherlands, only 63%. Granted, care given in certain American hospitals is very good indeed, but nationwide we have nothing to brag about.

However, it is quite likely that poor neonatal care is not solely responsible for our higher infant mortality. There are many reasons for it, and socioeconomic causes may well be more important than medical ones. But we should try in every way to reduce infant mortality, and better neonatal care is one of those ways. Certainly we must guard against the natural tendency to accept old prac-

tices as being good enough. They have to be improved.

Routine Care in the Delivery Room
Nasal, Esophageal, and Gastric Catheterization. In my opinion, subjecting all normal newborns to nasal, esophageal, or gastric catheterization is more hazardous than performing these procedures only when choanal obstruction or a tracheo-esophageal fistula is suspected. To exclude choanal obstruction, cover the baby's mouth and then separately block each nostril. Only if air does not pass through one or both nares need you pass a catheter to determine whether thick mucus or a true anatomical obstruction accounts for the blockage. Even then, he cautions about diagnosing an obstruction based on catheterization; the canal may be too narrow to admit any but the smallest

The American Academy of Pediatrics has recently revised its "Standard and Recommendations for Hospital Care of Newborn Infants" (May, 1964). Those who assume responsibility for newborns should review this carefully.

catheter yet may permit air to pass freely.

Nor do I believe that the benefits of gastric aspiration justify routine gastric intubation, as some have recommended. Recent data do not confirm that gastric aspiration influences the clinical course of the respiratory distress syndrome; moreover, gastric intubation may rarely cause gastric perforation. Naso-esophageal intubation with even a soft, blunt-ended catheter may cause hematomas of the turbinates or the posterior pharyngeal wall, esophageal perforation and laryngeal or tracheal irritation, which may be associated with edema and infection. I, therefore, prefer to reserve intubation for those cases which show clinical symptoms, even though these are minimal. When an infant shows signs of respiratory distress, excessive mucus or other evidence of tracheo-esophageal fistula, the patency of his esophagus must be checked immediately.

Preventing Gonorrheal Ophthalmia. Recent studies have again demonstrated the value of instilling silver nitrate in the infant's eyes, as required by law. However, it does not protect every infant, so always take a smear if purulent conjunctivitis develops. Whether gonorrheal ophthalmia occurs in infants who are given silver nitrate prophylaxis because we use a "modified" Credé method cannot be determined. Credé's original method called for the use of 2% silver nitrate (not 1%) and did not include immediate flushing of the eyes with a salt solution.

Giving Vitamin K Routinely. Some have questioned the need for and the safety of giving vitamin K to all newborns. In our clinic, controlled studies in premature infants have shown that

a single dose of 2½ mg. of vitamin K₁ (Konakion) given either orally or intramuscularly increases survival significantly. Repeated doses, however, serve no purpose; in fact, when given parenterally they increase the risk of complications. Male full-term infants who are given vitamin K₁ bleed less following circumcision. The administration of vitamin K (rather than K₁) is potentially hazardous since it may lead to hyperbilirubinemia.

Umbilical Cord Ligature. Since we began using rubber tubing for umbilical cord ligature in our clinic, only one of thousands of infants has had umbilical cord hemorrhage because the ligature slipped. Previously, when we used linen cord ligatures, several dozen infants developed severe umbilical cord hemorrhage. In some this was severe enough to cause hypovolemic shock. The hemorrhage was usually attributed to hemorrhagic disease of the newborn because the prothrombin time was prolonged. Yet, because in each case the ligature had slipped, we now believe that failure of the umbilical cord blood vessels to contract was the real problem. (Prothrombin time is prolonged in many otherwise-normal newborns.)

Based on our experience, we do not recommend leaving a long section of cord; pustules often form under the cord (see Figure). Nor can we recommend metal clamps because cellulitis often forms at the base of the cord. The rubber cord ligature method is superior to all others we have tried.

# Routine Nursery Care

Feeding. Formulas varying as much as 200% in protein, vitamin, and mineral content can be used safely for most newborn infants, but bear

Avoid: (1) formulas high in chlorides, which can cause hyperchloremic acidosis; (2) formulas high in vitamin D, which predispose infants to hypercalcemia; (3) formulas high in protein, which are associated with a higher mortality rate in immature infants as well as a higher incidence of allergy and an increased need to excrete urinary solutes; and (4) formulas high in phosphorus, which predispose to neonatal tetany.

Usually the first feeding, six to nine hours after birth, is a 5% sugar solution. Some doctors are convinced that an early feeding of sugar (or saline) benefits the newborn, but there is little published evidence to support their view except for one study of babies of diabetic mothers. In our clinic, we have evaluated concentrated formulas containing 34 rather than 20 calories per ounce for feeding premature infants. We have found that their use safely accelerates growth. The accelerated growth, however, does not exceed the physiologic rate, that is, the growth rate of the fetus in the uterus.

Many physicians were reluctant to use glucose and bicarbonate solutions for combating the respiratory distress syndrome until Doctor Robert Usher

![img-204.jpeg](img-204.jpeg)

Pustules found under a long, redundant umbilical cord.

of McGill University reported that this therapy, carefully timed and controlled, helped control acidosis and hyperkalemia, and thereby increased survival rates. However, very accurate biochemical studies are required to use the Usher regimen safely.

Venipuncture Techniques. Using any deep vein for obtaining blood carries a small but definite risk of major morbidity and mortality. Therefore, blood should be procured from a superficial vein, either the antecubital or external jugular vein, or from a capillary stab. Even from a premature baby weighing only 1 or 2 Kg., you can obtain 5 to 10 ml. of blood from a superficial vein. Do the venipuncture using a good light and a #21 or 22 needle with a trace of heparin on the barrel of the syringe.

# Rapidly Fatal Infection

Premature Rupture of the Membranes. Premature rupture threatens the fetus with infection that may be fatal even before the infant is born. There may be no time to culture the infecting organism from the infant before giving antimicrobial drugs. Nevertheless, it is possible to get circumstantial evidence of presence of a bacterial pathogen by obtaining a culture of the mother's cervix. If you find hemolytic streptococcus, enterococcus or pneumococcus, start penicillin therapy immediately. This should be given to the mother in large doses if the baby is unborn, and to the baby if already delivered. However, if any signs of infection (even though minimal) are present, antimicrobial therapy should be used to include at least the organisms obtained via cervical culture. Antimicrobial drugs are potentially harmful to the fetus and should be used as specifically and rationally as possible.

Choice of Antimicrobial Drug for Neonatal Infections. Therapy must begin promptly when you see any signs of infection such as unexplained fever, jaundice, apathy, or vomiting. For many years, many have given combinations of antibiotics such as chloramphenicol plus penicillin or streptomycin plus penicillin. Currently, I give the infant penicillin and two or three doses of kanamycin at 12-hour intervals, each dose exactly 7½ mg. per Kg. of body weight in a sufficiently dilute solution to minimize the danger of inadvertent over- or underdosage. (A dilute form of kanamycin for infant use will soon become available commercially.)

Why kanamycin? First, it kills most bacteria that cause serious infection in the newborn, including almost all strains of E. coli, as well as many strains of Staphylococci, Streptococci, and most strains of Pneumococci. Gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli now cause 60% or more of serious neonatal infections and the majority of strains have become resistant to chloramphenicol, streptomycin and tetracycline.

Second, although there is evidence that kanamycin is toxic when given in high doses over long periods, I believe it is safe as a stopgap antibiotic for treating possible neonatal sepsis. Two or three doses give an adequate blood level for 24 to 36 hours; by this time, one usually has the results of blood, urine, or spinal fluid cultures. If E. coli are recovered, kanamycin can be continued until sensitivity studies show that a less toxic drug is effective. If pneumococci or hemolytic streptococci are recovered, the penicillin should be continued and the kanamycin discontinued.

The two-to-three-dose kanamycin-penicillin regimen is adequate prophylaxis against suspected infection. However, when infection is probable, we add Staphicillin for penicillinase-producing staphylococci and tetracycline for Listeria. Since tetracycline (particularly the demethylchlor-analog) has reportedly caused dental staining, I recommend using oxytetracycline. This form of tetracycline has not been reported to cause cosmetically disfiguring dental staining. If Pseudomonas is a possible infecting organism, the use of colistin should be considered.

### Abnormalities in Older Children and Adults May Be Normal in Newborns

For several years, some have advocated establishing neonatology as a subspecialty of pediatrics. (There are cogent reasons for labeling it perinatology.) Many of the clinical signs and laboratory findings in newborns are quite different than at any other time in the life of man. For example, during the first two to four days, the majority of newborn infants develop one or more petechia, toxic erythema, and jaundice. In the first week, the majority of babies vomit once or twice (rarely is vomitus bile stained). Five percent of normal newborns do not void or pass meconium during the first 48 hours.

Unusual Blood Values. The following laboratory findings are found in normal newborn babies:

|  WBC | as high as 25,000 mm.³  |
| --- | --- |
|  Serum phosphorus | as high as 9 mg. %  |
|  Blood sugar | as low as 30 mg. %  |
|  Serum calcium | as low as 8 mg. %  |
|  Hemoglobin | from 15 to 23 gram. %  |

The urine of normal newborns may contain red blood cells and a considerable amount of protein. These are

Exchange Transfusions for Newborns with Hyperbilirubinemia. All newborn babies develop jaundice if adult bilirubin concentrations are used as the criterion. Most of those whose bilirubin concentrations exceed 20 mg. % reach this level between the third and fifth day after birth, then fall spontaneously. Not all recent data completely support the earlier recommendation that an exchange transfusion be performed whenever the indirect bilirubin concentration exceeds 20 mg. % during the first week of life. Before deciding to perform an exchange, consider two facts: first, the mortality from exchange transfusions ranges from 1 to 10%;

second, bilirubin concentrations under 25 mg. % cause brain damage in only a very small percent of infants—some estimate less than 0.1%.

# The Challenge

During the past few years, infant mortality has remained about the same in the U.S. One might conclude from this apparent lack of progress that we are approaching an irreducible minimal level. However, a growing number of nations have reduced their infant mortality rates well below ours. What a tragedy for the U.S. to become a nation of second rank in this regard. Whether socioeconomic reasons alone account for this difference remains to be determined, but even if they do, physicians should work to correct them.

349. Failing to appreciate fully the risks of exchange transfusion.

The basic question which must be raised is whether or not the risk of death due to the exchange (1 to 2 per cent) outweighs the small risk of brain damage (manifested at most by mild deafness) in asymptomatic patients who have bilirubin values under 25 (? 30) mg. per 100 ml. (See pitfall number 234.) The routine performance of an exchange if the bilirubin level rises to or approaches 20 mg. per 100 ml. in the first week of life is most unfortunate. We must have the fortitude to tell parents the whole truth and to inform them of the uncertainties and the risks. Many believe that it is far better to have a live child who has only a small chance of brain damage (if the bilirubin level does not rise over 25 mg. per 100 ml. for less than a day in the first week of life) than to risk the chances of a fatality.

## "Uncomplicated" Hyperbilirubinemia of Prematurity

The Lack of Association with Neurologic Deficit at 3 Years of Age

JACK G. SHILLER, M.D.

AND

WILLIAM A. SILVERMAN, M.D.

NEW YORK

The role that bilirubin plays in brain damage associated with prematurity has not been completely defined. The hazards in these infants of hyperbilirubinemia in association with isoimmunization and excessive

Accepted for publication Oct. 6, 1960.

20 Bay St., Westport, Conn.

Aided by a grant from the U.S. Public Health Service R.G. B-1067.

amounts of vitamin K analogue,¹ are well known; it has also been shown that when sulfisoxazole² is given to jaundiced premature infants, a significant proportion die with kernicterus. However, the magnitude of the risk of hyperbilirubinemia in the absence of these known complicating factors has not been established.

Meyer³ and Crosse et al.⁴ stated that hyperbilirubinemia is harmful to the newborn premature infant, and suggested that 18 mg/100 ml be considered the "critical" concentration of bilirubin in the blood, above which brain damage is likely to occur. Corner,⁵ Dundon,⁶ and Newns et al.⁷ agreed in principle but believed that the critical concentration is higher. Another group⁸ found a correlation between increasing concentrations of bilirubin in the blood of newborn premature infants and decreasing levels of gross motor development at one year of age. This correlation appeared to be more striking in boys than in girls.

Holman,⁹ Rapmund et al.,¹⁰ and Mores¹¹ have presented data which cast some doubt on these views. The latter authors questioned the advisability of routinely performing exchange transfusions on all premature infants in whom the concentration of bilirubin in the serum exceeds 18 to 20 mg per 100 ml.

The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the association between neurologic status at 3 years of age, and the maximal serum concentration of bilirubin in newborn premature infants who had not been exposed to influences (already discussed) which have been shown to affect the incidence of kernicterus. We also wished to learn whether brain damage in expremature children resembled the clinical kernicterus which has been observed in children who survived erythroblastosis fetalis.

HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA

591

No case of definite loss of perceptive hearing was found in any of the study patients. In the 9 patients diagnosed by the neurologists as definitely damaged, strabismus and palsy of extraocular muscles were most frequently observed. Spastic paraplegia was found in 1 case; quadriplegia was found in 2 cases. The remaining damaged patients demonstrated hypotonia, mental retardation, disorders of behavior and speech, and "nonspecific" signs of brain damage.

# Comment

The present study fails to demonstrate a significant correlation between uncomplicated hyperbilirubinemia in premature infants and neurologic deficit at 3 years of age. Damaged children were found to have had varying degrees of bilirubinemia in the neonatal period, and the differences which were observed in the groups with high and with low maximal concentrations of bilirubin in the serum could easily be explained on the basis of sampling variation alone.

The type of neurologic deficit noted in the damaged children in the present study does not resemble the classical picture of kernicterus residua described by Gerrard¹⁴ and by Evans and Polani.¹⁵ The most frequent findings described by the latter authors were opisthotonos, choreoathetosis, convulsions, muscular rigidity, ataxia, and hypotonia or atonic diplegia.

In this connection it is of some interest to recount the findings of Churchill¹⁶ in a recent study of a group of brain damaged children. He observed a close correlation between "simple spastic diplegia" (corticospinal and pyramidal tracts) and low birth weight or low gestational age. However, he found no significant correlation between "complex diplegia" (athetosis and extrapyramidal tract signs) and low birth weight or low gestational age.

We believe that the results of the present study suggest that premature infants may be able to tolerate moderately high concentrations of bilirubin in the serum when this

state is not complicated by erythroblastosis fetalis, excessive doses of vitamin K, or the administration of sulfisoxazole. Since it is possible that the concentration of bilirubin in the serum is only one of a number of factors which influence the penetration of this pigment into the brain, we wish to question whether the same criteria and treatment that are used for hyperbilirubinemia caused by erythroblastosis fetalis should be applied to uncomplicated hyperbilirubinemia of prematurity.

It should be emphasized that the evidence gathered in the present study did not result from experiment but rather from experience. The infants were "found" to have high or to have low concentrations of bilirubin in the serum; they were not allocated to these categories according to an experimental plan. Data from this and other similar observational studies can be used only to seek hypotheses. Proof of these hypotheses can be obtained only by carefully designed clinical trials. For example, Forfar et al.¹⁷ have undertaken a small trial (using concurrent controls) of the influence of exchange transfusion in the management of uncomplicated hyperbilirubinemia of prematurity. When the results of this and other experimental studies are known, answers may be available to the questions which have arisen from our experience.

# Conclusions

We reported on 110 expremature children who were examined at 3 years of age. Approximately one-fifth of these children exhibited signs that were interpreted as either suspicious or definite evidence of brain damage or mental retardation.

Although approximately one-fourth of the children had uncomplicated hyperbilirubinemia (maximal concentrations between 18 and 22 mg. per 100 ml.) in the neonatal period, there was no apparent association between hyperbilirubinemia and neurologic deficit or mental retardation. Moreover, none of the children exhibited signs which were suggestive of kernicterus residua.

# Studies in kernicterus

III. The saturation of serum proteins with bilirubin during neonatal life and its relationship to brain damage at five years

Psychometric studies were performed on a group of 5-year-old children who had been jaundiced during neonatal life. On the basis of the test results, 14 children were considered normal and 18 were classified as having brain damage. The presence or absence of brain damage was compared with clinical and laboratory determinations that had been made on the children during their period of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. No significant correlations were found between the presence or absence of brain damage and the maximum bilirubin concentration, birth weight, sex, presence or absence of hemolytic disease, or the use of exchange transfusion. A significant correlation was found between the presence or absence of brain damage and the saturation of the serum proteins with bilirubin during infancy.

Gerard B. Odell, M.D., G. N. Bruce Storey, M.D., and Leon A. Rosenberg, Ph.D.

BALTIMORE, MD.

A CAUSAL relationship between hyperbilirubinemia during neonatal life and kernicterus in infants is well established and has been reproduced in many animal species.¹⁻⁷ Chloroasthrosis, asymmetrical spasticity, and sensorineural hearing impairment are the most commonly described sequelae in infants who survive neonatal kernicterus.⁸⁻¹⁰ A few studies have reported a reduction of

the intelligence quotient as a manifestation of bilirubin encephalopathy, but others have not found such abnormalities in the absence of cerebral palsy.¹¹⁻¹⁸ However, the pathology of kernicterus indicates that other cranial nuclei are affected in addition to the basal ganglia.²⁰⁻²² Injury to many of these nuclei, particularly the hippocampus, may affect learning, memory, and adaptive behavior.²³⁻²⁵ Impairment of perceptual (interpretative) functioning may result without necessarily producing cerebral palsy or reducing the intelligence quotient (I.Q.) to subnormal levels.²⁶

Many of the published studies have depended upon disturbances of either sensory or motor performance in early infancy as criteria of central nervous system injury due

The purpose of the present study was to re-examine by comprehensive psychometric tests a group of children of 4 to 7 years of age who had been jaundiced during neonatal life. The results of the psychometric tests were correlated to a number of observations that had been made on the children during their period of neonatal jaundice. The results demonstrate a correlation between brain damage and the degree to which the serum proteins were saturated with bilirubin during the period of hyperbilirubinemia.

# MATERIALS AND METHODS

The 32 children reported in this study were between the ages of 4 and 7 years and had been patients on the nursery services of The Johns Hopkins Hospital. These children were from families which still resided in the Baltimore area and could be located. None of the families who were located refused to have their children examined. The 32 children represented only a third of the total population on whom studies were performed during neonatal life. The other families could not be traced.

Although all had been jaundiced, only 24 had been treated by exchange transfusion. None had physical signs of classical kernicterus (opisthotonus, shrill cry, or absent Moro reflex). Hemolytic disease due to a fetal-maternal blood group incompatibility was established as the cause of jaundice in 16 of the children, 8 due to Rh and 8 due to ABO isoimmunization. In addition to serial measurements of serum bilirubin and total protein concentrations, the saturation index of the serum proteins with bilirubin was determined by the salicylate displacement technique. The methodologies for these analyses of sera have been previously described by this laboratory.³³ The saturation indices in the present report are the values of either pre-exchange sera in the trans-

fused infants or the value obtained on the serum sample with the highest bilirubin concentration in the nonexchanged infants, except where noted in the tables.

When the children were 4 to 7 years of age, a complete medical history was obtained and a physical examination was performed. Abnormal neurologic signs were confirmed by a pediatric neurologist (Dr. William McLean). All the children were then examined by the same psychologist, who was unaware of the child's medical history apart from the history of jaundice.

The psychometric tests performed for evaluation of cognitive functioning were as follows: (1) Intelligence quotient was measured by the Stanford-Binet test for those children who were less than 5 years of age, and the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children for those 5 and over; (2) visual-motor coordination was assessed by the Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt test and the Sequin Form Board; (3) short-term memory and resistance to distraction were evaluated by the Children's Embedded Figures test and Reitan's Trail Making test adapted for children.

Two "scores" were determined for each subject: (1) the measured I.Q.; and (2) the designation "abnormal" or "normal" with reference to the presence or absence of cognitive dysfunction. The latter measure of brain damage involved the psychologist's over-all impression of the test data.

The most characteristic results from the test protocols which led to a designation of "abnormal" cognitive functioning were as follows:

1. Difficulties in visual-motor coordination were evidenced by slow, inaccurate, and "clumsy" performances on the Sequin Form Board. Disturbances on the Bender-Gestalt test were noted by distortion or loss of the shape of the designs, sketchy and tumulous lines, rotations, and a tendency toward perseveration.

2. Deficiencies in short-term memory tasks were found in "reding" on the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, digit-span, and picture-memory items on the Stanford-

The results in Table III indicate that 16 of the 18 damaged children had had a saturation index which equalled or exceeded 8.0. The 2 brain-damaged children with saturation indices less than 8.0 are Patients 2 and 20 of Table I. Patient 20 was born spontaneously at home and required repeated epinephrine injections because of apnea and bradycardia for the first 48 hours of life. Thus hypoxic injury related to her cardiorespiratory distress rather than the hyperbilirubinemia, may have been responsible for the cerebral injury. Patient 2 had an ABO incompatibility; the saturation index was done when the total bilirubin value was 15 mg. per 100 ml. The bilirubin concentration subsequently rose to 18 mg. per 100 ml., at

which time the saturation index might have exceeded 8.0.

Tables II and III indicate that 5 (Patients 3, 4, 16, 30, and 37) of the 14 children with normal psychometric test results had saturation indices which exceeded 8. Patient 30 was treated by exchange transfusion, the first of which was initiated at 30 minutes of age, and subsequently repeated 2 more times within the next 48 hours. The saturation of the serum with bilirubin to an index value above 8 was of less than 8 hours' duration. Patient 4 had a saturation index of 8.1 when the serum bilirubin level was 14.8 mg. per 100 ml. on the fourth day of life. The bilirubin concentration on the fifth day was still 14.0 mg. per 100 ml., but the saturation index had fallen to 2.0. Thus, the excessive saturation of this patient's serum with bilirubin may also have been of brief dura-

In contrast to the clinical course of the hyperbilirubinemia of the children with normal psychometric test results, the elevation of the serum bilirubins above 15 mg. per 100 ml. in the abnormal children was of relatively greater duration (3.29 days versus 1.73 days; the mean difference of 1.56 is significantly different, p < 0.01). Three of the 18 damaged children had physical findings of neurologic impairment in motor and/or sensory functions characteristic of kernicterus; choreiform movements were demonstrable in Patients 10 and 29, and spasticity with sensorineural deafness in Patient 5. One additional child, Patient 33, has defective enamel formation and staining of his incisors.

The comparison of the incidence and severity of complications of pregnancy and delivery could not be measured, but qualitatively, no particular events appeared to predispose in this series to subsequent cognitive dysfunction.

As has been found in other surveys on the incidence of hyperbilirubinemia¹⁷, ¹⁸ there was a preponderance of male infants in the present series. Clinically it was found that about half the damaged children demonstrated hyperkinesis, poor attention span, and more aggressive behavior.

# DISCUSSION

Any study which attempts to relate neonatal events to subsequent cognitive performance of the brain must recognize the many variables which can influence the maturation of the central nervous system, e.g., genetic endowment, maternal health during gestation, nutrition, critical-period imprinting, economic status, and educational opportunity, as well as inflammatory and toxic injuries during prenatal and postnatal life. In the present study, the only consistent feature of the children was the occurrence of jaundice during neonatal life. A correlation was not found between the maximum serum bilirubin concentration and the subsequent presence of either low I.Q. and psychometric scores or cerebral palsy. This observation is similar to those of previous reports in which neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, unrelated to hemolytic disease, was found not to correlate with the subsequent neurologic outcome of the children.¹⁷, ¹⁸, ²⁰ A relationship between hyperbilirubinemia and subsequent evidence of brain injury has occurred in infants with coexistent clinical disturbances such as hemolytic diseases,¹⁹, ²¹, ²², ²³ prematurity, ²⁴ respiratory insufficiency and acidosis, ²⁵ and the exogenous administration of organic anions. When a very large collaborative series of infants was

studied, a statistically significant relationship between hyperbilirubinemia, per se, and neurologic impairment was demonstrated.¹¹ Because of the relatively weak correlation of brain damage with hyperbilirubinemia and the absence of an abrupt change in incidence with increasing concentrations, the serum bilirubin concentration is not a precise measure of the risk of brain damage. We have previously emphasized that the absolute concentration of bilirubin is of less importance than the fraction of the serum bilirubin which is dissociated from albumin and therefore free to diffuse into cells.²⁴, ²⁵, ²⁶ It follows that the albumin concentration in extracellular fluids is as important as the total bilirubin in determining the concentration of the diffusible fraction. The previously cited clinical complications which have demonstrated a relationship of hyperbilirubinemia to neurologic damage are often associated with an increase in the concentration of diffusible bilirubin. The increase in diffusible bilirubin may be due to either hypoalbuminemia or to interference with the capacity of albumin to bind bilirubin. Under these circumstances the diffusible bilirubin can reach damaging concentrations at relatively low levels for the total serum bilirubin.

Currently there is no reliable method to measure the diffusible concentration of bilirubin in serum, but an indirect estimate can be made by determining the relative saturation of the serum albumin with bilirubin by the salicylate displacement technique.²⁸ When this saturation index was tested for a relationship to neurologic impairment, a significant correlation was found between poor psychometric performance and high saturations of the serum albumin with bilirubin during neonatal life. When I.Q. scores alone were compared to the saturation index a statistically significant relationship was not found, but all of the children with I.Q. scores of less than 80 were in the damaged group, and 8 of the 9 children with abnormal I.Q. scores also had had saturation indices greater than 8.0. As previously reported,¹⁰, ¹¹ the effect of hyperbilirubinemia on the I.Q. might have been demonstrable

if the scores were compared within sibships, but our distinction of normal and abnormal depended on the single criterion of scores above or below 80. Thus, it is quite possible the hyperbilirubinemia affected the I.Q. of the children, but not sufficiently to reduce it to frankly abnormal levels.

This study also demonstrated that neonatal hyperbilirubinemia can be associated with subsequent brain injury in the absence of cerebral palsy. Many clinicians have been under the impression that the encephalopathy characteristic of bilirubin toxicity will be manifested only as kernicterus with a depressed Moro reflex, opisthotonus, and shrill cry. The more recent reports of kernicterus in autopsied premature infants indicates that the classical signs of kernicterus were not present during life.²⁸, ²⁹ Three of the damaged patients in this report were found to have cerebral palsy characteristic of survivors of kernicterus without having had clinical signs during neonatal life.

The neuropathologic evidence of bilirubin encephalopathy indicates extensive nuclear involvement of the ventral cortex and suggests that the toxicity of bilirubin to the central nervous system is broad and might not be detectable until later life. The sensorineural hearing impairment is but one example.¹⁰, ¹¹ The frequent involvement of the hippocampus seen in brains of kernicteric infants and the role of the hippocampus in memory²⁴⁻²⁶ may be particularly relevant to the memory defects found in our patients with high saturation indices.

A number of the patients who had had high saturation indices during the period of neonatal jaundice were found to have normal psychometric test results. However, the duration of high saturation was considerably shorter than in the damaged children. Since the study was not designed to test temporal factors, these observations can only suggest that the duration of exposure, as well as the degree of saturation of the serum with bilirubin, may be important in determining the risk of bilirubin encephalopathy.

Although 16 of the 18 damaged children were treated by exchange transfusion, im-

pairment of cognitive functions was not prevented. The transfusions may have prevented lethal kernicterus, but were employed too late to prevent the milder injuries which were detectable at 5 years of age.

One optimistic finding in these studies is the indication that if hyperbilirubinemia is properly managed, the incidence of mental deficiency in premature infants may be significantly reduced. The use of the saturation index as a guide in the management of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia permits more precision in the identification of those infants at risk from the toxicity of bilirubin.

# SUMMARY

A group of 32 children who had been significantly jaundiced during neonatal life were re-examined at 5 years of age for neurologic and psychometric evidence of brain damage. From the results of the psychologic tests two scores were obtained: (1) the measured I.Q., and (2) the designation of presence or absence of brain damage derived from the performance of the children on psychometric tests of cognitive functions. These two determinants of mental function were tested for possible correlations to a number of clinical and laboratory measurements that had been performed on the children when they were infants.

Of the total, 18 of the children were found to have brain damage; 14 were considered normal. No correlations were found between the determinants of mental function at 5 years and the birth weights, sex, presence or absence of hemolytic disease, exchange transfusion, and the maximum serum bilirubin concentrations. A significant correlation (p < 0.01) was found between the presence or absence of brain damage and the degree to which the patients' sera had been saturated with bilirubin. It was found that 16 of the 18 damaged children had had a saturation index of 8.0 or greater, whereas this had occurred in only 5 of the 14 normal children. It was also found that the damaged children had had bilirubin concentrations in excess of 15 mg. per 100 ml. for 3.29 days, which was significantly longer than the 1.73 days in the normal children.

The results indicate that the determination of the saturation index is a more precise measurement than the serum bilirubin concentration for predicting which infants are at risk to central nervous system damage. These findings also indicate that impairment of cognitive functioning is associated with hyperbilirubinemia in the neonatal period without the occurrence of the classical findings of kernicterus during neonatal life or of cerebral palsy in later life. These results suggest that hyperbilirubinemia is associated with a continuum of morbidity of which classical neonatal kernicterus, with or without immediate death, is only one end of the spectrum of cerebral damage.

The authors are grateful to Joseph Dallas of the Department of Pediatrics who was able to locate many of the patients for us and encourage their cooperation with the evaluation.
